case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Worsening flushing, worsening diarrhea, and shortness of breath in the setting of metastatic neuroendocrine tumor.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic midgut neuroendocrine tumor (carcinoid) with hepatic metastases, mesenteric involvement, and later extensive osseous metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Repeat biopsy demonstrated interval increase in Ki-67 proliferation index and mitotic count compared with an earlier biopsy, consistent with higher-grade transformation/progression. Exact numeric values were not provided.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Prior to referral in 2003, metastatic midgut disease had been treated with radioembolization.  
- February 2015 imaging showed relatively stable disease with small liver metastases and one small lymph node.  
- May 2015 imaging showed marked interval increase in the number of liver lesions, described as innumerable small hepatic lesions, with new extensive bone metastases.  
- Disease progression between February 2015 and May 2015 was described as clear-cut on repeated scan review.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic test results were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2003: Radioembolization for metastatic midgut neuroendocrine tumor prior to transfer of care.  
- 2005: Pancreaticoduodenectomy and right hemicolectomy for mesenteric/root of mesentery involvement.  
- Long-term somatostatin analogue therapy with Sandostatin LAR 30 mg monthly for approximately 9 years.  
- Over subsequent years, hepatic recurrences/progression were managed with repeated local therapies, including percutaneous ablation and laparoscopic ablation.  
- Disease course had been relatively indolent over 7–8 years, with intermittent new hepatic lesions appearing every 1–2 years and treated locally. Symptoms had been relatively well controlled during much of this interval.

[ current disease status ]: Rapid systemic progression was present by May 2015, with innumerable hepatic metastases, extensive bone metastases, worsening carcinoid-type symptoms, and biopsy evidence of increased proliferative activity compared with prior pathology.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The patient had chronic diarrhea, attributed in part to prior pancreaticoduodenectomy.  
- Prior pancreaticoduodenectomy resulted in biliary-enteric anastomosis/hepaticojejunostomy anatomy, which was relevant to subsequent liver-directed procedural risk.

reference_discussion.text: So while everyone comes up, we'll tell you a little bit about at least our approach to the multidisciplinary team. We meet every Monday morning. We have anywhere from eight to maybe as many as 12 or 13 people in a room. And really, everybody that needs to be discussed, every patient that has an issue gets discussed at that meeting with at least our CEDARS group, because it's here. So who do we discuss? We discuss new diagnoses, anybody that's new to our program. We discuss people who've had a change in their course. Say, for example, a new spot showed up, new symptoms showed up, or something like that. And the person who identified it brings it to the group to discuss it. And then we discuss, we present patients who've had a completed therapy and we just want to see how they're doing. So for example, someone has a chemoembolization and we've got new films to look at and so their films will be shown at that time. So we don't say that every single time a patient's seen by one of us that they're discussed on Monday, but every time there's a change. there's something that needs to be reviewed or there's a new diagnosis, your name is brought up to our group. So I've tried to stall to let everybody grab their seat. We are planning to just do some short cases to get some discussion from everybody. Andrew Hendifar has a case as well he's going to talk about. When we do the true tumor board, it's a little more goal-directed, so we'll present a case and we'll roundtable it. We don't really have the ability to do that today. We did stage one of these for the LACNITS group a few months ago. All of our CEDARS team got together and we actually tried pretend some cases, and it was well-received, but today I'll be just more discussing some aspects of cases. I think everyone on the panel has spoken today except the two people in the middle, Dr. Mark Friedman and Dr. Gabriel Lipschitz, and they are our interventional radiology experts here at Cedars-Sinai. Mark Friedman, many of you know for a long, long time. He's done a tremendous amount of work on probably most people in the room. Gabe Lipschitz joined a couple years ago from UCLA. So Mark mostly does the hepatic artery therapies in terms of the stuff that we're discussing today. Gabriel does that, but Gabriel also wears the hat of a person that does these ablations that we talked about earlier. And a person missing from that panel is Ashley Waxman. Ashley's got some things going on, but never fear, Gabe covers for him as well. He wears that hat very well. So we're going to start with a case, 70-year-old female. And, you know, obviously the course, the disease course is very long. This isn't meant to be mysterious. There's no guessing here. We're just going to try to ask questions about what you think and how we should manage it. And we have, what, 15, 20 minutes. 70-year-old female had radioembolization in 2003 prior to coming to Cedars for a metastatic midgut and then had a very complicated recurrence pattern where there was involvement of the mesentery and underwent a pancreatic odontectomy, a right hemicolectomy back in 2005. Over the next several years, fairly slow disease course, things would show up in the liver and she was on Sandestatin that whole time. things might show up in the liver, and she had percutaneous ablation by Dr. Waxman, a laparoscopic ablation in my case, and we have a new scan that we wanted to discuss and just bring to the group in terms of what they would do. And this is an example where we would say, I would tell this person's name, the story, and I would say, here's why I'm presenting her, because there's a new problem, and I'd need advice from the group on what we should do. So, maybe we can pause for a second before going to the next slide. Is this the right treatment? We've gone through this seven-year course of things popping up every year or two, not really symptomatic, well-controlled in terms of symptoms, a lot of diarrhea because of the Whipple and other things. Sandastatin LAR, 30 milligrams a month for the last nine years. Should we have changed something earlier as we saw disease pop up? Maybe we can start at the end with Dr. Phan. Is this chronic maintenance therapy for metastatic midgut carcinoid doing well, relatively asymptomatic, but things are popping up every few years? We tend to try to get rid of what pops up and then suppress it with octreotide or sandastatin.
Thank you for picking me first. Actually, I'm not sure if this is a midgut or is it a pancreas?
It was midgut. It was just involving the root of the mesentery, and that's why the whipple. It was relatively complicated.

So, you know, asymptomatic, somewhat progressive neuroendocrine tumor on somatostatin analog. Nowadays, there's, going back, if I were to have this person with progressive disease, especially things that are not resectable. First question in any patient is, is this operable? Can most or all of the disease can be removed, whether it's metastatic recurrence or not? If the answer is no, I try to find standard of care. If there's none, then I go to clinical trials. So at the time this is going on, I think there is the radian 2 that is possibly an option for the patient if she or he is not a surgical candidate. In this era, the question to ask is that should we give not yet FDA-approved Afinitor or Evalimus for a progressing neuroendocrine tumor of the midgut? That is a question that I think everybody has to decide with the patient on one-on-one discussion with the result. The RADIAN4 result is back, or it's been announced. So perhaps there's more data. And I think the RADIAN2 is enough data for me to start using that affinitory and adding to the somatostatin analog.

So before we go to the next slide, Mark and Gabe, can I ask you, she's had a Whipple, so she's got a, again, that means the bile duct's been connected to the intestine. As the years have gone by, we've avoided arterial therapy. She did have a radioembolization in the past. How scared should we be, Mark, for arterial therapy and Gabriel for poking needles in and burning things in the liver? Or is this overkill, we can use a Mad Lib?

I think each patient needs to be looked at on an individual basis, but I still have significant reservation about going forward with regional therapy in patients who've had any kind of compromise of the bile duct connection to the small intestines. The risk of hepatic abscess after chemoembolization or radioembolization is very small. It's probably less than 1%. But if you look at retrospective series of patients who have developed hepatic abscess, the very large majority of them have had an incompetent sphincter. And that hepatic abscess complication can be a very severe, life-threatening complication. So you really have to look at each patient individually, but I still have relatively strong reservation about being aggressive in those circumstances.
Gabe, what about alcohol, nano knife, are these things okay? Or is all ablation bad in a liver with a hepatical jejunostomy?

I think, you know, you run the same risks. And so, you know, for patients who we decided the risk is worth taking, we also we do a bowel prep. We treat with antibiotics before and after the procedure for a certain amount of time. And since we've been doing that in the literature, infection rates have been less, but the risk is still, you know, fairly significant.

Well, the question at hand was this, and that is that in February 2005, things looked pretty stable. There were some small liver metastases. Again, we did intervene periodically with ablation nervously when these grew, but we're talking a seven or eight year time period. One small lymph node. But then in March, more flushing, some shortness of breath actually, some worsening diarrhea. And the May 2015 report comes back with marked increase in the number of liver lesions and now extensive bone metastases. We went over the scan repeatedly, and there really was a very clear-cut progression between February and May. Innumerable small liver lesions with bone lesions. I guess the first question is, what happened? And I'll show you, in fact, I will show you the films now. what happened here with this biology? Did the biology change? Did we miss something? What does the whole group think? Have they seen this? And this concept of rapid progression from stable to seems to be growing fast. Yeah, jump in.

All right, I'll be happy to give a jump in. A couple of things. First of all, I agree entirely with what's been said about surgery up front. I think it's really important. Debulking really makes a big impact in terms of the long-term outcome. I'm not so sure that I would repetitively do it, though. I think you need to realize that eventually you're losing more and you're gaining less with repetitive interventions. But if you can render somebody R0 or R1 early, I think it's very, very important. I think the issue here is that this is the natural history of the disease. This is what actually will occur. As time goes on, you're going to start selecting out clones that are going to be more resistant, and you're going to have, you know, the old VINIC slide where you get the sort of ramping up effect many, many years later. And I think in this particular situation, you've probably going to have selected out a higher grade lesion that is going to be less amenable to therapy, and in fact may not even necessarily be octreotide avid at this point. So a couple of issues here. This person needs systemic therapy, there's no doubt about it. And I think going and working on specific lesions in the liver is not going to make an impact. The reason to focus therapy on the liver early on is really important, because many patients ultimately are going to succumb to liver disease. So you'll have a bigger bulk in the liver, and you're going to have to hammer the liver. But if you reach a point where you've broken out of the liver and you now have systemic disease, I think you really need some kind of systemic therapy. So you're going to have to have a discussion here. This is going to be some kind of clinical trial, which I would certainly support. I'd be personally wary in this particular patient of PRRT having previously seen radiospheres. There's certainly a dose effect, but we've had some unhappy outcomes in that situation, although I think it is something that should be considered here seriously. And I'm sure the man on my left is going to be supporting that. We actually have an MIBG trial at the University of Pennsylvania that is something to consider. That's another radio pharmaceutical. But something needs to be done at this situation. So I think you've reached a point now where you've got to go global.

In order to answer your questions, there are things that can be done in understanding the pathophysiology that we're dealing with. What we do is a combination of F18, FDG, PET, CT, as well as either gallium or actuarial scan, mostly gallium. And we are, in some of these patients, we see, for instance, that a previously negative FDG PET CT scan becomes positive in certain areas. That tells us that the tumor is becoming more aggressive and confirms our sort of guess that these tumors, they are changing their behavior, actually. At this point, obviously, the patient is progressing, is not responding to the prior therapies. Systemic therapy is definitely an indication because of the bone lesions, because of other new lesions that you're seeing. And regarding previously treated patients with SIRT, of course, depending on the number of procedures, Still, we can guesstimate in terms of the dose that liver has received and based on that, essentially justify the PRRT. I don't think this patient, there is, I mean, necessarily there is an absolute contraindication for PRRT. PRRT needs to be considered at this point as well.
So we've got PRRT, we've got Dr. Fan, midgut, but we're in trouble. What would you do? Outside of a trial, you know, with the available drugs right now.
Well, I think at this point you ask yourself if the patient has symptoms or not.
Yeah, a lot of flushing and actually worsening pulmonary issues as well from the heart, cardiac.

So remember I said that the two goals of treatment of patient would advanced disease is symptoms control and disease control. Both of these are not control at the moment. So if you can add an agent that actually potentially can treat both the symptoms and the disease, I think that is the ideal thing. So this person is on stomatostatin analog. In a sub-study of the RADIAN3, there is actually some benefit of adding Afinitor to stomatostatin analog to improve symptoms control as well. It is something that, again, I would probably do at this time. The only question is that looking at the KI-67 and the mitotic figure, what if that was 20? That's actually more of an interesting question, is that it's 20 or more, it becomes high-grade neuroendocrine tumor, regardless of the primary site. So then you have to question whether somatostatin analog, TKI, are they adequately treating the patient or not?

And we did a biopsy, and in fact, as you pointed out, it had changed quite a bit from the one a few years ago, a much higher Ki67 and mitotic count. Here are the two biopsies side by side, but I don't want to get stuck on this case, so we'll move on to another case. Any other comments from the panel? Is this, by the way, the expectation that a person who's five, six, seven years with stable disease, do they unfortunately have to always be worried that their next scan might show this? Is there a way to predict this? Is there a way to not Select out these clones immunotherapy. What's the role of that? I mean, maybe it's not here yet Is there anything we can do or do we just get scans month to month and hope? That's not our turn

Well, so in terms of immunotherapy, I suppose, and maybe Alex can comment, is the PD-L1 inhibitors may be well something that would be reasonable to consider here, but you need a biopsy and you need to show that the receptor is present. I must tell you, we're zero for about 20 tries at Penn. We haven't yet found one person, but that's something I think to consider. In terms of our kind, you know, standard immunotherapy, we're a long way away from that. I mean, one day we certainly will be hoping that that would be the way to go here.

It's very important to remember a patient is symptomatic. You need to address it now. And being on a clinical trial, that there's still some option that you have to try. I think that's first. PD-L1 expression or overexpression in immunohistochemistry does not predict respond to an immuno checkpoint inhibitor. So I'm not sure. I mean, I think that's why there's study that's going on. I'm not sure that would rule my out for a patient being referred to immuno-checkpoint therapy on clinical trials. But, yeah. So if you keep remembering those tenets, symptoms control and disease control, and if you can find one that treat both, that's the ideal thing. And if you can't, you address the symptoms because oftentimes disease is very hard to control and the patient's quality of life is very important.

So, when you respond to our question about markers of prognosis, for small bowel carcinoma, there's really not a lot of great markers other than the clinical markers such as grade and stage. But for pancreatic, there are a few experimental markers, even including somatic mutations that are sort of in development. But for small bowel carcinoma, there really has not been a clear molecular marker to predict the natural history of the tumor.

reference_conclusion: The tumor board concluded that the patient has biologically progressive metastatic midgut neuroendocrine tumor with extensive hepatic and osseous disease and requires systemic rather than further focal liver-directed therapy. Clinical trial enrollment was supported, with peptide receptor radionuclide therapy to be considered despite prior radioembolization if dosimetry is acceptable. Outside a trial, addition of everolimus to ongoing somatostatin analogue therapy was identified as a reasonable option to address both symptom burden and disease progression, with management prioritizing symptom control given active flushing, diarrhea, and cardiopulmonary manifestations.
reference_conclusion_quote: This person needs systemic therapy, there's no doubt about it. And I think going and working on specific lesions in the liver is not going to make an impact. [...] This is going to be some kind of clinical trial, which I would certainly support. [...] PRRT needs to be considered at this point as well. [...] It is something that, again, I would probably do at this time. [...] It's very important to remember a patient is symptomatic. You need to address it now.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 63-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Abdominal pain, diarrhea, flushing, and occasional nausea.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic low-grade neuroendocrine tumor, presumed midgut/small bowel primary, with mesenteric mass and hepatic metastases. Carcinoid syndrome symptoms were present.

[ histopathology results ]: Pathology demonstrated low-grade neuroendocrine tumor.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial MRI demonstrated multiple large liver masses, a mid-mesenteric mass, and a small bowel mass. Disease was described as bulky and predominantly hepatic. Octreoscan was positive. After two operations, follow-up imaging demonstrated residual bilobar hepatic disease with lesions measuring approximately 1-2 cm. No extra-abdominal metastases were identified; no metastases outside the liver were known at that time.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent small bowel resection for symptomatic bowel disease. Hepatic disease was not addressed at the time of the initial bowel operation because of the extent of liver involvement. He subsequently underwent a second operation for hepatic tumor removal using a parenchymal-preserving approach. He recovered well after both operations. He was treated with Sandostatin LAR. Approximately 9 months after surgery, he developed increasing diarrhea and flushing while on Sandostatin LAR.

[ current disease status ]: Residual metastatic disease remained in both hepatic lobes, with small-volume lesions measuring approximately 1-2 cm. He was asymptomatic immediately after surgery, but by approximately 9 months postoperatively he had recurrent mild carcinoid-type symptoms, including increased diarrhea and flushing, while receiving Sandostatin LAR. Known disease at that time was confined to the liver.

[ other clinical data ]: He was otherwise described as healthy.

reference_discussion.text: All right, let's move to another case, get Dr. Amersi involved. 63-year-old male, abdominal pain, diarrhea, flushing, a lot of stuff going on, liver masses, a mass seen in bowel or next to bowel on the MRI, a mesenteric mass, noted otherwise healthy. These are the scans. The scans on the left are focusing on the liver, the two different projections on the liver. The scan on the right is meant to show, it shows some liver, but it's meant to show a mass sort of mid-mesentery. And again, you can't really see it here, but there's also a small bowel mass. It's got abdominal pain. You want to walk us through what we should do here? He's symptomatic with abdominal pain and occasional nausea and this amount of tumor.
I'll choose scan positive.
Pardon?
Octreoscan.
Octreoscan positive. What are you thinking? Early PRRT?
Well, I mean, to keep the disease, I mean, we can make it stable. I mean, the lesions are pretty big, very large lesions. But still, I mean, it works. We have treated many of these patients.
All right.

Sure. So I think, you know, with this patient, obviously, where would the primary be in terms of small bowel? Do you need to do double balloon on these patients? I can tell you that a lot of times when you go in for these patients, if they didn't have the mesenteric mass and just the liver metastases, then I think there's a role for a double balloon and aroscopy to try to identify the primary. Most of these patients, when you do go in for a surgical exploration, Wherever the mesenteric mass is, you can find the primary within the bowel in that area. And really, the question is looking at more cuts of the MRI in terms of the mesenteric mass. Is this involving what we call the superior mesenteric artery and vein, which is the blood supply to the entire small bowel? And trying to get all this disease out, are we going to compromise the potential blood supply to whatever else that's left behind? I think that's one important factor in consideration for surgery. And then more importantly, addressing it with a liver surgeon, is there something that's going to be done surgically at the same time to address the liver disease, or are we going to turn it over to our intervention colleagues after surgery and do something more in terms of chemoembolization or radioembolization or other targeted therapy?
I know you can't see the bowel mass, but laparoscopic, or is that mass too central and you just do this as an open case?
For this, I would do it open. I would not do it laparoscopic, purely because of the blood supply issue.

Let me say, this is a great example that you've chosen here of why you need a multidisciplinary center, because there are many ways to skin the cat here. So one option is to take out the primary and deal with the mesenteric nodes first, and go back and sort out the liver at a later stage with interventional radiology, making sure you do a COLI at the same time. We have that discussion. An alternative is to go in there laparoscopically, do as much as you can in terms of the liver, sort out what you're going to do with the mesenteric nodes, and then come back at a later stage and, sorry, start off with the liver directed therapy and then come back at a later stage and see what you're going to be doing with the surgical point of view. In terms of your scanning, you're going to certainly in this patient look for bony metastases and extensive disease out of the abdomen at this stage. And that may change you and make you want to go with some kind of systemic therapy. So this is a perfect example of why multidisciplinary care is everything that counts here. Because there's no one right or wrong way to do this patient's therapy. And you can change. And certainly, you can move as time goes, come back six months later and say, well, we've done X. Now the problem is Y. How are we going to deal with that? So I think it's a perfect example of why a multidisciplinary approach is so important.

In his case, the thought, and this is a great point, that's how we discussed it, and there was question about which direction. The thought was that he was symptomatic from the bowel lesion, so we as a group prioritized that. Mark and Gabe, anything interventional here? Let's take the bowel part out of the equation, because what ended up happening is a small bowel resection. There was a question, should the liver be dealt with surgically? Should the liver be dealt with interventional radiology? Should we use PRRT or just watch it for a while? What should we do? These big, bulky tumors, kind of one-sided.

Well, once these big bulky tumors really take a hold like this, get to be this size, my experience with radioembolization is that it's not quite as effective as we'd like it to be. So I think if we were going to go on the regional therapy tack, I think chemoembolization would probably be a better way to go in this situation. I think it's doable, but, you know, if surgery is an option in the clinical setting, I got to believe that that's going to be the best way of going about it, to debulk the liver at the time or at a separate time than the other surgery is done, and then come back. And if there has to be any kind of cleanup at that time, then we can address regional therapy then. That would be my opinion on that.
Gabe, what's the limit on ablation? What size would you no longer try or is there no limit?
There's no limit.
Perfect.

I think that you can use, you know, various strategies and you can combine therapies. So, you know, for tumors that are bigger than four centimeters, Ablation or chemoembolization alone tend not to be as efficacious, so you can combine the two, really, and chemoembolize before and then ablate the next day or a week later. And, you know, larger tumors, you can get a pretty good response with that.

So we didn't script this. I don't know that any of these people remember this case, but this is exactly the same dialogue we had in the multidisciplinary group. And ultimately, Dr. Amersi took this patient for a small bowel resection, and we felt that it was simply too much to tackle the liver at that time. It's a fairly big liver operation. After the fact, the case went to Dr. Friedman, who said, if you can do something surgically, that's going to put us miles ahead. So one of the videos we skipped over this morning was removal of that large lesion through kind of a parenchymal preserving approach. So that's just the pathology. It's a low grade. Let's move to his new scan. So this is now after two operations, which both he recovered quite well from. A little bit of disease left in the liver, both lobes, one centimeter, two centimeters, asymptomatic at this point in time. Again, this is mid-gut as far as we know, all the bowel, there's no other metastases, just some small disease left in the liver. What should we do, if anything? Now, I will tell you, just to add a bit, this was about nine months after the surgery, and he was actually starting to become symptomatic. He was having a little bit more diarrhea and flushing at this point in time. So, we have to do something, and he's already on his Sanistatin LAR. And this is all the disease we know of. What's the best way to tackle this small leftover disease by lobar in the liver? Andrew?

I mean, one thing that I would consider is that the clinical course doesn't seem typical. It seems to be rapidly progressing clinically. And I would probably want better imaging. Maybe this is the kind of patient you might get a gallium 68 to get more information.
All right. Still costs money. They're not covered yet. Any other thoughts? Mark, radioembo, chemoembo, it's not very big disease. You know, but he's symptomatic. Yeah.

At this point, based upon the carcinoid syndrome that you're describing, I think regional therapy would be an option at this point. And I would choose radioembolization because there's not that much disease, number one. Number two, it's much, easier to tolerate for most patients, radioembolization. It's outpatient. So I think in that setting, if the decision is made that something needs to be done, that's what I think would be the way to go.
Dr. Delbasan, where does PRRT fit? Any course in this illness, where does it fit?

Number one, I agree with Andrew regarding doing a more sensitive test. For a patient with this course, with those large lesions and essentially progressive disease, I won't be surprised that a diagnostic test like Allium shows more lesions at this point, or more lesions as our typical structural imaging modalities are showing. And you mentioned that the Arcturus scan has been positive. Of course, depending on how positive is that and how intense these tumors are expressing somatostatin receptors, I think PRRT is an option for this patient.

Would you choose, again, just because you mentioned earlier, you actually, the wheels were turning, you were wondering about doing it early on. Do you have experience with bulky liver disease before any other therapy? Do they do better to have it before we've done other things to their liver? Does it matter?

Actually, we have had very good responses with the, I mean, obviously seeing the bigger lesions initially, I mean, you feel, oh, wow, I mean, is this going to be really effective? But we have had several patients that I can tell with larger lesions, they have responded very well. And the way that the response is, I mean, we see the stabilization of the previously progressive disease for a relatively long time. And then, you know, kind of surveillance down the road just to make sure that they are staying stable. This has been our experience. I mean, still we can control this disease and function actually for the symptoms. I mean, our experience, about 77% of the patient, they experience symptomatic relief from the therapy. a structurally objective response by resist criteria might not really give the whole story to us. We see, I mean, our radiologists report this as a stable disease, but really, when you see a patient after two cycles, I mean, totally the clinic, the quality of life has changed. They say, okay, you know, I was having flushing, you know, five times a day. Now, occasionally I get it maybe, every, you know, two weeks. So that part, actually, we have seen very good response when they are functional.

I doubt his diarrhea and flushing actually due to the either new recurrent or residual tumor. I agree with Dr. Andrew Hanifar. Either he has actual hepatic diseases, significant advancement, or these are due to some dumping syndrome as a result of the bowel resection.

Let's just, all we found on it, because I'm just trying to create discussion points, forget this individual specifics. If all we found after an extensive workup was this liver disease, bilobar, relatively small volume disease, mildly symptomatic on Sandostatin LAR. Ablate it, inject it, change drugs, change to lanreotide, try a systemic agent. Where are we in this day and age? Because we've got six things to choose from now.

So there's another approach that actually hasn't been mentioned and I think is reasonable to consider. If you have a patient like this who's been maximally debulked, has very little residual disease. The residual disease doesn't look as if it's too aggressive, so it's reasonable to say, I want to wait a couple of months here, and I'll get another scan. And if this looks the same to me, and the progression of the tumor is mild and slow, it's reasonable to consider asymptomatic management, and that may be very well the place where a drug like Telotrastat could be useful here. I have a number of patients now that have done You know, I'm way in favor of being very aggressive up front. Take out as much tumor as you can, get us to an R0 if you possibly can. reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary review prioritized resection of the symptomatic small-bowel primary, and small-bowel resection was performed. Hepatic disease was deferred initially because the liver tumor burden was considered too extensive to address at the same operation; subsequent surgical debulking was favored when feasible to achieve maximal cytoreduction. For residual small-volume bilobar liver metastases with carcinoid symptoms despite Sandostatin LAR, regional liver-directed therapy was considered appropriate, with radioembolization favored in the setting of limited hepatic disease and PRRT considered an option after more sensitive imaging to better define disease extent.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 49-year-old woman from São Paulo, Brazil.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive visual field loss over approximately 1 year; headaches for 2 weeks prior to presentation. Additional symptoms before initial admission included headache associated with nausea, vomiting, and confusion.

[ diagnosis ]: Giant pituitary macroadenoma with sellar and suprasellar extension, associated obstructive hydrocephalus and visual pathway compression. Intratumoral hemorrhagic change/apoplexy was present at surgery.

[ histopathology results ]: Tumor consistency at resection was described as soft/suckable. No formal histopathology report was provided.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT head demonstrated a large sellar/suprasellar mass with hydrocephalus.  
- Post-shunt MRI demonstrated persistent ventricular asymmetry, with one lateral ventricle less dilated than the other, and a dumbbell-shaped lesion centered in the pituitary region with sellar and suprasellar extension, consistent with pituitary adenoma.  
- The lesion extended superiorly into the third ventricle.  
- Postoperative imaging showed a residual radiographic abnormality.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Prolactin level was normal.  
- Cortisol was reported as 0.9 on initial evaluation; no steroid replacement had been started at that time, and the low value was attributed to timing of sampling.  
- No postoperative diabetes insipidus was reported.  
- No postoperative cortisol change was reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- At initial presentation in 2020, cerebrospinal fluid diversion was performed with ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement under endoscopic guidance with septostomy because of hydrocephalus.  
- After shunt placement, the patient was discharged and was subsequently lost to follow-up during the COVID-19 period.  
- She later re-presented to the emergency department with visual loss and no headache.  
- Definitive tumor surgery was then performed as a combined procedure in a single anesthetic session: endonasal resection followed by transcallosal, transchoroidal/transfissural approach to the third ventricle for removal of remaining tumor.  
- Nasoseptal flap closure was performed after the endonasal stage.  
- Gross resection was achieved, with residual concern on postoperative imaging.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Immediately postoperative after combined endonasal and transcallosal resection, with a residual radiographic abnormality on postoperative imaging.  
- No CSF leak was reported postoperatively.  
- No diabetes insipidus was reported postoperatively.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Neurological examination at presentation showed reduced consciousness with Glasgow Coma Scale 13.  
- Visual assessment documented visual acuity of 20/50 in the right eye and 20/30 in the left eye.  
- Bitemporal hemianopsia and papilledema were present.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Three-month history of worsening deep-seated headaches unresponsive to medication, diplopia worse on left gaze, impaired coordination, dropping objects, difficulty walking, and altered speech/articulation. There was no history of seizures.

[ diagnosis ]: Clival/petroclival meningioma causing brainstem compression, left cranial nerve VI palsy, left pupillary abnormality, and cerebellar signs predominantly affecting the right side.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology was available.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI demonstrated a midline clival mass with imaging features described as classical for meningioma. The lesion extended superiorly into the suprasellar cistern, abutted both internal carotid arteries, and displaced the optic chiasm with greater left-sided effect. It displaced the midbrain and pons posteriorly and caused slight abutment/displacement of the fourth ventricle. There was approximately 270-degree envelopment of the basilar artery and encasement of both posterior communicating arteries. The lesion also encased and thickened the left cranial nerve VI. There was no restricted diffusion and no susceptibility blooming on SWI. T2 signal was described as very high.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No tumor-directed treatment had been administered. The patient had been discharged home and was awaiting return for surgery.

[ current disease status ]: Symptomatic untreated skull base meningioma with persistent cranial neuropathy and cerebellar dysfunction. At the time of reporting, the patient was at home pending operative management.

[ other clinical data ]: Neurological examination showed a dilated left pupil measuring 6 mm with poor direct light response and preserved consensual reflex. Visual acuity was unaffected, and confrontation visual fields were intact; formal visual acuity and visual field testing were pending as an outpatient. There was a left lateral rectus palsy without other gross cranial nerve deficits on examination. Dysarthria, right-sided dysdiadochokinesia, and dysmetria were present. The remainder of the neurological examination was normal.

reference_conclusion: The panel favored operative management with maximal safe resection focused on brainstem decompression. The preferred transcranial strategy was an anterior petrosectomy/anterior petrosal approach, with residual tumor adherent to the basilar trunk left in situ if no safe arachnoid plane is present; an endoscopic transclival approach was also considered reasonable, particularly for the inferior retroclival component, with possible staged transpetrosal surgery for residual disease. reference_discussion.text: But unfortunately, there was a 0% response rate and a median PFS of only 1.8 months. And in fact, there was an amendment after the first 23 patients were treated to include only fish-positive patients. But again, there was really not much response seen in this single-agent study. And similar disappointing results was also seen with lapatinib, which, as you know, is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor inhibiting the tyrosine kinase component of HER2 in an unselected population which only had a response rate of 3.3%. However, the impact of HER2 targeting has been transformed with this study by Fader and colleagues looking at the use of chemotherapy plus trastuzumab in a population of HER2 overexpressed or amplified uterine series carcinomas. And this was a trial that looked at patients with either primary advanced endometrial cancer or recurrent disease. And in this study, 71% of patients had primary disease, 29% had recurrent disease, and they had to have a treatment-free interval of more than six months from the last platinum treatment. And so the primary endpoint here was progression-free survival. And what has been shown here is a significant improvement in progression-free survival of 12.6 months versus 8 months in the entire intention-to-treat population. But when this was broken down to patients who got first-line versus treatment in the recurrent setting, what they found was that there was a huge amount of benefit in the first-line setting of a difference in 17.9 months, almost 18 months versus 9 months. in terms of progression-free survival whereas you still saw the benefit in the recurrent setting but this was a much smaller PFS benefit of 9 versus 6 months. It's sort of a surrogate marker for neoantigen load. It's highly variable across cancers. And you can see in this diagram, the reason why the high tumor mutational burden is important is because it may have an impact on subsequent response to immunotherapy. So you can see here, you've got lots of mutations. Then some of these mutations can be presented as neoantigens on the surface of the tumor cell by the MHC protein to these killer T cells. And you can see that the endometrial cancers, the cervix, at cancer of the cervix and the uterus also sort of fall into a relatively group of these uterine and cervical cancers that have relatively high number of mutations per megabase. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 76-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Painful chest wall mass developing approximately 4 years after prior treatment for colon cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage II colon adenocarcinoma diagnosed in 2017, subsequently recurrent/metastatic disease with biopsy-proven chest wall metastasis and a PET-avid suspicious right upper quadrant abdominal mass.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of the chest wall mass showed immunohistochemistry consistent with the original colon adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- PET scan demonstrated a painful chest wall mass and a minor suspicious mass in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen.  
- Repeat PET/CT after systemic therapy demonstrated response in the chest wall mass and resolution of the right upper quadrant abdominal mass, with persistent residual chest wall mass and ongoing chest wall discomfort.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: FoundationOne genomic profiling identified:  
- KRAS G12C mutation  
- NRAS wild type  
- Two PIK3CA mutations  
- Two APC mutations  
- SMAD4 mutation

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2017: No adjuvant therapy was administered after resection/diagnosis of stage II colon adenocarcinoma because no high-risk features were present.  
- The patient remained without evident disease for approximately 4 years.  
- After recurrence, treatment was initiated with FOLFOX plus bevacizumab.  
- The first cycle was poorly tolerated, with significant nausea and peripheral neuropathy.  
- Oxaliplatin was discontinued; treatment continued with infusional 5-FU plus bevacizumab.  
- The patient subsequently developed severe diarrheal syndrome and was diagnosed with enteritis.  
- The patient refused further 5-FU therapy.  
- Bevacizumab was tolerated.  
- Sotorasib was obtained for the patient.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent residual chest wall mass with associated discomfort remained after initial systemic therapy; the previously seen right upper quadrant abdominal lesion had resolved on repeat PET/CT.

[ other clinical data ]: Severe treatment-related gastrointestinal toxicity was documented during fluoropyrimidine-based therapy, including severe diarrhea/enteritis.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 75-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive bladder cancer with pelvic pain, back pain, obstructive acute kidney injury, and declining performance status.

[ diagnosis ]: Urothelial bladder cancer initially diagnosed in 2019, previously treated with intravesical BCG. Disease progressed in 2021 to muscle-invasive bladder cancer with a large bladder mass and metastatic retroperitoneal and pelvic adenopathy.

[ histopathology results ]: Transurethral resection of bladder tumor demonstrated muscle invasion.

[ imaging findings ]: PET-CT showed a large bladder mass with widespread retroperitoneal and pelvic adenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Comprehensive genomic profiling showed ERBB2 (HER2) amplification and ERBB2 R103Q mutation; TP53 alteration; CCND3 amplification. Tumor mutational burden was not high. Microsatellite status was stable. No FGFR mutation was identified. ERBB2 R103Q variant allele frequency was 3.6%. PD-L1 immunohistochemistry was positive.

[ laboratory results ]: Creatinine was approximately 2.5 mg/dL in the setting of obstruction-associated acute kidney injury.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:
- Intravesical BCG for bladder cancer after initial diagnosis in 2019.
- Nephrostomy tubes were replaced for obstructive uropathy.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic muscle-invasive urothelial bladder cancer with a large bladder mass and widespread retroperitoneal and pelvic adenopathy, complicated by obstruction-associated acute kidney injury.

[ other clinical data ]: ECOG performance status was 2 and had worsened over the preceding 4 weeks. No contraindications to pembrolizumab were documented. The patient was otherwise described as healthy apart from the current malignancy-related issues.

[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old female. Active smoker. Comorbid chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and congestive heart failure.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented with a large malignant pleural effusion.

[ diagnosis ]: Pulmonary adenocarcinoma / non-small cell lung cancer with malignant pleural effusion, subcentimeter pulmonary nodules, and mediastinal mass.

[ current disease status ]: At the time of referral, the patient had newly identified ERBB2-mutated pulmonary adenocarcinoma with malignant pleural effusion and thoracic disease burden including pulmonary nodules and mediastinal mass.

[ other clinical data ]: None.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult female with breast cancer. Initial presentation occurred in 2010.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic breast cancer with disease progression after multiple prior systemic therapies; new liver lesion identified in July of the current year.

[ diagnosis ]: Initially diagnosed in 2010 with triple-positive breast cancer (ER-positive, PR-positive, HER2-positive). Metastatic recurrence/progression was documented in 2014 with bone metastases. Subsequent metastatic progression involved lung, adrenal gland, and liver. On later biopsy of a liver lesion, the tumor remained ER-positive, became PR-negative, and was HER2-negative.

[ histopathology results ]: Liver lesion biopsy performed in July of the current year showed metastatic breast carcinoma that was ER-positive, PR-negative, and HER2-negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Bone metastases were identified in 2014. Later progression occurred in the lung and adrenal gland. Within 1 year of second-line ado-trastuzumab emtansine, enlarging lung lesions were documented. A new liver lesion was identified in July of the current year.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Comprehensive genomic profiling identified:
- PIK3CA p.H1047R mutation
- High tumor mutational burden
- BRCA2 alteration
- BRCA2 reversion alteration

Tumor mutational burden was 19 mutations/megabase.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: 
- 2010: Received TCH (docetaxel, carboplatin, trastuzumab), followed by trastuzumab, then maintenance endocrine therapy with a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor.
- 2014 metastatic progression to bone: Received first-line paclitaxel, trastuzumab, and pertuzumab; subsequently continued trastuzumab plus pertuzumab, with fulvestrant added.
- This regimen achieved disease control for approximately 5 years.
- After progression in lung and adrenal gland: Switched to second-line ado-trastuzumab emtansine (T-DM1).
- Within 1 year on T-DM1: Developed enlarging lung lesions.
- Subsequently received trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd); treatment was discontinued because of interstitial lung disease of sufficient severity to require cessation.
- Thereafter received ribociclib plus fulvestrant.
- After identification of a new liver lesion in July of the current year, started capecitabine; capecitabine was poorly tolerated.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic breast cancer with prior receptor conversion from HER2-positive disease to HER2-negative disease on liver biopsy, persistent ER positivity, PR negativity, and recent progression following multiple prior lines of therapy. Most recent documented disease sites included liver, lung, adrenal gland, and bone.

[ other clinical data ]: Interstitial lung disease occurred during trastuzumab deruxtecan therapy and led to treatment discontinuation.

[ patient demographics ]: 77-year-old man. He was documented as homeless. He had a history of very heavy tobacco use. Family history was unknown.

[ chief complaint ]: Profound weight loss and urinary retention.

[ diagnosis ]: De novo neuroendocrine small cell carcinoma arising from the prostate, with metastatic disease involving pelvic/inguinal and abdominopelvic lymph nodes.

[ histopathology results ]: CT-guided biopsy was consistent with neuroendocrine small cell carcinoma arising from the prostate.

Bulky lymphadenopathy was present in the abdomen and pelvis. CT chest and bone scan showed no other evidence of metastasis. PET scan demonstrated extensive metastatic disease. No brain metastases were identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Liquid biopsy identified an NTRK-FMO1 non-canonical fusion, NF1 frameshift alteration, and STK11 alteration. Additional findings were reported as consistent with clonal hematopoiesis. Tumor fraction on liquid assay was reported at 45%.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA was 11.8.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Systemic treatment was initiated with carboplatin, etoposide, and atezolizumab. No treatment response or outcome data were available.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic small cell/neuroendocrine prostate carcinoma with bulky pelvic primary tumor and extensive nodal metastatic disease on PET imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: No family history was available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive fatigue and dyspnea on exertion over approximately 1 month.

[ diagnosis ]: Acute myeloid leukemia with monocytic differentiation. Peripheral blood smear and bone marrow morphology showed monoblasts/promonocytes. Bone marrow was hypercellular. Cytogenetics showed a normal female karyotype.

[ histopathology results ]:  
Peripheral blood smear showed large immature cells with abundant pale cytoplasm, irregular nuclei, finely dispersed chromatin, vacuolation, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio, and features consistent with promonocytes/monoblasts.  
Bone marrow core biopsy was markedly hypercellular for age with near absence of fat spaces and diffuse blast infiltration. There was reduced normal maturation of neutrophilic and erythroid lineages. Small megakaryocytes with hypolobated nuclei were present in the background.  
Bone marrow aspirate showed monocytic blasts/promonocytes with irregular nuclei and cytoplasmic vacuoles. Background dysplastic erythroid cells and some hypergranulation of myeloid cells were described, but the threshold for AML with myelodysplasia-related changes was not met on the material reviewed.

[ imaging findings ]: No imaging results were available.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
Bone marrow next-generation sequencing panel identified mutations in NPM1, DNMT3A, and TET2.  
FLT3 was negative.  
CEBPA was negative.  
KIT was negative.  
IDH mutations were negative.  
KRAS was negative.  
Conventional cytogenetics demonstrated a normal female karyotype.

[ laboratory results ]:  
Initial complete blood count:  
- White blood cell count: 11.9 x10^9/L  
- Absolute neutrophil count: 1.1 x10^9/L  
- Hemoglobin: 7 g/dL  
- Platelets: 36,000/µL  

Chemistry/liver profile:  
- Creatinine: 1.1 mg/dL  
- AST: elevated  
- ALT: elevated  
- Bilirubin: normal  
- LDH: slightly elevated  
- Albumin: 2.8 g/dL  
- Uric acid: normal  
- Fibrinogen: normal  

Red cell indices were described as consistent with normocytic anemia with increased RDW.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior leukemia-directed treatment was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed AML with monocytic differentiation at initial evaluation. The patient was symptomatic from cytopenias, with anemia, thrombocytopenia, mild leukocytosis, and neutropenia. Karnofsky performance status was 80.

[ other clinical data ]:  
Past medical history: hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, arthritis.  
Home medications: hydrochlorothiazide, losartan, rosuvastatin, metformin.  
Family history: prostate cancer, coronary artery disease, diabetes.  
Review of systems: denied chest discomfort, lower extremity swelling, fever, and bleeding symptoms.  
Physical examination: afebrile; heart rate in the 90s; blood pressure approximately 140/90 mmHg; oxygen saturation 95%. Conjunctival pallor, bruising on extremities, and a soft systolic murmur were present. Cardiac rhythm was regular. Lungs were clear. Abdomen was normal without palpable organomegaly. No lymphadenopathy was present. Neurologic examination was nonfocal.

There are some scales that might have some relatedness to help make these decisions in terms of comorbidity scales and things like that. And as you said, I think I would argue the one thing missing from here is very much patient preference. And it's, I think, incumbent upon all of us with all interdisciplinary roles to make sure that the patients have the information they need to make that preference an educated one. And so you know really I think we're we're in a great place with AML diagnosis and treatment right now and Making some some great advances that all of these things really do Can play into prognosis and overall outcomes?
Just as an example. This was what her this patient's fitness assessment was predicted to be Not not so bad

But importantly, also social support is something that we all need to think about with our patients. So it really is kind of combined, but I think we think about activities of daily living, mobility, exercise, and cognition, a normal three-word recall, something that's very simple that can be done at bedside.
Wonderful. So I'll turn to Marty to just summarize the treatment discussion that he would be having with this patient.

Well, again, I think the treatment, the three bullets here are important. First of all, again, I can't emphasize enough, I hope everyone agrees that we think that all patients should participate in some clinical trial so that we can give them the optimal therapy and we can make progress in the disease. And then beyond that, the decision comes to really one of standard intensive chemotherapy or low-dose low-intensity chemotherapy with a hypomethylating agent, or what is very popular today, particularly, again, in the context of a clinical trial, are hypomethylating agents plus a novel agent, such as venetoclax or other agents. And I think this is the decision, and there's no absolute right or wrong decision. It's a decision that has to be made carefully, seeing the patient, examining the patient, and talking to the patient and the patient's family. So I think there's no right or wrong here. It sounds like most people here would argue for intensive chemotherapy, which I think is reasonable. This is the initial therapy. I think time will preclude a lengthy discussion, but we've touched upon the issue of transplant, which is likely, in an older adult, the only reliable curative strategy. But of course, it's associated with certain morbidity and risk of mortality, which I think is less than it used to be, but I think it's not zero or five percent. So that has to be taken into account. It's possible some patients with enough morbidity will actually live longer and happier. with one, two, or three years of hypomethylating agent or subsequent studies and subsequent therapy after that. But I think most the thrust in the field now is to try to do what you can to get a patient in first remission and then certainly at age 70 and this patient doesn't have many prohibitive comorbidities to try to move to some kind of an allograft.
Wonderful, thank you. And Katie, if you could go through just comments on reducing risk of treatment-related complications.

Yeah, so I mean, certainly lots of great treatment options, but then once we do go down that road, we have to be ready to try to optimize outcomes and make sure that the patient's able to get all of the intended dosing so we're not needing to face those dose-limiting toxicities. And some of the most common ones we can see, especially with these highly intensive therapies, deconditioning and mucositis and make sure we know kind of what's our threshold for parenteral nutrition, trying to optimize oral intake, certainly nausea and vomiting and making sure that we're following the NCCN guidelines for anti-emetic prophylaxis. And then certainly infection with this population and do we have the right prophylactic antimicrobials on board. making sure that we're following neutropenic guidelines and starting those broad-spectrum antibiotics at first sign of fever. But so these are certainly the most common of the dose-limiting toxicities that we'll see, especially with these intensive treatments. And so just making sure that we're staying on top of assessment and early intervention for these patients.

I want to add that if you were at ASCO this year, one of the plenary session presentations was about showing four or five months survival benefit by enrolling them, exactly what Kathleen said. Standard chemo, half the patients got online, almost 80 day access to send their symptoms and manage it, versus not. Survival was better four months than that. So I hope that we will be doing something similar to that in AML too.

reference_conclusion: Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy should be performed to confirm suspected acute myeloid leukemia, with comprehensive diagnostic evaluation including flow cytometry, conventional cytogenetics/G-banding, and molecular testing including at minimum NPM1, CEBPA, RUNX1, and FLT3; peripheral blood flow cytometry and HLA typing at diagnosis before induction therapy should also be obtained. Additional pretreatment assessment should include echocardiography, evaluation of abnormal liver function tests, and planning for central venous access as indicated. Enrollment in a clinical trial is the preferred treatment approach. If no trial is available, management should be individualized between intensive induction chemotherapy and lower-intensity hypomethylating agent–based therapy, with consideration of allogeneic transplantation in first remission as the only reliable curative strategy in an older adult fit for transplant.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female; age 32 years at initial presentation in 2004.

[ chief complaint ]: Surveillance imaging in 2021 demonstrated new bilateral pulmonary nodules.

[ diagnosis ]: Cribriform-type adenoid cystic carcinoma originating in the right maxillary sinus, initially diagnosed in 2004; recurrent metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma to the lungs confirmed in 2021.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Primary tumor: cribriform-type adenoid cystic carcinoma of the right maxillary sinus.  
- CT-guided biopsy of the left upper lobe lung nodule in 2021 confirmed recurrent metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma.  
- Left upper lobe lung resection specimen showed a 2.0 cm adenoid cystic carcinoma involving the inked pleural surface, with resection margins negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Surveillance CT chest in 2021 showed approximately 3-4 new bilateral pulmonary nodules.  
- Largest pulmonary lesion measured 2.1 cm in the left upper lobe.  
- PET-CT demonstrated a metabolically avid cavitary left upper lobe lung nodule measuring approximately 2.0 cm, corresponding to the CT abnormality.  
- Additional small pulmonary nodules were present, including a small right lung lesion and another lesion near the liver.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2004: Surgery followed by radiation for primary right maxillary sinus adenoid cystic carcinoma.  
- 2021: CT-guided biopsy of left upper lobe pulmonary nodule confirmed metastatic recurrence.  
- Left upper lobe lung resection was performed for the dominant pulmonary lesion.  
- Postoperative course was complicated by significant postoperative pain.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Residual small pulmonary metastases remained after resection of the dominant left upper lobe lesion.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Long interval between initial diagnosis in 2004 and detection of pulmonary metastatic disease in 2021.
