reference_discussion.text: Thank you. It's really a privilege to be here this morning. Thank you for the invitation. And I will bring up my slides. So, in a, in a normal tumor board, we would have a number of cases to discuss and typically the discussion starts with 1 of the members of the team presenting a case. And so I will present the 1st case, and then we'll have some discussion as we would in a real tumor board. And so this case begins back in 2004, at which point in time, the patient who came to us for care was 32 years old. And this woman developed a cribriform type adenoid cystic carcinoma that originated in the right maxillary sinus. Now, the focus of this patient's original treatment is not the topic of this tumor board, but she originally was treated with surgery followed by radiation. So a pretty typical initial treatment course. And then was seen regularly in follow up until more recently when in 2021, she had a surveillance cat scan of the chest. So a CT or cat scan of the chest, which demonstrated new bilateral lung nodules. So, lung nodules on both sides of the lungs, approximately 3 to 4 as determined by our radiologist. The largest was 2.1 centimeters within the left upper lobe of the lung. And on the right, you can see the patient went on to have a PET-CT. And this is the PET-CT. PET-CT shows activity, or what we call avidity, within normal tissues, such as the heart, that are metabolically active, such as the heart muscle, but also within tumors. And so this here in the lung, and this is the left lung, is a 2 centimeter cavitary left upper lobe lung nodule corresponding to the abnormality that was seen on the CT imaging. And this is kind of a view from the front. So, looking at the patient scan kind of head on. And this patient went on to have a CT guided. So using the CAT scan as guidance to do a biopsy of this left upper lung nodule. And when the pathologist looked at this biopsy tissue, it confirmed that the lung nodule that was seen was recurrent metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma. So, you know, normally during a tumor board at multiple points, when we're thinking about decisions, we would stop and have a discussion about management or what we think of scans and treatment course. And so maybe at this point, I'll stop and we'll, we'll have a little bit of a discussion. Um, you know, the 1st, the 1st question that comes up and management is, you know. What should we do for surveillance? Um, and that means after a patient is treated, uh, you know, in this case, it was surgery and radiation, uh, back in 2004, you know, how is the, what is the best way to follow these patients? Um, and subsequently, when, um, this patient developed a nodule. what defines a suspicious nodule? So maybe I'll ask Paul to comment first on what his practice is, and then I'll comment also.

Boy, it's a fantastic question. Once again, thank you for hosting. Surveillance is difficult. Typically, most cancers, breast cancer, colon cancer, we think 5 years and your risk of recurrence is very low. What we've seen for adenoids, it's extremely variable, shown by this case in 2004, the original case, and now 2021 and finally recurring. ACCRF actually has been funding some research, both at our institution and others, to look at how often we should be screening people for how long. And I think that will be very useful. Overall, this is for some time, because recurrences can happen 20, 30, even 40 years later. In general, our practice at University of Michigan has been yearly CT scans. And if there's something suspicious, follow up with a little bit closer interval scans every six months. Hopefully with research between different endocytic sites, we can have a more precision type surveillance strategy. In terms of when and how to biopsy, that's a multidisciplinary discussion. between ourselves, the thoracic surgeons, the radiation oncologists, and the radiologists. Normally we look for it to be growing over time. And once again, that's very, it changes from case to case. It's very hard to define. Often we wait for it to get at least to about a centimeter. And then if there's only one lesion, we actually may do a surgery to remove it. Once again, we defer to our thoracic surgeons. If there's several spots in both lungs, then we might just do a CT guided biopsy as shown here. The reason of the difference is if there's a single spot, we do remove it with a surgery, we're done with it. There's no other spots to deal with. However, if there's multiple spots, then we can just biopsy it with a needle. Then it brings up the question of how do we address it appropriately? I think that's what Dr. Schoenfeld is about to discuss. But I'm curious, what about at Brigham? What's your practice?

Yeah, it's pretty pretty similar. I mean, I think we, we admittedly wish we had more kind of data. So it's very helpful to continue to do research to really see what the best way is to to follow patients. But I completely agree. I mean, we, we treat this differently than. Uh, other types of head and neck cancers, you know, other types of cancers that we see, and that we typically don't think there is an interval, um, after which we stop doing surveillance. So, you know, and other types of cancers, you might stop after 3 years or 5 years. Um, in patients with, we typically would do maybe some more frequent scans the 1st, few years after initial treatment, um, and then, you know, enter what we call kind of longer term follow up where we typically would still kind of do imaging about once a year in most cases. But that's also a discussion with patients because we admit we don't have the data to really guide us about the frequency of scans or what types of scans we want to do. So usually we will do a CAT scan of the chest and we'd recommend a CAT scan of the chest once a year. Sorry, just a quick follow up.
Should should every scan also include the abdomen to view the liver and how do you recommend that?

So, we typically don't, um, you know, I think that's a good question and that gets back to the fact that we, you know, we can't no scan is perfect and no scan is going to catch, you know, kind of everything and scans also have what we call false positives. And, you know, if you scan. people that have no cancer, with a history of cancer, without a history of cancer, you will get abnormalities that turn out to be just scar tissue or evidence of a prior infection or things completely unrelated. So we always are balancing kind of the risks and benefits of doing scans. And that is how frequently we do scans, but also what types of scans to do. And for ACC, we usually just focus on the lungs or the site in the head and neck. That was originally treated because we think at least according to the data that we have for most patients, those are going to be the areas of most risk. But what do you think?

I think that it's a couple of very important points. For 1, our technology is getting better over time. And 1 thing that we run to an issue with is technology gets better that sometimes presents new diagnostic challenges because now they see things smaller and smaller and smaller. And after you've had. a viral infection, or even after you've done a beautiful fall day, you actually develop pulmonary nodules, which are very, very common. And now we can see very, you know, sub-centimeter, three, four millimeter spots, and that's completely benign. However, of course, in cancer, we always get concerned. And so that's why it's so important. I think in the coming slides, we're going to discuss how do we follow this over time? I think the other question I hear very frequently is, well, why CT? Why not PET scan? You know, it's beautiful colors. Why can't we do that? CT and what I tell all my patients is actually much more high definition. You can see spots in much better anatomic resolution. I always give the analogy of a 1990s TV and watching football being in Ann Arbor here. versus a high-definition TV of today where you can see sweat rolling down people's faces. You can see very, very small spots on CAT scans and follow it over time. And so in general, our practice has actually been to favor CTs when at all possible. There's some contradications there. If I had a question about liver metastases, it's a great topic, but in general, if you look at the statistics, when people develop metastases outside of the lungs, for example, liver, the bones, the right leg, most of those people have lung metastases. And so we would have caught it if we're just scanning the chest and avoiding unnecessary radiation.

Yeah. And I will just add that if we do see something in the chest, like what was seen in this case, then we will go on to do more imaging. So then we would do either a PET scan or a CAT scan for high resolution. And we typically would do the entire body or kind of restage patients at that point. Um, and so I think here, we've talked about, you know, surveillance, we talked about suspicious nodules again, you know, there's, we would always discuss with our radiologists and tumor board and with our surgeons about radio, you know, how best to biopsy it. And often we would do, you know, as we did in this case, a CT or CAT scan guided biopsy. So maybe I'll go on in the interest of time. Um. And and so, you know, in this case, you know, getting to the management options, we had a biopsy that that showed, um, you know, recurrent. And so at this point, we think about various management options. And then, in terms of the general options that we always consider, is one, not every cancer, not every ACC that spreads to the lung, especially with very small metastases, needs treatment. And we'll talk more about that. So one option that we always think about is just watch it and watch it closely. The other option we think about is systemic therapy. So that would be, you know, Paul's area of expertise and expertise and he'll talk more about it in a minute. But and then finally would be local treatment. Would be, you know, should we treat just the lesions that we see and within local treatment is a kind of some nested questions. How many so in this patient, there were a few lesions that we're seeing that we think we're suspicious. Do we treat all of the lesions or do we treat some of them? And what type of local treatment should we should we pursue? So, should we do surgery? Should we do what we call ablation and the several different types of ablation such as cryo ablation using cold thermal energy to kind of ablate the tumor radio frequency ablation or my specialty, which is to do therapeutic radiation. And often we think about a very focused type of radiation called stereotactic body radiotherapy, otherwise known as, as for short, as an acronym. So, you know, I think there's a lot of considerations. How would you, how would this discussion typically go at University of Michigan, Paul?

Yeah. So it's a great multidisciplinary case here. And I always really depend on the expertise in my head and neck radiation oncologist. I think this is very important to engage people that specialize in this type of cancer. In this case, we would follow up the patient with probably scans at approximately six months to judge the pace of disease and understand really how this is growing. Because it looks like the original case was 04, Now we're seeing lesions in 2021. The largest was 2.1 centimeters. And to really assess, is that disease velocity increasing rapidly? Or does it sound like they're symptomatic? And based on that change in disease, if they're stable, if they're growing, then we would consider radiation to all of them, given the limited number, versus active surveillance.

Great. And so, you know, I think You know, 1 of the things I wanted to highlight just in terms of those different options is, um, is that there is a lot of uncertainty and I think, you know, when we talk about the case, this, this type of case, all of those issues that that Paul brought up, you know, do we monitored how stable have the lesions been? You know, we really, I think, as a field. Um, you know, don't know the right answer in many cases. Um, and so it's a very individualized discussion about. You know, what we think where the, where the nodules are located, how easy are they to treat? You know, what's the risk? Um, what are the side effects that are associated with each of the treatment? What's the best treatment? Um, but more broadly. Um, is conceptually a question that I think we all struggle with in the field, which is, you know, how aggressive, you know, what should our general philosophy be? Um, and, you know, in that context, I wanted to mention that a trial that we have started at the Brigham and Women's Hospital Dana Farber, which is the solar trial. And as I'll talk about in a minute, we found that the early treatment of oligo metastases may improve outcomes in patients we had treated over the last few decades. And so what does that mean? You know, I think in historically, we've kind of. Divided cancer patients into 2 kind of groups. Um, so people that have what we call localized cancer and patients that have metastatic cancer that spread to other parts of the body. But that we're learning over time that probably in many cases, as we learn more about the biology, as we get as our anatomy is our ways of following patients get more sophisticated that there's kind of this intermediate group and oligo means that these patients may just have a few kind of areas. Um, and so, you know, there's a thought that maybe treating these few areas aggressive locally might be beneficial. But we don't know that and what we always like to do is, you know, not just look back at our outcomes over historically. but also just actually test the question by doing a randomized trial of early radiation of metastases versus observation. And so this follows on a number of other trials that have been done in the United States and other countries. for patients with this type of condition, oligometastases, and they've really had mixed results. You might have strong feelings one way or the other, and we certainly see patients and doctors that feel strongly, like, of course, if you see a few cancer spots, why wouldn't you treat them? And then another school of thought is, well, what are you really doing to benefit the patient if there's still a risk that the cancer comes back somewhere else? And so I think it really depends on the situation and you can see that by results of other trials. So there was a trial called the saber comment trial, and that was multiple different types of cancers, including some salivary cancers. And they're treating these oligo metastases actually. Seem to improve survival. Similarly, in patients with prostate cancer, there's been a couple of trials. All these trials have, you know, they try to get good acronyms for the trials. So, STAMP and ORIEL were the names of 2 of these other trials. And there was a benefit in prostate cancer for localized treatment. But in contrast, just to show that it can be different from 1 cancer to another, just recently, we've had results from 2, 2 trials that were done on what we call a cooperative group. So, within the United States, and that was the energy is the name of the cooperative group. And so there was a lung cancer trial that was negative. It showed that treating these oligo metastases with radiation or localized treatment didn't benefit patients overall. And similarly, for patients with breast cancer, there was a recent report of a trial that was negative.

I don't know about you, but I always find it difficult to interpret these because there's a little bit of patient selection that goes into these. And it's always judging. Each cancer is completely different, especially an adenoid cystic. And sometimes the patients may be driving benefit, as you've kind of implied, or those that are growing slowly over time are very stable versus those are you know, tripling oversize, developing new lesions within a matter of a couple of months, and it's parsing out which group of patients, which disease biology may be driving a benefit oligomet. And so, as you're putting it here, I think that it's, your prospective study will be so important to address that, about who can we really address in that early setting, and how do we really prescreen them with, you know, scans a couple of months apart to figure out what that best therapy is.

Yeah, yeah, that's a great point. It's really comes, and that's the discussions, right, we have in Tumor Board all the time. It's like, what are the patient factors that really kind of drive us to think one way or the other? Here's the data that I mentioned. This is what we call retrospective data, so it's not a trial. We just looked back at the patients that we treated over many years, and this was research that was supported by the ACCRF, where we looked back and saw how many of our ACC patients had oligometastatic versus polymetastatic disease, and so might be eligible for kind of this type of approach. And we saw that, especially with our way of monitoring patients, we did see patients with just a few lung metastases or other metastases. And that when we looked back, it was some suggestion that maybe patients did better with earlier treatment. Now, I will say that there's a lot of caveats because, again, what Paul just said goes into this data that we do our best. This wasn't randomized. We selected the patients for local treatment based on maybe some favorable factors, and that might have contributed to this. But at least it makes us think that it's a question that's worth testing. And so this is the trial. This is the SOLAR trial. This is what we call a trial schema. where we have, I won't go through all the details of the trial, but basically we take patients that come to us and we say, we don't know what the best option is. So, we are going to follow you closely and either monitor things closely or be more aggressive and treat with radiation, SBRT. or other types of local therapy. And then really look to see over time, is there a benefit in how quickly the cancer progresses in your quality of life, in the toxicities, and how well do our treatments work? And so that's the goal of this ongoing trial. So to go back to this first case, so this patient had a, we discussed all the issues and we decided because they had that one larger lesion to go ahead with surgery. And so the patient had a left upper lobe lung resection, which showed a 2 centimeter lesion of adenoid cystic carcinoma involving the inked plural surface, but not at the resection margins. And I will just say that, you know, it is a, it is a good question. So everybody, of course, feels reassured that the cancer comes out, but there are downsides, obviously, to any procedure. And so one of the side effects of surgery is that this patient had significant post-operative pain. And then we're still left with the question of what to do about the other lung metastasis. And so getting back to Paul's points that he was making before, Um, you know, here are the other lesions that we saw, you know, 1 was small and was close to the liver. Another 1 was very small. You can see here in the right lung. You can see that it's just a little bit of a dot here. That's not present on the other side. And so actually, for this case, when we then gave advice to this patient after discussing it in our tumor board, just like Paul was commenting, we thought given the long interval between the initial presentation and metastases, the low overall tumor burden, And the trickier location to treat, because it was closer to the liver, we decided to observe. And just to highlight, as Paul mentioned, there are data that suggests that certain factors, such as the long interval from initial diagnosis, predict more slow growth. And this patient has fortunately gone on to have stability of these other small lesions for approximately 2 years, which brings us to the current time. So, I think that was the end of the 1st case. Do you have any final comments, Paul? on this case?
No, not at all. This is a great case to cover some very important points and some important trials.

Dr. Schoenfeld, can I just ask one question that we saw in the chat that relates to this last point about the interval between initial presentation of metastases? Is there generally a breakpoint at which you say, oh, this is a case where it's clearly less aggressive versus perhaps more aggressive?

Uh, that's a great question. You know, I don't I don't think we, we know what that that cut off is. Um, I think again, it depends on a number of factors. The way. We typically think about it is, is, is like we were saying, you know, for for other types of cancers, you know, we use that kind of 3 year, roughly 3 year time point, or even like a shorter time span where. you know, these cancers would grow and if they've grown within the 1st, certainly within the 1st year, but within the 1st, you know, couple years, um, it, it, it, we do think about treating more broadly, but, but clearly when there's been, you know, decades or more than 5 years, then we think that we hope that even if there's cancer growing somewhere else, it's more indolent, slow growing. Okay. So, I'll go ahead and then the 2nd case brings up some of the same issues a little bit different. This was a 61 year old man who was diagnosed with a 6.8 centimeter ACC of the right maxilla in 2021, underwent surgery, and then developed 4 lung nodules in late 2023. So, for lung lesions, 1.3 centimeter sub plural nodule in the left lower lobe biopsy confirmed adenoid cystic carcinoma and then 3 additional what we call sub centimeter nodules 2 in the left lower lobe and then 1 in the right upper lobe. And so here are the scans that we would review in our, in our tumor board, and you can see this 1.2 centimeter left lower lobe, what we call power vertebral. So it's next to the vertebral body lesion. You can see this other nodule here in the left lower lobe looking kind of face on. You can see this nodule here in the left lobe of the lung. And here you can see, you know, this peripheral, so kind of this smaller lung lesion kind of here and here, as I had mentioned. And then a very small lesion that's very, you know, it's hard to even see, but this tinier lesion right here, left lower lobe. And then the right upper lobe, again, you can see a small lesion here in the right upper lobe. So we would go through these in our tumor board with our radiologists and discuss. And so here we decided on a little bit of a different approach. Again, it was a shorter interval. These areas are more tricky to remove for surgery. There's fewer nodules. And we were a little bit worried that this nodule here close to the vertebral body might eventually start to cause pain because it's close to the chest wall. And so we actually discussed the protocol with this patient. This patient enrolled in our solar protocol, and we did radiation to the 2 largest lesions that we saw in the left lower lobe. And here's a typical, what we call a radiation isodose curve or heat map, and it just shows where the radiation goes. you know, the colors are what radiation dose, and you can see how targeted we try to be with our radiation, giving the highest dose, you know, right around the tumor and a much lower dose to the normal lung tissue and to the heart and to other tissues in the body. And, you know, again, we did this on protocol, but we also discussed, you know, in our tumor board, you know, whether or not we should treat this patient, and if so, what approach. And so maybe, you know, would this patient have been considered for radiation at Michigan, Paul?

reference_conclusion: Following multidisciplinary review of biopsy-confirmed pulmonary metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma, the dominant left upper lobe lesion was managed with left upper lobe lung resection. Given the prolonged interval from initial diagnosis to metastatic presentation, low overall pulmonary tumor burden, and the technically challenging location of the remaining small lesions near the liver, the residual lung metastases were managed with observation and close surveillance. The remaining lesions have remained stable for approximately 2 years.
reference_conclusion_quote: we discussed all the issues and we decided because they had that one larger lesion to go ahead with surgery. And so the patient had a left upper lobe lung resection [...] for this case, when we then gave advice to this patient after discussing it in our tumor board, just like Paul was commenting, we thought given the long interval between the initial presentation and metastases, the low overall tumor burden, And the trickier location to treat, because it was closer to the liver, we decided to observe. [...] this patient has fortunately gone on to have stability of these other small lesions for approximately 2 years

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 47-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Floor-of-mouth swelling in August 2016.

[ diagnosis ]: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the left floor of mouth with synchronous metastatic pulmonary disease at initial staging; later metastatic involvement included pleural-based thoracic lesions and a renal lesion.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy of the floor-of-mouth lesion demonstrated adenoid cystic carcinoma. Surgical resection of the primary floor-of-mouth tumor was performed; the resection specimen showed high-risk pathologic features. Because the pulmonary nodules were too small for CT-guided biopsy at presentation, one lung lesion was surgically excised, and pathology confirmed metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial staging CT in August 2016 showed approximately 7 bilateral pulmonary nodules, all subcentimeter, involving all 5 lobes.  
- Serial CT surveillance was performed every 6 months.  
- By 2018, the pulmonary nodules had shown slow interval enlargement, increasing by approximately 2-3 mm on each 6-month scan; only one lesion was greater than 1 cm at that time.  
- In 2018, imaging also showed a renal mass of uncertain etiology and pleural thickening.  
- By 2019, there were greater than 10 pulmonary lesions, with multiple lesions measuring 1.5-2 cm.  
- In January 2020, the pulmonary lesions had continued to enlarge; the largest lung lesion measured 3.5 cm. The renal lesion measured 4 cm. Imaging demonstrated pleural-based nodularity/lesions along the outer lung/chest wall region, including lesions enlarging over time and appearing to abut/push toward the rib. Additional fissural and pulmonary nodules were also present.  
- Approximately 6 months after local radiation treatments, follow-up imaging showed further progression, including increase of one lesion from 2.2 cm to 3.6 cm (>20% growth over 6 months), with additional enlarging and new lesions seen by 2021.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Repeat biopsy in 2019 for molecular testing identified a MYB-NFIB fusion, described as common in adenoid cystic carcinoma.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Primary surgery was performed to remove the left floor-of-mouth primary tumor.  
- Adjuvant radiation therapy was delivered to the floor of mouth after surgery.  
- The metastatic pulmonary disease was initially managed with surveillance only, with CT imaging every 6 months, for approximately 4 years from diagnosis because of indolent growth and lack of significant symptoms.  
- In 2020, radiation therapy was delivered to pleural-based thoracic lesions because of concern for current or impending symptoms; this improved the patient's intermittent side discomfort/twinge.  
- Radiation therapy was subsequently delivered to the renal lesion because of concern for future renal complications.  
- Radiation therapy was also later delivered to a lung lesion.  
- Despite local therapies, imaging approximately 6 months later demonstrated continued disease progression, with enlarging and new lesions.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma after a prolonged indolent course, with multiple enlarging pulmonary metastases, pleural-based thoracic disease, and a renal lesion. Disease progression was documented despite local radiation treatments, including >20% growth over 6 months and development of new lesions.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- At multiple time points through progression, the patient remained highly functional and largely asymptomatic.  
- In January 2020, he remained active enough to run 10 km and reported only an occasional side twinge/pulling sensation.

reference_discussion.text: Either that or observation, I personally will talk about an upcoming case. I would at least push for radiation or advocate for radiation for that subplural lesion, the 1.2 centimeter. That is a high likelihood of becoming symptomatic either in the very near future or possibly even now, just based on that location. So even off trial, I'd consider radiation for that lesion.
Dr. Schoenfeld, I feel I need to stand up for the surgeons. What do you think the surgical perspective would be on this?

Again, as not a surgeon, I'll do my best. The surgeons always, I think, as Paul was saying in the beginning, there's some situations where we do, I think, really do try to favor surgery and that's kind of uniform in our tumor boards. And that's when it's a single nodule, especially if we don't have a diagnosis and it's an easier spot to remove. because then we answer multiple questions at once. We get a diagnosis, we remove potentially all the disease we can see, and hopefully patients do well, not just from a tumor perspective, but also from a quality of life perspective, in terms of a quick recovery. Um, we think less about surgery, the more nodules there are generally because again, you know, every time we're doing surgery, that's time on 1 nodule. We're not addressing the other nodule. We also shy away from surgery when we think that the recovery is going to be more challenging. Sometimes these nodules right at the chest wall can be a little bit of an issue because they're right by kind of the lining of the lung. and that can be a little bit riskier in some situations. But again, we would discuss, that's one of the important roles of the tumor board, because we would have a surgeon and a radiologist and usually multiple surgeons there to discuss kind of the pros and cons for each individual situation.
So there's some questions here about, are you always biopsying these lesions? Did you biopsy both before you would treat? Talk a little bit about that.

I think that's a great question. And in general, the 1st time lung lesions or bone lesions, anything appear after the initial diagnosis, you have the initial surgery. After that, there's a new spot that shows up in the lung. It's worth biopsying that to confirm it is in fact, to even consider molecular testing at that point. That being said, when there's subsequent spots that show up, we don't biopsy every single one. And in general, there may even be a lag time from when the spot shows up in the lung to when we find the stick and needle in it. And that's because we wait until it's a safer size. When spots are very, very small, there's a possibility we don't get a sample of it and we just get normal lung and have complications. And so it's a complex decision-making process that the multidisciplinary tumor board always talks about.

We don't just talk about treatment. We often talk about imaging and other management questions too in the tumor board. That's a great point. And so, after treatment for this patient, there were what we call post-treatment changes. Sometimes right after radiation, it can be challenging to kind of see exactly what's happening because of the changes caused by radiation. But we usually follow these changes over time. and the other lung tumors remain stable. And I will just add that we've done a previous study where we looked at SBRT kind of prospectively, either with or without immune therapy, and we really did show that radiation is a good local treatment where we give the radiation. It's just a matter of trying to select the patients who would benefit the most from this type of approach. So, I think that wraps up my 2 cases and so I will stop sharing and turn it over to Paul.
John, a quick question. A couple of people are asking versus proton. Can you can you comment at all?

Yeah, it's a complicated question that I don't know that I'll have time to do complete justice to. There's multiple different types of radiation that we give that might have some advantages versus another. Photons is the most common type of radiation that we give. And then there's another type, protons. Sometimes we think about protons, especially in the head and neck area. for a variety of reasons. Usually when we're treating metastases in the lung or in some other organs of the body, some centers will think about protons in specialized situations, but usually we do photons because we do a stereotactic body radiotherapy. And because of some of the uncertainty within the air, for physic reasons, we often would not use protons for this type of situation.
And I would also recommend anybody interested in the SBRT proton conversation, check out our 3rd webinar, because there was a good discussion among docs within that webinar as well. Okay.

So, this case that I'm presenting is 1 that goes over a pattern of years, and we're going to have a repeated discussion about treatment decisions, because I think it gets at many of these points we've been talking about. So this is a 47-year-old gentleman who had a newly diagnosed metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma involving the lung. So to go back, just to keep this in perspective, it's August, 2016, and this person had flora mouth swelling. The dentist, very full, body age with an infection. Fortunately, this was biopsied and found to be adenoid cystic carcinoma of the left bottom of the mouth. At that point, just for reasons of staging, CAT scan was done, showed very many, I think it was about 7 pulmonary nodules. The largest was under a centimeter on both sides of the chest, all 5 lobes of the lungs. So it wasn't something we could just remove with surgery. in order to get an accurate biopsy, because they're so small, we couldn't do a CT guided biopsy. We had to do a surgery to remove one of the spots. And in fact, that was shown to be adenoid cystic carcinoma. So the question was how to treat this person with adenoids that was found to have metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma upfront. So, we chose to do a primary surgery to remove the cancer at the bottom of the mouth. And also, this person had, when they removed it, had high risk features. We looked at it under the microscope. And so the question was, do we do radiation to the mouth afterwards as well? So, what would you guys have done at Brigham, out of curiosity?

Yeah, first and foremost, I think we want to treat patients who are having symptoms to see if we could help. And so in this type of case, there are multiple kind of small lung nodules. Hopefully those are not growing too quickly. And then there's kind of a symptomatic area in the floor of the mouth. And so then it's always a question, you know, we're really talking about, in addition to trying to control the disease, what would what would provide the most palliative symptomatic benefit? And that's always a discussion with medical oncology usually or surgery about, you know, what are the options in terms of drug treatments? What are the options in terms of surgery? We do often consider radiation for these type of situations to try to stabilize or shrink the swelling in the floor of the mouth. The issue with radiation in the mouth can be that we're trying to relieve symptoms, but it's a tough area to give radiation to because it also causes significant symptoms. And so it's always a discussion to think about whether or not we should do radiation. So, I think in this type of situation, sometimes doing surgery 1st would be reasonable to kind of remove the mass because it's on the larger side. And then in patients that have gone through a surgery, who have these high-risk features in the setting of kind of small lung disease, we would think about them in some way similar to an initial presentation of a patient, and then actually talk to the patient about giving radiation after surgery to try to make sure what we call consolidate that local treatment and reduce the risk the tumor came back.

In fact, that's the same thing we did. We have adjunct radiation, as you said, to ensure it doesn't come back to the bottom of the mouth. and followed this person with a CAT scans every 6 months. And over time, I have pictures here and even as a medical oncologist, I think I can do this and please don't get angry at me. I'm not a radiation oncologist, but we saw a slow increase in these pulmonary nodules. Going up top here, we can see the small lesion right there, that white spot, perhaps that's the most prominent, and that was in 2018. And every scan, every six months, it increased by about two to three millimeters. Each time, asthmatic, and only one was greater than one centimeter. And six months later, as you can see in 2018, we were accused of having a renal mass, but it was hard to say, couldn't really say if it was cancer or not. And he also was noted at pleural thickening. So that's where the lung joins up with the outer portion. Once again, continue to follow his lung spots. We had this discussion repeatedly. This patient was very well-informed and very involved with the research area. And finally, in 2019, we decided to biopsy it again, just for molecular testing. At that point, we were looking mainly to see if there's anything we could do treatments with. And we found this MIB-NFIB fusion, which is very common in ACC. We'll talk about in just a second with some emerging therapeutics that are very promising. And so at this point, slowly increasing in size over time, What would you guys do? I think he had greater than 10 lesions by 2019, multiple lesions over 1.5 to 2 centimeters. Would you consider treating this as oligo and going for the lesions greater than 1 centimeter or continued after surveillance given less than 20% growth?

Yeah, this is a tough one. I mean, I think that typically Historically, 5 lesions have been our cutoff for what we think of as oligometastases. And even there, I think, once you start getting more than 3, there's some question. Now, there's also a question, maybe 5 to 10 counts as oligometastases as our radiation techniques improve. But I would say generally when there's more than 5, you know, we, we, we don't treat locally unless there's, we're worried about symptoms or growth in that area. And then we would have a discussion, I think about, you know, given that growth, you know, whether it's time to initiate systemic treatment.

Perfect. I'm glad we're all on the same page. We didn't commit malpractice. Sure enough, in January 2020, continued to increase in size, asymptomatic. Finally, as we saw, I think we kind of alluded to before, adenoid cystic over time increases in the speed it's growing. I think about this and discuss it with my patients. It's like a stone rolling down the side of a mountain. At first it's going slowly, but at some point it starts to speed up quicker and quicker and quicker. And what we saw was that these lesions were getting larger, but he was still asymptomatic. The largest spot in the lung was now 3.5 centimeters. The kidney spot was up to four centimeters. So it was getting rather sizable. He was still running a 10K faster than I could, which is saying a lot. This person had an occasional twinge in his side, but it was running six mile, and the twinge could be just sitting around. And here we can see his scans, once again, 2018 versus 2020. To make this confusing, the 2018 scans are at the top and 2020 are at the bottom. And we can see this is the pleural base nodularity, very similar to the previous case he presented. You can see a little bump here, and a couple of years later, this large lesion kind of pushing into the rib here. And similarly, we can see maybe nothing here, maybe a little bit of thickness. And once again, a bump at the rib here on the outside of the lung. Same thing, this little white speck. And now there's a larger white lesion, significantly increased in size over those two years. And then along this fissure of the lung here, a little bit of thickness. And now you can see definitely more nodularity bumps there. You can also see a small lesion that was present. You can't really see it now, but several other metastatic cancer spots just in that field of vision alone. So at that point, especially given these spots on the outside of the lung, per our conversation earlier, we already got to it. These were starting to be concerning for either symptoms now or symptoms in the near future. And so talking to radiation oncology, we pursued radiation to those pleural base lesions. And that actually did help this patient's twinge, still kept to the six minute mile, unfortunately. And shortly thereafter, we were getting concerned about the kidney spot, that that could actually cause some kidney problems in the future. And so we performed radiation to the kidney spot and eventually to a lesion in the lungs too. But despite all of that, about six months later, we performed scans and we could see that it was once again, picking up in size. Compared to six months prior, it went from 2.2 centimeters to 3.1. 3.6, so greater than 20% growth in six months, despite our local therapies. Still active, but occasional pulling sensation.

Can I ask a quick question before you move on? Yeah. John, they've irradiated at several sites. Could you go back if a new lesion showed up in a similar location? Can you re-irradiate that site, or does that change how you might do a treatment?

That's a great question. We often try to avoid giving radiation to the same site. There's some side effects of radiation that can be cumulative, depending on the total dose that's given. but it varies. I mean, it depends on the timing when the radiation was given, the dose of radiation, the situation. So I would say that's a really individualized discussion, but in general, a prior course of radiation to that same area, we can give radiation to other areas, but prior radiation to one area does make the discussion about future radiation to that same area more complicated.

So once again, pictures here to kind of put it in perspective this time. This is out of order to like we do in tumor boards. So actually 2020 is over here, 2021 is over here to keep us out of just paying attention. We can see that the lesions are increasing in size even within the matter of year, almost double. Once again, here's another lesion slowly increasing in size. And also we saw new lesions popping up. So what's the point of the story? We went from 2016 with the initial diagnosis of metastatic adenoid cystic. He eventually got radiation almost four years later. And finally, because it's increased growth, new lesions, that's when we finally started systemic therapy. So here's a person asymptomatic and we're able to just watch for four years with nothing at all and no impairment in the patient's quality of life. So I think this points to the fact of the multidisciplinary discussion and when to finally Choose those tricks out of our belt and it's also a complex discussion with our patients and, you know, in the end of the day, it's you all are very, you know, the ultimate decision makers here. But I think this is points the complexity around to some of these things. And I think it gets the question to about when is a medical oncologist do we do we reach for a systemic therapy? I think that goes into here. Yep. And so it's hard given the variable history of adenoid cystic cancer, how these grow in every single cancer is different. What we're realizing more and more is that we wait until it's picked up that disease trajectory when it's growing faster and faster, at least increasing in size by 20%. within six to 12 months, as well as being at least two centimeters in multiple spots. We can't just radiate those two spots that John's talked about. It's something that's many, many spots, and it's growing quicker. That's when we start talking about a systemic therapy. And our go-to, if available, is a clinical trial, because we really think clinical trials offer us a way to move the field forward and offer us something better than what we currently have. Um, right now targeted therapies, um, they're called, um, all these, what's called a VEGF inhibitor are typically our go to based on some clinical trials. It gets kind of complicated here, but I have some of the information shown here showing that we were making a ground, but still have some, some room to grow. Um, what we see with a lot of these drugs. Here are 2 typical agents, exitinib and lindatinib, is that tumors very rarely shrink. In fact, no growth is a very good thing. We're just looking to stabilize the cancer. However, what we're hoping to do is just stabilize that growth for some period. On average, with our oral pills, with some of our agents, it stabilizes it for about six months to about a year. And then we just look for the next tool on our belt. Immunotherapy has been tested, including by the Harvard group. And unfortunately, it hasn't been as effective as other head and neck cancers, but we're looking at different combinations there. But so far, it hasn't really made the change that we would hope for. Currently, some areas that are clinical trials are evolving. There's directed clinical trials for this MIB fusion I mentioned before. Adenoid cystic, when we started doing molecular testing, we thought it'd be like lung cancer or melanoma, where there's a very specific mutation. We could use a pill and it would reverse the cancer and get rid of it right away. Unfortunately, it hasn't been that easy. But there's now a fusion about 80% of patients, which there's several companies coming up with a drug that might be able to at least stabilize the growth in those patients. And those studies are ongoing. And so hopefully within the next couple of years, we can get a sense of how those targeted therapies will work. There's also some next generation kind of chemotherapy type drugs that are IV called antibody drug conjugates. The idea of kind of depositing chemo just inside the adenoid cystic cancer cells. And I think those are very promising in the next couple of years. But once again, these are all clinical trials. And for the first time ever, we have several clinical trials in this area. So it's an exciting time to be moving the field forward. So I think that's it for that case. We have one more, but I think in the interest of time, we could stop there if you want, Jeff. It's up to you.

reference_conclusion: The primary floor-of-mouth adenoid cystic carcinoma was managed with surgical resection followed by adjuvant radiation to consolidate local control, with surveillance imaging performed at 6-month intervals. Given the multiplicity of pulmonary metastases, local therapy was deferred initially in favor of observation. As pleural-based and renal lesions enlarged and became concerning for current or impending symptoms, radiation was delivered to those sites and subsequently to a lung lesion. With further progression characterized by new lesions and accelerated growth despite local therapy, systemic therapy was initiated; clinical trial enrollment was identified as the preferred approach when available.

[...] And shortly thereafter, we were getting concerned about the kidney spot, that that could actually cause some kidney problems in the future. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic recurrence of adenoid cystic carcinoma with disease involving the left neck, lungs, and a liver lesion.

[ diagnosis ]: Intermediate-grade adenoid cystic carcinoma, initially diagnosed 4 years earlier, with subsequent metastatic recurrence.

[ histopathology results ]: Intermediate-grade adenoid cystic carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- After 3 years without evident disease following initial treatment, recurrent disease was identified in the left neck and lungs, with a possible liver lesion; lesions were described as subcentimeter at that time.  
- Repeat imaging 3 months later showed new pulmonary lesions and interval enlargement of a liver lesion to 6.1 cm.  
- During treatment on a clinical trial, pulmonary lesions decreased in size and liver lesions ceased growing initially.  
- Approximately 1 year after trial initiation, pulmonary lesions remained stable, while a dominant liver lesion enlarged from 6.1-6.5 cm to 8 cm.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial treatment consisted of surgery followed by radiation therapy.  
- She remained without evident cancer for 3 years after initial treatment.  
- Radiation to all recurrent sites was discussed at the time of metastatic recurrence, but this was not pursued.  
- She subsequently enrolled on a clinical trial of a targeted agent.  
- On trial therapy, she had a marked response in the lungs, with shrinkage of pulmonary metastases, and initial stabilization of liver disease.  
- After approximately 1 year on trial, isolated progression occurred in the liver while other disease sites remained stable.

[ current disease status ]: Oligoprogressive metastatic disease, with stable pulmonary metastases and isolated progression of a dominant liver lesion to 8 cm.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- She was described as very active and working full time at the time of metastatic recurrence.

reference_discussion.text: This one's a pretty quick case. And so this 53 year old lady with metastatic adenocystic carcinoma was diagnosed 4 years ago with intermediate grade. She was treated surgery, followed by radiation and had no cancer for 3 years. And then, unfortunately, the cancer came back in her left neck, her lungs, and actually kind of concerning for her liver. Couldn't say for sure. It was all quite small, below a centimeter, even hard to tell. She decided she was very active, works full time, didn't want radiation. We talked to her actually about treating with radiation to all the spots they saw. And unfortunately, 3 months later, there was new spots in the lungs. There was a liver spot that was now 6.1 centimeters, so very large. So, at that point, she enrolled onto a clinical trial of a targeted drug we had at our institution as well as other places. And she had a great response. Her lung spots all shrink. She was doing very, very well, and her liver spots stopped growing. And the issue is that about a year into this, Her lung spots, although stable, finally her liver started to grow, went from 6.1, 6.5 centimeters to up to 8 centimeters. And here's what a picture of that would look like. Here's before the clinical trial. and here is now a year later. And per the clinical trial, there's very tight rules. What you do under certain circumstances should have to come off the clinical trial. But now we're having the question, everything's stable except for this one liver lesion. So what do we do? And so throw this to you. If this was in your clinic, what would you do?

Yeah. You know, Again, with with 1 dominant lesion, so sometimes there's oligo metastases as we talked about. There's another concept that we're kind of or another scenario, which is oligo progression, which is patients that are benefiting. So, you know, whatever drug usually that they're on and then have 1 area that's causing problems. And so we do try to try to target that area. The liver is a hard area for what I do, radiation often, because you want to preserve the liver. For smaller lesions, we often think about SBRT. That's most common for gastrointestinal tumors, but we do sometimes do ablations and SBRT for adenoid cystic carcinoma as well. When lesions typically grow this size, we often consider other options because we can't do SBRT usually for lesions this size.
John, what's the size in a small like, what do you mean by small.

Yeah, it's usually, I mean, there's, it depends on the, to be honest, it depends on the normal liver. I mean, this, this, this, this is complicated because it's, it's away from, you know, it's kind of at the side of the liver, but it's also close to the stomach. And so it depends on the other organs that it's close to. Um, but usually once we start to, you know, 5 centimeters or larger in most locations is not really appropriate for SBRT. Even once, you know, in many locations when it's larger than about 3 centimeters, 3 to 5 centimeters, we really start kind of thinking about other options.
Thank you.

And in this case, as you were saying, was progressing in a single lesion. All the others were doing quite well. She wanted some time off therapy. And so we decided to treat this aggressively with radiation. There's actually a clinical trial that's available here regarding treatment of liver lesions, and so they treated it quite aggressively with different types of radiation in combination, which I won't go into because I don't presume to step on your toes there with all the types of radiation. But the result here was that she was able to handle that spot well, developed a result, no symptoms there, and had endotherapy for some time.

reference_conclusion: In the setting of oligoprogression with a single enlarging hepatic metastasis and otherwise stable systemic disease on targeted therapy, the consensus plan was to pursue aggressive local treatment to the liver lesion with radiation. This approach was selected in the context of an available clinical trial for liver lesions, using combined radiation modalities, with the goal of controlling the progressing site and permitting time off systemic therapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 57-year-old man; otherwise healthy.

[ chief complaint ]: Multiply recurrent sinonasal adenoid cystic carcinoma with severe facial/orbital pain, ectropion, and worsening diplopia; visual acuity in the affected eye had been preserved.

[ diagnosis ]: Multiply recurrent intermediate-grade adenoid cystic carcinoma of the left sinonasal/maxillary region with involvement of the left orbit, pterygoid skull base region, sphenoid sinus, infratemporal fossa, and nasopharyngeal bulging; prior isolated pulmonary metastasis had been resected in 2022.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 1999: Adenoid cystic carcinoma of the maxilla.  
- 2018 resection: R2 resection with positive margins along the orbital floor and pterygoid plates.  
- 2023 biopsy: Recurrent intermediate-grade adenoid cystic carcinoma.  
- Pathology over time had been described as possibly initially lower grade, subsequently read as intermediate grade.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- 2021 imaging showed soft tissue prominence in the posterior left nasal cavity at the pterygoid plate, masticator space, and orbit; this was observed.  
- MRI demonstrated recurrent tumor in the left orbit involving the rectus muscles and lacrimal gland, without intracranial extension.  
- MRI also demonstrated a second component at the pterygoid base extending into the sphenoid sinus and infratemporal fossa, with bulging into the nasopharynx.  
- Tumor involved the foramen rotundum below the skull base and encroached on the foramen ovale.  
- No overt intracranial extension or cavernous sinus extension was identified on imaging.  
- PET demonstrated a large hypermetabolic exophytic tumor at the nasal-maxillary junction.  
- PET showed no evidence of distant metastatic disease at the time of current evaluation.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Oncomine/targeted molecular profiling was negative for actionable alterations.  
- No NOTCH mutation was detected.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 1999: Infrastructure maxillectomy for maxillary adenoid cystic carcinoma followed by adjuvant neutron radiotherapy.  
- Approximately 2009: Revision surgery for recurrence at a second center.  
- 2018: Total maxillectomy without orbital exenteration with fibula free flap reconstruction for recurrence in the maxillectomy bed with orbital and masticator space extension; resection was R2 with positive margins at the orbital floor and pterygoid plates.  
- 2021: Imaging-detected soft tissue recurrence was observed.  
- 2022: Isolated lung metastasis underwent resection.  
- 2023: Hardware removal for hardware exposure and cutaneous deformity; radial forearm free flap reconstruction was performed. Residual skull base disease was not dissected.  
- 2023: Biopsy confirmed recurrent intermediate-grade adenoid cystic carcinoma.

[ current disease status ]:  
Locoregionally recurrent disease remained present in the left orbit and skull base/pterygoid region, with orbital muscle and lacrimal gland involvement, extension into the sphenoid sinus and infratemporal fossa, and involvement of the foramen rotundum with encroachment on the foramen ovale. No overt intracranial or cavernous sinus extension was identified. No distant metastatic disease was identified on current PET imaging. Symptoms included severe facial/orbital pain, ectropion, and worsening diplopia with preserved visual acuity.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Prior neutron radiotherapy records from 1999 were not available despite attempts to obtain the treatment profile.  
- Chronic opioid therapy had been used over more than a decade, with opioid dependence/addiction reported.  
- Possible infected mesh had been considered as a contributor to pain prior to hardware removal.

reference_discussion.text: Thanks for the opportunity. For discussion today, we have Mr. G, who is a 57-year-old gentleman, otherwise healthy, with a 26-year history of multiply recurrent adenoid cystic carcinoma of the sinonasal cavity. He's been treated at several centers across the United States. So to briefly recap, his journey started in 1999 when he developed an ACC of the maxilla. He underwent a infrastructure maxillectomy and adjuvant neutron therapy. He did well for about a decade until about 2009 when he presented to a second center and got revision surgery. The notes on that are a little bit sparse, but we do know well that he did well for about another decade until about 2018 when he developed a second recurrence in the maxilectomy bed with orbital and masticator space extension. He then went to his sort of third surgical team where he underwent a total maxillectomy without orbital exteneration and reconstructed with a fibula free flap reconstruction. This was an R2 resection with positive margins along both the orbital floor and pterygoid plates. The imaging done about 2 years later in 2021 showed that he had a soft tissue prominence in the posterior left nasal cavity at the pterygoid plate, masticator space, and orbit. This was observed. He later developed an isolated lung met and underwent a red trasection in 2022. In 2023, he developed some hardware exposure and a bit of a cutaneous deformity so that the hardware was removed. He had a second free flap, a radial forearm done at that time, but the residual disease in his skull vase was undissected. And then he finally had a biopsy done later that year by a rhinologist, which confirmed recurrent intermediate grade adenoid cystic carcinoma. So that brings us to kind of earlier this year, where he presented to us for really kind of a second opinion, and he's really just seeking further treatment options. He was really suffering from severe facial pain, ectropion, and worsening diplopia, though his visual acuity in that eye was preserved. I think the tumor is best captured with MR. So starting with the coronal, he's got a recurrent tumor in the left orbit that involves the rectus muscles and lacrimal gland without intracranial extension. There's a second component at the pterygoid base that extends into the sphenoid sinus and for temporal fossa, kind of bulges into nasal pharynx. The tumor involves the foramen rotundum below the skull base and kind of encroaches on ovale, but there's no, overt sort of intracranial or cavernous sinus extension. He's had a, we had a PET done as well, which sort of re-demonstrates this large hypermetabolic exophytic tumor at the nasal maxillary junction. Notably, though I don't show it here, there's no evidence of any distant or metastatic disease. So we thought this was a good time to bring it up to sort of turn it to the discussants. I guess we have a couple questions that we've prepared just to shape the conversation a little bit.

Chris, maybe to sort of facilitate discussion, can you bring up your imaging again? Sure. And then we'll turn it around to, we'll start with our... I just paused at a good spot. faculty members and then turn it to our senior discussants. Maybe we'll start with Dr. Levine, if that's okay, your thoughts on receptability and we'll go around the table.

Yeah, this is always, you know, an area that's gonna be a challenge because, you know, resectability at a rate cystic carcinoma is, you know, kind of variable, right? You know, there's great studies to show that, you know, gross total resection and getting decent margins is going to make a difference for you. And that even in some cases, close margins are still gonna have very similar prognosis. I think the the real challenge here is that. you don't know how much perineural invasion or skip lesions or other things you have. But in theory, this is still a resectable tumor, at least by what you can get access to. It hasn't gone completely into the skull base. It hasn't gotten into any of the areas that you really can't get to. But I do think that I would hesitate to say that you're gonna get a gross total resection on it just because of the nature of this disease.
Dr. Monteiro, your thoughts on resectability of this, and are we prepared to accept positive margins here?

Yeah, Chris, nice to see you, by the way, Chris. Nice to see you. Yeah, can you just show the stuff in the orbit again? It looks like the tumor in the orbit's probably gone in through the inforbital fissure. It's hard to tell. or where the inferior orbital fissure used to be. Is that just in the apex there?
Is there anything? I think it's all contiguous. It looks sort of like two separate masses, but I think they are kind of contiguous with each other.

So I mean, I guess the way I would, yeah, I agree with what Karina was saying. I mean, he's got incurable disease. He's already had metastatic disease to his lungs. So to me, this is all about how do we try and maintain him going, he's gone for almost 25 years now, and how do we maintain him going as long as possible with the least amount of morbidity possible? That's kind of how I think about this. because this is no longer a curable tumor. So anything we do here, regardless of whether it's surgery, radiation or chemotherapy, is all about controlling things for as long as possible. So that's kind of, I don't know what the conversation was that you framed with him, but I suspect the reason he's coming to you is because currently his quality of life is horrible because he's got a lot of pain. So really, at the end of the day, what he's probably looking for is treatment of his pain. And that can always be tricky because it's hard to know what's going to be causing his pain. I don't think, you can't get that orbital apex disease without taking out his eye, and if he's got a functioning eye and he's got incurable disease, I'd be reluctant to go down that road knowing that I'm probably not going to give him long-term disease control, as opposed to someone who has a non-functioning eye that's very, very painful. As we all know, that's a little bit of a different scenario. So for me, that orbital apex involvement is very hard to not only get out fully, but you can see it's funneling towards the apex. That's basically impossible to get out. And not only that, if he's got visible, good vision preserved, I'd be reluctant to do that. So for me, this is very difficult because the symptom I'd be wanting to treat is pain. and it's very hard to know how we would address that surgically. I agree with Karina, the lower stuff down is technically resectable. You're going to have positive margins for sure at foramen rotundum and those various other, in my opinion, even if they look normal radiologically. However, I sort of wonder whether the source of his pain is potentially coming from either branches of V2 or V3, which is not uncommon in these multiply recurrent tumors. So, I don't really have a great answer, Chris, because I think the treatment here is really to manage this guy's pain. And I don't know if you and Kyle have a better idea of where it's coming from, but that's the difficult part for me to know. And I wouldn't take out his eye at this stage unless it was non-functional or the eye itself was giving him a lot of pain.
Kyle, Dr. Vancouvering, this is probably your case. So what did we do here?

Yeah, so both great points from Dr. Levine and Dr. Montero. It's, you know, just even understanding this guy's disease history was like reading a novel. And fortunately, he was extremely well educated. And so there were so many complicating factors, prior neutron therapy, and what does that mean now, 25 years later, all of this pain that he was having, and I totally agree with you that You know, the infratemporal fossa and the pterygoid involvement was going to be tough surgically, but the apex and the orbit was really the crux of our discussion. And he had a lot of pretty severe pain. Part of it, I think, was an infected mesh that was there. He had severe atropion and was beginning to have more and more dysfunction with worsening diplopia. Although the acuity was intact, the orbital pain was starting to be debilitating for him. As we talked more, I realized there was some underlying opioid addiction or dependence that he has been dealing with for over a decade as all of his chronic treatments have included opioid therapy along the way. And it was really difficult to distinguish what was flap, what was tumor, what was infection, et cetera. So that's why we got the PET scan to kind of help delineate that to some degree. So we had a long conversation, multiple clinic visits, just like you said. And then, you know, I ultimately told him that I thought that if we entertained a definitive approach, this was the last shot at doing it. If we were going to entertain surgery, it would have to include an exenteration, infertemporal exenteration, nasal pharyngectomy. And at best, my plan or goal would be an R1 resection for this. But there is very compelling data, as Dr. Levine highlighted, that an R1 resection with adjuvant radiation has durable local disease control in the five to 10 year range, you know, looking at 75, 80%. And so basically what I told him to your point, Eric, is I'm, if we're going to do it, it's the goal is to try and buy you five to 10 years, but I don't know if you're going to have a metastatic focus pop up and I can't guarantee you won't have disease that progresses intracranially. Um, so that's where we started the conversation.

It's interesting, Kyle, as you said, like with the recent data, like I think it was a Sears study, right, which looked at sort of R1 resections in T4B tumors followed by postoperative radiation do better as opposed to upfront chemoradiation. So we're going to probably be having these conversations a lot more moving into the future. And I think both you and Corinne alluded to that. No, that was a good clarification. Cause you're right. Like if the pain is coming from the eye, then you, you know, that would potentially palliate him to some degree, but yeah, I agree. It's kind of his last shot. And, um, you know, what did your radiation oncologist think out of curiosity in terms of room for additional radiation?

So that was my, my first question, because that data is only valid if you can give definitive or fairly definitive doses of adjuvant radiation. And so we had a long discussion. We tried to track down the neutron treatment profile from 1999. Uh, but that was a futile effort, unfortunately. Uh, so this evolved fortunately over about a month and a half of discussion points, because it was a slow growing tumor. We had time to really work all this out. Um, but they said, you know, 25 years later, particularly if we were going to be putting a free flap into the, into the cavity to bring fresh vascularized tissue, they were willing to give him definitive. Radiation with protons, which is also another discussion point about what, what type of radiation you'd want to entertain here. And so, because that package, you know, the full package was available on the table with R1 and definitive protons at full dose, I thought it was reasonable to at least offer him definitive resection followed by adjuvant treatment.

I think the point is worth making here that Just for the fellows on the call, you know, neutron radiotherapy is something that has, to the best of my knowledge, largely fallen out of favor, but had its kind of time in the sun where some of the side effects were quite significant locally, and this is part of the reason why it's fallen out of favor. Feel free to correct me if I'm wrong. Any of the panelists on the call, but that would be a consideration here. The local toxicities further radiation, maybe to to the senior discussants. Any any argument to not proceed with surgery here? I think we have arguments in favor of an orbital exoneration, mainly for symptom palliation and possibly achieving an R1 resection may give him some local control. Dr. Wong and Dr. Wang, any thoughts on non-surgical approaches maybe? Do we have some alternate approaches we could offer here?

Well, I think you've done a great job of outlining, you know, discussing with him his goals of treatment. And, you know, you're trying to buy him some more time. He's not probably curable in the long, long term, but we know that adenocystic can be indolent. I would potentially explore some of the clinical trials out there. You could talk with your mental oncologist, see if there's any immunotherapy. I don't think they've had great results, but at least it might be another discussion to have if he were really against having surgery.

That's perfect. And I will add, he's, like I said, very well-educated and well-prepared in gnosis. He actually came asking that question. He had a trial or two that he had looked at that was actively recruiting. We talked with medical oncology about that as well. I'm happy to go into detail there.
Kyle, has there been a change in the pathology over time?
I think originally it may have been more of a low grade or primiform, but now it's being read as intermediate grade.

So, I mean, that's more consistent with the history, right? Whether you do the formal MD Anderson, ACC one and two, or you just look at the solid pattern of it versus not. But given his long drawn out course, I mean, 20 something years, I think that you make that assumption that it was actually low grade at first and it is getting more aggressive. So I would say that if he does anything besides pure palliation as Eric suggested, or maybe mesh removal if you really think the mesh is infected and causing some of the pain. But if you really are trying to manage that orbit, the likelihood is with this much disease along V2, that orbit with a transition in its pathology is likely not gonna be a very functional orbit for very long. Pain or no pain aside. So I think most centers, and I'm sure you guys did this, Kyle, you know, you would have gotten some sort of oncomine sort of panel on this to see if he has any targetable options. I'm sure you went, no?
We did, and it was negative.

Yeah. I mean, so I would say, and that's kind of the pattern with anoint cystic, right? And that's been the challenge with most of these trials is that in truth, we have very, very few targetables. If you lived in Italy or Japan, I guess you would think about carbon ion, but again, that would sacrifice the eye just in a different way than sacrificing the eye surgically. And it's unclear if that would actually result in any more or less pain. And I think the radiotoxicity to the frontal lobe, and to be truthful, the sparing of the contralateral eye becomes a little bit of an issue. Chris, if you could scroll back for me a little bit on that orbital apex on either side, doesn't really matter. posteriorly if you can. You're close. I mean, you're sort of knocking on the front door of the cavernous sinus, at least in my view of it. It's not invaded yet. But, you know, you really do. I mean, if you think about quality of life, preserving his right eye has some value too. I think I would probably either go complete palliation, like pain control palliation, which seems, you know, like a very reasonable option. I think that the trial options are pretty limited, or I think Kyle's making the right If you're going to make a surgical decision, it's the right decision. Free tissue transfer in there gives you some degree of protection. The neutrons are a long time ago. Most of, as I recall, John, most of the side effect profiles were pretty early, like in the first three to three years from neutrons. And I think the only place left in the United States that gives it is University of Washington. So I would probably have to admit, I probably would fall under Kyle's if I thought the orbital pain was the significant driver, because I do think in some ways this orbit is probably past the point of doing much, except for literally just palliating it.

Yeah, and just to add to the neutrons, again, correct me if I'm wrong, everybody, but I think there was like the 90s was a time when we thought neutrons was the secret to adenoid cystic carcinoma, right? But the data didn't, because it wasn't routinely used for other pathologies. It was really commonly used for adenoid cystic, but I think as more data's come about, it hasn't really shown. to be much beneficial. And I think, speaking to a colleague from Austria who does carbon ion, and again, I think carbon ion hasn't been particularly amazing for this disease either. I think it has been quite helpful for other challenging diseases that we face, like mucosal melanoma in particular has had some pretty decent results with carbon ion. But again, I could be wrong, but I don't think it's been particularly amazingly helpful for adenoid cystic when compared to other available usual radiation treatment options that we have.

So I think, Eric, there's a little bit of controversy in that. If you were to ask the Italian group, I know we're out of time for this case, but the Italian group has largely moved to carbon ion for almost every site on nasal adenoids as to carcinoma now. And it's really kind of their primary treatment algorithm as an ablative radiation source, you know, not adjuvant cleanup, but as an ablative source.
Yeah.

You know, I think that there's, It may be like neutrons too. I mean, it may, as you say, the data is still maturing. And we can see that the challenge here is that we really need long follow-up to really understand how these patients do. And that's a challenge of many sinonasal disorders, but this one in particular.

All right, just to sort of really quickly wrap up with this case, and Dr. Vancouvering alluded to this, because this is important, even though we're primarily a surgical group here. Kyle, can you quickly talk about mutations and your conversations with MedOnc? I will say that there are some mutations and targetable agents here. And I'm not a medical oncologist, but we know about MIB-NFIB fusions, notch mutations, and there's data around notched targetable agents. And of course, TKIs with lenbatinib. So what were your, just to wrap up, what were your conversations with medical oncology around potential targets?

Yeah, the short answer is we did not detect a notch mutation. And Our medical oncologist, you know, he basically said that of all the trials that are out there, fadenoid cystic, not any of them have really panned out very, uh, with, with a lot of positive results to date, you know, there's some tyrosine kinase inhibitors and some other trials that are ongoing. I talked to the patient about that option and frankly told him that it's very hit or miss. And he frankly wasn't willing to take the risk because his disease seems to be progressing a little more quickly now. And if we give him six months on a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, and now it's in cavernous sinus, the conversation changes a little bit, frankly. And so he actually, after a long discussion and talking about his oral pain, really wanted to move forward with surgery because the medical oncology landscape just did not seem very promising as a definitive option.

reference_conclusion: Given multiply recurrent sinonasal adenoid cystic carcinoma with debilitating orbital pain, progressive diplopia, and preserved visual acuity, the board supported offering definitive surgical resection as the final local treatment opportunity. The proposed operation would include orbital exenteration, infratemporal fossa resection, and nasopharyngectomy, with the goal of achieving an R1 resection, followed by full-dose adjuvant proton radiotherapy with free tissue transfer to facilitate reirradiation. Systemic therapy and clinical trial options were reviewed with medical oncology but were not favored as a definitive strategy, and the patient elected to proceed with surgery.

[...] they were willing to give him definitive. Radiation with protons [...] because that package, you know, the full package was available on the table with R1 and definitive protons at full dose, I thought it was reasonable to at least offer him definitive resection followed by adjuvant treatment. [...] he actually, after a long discussion and talking about his oral pain, really wanted to move forward with surgery because the medical oncology landscape just did not seem very promising as a definitive option.
