case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 31-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Left temporomandibular joint region swelling for approximately 11 months, with associated jaw pain, xerostomia, and oral fullness. No upper aerodigestive tract symptoms were reported.

[ diagnosis ]: Left TMJ lesion with preliminary pathologic diagnosis of calcified chondromesenchymal neoplasm.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsies were non-diagnostic. Subsequent biopsy demonstrated features less concerning for malignancy, with no atypia, no mitotic activity, and no necrosis. Preliminary diagnosis was calcified chondromesenchymal neoplasm.

[ imaging findings ]: CT and MRI demonstrated a soft tissue lesion surrounding the left TMJ capsule with skull base involvement extending into the floor of the middle cranial fossa. MRI showed enhancement within the joint space with encroachment on the middle cranial fossa and sparing of the dura. Axial imaging showed the lesion in close proximity to the horizontal petrous internal carotid artery. Imaging also demonstrated extension into the parotid region.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Fusion profiling was referenced for this tumor type, but no specific molecular alteration was documented.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient initially underwent multiple non-diagnostic biopsies.

[ current disease status ]: Left TMJ calcified chondromesenchymal neoplasm with extradural extension to the floor of the middle cranial fossa and into the parotid region, in close proximity to the horizontal petrous internal carotid artery.

[ other clinical data ]: The lesion was described radiographically as extradural at the middle cranial fossa floor. The disease had progressed between imaging and the planned operation.

reference_discussion.text: So the case I'm presenting is more so a school-based case. and hopefully a lot of interesting discussion points to highlight here. So it's a 31-year-old male who presents with a left TMJ lesion. Diagnosis preliminary is a calcified chondromysclimal neoplasm. Essentially noticed swelling over the TMJ area for about 11 months. Initially had a few non-diagnostic biopsies, only had some associated jaw pain, xerostomia, and oral fullness, and otherwise no upper air digest tract symptoms. Imaging, which I'll show in a second, showed a lesion in the TMJ involving the middle cranial fossa floor. And there was initially concern for possible sarcoma prompting further biopsy, which clarified the diagnosis. So I'll show you the imaging here. So you can see this soft tissue lesion surrounding the TMJ capsule. And on the coronal, You can more clearly see its skull base involvement extending into the middle cranial fossa floor on this image. And on the patient's MRI, you can see the similar lesion enhancing the joint space there, encroaching on the middle cranial fossa, but sparing the dura. And then in the axial imaging, you can see that it gets very close to the petrous horizontal internal carotid arteries here. And so before moving on to the discussion part, I just want to highlight that the initial biopsy came back with some features less concerning for malignancy with no atypia, no mitotic activity or necrosis, and the preliminary diagnosis as discussed was a calcified chondromedial mesenchymal neoplasm. In terms of discussion, I had a few points to highlight here and then I can move on to the rest of the case if there's no further points, but essentially, are there any additional concerns about the preliminary pathologic diagnosis given the extent of the lesion? Would anyone consider any radiation in the role of management of this lesion? And then since we're talking about surgical approaches for treatment, would anyone have any recommendations for any approaches that would achieve an on block resection? And then additionally, given the location of lesion and function, Any considerations for reconstruction?

OK, Michael, let's let's break there and maybe get some input from our. from our faculty members. Maybe let's start with Dr. Vancouvering, if that's okay. Obviously not your run-of-the-mill skull-based tumor, just a very weird and wonderful.
We see like 20 of these a year. I don't know, what are you guys doing in Canada?

You guys are the highest volume center in the world for this, for sure. Yeah, definitely. So this is a benign sort of locally aggressive pathology, obviously with resectability issues on imaging. Let's say you are going to offer this patient surgery. How are you going to? How are you thinking of approaching this co?

Yeah, great point. And maybe can you pull up the axials down into the window there? And so for me, this would obviously be an open approach where I would do a preauricular and extend that into at least a hemicoronal, if not a full coronal. uh, incision, depending on some of your cosmetic preferences on how you'd like to make that incision and bring that down. Uh, it looks like it's going well into the parotid as well. And so you probably are going to need to dissect the facial nerve in order to help deliver this tumor and get the TMJ, uh, exposed through a pre-auricular route. Uh, so sort of defining that frontal branch and the upper division of the, of the facial nerve may be needed here. Um, so I would probably extend that into some degree of a modified Blair incision, to get the exposure. And then, uh, you know, in a combined fashion with neurosurgery, this is going to involve a sub-temporal craniotomy to try and get around this tumor on block from above and below. And you'll have to take a cut across the, the, uh, the condyle, uh, or, or through the ramus, perhaps even, I can't remember how far down the TMJ it goes there on the coronal. Once you have that mobilized, the deep dissection is really the hard part where the, where the, where the carotid comes into play. And so it's really a slow dissection, probably working over top of the tumor to get to the petrous segment at the floor of the middle fossa, trying to peel dura the whole way. That's a tough dissection, no doubt about it. But that would be the approach I would probably take.
Dr. Montero, can we get this out on block, you think, in one piece?

You're going to try, but I think you probably can, John. It's going to be a little bit challenging, but I think you can. I agree with Kyle that that's how I would approach it as well. This wasn't my case, but I think a hemi-coronal probably would be enough here. Sometimes you have to extend a little bit over just to get enough mobility of the skin flap. Neurosurgery could go from above to sort of clear the middle cranial fossa floor. It looks all extradural on the imaging. Yeah, I agree with Kyle. It looks like it's quite a lot into the parotid gland, so I would dissect out the facial nerve and particularly just mobilize the upper branch because it'll all be deep to those upper branches. I think some of the zygoma has to go anteriorly as well and then the carotid could probably be approached through the neurosurgical approach of the middle cranial fossa four because that will give you some exposure to the petrous carotid and then similar to what Kyle said you can also approach the cervical and parapharyngeal carotid through the neck just to kind of protect that. So I agree with what he said and I think you know, an on block resection is going to be doable. Positive margins might be risky for microscopic positive margins, depending on how close it is to the facial nerve on the deep side of the facial nerve. So I'm not sure what you encountered, John, when you did the case, but I suspect it'll be a little close there.

And maybe from our senior discussants or Karina, any other approaches other than what Dr. Vancouver suggested, preauricular to a hemichronal or full coronal? Are there any other approaches to get to this?
It would not go endoscopically.

I agree. I think the concerns are definitely the carotid and the facial nerve. And I think that approach is probably the best and the safest so you can identify those structures and try to preserve them. I would be concerned a little bit about pathology. It's not a common tumor that we see a lot and it wouldn't hurt to maybe send it out for another opinion just to make sure it's not another rare type of mesenchymal tumor because you'll, or it could be sent out, you know, after the tumor is out, that might actually be more helpful when they have a lot of tissue to look at.

Yeah, that's generally what happens, Marlene. I think John can speak to it because I think it was his case, but we, all the sort of starcoma type lesions basically get regionalized to one center that both John and I work at just because the pathologists have basically been regionalized for our entire province to the one center. So I can't remember whether the initial biopsy, John, was read at Sinai or whether it was the post-op, but that's exactly right. The pathologist will often just reflexively send it to the sarcoma center for the reasons that you spoke about. It's just that these can be really challenging. And sometimes, you know, even after the post-op and they have a lot of tissue, they always can't properly characterize these things 100% either, right? They'll sometimes hedge on what they think it is.
Yeah, these rare pathologies are tough, but your radiation oncologist is going to want to know. They're very reluctant to radiate anything that's benign.

Dr. Delmeda, I think this tumor has some fusion profile that I can't quite remember, growth factor something or other. Oh, yeah. OK, there we go at the bottom there. I have no idea, to be honest with you. Is that amenable to any targeted therapies?

Yeah, that was a good question. We actually had one of our sarcoma med-oncs enter into the discussion before we proceeded with surgery, which we did. This is amenable on clinical trial to what are called CSF inhibitors or colony stimulating factor inhibitors. There's some data on that in the clinical trial space. These tumors are actually probably seen a lot more by oral maxillofacial surgeons. And so it's probably not in the average sort of skull-based surgeons' wheelhouse. It's kind of rare, but they're not as rare, I think, for maxillofacial surgeons. And the data generally supports, you know, why local resection where possible, and where concerning margins, there is a role for radiation treatment to minimize the risk of local recurrence, particularly in areas where it's close to unresectable structures. So that's kind of where the general thinking is with this approach. Maybe we'll switch over to Eric Wong. Your thoughts, I know you have an interest in reconstructive surgery. Do we need to reconstruct this? What do you think? How would you approach this and what would be your considerations here?

I think I would in a 31 year old. He's obviously have significant shortening of his ramus, I mean, it's almost. Yeah, that's a beautiful cut. Thank you, Michael. I mean that you're going to have, you're going to shorten his ramus by three or four centimeters. So it seems like he will have long-term dysfunction of his jaw, of his mandible, excuse me, if there's not a reconstructive option. You know, it looks like it's going to be extradural, but, you know, that's going to be close as you go through it. It's going to need sort of almost a patrosal approach as they come down from above. And then obviously there's the, so then there's going to be that portion of the temporalis that you're going to sacrifice as it attaches all of the muscles of mastication to that space. You're going to have a pretty large dead space. So John, you are definitely a better reconstructive surgeon than I, but I would guess that you're going to try to do something to restore some of that height, even maybe with one of those TMJ prosthesis that oral surgery sometimes uses for very recalcitrant situations. I guess the question is whether you do it at the same time as your resection or if you go back and do it later. I'm guessing it'd probably be best because you're going to come from above and below and it's really quite an impressive approach you'd have to take for it. I was trying to contemplate if there was any way um, to not have to do a, uh, you know, a full, um, hemichrono to a Blair like incision, but it just feels like the product has to be dissected to get this clear. So, um, I don't know that there's another option at first. I was trying to contemplate if you could get, you know, if you just pop up, Eric mentioned, you're going to have to take probably the, um, zygomatic arch, if that would allow you to rotate enough out that you could make an inferior incision, like, through a cervical approach, and then deliver it without the prodded, but it sure seems like the prodded is directly involved with this. Is that accurate, John?

Yeah, yeah, yeah, it definitely was, and that's kind of how we approached it. Michael will kind of wrap up the case in a second, but I want to just address one other issue, and maybe with Dr. Wang, Marilyn, your thoughts. This is very close, as you can see, on the CT to the carotid. What are your approaches here? How do you prepare for, you know, for potential carotid injury? Are there any things you do in terms of investigations, either preoperatively or or considerations intraoperatively for carotid management.

Yeah, there's things to consider. He's a young person, so you do worry that he doesn't have a lot of collateral if you do injure the left carotid. But you certainly could do an angiogram, you could do a carotid balloon occlusion in advance just to see if it were necessary. I don't think it would be, but it certainly wouldn't hurt to do an angiogram and see what the circulation looks like.

And intraoperatively, let's say you get into it at the petrous carotid, which is where it's very close. What are the options here if we injure the carotid intraoperatively? We're very close to the horizontal petrous carotid, taking the tumor out.

Yeah, I think you have to be prepared for that to harvest some muscle, some kind of a graft to put there. Fortunately, with an open approach, you have a little bit more access. I think you can plug it, so to speak, a little easier than endoscopically. And then, of course, he would need an angiopost-op just to make sure there wasn't any embolus or a clot there.

I agree with Marilyn. I mean, you definitely need to get immediate control, probably through directed packing. And then subsequently, Angiography is going to be the answer because actually I think in most 31-year-olds, they tend to have pretty reasonable collateral. Certainly pediatric patients have really great collaterals. So they can sometimes tolerate quite well the sacrifice. John, did you consider like reflecting the temporalis down and then actually drilling the floor anteriorly to give you even more access with, like in this cut that we see here?
Yeah. Yeah. So, um, maybe Michael, why don't you pick, pick the, show the pictures of what we actually did.
We did follow the temporal fossa, right. And actually remove some of that to give you more access to the anterior portion of the Petrus.

That's right. Yeah, we did. I mean, we did essentially neurosurgery came in to do a, uh, teratonal crania. And as Kyle mentioned, uh, we, he needed a sub-temporal sort of craniotomy, uh, to get rid of the disease that was extradural. So Michael, why don't, why don't you show kind of how we managed it?

Sure, yeah, I'll highlight some of the points I've mentioned. So the hemichronal blare and then the neck dissection incision. This is the final resection. We have basically a total parotidectomy. We mobilize the facial nerve and we did a transparotid approach into the TMJ. The toronial approach, subcranial craniectomy as shown here. And then we did take essentially the posterior part of the mandible, just a vertical osteotomy through the sigmoid notch down. And some of the other points that I wanted to highlight was obviously occlusion is important in this case and MMF we performed with rapid arch bars, which you can see here. And one of the learning points we had was you can't mobilize the TMJ when the patient's in MMF. you have to take the patient out of MMF to do your cuts, remove the tumor, and then go back to MMF for your reconstruction. And I think Dr. Montero mentioned taking out part of the ligoma, so we did also take out a segment of the lateral ligoma for access from a neurosurgery perspective. And then we, in terms of managing the infernal carotid artery, followed it from the neck through the peripheral space up to the skull base for not only control during a resection, but as we mentioned, in case there's any concern about injuring it at the petrous intracranial portion. And in terms of reconstruction, we performed a chimeric scapula tip myogenous latissimus dorsi free flap. So you can see the scapula tip here sitting, reconstructing TMJ with the tip into the TMJ fossa, and then the latissimus dorsi was used to cover. We had a free bone graft to reconstruct the zygoma. We mentioned and discussed previously about these custom TMJ prostheses, which you can actually modify them so that they don't need to sit specifically in the glenoid fossa, but you can actually butt them against, for example, the zygoma, as well as the cranium itself. But the concern was, given that medial margin and potential need for radiation afterwards, we want to reduce the risk of any hardware complications associated in that region. So that's why we chose to go for a free flat reconstruction. And just to end the case, I can show you the post-op imaging here, which shows some of the structures that we've reconstructed. So you can see here that that's the zygoma free bone graft. As we go down, we can see the scapula tip on the posterior mandible there.
So John, it looks like you just brought the scapula a little bit forward so that it's sitting below floating below the middle cranial fossa floor that wasn't resected. Is that right?

Yeah, that's right. We buttressed it against some residual sphenoid bone. There is a thought around doing a custom TMJ prosthesis, but the concern there, obviously, in patients who, if they do get radiated, you know, that we'll see a hardware complication, almost like that first case that we saw. And there really is still a possibility of coming in secondarily down the road and putting in a secondary TMJ implant. The other thing in our center, custom TMJ prostheses take three months to develop or to get them manufactured. And this was progressing. In fact, it progressed from imaging to surgery. And so that's a consideration as well. But when you put the patient in MMF for a period of four to six weeks, you almost let them create a pseudoarthrosis there and they kind of scar into place and their occlusion actually prevents migration of the scapula into the middle fossa because their bite prevents that scapula from actually pushing intracranial. So that was kind of the thought around that. So maybe in the interest of time, we'll move to the last case. Nadine and Dr. Levine, please take it away. Yes.

reference_conclusion: Tumor board consensus favored primary surgical management with attempted en bloc resection via an open preauricular to hemicoronal/Blair-type transparotid approach combined with neurosurgical subtemporal craniotomy/craniectomy to clear the extradural middle cranial fossa component, with facial nerve mobilization and carotid control from the neck to the skull base. Reconstruction was planned with vascularized free flap restoration of mandibular/TMJ height and soft-tissue obliteration of the defect; a custom TMJ prosthesis was deferred because of disease progression and concern for hardware complications if postoperative radiation were required. Additional pathology review at a sarcoma center was considered appropriate given the rarity of the mesenchymal neoplasm, and adjuvant radiation was recognized as a consideration in the setting of concerning or close margins near unresectable structures to reduce local recurrence risk.

[...] it wouldn't hurt to maybe send it out for another opinion just to make sure it's not another rare type of mesenchymal tumor [...] The data generally supports, you know, why local resection where possible, and where concerning margins, there is a role for radiation treatment to minimize the risk of local recurrence, particularly in areas where it's close to unresectable structures. [...] We have basically a total parotidectomy. We mobilize the facial nerve and we did a transparotid approach into the TMJ. The toronial approach, subcranial craniectomy as shown here. [...] in terms of managing the infernal carotid artery, followed it from the neck through the peripheral space up to the skull base for not only control during a resection [...] in terms of reconstruction, we performed a chimeric scapula tip myogenous latissimus dorsi free flap. [...] the concern was, given that medial margin and potential need for radiation afterwards, we want to reduce the risk of any hardware complications associated in that region. So that's why we chose to go for a free flat reconstruction.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive left nasal obstruction with rhinorrhea and hyposmia for 5-6 months, with associated dizziness, headache, and diplopia.

[ diagnosis ]: Olfactory neuroblastoma (esthesioneuroblastoma) of the left sinonasal cavity with skull base invasion, intracranial extension, meningeal/dural enhancement, and cervical nodal metastasis. Staged as Kadish D. Neck disease was identified on CT neck as a positive left cervical lymph node.

[ histopathology results ]: Intraoperative biopsy with frozen section demonstrated a malignant neoplasm suggestive of carcinoma. Final pathology was olfactory neuroblastoma, Hyams grade 3. Pathology demonstrated pseudorosettes.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI demonstrated a large mass in the left nasal cavity obstructing nearly all left-sided sinuses, with intracranial extension and abutment of the left orbit. CT demonstrated no invasion of the medial orbital wall, with chronic bony changes involving the sphenoid, clivus, and ethmoid roof. CT neck demonstrated a positive lymph node on the left. DOTATATE PET demonstrated tumor involvement in the primary site and neck.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Past surgical history included prior nasal polypectomy performed outside the United States and prior tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy. Office biopsy was not performed because of marked lesion vascularity and patient anxiety. The patient underwent intraoperative biopsy.

[ current disease status ]: Hyams grade 3 olfactory neuroblastoma of the left sinonasal cavity with skull base invasion and intracranial extension, and a positive left cervical lymph node, staged as Kadish D.

[ other clinical data ]: On examination, there was no neurologic deficit and cranial nerves were intact. Nasal endoscopy demonstrated a highly vascular, pulsatile mass filling the left nasal cavity, extending beyond the middle turbinate without reaching the nasal floor or nasopharynx, with surrounding watery polyps. Fibrous dysplasia of the skull base was present.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, so hello everyone. We'll be presenting our case for today. This is a 68-year-old patient who presented to our clinic with an MRI finding of a large sinonasal mass. I'll be showing his MRI shortly. His symptoms were a five to six month duration of a progressive left nasal obstruction with rhinorrhea and hyposmia, along with dizziness, headache and diplopia. Previous past medical history that is a bit related to us is he had a nasal polypectomy outside the US and a tonsil and adenoidectomy. On exam, he had no neurologic deficit and his cranial nerves were intact. On scope exam, he had a highly vascular pulsatile nasal mass that was filling the left nasal cavity. However, this mass was extending beyond the middle turbinate but not reaching the nasal floor nor the nasopharynx. And he had surrounding that watery polyps. This is his MRI. So as you can see, he has this large mass in the left nasal cavity obstructing almost all of his left sinuses with intracranial extension as well, and abutting the left orbit as well. This is his CT scan. to assess for any further bone involvement. His medial orbital wall did not look invaded, but he had some chronic bone changes, mostly in the sphenoid and in the clivus, and the roof of the ethmoid as well. We needed to get tissue biopsy to get further assessment of what this patient was presenting to our clinic with, but given the vascularity of the lesion that was on our exam and the anxiety of the patient, we were unable to have the biopsy in a clinic setting. And we could not also ask for a PET scan early on because the insurance company refused to get clearances before a biopsy proven malignancy, which was highly suspected on those imaging findings. So we ended up taking the patient for an intra-op biopsy and on frozen section, the patient had a malignant neoplasm that was suggestive of carcinoma. Thinking of what could be part of our differential diagnosis for malignant nasal mass, these can be a long list, but if we want to name some of them, we have the neuroendocrine tumors, the pituitary adenomas, melanomas, lymphomas, SCC, snot, rhabdomyosarcomas, or even Ewing sarcomas. And if we want to compare neuroendocrine tumors to olfactory neuroblastomas, usually, astesial neuroblastomas, they have a less aggressive clinical course compared to the neuroendocrine tumors. So the pathology of our frozen section ended up being indeed an olfactory neuroblastoma, and it was read as a grade three on HIAMS. Basically, the high M grading system is what will be categorizing the pathology or the histopathology of these tumors based on their architecture of the cells that they have, and this will further give us information on the prognosis with higher grades. meaning that the patient will likely have or present with metastasis, mostly in the neck, and will have a worse survivor rate. These are our own patients' pathological slides. These were provided by our pathology department, in which you can see some of the clinical findings that points out to the olfactory neuroblastoma with the grade three, and some of the key points or key cellular structures related to the diagnosis of the olfactory neuroblastoma. We have specific pseudorosette in him as well. So my question for the panel are the following. What would you order for additional imaging for a patient that presents with such a scenario to your clinic? What are some of the referrals you might consider? And if his neck is negative, what would you actually do with the treatment of the neck?

OK, maybe that's a good opportunity to stop and focus on some of these questions that you've posed here. Dr. Montero, maybe your thoughts on, let's just focus, let's focus on maybe the neck for now. He or she is N0, I believe, Nadine, is that right on imaging?
So this is my initial question. Would you ask for imaging for the neck to start with?

OK, let's say the imaging is done and it's negative. Eric, what are you doing for the neck? Himes 3 or high grade Himes? Are you doing an elective neck dissection? Are you? observing the neck or elective neck irradiation? What are you thinking for this patient?

Sorry, right now I'm just trying to deal with my post-viral cough, which I think is becoming more functional in nature than actually pathologic. But yeah, so that's a good question, Nadine, and it's a topic of controversy, as many will talk about how to manage the neck. Generally, so generally we would not operate on an N0 neck in the setting of anesthesia neuroblastoma. I don't know how my esteemed panelists, whether they would agree with that, but generally we would not approach that with primary surgery. However, where it's controversial is the radiation side of things and whether you give elective neck radiation to patients with Ends your neck disease. There's been lots of studies on this. And, you know, in our study actually Himes grade was not predictive of neck metastases. John can speak to this as well, but we did a study where there's actually comparable rates of neck failure in low grade and versus high grade hymes. So we're not sure whether that's necessarily true. However, other things can predict regional failure. I think out of the Pittsburgh group, Eric can correct me if I'm wrong, but when you look at something like dural invasion, for example, is actually quite predictable of neck neck failure as opposed to Heim's grade. So, our radiation doctors sometimes do treat the neck electively as part of management, about 20 to 25% of patients will fail on the neck over time generally I think was most of the studies have shown. And actually, the neck has also been shown to be relatively salvageable surgically. And when you add postoperative radiation to a previously non radiated neck in the salvage setting that can show some decent control options. Long answer is that we don't tend to treat the neck electively in these scenarios. However, the neck is often treated to some degree, whether that's microscopic radiotherapy, dosages of 50 gray or more, kind of is dependent on our radiation doctors. But I do tell patients that they do have about a 20 to 25% chance over time of failing regionally.
Kyle, are you guys, how are you guys addressing the neck at Ohio State?

Yeah, great question. I think Eric brought up a lot of key points. And like he said, there's been some several retrospective analyses that have looked at nodal failure rates. And like he said, for K-B and especially K-C disease, which this is, the risk of nodal disease or nodal failure is significantly higher. And so for us at Ohio State, we would routinely treat the neck with elective nodal radiation. And that allows us to include level one as well as the retropharyngeal basin. which is tough for the patients. Um, but that, that can be pretty comprehensive there.

Yeah. In Toronto, we, we electively treat high grade tumors, bilateral level two, three, actually, and RP nodes. Um, the, uh, um, we don't treat electively level one, Eric, to your point about regional failure, there's actually a lot of data with elective nodal irradiation that the regional failure rate is very low. In fact, in the Michigan series, and I think MD Anderson series with elective nodal radiation close to zero, that 20 to 30 percent is when you don't treat the neck. In fact, yeah, we did a neck dissection recently on a a low Himes grade patient who recurred isolated level two in the neck. Marilyn, your thoughts on neck management? Is anyone doing neck dissections here?

Not for clinically negative neck. You know, I agree with what's been said that because of the risk, especially in this patient with the intracranial extension, I would, well, my radiation oncologist would radiate the neck because you can't really access this retropharyngeal nose real well. With elective neck dissection, you can't really argue to do an elective neck dissection when there's no clinical or radiographic evidence of disease. So, you know, I think after the surgery, they would see our radiation oncologist who would very likely recommend post-op radiation, including the neck.

Yeah, sorry, John, I should have clarified that before, but yeah, I meant that 20 to 25% is exactly why most of our adults give it, right? Because I think our data shows it's less than, we've had less than 5% failures with elective neck radiation, right? Which I think is similar to the Michigan data. I don't know if it's 0%, but I remember something between less than six or 7% sort of the data, but I could be wrong.

And Dr. Levine, let's say this is a 20 year old patient with a, a Hymes I with the same volume of disease on imaging, so a low Hymes grade, asthesio-neuroblastoma. What are you thinking at your institution in terms of managing the neck or not managing the neck?

Yeah, that's a great question. You know, we, I think one of the great advantages is to kind of go through that at tumor board and we'll often, you know, have that discussion. You know, this is a young person then who has a high volume of disease and a long life in front of them. And I think they really also need to be part of that discussion. We know that neck recurrence is one of the most likely areas and that can be very delayed in this pathology. So we do really want to make sure that they understand that if we decide not to do the neck, there's a possibility that this is going to be the recurrence. I did have a significantly younger person, I want to say 16 or 18, that had an anesthesio-neuroblastoma with a clinically negative neck. And after talking with the patient as well as the family and our radiation oncologist and looking at the intracranial extension, we did actually decide to do treatment to the neck as well. that was very much a discussion that they were involved with. But I do think that that ends up being a much more kind of personalized decision and also a little bit focused on what kind of the risk tolerance level is of the patient and the family.

I think for the fellows, it's important that, you know, in young patients, these bilateral neck irradiation doesn't come without side effects. And salvage rates on recurrent neck disease anesthesia are not small. What I mean by that is you probably have a 70 to 80% likelihood of salvaging a nodal recurrence. So that should definitely be a point of discussion. If they recur, it's not like those are going to be catastrophic recurrences necessarily. They're very salvageable typically. So maybe Nadine, take us through what you guys did here.

So we did order imaging of the neck. We ordered a CT scan of the neck that showed a positive lymph node on the left. And we asked for also referrers to have the neck and neurosurgery for the extent of the disease in the neck and through the skull base. As for additional imaging, we also asked for a DOTATATE PET. And I want to talk a bit about this studying specifically because Esthesia neuroblastomas are known to express somatostatin, and the DOTADATE PET scan is a somatostatin receptor-targeted PET. It has multiple advantages over the regular FTG PET CT. Mostly it has better resolution and accuracy. We have less radiation dose on the patient. It costs less and it's much more comfortable for the patient. Most of the time it's used when the tumor is difficult to visualize, when we have extension through the brain or through the skull. skull base, and with the regular FTG PET scan, usually with Estesio, these have low metabolic activity, so the PET scan might be falsely negative. So many authors now are recommending the Delta Tate PET scan to detect lymph node metastases rather than the regular FTG PET scan. So as all the panelists have been discussing with the N0 or the N1 neck, we all agree that with the N1 neck, the patient will undergo a neck dissection. Most of the literature also recommends radiotherapy after that, plus or minus chemotherapy, which I'll be asking you about that in a few minutes. And with the N0 neck, the literature also is being geared into going with the prophylactic radiotherapy to the neck, given the high rate of regional failures in patients who do not receive this elective neck radiation, even in those Kaddish stage B or C tumors. So this is the DOTATATE PET scan of the patient. You can see the tumor involvement in here, and this is his neck scan. Next would be how would we stage our tumor and we have multiple staging system. The most common one is the Kaddish versus the Dolgorov stage. We are mostly familiar with those stages. the Kaddish is less detailed about where the tumor actually invades versus the other staging system, which is the Dilgarov, it goes more into details of what which entity is the tumor is invading. This will also help us if we follow one of those stages, let it be the Dulgerov, to know what approach the surgery should be or the surgeon should follow and it will correlate with further assessment of this tumor based on the involvement of either the crib reform, the orbit, or the dura, which will eventually play a role in the risk of recurrence and the death over time. Versus with the Kaddish, mostly like the Kaddish stage C, will have all of the tumors grouped in a single entity, regardless of which structures they are invading.
This is an interesting study. For the sake of time, I think we can skip forward since we're a little slow for where we are to talking a little bit about the risk action.

Okay, so this is in summary our tumor. It's a tumor that is invading the skull base. It has intracranial extension with meningeal enhancement at the positive neck. It is staged as a Kaddish D and a high M3 on pathology. So what would be your approach for surgery for this patient?
Maybe Nadine, why don't you show us what you guys did and then we can get some feedback from the panelists.

Okay, so what we ended up doing is a combined approach with neurosurgery going from above and below at the same time. This is our endoscopic view working on the ethmoid and this is the above the view. We ended up just like we would treat with any craniofacial approach following the tumor opening up the maxillary sinuses, the sphenoid, clearing it from different areas to get better access and to control the bleeding. So this is our endoscopic approach. This is the repair that was eventually done with the alloderm being sutured to the dura. And this is the immediate post-op CT showing the resection and the repair. These secretions are from the packing that were placed in the nose.
Can you just clarify, did you guys go from above with the craniotomy or everything entirely from below?
So this is the above procedure. So a craniotomy was done at the same time as the tumor from the endoscopic approach.

Okay, maybe pull up your images and we'll get some feedback from the group. Dr. Wong from UPMC. Eric, your thoughts on combined craniofacial resection with endoscopic assist versus strictly endo approach here?

So, I mean, I think actually in our team, we probably would have done this purely endoscopic, but in truth, I don't know that it matters as long as you get an R0 resection from a margin standpoint. If your team is more comfortable using a craniotomy to achieve that, I think it's... It doesn't, it doesn't matter. I mean our team we probably would have done this because it's behind enough. It's behind the frontal enough it certainly has a reasonable lateral extension, but I think it's well within the reach of the midplane in the orbit. So we probably would have done this and the nasal. I will say though, I probably, these surgeries are pretty long. So in my hands, I probably would have done the neck dissection actually on stage one. And I like to do the neck first because I don't really love re-intubating my fresh, you know, open craniofacial resection or endoscopic craniofacial resection with the re-intubation of the neck. So I tend to do the neck first, because I think it's a pretty straightforward operation. At least the node that you show, Nadine, was pretty significant in size. So I would have at least done the left neck first, and then probably done an endoscopic craniofacial resection for clearance.
Marilyn, your thoughts on when to do a craniotomy versus, indications for a craniotomy versus endoscopic approach.
Yeah, Corrina, how did you reconstruct the defect? Did you use a paracranoflap or a nasoceptal flap? Because that is one of the things we think about in deciding on the approach.

There was no nasoceptal flap that was going to be available because of the involvement with the sphenoid and the extension. We knew we wouldn't have one. And the, you know, I think one of the things that is an advantage here that you don't get to see is that for us, when we talk to the patient and I took him for an intraoperative biopsy, I said, well, if we know that it's something that we expect to be resectable, I can debulk some of it at the time. So when you can breathe into our second stage surgery will be much faster. So I think Eric's point is excellent. And for us, this was about half the size of what you see by the time that we went to do the second stage where we did it from above and below. And then we actually did the neck all in the same day. And because we do above and below at the same time, we actually work simultaneously. that saves us a lot of time to do it that way. But I think that's part of the reason is that we knew we wouldn't have a nasal septal flap. This is an older gentleman. And so this was a pericranial flap that we used.

Yeah, I think that would definitely weigh into the decision. I think that the tumor itself looks accessible and resectable from below. But if there's a concern about reconstruction, it's good to have that option of coming from above so you can do the pericranial flap.

Karina, correct me if I'm wrong, I imagine you guys chose to go from above because of that dural enhancement that goes almost to about the pupil on the left-hand side. Was that, because to me, you kind of scrolled over, it looks like the dural enhancement goes about to the level of the pupil, but maybe I'm just right there, a little bit back. So is that kind of what tipped your neurosurgeons? Because that's hard to get endoscopically if it really does go towards the pupil and beyond.

Yes, and I think that, you know, our concern was that we wanted to make sure that we got good margins on him we definitely wanted to get a good reception. And we were worried that, you know, if we were there and struggling and then we had to stage it versus doing it all at once. We really felt that then we got a better reconstruction, we got a better opportunity to get the really good resection for him, and then to make sure that we can really get him to radiation. You know, sometimes we will do this at Miami with just an allergy reconstruction and no, you know, vascularized covering there. But if we're going to try to get him as an older person to radiation quickly, and we knew that we would want to do that, this was, I thought, just a better option for him in general.

And then I guess a quick second question is the fibrosius appearing bone throughout the entire skull base. Did you biopsy that just to confirm that that was a separate fibrosius lesion or how did you manage that?

Yeah. So we, um, he definitely has a whole bunch of, um, fibrous dysplasia. And so a lot of it does come back as fibrous dysplasia, but we also then had to drill quite a bit of that bone, um, to get kind of all the stuff that was in the nooks and crannies, which, um, was less than pleasant.
OK, Kyle, final word. Combined crani endo versus endo alone and reconstructive options at Ohio State.

Yeah, great question. I think if you go through that MRI, the one thing that kind of leans me slightly towards the combined approach in addition to the reconstructive ability, because you're going to need a pair of cranium either way. is that the tumor has a fairly narrow waste right there that you're kind of working through, and then it kind of mushrooms out. So you're going to be fighting with that right frontal lobe quite a bit endoscopically, and you're going to be able to manage that perhaps a little bit better in an open approach, and then the extension up over the orbit on that left side. So, you know, we might start endoscopically, and then After we've struggled long enough, decided to go open or maybe just plan for it straight ahead of time. Frankly, I think, you know, it depends a little bit on the patient's age and all those things. This has been noted, but I would perhaps lean a little bit towards a combined approach here.

reference_conclusion: Additional staging included CT imaging of the neck and DOTATATE PET, with referral to neurosurgery for skull base involvement. Given the radiographically positive left cervical lymph node, management proceeded with combined craniofacial resection using simultaneous endoscopic and craniotomy approaches, with neck dissection performed the same day. Postoperative radiation therapy, including treatment of the neck, was planned.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 86-year-old female from Louisville, Kentucky. She lived independently and was described as relatively functional. She was a never smoker and had no history of alcohol use.

[ chief complaint ]: New ventral tongue lesion present for approximately 3 months, associated with mild discomfort.

[ diagnosis ]: Oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma of the ventral tongue, predominantly right-sided with extension to the midline region. Final pathologic findings were consistent with node-positive oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy performed by an oral surgeon showed squamous cell carcinoma with an estimated depth of invasion of approximately 3.6 mm. The lesion was described at biopsy as an erythematous lesion measuring approximately 1.5 cm. Final surgical pathology after partial glossectomy showed a 3.0 cm squamous cell carcinoma with depth of invasion 7.5 mm. Margins were negative; closest margin was 4 mm. Perineural invasion was present. Three lymph nodes were positive for metastatic disease: one level IB node on each side and one ipsilateral level III node. The largest positive node measured 0.9 cm.

[ imaging findings ]: Cross-sectional imaging of the neck/oral cavity was limited by dental artifact, with poor visualization of the oral cavity tumor. Imaging report indicated no appreciable cervical adenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Past medical history included breast cancer treated approximately 10 years earlier. She had a history of DVT at that time and remained on anticoagulation. Additional history included hypertension and idiopathic left vocal cord paralysis diagnosed approximately 7 years earlier; medialization had previously been discussed but not performed at that time.

For the current malignancy, she underwent partial glossectomy with bilateral neck dissection. Reconstruction was performed with a radial forearm free flap because of concern for tethering related to ventral tongue/floor-of-mouth involvement. During the postoperative hospitalization, left vocal cord medialization injection was performed approximately 6-7 days after flap surgery to support swallowing function. A feeding tube was placed. Postoperatively, she was hospitalized for approximately 1 week, then discharged to rehabilitation for approximately 1 additional week. By discharge from rehabilitation, she was eating by mouth while also receiving nutrition via gastrostomy tube.

[ current disease status ]: Status post surgical resection of ventral tongue squamous cell carcinoma with bilateral nodal metastases identified on final pathology. She tolerated surgery and postoperative recovery well.

[ other clinical data ]: On preoperative examination, the ventral tongue lesion was estimated clinically at approximately 2.5 cm, with mild induration and tenderness. It was predominantly right-sided but approached the midline. No palpable cervical adenopathy was appreciated clinically. Flexible laryngoscopy confirmed persistent left vocal cord paralysis. She had breathy dysphonia consistent with the vocal cord paralysis. She maintained oral intake preoperatively without significant weight loss. Dentition was described as moderate, with a lower partial denture in place.

reference_discussion.text: My name is Mia. I am in Louisville, Kentucky, and I'm going to present a case of a early stage oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma, so we can discuss a little bit about different management options for that. Okay, so our patient today, she's an 86-year-old female. She has a past medical history of breast cancer that was treated about 10 years ago, so this is a semi-recent patient, so you can take the years to be accurate. She had a history of ADVT at that time, so she's on a blood thinner. Hypertension, a little bit of a strange history of an idiopathic vocal cord paralysis that was diagnosed about seven years ago. Saw an ENT at that time. They said it's idiopathic, discussed medialization, ultimately decided not to do anything. But she is coming to see you today because she has a new ventral tongue lesion. So this has been present for about three months. Initially it was thought to be due to irritation. Got a new lower partial denture. Her dentist said it's probably nothing to worry about. Let's watch it persisted, so she got sent to an oral surgeon who did a biopsy of it. This confirms squamous cell carcinoma, so she got sent to us. The lesion is causing her a little bit of mild discomfort, but she's eating and drinking well. She hasn't had any significant weight loss. She's a never smoker, no history of alcohol use. She is 86 years old, but she lives independently and is relatively functional. So this is the biopsy report that comes with her from the oral surgeons. They called it about a one and a half centimeter lesion, erythematous. They biopsied it and on the path report it comes back as showing you at approximately 3.6 millimeter depth of invasion on this is how they marked it. The next slide. And then on your physical exam you see a very pleasant, alert, elderly female. She does have breathy dysphonia that's consistent with her previous vocal cord paralysis. On exam, it's a little bit bigger than they described. They're probably about a two and a half centimeter ventricle. Predominantly right-sided, but really does encroach upon the midline and Not quite to the other side, but close enough that you are thinking that it does involve really the center of the tongue. It's got some mild induration, a little bit of tenderness when you feel it. It's got moderate dentition. She's got that lower partial that's in place. Clinically, you don't appreciate any palpable adenopathy, and then your flexible inner gospe does confirm that she has that left-sided vocal cord paralysis. These are the scans that we obtain on this patient. A lot of dental artifacts, so difficult to see into the oral cavity. But I don't know if anyone wants to comment on it. The read that she comes to you with is can't really see the tumor, and there's no appreciable adenopathy on the skin.
Is it possible to scroll through the oral cavity a little bit slower?
It might. Can you toggle on the bar and see if we can hold the bar down?
No.
No. I don't think I can.
That's fine. No worries.
OK. Next time? Oh, apologies.

OK. So topic of discussion, what would be treatment recommendations from everyone on this with regard to her primary tumor site, the neck management, affecting any reconstruction? And then, as we mentioned, this patient's an 86-year-old lady. So does that impact how you are treating this malignancy?
But I guess we can start with, on this list, what is the, what do the experts think about how would you approach neck management and counseling the patient about the neck?

Okay, I'm going to speak up first. So, you know, the. I was, I would say if this was a young patient, be healthy, you know I would first think about and think about a neck dissection, with regard to manage management of a neck. But there are two factors that are in consideration here. The fact that her left true vocal fold is paralyzed and the fact that she's 86 years old is a drive to get her off the table as soon as possible. If you are to employ a neck dissection as a management strategy for her neck, it sounds like it'll have to be a bilateral neck dissection. If she was healthy and getting her off the table is not a consideration since the tumor does go up to the midline. But, you know, in doing so, you know, she's got a lecture vocal for paralysis. And so, you know, if you injure the vagus on the right side, then it's going to be a big problem with a little vocal for paralysis and doing bilateral neck dissection. In addition to the primary tumor, it's not take a good five, six hour surgery to get the surgery done. So that may not be for an 86 year old patient. So either you can go with just unilateral neck dissection, or the other option would be, I think, sentinel lymphobiopsy may not be a bad option for this patient.

That's great comments. I would look at it slightly differently. It seems like from the history that this is a pretty spirited 85-year-old who would seem to me would want to have everything done to be able to, um, sorry about that, to be able to get, get treated. Um, I think if we, um, if we, I would consider doing basically, um, treating them as, as though they were like any other patient, um, you know, um, hemiglossectomy with a neck dissection, I think the likelihood of injuring the vagus in a selective neck dissection is extremely low. And so, you know, I think, you know, this is one of those cases where, you know, you would want to take ownership of, you know, making sure that the fellow or yourself are doing the neck dissection and and get through the case. You can be temperate in how much you dissect and do a selective right-sided one through four neck dissection, but then you don't have to be as aggressive on the opposite side, if at all it's required. But given the fact that this is a pretty thick tumor, I would consider just a one-sided neck dissection and then post-operative radiation may be a consideration in this case, which could cover the opposite neck. That's how I would think about it. And as far as the vocal cord paralysis, I think that's definitely a consideration and I would have a conversation about that with the patient, but You know, I think this patient has an opportunity to get a full-fledged comprehensive treatment. So I would try to go for that.

Yeah, I agree with both comments. I think it all comes down to just the overall performance status of the patient. The challenging part of this case is that you actually have a depth of invasion up front on biopsy. That's usually a lot of times not the case. And certainly with it approaching, you know, four millimeters, we do worry about occult nodal metastasis. If she had come to me just to give another scenario and we didn't know for sure the depth of invasion and it felt pretty thin, this is the type of patient that I actually stage and would resect the primary, figure out what is her real depth of invasion, and then base my next steps off of that. I do think if you're going to do a neck dissection, you just need to commit to it, and I thought that was just nicely described.
Thank you all. Would any of you consider a Sentinel lymph node mapping on this patient? And if so, great. Why? If not, why not?

You know, I brought up the sentinel lymph node biopsy, so I guess I should comment on that. Again, a lot of it depends on the patient's overall health status. And so I do agree that if she is a spry, healthy 86-year-old patient, a bilateral neck dissection would be the first choice. But, you know, let's say she was not healthy and there was some concern about putting her through a major resection. I think in that situation, I think a sentinel lymph node biopsy is not an unreasonable option for her.

If we had Dr. Smallvox presentation where they came, there's no depth of invasion, would you consider when you do your staging doing a Sentinel node at that time or would you just wait for depth of invasion?

One is I don't do as many Sentinel lymph node biopsies. But irrespective, I think I would probably just do a primary resection. I think there's a lot of value you get when you actually, you know, resect the tumor and feel the tumor three dimensionally, you kind of get a sense of how deep it is also. And I think that's extremely valuable in making your decisions about the neck in an 85, 86-year-old. I think if I was not sure of the depth, I would definitely consider finding the distinction and then staging the neck.
I will add, just to help, my suspicion was that the depth of invasion was slightly more than what the pathology report was telling me. So I didn't quite fully agree with that DOI.
In the physical examination, was it apparent on bimanual palpation, whether this was a thicker tumor versus more superficial? Was there any?
I thought the depth of invasion would be more than four. I wasn't expecting it to be like centimeters big, but more than four for sure.

And that gets into the next challenge of the patient that gets sent in, biopsy done, how much of that thickening at the time of your evaluation is a reaction to the biopsy? How much of it is actually the tumor? And what if they take the whole thing out and you can't see anything? Those are all challenges we face. How about management of the mucosal margins on the primary site? How much of a margin are you shooting for? Are you taking margins off the specimen or off the patient? And then what are you doing to close?

i'm happy to start with that, so you know i'm going to try and achieve a one centimeter margin. That includes both peripheral, but I think where we really oftentimes will lose is with the deep margin, so I'm very cognizant of that. I try and walk the specimen up to pathology and mark it with them and point out which areas I'm most concerned about. Then at times, if I'm unsure about that deep margin, I don't mind taking a second deep margin from the patient himself or herself. Whenever possible, again, I'm sitting with the pathologist getting the margins off of the main specimen. So that's how I address that. And then, I'm sorry, did you ask about reconstruction too there, Trevor?

Yeah, because it's a two and a half centimeter lesion. So if you're taking a centimeter margin throughout, that becomes a four and a half centimeter defect in one direction. So what are we doing for recon?

Yeah, so it all, to me, depends on if this extends by the time you get your surgical margin, if it extends onto the floor of mouth. So I like to teach my residents that, you know, you really should treat the floor of mouth and the oral tongue as two different subunits, much like we have the subunits of the nose. And so I may, if it's small, let the floor of mouth granulate in, assuming we always have to think about the submandibular gland duct. And I'll close, for example, the tongue primarily without seeing a picture. It's a little bit challenging for me to know. I'll be curious, Mia, to learn from you about what you did. The other thing I've come to appreciate over the years is when I am, if I am primarily closing, oral tongue, I actually try to do so in an anterior and posterior direction, as opposed to dorsal ventral, because otherwise you wind up tethering the tongue, and really what you want to ensure that they have is excellent mobility. That kind of goes back to my original point of treating the floor of mouth and oral tongue as two different subunits. At times, I will say I have used alloderm, though in my hands, I feel like it's more of a biologic dressing, giving them some, you know, maybe a little bit of relief from pain. So those are just some pearls to throw out.

Trevor, you had asked about where to take the frozen section from, specimen or the defect. So I think the latest studies, including the studies here out of UPMC, have shown that the frozen should be taken from the specimen, not from the patient defect. And that's more predictive of the true margin status. So that would be my answer to that. With regard to the reconstruction, I do agree with all of Cecilia's comments. The thing that you've got to watch out for here is they don't want tethering of that tongue onto the floor of mouth as she heals. And so depending on the size of the defect, sometimes skin graft is adequate. The other consideration is that when you remove the ventral surface tuner, the dorsal surface that is left is very thin, it's very devascularized. And so that's going to die if you leave it like that. In a patient like that, I would just sort of chop off the anterior tongue, you know, the anterior parsoplastectomy. But in those kind of situations, often you tune them to a free flap reconstruction. So again, it depends on the defect size, but the thing that you got to be cognizant of is try to minimize the tethering by utilizing skin graft or free flap or whatever is necessary.

I'm happy to comment as well. I think I agree with all the comments. In my particular practice, I tend to take the specimens of the, you know, the remnant tongue. And I sometimes, if I'm really close on something and I feel like I need to, you know, I'm going to compromise some function, I won't hesitate to mix it up and take a specimen, a particular margin of the tumor, if I'm going to save function in a particular case. But in general, I do take circumferential margins of the residual dung. I was pleasantly surprised to hear that primary closure is a consideration, because I think we constantly think about free flaps. But even with the hemigloss, I My time at Tata Hospital in my fellowship in India, we did so many hemiglossectomies and just rotated the tip of the tongue to close the defect. And it's not always pretty, but it's very functional. So in an 85-year-old, that could be a consideration. And you can get pretty good function with just a primary closure of that tongue.

You know, just to throw it out there on the slide here, I've listed under reconstruction, pedicle flap is listed here as a possible option. So, you know, would anyone here ever consider submental island flap to reconstruct eventual tongue defect like this?

I've done it, so I will say sure, I will consider it. I'll use a subventilating flap for a lot of defects, including the ventral tongue. There's no risk to transferring lymph nodes into the defect. You can remove the lymph nodes from the flap safely. And I think it's a pretty good flap. But I think going back to Cecilia's point, and it should be underscored for the trainees, The floor of mouth is critical. You have to create a trampoline between the tongue and the mandible. Without doing that, you tether your tongue to your mandible, you lose the articulation, you lose swelling. So the floor of mouth is critical, even more critical than the tongue per what Dr. Kim and Dr. Walker-Ross were saying. You could take half a tongue, but if you take any of the floor of mouth, it matters a lot. Why don't we keep moving forward so we can get through this case to the next ones as well. So next slide.
So I took the aggressive route.
Don weed in the chat, put down a forum flap is a good choice for floor of mouth. If the patient is healthy and she drives the decision making. So there you go. Don weed is on your side.

So she actually did really, she did a, we did a partial glossectomy on her. I did address bilateral necks to me. It didn't seem like it added a whole lot. If we were doing a neck dissection on one side, I was worried enough about it encroaching the opposite side that I felt like it needed to be addressed. And then we actually counseled her on. Let's see how the defect looks. And then based on that, we'll talk about if it's something we can leave open, something we can close, do a form. After doing the risk section, my concern was the tethering that everybody else has kind of talked about it. Just being in the ventral tongue and extending to the floor of mouth. And so my partner did a beautiful radial form free flap on it. And I did not list it in here. One of the other things we did do during her hospitalization, we medialized her vocal cord. We knew that this was gonna give her enough swallowing dysfunction just from having new anatomy in her mouth that we wanted to try to do anything we could to try to improve her swallow function. So did go ahead and do that. And then the next slide has her pathology.
Mia, I was just curious, did you do the vocal cord medialization before the big resection or after the big resection?

No, so after. Had kind of honestly intended to do it at the same time, but because I wasn't sure what the reconstruction was going to look like, didn't do it up front. And then when we did the free flop, decided to delay it. And actually she, we waited for the pathology report to come back. We had some like questions about dentition. And so when she got her teeth Well, spoiler alert, but when she ended up going back for something else, we did the injection at the same time, probably about six days later. I think something like six, seven days after the flap did the injection. So her pathology came back as a 3 centimeter squamous cell carcinoma. Her DOI was 7.5 millimeters on the permanent pathology, had negative margins, 4 millimeters was the closest margin, and then did have, I believe it had positive, oh yeah, I'm trying to find it. Yes, no, positive PNI on it. She had three positive lymph nodes. Bilaterally, each one B had a positive lymph node, and then on the right side, the epsilateral side to the tumor, a level 3 node was positive. All of them were sub centimeter 0.9 was the largest one. Then kind of came the second question. So we did this surgery on this 86 year old lady. So adjuvant therapy recommendations and what to do with her pathology.
That's like a really tough question because it really depends upon how did the patient do with the whole surgery? Like, I mean, did she do well?

Yeah, so she did well. She was in the hospital for about a week. We sent her to rehab for about a week afterwards. She, by the time she left rehab was eating by mouth. We did an anticipated, she got a feeding two place at the same time. So it was kind of combining doing some nutrition. through her G-tube doing some nutrition by mouth. Yeah, it's actually tolerated it really well.
She didn't have a, did she have a trach that was removed later or no trach?
No, she was never trached. Yeah.

Yeah, I think I would lean towards post-operative radiation both to the primary side, more aggressive to the ipsilateral neck, and talk to the radiation oncologist about maybe, you know, the contralateral neck didn't have any positive nodes, right?
It did. Each 1B had a positive node, and then the ipsilateral had a lateral neck.
Yeah, then I would give them, you know, the radiation that they could tolerate, but I would obviously not recommend any chemotherapy for the station.

No, I agree with Rohan. I mean, if the patient did OK after surgery, it sounds like she did, which then indicates that she's a relatively healthy person. So I think that in this case, she should definitely get at least adjuvant radiation therapy. And I would advocate radiating both the primary site and both sides of her neck.
All right. We are. That was a great first case. So we can keep on time. We'll go to our next case. I think it sounds like adjuvant radiation therapy.
That's what we did. She did great. She's finishing now.

Given final pathology demonstrating perineural invasion and bilateral nodal metastases, adjuvant radiation therapy to the primary site and bilateral neck was recommended; chemotherapy was not recommended.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 82-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistent pain involving the right mandibular teeth/mandible with nonhealing extraction sockets 6 months after extraction of two right mandibular molars.

[ diagnosis ]: Squamous cell carcinoma of the right mandibular alveolus/gingiva.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial oral surgeon biopsy demonstrated squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: PET/CT demonstrated FDG uptake at the primary right mandibular site without evidence of cervical nodal disease or distant metastatic disease. Contrast-enhanced CT soft tissue neck was interpreted as demonstrating cortical bone involvement of the mandible. Clinically, the lesion measured approximately 1-2 cm, involved the right mandibular alveolus with submucosal extension, appeared fixed to the mandible, and had no palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. The lesion was described as isolated to the right mandible/gingiva without midline involvement and with minimal to no floor-of-mouth or buccal involvement.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Two right mandibular molars were extracted by a dentist prior to cancer diagnosis; pain persisted and extraction sites remained unhealed at 6 months.

[ current disease status ]: Squamous cell carcinoma of the right mandibular alveolus/gingiva, clinically approximately 1-2 cm and fixed to the mandible, with cortical mandibular involvement on CT, no palpable or radiographic cervical nodal disease, and no distant metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Past history included remote tobacco use, discontinued approximately 20 years earlier. Baseline medications included metoprolol and simvastatin. The patient was otherwise described as healthy for age.
