reference_discussion.text: All right, so we're now going to jump to Jeremiah Tracy, who has the next case for us.
I think you're muted, Jeremiah. Let's try that again. There you go.

Thanks to the organizers for having me present. And thanks, Dr. Yusefbegovich. That first case was very interesting. I like there are a lot of margin calls there. The case I have may be more straightforward. This is a 82-year-old who first presented with pain of what he thought were his mandibular teeth, possibly the mandible. His dentist pulled two of his right mandibular molars. Unfortunately, the pain persisted, and his two sockets had not yet healed six months later. He was seen by an oral surgeon who did a biopsy. And so when he got to me, he did have a pathologic diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma. He was quite healthy for an 82-year-old. He had a history of tobacco use, but not for, I think, almost 20 years. And really, metoprolol and simvastatin were his only medications. He had this about 1 to 2 centimeter a lesion involving the right mandibular alveolus, kind of visible submucosal extension. It seemed to be fixed the mandible and there were no palpable lymph nodes. He had a PET CT scan at the time of my evaluation showing FDG uptake at the primary site, but no concern for nodal disease or metastatic disease. And I actually got a CT scan of the neck, soft tissue neck with contrast as part of preoperative planning. which we read as demonstrating cortical bone involvement. So I guess this would be my first pause. Any further workup to complete staging and initial management recommendation?
So he has a biopsy and a PET CT scan?
That's right.
OK. So with regard to the evaluation of the tumor, to me, that's pretty adequate.
And what was the time frame between the biopsy and the dental extraction?
So the dental extraction was six months prior. That's where the delay occurred. But between the biopsy and him seeing me was quite quick, a few weeks.
And the PET CT scan is pretty recent too, right? That's not that old.
That, yes, that was all ordered by the oral surgeon to identify the cancer. And then I did have also a CT soft tissue neck with contrast.

So we've all unfortunately seen these patients. First of all, you guys can't operate on anybody under the age of 80 apparently, but we've all seen these patients who come in, right, with loose dentition or stuff around the tooth. They pull the tooth and you've got cancer around the socket. So what's the, on Dr. Tracy's slide, are we doing a marginal mandibulectomy? Are you doing a segmental? What are you doing? And what are you doing with the neck?

In this case, I'm definitely doing a segmental mandibulectomy. The one thing is it's pretty straightforward with respect to the bony erosion. I also to your point, Trevor, just to again underscore for the fellows, you know, when there is a tooth extracted, presumably in the bed of where cancer was, you know, you almost have to assume that it's in the medullary space, meaning you can't afford to leave cancer behind there. And that's why I would err towards a segmental over a marginal But again, very straightforward with these nice images. And then I would do, certainly do a neck dissection as well on that side. It looks like from your photo that this is right-sided and that even with a good one centimeter margin, it's still right-sided. Is that fair to say there was no midline involvement?
That's right. It was very, very isolated to the mandible and the gingiva. There was really pretty minimal to no, you know, floor of mouth or buccal involvement.
Yeah, I agree with all the comments.

I'd just like to say that on the scans, like whenever you look at assessing mandibular tumors, you know, look for paramandibular spread, you know, look for the sublingual space and, you know, whether that is asymmetric as compared to the other side. Look at the symmetry of the, you know, midline tongue musculature. All of those things are important to decide whether this is truly sort of a lateralized tumor that has some medial component to it. I agree that in this case, it looks pretty obvious that the patient needs a segmental. There's too much of a body involvement to consider anything else.

Yeah, I agree. Segmental is a standard of care in this situation. But just to make the discussion a little bit more interesting, what if the patient said, hey, doc, for whatever reason, he loves his mandible, and he does not want to go through a segmental mandibulectomy? He says, there is no way I'm going to go through a segmental mandibulectomy. Explain to the patient that even if you do a marginal, the soft tissue defect will be large enough that he's going to need a flap to cover the soft tissue defect anyway. But for whatever reason, he does not want a fibular free flap in a segmental. How would you proceed? Would you do a marginal?

That's a really great sort of scenario, which I hope I never have to encounter. But if it did come down to that, then I have to be true to, you know, what I think is going to work. And in that situation, it could be an inadequate surgery, it wouldn't even be palliative, because you're going to kind of, you know, cut through tumor for the most part. and sort of leave the patient in a greater disadvantage. And I would just have them consider a non-surgical treatment option at that point, even though it's probably not the right option for them.

Yeah. Tracy, can you go back to the CT scan that you had shown previously? So on that axial, on that coronal cut, you can see the degree of bone invasion into the mandible there. Now, I had patients like this, a handful of patients in my career, who for whatever reason, they refused a segmental. And their tumor was eroding the mandible from the occlusal surface like we have here. So I've done I've relented on these patients, and I have done marginal on these people, but doing the marginal, but taking a very significant portion of the mandible, leaving a fairly thin rim along the inferior aspect and plating that to bolster it. By doing that, on three of these patients who had refusal segmental, I was able to get a negative margin on the bone, and with adjuvant therapy, they turned okay. On some of those cases, I have taken that approach. But I do agree with everyone that the standard care is. Sorry, I'll put one more step forward.

And that's why I asked Jeremiah the dental extraction was six months prior. So are you sure that this, this amount of bone loss is due to. the cancer or could it be from the dental extraction and from six months ago. And then, just to be devil's advocate, and, and there's a pretty big distance between that and where the nerve is that the patient doesn't have mental numbness they're not involved in the marrow space I still think is segmental is what most of us would do. But if you do a marginal. Steve, do you do a marginal and then wait for final path, and then go back and do a segmental neck if you need to, or are you doing a neck when you're doing the marginal, if you're doing a marginal and then you'd be like?

So if I'm doing a marginal on this patient, I'm doing the neck at the same time. The main reason is that to, in order to put the plate on, it's easier if you make a neck incision and raise the flap over the mandible. And so if patients have a neck incision, the neck's gonna be opened up, I'll do the neck dissection at that same time.
Yeah.

I mean, I, you know, it is, it is true that like sometimes you can get away with marginal mandiblectomies. Uh, I, this particular case, I think it would be really difficult to get away with one of those. Uh, but, but, you know, there are certainly something to consider. And I think if you have a proper discussion with the patient preoperatively and, um, look at all your options and say that I'm going to consider doing a marginal. But if things don't look, you can always have a backup of a segmental resection. And sometimes you can get away with it.

Yeah, I think there's a difference between mild cortical erosion and irregularity versus involvement in the medullary space. And this is actually, and Jeremiah, I don't know if you were hinting at this earlier, most neuroradiologists would actually prefer an MRI if we are really questioning bony involvement into that medullary space because they can look at the enhancement better. So that's just one thing to think about. But I will still stick to my segmental.

I would agree. That's a great point, Cecilia. And the last thing I'll put on there is if you're going to do a segmental for the trainees, you're going to take their mental nerve. So when you're doing the neck, you have to be very careful you don't take their marge. Because if you give them a numb lip and a weak lip, you affect their oral competence, which could be a big factor in the quality of life of anybody, especially this 82-year-old. So you have to be very careful. Once you've taken their sensation, don't also take their power. Go ahead, Jeremiah.

So this patient did indeed have a segmental mandibulectomy, an ipsilateral selective one through four neck dissection, and was reconstructed with a fibula. He did well perioperatively. The surgical pathology actually showed a 1.4 centimeter tumor, seven millimeter depth of invasion with no bone involvement. And this was confirmed with the pathologist pretty extensively. LVI, PNI negative, negative margins, no lymph nodes. So finally, final pathologic staging was T2, N0, M0. And I guess my question for concern is, I guess what I'm hinting at is, do we have any remorse for doing a segmental on this patient with the T2 disease? And any pearls that you have for identifying bone involvement preoperatively? And I guess final would be any role for adjuvant treatment in this case.

Yeah, first of all, no remorse at all. You've done the surgery that you thought was indicated based on the preoperative information. What I will tell the patient is, you know, emphasize the positive. Listen, you know, your cancer did not invade a bone. Your cancer has been taken care of. You don't need to adjuvate treatment. You're good. So I would reinforce the positive. But the surgery, if this was my patient and I'd done the segmental, then you've done the surgery that you thought were indicated based on the preoperative scan. So there's no remorse on that. In terms of identifying bone involvement, obviously, CT scan is what you start out with. And as Cecilia said, if you have any concern, MRI would be your second line study. But I have patients who on CT scan who had no evidence of bone invasion, and I do a marginal, and the path comes back with T4 cancer with positive bone margin. So that has happened to me as well. But I would say relying on the CT scan, using the MRI as necessary, and your clinical assessment is what you have to rely upon to assess for bone invasion.

I agree, Steve. And I think the onus is really on us as surgeons operatively to say, you know, please realize there's a chance we're going to go in. And despite, you know, thinking we need to do this segmental, we may not find bony erosion. And it's easy to look back and say, gee, I wish I didn't, but it's A, the only way to know and B, if that happens, we're going to celebrate because you don't need radiation. And that's just a great sign. It's early stage. So I think being transparent up front, explaining the why, and then finding the positive, as Steve was saying. And that's easier to do up front before you go to surgery, and then you can just reinforce it on the back end.

I think sometimes also, and again, I wouldn't say that this trumps getting a CT, but sometimes when patients come with OPGs or orthopentomograms, you get some really cool bone architecture and perspective that you don't get with a CT. And sometimes it's worth looking at that also. But again, there will be no doubt in my mind that I will change my management based on the scans that you showed us. So yeah, and no remorse, like Dr. Kim said, you did the right operation for the tumor.

Thank you, Jeremiah. That is a great case. And it is a challenging case. This one's maybe seemed like it was more straightforward because of bone erosion. And that was my question to you, Steve, is that sometimes I'll do a marginal, but I don't do the neck at the time of the marginal. And the main reason I don't is because if the bone is positive, then I haven't violated my neck and I can go back in and do my segmental and free flap. But what I would say in this case, too, is sometimes and you might speak to the Steve, sometimes the soft tissue margins are easier to get widely negative when you do a segmental when you're doing a marginal sometimes you don't get as good because because you're approaching it in a different way. or maybe your soft tissue margins on your path report, Dr. Tracy, wouldn't have been as widely negative if you had done a marginal. You may not have taken the same cuff of tissue because you're trying to kind of get the saw in there. And so doing the segmental may also not take the care of the bone, but expand a little bit how you manage the soft tissue around it too. Great. All right, Caitlin.
Before we move on, did you radiate this patient or observe?

No, and so I appreciate everyone's input and that's exactly what I think about it. I kind of think about it as, you know, the classic teaching for appendicitis, right? In general surgery, like they should remove a certain percentage of normal appendices to make sure they're not leaving appendicitis behind and having ruptures, right? And in this patient, it worked out great since he did have no nodes, otherwise no high-risk features. He had no radiation. He's two years out. He's getting implants placed shortly, so he's happy.

I think the other important point, I realize we're a little bit almost out of time, but he's fully dentate. So by doing that fibula, you now gave the opportunity to do dental restoration, whereas with a marginal mandibulectomy, I think for this particular case, that would have been nearly impossible.
Very good point.
Having dental

is not something which is commonly, like, you know, we don't commonly think about it as a part that at least we do as head and neck, you know, ablative surgeons. But a lot of the OMFS literature talks about, like, actually having the implants in the fibula at the time of reconstruction. And that has several advantages of, you know, not exposing that, you know, radiated fibula then to implants later on. So that's just something to consider.
All right. Thank you, Jeremiah. All right. Caitlin. Hey, sort of a less fun case, more depressing.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary consensus supported primary surgical management with segmental mandibulectomy and ipsilateral neck dissection, given the extent of mandibular involvement on preoperative assessment. Following resection, reconstruction with a fibular free flap was performed. Final pathology demonstrated pT2N0M0 squamous cell carcinoma with negative margins, no lymphovascular invasion, no perineural invasion, no nodal metastases, and no bone involvement; therefore, observation without adjuvant therapy was recommended.
reference_conclusion_quote: In this case, I'm definitely doing a segmental mandibulectomy. [...] And then I would do, certainly do a neck dissection as well on that side. [...] Segmental is a standard of care in this situation. [...] So this patient did indeed have a segmental mandibulectomy, an ipsilateral selective one through four neck dissection, and was reconstructed with a fibula. [...] You don't need to adjuvate treatment. You're good. [...] He had no radiation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Advanced oral cavity/oropharyngeal mass with severe trismus, weight loss, frailty, and left lip numbness.

[ diagnosis ]: Keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma of the oral cavity/oropharyngeal region, involving the retromolar trigone, posterior buccal mucosa, posterior maxilla, lateral pharynx, mandible, and tongue. Clinical stage based on imaging was cT4b cN2c cM0.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside biopsy showed squamous cell carcinoma. Pathology review confirmed keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. p16 was negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Cross-sectional imaging demonstrated extensive mandibular destruction crossing the midline, with tumor extension under the gingiva nearly to the midline. There was invasion of approximately half of the tongue, nearly to the midline, with involvement of the hemitongue. Tumor extended posteriorly into the medial pterygoid with masticator space involvement. The pterygoid plate was not clearly eroded. There was extensive pharyngeal involvement and extension into the posterior maxilla. Anterior soft tissue involvement approached but did not invade the skin. PET imaging demonstrated a contralateral cervical lymph node, consistent with bilateral nodal disease (N2c). No distant metastatic disease was reported (M0).

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: p16 negative.

[ laboratory results ]: Liver function tests were normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial management focused on supportive optimization because of poor nutritional status and frailty. A gastrostomy tube was placed. Nutrition and social work were involved. Pain control was improved. Smoking cessation efforts were initiated. The patient was evaluated by radiation oncology and medical oncology. Medical oncology determined he was not fit for concurrent chemotherapy.

[ current disease status ]: Locally advanced, unresected head and neck squamous cell carcinoma with masticator space invasion and bilateral cervical nodal involvement, without documented distant metastasis. The patient remained frail with severe trismus and malnutrition.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had mild to moderate dementia and was taking memantine. He was able to answer questions appropriately and understood his condition, but was not fully independent in daily activities. He had a history of cirrhosis. He was a former heavy drinker and former heavy smoker; he was still actively smoking at the time of evaluation. Nutritional status was poor, with significant weight loss, BMI 17, temporal wasting, and marked frailty. Examination was limited by severe trismus. There was decreased sensation/numbness of the left lip. Airway was reported to be adequate. He lived at home with his wife, who was his primary support.

reference_discussion.text: Okay. So this was actually a patient I saw recently, so I don't have a long-term follow-up for him, but, uh, 54 years old, 56 years old, excuse me. but he does have some mild to moderate dementia. He's not entirely independent, but he does kind of understand what's going on. He can answer questions appropriately. He's on amenda for that. He has a history of cirrhosis in the past, but his LFTs are currently normal. He's not actively drinking, but he was a former heavy drinker and a former heavy smoker. When I saw him, there had been some delays in his care and he had lost a significant amount of weight. His BMI was 17. He had temporal wasting. He looked quite frail. In pretty severe trismus, it was a limited exam. This is pretty much all I could see. But if I really got in there, I could tell that the tumor was creeping up the retromolar trigone, was extended to the posterior buccal mucosa, and was along the posterior maxilla as well, and then into the lateral pharynx. And you can see in the midline there, there's extension under the gingiva almost to the midline. So he had no, that was it. That was what I saw when I first saw him. He had nothing else available besides a biopsy showing squamous cell carcinoma. What would our experts do for their next steps in management?

I would get some imaging done first. Obviously, you know, a full head and neck examination of the clinic, scope the patient, just understand the airway, and then get some imaging before, you know, doing anything intraoperatively. Patient will probably require a proper EUA, you know, but that's, you know, we run the risk of requiring a trach at that time. So I'd get the imaging done first. And my imaging of choice would be a CT scan, you know, one millimeter cuts with and without contrast.

And of course, PET scan also at the same time. Anything else? I assume that you don't have a tissue diagnosis yet, correct? No, we do. It was a squamous cell carcinoma. That's the only thing he came in with. Okay. All right. Shall I carry on?

Well, I was going to say there are a lot of consultants that you need beyond me. Oh, yeah. Go for it. Go for it. You know, my biggest concern is that BMI is 17. I imagine this patient came in a wheelchair and probably never even made it into your exam chair. And you mentioned temporal wasting, and so I just worry about this individual being able to make it through any treatment. A lot of times with the dementia, they don't have a whole lot of social support, so getting social work involved. Depending on how frail they are, you know, I'd want to know more about their swallowing, so certainly would do a formal consult to SLP. from that aspect as well. And there, it looks like there was pretty poor dentition there. So eventually getting a dental evaluation, which is going to be exceedingly hard with that trismus. But from a practical standpoint for the fellows, like you have to prioritize of like, where do you start? Because those are a lot of appointments and really long days for someone who's probably exceedingly debilitated.
Is there anyone else based on the trismus and the, I think, was there was there mental numbness or anything? Was there any signs of V3?
Yeah, he did have some lip numbness, but it was kind of a little bit hard to elucidate from him. But it did appear he had some decreased sensation on the left lip.
Would that prompt any additional or different imaging from any of the faculty besides the CT and the PET?

Yeah, I mean, if you're worried about perineal involvement of a major name, cranial nerve MRI should be done to make sure there's no intracranial extension. But I have another question about this patient. What is his social situation? Is he living at home with family by himself? Is he institutionalized? What is his situation?

Yeah, great question. Great points brought up about a social situation. He actually has a very dedicated wife who married him when they met in high school. So they're longtime partners. He lives at home with her, but she works full time. And their insurance and stuff like that depends on her work schedule. And she has very limited time off. So it took a long time to get the stuff done that I wanted to get done.

Yeah, I totally agree with the idea that you have to think about this patient holistically. I think the reason why I jumped to CT scans and PET scans and EUAs is because ultimately, the first thing I want to assess is receptability of this patient. However, whether that's even a possibility or not. Because if I know with the CT scan that this patient has extensive soft tissue involvement and high infratemporal fossa involvement, then I'm going to activate, you know, my thought process in a very different direction. But you're absolutely an extremely challenging patient and requires a lot more sort of in-depth, you know, considerations before you make any formal decisions.

Thank you, guys. So, uh, you know, when I saw my priority really was, uh, at the time his nutritional status and social work, just to get that stuff lined up, he wasn't going to be able to tolerate really any kind of treatment in his current condition. So G tube was priority. Number one, his airway was actually fine. Um, so he got his G tube. Um, he saw nutrition, social work was, was, uh, working with them. We got his pain under better control. He was actually still actively smoking. So we worked on that too. and I ordered some imaging. I sent him, you know, kind of shotgun ordered all this stuff. I sent him for multi-D discussion with also radiation medical oncology. I like to establish with them early, even if I am going to think about going to surgery, our radiation oncologists do appreciate examining the patient prior to surgery so they can understand the lesion and margins, what they're going to do postoperatively. So I usually consult them early on, especially for advanced tumors where they're probably going to need adjuvant if we get to surgery. And then we brought the tissue over to Moffitt and we reviewed it and agreed it was a keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma, P16 negative. So I'll just go through some of his imaging. These are just some screenshots, but you can see extensive destruction of the mandible across midline, invading half the tongue, almost to the midline of the tongue as well. and extending on the posterior aspect up into the medial pterygoid there. Pterygoid plate wasn't quite clear. It looked okay. It wasn't quite eroded, but certainly masticator space involvement. You can see on the axial here the extent of the pharynx involvement, okay, and the hemitongue. And you can see anteriorly all the soft tissue. It wasn't quite invading skin, but you can see it's quite close. This is the PET scan. He did have a contralateral lymph node. So he had N2C disease in the neck. And you can just see how absolutely massive this is, extending in the posterior maxilla there as well. I looked at the nerve on the PET scan. Obviously it's not the best modality, Honestly, I was not optimistic about surgery for him, and so I didn't want to put him through an MRI. But if I were really going to consider going to surgery, I probably would have ordered that. So this was staging based on imaging, T4B, mastigator space involvement, and 2CM0. So what would our experts do next?

Yeah, no, I agree with that T4B designation. I think that this tumor is, at that presentation, unresectable. If you had a patient with this type of tumor and they really wanted you to do everything possible, including consideration of surgery, I think one option is neoadjuvant treatment, whether that be chemo or a combination of chemo and immunotherapy and see how the patient's tumor responds. And in some cases, we have seen patients who do respond significantly where we think that surgery does become feasible, not easy, but feasible. So that's an option. But otherwise, I would say most patients would recommend probably non-surgical chemoradiotherapy for a tumor like this.
Yeah, I definitely would lean on our tumor board You know, it's interesting, Caitlin, from the dementia standpoint, like, was he able to participate in his decision making?
He was. He could answer questions appropriately. He understood what was going on. But in terms of his day to day, he's not driving the car. He's not, you know, doing his bills.

Sure. So, you know, I think that you have a couple of options. Any surgery in this case would be heroic. There would certainly be positive margins. I just want to reiterate, I thought you brought up a great point for the fellows, Caitlin, that, you know, when you start seeing trismus, you think pterygoid invasion, and you need to think about the sphenopalatine, pterygopalatine fossa, and the MRI can be really helpful in evaluating that. Looking at a non-surgical option, I think one of the priorities, assuming they want to continue with treatment, is actually to get a feeding tube in and start getting him some better nutrition so that he can look at some aspects with respect to systemic therapy and or radiation. Then I think you also need to be candid and talk about palliative treatment and hospice as well.

Yeah, no, I agree with that, Cecilia, for sure. This tumor, I think, is unlikely to be curable regardless of what we employ here. So I think that consideration of palliative treatment and hospice is a very important aspect of this patient's treatment plan.

Yeah, I just, I totally agree. I just want to say that, like, you know, from the fellows perspective, that there are T4Bs, and then there are T4Bs, you know. So I think when we look at scans, everything looks sometimes unresectable. And you have to, you know, rely on the scans. But sometimes an examination or an anesthesia is so important for you to be able to understand how those tissue dynamics work. And many of the times when you have really advanced looking tumors, you'll actually, you know, once you do an EUA, you feel like you may be able to get around it. And again, you know, it's a very tricky situation, right, because if this patient was, say, 10 years younger, and he was like, absolutely with it, and had like a young family, you would want to do everything that you want that it possibly can for this patient. So every case is unique and presents its own sort of decision-making challenges. But I often find that people at tumor conferences are very quick to make decisions based on just imaging. And so just make sure that don't hesitate to don't hesitate to take the patient back and do a proper examination of the anesthesia before you make any final calls.

And to bring up, that's a great point, Rohan, and to bring up from the chat, Don, we put in there to not forget this guy has some cirrhosis too, so he may not be the best wound healer. And even if you did a heroic surgery with a flap, it's going to be two, three months of recovery. And then what happens is that the cancer occurs literally at the margin of your section three months afterwards. And so I think that's the, those are the cases I think that we all regret, the ones that we pushed and then, basically just they were recovering, they recurred. And so the saying that I've given to patients and thankfully not very often is there's worse things than dying, it's what I could do to you before you die. And I think that's the mentality I would take into this case. And even think about radiation therapy, if you've had a great response, I think that might also be toxic. So it may be palliative or palliative immuno alone.

Yeah, I agree. You know, I agree. I mean, I see where Ron is coming from, you know, we see these patients, of course, our gut reaction is we want to help them, you know, with regard to the cancer. But on the other hand, sometimes helping them is guiding them, guiding them away from surgery that is not going to help them, in fact, is going to make things a lot worse for them. Just like Trevor said, I think that this is one of those patients.

Yeah, absolutely agree. Very well said. And I just want to you know, for the fellows, I think you have to have both those perspectives in the back of your mind and sort of, you know, think about what's right for which patient and do the best you can. And that's where the tumor board comes into play, right? I mean, because as a surgical, you know, oncologist and a patient coming to you, you want to help everybody, but then your colleagues will help put things into perspective at times. And so that's how you sort of lean on each other to make those decisions.

Yeah, I think the hardest thing we do as surgeons is say surgery is not the right answer because you can almost always cut something out of the question, should you? And so when I think about resectability, I put it into three different categories. First, you have the anatomic resectability. So masseter space here, skull base, et cetera. Then you have what's functionally resectable. And I would argue this almost borders on not being functionally resectable, even if you could get widely around it. And then lastly, I like to teach that there's, you know, you have to ask, what is biologically resectable? You know, is this someone that's had three resections already, failed radiation, chemo, et cetera? Are they immunosuppressed organ transplant? Obviously not Caitlin's case, but those are things that I consider when I look at resectability on an individual basis.

I think that's a great point Cecilia and then there's probably a fourth one which is just like the patient themselves like this patient. What would a 10 hour surgery due to this patient with dementia, what would it do to their dementia. what would all that treatment do? All the anesthetic, you start worrying about what if they wake up and they're not the same person when they went to sleep. So there's that point of, did you help them globally? This is a sad case, like you mentioned it would be, but it's a case that I think is great for the fellows to really think about that this is, it's not easy. And it's not easy to be in that position.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 26-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: One-year history of neck swelling.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with bilateral cervical nodal metastases, central neck nodal disease, and left retropharyngeal nodal metastasis. Background history of Graves’ disease diagnosed at age 18.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid lesion had shown papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Physical examination had demonstrated an easily palpable left thyroid nodule measuring approximately 3 cm, massive left-sided cervical adenopathy with multiple mobile lymph nodes greater than 5 cm in levels II-IV, and a mobile right level IV lymph node measuring approximately 4-5 cm. Vocal cords were mobile on examination. Office ultrasound had shown a 3 cm left thyroid nodule that was hypoechoic, solid, with ill-defined borders and microcalcifications. Ultrasound had also shown bulky cystic adenopathy in the left lateral neck, involving levels III and IV, suspicious nodes in left level II, concerning right-sided cervical nodes, and central neck disease. Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck had demonstrated bilateral lateral neck adenopathy, central neck adenopathy, and left retropharyngeal adenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic testing data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had previously been evaluated by another surgeon and then sought a second opinion.

[ current disease status ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with bilateral cervical nodal metastases, central neck nodal disease, and left retropharyngeal nodal metastasis, referred for a second surgical opinion.

[ other clinical data ]: There was no family history of thyroid cancer. Other physical examination findings were otherwise unremarkable. Evaluation had been delayed during the COVID-19 pandemic.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Three- to four-month history of dysphagia, globus sensation, and palpable low right neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe with regional nodal metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the thyroid lesion demonstrated medullary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound identified a thyroid lesion and suspicious lateral neck adenopathy. Contrast-enhanced CT neck demonstrated a multilobulated right-predominant thyroid mass with a right lateral neck lymph node. The mass abutted the tracheal wall and caused compression without tracheal invasion. Flexible laryngoscopy demonstrated right vocal cord paresis.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline RET mutation was positive.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-proven medullary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe with suspicious right lateral neck adenopathy, tracheal compression without invasion, and right vocal cord paresis.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included lung disease and hypertension. There was no prior head and neck surgery. Social tobacco use was reported. No known family history of thyroid cancer was available; the patient was adopted. Examination demonstrated mild breathy dysphonia, right lower neck/thyroid asymmetry, and a palpable focal lower neck lymph node without other palpable lateral neck nodes.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 85-year-old Taiwanese male.

[ chief complaint ]: Intermittent hemoptysis beginning in June, with progression over weeks to intermittent stridor. Associated cough was present. He had known right thyroid fullness and induration.

[ diagnosis ]: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, stage IVC, with pulmonary metastatic disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid demonstrated high-grade carcinoma with squamous features, interpreted as most consistent with anaplastic thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Fiberoptic laryngoscopy showed normal vocal cords with a lesion beyond the cords in the subglottic/tracheal region. CT neck/chest demonstrated a thyroid mass involving the right side, invading the right lateral aspect of the trachea, with tracheal deviation and suspected tracheal erosion/invasion. CT chest demonstrated bilateral pulmonary nodules, including a large spiculated lesion in the left lung and additional right-sided and left lower lung nodules, reported as consistent with pulmonary metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF V600E testing was negative. PAX8 was positive. Thyroglobulin was negative. TTF-1 was negative. Tumor mutation burden was low. PD-L1 status was low or negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: He had no prior surgery and was not taking thyroid medication. He was hospitalized for approximately 1 week with worsening airway distress. He declined tracheostomy, tracheal resection, radiation therapy, and toxic chemotherapy.

[ current disease status ]: Stage IVC anaplastic thyroid carcinoma with pulmonary metastases and progressive airway compromise manifested by intermittent stridor and hemoptysis.

[ other clinical data ]: Otherwise healthy prior to presentation. No family history of thyroid cancer.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 26-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidentally identified thyroid nodule. The patient was asymptomatic, without dysphonia, dysphagia, or dyspnea.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- Left thyroid papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), classic type.  
- Left thyroid follicular carcinoma, minimally invasive.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Fine-needle aspiration of the left superior thyroid nodule: malignant papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Fine-needle aspiration of the left mid-thyroid nodule: benign, consistent with benign follicular nodule.  
- Left hemithyroidectomy pathology:  
  - Lesion 1: 1.6 cm papillary thyroid carcinoma, classic type, with lymphovascular invasion; posterior margin focally positive.  
  - Lesion 2: minimally invasive follicular carcinoma; no lymphovascular invasion; no perineural invasion; margins negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated:  
  - Right thyroid nodule not meeting criteria for biopsy.  
  - Two left thyroid nodules meeting criteria for biopsy.  
  - Left superior nodule measured 1.8 cm and was TI-RADS 5/highly suspicious. Sonographic features included mostly solid/almost completely solid composition, hypoechogenicity, taller-than-wide shape, microcalcifications, and punctate echogenic foci.  
  - Second left thyroid nodule measured 1.8 cm and was TI-RADS 4.  
  - Isthmus was normal.  
  - No notable cervical lymphadenopathy.  
- Laryngoscopy demonstrated normal bilateral vocal fold mobility.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- TSH: 1.552 (normal).  
- Free T4: 0.8 (normal).

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Left hemithyroidectomy was performed.

She is asymptomatic. And on presentation, she didn't have any dysphonia or dysphagia or dyspnea. She had no history of radiation exposure or any family history of thyroid cancer. Finished, Erin. Sorry.
Oh, hey, Vinnie. Oh, sorry. Hi. Hey, it's OK. We're doing your case next.
I'm talking to my kids. I apologize.

That's OK. Feel free to chime in any time. A physical exam was unremarkable. The thyroid nodule was not palpable and her scope demonstrated normal bilateral vocal fold mobility. So her workup showed the following lab studies with normal TSH 1.552 and free T4 0.8. On her imaging, she had a right thyroid nodule that did not meet criteria for biopsy. And she had two nodules on the left that did meet criteria. One was thyroids five or highly suspicious with the biggest measurement at 1.8 centimeters. And the other also 1.8 centimeters was a thyroid score of four. The isthmus was normal and she had no notable lymphadenopathy.
But before you move on, let's just take a look at this ultrasound. Do you want to comment a little bit on the appearance of that nodule?

Yeah, so this nodule is, I would say, some mostly solid or almost completely solid. I would call it hypoechoic to the surrounding tissue and taller than wide. So based on that, there are, this would be characterized as Tyrods 5 because there's also microcalcification speckled throughout. and there are also punctate echogenic foci within. So this meets criteria for biopsy over the size of one centimeter, so they did biopsy this one.
Dr. Teresova and Dr. Wong, do you have any other things that are jumping out to you about this nodule?

I'm always interested in its relationship with the capsule and the, you know, in here, the strap muscles, and you can see there's a little bit of an anterior push. Nothing I would say that's overt extrathiral extension, but I'm always interested in the boundaries. There's a good margin there with the carotid. And then the things that are more concerning are when they're irregular or they have posterior extracapsular extension or immediate extracapsular extension. Those are the more concerning ones.

Yeah, I think that it's heterogeneous nodules with somewhat levelated margins. So somewhat suspicious, not necessarily something that immediately raising high concern for cancer, but definitely something that requires biopsy in the younger patient.

I think one other thing that bothers me is the margin with the nodule on the cartilaginous structures. It's very kind of a flat and not an acute angle. There's not any cushion of normal thyroid tissue there. So these are the kinds of things that we look out for. Okay. I guess let's keep going. Thank you, Sita.

Thank you. That's great. So biopsy with FNA, the superior nodule, the thyroid's five came back as malignant PTC. And the second nodule in the mid area of the thyroid came back as benign consistent with benign follicular nodule. And so next steps, we have options, active surveillance with interval ultrasound, we have hemothyroid, we have total thyroid.
So let's talk about these options. So what kinds of things would lean you towards or away active surveillance for this patient, Sita? Do you want to comment a little bit on that?

So I think that based on my understanding of thyroid cancer, it's really rare that I would be offering somebody young and healthy and otherwise able to undergo surgery active surveillance. I think that with the PTC nodule, she meets criteria for at least PEMI. So active surveillance might fall under the category of somebody that either cannot undergo surgery or absolutely is unwilling to undergo. But I think in this case, in this case of this young, healthy patient, it isn't something that I would necessarily offer or discuss at length. I would probably talk about...

Sorry, Sita. I'm sorry, Caitlin. Maybe a good time to bring up the new guidelines on the recommendations for active surveillance, which... Sure. Or maybe we can ask one of our expert panelists to bring it in. But in my reading of it, they're pretty close on the one centimeter unless there is like you have a clinical trial at your institution or something else that you're going to be working within. So I think that also kind of brings to bear in this patient.
Yeah. Dr. Tarasova, do you want to comment on that a little bit?

Definitely. So active surveillance was initially introduced in 2015 guidelines and was now in 2025 ATA guidelines on differentiated thyroid cancer. Now it's endorsed as one of the recommendations for management of smaller thyroid cancers, less than 1 centimeters PT, 1A, and 0. So we need to really assess the lymph nodes on the neck to ensure that there is no lymph node involvement to qualify for active surveillance. Also, for smaller papillary thyroid carcinoma, now radiofrequency ablations could be considered, but it's out of the scope for that case. That case is slightly above the threshold for us to consider for biopsy and it makes it not ideal candidate for active surveillance. Typically, the ideal candidate will be patients with smaller biopsy-proven papillary microcarcinomas that in all the patients in the absence of other you know, like the absence of suspicious lymph nodes in the neck, then we have also to ensure that the patient is on board with active surgeries and they are interested and willing to follow without surgery. And we have an expert team who is also interested to provide, have ability to provide high quality ultrasounds for the patients. So many factors have to come together to really qualify for active surveillance. This is a little bit above the threshold that we offer active surveillance. However, there could be circumstances that, you know, let's say if this patient will be pregnant, we'll be naturally offering active surveillance until she will deliver. But in general, not ideal candidate based on the age, appearance of the nodule, the size, and more workup is necessary, definitely.
Dr. Wang, I know you guys have a lot of experience with this and sometimes even larger nodules. What do you think about active surveillance in this case?

Yeah, so I agree completely with Valentina and Saida. It was really well, really eloquently described by both of you. In this case, as you pointed out, Caitlin, you know, it's abutting the trachea. It has this anterior push into the straps. So the location of it within the thyroid is another component that's important. You know, the ideal candidate has a cushion of thyroid around it. The second is that this patient is really young, and if you look at the Miyayuchi data, the younger they are, the more likely they are to fall out over time. Every decade increases their risk that they're going to fall out. And so in aggregate, this patient has a very high chance that she will need surgery at some point because she's so young, and we don't want her to be disappointed with that. The other thing is that if someone like this fails and they progress, it could become adherent to the trachea, it could become extrathyroidal, and then instead of doing a hemithyrectomy, you're suddenly talking about a total thyrotomy. So, the penalty for failed active surveillance with progression, if you select poorly, is more radical therapy in the end. They're all fine in the end. Nobody dies, but there's more radical treatment that's delivered. So I agree with everything that's been said already. At MSK, we do have guidelines for our own protocols where we accept up to 1.5 centimeters of carefully selected lesions. And because we have lots of older patients here that have been through lung cancer and colon cancer, and you find something that's 1.5 and in a good location, this guy's been through chemo and everything, and you just don't want to touch him. So we have tons of people like that here.

There's a lot of that at Moffitt too. Awesome. All right, so I guess our next option there is hemothyroidectomy versus total thyroidectomy if active surveillance is not looking. like the best option for this patient. So let's talk a little about that. Saida, do you want to start about the discussion?

So in discussing the options of the patient, for nodules that are on the smaller end, like often less than one centimeter, there's a stronger recommendation for hemothyroid, even for PTC with the final decision dependent on the pathology after excision. From one to four centimeters, traditionally what I've learned is there's a bit of a gray area. You can offer both options, but you don't have to really push for a total thyroid unless the mass starts to go over four centimeters. In her case, she has a couple of concerning signs that have been discussed on her nodule based on positioning, based on the contours of the nodule, based on, obviously, its diagnosis as PTC. I would probably still offer her a hemihythyridectomy to start off with and see if I can achieve good margins around the tumor, see what the qualities of the nodule are after excision, and then base a decision to do a completion on what pathology results, just to try and save for some of the slight elevated morbidity of a total third, and go from there probably.
What are some of the risks of HEMI versus total in terms of surgical side effects?

You do, of course, there is a slightly higher risk of hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism. I think that's the major one. Anytime that you're doing total, there's a possibility of damage to both nerves, but typically I believe surgeons will, if they lose stem, stop, wait for the nerve to come back and proceed to the other side. I think it would be very rare that you would move forward with surgery if you had suspicion that one side of the nerve was damaged. I think those are the major ones that come to mind. Of course, you have to take Synthroid for the rest of your life. Patients that have a hemithyroid do have, I think, like about a 20% chance of needing a little bit of Synthroid for support. But often, if you proceed with a hemi, many of them don't need to take that additional medication.

We usually quote patients about a 30 to 50% chance of ending up needing thyroid hormone after a lobectomy. So it's actually a bit higher than you would think. reference_conclusion: Following left hemithyroidectomy demonstrating a 1.6 cm classic papillary thyroid carcinoma with lymphovascular invasion and a focally positive posterior margin, as well as a minimally invasive follicular carcinoma without vascular invasion or other high-risk features, the consensus favored surveillance rather than completion thyroidectomy. Management should consist of serial neck ultrasound, thyroglobulin monitoring, and clinical follow-up, with prognosis considered very favorable provided the resection was clinically clean. Completion thyroidectomy was considered reasonable only if operative findings suggested gross residual disease or if additional concern arose from the surgical assessment.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 85-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidentally identified right thyroid nodule.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe with nodal metastases, including a metastatic left level II cervical lymph node.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside biopsy of the right thyroid nodule confirmed papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Clinic ultrasound demonstrated a right thyroid nodule measuring 4.2 x 2.6 x 1.9 cm with microcalcifications and irregular lateral borders. The interface between the right thyroid and trachea was difficult to define, and the strap musculature was difficult to ascertain. Minimal to no thyroid tissue was present on the left. One right level III lateral lymph node contained microcalcifications; central neck nodes were difficult to assess. Formal neck ultrasound showed indeterminate right level IV lymph nodes and indeterminate left level IA and IIA lymph nodes. CT neck demonstrated a large right thyroid nodule measuring 4.4 x 4.0 x 4.3 cm with several internal calcifications and no obvious concerning cervical lymph nodes. CT chest was negative.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF V600E positive.

[ current disease status ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe with a metastatic left level II cervical lymph node confirmed on fine-needle aspiration.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient was asymptomatic at presentation. He had no history of radiation exposure. Examination showed a palpable right thyroid nodule that was firm and fixed along the trachea; voice was strong without breathiness. Flexible laryngoscopic examination was unremarkable. Fine-needle aspiration of a left level II lymph node was positive for metastatic disease, and thyroglobulin washout was positive. Past medical history included coronary artery disease with two coronary stents, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia. Medications included aspirin 81 mg, metformin, levothyroxine, amlodipine, and lisinopril. No prior relevant head and neck surgery or prior anesthesia complications were reported.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, great. Can you see my screen? My name's Annie. I'm one of the PGY-3 residents from Walter Reed. I spent the last four months with Dr. Dillon, so thank you for having me tonight. I will be presenting a moderate case complexity on another PTC. So this was an 85-year-old male who presented back in August with a 3.5-centimeter right thyroid nodule. It was incidentally found during a hearing aid consult with a community ENT and he had an outside biopsy of his nodule and it was proven to be PTC. It was BRAF V600E positive on a firm of testing. And on presentation to Dr. Dillon's clinic, he was completely asymptomatic. He had no history of radiation exposure. In terms of past medical history, he has coronary artery disease with two stents in place on 81 milligrams of aspirin, type 2 diabetes on metformin. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 17-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistent abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma with bulky thyroid primary causing severe tracheal compression; regional nodal metastasis in the right lateral neck; distant metastatic disease was suspected based on markedly elevated calcitonin and indeterminate pulmonary nodules. Germline RET M918T mutation was present, consistent with MEN2B.

[ histopathology results ]: Thyroid biopsy performed at the time of tracheostomy showed medullary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT neck/chest demonstrated a thyroid mass with significant tracheal compression.  
- A pathologic right lateral neck lymph node was present at level II.  
- The common carotid artery was abutted/partially encased by tumor on imaging.  
- The innominate artery was completely encased by tumor.  
- DOTATATE PET demonstrated the known right level II nodal disease, multiple small pulmonary nodules interpreted as indeterminate, and no other evidence of disease elsewhere in the body at baseline.  
- Airway evaluation including bronchoscopy and esophagoscopy showed no transmural tracheal invasion and no transmural esophageal invasion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Germline RET M918T pathogenic mutation was identified.  
- Somatic RET mutation was also identified in the tumor.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Calcitonin was >11,000 at initial workup.  
- BMI was 13 at presentation.  
- Other initial laboratory testing was reported as otherwise unremarkable/within normal limits.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- During EGD/colonoscopy, the patient developed ventilation difficulty followed by significant respiratory distress in recovery.  
- Urgent airway management was performed by pediatric otolaryngology with intubation using a size 5 endotracheal tube.  
- Urgent tracheostomy and thyroid biopsy were performed.  
- The patient was initially tracheostomy-dependent and unable to tolerate capping.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Medullary thyroid carcinoma in the setting of MEN2B, with a bulky thyroid primary causing severe tracheal compression, complete encasement of the innominate artery, right level II nodal metastasis, and indeterminate pulmonary nodules.  
- Calcitonin was >11,000.  
- He remained tracheostomy-dependent and unable to tolerate capping.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Left vocal cord paralysis was present at initial specialist evaluation; right vocal cord function was intact at that time.  
- Mucosal neuromas were present.  
- Phenotypic features characteristic of MEN2B were present.  
- Past medical history and social history were otherwise unremarkable.

And he showed like an over 50% major response rate. And I think in his study, almost everyone made it to surgery and they had like an over 90% R0, R1 resection rate. So this definitely has legs and we do, we do it too here. This is definitely a target you want to go after. So congratulations. That's a fantastic surgery, Dr. Jethwa. Fantastic.

reference_conclusion: The tumor board determined that the disease was not surgically resectable at presentation because of innominate vessel encasement and therefore recommended RET-targeted systemic therapy with selpercatinib as initial management. Following a marked radiographic response after approximately four months of therapy, resection was undertaken with total thyroidectomy, central neck dissection, and right neck dissection, with cardiovascular surgical support available for possible innominate resection. Postoperatively, decannulation was achieved; DOTATATE PET showed no evidence of disease, although calcitonin remained elevated at approximately 500, consistent with persistent disease.
reference_conclusion_quote: I think we can all agree though, that with a nominate encasement like that, this is not a surgical case up front. Unreceptible. [...] So in this specific case, the presence of rat somatic and germline obviously like mutations opens opportunities for selective rat inhibitors and they change the landscape of management for patients with medullary thyroid cancer. they are very well-tolerated. Basically, initially, it was silprocaltenib and pralseltenib, but like the silprocaltenib is the only one that is approved for the treatment of medullary thyroid cancer, red mutant medullary thyroid cancer. So that could be used as a neoadjuvant agent with great tolerability, great response. And so I think that that's something that could be considered. [...] So you got, he had suffragette and maybe he was on it for four months, had a pretty remarkable response. [...] And so I actually did take him to surgery. I did have a cardiovascular surgery who was willing to resect the anominate if needed. [...] did the right neck dissection, total thyroid and central neck [...] I was able to get him decannulated. He is eating everything by mouth, so I got his G-tube out. And his DOTATATE PET showed no evidence of disease. His calcitonin is ranging around 500, so still diseased.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 30-year-old woman; lifelong non-smoker; never drinker.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive oral tongue lesion present for approximately 2 years, with progressive pain, intermittent tongue bleeding, dysphagia/odynophagia, and approximately 20-pound weight loss over the preceding few months.

[ diagnosis ]: Well-differentiated papillary squamous cell carcinoma of the oral tongue, with possible anterior floor-of-mouth involvement and no clinical or radiographic nodal or distant metastatic disease at presentation.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial incisional biopsy of the tongue lesion demonstrated well-differentiated papillary squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- CT imaging demonstrated a 3.1 x 2.8 x 3.0 cm exophytic mass of the oral tongue.  
- Possible involvement of the anterior floor of mouth was reported.  
- No extension to the base of tongue was identified on CT.  
- No cervical adenopathy was identified on imaging.  
- No mandibular involvement was identified clinically or on CT.  
- Metastatic workup was negative.  
- Clinical head and neck examination showed no palpable adenopathy.  
- Endoscopic examination showed clear base of tongue, vallecula, and lateral pharyngeal walls.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- A biopsy had been offered by a local otolaryngologist approximately 2 years earlier, but was declined at that time.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-proven squamous cell carcinoma of the oral tongue with possible anterior floor-of-mouth involvement; no clinical or radiographic nodal or distant metastatic disease had been identified on staging workup.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history included leukemia at approximately 2 years of age, treated with total body radiation and bone marrow transplant.  
- Leukemia had remained in remission.  
- There was no prior history of head and neck cancer.  
- At presentation, the lesion was described clinically as a fungating exophytic mass involving most of the visible oral tongue and extending to the junction of the ventral tongue and floor of mouth.
