reference_discussion.text: All right. Good evening, everyone. It's an honor and a pleasure to be kicking off the virtual activities for this academic year. I'm Fab Al-Bahari. I'm a fellow at the University of Florida. The case that we'll be presenting today is around a patient that we saw not too long ago. She is a 30-year-old woman, a lifelong non-smoker, that presented to our clinic with progressive tongue lesion, with a progressive tongue lesion for about two years. She was offered a biopsy by her local ENT in Panama City two years ago, but refused. And then she presented for an assessment secondary to progressive pain and intermittent tongue bleeding, now two years later, referred by her local otolaryngologist. In terms of other head and neck symptoms, she had some dysphagia or dynaphagia and weight loss of about 20 pounds over the last few months of her symptoms. In terms of her risk factors, she had full body radiation at age of about two years for leukemia. She also had a bone marrow transplant around that time, but she has been in remission since. She's a never smoker, never drinker, and she has no previous head and neck cancers. And she presented to our clinic with no workup. So this is essentially what she presented with, a sort of a fungating exophytic lesion that was covering most of her visible oral tongue and reaching the junction of the eventual tongue with the floor mouth. In terms of her initial work, we did a full head and neck assessment. There were no palpable adenopathies. We scoped her. The base of tongue and molecular were clear. The lateral pharyngeal walls were clear. We also performed an initial incisional biopsy, and we got some head and neck imaging and metastatic workup going.

Just before we go on from there, how do you typically, maybe I'll start with Jen, when you see a patient like this in your office, obviously malignancy is high on the index of suspicion. So assessing somebody like that has got obviously a very large, I imagine quite tender tumor. How would you assess this relationship to the mandible if it's too tender for them to really touch it much on the tongue itself? And then how do you get your tissue diagnosis for these patients?
You're asking me?
Yes.

Okay. I mean, I try and do as good of an exam as I can. Sometimes I'll spray them with some topical anesthetic to get a better exam, um, and assess the mobility from the mandible. Um, obviously imaging is helpful with that. Um, obviously if they have any kind of, um, symptoms of V3 numbness, then I, you know, that will tell me that there is involvement in the mandible. Um, In terms of, sorry, in terms of how I would do a biopsy, I would also do a very basic incisional biopsy of trying to get a good piece of tissue using probably just a scalpel and pickups. Were those your two questions?

It is. Yeah, no, I think I have a very similar approach. I would say the only other subtle thing that you can add, sometimes just pushing under the chin, if it's really painful for them in the mouth, you can actually see how much it wiggles from the mandible. If it's one that's kind of endophytic onto the floor mouth and although not excellent, it gives you a little bit of appreciation for it. Incisional versus a version of that, sometimes doing a punch biopsy, the three millimeter is nice because it's about the exact size of a silver nitrate Q-tip as well. All right, Pod. Talk us through the rest of what you found.

Yeah, so her CT scan showed a 3.1 by 2.8 by 3 centimeter exophytic mass of the oral tongue with possible involvement of the anterior floor of mouth, but there was no extension to the base of tongue again, no adenopathy. Her pathology came back as well differentiated papillary squamous cell carcinoma. And again, this is sort of in the context of a slowly progressive over two years sort of lesion and her metastatic workup was negative. So, you know, in terms of the treatment options, we offered the patient our usual treatment options for oral cavity sclerosal carcinoma. Essentially, you know, on the top, we offered surgery followed by possible radiotherapy. We spoke to her about the extent, possible extent of a resection, her need for neck dissection, and her reconstructive options. We also offered her primary chemo and radiotherapy. We offered her as an option chemo and immuno-oncology or immunotherapy, and obviously no intervention or palliation.

She, after a thorough discussion, she... Before we, why don't we stop there just for a second, just to kind of get the thoughts of the group as well, and then we can maybe go through how you guys proceeded. So on the imaging, what, Peter, what imaging would you get for a patient like this with a pretty advanced oral tongue cancer? I guess more than anything to assess the extent of the primary, and why would you get that?

So for me, typical imaging would be a CT neck and chest or we call it here a CT max face neck you need both order them both of them to get the entire oral cavity so we get that. If there's too much dental artifact and I can't tell the relationship of the tumor to the mandible I'll get an MRI as well. In some cases, I'll also get a PET scan. I can't remember if we got one in this case, but in a case with something unusual like recurrence or someone with suspected aggressive pathology, I might get a PET scan right off the bat as well. But for most of them, a CT neck and chest is what I'll start with.
All right. And Jen, you have similar approach to that as far as when you get a pet. Do you look for adenopathy before considering a pet or?

We generally get pets on every start, unless there is limited time. and or the schedule is too full for a PET scan. And then we can just get a CT neck chest kind of faster. But we really try to get a PET on everyone to start.

As you guys were presenting this at your tumor board, did the history of leukemia and their prior therapy for that at all impact or what it impacted your institution? approach to treatment. And obviously there's still, there's no exact science to that. It sounds like I would imagine fairly low dose radiation for kind of whole body ablation, but also just your counseling with the patient on how the biology of the disease may behave in a patient whose status post prior kind of whole body ablative therapy, even if it was in the distant past. And Peter or Jenny, either one.

In our case up front, didn't really come into the treatment decision algorithm for this patient. Kind of kept it in the back of our mind. Discussing it with the patient, you know, her having been a lifetime non-smoker, she's already had a previous cancer. We discussed with her that she probably has some kind of a genetic defect that we don't know about, and this tumor may not behave like a usual one. That being said, she had it for two years, and it really hadn't spread anywhere, and it was just slowly growing. So we can't really predict exactly how things are going to go for her. She's young, so it's not a common age to get this type of cancer. So we had that discussion with the patient, but it didn't really factor much into the treatment decision, other than the fact she wanted the most aggressive treatment available, which for us was surgery followed by adequate treatment as needed. And then we haven't gotten that part yet, but post-op, you know, it did come in a little bit into the discussion and we can mention that once we get there.
Sure. All right. Well, Fahad, why don't you walk us through how you guys approached it?

Yeah, so one, you know, she opted obviously for surgery after discussing all the options. We essentially explained to her that she will require, you know, an ablative approach to the tongue with a wide resection, hopefully with negative margins. And then we discussed with her the need for neck dissection and reconstruction afterwards, both from a functional perspective and from a holistic treatment approach. The things that came up to mind when we were thinking about her consent were, are we gonna spare her base of tongue or not? Obviously there wasn't any obvious involvement on the CT scan. And we also had in the back of our minds, both pre-op and intra-op, you know, whether we will need a marginal mandibular ectomy or not. She did not have any obvious disease that was close to the mandible upon assessment in the clinic, nor on the CT scan, and interoperatively, we did not think that there was anything involving the mandible.

Which approach, yeah, oh, there you go. Yeah, so this is a great, great point. So what approach would you guys consider? Maybe I'll start with Jen, since Peter, I think this may have been your case. So why don't we get to Dr. Gross's thoughts.

actually have never found the need to do a mandibulotomy. I always try and do anything else. So, and especially in a patient like this, where you really don't, I don't think need one for the approach. I would just make, you know, a gingival incision intra-orally and just drop the whole tongue into the neck to make the posterior cuts. So pull through.

And we didn't really mention this earlier, but I think just since this is one of the first sessions of the year, this patient would obviously need a thorough dental evaluation, you know, high likelihood they may need some additional adjuvant therapy afterwards. These are going to be right in the high dose field for that. So if there are any teeth that need to be removed, especially if you're going to be doing, you know, some sort of a, you know, a lingual release or, or a pull through approach where you're going to be degloving the inner surface of the mandible, that's the time to get the teeth out of there. Cause you would then just overlay the sockets with your flap. And when you do your reconstruction. Yeah, I would say I would certainly use a similar approach. The only caveat of times where I sometimes consider a mandibulotomy is if there's a lot of the floor mouth musculature on one side that may give them some semblance of function. And, and you feel like that's your only chance to preserve that just given how, um, it's growth pattern would, uh, threaten things like the contralateral lingual artery. Uh, usually you can still do those just working above and below, but that's kind of one of the rare times if you're trying to really keep that mylohyoid and kind of the suprahyoid muscles on one side, it would give some semblance of, rather than just resuspending it, that can sometimes help. All right, why don't you talk us through that after the verse action there.

All right. We obviously consider her for bilateral neck dissection. We did not involve level four as she was an N0 neck. And then we also spoke to her about reconstruction. So this was the extent of our resection. We were all the way back to the circumvallic papillae, but we We did it through a pull-through approach, like a hemi-pull-through approach. So we saved, we preserved the super hard muscles on the left side and only sacrificed them on the right side, the side of the pull-through. And this essentially the defect that we ended up with intraoperatively. So that's the base of tongue at the very back and essentially the floor of mouth along with the oral tongue were all removed. So the next question for us was, you know, what are the goals of our reconstruction? Obviously we wanted to separate the oral cavity from the neck. We want to create and maintain bulk for deglutition, for speech intelligibility, to try and prevent aspiration. And the, you know, the famous question is, you know, how do you try to get back sensation by doing any neurophys or nerve transfers? And then also the choice of reconstruction, you know, as in terms of would you go for an ALT or rectus free flap, a thoracodorsal artery flap, rate of form with a beaver tail, or a regional flap in that case.

I see in our participant group here, Dr. Hoey, B. Hoey. I don't know if you can, if it's Dr. Hoey out of South Florida, if you can comment on your approach to reconstruction in this patient. I don't know if you're able to unmute. if he's available to comment. In the meantime, Dr. Gross, maybe you could comment on how you would approach it. Maybe first off, your choice of flap, and then whether or not you have any subtle tricks of the trade, and then whether you consider the nerve repair as well.

You know, I try to get something that has sub-q fat because I find that that doesn't atrophy as much as muscle. So, you know, especially in a female, I would say that an ALT would be my go-to option. You can also two-team, of course. I haven't done erectus, so I can't really comment on that, but my thought is that the donor site morbidity is probably higher with erectus than with an ALT. I also like getting the tensor fasciae latae with ALT for suspension reasons. I think regardless though of what you use, you know, you're trying to get the bulk to get that tongue, that neotongue to touch the hard palate to help with swallowing and speech if they can do that. But all these flaps do end up atrophying over time. I try to suture the TFL to the cutaneous paddle to the gingiva to try and suspend that tissue so it doesn't fall into the neck. But I wouldn't do a regional flap and a young person. I really try not to do tech flaps primarily unless I really have to. And then a radio forum generally just isn't enough bulk, I think.
Absolutely.

Dr. Zygielewski, your thought as well. I know you did this reconstruction, but if you can comment on it, as far as your approach, any subtle ways you do to minimize, kind of help it bunch up for you in a way that doesn't compromise the perforator circulation to the flap and your flap of choice for this.

I think the flap of choice, first of all, I agree. I want something with a lot of sub-Q fat, ideally, and it's going to depend on the patient's body habits. I've seen forearms that are as thick as ALTs, ALTs as thin as forearms. It depends on the patient. This young lady, she was somewhere around like 90 pounds, very, very tiny, very small BMI. Forearm definitely was completely out. Even her rectus was too thin. We looked at rectus versus ALT, and her ALT actually looked better than the rectus would have been in this case. So certainly want something with bulk. I usually measure it to overcorrect, kind of measure from one part of the defect. So like we'll say from one side of the teeth to the other with an arch that'll touch the palate to try to get a sense of some extra width on it. And then I don't have any really good tricks to get it to bunch up other than just travel along the flap more than I would around the teeth. It's pretty rare that you'd put too much in there and congest the flap or your perforators, but I have seen that happen before where I had to cut out a bunch of flap because it was too much. I think I've seen that once. Most of the other time, if it feels like it's too much and it's difficult to suture, you're probably doing it right, is what I tell our fellows. And then I like to use a TFL to suspend it. I do it on the undersurface of the mandible by drilling little holes into the mandible and suturing through there. And Fahad will show you what we did. Those are the main things. If it's a huge defect and I'm taking some muscle as well, like with an ALT, I'll do a neuroraphy between the nerve to the vastus to the hypoglossal nerve to try to maintain some of the muscle to keep some bulk over time, even though a lot of it's still going to atrophy, but if you reinnervate it, it'll keep some bulk. Um, you know, those are kind of the main things that I try to go for over correction and some suspension. And if you can keep some of the super high muscles, like we were able to in this case on one side, that's great. Um, I think those would be the main things I would think of.

Absolutely is a great case. I think it highlights so many important points. Um, You know, I think it is important to remember, you know, there were studies in years past to look at, and it was actually out of the Wash U group, that looked at using latissimus free flap and reinnervating the thoracodorsal nerve to the hypoglossal nerve, and they would kind of put it crossways. in a delayed fashion, you could see it kind of contract. And although you could see some movement, it didn't actually, there was a question of whether it actually had significant benefit to swallowing. And so I think it's not been used as much for that. Spending a little bit more time here because I think you're one a lot of great points and I'm not sure if Natalia is going to be able to join us we're still trying to reach her. So, while before we move on from this case maybe one additional points so for the subtotal or maybe if they say this had extended back to involve the base of tongue. When do you consider doing just a total glassectomy versus including a laryngectomy? Obviously, for a young person, that's a very difficult conversation. Dr. Gross, do you have a cut off? Do you offer a total glassectomy just by itself with necks and reconstruction? Or do you, you know, some some people I know have a philosophy of strongly considering an upfront laryngectomy in those patients?

I try and preserve the larynx at all costs, and even if, you know, a segment of the hyoid is, has to be resected, as long as the epiglottis is maintained, I will, you know, I'm going to try and save the larynx. And of course, I do warn them that there could be intractable aspiration if I'm getting kind of a little bit close, or I have to take even you know, some of the mucosa off of the epiglottis, for example. And we would, if that was the case, go back at a later date.
And Peter, do you have a similar approach?

Yeah, I agree. I like to preserve the larynx if possible, pretty much at all costs. I think patients can do very well that way. But once you're starting to remove part of the supraglottic structure like the epiglottis, then you're just creating a nice conduit for any food and liquid to just go straight down there. So once it's starting to involve resecting part of the supraglottic structures, then I would opt for a total laryngectomy. I agree, the hyoid doesn't play a huge role in it, you can still suspend the larynx through the thyroid cartilage if you want to do sutures to the mandible so that can help. If the patients had radiation therapy, I would be much more quick to do a total gloss total laryngectomy because those patients already have a huge swallowing deficit and they're probably going to be chronically aspirating. in a patient who's had a full dose of radiation before, I would push probably more towards a total laryngectomy with a total vasectomy. But otherwise, I think it's a good option in most patients to preserve the larynx.

Sometimes for these patients, we will offer them a neoadjuvant Um, chemo or, you know, just because obviously, I don't think she would be a trial candidate. So it might just be chemo. But because. If you're worried about a laryngectomy, that is with the hopes of trying to spare the larynx, because in the end, they're going to need a laryngectomy anyway, but I don't think that would be the case necessarily for this patient.

Yeah, I would agree that in surgery, if it persists, you know, it's a rare instance you consider something like that, because especially without a lot of nodal disease, it's unlikely you're going to go from that to an incurable cancer and the surgery would likely be similar. So there are certainly some patients who would would balk at, you know, that and would consider doing some sort of a non-surgical neoadjuvant. And it also gives you a sense on the biology of the disease, you know, as well. All right, well, why don't we transition to our next case. Dr. Chang, maybe if you could stop sharing. We'll have Dr. Chang call hers up and then.

reference_conclusion: The patient elected primary surgical management for oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma. The agreed operative plan was wide ablative resection of the tongue and involved floor of mouth with the goal of negative margins, bilateral neck dissection excluding level IV in the clinically N0 neck, and immediate reconstruction. Mandibular resection was not planned because there was no clinical, radiographic, or intraoperative evidence of mandibular involvement.

We did not involve level four as she was an N0 neck. And then we also spoke to her about reconstruction. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 47-year-old male. Past medical history included hypertension and asthma. He was a never smoker and never drinker.

[ chief complaint ]: Five months of left facial swelling and pain, with progressive trismus and odynophagia. Oral intake had been mostly liquids. Associated symptoms included 20-pound weight loss and two weeks of numbness of the left lower face and chin. He had initially been treated for presumed dental infection with mandibular molar extractions and antibiotics without improvement.

[ diagnosis ]: Invasive moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the left oral cavity/buccal region, clinically staged cT4b cN2b cM0. Primary tumor involved the left buccal cheek/retromolar trigone region with extension into the masticator space and infratemporal fossa, with perineural spread along the mandibular nerve to the skull base. Regional nodal disease involved left level IB and level II nodes.

[ histopathology results ]: Buccal biopsy showed invasive moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- CT neck demonstrated an endophytic mass involving the retromolar trigone and masticator space, with erosion of the pterygoid plates and posterior maxilla, and involvement of the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles. Tumor approached the coronoid attachment of the temporalis and extended into the buccal space. No clear cortical invasion of the mandible was identified.  
- MRI with contrast demonstrated tumor between the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles with thickening, inflammation, and enhancement of the mandibular nerve tracking to the skull base/foramen, concerning for perineural spread to the skull base. Coronal imaging showed extensive buccal edema and enhancement.  
- PET-CT demonstrated FDG-avid primary tumor centered in the masticator space and FDG-avid level II and level IB lymph nodes. No pulmonary, hepatic, or other distant metastatic disease was identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]: Not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Prior to oncologic evaluation, mandibular molars were extracted and antibiotics were administered for presumed dental infection, without improvement.

[ current disease status ]: Very locally advanced squamous cell carcinoma of the left oral cavity, clinically staged cT4b cN2b cM0, with extension into the masticator space and infratemporal fossa and perineural spread along the mandibular nerve to the skull base, and clinically involved left level IB and level II nodes. No distant metastatic disease had been identified on PET-CT.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Examination showed left facial swelling, severe trismus to approximately 1 cm, and an ulcerated endophytic mass of the left buccal cheek extending to the retromolar trigone, tonsil, lateral soft palate, maxillary alveolar ridge, hard palate, and second and third mandibular molars.  
- Tumor extension onto the buccal cheek was near full thickness without skin involvement and approached the oral commissure.  
- Left V3 numbness was present.  
- Palpable mobile left level IB and level II lymph nodes were present.  
- Endoscopic examination showed no extension to the posterior pharynx, base of tongue, or nasopharynx.

For this one, I would certainly do CT max face, neck, and chest. This looks like it's probably going to be involving bone most likely I would also get an MRI to get a better sense of the bone involvement as well as the soft tissue involvement through the terror goads, sometimes the MRI is going to show that a little bit better. Now, if it's possible to get a PET scan within a reasonable amount of time, I might do that instead of the CT chest. It's not always the case since our patients are often traveling longer distances and sometimes getting the CT chest is just more practical, but that's where I would start.
All right. Jen, I don't know if you're available or not to comment on that.
I agree with all of that.

And you can see how, although it's very advanced in its presentation, it's not that easy to actually expose and visualize the tumor, I would imagine, at least based on the fact this is an endoscopic exam with the trismus and everything. So it's certainly one of those that can oftentimes come into your office fairly far along in their presentation. All right, so maybe we can see how the imaging looked here.

Yes, so the first thing we did was a CT neck. So I can play this on the left, but basically we're going to get to the vertebral fossa masticator space and there's a mass that's eroding through involving the retromolar trigon and eroding through the pterygoid plates with clear involvement of the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles. It's also approaching kind of the coronoid attachment of the temporalis. and there's extension also onto the buccal space down here. So it's a pretty endophytic tumor. There's no clear cortical invasion of the mandible, but certainly obviously cortical invasion of the pterygoid plates and the posterior maxilla. And then on the right is just a snapshot of the tumor at the level of the pterygoid plates with erosion of the plates and then clear involvement of the pterygoid muscles. We also obtained an MRI on this patient, and this is a T1 with contrast given the lower lip, lower chin and facial numbness. There was concern for mandibular nerve invasion. So this is a T1 with contrast, and we can see that tumor sort of redemonstrated. And if you look in between sort of the lateral medial pterygoid muscles, and follow it up, you can see that the mandibular nerve, there's thickening and inflammation of the mandibular nerve and enhancement, and it tracks all the way to the foramen. And then this is a coronal, you can see extensive sort of buckle edema and enhancement, and re-demonstrated is the nerve as it goes into the skull base. So we were concerned obviously at this point that there was perigross intraneural or perineural invasion to the level of the skull base. And we did end up getting a PET-CT scan like we do for many of our patients, but especially in someone with pretty concern for novel disease, but it's such advanced oral cavity cancer. We did obtain a PET scan. It redemonstrates that tumor centered in the masticator space and then some level two and level one B nodes that are FDG avid. The scan doesn't show this, but there was no pulmonary or liver or any other distant metastatic disease on the pet. So the buccal biopsy was positive for invasive moderately differentiated squamous cell cancer. We tentatively staged this clinically as a T4B, N2B, M0. T4B, given there was invasion of the masticator space and the infratemporal fossa, the pterygoid plates, and also imaging and clinical evidence of perinatal invasion to the skull base. And so, management of this patient, you know, our first initial questions were, you know, which T4B tumors are considered resectable? You know, we're sort of classically taught that T4B tumors are unresectable. but we know from practice that not all T4V tumors are the same and that we do tend to offer definitive surgery to many patients. And if we do offer surgery, you know, what is the goal of surgery? Is it truly that we think we can get an R0 resection versus, you know, resecting macroscopic disease knowing that we may leave some microscopic disease behind? And what is the goal in terms of, are we trying to truly improve survival or disease control in these patients? or is this more of a palliative surgery as these surgery, I mean, these patients can be very difficult to palliate with non-surgical treatment. And then with regards to skull base management, you know, how much skull base disease is too much for surgery. And then, you know, later we'll sort of get into what the decision-making was at tumor board, but what is the role of, you know, induction or new adjuvant chemotherapy in patients with very locally advanced oral cavity cancer.

Catherine, this is a very challenging case. Maybe we'll start with Peter on this one. What's your thought on discussions with a patient like this? Obviously young, sounds like fairly robust and healthy individual who has obviously a very advanced tumor, the likelihood of getting, well, maybe you can comment on whether you think that it's surgically perceptible or not and how you would approach this in your conversations with the patient.

Sure, I would be very realistic with the patient, starting off with discussing how extensive disease is and what the reality is of every treatment option. You know, the survival rate is not going to be high no matter what we do. But if we do nothing or opt for non-surgical treatments, the outcome is going to be miserable. And, you know, as you mentioned, you know, palliation through surgery might be the best option in any way you look at it. And then is surgery, is the goal of surgery and RZO resection possible? And I think it is possible in this case. I don't think you're gonna get wide margins on this. That's, I think, probably quite impossible to do, but the best chance of this patient surviving with any decent outcome would be to start with surgery. So that's how I would look at it, but have a very frank discussion with the patient about exactly what that means and how big the surgery is going to be and what the recovery is going to be like and the importance of recovering in a way that he can get to the next step of treatment because surgery alone is not going to do it. He's obviously going to need adjuvant treatment as well.

What's your thoughts on the last line there, the consideration of neoadjuvant therapy in a patient like this? A lot of times it sounds great, but in practice, it's always a question of whether it has a role or not. I'm curious how it's managed at your institution. Obviously, I'd love to get Jen's thoughts as well.

Yeah, every now and then we get a patient who really wants to do something like that and the reality is in a situation like this, we don't have a lot of room for this tumor to get worse. So, if we did neoadjuvant chemo or neoadjuvant immunotherapy and the tumor grew, the next place it's going to grow through is the skull base or in case the carotid or you know, or grow in any number of directions. So I think discussing that with the patient would be like, it's very risky, but it could get much worse. And then we're not gonna be left with any other option. On the other hand, you know, there's a small chance it could get better, but I haven't seen that. I haven't seen this play out in a good way. I haven't seen it many times, but the times I've seen it, it's always gone south.
Dr. Gross, your thoughts?

If this was a T4A tumor, we have some trial options for neoadjuvant immunotherapy. I think for chemotherapy, I agree with Peter. It's really all about having a frank discussion with the patient and the family and seeing, you know, sometimes they I feel one way versus another. I think one thing to note is that with the extent of disease and especially intraneural and just the size of it, I would expect there's a very high probability of positive margins with this surgical resection. I mean, it's not impossible to get our zero, but so. Keeping that in mind, I think we are, we do offer chemotherapy, induction chemotherapy in these cases, kind of depending on the medical oncologist because of that reason. And knowing that, you know, regardless of what we offer them, they're not gonna do well. So it's a very unfortunate kind of place to be in.

With regards to the skull base involvement here, it looks like it's primarily perineural invasion. Uh, it looked like obviously the, the pterygoid plates and the, the medial and lateral pterygoid muscles were involved, but as far as bone erosion, and maybe I missed it, it looked like it was primarily going up B3 through a valley into the lower, you know, basically, um, the lower part of the trigeminal. nerve. And so on those, you know, if you're approaching them surgically, sometimes they have a little bit, you feel a little bit better about being able to at least more precisely address the area of concern. I think you recognize it's still going to be almost a certainty there's going to be some microscopic residual disease, at least in my practice. I've never seen one where there's a fat nerve on an MRI that's going through a skull base foramen. that you can then get a very widely clear proximal margin that's negative. You may be able to, you know, I guess the only one is sometimes the facial nerve because you have a larger, you know, area that you can resect of that. But, you know, things like V3, you know, you can sometimes go and find ovale and rotundum, remove the intervening bone, and that gives you a little bit more wiggle room to get up and resect more of the nerve. you know, if, and I'm curious to see in the next slides, what was done here, but if you're going to approach this surgically, what sort of soft tissue approach would you do? And then for the diffuse, you know, even with the absence of bone erosion on the mandible, how would you address kind of the diffuse pterygoid muscle involvement here? As far, as far as that goes, maybe I'll start with you, Peter.

And this is always a challenge, number one, to get to that area. And in a case like this, I would want big exposure, lots of comfort. I would split the lip and peel the face off laterally. We don't need a mandibulotomy because we're going to be taking bone anyway. So we're essentially making a mandibulotomy. And it's probably going to be a hemimandibulotomy in this case, all the way up to the TMJ. So it probably makes the cut somewhere around maybe down the midline or parasympathesis, and then essentially you're creating a mandibulotomy that way. The other part is it looked like it may have been invading the posterior aspect of the maxilla. So I would make that maxillary cut posteriorly as well to kind of detach the pterygoids from there, and then work my way up towards the skull base. And in this case, it may even remove a zygoma and potentially replace it later, plate it back together to get into the infratemporal fossa. But I'd want to get all along the sphenoid bone and the skull base as much as possible to get all the pterygoids and their attachments out as much as we can. That's our best chance for, I think, getting a R0 resection, though we know there's a good chance we're going to be leaving some microscopic disease behind somewhere. And then as I do that, I expect lots of bleeding from the pterygoid plexus. So keep my bipolar up really high, like at 80. Use, you know, other energy devices like ligature or harmonic scalpel. Crank the bovie up pretty high. And just work my way around that with the idea being I want to clear everything off that skull base out of the infratemporal fall zone.
Jen, do you have any additional thoughts on how you tackle it, you know, these tumors extending to the pterygoid muscles?

Yeah, so I think that I've been able to, obviously totally case dependent, do a segmental mandible where you just remove the coronoid, you know, like the anterior mandible, so you don't have to Late or recon the bone and then by. Removing the anterior segment of the mandible there, you can then get access to, like, the lateral terracotta. Origin at the condyle and kind of go all the way to the condor head. If you need to, you can get the entire the terracotta muscles. It also helps. to get the teragoid plates. This patient in particular did have cutaneous involvement, so it made that part, it would make that part a lot easier for access as well. But generally for these patients, it will require some radical parotidectomy just because of the proximity to the parotid. And just the multi directional approach, if you don't have the continuous involvement, you know, obviously, you have to go trans oral trans cervical. I, I mentioned, I don't like doing him and a lot of me if I don't have to. So, with this patient, you know, I would. if there wasn't the cutaneous involvement, extend the incision kind of like a parotid and lift the skin as high as possible to get access because of the trismus and just kind of go from all angles to get what I need to do.

You know, and I think one of the things that's a challenge when things get into the pterygoid is there's so little resistance for tumor spread. And, you know, I think when instances like that happen, it's sometimes at least I've found it's helpful. Think of the muscle going to attach its attachments and depending on the morbidity it would impart, you know, you sometimes need to actually take those areas out on block. So here, you know, if it's extending to the pterygoid plates, you know, you have to take those out. You know, the, you know, depending on how lateral the, um, tumor extension is, you know, it's to the mandible, uh, you know, at, right at the retromolar trigone, it would be a little tricky to save the posterior ramus. If possibly you could, I think I'd have to look at the image again, but sometimes then if you unblock or removing the ramus as part of the resection, then it, it helps to just think about what is it. It's always tight to deliver that down. So what are your attachments? So you can detach. you know, the condyle of the mandible. You can obviously detach the temporalis muscle attachments. You got the spheno-mandibular and the stylo-mandibular ligaments down below. And then a lot of times, mainly what you're set on, if you've made your pterygoid plate cuts, that's usually an attachment as well. You take your distal and your proximal, you know, ECA branches. And then, as Peter mentioned, obviously there's always bleeding either in the pterygoid plexus or in those distal kind of terminal branches off the external carotid going up to, you know, spinosum with the middle meningeal. You'll want to address also coming right back behind the mandible, the auriculotemporal nerve, But sometimes that and the lingual nerve can kind of help guide you towards where that's going up to a valley. Cause they're both going to join V3 near the skull base. And that's usually your last attachment. So you've detached all these other ones cause they're easier to address on the way in. And then it's that last kind of battle to be able to dissect down. And, and, uh, Peter mentioned a great approach, you know, sometimes going from up above, um, you know, either taking down the zygoma and peeling down the temporalis muscle. or if you come at it from below and are able to move the facial nerve branches out of the way and still get access and divide through some of the temporalis, you can get, you know, to the skull base and then, you know, dissect down and looking back kind of back behind where those kind of lateral turquoise plates extend, you can see a valley there and address it almost from up above where the tumor is. These are hard, though, because it's always a challenge. You never, unless you kind of take those wider approaches, you never really feel like you get a legitimate margin when they get into the kind of these muscular beds like this. Well, Catherine, you want to take us through the rest of the case here?

Okay, so So we discussed this patient at our tumor board and we essentially offered two treatment options. One was induction TPF followed by surgery and adjuvant chemoradiation versus surgery and adjuvant chemoradiation. And we did have a frank discussion that obtaining negative surgical margins would be difficult and that his prognosis was fairly poor, especially given the perineural invasion either way. And there was a discussion of proton therapy as an adjuvant treatment for the perineural skull base disease. Ultimately, the patient chose option two. And we did discuss that with induction, you know, chemotherapy, there was no guarantee at all that he would have any regression of disease. But certainly there was potential that he would have progression of disease and he didn't have a lot of space to go there. So the patient underwent surgery, which was a subtotal maxillectomy, sparing the orbital floor with an infratemporal fossa resection. Um, because the, um, tumor and the buckle space approach the skin, we did start with just sort of a wide local excision, um, of the cheek, um, full thickness, um, and we were able to access the mandible and connect that with our neck incision. Um, we did do a segmental or, um, uh, marginal mandibular ectomy of just the ramus and took the coronoid and release the temporalis muscle, which gave us a little more mouth opening. And we did take, release the masseter and we're able to make some of those cuts through the external facial incision. And then we were able to get enough mouth opening after doing those maneuvers to do some of this intraorally as well. We then did a bilateral neck dissection and reconstructed with a fibula free flap. We ended up taking the hard palate basically to the K9 and did a subtotal maxillectomy, resected the pterygoid plates, and then we followed…we resected most…basically the entirety of the masticator muscles with the exception of the temporalis that was sitting in the temporalis fossa…temporal fossa. Of note, so the maxillary mandibular nerve did have positive margins intraoperatively, and so those nerves were followed back to their respective foramen. and were drilled down actually to obtain additional margins, which were set for permanent. We did note, unfortunately, gross disease in the foramen ovale. And then initially in our resection specimen, we had two margins that had microscopic disease, the infratemporal fossa muscles kind of superiorly, and then also the posterior pharyngeal margin. We had to take our cuts kind of almost to the lateral soft palate. Those were actually positive and we had to resect twice and we ended up sending them both for just permanence on final. And this is just a picture of the resection. You can see sort of extended all the way to, we actually ended up having to take part of the commissure. You can see the buckle space and then sort of the maxillectomy. And then posteriorly, you can see the pterygoid muscles that we had to take. And then on the superior aspect is the hard palate and the nasal floor. And then the bottom right shows kind of a superior view of that specimen and the sort of extra oral resection that we had to do. So final pathology, this was a really large 7.7 centimeter tumor with a depth of invasion of 23 millimeters with LVI and gross PNI. The final specimen margins did end up being negative. We were able to clear the infratemporal fossa and pharyngeal margins, but again, they were resected twice due to microscopic disease on frozen. And then the final on the mandibular maxillary nerve were positive for carcinoma with intraneural involvement with the mandibular nerve. And then four of the 31 lymph nodes were positive with major E and E. Um, and so sort of my last set of questions, you know, obviously we discussed that this patient would certainly need chemo radiation. Um, we discussed with them. Discuss that option with an upfront, given just how aggressive, um, locally the cancer was. Um, and then sort of what our other thoughts about this case, um, were, you know, management of skull base disease in the setting of perineural invasion. And so initially on the scan, we didn't see sort of the gross tumor kind of going up to the level of the skull base. It was mostly tracking along the mandibular nerve. And so how far do you chase PNI into the skull base? And what is the role of adjuvant proton therapy in patients with gross paranormal invasion, especially if you are unable to clear that margin? And then the last question is like kind of a loaded question, but how far do you chase a positive margin in a patient like this? How much benefit are they really getting in this setting?

Well, this is a great case, Dr Chang, and thank you so much for putting it together and really amazing surgery. I'll comment briefly. Actually, I know Natalia has been able to join us. I do want to give her a little time to present here in a moment. So maybe we could just go briefly through this. I know my mentor at one point when I was in training always said, you know, your closest margin is your closest margin. So at least my take on chasing margins is if you feel like without a lot of additional morbidity, you're going to actually improve their margin status, I consider doing it. But if it's something where you already have a known positive margin. How much you're going to go chasing after other ones, especially if you're imparting a lot of additional morbidity, is something that I typically would shy away from just depending, because you know at that point you're really dependent on the biology of the disease, whether it's going to respond to this adjuvant therapy or not. Certainly, with proximal nerve involvement near the skull base, we'd consider protons if available here. But at the same time, I think IMRT can also offer it. One question came up from the audience I'd love to briefly get. Maybe I'll have Jen comment on this just because, you know, she was involved in the case. Commenting on the approach to reconstruction, this was, it sounds like accomplished with a fibula. I don't know if there was an additional soft tissue flap on top of that. It sounds like the fibula was used more for maxillary reconstruction since you did a marginal mandibulectomy and left the lower ramus of the mandible. Was there additional soft tissue component or just a massive fibula skin paddle?
So, I'm actually on maternity leave, so I did not do this case. I haven't even seen Catherine in person yet. Catherine, do you want to comment? My, my guess is the city was for the maxilla though.

Yeah. Yes. So, um, we did a one segment fibula to reconstruct the maxilla and we did use a very massive, um, fibula skin paddle. Um, initially we were going to try to do like a chimeric skin, um, skin paddle where, cause we did find, um, a proximal and a distal perforator, but we use like spy fluorescence and actually saw that this like huge, like 15, 16 meters centimeter skin paddle was supplied by that one perforator. And we just de-upped it and sort of folded it to reconstruct the intraoral component. And then at the commissure was sort of where the DF portion, we sutured it sort of to the mucosal, I guess, lip or mucosal lip and then the external paddle within just to reconstruct the face.
So just because this is such an interesting reconstructive challenge, Peter, your approach to that one, how would you have tackled it?
You know, it sounds like a fairly, you know, subtotal maxillectomy, a large soft tissue void that's there, but the mandible itself has continuity in it.

The way I would think about this is a couple of things that don't always come to mind. Number one would be the infratemporal fossa. You're going to leave a big dead space in there if you don't fill it with something. You have some facial skin and then you have some mid-face as well to reconstruct. So I would think I need some bulk. A little bit of bone would be good. You could do this whole thing with soft tissue. I mean, you could say, this prognosis is terrible. Let's do the quickest possible flap just to have a safe wound and get the patient off the table. I think that would be perfectly reasonable. You could do a big rectus, ALT, or latissimus. But if you wanted to achieve all the goals, I think scap tip with a pedicle lat with skin, not necessarily a Tdap, but latissimus with skin would be good. You can also take some serratus anterior if you need to fill in that infratemporal fossa so you don't get this big, hollowed, sunken in look after the patient gets out of your treatment. that'd probably be my first choice. But if this patient wasn't in the best of health and we needed to get them off the table sooner, I might say, let's do something that we can do a little quicker in a two-team manner and maybe just soft tissue, a big ALT or a rectus flap.
Yeah, I think that's a great point.

And, Catherine, maybe I'll have you stop sharing just so we can be getting Natalia's slides loaded up. While we're making that transition, the comment on the infratemporal vasa dead space is a critical one because you're going to basically clear off the entire skull base and then radiate it. So getting some sort of soft tissue bulk in there to fill that, because if it starts to fall down, there's no way to get it back up there. And so, you know, not only getting something in, but trying to tack it up in a way that it's favored to swell and almost push against that bone really gives the best chance of it kind of sealing in. Occasionally you can get these little kind of potential spaces in there that become a big hassle down the road because they're virtually impossible to repair. Well, Natalia Hodges, I appreciate very much you joining us. I know it sounds like you've had a busy day. So thank you for being nimble and being here at UT Southwestern. Welcome to fellowship. I'm glad to have you a part of the session. We're a little late on time, but I think we'll still be able to get through this case. We may just abbreviate it a little more than some, but we'll probably just spill over a little bit past the normal time. So yeah, if you will, why don't you take it away.

reference_conclusion: Tumor board consensus was to offer either induction TPF followed by surgery and adjuvant chemoradiation or upfront surgery followed by adjuvant chemoradiation, with counseling that negative margins would be difficult to achieve and prognosis remained poor given perineural skull base involvement. The patient elected upfront surgical management. Resection was performed with subtotal maxillectomy sparing the orbital floor, infratemporal fossa resection, bilateral neck dissection, and fibula free flap reconstruction. Postoperatively, adjuvant chemoradiation was indicated, and proton therapy was discussed as a potential adjuvant option for perineural skull base disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 18-year-old female at initial diagnosis in 2011; age 32 years at most recent documented follow-up.

[ chief complaint ]: Right ventral lateral tongue lesion present for approximately 3 months at initial presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent right oral tongue squamous neoplasia, including well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma and multiple episodes of carcinoma in situ/dysplasia. Initial stage was documented as T1N0 in 2011. A recurrent invasive lesion in 2018 was documented as T1.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial outside excision in 2011 showed well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma arising in a papilloma; p16 negative; excision margin 0.2 mm. Subsequent partial glossectomy in 2011 showed squamous mucosa with focal mild dysplasia; margins negative for dysplasia and carcinoma. Right selective neck dissection levels I-IV in 2011 showed 0/19 lymph nodes positive. In 2014, direct laryngoscopy with biopsies of the base of tongue and oral tongue showed carcinoma in situ, suspicious for invasion; subsequent partial glossectomy from the same site showed carcinoma in situ. In 2016, partial glossectomy again showed carcinoma in situ. In 2017, there were benign biopsies, followed by partial glossectomy with final pathology showing well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma measuring 0.2 cm, depth of invasion 0.5 mm, no lymphovascular invasion, no perineural invasion, and closest margin 2.5 mm at the deep margin. In 2021, partial glossectomy showed moderate to severe dysplasia, with severe dysplasia 1 mm from the lateral margin. In April of the most recent documented year, partial glossectomy specimen was benign.

[ imaging findings ]: In 2011, CT neck and PET demonstrated FDG avidity corresponding to the oral tongue lesion; otherwise unremarkable. The lesion was initially misread as tongue base on imaging but clinically represented oral tongue disease. Over subsequent surveillance, there were two additional CT neck studies and two additional PET scans. Neck ultrasound was used as the primary surveillance imaging modality thereafter. Initial examination documented a 1.4 cm right ventral lateral tongue lesion sparing the floor of mouth, with no cervical lymphadenopathy; endoscopic examination was normal.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: p16 negative on the initial 2011 squamous cell carcinoma specimen. Formal genetic evaluation assessed low likelihood for Fanconi anemia; no formal genetic testing was performed because further testing was declined.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Outside hospital local resection of tongue lesion was performed in 2011 and identified squamous cell carcinoma. Re-resection with partial glossectomy was performed in 2011 and showed no residual carcinoma, with negative margins for dysplasia and carcinoma. Right selective neck dissection levels I-IV was performed in 2011 and was node-negative (0/19). In 2014, direct laryngoscopy with biopsies followed by partial glossectomy was performed for recurrent lesion; final pathology showed carcinoma in situ. In 2016, recurrent lesion was treated with partial glossectomy; pathology showed carcinoma in situ. In 2017, benign biopsies were followed by partial glossectomy; pathology showed a 0.2 cm well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma with 0.5 mm depth of invasion, no LVI/PNI, and negative margins. In 2021, another recurrent lesion was resected by partial glossectomy; pathology showed moderate to severe dysplasia. In April of the most recent documented year, another partial glossectomy was performed for a new lesion; pathology was benign. No adjuvant therapy was administered.

[ current disease status ]: Most recent documented resection in April showed benign pathology. The patient remained under close surveillance approximately every 3 months.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history was significant for beta-mannosidosis deficiency, described as a lysosomal storage disease. She was a non-smoker and non-drinker. Initial examination at referral after outside excision showed granulation tissue at the prior excision site. No cervical lymphadenopathy was documented at initial presentation.

So this is an 18 year old female initially when she presented, she had a tongue lesion for three months and outside hospital, otolaryngologist kind of resected it. and had found that there was squamous cell carcinoma and had referred her over to Dr. Sumer. Non-smoker, non-drinker, and nothing particular about her social history otherwise either. on her physical exam, she had, this is like her physical exam when she had initially presented to the outside, ENT 1.4 centimeters, right ventral lateral tongue lesion, sparing the floor of mouth, no cervical lymphadenopathy, and her scope was normal. When she came to us, she had a like kind of just granulation tissue evidence of where this excision occurred. CT, neck, and pet at that time. This is from 2011, so unfortunately I didn't have access to the images for this, but it was misread as tongue-based. It really was the oral tongue and had corresponding FDG ability in that area, otherwise unremarkable. So her initial biopsy from the outside was well-differentiated squamous low carcinoma, arising in a papilloma, P16 negative, and the excision margins were 0.2 millimeters. She was counseled on re-resection with wide margins, knowing that, you know, the final pathology may not reveal carcinoma. That was done, and so she had a partial glassectomy. That pathology revealed squamous mucosal focal mouth dysplasia. Margins were negative for both dysplasia and carcinoma. The decision was also made to perform a right neck dissection, levels one through four, selective neck dissection. There were zero out of 19 lymph nodes that were positive. The reason for that was based on the description of how the lesion initially looked and the size in order to try to avoid any kind of radiation therapy. That's kind of the thought process behind the neck dissection at that time.

Can I just ask a quick question? So Peter, when do you consider doing, so say you have a fairly, you know, an oral lesion, doesn't feel overly deep. And, you know, your question whether it was just a surface lesion or a truly invasive, when do you make the cutoff or when you do an upfront neck dissection versus not, and do you ever base that on frozen section or wait for permanent pathology?

Good question. So I start off doing a punch biopsy in clinic, like you were mentioning earlier, and I try to get something that helps the punch so I can get a good sense of the thickness. So I'll start with that. If that can give me a definitive answer, then I can make the call up front. And I like to use two millimeters as a cutoff. Anything more than two, that's my cutoff for recommending a neck dissection in most oral cavity cancers. And if I don't have the depth of invasion on the biopsy, then I discuss the option with the patient and tell them, you know, we could do an FAS on front, it might be overkill, or we can do it in a staged fashion, cut it out, wait for the final. the final pathology and then come back and do the neck dissection after. I've talked to our pathologists and they haven't been able to tell me that they can do a reliable depth of invasion on frozen sections. They've always said what they prefer to do, final pathology. I would stage it if that's what the patient preferred to do.
Excellent. Thank you.

All right, so moving on a few years, in 2014 now, she had a recurrence of a suspicious lesion. She underwent a biopsy in the operating room, a drug laryngoscopy with biopsies of the base of tongue as well as the oral tongue. That revealed carcinoma in situ and suspicious for invasion, and so then was recommended to have a partial glaucectomy. Same site, that final pathology revealed carcinoma in situ.
Quick question, I guess, before we go from there.
On the invasive disease, Dr. Gross, how do you assess the margins at the time of surgery for those who have partial glassectomy for an invasive, like lateral tongue cancer, for example?
You mean with frozen section?
Right. Yeah. Do you do it as a specimen-based or a wound bed?

Oh, specimen base, I mean, I think there's enough literature out there showing that the. Outcomes are better and the risk of having to do a section is lower. And then, of course. If you had, if you're doing tumor bed based margins and it's positive, you know, the likelihood of getting to that same spot to re resect is pretty low. There's, I can't remember what percent it is, but it's, it's pretty low. So we at Emory, at least we do it all tumor based margins. We walk it over to the pathologist and review it. And we, you know, if I have any questions at all, we'll actually stay there and cut it with the pathologist so I can see exactly where the closest margin is, re-resect if needed. But hopefully you get it right on the first go around.
Peter, you have a similar approach?

Yeah, the way I do it is before cutting out the tumor, I kind of map out where my resection is going to be. And so I take a ruler, I like to do two centimeter surgical margins. So I measure out two centimeters all the way around. And then I take circumferential margins all the way around my plan resection, then do the resection and take the deepest margin off right before we remove the entire tumor. knowing that that's probably the least reliable of all the margins. I think the superficial mucosal ones are the most reliable and the easiest to re-excise if you have to, but I agree with Jen. It's that deep one that the chance of you getting right back to where it was is pretty pretty low. And then I do think that taking the specimen to the pathologist is key, not only for assessing, you know, potentially close margins that you can re-excise, but also for orienting the specimen for analysis afterwards. Many times they don't always understand the three-dimensional anatomy. So if you can show it to them, draw a picture, help them ink it, it can make a big difference in your pathology reporting.

Great question came up from Fahad on the role of sentinel node biopsy in this original one. Do you ever consider doing that for early oral cancers that are clinically in zero? Either Jen or Peter, either one of you have experience in that.

Yeah, I mean, we participate in the HN006 trial. So we actually are only offering sentinel node trials for oral cavity if they're, sorry, sentinel lymph node biopsies for oral cavity if they're on that trial. I think we tend to err on the side of neck dissection, especially if it's oral tongue, just because, you know, they can be very aggressive, they can come back even if it looks like it might be really superficial. It might be more, have more depth than you initially think. So we tend to just do a neck dissection on most patients unless they are not a good surgical candidate or they really, really, you know, insist, or if they are interested in the HN 066 trial and get randomized into the sentinel lymph node arm.

Sounds good. Yeah. And just remember, we do have level one evidence to show that you need to manage the neck somehow once it's above three millimeters deep. And some people certainly use a little lower cutoff from the D'Cruz study, you know, conspiring observation with close surveillance and therapeutic dissection if they develop nodes versus an up to front elective neck dissection. They shared a significant survival advantage when they did the upfront dissection, but that's what this HN006 is designed to look at. Well, would the sentinel node offer a similar benefit by kind of stratifying which one of those need the formal dissection by testing the most adverse nodes? Very good. Natalia, you want to continue on?

All right, so similarly, a couple of years later, in 2016, she had another recurrence of the lesion, had a partial glaucectomy, and that showed carcinoma in situ once again. A couple of benign biopsies in 2017, followed by another partial glaucectomy. This is probably the one that we have the most information from. Here she had final pathology showing a well-differentiated swing-missile carcinoma, 0.2 centimeters in size. Depth of invasion was 0.5 millimeters. No lymphovascular invasion, no perineural invasion. And then the closest margin was 2.5 millimeters away, and that was the deep margin. She then continued follow-up. Again, another lesion. She had no adjuvant treatment at that time. She had another recurrence of a lesion in 2021. Had that resected with partial gloss, moderate to severe dysplasia on that with severe dysplasia one millimeter away from the lateral margin. And then finally another lesion this year in April for which she went another partial glaucectomy and that was benign. So here's like a just summary kind of of her treatment history that we had just reviewed. So she was diagnosed at 18, she's now 32. Her staging as follows with T1 and zero, 2011 recurrence, T1 in 2018 with that summary of pathology right there that I just discussed. and kind of her entire history right there with the surgeries that she had.

So this is obviously one of the most challenging scenarios, and I'm glad I'm on this session because I'm hoping that you guys all tell me how to manage these people, because they are very, very difficult. I certainly have not found a great way. Peter, maybe I'll start with you. These patients with just kind of multifocal, this one seems like it's centered a bit more in one area, the right tongue, but certainly there are ones where it's proliferative rucous leukoplakia or like implantists where it's just popping up everywhere as dysplasia or pre-cancer, sometimes early invasive disease. How do you manage those? Your surveillance regimen, do you have any other non-surgical approaches that you use like topical agents or other chemopreventive agents that you believe in.

A great question. I think, just like you said, these are very challenging patients. I've got a number of these in my practice. For surveillance, they're usually very in tune. And so I tell them, we're going to see you every three months or so. Anytime you notice something new, call the office and I'll see you right away. And anytime they find something new, they're typically in there pretty quickly. And eventually, from my experience, they'll end up with something that needs a much bigger surgery. I had one recently that eventually ended up needing a mandibulectomy with these multiple recurrent areas. Some of the other ones, I tried to convince one of our medical oncologists to just give immunotherapy to them to see if this would help, because we had nothing else to offer. And we came up with a compromise. I don't know if you guys are using any of the circulating tumor DNA tests, but there's one signataria that we've been using. And so we decided, let's do that. And if it comes back positive, maybe we can convince the insurance company to pay for some rounds of Keytruda. Luckily, it was negative, but that was kind of our thinking about something we might be able to offer these patients that if they still have circulating tumor DNA after their latest resection, perhaps we can add in some immunotherapy as sort of a treatment slash preventative measure. But I don't have the answer to these, unfortunately.
Any topical agents or any other tricks of the trade, Dr. Gross?

Yeah, I mean, these are very challenging. I think there aren't great chemo preventative options for this problem. You know, we have a trial for active or previous smokers who can take metformin as a chemo prevention if they have any type of dysplasia. And there is some data from a phase 2 trial showing that in these patients. There is a greater likelihood that the dysplasia resolves so. I mean, if they aren't a smoker, I don't really have a good option for them. And kind of like what Peter said, unfortunately, I, in my, you know, few years of practice, have seen that these often progress to larger cancers, and you just have to keep a very close eye on them. So, preserving…sorry. So, preserving the radiation for the large cancer is kind of what we tend to do.

Yeah, I agree. I think one of the most tricky situations is people kind of overreact to a close margin or displeasure or something and try and then throw like radiation or some other adjuvant therapy at it. And like you said, you almost want to save that for a later time. I have heard of a clinical trial of using topical 5-FU, which is similar to what you use in early skin cancers, but not for invasive disease, for pre-cancers. There's a place out of Ohio, it's actually not an academic, it's a private practice group, but I've had a couple of patients who've interacted with, and actually so far I've been very impressed with the patients I've sent over there, And I think there actually may be one for ones where they have multifocal invasive disease. I believe there's an ongoing clinical trial that actually does use immunotherapy for that, I think for the similar reasons, but since it's done on trial, I think they were able to get it passed, but obviously it's a very challenging situation. One question from the audience came in, I think that leads to your next slide, Natalia, is, you know, was Fanconi's anemia ruled out or what other testing was done?

Yeah, so we she did formally see the genetic team over here. And they, they just clinically kind of determine her risk factors and whatnot and didn't do any formal genetic testing but they decided that she had a low likelihood for pancomenemia. Actually, she declined further genetic testing, I should say. Her surveillance with us has been kind of similar to what others have said about every three months or so she has been coming in. Over the course of these years, she had Aside from the initial CT and PET, she had like one other CT neck, or sorry, two other CT necks and two other PET scans. And then other than that, her main surveillance imaging modality has been a neck ultrasound. And yeah, that's no other kind of adjuvant treatments or adjuvant therapies or testing besides that.

reference_conclusion: The patient is to continue close surveillance with clinical follow-up approximately every three months and expedited evaluation for any new oral lesion. No adjuvant therapy is planned at this time; management remains surgical surveillance, with radiation reserved for development of a larger cancer. Surveillance imaging has primarily consisted of neck ultrasound.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Male patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent epistaxis. At the current recurrence, the only symptom was mild bloody nose. He had no orbital symptoms, vision was intact, and extraocular movements were intact.

[ diagnosis ]: SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma. Initial diagnosis was biopsy proven. A first local recurrence in the right ethmoid region was biopsy proven and treated. A later recurrence was also biopsy proven and showed the same tumor type. Disease recurred locally without evidence of systemic metastatic disease at the times described.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy confirmed SMARCB1-deficient sinus carcinoma. Tissue specimens obtained during bilateral sinus surgery performed for post-radiation sinusitis were negative for tumor. Biopsy of a right-sided ethmoid mass confirmed recurrent disease. After two cycles of additional neoadjuvant chemotherapy, surgical resection yielded no tumor in the specimen; frozen sections and all margins were negative. A subsequent later lesion was again biopsy proven recurrent disease of the same histologic type.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- PET/CT performed one year after bilateral sinus surgery showed no evidence of disease.  
- Surveillance MRI obtained three months later demonstrated a right-sided ethmoid mass.  
- At the first recurrence, disease was described as localized, in the frontal ethmoid region/medial orbit, within the prior radiation field.  
- Repeat imaging after two cycles of additional neoadjuvant chemotherapy showed interval increase in tumor size in the vertical dimension inferiorly.  
- Postoperative PET imaging performed soon after that resection showed no additional disease.  
- Approximately one year later, imaging demonstrated a new recurrence in a slightly more anterior location, with greater orbital involvement than previously described.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: SMARCB1 deficiency was identified. No additional molecular profiling results were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial treatment consisted of induction chemotherapy followed by chemoradiation, with a complete response.  
- Nine months after completion of treatment, bilateral sinus surgery was performed for post-radiation sinusitis; pathology was negative for tumor.  
- At the first local recurrence, the patient received additional neoadjuvant chemotherapy for two cycles.  
- Repeat imaging after these two cycles showed progression, with increased inferior vertical extent of the mass.  
- Surgical resection was then performed. Pathology from the resection specimen showed no residual tumor; frozen sections and margins were negative.  
- Approximately one year later, a further biopsy-proven local recurrence developed.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-proven second local recurrence of SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, more anterior than the prior recurrence and with greater orbital involvement, within a previously irradiated field and without documented systemic disease.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The recurrent disease occurred less than two years from primary treatment.  
- The patient had previously received a full course of radiation to the local site.
