reference_discussion.text: Yeah, well, the basic facts about doing a history and physical examination and seeing what the orbit is doing, and then often we get a pathology review, so assuming that it is what it is, and then review what imaging we have, and then decide on other imaging, so obviously an MRI would be appropriate here, and then whatever type of metastatic workup that you would normally do. In this case, I think a PET CT would be very worthwhile to look at for metastatic disease. And then putting that all together then would be discussed in a multidisciplinary tumor board.

Great. And then knowing that it is now a SMARCB1 deficient sinus carcinoma where you have the biopsy proven diagnosis, what is, how would you recommend treatment if there is no metastatic disease in this patient?

Well, we would normally start with discussions around neoadjuvant type treatment and then look at the response and then go on to consider chemoradiation and look at the response there and then versus surgery with that. So we have to look at a whole host of factors and patient preference.

Wonderful. Thank you so much for sharing that. It's very, very comprehensive and well said. So we did cover this in the Icarcine nasal tumors document where we talk a little bit about management options for different tumors based on histopathology. So in this case, as you mentioned earlier, Dr. Widerich, we do look at neoadjuvant chemotherapy response as a guide for treatment based off of the MD Anderson paper, And it was provided really strong evidence for us to be able to delineate out responses and subsequent treatment methods. So then this patient underwent initial treatment with induction chemotherapy followed by chemo radiation and he had a complete response. Nine months after his treatment, he continued to have really bothersome quality of life issues. So he underwent a bilateral sinus surgery for post-radiation sinusitis. Tissue specimens sent during the sinus surgery were all negative for tumor. He did not have any signs of that. One year after his sinus surgery, his PET CT demonstrated no evidence of any disease. So he was still disease-free. And then three months later, in surveillance MRI, he developed a right-sided ethmoid mass, and the biopsy confirms recurrent disease. Dr. Gelsiler, what are your thoughts about this phenomenon at this point?

Yeah, that's a rapid recurrence, unfortunately. So we're looking at basically less than two years from primary treatment. Yes. Which isn't surprising. I would want to completely restate this patient with another PET scan just to make sure it didn't pop up with any regional or distant metastatic disease. Um, and then, you know, assuming that he was able to get full dose radiation to the local site, he's within two years. Um, I would want to know more about how that orbit's doing. Um, Is he having any double vision? And then, you know, it's hard to tell from this single slice if, you know, how, what that dura too is exactly doing. I would kind of want to look more closely also at a CT scan, just to kind of get a better sense. And if I felt like there was dural involvement, but general principle would be, I would send this tumor off for genetic analysis to see if there was any systemic therapy. But I would likely offer this patient surgery, assuming that there's no T2 signal change in the brain. And then regarding the orbit, I'd have a pretty low threshold to exonerate a patient like this, although it almost looks like on this slice that you could maybe try to preserve it. But I would go into the surgery telling the patient that if we couldn't clear that orbital margin, we would have to take it.

Very well said, and definitely a little additional information is he did have no evidence of other systemic disease, just localized. A couple of questions in, since you brought up some of the treatment algorithms and possibilities for this patient. Dr. Liao, would you consider re-irradiation if the patient had a full course of radiation in this case?

Yeah, that's a good question. I think this soon from his prior treatment, I would be reluctant. We're pretty selective about re-radiation in general, you know, in this region. This looks to be kind of within field recurrence, you know, along this frontal ethmoid region and medial orbit. So it would have been, I think, within his prior field and received full dose. I don't see relationship to the, you know, orbital apex there, but the frontal lobe there would have received full dose and would have had 60 gray. I think if this is resectable disease, and that's an option, I think that would be preferred versus systemic therapy. But tough case, I definitely have seen cases of local infield relapse for this entity.

Appreciate it. And also to Dr. Gelsinger, back to your question. He actually had no orbital symptoms at all. Yeah. Intact vision, extraocular movements intact. The only symptom he had was a little bit of bloody nose. So of course these are very challenging. Repeating chemotherapy, Dr. Price, what is your thought on about this regarding, you know, he just had quite a few doses and he has this local recurrence.

So I would definitely consider that as an option. I would look to see, you know, what his response was to the induction chemotherapy by itself to see if he did have chemotherapy sensitive disease at that time. This is a relatively fast recurrence, but it still would have been quite a while since his last chemotherapy dose. So I wouldn't take that off the table. We don't have a, you know, you know, huge list of effective chemotherapies for this disease. So, you know, I wouldn't want to throw something out too early. So I would definitely, you know, look back at his original regimen if he'd had a good response to reduction chemotherapy, you know, offer that as an option to retreat. Agree completely with getting, you know, molecular testing to see is there something targetable because even if, you know, best case scenario, he'd responded to that initial therapy, which was probably a platinum-based regimen and you retreat, you know, that still is only going to buy you a certain amount of time. You know, you can't continue somebody on platinum doublet chemotherapy indefinitely, so you kind of have to start in parallel looking for other options, you know, that you might be able to use, you know, as kind of a maintenance therapy if you're successful at debulking it initially, or just to have in the future, certainly if this patient were to go to surgery and then be followed afterwards, you might put those in your back pocket immediately. You know, in my experience with these cancers, they're often not as chemotherapy sensitive as some of the other sinonasal cancers that we see. So I think it's a little bit tricky. And so looking at kind of what actually happened in vivo with somebody with chemotherapy response can be helpful.

Thank you for sharing that. Yeah, his initial response to the chemotherapy was pretty dramatic. So he actually did fortunately have a good response to the neoadjuvant treatment. So we're also brought up a little bit when touched upon it by Dr. Geldseiler, management considerations for the orbit. Dr. Levine, any additional commentary on just what you would do with the orbit in this case, knowing that there's no symptoms related to it?

Yeah, I mean, obviously it's much harder when there's no symptoms. I think that some of that is a discussion with the patient themselves and kind of talking to them about their prognosis now that they've had a recurrence. One thing that we have done previously is to take periorbita and take orbital fat and then try to kind of recover that area so that we're still taking a margin on it. It's not always the best margin, but we've had some success with that. And I do think that that would be something I would talk to them about as an option, especially since that could preserve a lot of the function and still give you a little bit more cushion. But I do think that that is a really tough discussion with a patient, especially when they have really good function.

Great points. and definitely not a lot of consensus in that, as you'll see in the ICAR document. Dr. Gardner, if we resected the skull base regarding reconstruction, especially with the history of recent radiation, what are some considerations and any changes in the strategy for you?

Sure. I think this appears to have pretty clear dural involvement. And even if you're unsure, I think if you're doing surgery for this, you're trying to get margin on it. And that would mean an anterior craniofacial resection. In this setting, a vascularized reconstruction, which usually would involve pericranial flap, but the absence of any nasal tissues and also the aggressiveness of the tumor, we would probably do a pericranial flap. I like to take out just the frontal sinus itself, the anterior table, the frontal sinus, so it's not perhaps a true craniotomy, but a transfrontal sinus approach. take out the anterior sable, remove the posterior table so you cranialize it and use a pericranial flap with temporalis fascia as your dural substitute and suture in as much as you can the temporalis fascia and lay the extra durally tunneled pericranial flap on top of that. And that creates a very nice barrier. And at least you have a two layer, one of which is vascularized reconstruction. And that's really quite a good option in this setting.

Yeah, these are challenging reconstructions because of the radiation as well. And then role of immunotherapy, and we briefly touched on this. Dr. Price, can you expand a little bit more on kind of your experience with immunotherapy in patients with these problems?

So definitely a tough question. I don't think we have a lot of really good data. I think in the face of a bad tumor, especially a recurrent one, you know, we'll often throw a lot of things at it. And so, you know, thinking about chemo immunotherapy, you know, is reasonable, but, you know, it would be better or nice to see if there are some markers of immunotherapy response, you know, if you were doing some additional sequencing or testing, if you saw, you know, higher mutation burden, or had other surrogate markers. PD-L1 can be done, although it's an imperfect predictor of response. Again, I haven't seen a lot of great responses with immunotherapy as single agents in these tumors. So I tend to incorporate it with chemotherapy if there's a reason to do that. That's not to say still wouldn't do it, especially if they had a marker that would suggest benefit. But I, you know, I haven't seen a lot of sort of really durable, good responses like we'll see, you know, a little bit more frequently in some of the squamous cell cancers. Great.

So he underwent, we talked about his case at Tumor Board again. He actually underwent additional courses of neoadjuvant chemotherapy. He went through two cycles and had a repeat scan. That was his new repeat scan. It looks like the tumor grew a little bit more in the vertical dimension inferiorly. So the thought was, okay, well, he's not responding. He's progressing through something that he responded to earlier. So to surgery we go. I took him to surgery, I sent frozens, there's no tumor in the specimen anywhere, all margins were negative, and then he had a PET done relatively soon afterwards, which also showed no additional disease anywhere. that's what it looked like post-op. Very limited resection really because there was no tumor in the specimen, nothing along the lamina, nothing along the skull base. So Dr. London, have you seen this type of phenomenon before and what are your thoughts about it?

That's actually quite surprising. So he previously biopsy positive when you said after three months of that PET-CT, that was biopsied in clinic, it was positive, and then got two more rounds of chemo? Yes. Interesting. I don't know that I've seen that with chemo, maybe with some patients with immunotherapy, but not necessarily for SMART-B1 deficient carcinoma. Very surprising.

Yeah, this was a huge surprise to me. I actually asked a couple of colleagues around and some people have seen it before just because I think it worked so well the first time and I guess it did work really well this time. It's just that the mass itself did not fully regress at this point. So I thought that was just really interesting. And I think we're gonna probably see it more and more as we adopt this treatment strategy for different tumors.
How long ago was that?

That was a year ago, and then I have the next part of the story. So he then developed this about a year afterwards, being completely free of disease, but this is different appearing and in a different location or close, but it's actually a little more anterior. Okay. So this was interesting as well. So actually, Dr. Geltzer, I listened to you, brought it up. What do you think, options at this point?

I mean, it's the same thing I said. I would restage him again. I mean, this disease has a propensity to have distant metastatic failure. So I would worry that's going to happen at some point. This looks like, at least in the left-sided image, that it's even more in his orbit. Again, I would ask him about symptoms related to that. And I mean, it's, it almost looks more unilateral than it did last time. You know, this, if I was going to, I would definitely offer upfront surgery. Now that he's kind of failed this treatment strategy twice, you certainly could do it again, give him another more induction and do it again. But I mean, this thing keeps on recurring and now the interval is actually earlier. And I would, I wouldn't try to preserve the orbit with that scan. I would do. an orbital exoneration with neurosurgery and we could take out that adjacent dura directly through the orbit and then reconstruct it with a free flap.
Yeah. So, you know, the, it's interesting to say that he again had no symptoms except for nose bleeding, that's really what it turned out to be.
You biopsy that, that was biopsy proven recurrence.

Yeah, same tumor type as well. So this patient is very much against highly aggressive surgery, of course, so we had the discussion. He ended up getting, he ended up wanting to go with the option of getting treated again with a similar regimen, although he's now also on immunotherapy. He's about six months out again, without any disease again, and also no metastasis. So the saga continues, but I felt this case was not your typical scenario for an undifferentiated carcinoma and felt like it was a worthwhile discussion. I learned so much from everybody. So appreciate all of your thoughts. I think the next case is going to be Dr. Chobi. So Dr. Chobi, go ahead and take it away.

reference_conclusion: For localized recurrent SMARCB1-deficient sinonasal carcinoma, repeat staging with PET/CT was recommended to exclude regional or distant metastatic disease, with additional assessment of orbital and possible dural involvement and molecular/genetic analysis to identify potential systemic therapy options. If the recurrence remained resectable and confined locally, surgical salvage was favored over re-irradiation or systemic therapy; given repeated recurrence after prior induction chemotherapy, upfront surgery was advised, with low threshold for orbital exenteration if orbital margins could not be cleared and consideration of craniofacial resection with dural resection/reconstruction when indicated. Re-treatment with the prior chemotherapy regimen was considered a possible option because of the prior dramatic response, with immunotherapy viewed primarily in combination with chemotherapy rather than as a single agent.

So I tend to incorporate it with chemotherapy if there's a reason to do that. [...] I would definitely offer upfront surgery. Now that he's kind of failed this treatment strategy twice [...] I wouldn't try to preserve the orbit with that scan. I would do an orbital exoneration with neurosurgery and we could take out that adjacent dura directly through the orbit and then reconstruct it with a free flap.

reference_discussion.text: Thanks, Ed. Really interesting case. Thanks for presenting that and appreciate all the insights from the panelists. So we're going to change gears a little bit, and I'm going to present a cyanasome mucosal melanoma case. Go to the next slide, please. Certainly, this disease entity is one we discussed quite a bit and is rapidly evolving in treatment. On the Carl Snyderman good, bad, and ugly scale, I think we all consider melanoma to be on the ugly, ugly side of that scale. So this is a middle-aged woman who presented to me with six months of some decreased sense of smell, nosebleeds as well. There's the initial MRI scan, just a quick shot of what she has there, and got a biopsy before she was sent to me, which showed it to be mucosal melanoma. That was reviewed at our institution. And the next few slides, just some CT scan sort of sample images showing this right-sided ethmoidal tumor abutting the skull base. based on the MRI scans, CT scans. The bone is relatively intact, and perhaps a little bit of dural touching, but probably not direct involvement of the dural on that MRI scan. Go to the next slide, Ed. Perfect. So this was her biopsy. The genetic panel was negative, which is not altogether uncommon in mucosa melanoma. K67 was 32%, so high for most tumors, but in melanoma, we see many of them above 40%, so kind of moderate to high in K67. PET scan was clean, and there's an endoscopic image there just below. We can go to the next slide, and perfect, to the next one. So the first question to the panelists is, in my practice, we have moved quite a bit towards induction immunotherapy for most mucosal melanomas, again, because of their aggressiveness, their propensity for distance spread. But this is a bit more of a unique case. This is a limited disease case. This would be a T3N0M0 mucosal melanoma, so limited disease. So in a case like this, what I wanted to discuss with a limited local disease burden, no regional metastatic disease, what would people's thoughts be on the role of surgery for this disease? And perhaps I'll start with Dr. Widerich, if you would chime in first on, again, local only, a respectable mucosal melanoma in the role for upfront surgery.

Yeah, I never know what to do with mucosal melanoma anymore. Um, it's like an open season on that. It typically, um, we're not in Toronto. We're not quite at the stage where we're giving induction immuno, although we talk about it all the time. Uh, we just haven't done it. And so typically what happens is, is that I reset or we resect it and then it comes back to tumor board. Then there's a discussion about, do we radiate it or do we do immuno? And, um, we're typically going more to immuno now and sort of saving the radiation for when and if they recur later on. That's sort of, because radiation, we can, Dr. Liao, but, you know, it sort of helps with local control. Maybe local regional control doesn't really impact overall survival much. It's really the immuno that's been the game changer.

Yeah, I agree. We have those same conversations, it seems like, every other week in tumor board about, you know, these pluses and minuses. Dr. Price, if I could ask you to chime in, you know, we use a lot of immunotherapy now for mucosal melanoma. Maybe chime in a little bit on your thought on that as an upfront treatment strategy and or as an adjuvant treatment strategy.

Yeah, so I think, Toph, I mean certainly immunotherapy, you know, melanoma is the original tumor for immunotherapy. I think it's challenging for mucosal melanoma because the response rates are not really as robust as you'd see, you know, with cutaneous, so it's always a little bit hard. This case would be really hard just because it is, you know, kind of earlier stage and, you know, you could potentially just resect it. So I'm not sure what the right answer is here. You know, our groups here tend to do, you know, induction of olumab, ipilimumab, either alone or sometimes even with radiation prior to surgery, and then, you know, offer some adjuvant nivolumab, kind of borrowing from some of the stage three melanoma. So, you know, I think we are pretty aggressive about incorporating immunotherapy, in part because we don't have a lot of other really good options, too, and these don't tend to be you know, BRAF mutant or is sensitive, you know, to chemotherapy and things like that. So we do use it a lot. I think this case is a true gray area.

Yeah. And if you just click to the next slide, and Dr. Price, just one follow-up question for you, and you alluded to this already. You know, obviously in cutaneous melanoma, BRAF inhibitor therapy is a game changer. You know, 60 to 70% of cutaneous melanomas have a BRAF mutation. Unfortunately, mucosal melanoma, it's in that sort of 2% to 4% range across the board. In your experience, though, if this did have a BRAF mutation, would you consider a BRAF inhibitor therapy as opposed to more non-targeted immunotherapy?

Oh, that's a good question. And I'm trying to think if I've had a BRAF-mutated mucosal melanoma. But you know, I think I would probably still, you know, lean towards immunotherapy as frontline treatment.

Next slide, Ed. Can I ask her a quick question? Go ahead, Matt. So do you find a role for immunotherapy in a strictly adjuvant setting in this disease, or would you only give it adjuvantly if you had given it in the neoadjuvant context prior?

Yeah, I mean, we, you know, tend to, do it if we've done it up front, you know, and you have some, you know, at least some sense potentially of, you know, pathologic response and tolerance and all of that.

Yeah. Just because, and the rest of the head and neck, and just correct me if I'm wrong, we've been finding that unless there's gross tumor up front, like in just a strictly adjuvant setting after surgery, we found that immunotherapy doesn't really work all that great. Is that fair?

Yeah. I mean, for, are you talking about for squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck? I mean, we really don't use it. I mean, there's trials ongoing. We don't use it for squamous cell cancers in the head and neck in the adjuvant setting. We don't use it with radiation either in the definitive setting. Occasionally we'll use it as part of a kind of neoadjuvant regimen. Usually we would like to do that more on trial, but occasionally we do it off trial. But I agree in the adjuvant setting for just head and neck cancer in general, You know, we really don't use it. Yeah.

Dr. Liao, just to sort of get some input here, and Dr. Widerich, you know, astutely mentioned earlier that radiation has been shown to increase local control for mucosal melanoma, but at least to date, there's not much data showing survival benefit, yet we oftentimes use it because of local control, as well as sort of, you know, what else do we have to use for this disease process. What are your thoughts on radiation for mucosal melanoma, either as an adjuvant treatment or as a definitive treatment, perhaps with upfront immunotherapy?

Yeah, great question. We debate also the same questions of what is the optimal sequence with these, so it's just such a challenge. I would say from the patients I've seen, there's also pretty diverse natural history with these patients. Some of them definitely do blossom with distant metastatic disease very quickly, but I have some that have had a more indolent kind of disease course or just a tendency towards local recurrence. We will usually discuss these in multidisciplinary fashion, you know, and having patients meet with all services. And in a patient with more kind of confined, localized disease like this that's amenable to endoscopic resection, we usually go for surgery and then we discuss the possibility of postoperative radiation and immunotherapy. Uh, well, I do tell patients exactly that, that there seems to be a signal towards reduction in local recurrence, but not a clear impact on survival, you know, or just a metastasis, which kind of mirrors our experience with cutaneous melanoma. Yeah. Um, but I have had patients, you know, they're long-term survivors that had more localized disease like this, where we treat it with surgery. We treat it with postoperative radiation to optimize or local control and then plus minus, you know, adjuvant immunotherapy.

Yeah, I think I know the answer to this question, but I'll ask it anyway. Any data on proton versus photon, does it make a difference, or do you personally think it makes a difference in your experience?

Good question. We were just reviewing that actually coincidentally and working on a manuscript now. We have a very small series. It's about 10 or 15 patients that were treated with endoscopic resection, post-op proton radiation, and then plus minus adjuvant systemic therapy with immunotherapy. From that, the local control was very favorable on that, but it was very short-term follow-up. It was in like the 90% range, but patients failed with distant metastatic disease, unfortunately. And it was a small series, but it wasn't clear that adjuvant immunotherapy made a difference. As far as radiation technique, we tend to treat patients with protons a little bit preferentially over IMRT. The differences as far as toxicity, acute toxicity are probably pretty modest, and as far as improvements in local control, admittedly, it's probably pretty modest, but in this anatomic region where you're in close proximity to neural structures of the optics, the brain, there's some reduction in the overall integral dose exposure with protons over IMRT.
I think you had a question.

Oh, yeah, I was just going to sort of anecdotes but the recurrence is when they have in the nose and in the skull base, and then they start to bleed, and it's a real management and horrible problem for the patient. So that's why my bias is often towards saying radiation to try and slow down or prevent some of that if possible, because if they're not responding to immuno, then you're trying that and they're in and out of the eMERGE and in and out of hospital, and it's a real horrible thing for the patient. If we can control it, it's nice.

Yeah, that's a very good point. Go to the next slide, Ed, if you don't mind. Fantastic. Paul, for a case like this, who is a bad disease player, potentially amenable to surgery currently, when you think about a tumor like this, what would you recommend for a surgical resection if you were to do upfront surgery for this patient?

Well, I wouldn't let them think that that's going to be probably curative because of the concern for skip lesion that you mentioned. I think with a lesion like this, if you're going to do surgery and your plan is to do something close to curative, you need to be aggressive with it. And that would mean a margin, which in this case is not quite so straightforward as predictable, but at least the lamina paprecia, perhaps periorbita, skull base, and plus or minus dura in this situation. I think you can get a sense for what the involvement of dura is, but it is less predictable in this case. And I don't know that dura has to be resected in this. I would be curious to hear what the rest of the panelists think. And in general, I would say that we probably stop shy of it unless the tumor clearly invades the bony skull base.

Yeah, good points. Just kind of building on that, Dr. London, if you don't mind offering your thoughts on sort of Paul's point about the dura, but also the role of frozen section. So historically, melanoma frozen section is difficult for pathologists. What's your experience with frozen and melanoma? Things like dura resection, would you rely on a frozen to make that intraoperative decision?

Yeah, those are all good questions. You know, typically, frozens are inaccurate or, you know, at best, not very helpful for melanoma. So it's really hard to be guided by those. In terms of whether, you know, our group would take or consider resecting the dura, to me, it depends on where the tumor is attached to and where it's kind of invading along, whether it's of filling that sinus or if it's, you know, along the entire skull base mucosa, then, you know, there's a good chance it could be invading the olfactory phyla, in which case we would lean towards taking the dura and, as Dr. Gardner said, you know, an aggressive surgery if you're going to go for surgery for this patient.

Yeah. And last question on the surgical aspect, Dr. Levine, just mind commenting for us frequently these have skip lesions. So we have the main tumor, we're going to resect that. But then as I show in that picture in a separate case, there's skip lesions in various other areas. What is your approach to those? Do you try to chase and resect all those? Do you consider the cats out of the bag at that point in time? What are your thoughts on skip lesions in mucosal melanoma?

So I think, you know, the reality is that once you have skipped lesions that are visible in multiple areas, there are probably ones that are visible, that aren't visible, that you're just not going to be able to see. So I do think that anything really obvious that's easy to resect, you know, we're all surgeons, we like to try to do our best to get as much disease out as possible. I think that that's reasonable. But I think that it's naive to believe that once you have seen a number of skip lesions that you're going to be able to get all of them during your surgery, it's extremely unlikely.

Yeah, good point. Perfect. So I did just want to briefly show that there is a decent amount of evidence for mucosal melanoma. So I had the good fortune of writing this part of the document. And what I want to show here is that surgery with negative margins does have a survival benefit. So important to know. So if something is resectable, at least most data out there shows that there is a survival benefit to surgical resection. My fear, of course, that if I resect something and they heal from surgery for six weeks, by the time we scan them for staging, they've met it out in those six weeks. That's something to think about as well with immunotherapy. Next slide, please. This is what's out there as far as the role of immunotherapy. We have really just an early experience with immunotherapy for mucosal melanoma. There's more data being investigated now and being published currently. But likely in those cases with advanced or metastatic disease, it's probably effective. And then there is some emerging data for induction immunotherapy as well. So certainly something to consider. Typically, it's undifferentiated. So it's going to be something like ipinevo as opposed to a BRF-targeted therapy. But certainly, we use that more and more in our practice, both here in Pittsburgh as well as at Mayo Clinic as well. Awesome. So thanks for your input on that case. And I think the third case is back to Ed.

reference_conclusion: For localized sinonasal mucosal melanoma amenable to endoscopic resection, the multidisciplinary consensus favored upfront surgical resection. Postoperative management should include discussion of adjuvant radiation to improve local control, with consideration of adjuvant immunotherapy in multidisciplinary follow-up. If surgery is undertaken with curative intent, resection should be aggressive, including appropriate skull base margins with consideration of lamina papyracea, periorbita, and selective dura resection based on extent of involvement.
reference_conclusion_quote: in a patient with more kind of confined, localized disease like this that's amenable to endoscopic resection, we usually go for surgery and then we discuss the possibility of postoperative radiation and immunotherapy. [...] but I have had patients, you know, they're long-term survivors that had more localized disease like this, where we treat it with surgery. We treat it with postoperative radiation to optimize or local control and then plus minus, you know, adjuvant immunotherapy. [...] I think with a lesion like this, if you're going to do surgery and your plan is to do something close to curative, you need to be aggressive with it. And that would mean a margin, which in this case is not quite so straightforward as predictable, but at least the lamina paprecia, perhaps periorbita, skull base, and plus or minus dura in this situation.

[ patient demographics ]: Demographic details were not provided.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent nasopharyngeal carcinoma with new PET/CT abnormality after prior definitive chemoradiation, salvage stereotactic radiation, and pembrolizumab.

[ diagnosis ]: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma, initially stage IIIB. The patient achieved a complete response after definitive chemoradiation. Five years later, recurrent disease developed in the right masticator space. Subsequent biopsy-proven recurrent disease in the nasopharynx was identified. A right temporal lobe lesion was present.

[ histopathology results ]: Recurrent nasopharyngeal carcinoma in the nasopharynx was biopsy proven.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial recurrence occurred in the right masticator space 5 years after definitive treatment.  
- A subsequent PET/CT demonstrated a nasopharyngeal-region abnormality and a right temporal lobe lesion.  
- CT imaging demonstrated bony involvement.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic findings were reported.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory results were reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Definitive chemoradiation was administered for stage IIIB nasopharyngeal carcinoma, with complete response.  
- Five years later, recurrence in the right masticator space was treated with stereotactic radiation in 5 fractions and pembrolizumab for 5 cycles.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-proven locally recurrent nasopharyngeal carcinoma of the nasopharynx after prior definitive chemoradiation, salvage stereotactic re-irradiation, and pembrolizumab, with bony involvement demonstrated on CT. A right temporal lobe lesion was also present.

[ other clinical data ]: Prior radiation exposure included definitive chemoradiation followed by salvage stereotactic re-irradiation.

reference_discussion.text: Great, thank you very much, Dr. Choby. So, the third case is going to shift gears a little bit to another very well developed area but also kind of a frontier in many other senses. So nasopharyngeal carcinoma which really has a lot of challenges of its own. This is a patient who initially presented stage 3b and was treated with definitive chemoradiation with a complete response. Five years later, the patient developed a recurrence within the right masticator space and was treated with stereotactic radiation, five rounds, and then also Pembroke for five cycles, and now moves over to a different area and now presents with a new PET CT demonstrating this finding right here. I'm going to start by pulling the panel and asking, how do you surveillance patients? Dr. Price, what is your paradigm for this?

So I think if you look at the head and neck guidelines for NCCN, they talk about doing pre-treatment imaging, doing your post-treatment kind of curative imaging. And then there's not a lot of really recommended imaging when there aren't any symptoms. So it's kind of left up as clinically indicated. I always struggle with this for nasopharynx because you can't really see, or at least those of us without fun scopes can't really see very well. And it's kind of like with some of the sinus tumors too, you sort of feel a little bit blind because you can't really feel as well or see as well. we do tend to kind of get some intermittent imaging on these patients, both MRI imaging generally to look at the nasopharynx as well as some form of distant metastatic assessment, whether that's PET or whether that's CT scans. For those that are EBV related, we'll incorporate the EBV quantitative DNA in the blood as kind of a biomarker. And of course, history and physical exam and all of the important things that we do for everyone.
Thank you. And then, Dr. Liao, just to add to that, what is your intervals for assessing surveillance for these patients?

Yeah, like Dr. Price said, there's not great guidance as far as national guidelines with this, with what exactly to do. It is a little bit individualized, I think, from risk from patient to patient, but our starting point is usually Q3 to four months with office visit, endoscopy, MRI, and then Q6 months after that, and a little bit more space with systemic imaging, either CT, chest, abdomen, pelvis, sort of Q6 months. We don't routinely get PET-CT scan, necessarily, unless we're concerned the patient hasn't had a CR. You know, sometimes we'll get that in three or six months to verify that, but I know there's many institutions that do.

Great, thank you. So just wanted to also point out, we do cover this partly within the document itself and especially for the ones that are EBV positive, there was a recommendation that was very strong from the Asian literature on the use of the EBV DNA serum test for surveillance and assessing recurrence. So this is some representative scans of the patient once we saw that PET CT. So we draw your attention to this very cloudy area, as well as the temporal lobe lesion that you're seeing very obviously on the bottom there. Dr. Gardner, would you biopsy the right temporal lobe lesion if you see something like this, knowing the patient has had prior treatment as well as a little bit more radiation treatment than the typical course?

I definitely would not. I fight this battle on a regular basis where patients with sinonasal tumors of any sort get temporal lesions in any time period from even six months to three and four or five years later. And it often is read as tumor recurrence, but these tumors, it's not the right substrate. These are not brain tumors. They don't grow in the brain. They don't like the brain. This is not a solid looking lesion. And I always have to fight back about biopsy, and I definitely would not biopsy the temporal lobe.

Thank you. Yeah, I love the way you said that. All right. And then one representative scan for the CT, you can see a little bit of that bony involvement. Dr. London, when would you consider nasal pharyngectomy for nasopharyngeal cancer patients?

In the question, that would be, you know, in the setting of a recurrent NPC, you know, this patient you said has already had CRT with a recurrence and even already had immunotherapy. This looks like a fairly easy recyclable lesion. So, you know, I would recommend proceeding with endoscopic nasopharyngectomy at this point.
Yeah, it was biopsy proven again so technical considerations for surgery if elected Dr. Levine with regards to nasal pharyngectomy.

Yeah, I think, you know, there's some of the kind of the classic ones here, you know, whenever you're, you're doing this type of surgery, obviously, you want to have enough imaging to really see, you know, that you don't have any aberrant carotid lesions, that you're not going to be super close to anything that, that is a abnormal, but a lot of times that when you're doing this type of a a resection, I think the biggest part of this in many ways is just preparing the patient for what it's going to be like afterwards and making sure that you have a really good frank discussion with them about that. A lot of times, the biggest challenge is not actually the surgery itself, although I can say it can be challenging, it's really getting the patient through that post-operative period and making sure that they can cooperate with you in that process. Going through that with them, I think is really helpful.

Just kind of to piggyback off of that, I know we always worry about critical neurovascular structures for nasal pharyngectomy, especially the carotid artery. Do you counsel them about eustachian tube symptoms? I know they probably have a pre-op, but it's likely to be a permanent problem going forward. So what is your strategy for talking to patients on that?

So usually I tell them that what they have at that time, which most people, you're right, have symptoms, is going to either stay the same or get worse. So I try to usually set low expectations, and then if it's anything better than that, they tend to be pretty happy. But I think it's really important to discuss that because often patients have this idea that you do surgery and then everything will get better. And I think it's just very important to dissuade them of that notion and to have a really realistic set of things like this is the bad part through the healing period, but these are the long-term things that you're going to be dealing with. And I think that's the piece that everybody needs to have the right expectations for. And usually they need to hear that more than once.

Great. So we do also cover nasal pharyngectomy in the document itself. So it's been getting a lot of growing evidence base, especially also pioneered in Asia, especially for select early stage and maybe a couple of more advanced stage lesions. Of course, there's some frontiers being pushed on this where you see very amazing videos of carotid bypasses and sacrifices and, you know, I think it's probably going to get a lot more adoption as we learn more about this disease. Dr. Gardner, you had a comment?

It's a question for really anyone in the panel is, what do people do for coverage after an endoscopic nasopharyngectomy, especially these patients who have been radiated and you may have exposed a clival bone in that setting? Just curious as to thoughts on that.

I mean, I think in this setting, it's really important to cover, you know, the great vessels after surgery. If you can use a contralateral and there's a septal flap, that's helpful, or a, you know, pedicled temporal parietal fascia flap, or even, you know, if there's a really big defect, you know, free flap, if you really had to. Those would be some things I would think about.
Would you do that if the carotid is, only if the carotid is exposed, or would you routinely do it, Dr. London?

I mean, I think it's hard to tell based on those two cuts from the CT, but for that particular patient, I'd probably try to use a contralateral nasoceptal flap to cover that area. It should be usable.
Dr. Roderick?

Yeah, thanks. I would do exactly the same as what Dr. London had said. But the ICAR document is absolutely wonderful, but there's been Chinese guidelines from several communities of care there that are really quite good that were recently published. And they go through different scenarios of also nasopharyngeal cancer, but osteomyelitis of the skull base, which is also a terrible problem as well. So I'd encourage anybody to take a look at that who's interested.

Definitely. I remember seeing that as well. Okay. So the patient ended up getting the nasopharyngectomy, negative margins, and then end up having bevacizumab and some steroids for the temporal lobe necrosis, and it ended up getting better. But of course, the saga always continues. So question kind of before we get to kind of the end of the saga, Dr. Price, when would you consider immunotherapy for MPC patients? What are your main indications for using it?

So we're using immunotherapy now routinely in recurrent metastatic disease for nasopharynx cancer. So there was a recent phase three study from Asia, the Jupiter study, that used it for first-line treatment in combination with cisplatin gemcitabine and showed survival benefit. But even before that study, there had been a number of phase two studies looking at single agent immunotherapy, typically after platinum chemotherapy, similar to mucosal head and neck that showed activity. So we routinely will use it in the recurrent metastatic setting, either by itself or with chemotherapy, depending on the amount of disease, whether the patient's symptomatic from their disease. a good tool, of course, you know, not everybody responds to immunotherapy, but it is part of standard care now.

Great, thank you for sharing that. So, this is also kind of summarized also in the document as well. Again, for recurrent and metastatic MPC as you had mentioned. And we briefly already, our STOOT panelists already talked about this a little bit. So several months post-treatment, of course, there's new clival enhancement and the nasal pharynx is demonstrating a little bit of mucosal necrosis. So I think this is a great segue into how do you manage a likely impending ORN of the skull base? So Dr. Widerich, I know we were just talking about this, so. I'll share your thoughts.

Yeah, you know, it's the bane of existence on this. So, I mean, we have a late effects clinic and there's various medications that can be used to try to increase blood flow and I'm not really sure they work. And then we also have hyperbaric and I'm not sure that works. And if we really think that there's something going on, you know, you can watch for a while, but if it's progressing, then I would move towards putting some sort of vascularized tissue on it to try and prevent a carotid blowout. So it all depends on how it's progressing. Some of it stays stable. You know, I think of hyperbaric oxygen as just sort of delaying. It's like a delaying tactic. It's something to do while you're waiting to see what happens. Maybe I'm offending some people by saying that, but I think definitively you have to decide whether they really need surgery and a flap.
And then when you offer them surgery, you would debride it to, what is your end point that you use for debride?

It's until my coronaries act up enough that I have to put nitrates on, because sometimes you just can't get the bone to bleed and it's terrible moth-eaten, And you just sort of, you know, your coronaries go into spasm. Yeah, so that's the limits.
Dr. Gardner, do you ever chase it to incorporate resection of dura? I think I know the answer, but what is your thought on that?

Usually, you know, we're monitoring Ian's coronary vessels throughout the procedure, and we use that as our marker as well. But it is, all kidding aside, you take it until your degree of comfort. I would never resect dura in this setting. reference_conclusion: For biopsy-proven locally recurrent nasopharyngeal carcinoma after prior chemoradiation, stereotactic radiation, and immunotherapy, the agreed management was to proceed with endoscopic nasopharyngectomy. Reconstruction should include vascularized coverage of exposed critical structures, with a contralateral nasoseptal flap favored for this defect. The temporal lobe lesion was not recommended for biopsy and was managed as radiation necrosis with bevacizumab and corticosteroids, with subsequent radiographic improvement. Ongoing management consisted of active surveillance while receiving immunotherapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 74-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Right facial numbness in the V2 distribution.

[ diagnosis ]: Keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma involving the right midface/maxillary sinus region with cutaneous lesion overlying the involved area and clinical perineural involvement of V2/infraorbital nerve.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of the lesion in the involved midface/maxillary sinus region showed keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. Biopsy of an overlying skin lesion in the same region also showed keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. Biopsy of V2/infraorbital nerve tissue was benign at initial diagnostic workup. Additional sinus contents sampled were reported as normal tissue. The initial diagnostic procedure was described as an aggressive biopsy rather than an en bloc resection.

[ imaging findings ]: Coronal CT demonstrated a soft tissue lesion in the midface with extension along the infraorbital nerve and a component within the maxillary sinus. MRI demonstrated enhancement along V2; foramen rotundum was mildly enlarged. No pterygopalatine fossa involvement was identified. No other involved areas were described posteriorly.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had a history of right facial cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma treated with unspecified office-based radiation completed approximately 4 months before presentation. During that treatment period, facial numbness developed. Further treatment of the skin cancer was discontinued at that time. The patient had prior sinus surgery, with prior sphenoethmoidectomy noted on nasal endoscopy. On examination before oncologic treatment, palpable nodularity was present in the midface; V2 sensation was impaired, while V1 and V3 were intact. Ocular examination was normal, with normal extraocular movements and vision. Nasal endoscopy did not show a visible maxillary sinus mass with a 0-degree scope; polyploid tissue was seen anteriorly in the sinus with a 70-degree scope. Definitive surgery was declined because of the extent of proposed resection.

[ current disease status ]: Keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma of the right midface and maxillary sinus region with clinical perineural involvement of V2, manifest as impaired V2 sensation and palpable midface nodularity. MRI demonstrated enhancement along V2 with mild enlargement of foramen rotundum, and no pterygopalatine fossa involvement was identified.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial neurologic evaluation had identified bilateral petrous cephaloceles, which were subsequently considered unrelated to the facial numbness by neurotology/neurosurgery assessment. The lesion extended through the anterior wall of the maxillary sinus into the subdermal midface soft tissues. The posterior aspect of V2 before the skull base was described as clear at initial assessment.

reference_conclusion: For this cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma with clinical perineural invasion along V2, the tumor board favored surgical resection with curative intent, using an open or combined open-endoscopic approach to obtain negative margins along the infraorbital nerve/foramen rotundum, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy. Neoadjuvant anti-PD-1 therapy with cemiplimab or pembrolizumab was considered appropriate to improve resectability, but not as a substitute for definitive local therapy. Because surgery was declined, cemiplimab was administered with interval MRI surveillance; the medical oncology recommendation was to continue treatment for 24 months. If surgery continues to be refused after immunotherapy, definitive radiotherapy may be offered as a reasonable nonstandard local therapy option rather than observation alone.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 45-year-old male; originally from Laos.

[ chief complaint ]: Initial presentation six years earlier with nasal obstruction and epistaxis. In 2024, presented four years after completion of treatment with 3–4 months of confusion and suspected seizures. Eight months later, developed progressive speech difficulty, dysarthria, bilateral hypoglossal nerve weakness (right greater than left), and mild aspiration.

[ diagnosis ]: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-related nasopharyngeal carcinoma, staged cT2N2 at initial diagnosis. Subsequent intracranial/temporal lobe process was clinically assessed as radiation necrosis rather than recurrent disease.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology data were provided.

[ imaging findings ]: At initial diagnosis, imaging demonstrated a large right nasopharyngeal mass encasing the carotid artery, PET-avid, with bilateral cervical adenopathy. No contrast-enhanced MRI had been obtained at that time. In 2024, MRI demonstrated a lesion with a classical appearance considered consistent with radiation necrosis. PET imaging showed asymmetry of intensity corresponding to the MRI abnormality. At later progression, imaging showed slight asymmetric enhancement near the right hypoglossal canal.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: EBV-related disease. No additional molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: Initial EBV titer was elevated at 540. At later progression, EBV remained negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Received definitive concurrent chemoradiation for nasopharyngeal carcinoma with 70 Gy plus cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil. Four years after treatment, developed neurologic symptoms with imaging findings felt to represent radiation necrosis. Eight months after that presentation, symptoms progressed with dysarthria, bilateral hypoglossal weakness, and mild aspiration.

[ current disease status ]: No visible nasopharyngeal mass was identified on serial nasal endoscopy. Nasal endoscopy showed no masses, no purulence, and no exposed bone. EBV remained negative. The patient had progressive neurologic deficits and swallowing dysfunction in the setting of imaging findings considered most consistent with radiation necrosis.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial physical examination reportedly showed no other abnormalities. At later evaluation, there was no vocal fold immobility. Coworkers had reported episodes concerning for seizures. Speech and swallowing impairment were present, with aspiration beginning at the later time point.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Evaluation of suspected local recurrence in the ipsilateral nasopharyngeal/pharyngeal region identified on MRI in 2020 during workup for transient ischemic attack symptoms.

[ diagnosis ]: Adenoid cystic carcinoma, initially staged T4N0M0. Suspected local recurrence in the ipsilateral deep nasopharyngeal/pharyngeal space approximately 15 years after initial treatment. Separate thoracic metastatic disease was present and remained stable.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial malignancy was adenoid cystic carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Last routine imaging before recurrence surveillance gap was in 2015.  
- MRI in 2020 demonstrated an area in the pharynx/deep nasopharyngeal space concerning for recurrence, ipsilateral to the original tumor.  
- CTA demonstrated some separation from the cervical carotid, with very close proximity along the petrous carotid.  
- Thoracic metastatic lesions were identified separately and had not changed over time.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic test results were reported.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial treatment for T4N0M0 adenoid cystic carcinoma consisted of partial palatectomy, pharyngectomy with free flap reconstruction, and postoperative IMRT to 62 Gy.  
- The patient underwent long-term follow-up with medical oncology and otolaryngology.  
- Thoracic metastases remained stable and had not required systemic therapy to date.

[ current disease status ]: Suspected localized recurrence on MRI in the previously operated and irradiated ipsilateral deep nasopharyngeal/pharyngeal space, approximately 15 years after initial treatment. Thoracic metastatic disease remained stable without systemic treatment requirement to date.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The suspected recurrent lesion was located in a previously operated and irradiated ipsilateral field.  
- Balloon test occlusion had not been performed.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 54-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Left anterolateral chest wall lesion at initial presentation; later developed recurrent disease with dyspnea in the setting of lung and pleural metastases.

[ diagnosis ]: Skin adnexal adenocarcinoma of the left chest wall, reported as syringocystadenocarcinoma/syringocystidinocarcinoma, with subsequent axillary nodal recurrence and later metastatic recurrence involving lungs and pleura.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- September 2023: Local excision of left chest wall lesion showed adenocarcinoma.  
- December 2023: Axillary lymph node dissection specimen showed syringocystidinocarcinoma.  
- Nodal status: 19 axillary lymph nodes were dissected; 1/19 was positive with extranodal extension.  
- Immunohistochemistry: CK7 positive, CK20 negative, CK19 positive, TTF1 negative, HER2 negative, GCDFP-15 negative, mammaglobin negative, GATA3 weak positive in <5% of cells. Breast markers were considered negative overall. ER and PR were not performed.  
- Clinicopathologic impression favored skin-origin adnexal adenocarcinoma; gastrointestinal primary was considered and investigated.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Baseline MRI (September 2023): Left-sided anterolateral chest wall lesion in the skin/subcutaneous plane, measuring 3.5 × 3.1 cm, with cystic degeneration.  
- Baseline PET-CT: No disease elsewhere.  
- After recurrence following adjuvant radiotherapy: Lung and pleural metastases were identified.  
- September 2025 PET-CT: Progressive disease with lung deposits, pleural deposits, and pleural effusion.  
- December 2025 PET-CT after 3 cycles of paclitaxel/carboplatin: Progressive disease.  
- Post second-line gemcitabine/cisplatin (after 4 cycles): Final PET-CT showed progressive disease.  
- At latest description: No local chest wall recurrence; disease was lung-limited with multiple lung nodules, pleural-based nodules, and left-sided massive pleural effusion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Comprehensive NGS on archival tissue showed PIK3CA mutation with variant allele frequency 76.5%.  
- PD-L1 immune cell score: 2%.  
- Tumor mutational burden could not be determined from the tested specimen.  
- Copy number variation assessment could not be determined from the tested specimen.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Pleural fluid cytology from initial tapping was negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- September 2023: Wide local excision/local excision of left chest wall lesion.  
- December 2023: Axillary lymph node dissection for nodal recurrence; 1/19 nodes positive with extranodal extension.  
- January 2024: Adjuvant radiotherapy to chest wall and axilla.  
- Subsequently remained on follow-up until metastatic recurrence approximately 1 year after completion of adjuvant radiation.  
- Palliative chemotherapy was advised at metastatic recurrence, but treatment was initially defaulted; patient underwent unspecified native therapy for approximately 8 months.  
- First-line palliative chemotherapy: Paclitaxel plus carboplatin for 3 cycles; outcome was primary progression.  
- Second-line palliative chemotherapy: Initially single-agent gemcitabine, then gemcitabine plus cisplatin; 4 cycles completed; outcome was progressive disease.

[ current disease status ]:  
Metastatic progressive disease after two lines of palliative chemotherapy, with multiple pulmonary nodules, pleural-based metastases, and left-sided pleural effusion. No local recurrence at the primary chest wall site was described.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Upper/lower gastrointestinal endoscopic evaluation was negative.  
- Repeat biopsy was not performed because the patient was unwilling due to pain and pleural disease burden.  
- NGS was performed on archival tissue block from the original specimen.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Initially presented with gastric outlet obstruction. Re-presented in December 2025 with abdominal pain and abdominal distension.

[ diagnosis ]: Gastric adenocarcinoma, status post radical subtotal gastrectomy, with subsequent progressive metastatic gastric cancer.

[ histopathology results ]: Postoperative histopathology showed pT2N0, grade 1 adenocarcinoma of the stomach. Lymph node dissection was inadequate: 5 lymph nodes were resected, with 0 positive nodes.

[ imaging findings ]: Outside PET-CT performed in December 2025 showed progressive metastatic gastric malignancy. Clinical progression included an umbilical nodule.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- MMR IHC showed isolated MLH1 loss.  
- HER2 IHC was negative.  
- PD-L1 was negative.  
- NGS showed no actionable mutations.  
- No BRAF mutation was detected on NGS.  
- Tissue NGS report noted poor sample quality.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent radical subtotal gastrectomy with modified Billroth II reconstruction on 31 December 2024 at an outside center.  
- Planned for adjuvant chemotherapy followed by adjuvant radiotherapy after referral.  
- Received 4 cycles of CAPOX, completed by March 2025, then defaulted further treatment.  
- After metastatic progression in December 2025, started palliative FOLFOX.  
- Tolerance after the first cycle of FOLFOX was poor.  
- Disease was clinically progressive on FOLFOX, with non-response of the umbilical nodule and severe pain; chemotherapy was stopped.  
- Received palliative radiotherapy to the umbilical nodule.  
- Subsequently declined further intravenous chemotherapy.  
- Was continued on single-agent oral capecitabine.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic gastric cancer after prior surgery, incomplete adjuvant systemic therapy, and poor tolerance/progression on first-line palliative FOLFOX. Symptomatic disease included abdominal pain, distension, severe pain, and an umbilical metastatic nodule. At last update, the patient was on oral capecitabine after palliative radiotherapy and was unwilling to receive further intravenous chemotherapy.

[ other clinical data ]: No additional objective clinical data were available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 41-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache.

[ diagnosis ]: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), diagnosed in April 2024. Recurrent disease was identified on 19 December 2025. Re-excision specimen showed recurrent high-grade glioma.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial intracranial space-occupying lesion was diagnosed as GBM. Following recurrence, re-excision histopathology showed high-grade glioma.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI performed at recurrence demonstrated a recurrent lesion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Next-generation sequencing on recurrent tumor identified TP53 mutation.  
- MGMT promoter methylation was positive.  
- IDH1/IDH2 alterations were not detected.  
- HRD was negative.  
- Tumor mutational burden was low.  
- Germline testing was positive for TP53.  
- TP53 variant allele fraction on tissue testing was reported as 42%.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent right frontoparietal craniotomy with near-total excision after initial diagnosis in April 2024.  
- Received adjuvant radiotherapy to 60 Gy with concurrent temozolomide.  
- Subsequently received adjuvant temozolomide.  
- Achieved a disease-free interval of approximately 1.5 years.  
- At recurrence in December 2025, underwent re-excision.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent intracranial high-grade glioma/GBM following prior surgery, chemoradiation, and adjuvant temozolomide; status post re-excision for recurrence in December 2025.

[ other clinical data ]: Intracranial lesion was located in the right frontal/parietal region.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent metastatic rectal cancer with bilateral pulmonary metastases after a disease-free interval of approximately 5–6 years following treatment for localized rectal cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Rectal adenocarcinoma, initially localized at first presentation; subsequently recurrent stage IV disease with unresectable bilateral lung metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy of a lung lesion at recurrence confirmed metastatic disease consistent with the primary rectal carcinoma. Mismatch repair protein testing by immunohistochemistry showed deficient MMR.

[ imaging findings ]: Metastatic disease involved both lungs with multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules/lesions. One pulmonary lesion was described as large. Disease was considered unresectable. One lesion had encroached on the bronchus and was associated with hemoptysis. Most recent HRCT thorax showed stable thoracic disease. No liver metastases were identified on the imaging referred to.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Initial molecular profile: BRAF wild type; KRAS wild type.  
- Liquid biopsy NGS (Guardant): KRAS mutation detected, specified as KRAS G12S; TP53 alteration detected; SMAD4 mutation detected.  
- ctDNA/tumor DNA fraction on liquid biopsy was approximately 0.8%.  
- Variant allele fractions of detected alterations were reported as less than 1%.  
- Tumor mutational burden on liquid biopsy was reported as low.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial localized rectal cancer had received protocol-based treatment.  
- After metastatic recurrence, first-line FOLFOX plus panitumumab was administered; disease progressed.  
- CAPOX plus bevacizumab was then administered; disease progressed.  
- TAS-102 (Lonsurf) plus bevacizumab was subsequently started and was associated with partial response/stable thoracic disease on latest HRCT.  
- Radiotherapy had been considered for a pulmonary lesion encroaching on the bronchus because of hemoptysis, but no radiotherapy administration was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic rectal cancer with lung-only disease, involving multiple bilateral pulmonary metastases. Disease remained unresectable. On current TAS-102 plus bevacizumab, the patient had partial response with low ctDNA fraction and stable disease on latest HRCT thorax. Hemoptysis had been settling. No hepatic metastases were documented.

[ other clinical data ]: Hemoptysis had occurred in relation to a pulmonary lesion with bronchial encroachment.

[ patient demographics ]: Male patient; described as young. Performance status was 4.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent/progressive glioma after multiple prior lines of therapy.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade glioma/GBM arising from a previously lower-grade glioma, with features consistent with transformed IDH-mutant, 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglial tumor. Disease had progressed multiple times after prior treatment.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial tumor tissue immunohistochemistry had identified an IDH1 mutation.

[ imaging findings ]: No imaging findings were provided.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- 1p/19q codeletion was present; this was identified after primary progression.  
- MGMT promoter methylation was present.  
- PD-L1 was negative.  
- Tissue NGS identified IDH1 R132C mutation.  
- PTEN mutation was present.  
- ATRX alteration was present.  
- MLH1 c.618 deletion was present.  
- MSH6 mutation was present.  
- Two TP53 mutations were present.  
- Microsatellite status was stable.  
- Tumor mutational burden was 66.76 mutations/Mb.  
- Variant allele fractions reported included ATRX 48%, MSH6 5%, and MLH1 1.1%.

[ laboratory results ]: No routine hematology or biochemistry results were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial surgical resection was performed.  
- Temozolomide was administered after surgery.  
- Subsequent disease progression occurred after temozolomide.  
- There were 2-3 episodes of progression overall.  
- Additional systemic treatments administered included bevacizumab, vincristine, and PCV regimen.  
- Disease progressed after multiple lines of therapy.

[ current disease status ]: Multiply relapsed/progressive high-grade glioma following surgery and several systemic regimens. Functional status was poor, with ECOG performance status 4.

[ other clinical data ]: The genomic profiling discussed was performed on tumor tissue rather than blood.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Postoperative management of carcinoma endometrium.

[ diagnosis ]: Endometrial endometrioid adenocarcinoma, FIGO stage IIIC, grade 1. Diagnosis date was recorded as 1 October.

[ histopathology results ]: Surgical pathology was reported as endometrioid carcinoma, grade 1.

[ imaging findings ]: No imaging findings were provided.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Mismatch repair immunohistochemistry demonstrated loss of MLH1 and PMS2 expression, consistent with deficient mismatch repair. MSI status was reported as MSI-high. Next-generation sequencing on an endometrial hotspot panel did not detect clinically significant variants in the MMR genes assessed. TP53 was reported as wild type in one report; a pathogenic loss-of-function TP53 mutation was also reported on NGS.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory results were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent surgery consisting of total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral oophorectomy. She subsequently received paclitaxel plus carboplatin every 3 weeks for 6 cycles. After completion of 6 cycles of chemotherapy, she was referred for radiotherapy. No treatment response or toxicity data were provided.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative stage IIIC endometrial carcinoma after completion of adjuvant paclitaxel/carboplatin x6; referred for radiotherapy. No documented evidence of recurrence or metastatic progression was provided.

[ other clinical data ]: Biomarker testing had been sent on the biopsy specimen for MMR immunohistochemistry and NGS panel analysis. No clinically significant variants were detected on the reported biomarker studies apart from the TP53 finding noted above.

[ patient demographics ]: 51-year-old female; performance status 1.

[ chief complaint ]: Cough and mild chest pain.

[ diagnosis ]: Inoperable pulmonary artery sarcoma with peripheral lung nodules/lung metastases. The lesion was described as an intraluminal pulmonary artery mass; intimal sarcoma was considered in the differential classification.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from a peripheral lung nodule showed undifferentiated sarcoma after extensive immunohistochemistry.

[ imaging findings ]: Echocardiography identified a space-occupying lesion. PET imaging demonstrated a pulmonary artery mass with peripheral lung nodules. The pulmonary artery lesion was described as intraluminal, with associated tumour thrombus. Cardiothoracic assessment deemed the pulmonary artery mass inoperable.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Soft tissue sarcoma-specific NGS panel identified two TP53 pathogenic missense variants. One TP53 variant had a variant allele frequency of approximately 40%. No sarcoma-associated fusion was detected on the panel.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Systemic chemotherapy with gemcitabine plus docetaxel was initiated for inoperable cardiothoracic sarcoma. The patient completed 2 cycles. Cough reduced and clinical symptoms improved after treatment.

[ current disease status ]: Clinically improved after 2 cycles of gemcitabine/docetaxel. No repeat imaging had yet been performed to assess radiologic response.

[ other clinical data ]: Cardiac function was reported to be preserved. No comorbidities were reported.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old male. Smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Lung squamous cell carcinoma with extensive bone metastases involving the spine; poor performance status related to bony metastatic disease.

[ diagnosis ]: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung with extensive osseous metastases in the spine. Performance status was ECOG/PS 3.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy did not show fully differentiated carcinoma. Subsequent biopsy reported squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Extensive bone metastases were present in the spine.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing identified a KRAS G12C mutation. EGFR testing showed an exon 20 point mutation classified as a variant of uncertain significance. EGFR variant allele frequency was reported as 44%. No STK11, KEAP1, or SMARCA4 co-mutations were reported.

[ laboratory results ]: PD-L1 testing by Dako 22C3 showed expression less than 1%. PD-L1 testing by Ventana SP263 showed approximately 1% expression (low expression).

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Radiation therapy was started after the initial biopsy, before final histologic classification. No systemic anticancer treatment outcome was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic squamous cell lung carcinoma with persistent extensive spinal bone metastases and poor performance status (PS 3).

[ other clinical data ]: Poor performance status was attributed to extensive bone metastases.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old man from Junagadh, Gujarat.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent/metastatic esophageal squamous cell carcinoma with new multiple pulmonary nodules and nodal recurrence on recent PET-CT after prior multimodality treatment.

[ diagnosis ]: Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus, initially diagnosed in 2024 as stage III disease; subsequently developed recurrent metastatic disease involving the paraesophageal region and lungs.

[ histopathology results ]: Residual disease was present after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy and surgery. Paraesophageal nodal recurrence and a lung nodule were surgically resected subsequently. Histologic subtype was squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Routine PET-CT performed during adjuvant nivolumab identified recurrence with a small paraesophageal nodule and a small lung nodule.  
- Most recent PET-CT demonstrated multiple lung nodules, one new paraesophageal lymph node, and a parietal lymph node.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Comprehensive genomic profiling performed on surgical tissue demonstrated PTEN mutation, TP53 mutation, CCND1 alteration/amplification, and CDK6 alteration/amplification.  
- Additional reported amplifications included FGF19, FGF3, and FGF4.  
- PD-L1 CPS: 10.  
- MSI/TMB were reported as low.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- In 2024, the patient underwent neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by surgery for stage III esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.  
- Due to residual disease after surgery, adjuvant nivolumab was administered for 1 year.  
- Approximately 6 months into adjuvant nivolumab, PET-CT showed recurrence with a paraesophageal lesion and a lung nodule.  
- Robotic-assisted surgery was performed with resection of the paraesophageal lymph node and the lung nodule.  
- The patient was subsequently rechallenged with paclitaxel plus carboplatin administered every 3 weeks. Two cycles were completed.  
- Paclitaxel/carboplatin was poorly tolerated, with recurrent malaise and difficulty tolerating chemotherapy.  
- Despite prior surgery and systemic therapy, subsequent PET-CT showed further progression with multiple lung nodules and new nodal disease.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent metastatic esophageal squamous cell carcinoma with progressive pulmonary and nodal disease after prior neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, surgery, adjuvant nivolumab, metastasectomy, and 2 cycles of paclitaxel/carboplatin.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- ECOG performance status had been 0 after surgery.  
- The patient subsequently experienced intermittent poor tolerance to systemic chemotherapy, including recurrent malaise.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 76-year-old woman. ECOG performance status was 3 at initial oncology assessment. Body surface area was 1.43 m². Comorbidities included coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension.

[ chief complaint ]: Initial presentation in 2022 followed post-COVID lower respiratory tract infection admission. Geriatric assessment identified anemia, weight loss, recurrent falls, and inguinal lymphadenopathy.

[ diagnosis ]: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocyte-depleted subtype, stage IIIB.

[ histopathology results ]: Excision biopsy of an inguinal lymph node showed lymphoma consistent on immunohistochemistry with classical Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocyte-depleted type.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Baseline whole-body PET-CT showed extensive lymphadenopathy with both supradiaphragmatic and infradiaphragmatic involvement.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Anemia was present at baseline; hemoglobin was 9.4 g/dL.  
- Albumin was 3.4 g/dL.  
- Creatinine was normal at baseline.  
- LDH was mildly elevated.  
- Left ventricular ejection fraction was preserved.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Comprehensive geriatric assessment was performed before treatment. Findings included: Charlson Comorbidity Index 7; CIRS-G 19; dependence in mobility and transfers; dependence in activities of daily living and instrumental activities of daily living; timed up-and-go test 20 seconds with difficulty; high fall risk; MMSE 24; Geriatric Depression Scale 11; significant weight loss over 6 months; malnourishment; frailty by Fried criteria; Clinical Frailty Scale 6 (moderately frail). Identified geriatric syndromes included falls, frailty, depression, probable pseudodementia, insomnia, malnourishment, and polypharmacy.

[ current disease status ]: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, lymphocyte-depleted subtype, stage IIIB, with extensive supradiaphragmatic and infradiaphragmatic lymphadenopathy on baseline PET-CT. ECOG performance status was 3, and comprehensive geriatric assessment performed before treatment identified frailty, malnourishment, depression, recurrent falls, dependence in mobility and activities of daily living, and polypharmacy.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- CARG score was 14, corresponding to high predicted chemotherapy toxicity risk.  
- Cardiac disease was described as stable at baseline.  
- Social assessment showed that she lived with her son and family and had good caregiver support and insurance/resources.  
- Vaccination history was incomplete.
