So, we are trying to find out other surrogate objective ways to figure out whether this patient is going to tolerate chemo or not. So, for that, First, we need to understand what is his survival due to comorbidities itself. For example, if you have a comorbidity that is life-threatening, then he would not qualify for anti-cancer therapy. So, therefore, you would assess each domain, including the CGA. I mean, that is there in the CGA. So, it's not practically possible to do a CGA in the clinic. It's time-consuming. We try and look for other surrogates. For example, you were seeing the comorbidity index score or the frailty score. We try and do these, but I agree we need to have a CGA and a geriatric assessment for this patient to objectively say whether he is going to tolerate and benefit from chemotherapy. It is not possible to do a CGA in an oncology clinic unless and until you have a proper geriatric assessment system in place.

Yeah, all right. If actually a proper CGA is not possible, is it possible to do a practical GA as suggested by ASCO or SCOPC, which is I think violated in Indian patients also. So, what's your take about that?
These are, there are online tools that are available. If I type the calculators, they open in the desktop and they can keep numbering and that will give you a rough estimate as to which way it goes.
And anyone actually among the panelists, are you following the PGA or SCOPE-C?
Not routinely.

So, my next question is to Dr. Krishnakumar. So, it is a practical question that is do this course like CARG or CRASH. We are using only CARG. Yeah, yeah. So is it realistically influence your chemotherapy choices or will you go?

It does, it does partly. So we are just in the transition from the so called gut feeling what comes to our mind to treat to reform ourself into something little more objective. and see many times the patient asks us when you know that many of the patients with old age who are still willing for treatment they are either related to doctors and so sometimes they come and ask us what's the risk of you know toxicity and sometimes we have to give them some obvious numbers so we are using CARG since last year we have just started using CARG score not crash but CARG score and then we use our clinical parameters including the nutritional and other things
All right. So, as the panel suggested, actually, we also did the comprehensive CTA in this patient. So, Dr. Gino, I think you can explain.

Good evening, everyone. So, in this patient, in fact, prior to the diagnosis itself, we had the opportunity to evaluate the patient because like Dr. Varun told us, the patient had actually was admitted with an LRTI post-COVID issues in pulmonary medicine where we were evaluating her for recurrent falls. So we thought that we generally do a CGA whenever we are called for a consultation. And in that process, we found out that she has a type 2 diabetes mellitus, which was fairly controlled. She had hypertension. She was taking medications. We always do a Brown Bag examination. And we found that she had five medicines for her diabetes and hypertension, plus multiple supplements. Because those days, following COVID, everybody was, the tendency was to take more supplements. We found that she had not taken vaccinations. At that point, COVID vaccine also was not available. We found that her comorbidity indexes, the Charleston comorbidity index was 7, and SIRS-C was 19. We went into deeper geriatric assessments where the functional assessments we found that she was actually dependent in her mobility and transverse. she was actually requiring, because of her recurrent falls, she required to hold on to somebody to walk. She required support for activities of daily living and IADLs as well because she was always dependent on a caretaker. The tuck test which we did showed that she had taken 20 seconds to complete with much difficulty when she was asked to walk alone. And we definitely considered she has a high fall risk. And moving on, our cognitive assessment actually showed that her MMSE was 24. Her geriatric depression scale was 11, indicative of clinical depression. And psychological depression was also assessed and found that she could be probably fitting into depression. However, what we found that she had an excellent social domain. stays with her son and family with adequate support. The family participation was very evident right from the beginning and when we started working her up and she was supported by good insurance and good resources otherwise. Nutritionally, like the initial presentation itself was weight loss. So we found that she had a significant weight loss in the past six months. Nutritional assessment also showed that she had malnourishment. And her frailty assessment, we use a frail criteria. And she was fitting into a category of frail. And with the CFS score, she had six, which was putting her as a moderately frail lady to begin with. So at the end of our CGA, we found that she has issues in multiple domains. And the issues which were identified included false frailty, depression, probably pseudodementia at that point, insomnia and malnourishment. So these were the syndromes identified in this lady who was otherwise probably when we were taking discussions on RMDT on whether we should treat or not, these were the issues which we had in our hand. So again, my questions to my fellow geriatricians in this board, I would like to begin with Dr. Rakesh Mishra. On These geriatric syndromes, mainly especially on this malnourishment, the depression and the polypharmacy, prior to the oncological treatment, how would you like to optimize and how do you want to generally take up the decisions on these issues, Dr. Rakesh?

Am I audible? Yes. Hi, thank you so much for this opportunity. Now, a very wonderful presentation and good approach. This is how we usually go about addressing an older person who has come to us prior to initiation of chemotherapy. Now I'd like to take a moment to say that G8 screening tool that we were talking about, it's actually a screening tool which actually identifies the patients who warrant a more comprehensive geriatric assessment. So in case they score higher on the G8 screening tool, here the radiation therapy people refer these patients to us. We're actually currently having a study with them, which is using the ES13 as well as G8 screening tools along with comprehensive geriatric assessment. Now, like Dr. Gino said, that polypharmacy was an issue here. This patient was on five different medications for her sugars. Definitely, when we do a comprehensive geriatric assessment, it also includes a detailed history and a thorough examination and a brown bag check. and if we find that the patient is on more than five medications, it qualifies as polypharmacy. Now, definitely, if possible, we would like to give her higher doses of, reach the maximal doses of one oral anti-hyperglycemic agent before introducing another. Then again, the causes of malnutrition in this patient, we have to see whether it is because of her depression itself, whether it is loss of appetite because of her malignancy, whether it is because of something like an edentulous state, which many of our older people have, or poor dentition. whether it is because of a lack of social support or whether it is because of a combination of all these. So this is something which is usually picked up quite well if you do a thorough comprehensive geriatric assessment. There are certain markers for malnutrition which we can use. For instance, this patient had an albumin of 3.4 and this patient also had a hemoglobin which was a little low, 9.4. Now, so we have to find out the cause for her anemia. Is it only because of malnutrition? Does she have any GI loss? Is it because of any vitamin deficiencies? So we would like to check her B12. We would like to check her iron stores. As regards depression, identifying depression in such a patient becomes a little difficult. So because she has scored so high on the geriatric depression scale, definitely she is having depression, whether it only warrants psychotherapy or whether it also warrants pharmacological therapy, something which needs to be seen. Having said that, initiating antidepressants if your psychotherapy is not working would be helpful in helping her regain her appetite as well. The problem is all the antidepressants that we start, they usually take some time to act. So before initiating the chemotherapy, it might make sense that if warranted, we start the appropriate antidepressants as well.

Thank you, Dr. Rakesh. So, Dr. Rakesh, you could continue on answering the questions. What you would think about the frailty factor in this patient? We found that the patient is very frail. So, what are the interventions you would think that is impactful in reversing the frailty or modifying the risk before or during the treatment?

So there are a few interventions, like if in a CGA we identify the patient has malnutrition, we do a mini nutritional assessment and we find that the patient has, or is at risk of malnutrition, definitely making the meals more palatable, making the meals, if it's an edentulous patient, making it more suitable for her. In case you need to increase the protein or the calories, work in tandem with dietary to help modify the meals, making them high calorie and high protein. look at the sugars and see whether you need to give a diabetic diet or not. This goes a long way. Nutrition goes a long way in addressing frailty. Apart from that, certain exercises, whatever the patient can tolerate, can be prescribed based on the patient's functional status.

Thank you. I think I'll, I mean, put this question to Dr. Divya Maul. So, Dr. Divya, I think everybody is worried about how to screen in busy clinics. So, I'm sure in all the discussions we had in the latest meeting which we had in Kochi also, we had a lot of debate how to screen this very fast. So, a CGA comes quite fast for a geriatrician, but then it comes with practice probably. So, any practical tips or how do you tell us, you know, how can we handle a CGA in a very busy clinic?

Thank you, Gino, for this opportunity. Basically, in many of this screening that we do in CGA involves basic questioning about how their routine day-to-day life is going about. So we can ask them regarding if it is the malnutrition, we can ask them regarding how many meals they have during the day. We can ask them what is there in their meal, meaning do they have rice alone. Sometimes when elderly leave alone, they have just rice and maybe one curry with them. So is it a balanced diet? We can explore through just that one question. What all do you have during the day? And also we can ask, have their appetite come down recently? that itself will give you an idea of whether the patient is eating well. Regarding depression, we can ask two questionnaires. There are simple questions regarding, have you been feeling low lately? Simple questions itself can screen most of the items that we do in a CGA, and which can actually hint us on what to dig in deeper.

Yeah, I think that's what the consensus which we reached last time when we had the discussion on geriatric oncology in Cochin under EGOS, that we all have kind of modified our CGAs. We have tailor-made CGAs to fit into our busy clinics. And we had shared a couple of our models last time, the Amrita model and the medical dress model, as well as the CMC Vellore model. So what we all have done is we have tailor-made into asking very significant questions and identifying things as we go on, so that the CG actually can be done in a much shorter time, but touching on most of the factors. So I think we'll move on with the case. So we had, I mean, as our team had decided to give the clearance for the patient and oncological treatment was undertaken and initiated by Dr. Varun and team. Also, our side, we thought we definitely need to treat the depression apart from the psychotherapy part. We initiated Mirtazapine, we chose Mirtazapine because we thought it will also boost their appetite. We taught her sleep hygiene measures, nutritional rehabilitation and diet supplements were started. Her occupational therapy, physiotherapy team both started working on her because of mobility issues, recurrent falls. We provided her walking aids, made her walk independently. We gave her vaccines in between. Influenza, pneumonia, and herpes zoster were considered from our side. And the government had issued COVID also subsequently to her. We ensured adequate diabetes and hypertension control. We were done with minimal medicines and insulin. And we took care of her polypharmacy. We reduced her overall medicines to just five medicines. And that's how we supported the journey in the oncology part with Dr. Varun.

So as Chinnam mentioned, actually, we have decided to proceed with the treatment of hot skin lymphoma in this elderly lady. As everybody knows, the hot skin and the myeloma, these all are the favorite topics for all madams. So we don't want to leave that disease, so we actually decided to treat it. So the issues to address here is that here we have an elderly lady who is frail, and we identified a lot of geriatric syndromes. So what about the use of anthracyclines in frail patients? So how would you approach this case, Dr. Chandrakant?

Yes, Chandrakant? Right, right, right. So well, again, it's tricky to assess for anthracycline. In fact, for any chemotherapy fitness, again, we should go back to the same CGA functional status, cognition and the frailty score. If all things are fine, then the cumulative dose of anthrax in Hodgkin's is not much. So you would have a cardiac assessment. In fact, we can do a GLS and a 3D echo and we can have a baseline cardiac biomarkers in the hand. So if by the CGA this patient is fit for anthracycline then we can actually use anthracycline and we have used dexrazoxane in some of our patients. So if you can use dexrazoxane it has yeah as a prophylactic measure you can use it in these patients and maybe you can prolong the infusion time of anthra. So maybe these are some ways to be a little cautious. Of course, we need to have a proper IV line in this patient because a PICC is important because they're frail and extravasation is common. So I think the CGA plus specifically assessing the cardiac status, the liver function, renal function, I think these are more important. We find the cumulative dose is not much. I think that's the way to go. We can use some protective agents like dexrazoxin.

Yeah. Yeah, all are valid points, Chandrakant. And so questions are actually, is there any cutoff for the use of BLEO in elderly? Because we all are actually scared to use BLEO in elderly because of the risk of pulmonary fibrosis, which is irreversible. So is there any cutoff? What about your practice in elderly patients?

Yeah, actually, bleomycin is an important drug in the treatment of Hodgkin's disease. But the issues are that what we are worried is about the lung toxicity. And this lung toxicity increases as the age advances. Because if the patient is above 70, risk of bleomycin toxicity is more than 25%. Like that, if the renal function is low, that is increased creatinine, or previous UOPD, or some lung disease, then smoking history. All these increases the risk of bleomycin toxicity. So if such risk factors are there, better to avoid. Otherwise, you can use it. But again, it depends on the number of cycles used. So if you use four cycles of ABBD versus two cycles, or two cycles of ABD and two cycles of ABBD, the risk of toxicity is almost same, ABVD versus two cycles of ABVD. So in a very fit patient, maybe you can use about 60. Maybe you can maximum maybe two cycles, not more than that, because as the dose increases, the risk of toxicity also increases. Yes, sir.
And now we have actually the better molecules.
There are other agents like you.

Yeah, yeah. So Krishnakumar, so what about your take on the use of brentoximab or immune checkpoint inhibitors? Actually, at that time, when I treated this patient, the NEVA was not approved as first line. Only brentoximab was approved. So how you approach this case if you omit BLEO?

There have been few patients for whom AVD backbone we are given, assuming that the echo with the GLS scoring is normal. There have been some rare patients where we haven't gone up to the extent to see the LV function properly to make sure that there is no even subtle cardiac dysfunction because as Pavitran sir mentioned, just like bleomycin has the cumulative dose, even if it has not reached a particular level, patients tend to have So baseline biomarkers in some patients who have real high risk. And when we do the, actually very recently, I can't tell you about our experience. We've just started incorporating slowly into the geriatric oncology assessment, which is the CGA, as well as we are doing for patients with very high risk, we do baseline biomarkers. Now I know that this is not the standard of care. We tried adopting it from the ESA recommendation, the first guidelines, which came on Asian, I mean, on the geriatric oncology guidelines for managing various toxicities, cardio-oncology. So they say that actually it's a two-year recommendation. We can do baseline troponin. So some of the patients who are very high risk, we even follow up with serial troponin. There's a sudden rise, then we stop. So we have done it for one patient, but now that is for the anthra. Then coming to avoiding BLEO, definitely yes. I would be scared even with one or two dose of BLEO. very apprehensive. I don't use bleomycin. I have AVD as my backbone. Even a choice, it would be Nivo first in today's context, followed by BV. Hopefully, post-COVID, there is no lung ILD issues or other problems, then Nivo would be my choice to go. Otherwise, we can go for a BV-AVD. BV with AVD. And now you have that split dosing also available sometimes in elderly and frail where you can just give 2 BVs and then follow it up with 4 AVD and then again give 2 BV later and keep under follow up. Yeah, you have a follow-up, like you have a patient who has been under geriatrician, they will know. We use it in our day-to-day practice, because that can be done in 10 minutes. And even a nurse, even my department attendant was doing it for us. And look at the components. Her cognition is assessed just by three-word recall. If she can recall at least two of the three words that you have told after some time, that means a cognitician is okay. Then comes depression. The question is, are you sad or depressed and how long? So everybody will be sad after a diagnosis of malignancy for sure. That we will not assess as depression. because depression means it has it should be there with the patient for some time. Then the third question that we ask is about incontinence and the fourth one that we ask is history of fall. So again, the patient has been following after patient developed malignancy. That means it is all due to malignancy. So we have to of course improve the nutritional condition, exercise, high protein diet, if she has sleep issues that has to be addressed. So all that we do for a geriatric patient, we have to continue to be doing while the oncologist assess the patient for fitness for chemotherapy in their own way. That is based on the toxicities of the drug. So, I was thinking that for cardiac assessment, even nitroproBNP is a very good biomarker because if they have subclinical heart failure already, such a patient may go into overt heart failure after your anthracycline. So, not only troponin, you can also do a nitroproBNP because many of the patients do have a subclinical heart failure already. in which case just giving anthracycline can push them off balance because all these frail patients they won't have exercised much they would just maybe walk to the washroom and come back but if a challenge if they put on a challenge they may develop overt heart failure so nitroproBNP is a very good biomarker that can be used because that if that is elevated already we know that there is a possibility of patient going into overt heart failure so that is also a good biomarker that we can use if it's very high you know this is not the patient for you but if it is just normal or just outside the reference range it's okay we can still take the patient and give the patient of course those I know for a frail patient you will adjust the dosage as well and then give the treatment. So if somebody has been really fit, like what we do in geriatrics is somebody who has been exercising regularly, okay, for maybe many years, 10 years, we assess their age as 10 years less. Whereas somebody who has been not exercising at all, mobility is restricted for a long time, such a patient is really frail and even if they are 60, probably we would put them as 70, like that. So all that matters. The fitness that they had before they developed cancer is what matters a lot. In addition to doing CGA at the point and then serially as we go through the chemotherapy and suppose the patient is becoming frail and frail with chemotherapy, we know, like we have to stop, watch, see what has happened. but if the patient is improving and improving, and what you did was absolutely right. You gave steroids first, with which many of these frailty markers will improve. There will be significant improvement with the steroid that you give, then the patient becomes fit, patient will eat better, nutritionally better, mobilize better, and then you have given chemo. I feel that's the right approach, I would say.

Yeah. Thank you for the Bible book. Yeah. Yeah. The next question, actually, it is actually this person is more or less like a. Now, which comes first, the chicken or the egg? That is, yeah, in this patient, the patient's CGA improved after treatment. So do you see this as evidence that treating cancer reverses frailty or the interventions by the treatment enhance cancer outcome? So Chandragana, what's your take about that? Or Dr. Ragesh also can answer that.
What was the question, Varun?

Yeah, in this patient, the patient's CGA improved. Actually, it was a dramatic improvement after treatment. So do you see this as an evidence that treating cancer, it reverses frailty or the geriatric intervention enhanced cancer outcome?

Yeah, so CGA is important to plan the initial treatment. And in this situation, what is the response to treatment? There's also a CGA can guide us. So if the CGA is worsening, then probably your initial selection of chemotherapeutic regimen is not good, or the disease is bad, then you need to probably change the plan. If there is an improvement in the CGA score, then probably you can add a better chemotherapy regimen. That's a good sign. Yeah. Supposing, let's say, I didn't give chemotherapy, I just give prednisone for this patient and the patient's CGA has improved over a period of time, then I would go ahead and add an anthracycline based chemo. So CGA is dynamic. The problem with static CGA is it's only a single time assessment, but this keeps changing. So if there is an improvement in CGA score, that means the treatment is working, the disease is becoming better, we can actually escalate on to the treatment.

Yeah, nice. So, let's move on to the next slide. So, the key takeaways from this case is the CGA is both diagnostic and prognostic, frailty and all other syndromes, that is geriatric syndromes, were as significant as malignancy in an elderly patient. So holistic intervention improved resilience because remission was accompanied by actually the reversal of frailty, malnutrition, and depression in our patient. So at the end of the initial, at the end of the treatment, then relapse, the patient was more fitter, more independent, and psychologically stronger. So it actually demonstrate the long-term benefit of integrated geriatric interventions. So, after this case, I think we can move on to the second case. It's a totally different case when compared to the first one. So, Dr. Chino, you can summarize.

reference_conclusion: Comprehensive geriatric assessment identified frailty, malnutrition, depression, recurrent falls, mobility impairment, and polypharmacy; multidisciplinary optimization was undertaken with mirtazapine, sleep hygiene measures, nutritional rehabilitation with supplements, occupational therapy and physiotherapy, provision of walking aids, vaccination, optimization of diabetes and hypertension control, and medication rationalization. Curative-intent treatment for classical Hodgkin lymphoma was initiated with prephase steroids followed by AVD alone because of financial constraints; treatment was completed for six cycles with supportive care for toxicities. At relapse, with preserved performance status and fitness on repeat geriatric assessment, treatment was administered with brentuximab plus bendamustine for three cycles, followed by brentuximab alone to complete six cycles after near-complete response, and the patient was subsequently continued on brentuximab maintenance.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 86-year-old man; widower; father of two children; occupation: farmer.

[ chief complaint ]: Bleeding per rectum and constipation for 3 weeks.

[ diagnosis ]: Locally advanced rectal adenocarcinoma, staged as cT4N1M0 / stage T4N1 with no distant metastases identified on PET. Lesion was located 5 cm from the anal verge. Mesorectal fascia involvement was present.

[ histopathology results ]: Colonoscopic biopsy showed moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Colonoscopy demonstrated a circumferential rectal lesion 5 cm from the anal verge. MRI pelvis showed locally advanced rectal disease with nodal involvement, staged T4N1, with mesorectal fascia involvement. Whole-body PET showed no distant metastatic disease and demonstrated local nodal involvement only.

[ laboratory results ]: Initial blood investigations were reported as within normal limits. Hemoglobin and albumin were available; despite rectal bleeding, anemia was not present.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior oncologic treatment was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Untreated locally advanced non-metastatic rectal cancer with local nodal involvement; performance status was reported as PS 1.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included systemic hypertension and obstructive airway disease. Regular medications included one antihypertensive tablet and one inhaler. No family history of malignancy or genetic disorders was reported. Baseline general and systemic examinations were unremarkable; vital signs were normal. Digital rectal examination identified a rectal mass. Comprehensive geriatric assessment showed independence in all activities of daily living, active involvement in farming, independent mobility, robust handgrip strength, normal 3-word recall, no documented cognitive impairment, negative PHQ-2 screening for depression, good family support, and no significant frailty identified. Additional findings included bilateral cataracts with minor visual impairment, nocturia/lower urinary tract symptoms, unintentional weight loss, mild loss of appetite, and constipation. He had received 2 doses of COVID vaccination.

reference_conclusion: The patient was considered fit for multimodality treatment following comprehensive geriatric assessment. For this locally advanced rectal cancer, the agreed approach was long-course chemoradiotherapy as the initial modality, followed by reassessment; if a good or clinical complete response is achieved, a nonoperative watch-and-wait strategy may be considered, whereas if feasible and acceptable, chemoradiation followed by surgery remains the preferred option. If systemic therapy is administered, treatment should favor single-agent fluoropyrimidine-based therapy such as capecitabine rather than oxaliplatin-containing combination chemotherapy because of age-related toxicity concerns.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old woman. Retired government employee. Good performance status. Lived with her younger brother. Past medical history included diabetes mellitus and hypertension for 15–20 years on regular medication, dyslipidemia for 4–5 years on statin therapy, and sleep disturbance/insomnia. She was taking more than five medications for comorbidities.

[ chief complaint ]: Right breast lump detected incidentally in April 2025, with associated vague bony pains.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic right breast carcinoma, hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative, with nodal and osseous metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsy from the right breast lesion showed invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 3. Immunohistochemistry showed estrogen receptor strongly positive at 90%; HER2 was 2+ by IHC and negative by FISH. Ki-67 was approximately 60%.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Mammogram: BI-RADS 5 right breast lesion measuring approximately 4 × 5 cm.  
- Initial PET-CT: primary right breast lesion with regional axillary nodal involvement, multiple non-regional nodal metastases in the cervical, mediastinal, and abdominal regions, and scattered bony metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- HER2 FISH negative.  
- Germline BRCA testing was performed.  
- Additional NGS testing was performed for potentially druggable targets.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Baseline frailty assessment was performed; no recent falls were reported.  
- Bone densitometry and cardiac evaluation were completed prior to systemic therapy.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic ER-positive/HER2-negative breast carcinoma with nodal and osseous metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Comorbidity burden included diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia with polypharmacy. Performance status was good.

reference_conclusion: Baseline frailty assessment with at least a G8 score, review of social support and financial considerations, evaluation for drug interactions, and pretreatment cardiac assessment and bone densitometry were undertaken prior to systemic therapy selection. Germline BRCA testing and additional NGS were obtained. The agreed first-line treatment was palbociclib plus letrozole for metastatic ER-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer, with initiation of bone-modifying therapy and calcium supplementation for osseous metastases. Following subsequent neurologic toxicity workup, the CDK4/6 inhibitor was re-challenged in hospital and was tolerated, and the patient was discharged on tapering oral steroids as advised by neurology.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 90-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Pain, loss of appetite, and weight loss.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV / extensive-stage large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, managed clinically as small cell carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Morphology was consistent with large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma. Tumor was described as highly proliferative with high Ki-67.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Hemoglobin: 10 g/dL.  
- Creatinine clearance: 47 mL/min.  
- Cardiac function was described as fairly preserved.

[ current disease status ]: Extensive-stage large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma in a 90-year-old man.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Functional assessment showed ADL and IADL largely preserved; he was able to perform most activities independently.  
- No falls were reported.  
- Cognition was intact on assessment.  
- Mild depression was present and was already on treatment.  
- Nutritional risk index indicated severe risk of malnutrition.  
- G8 screening indicated need for full comprehensive geriatric assessment.  
- Age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index predicted 10-year survival of 0%.  
- Chemotherapy toxicity score (CARG) was 12, indicating high risk for serious toxicity.  
- BMI was described as acceptable.  
- Social support was limited to one full-time helper.

reference_conclusion: Comprehensive geriatric assessment demonstrated marked vulnerability and a high predicted risk of chemotherapy toxicity; therefore, standard platinum-etoposide chemotherapy was not considered appropriate. After detailed discussion of the incurable, palliative intent of therapy and supportive care alternatives, treatment was initiated with weekly carboplatin AUC2, with etoposide added from the second week after initial tolerance, and delivered with supportive measures as needed. Following subsequent disease progression and treatment-related decline in quality of life on later-line therapy, chemotherapy was discontinued and management was transitioned to symptomatic supportive and palliative care.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old right-handed man. Retired from law enforcement. Newly divorced. Lived alone. No children. Residence was approximately 45 minutes from the treating medical facility.

[ chief complaint ]: Confusion and headache.

[ diagnosis ]: Glioblastoma, WHO grade 4.

[ histopathology results ]: Resected brain tumor tissue showed large pleomorphic tumor cells with mitotic activity and microvascular proliferation. Histopathologic and molecular classification was glioblastoma, WHO grade 4, IDH-wildtype.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial brain MRI demonstrated an aggressive-appearing enhancing mass in the right posterior temporal/inferior parietal region with central necrosis and surrounding edema, consistent with a high-grade glioma. Postoperative MRI obtained within 48 hours demonstrated gross total resection of the contrast-enhancing tumor.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH mutation negative. MGMT promoter hypermethylated. TERT promoter mutation present. EGFR amplification present. CDKN2A deletion present.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent surgical resection with gross total resection of the contrast-enhancing lesion. Postoperative course was uneventful; he was ambulatory the next day and headaches resolved. He received dexamethasone postoperatively. Despite no prior seizure history, he was discharged on antiseizure medication.

[ current disease status ]: Status post gross total resection of a right posterior temporal/inferior parietal glioblastoma, WHO grade 4, IDH-wildtype with MGMT promoter hypermethylation. Postoperative MRI within 48 hours demonstrated gross total resection of the contrast-enhancing tumor. He was ambulatory the day after surgery with resolution of headaches.

[ other clinical data ]: Symptoms began approximately 2 months before presentation with mild daily headaches that progressed to severe, intolerable headaches. Family noted confusion and forgetfulness for approximately 2 weeks before presentation. Past medical history included hypertension and pre-diabetes. Family history was notable for a father who died of colon cancer. Visual field assessment was considered preoperatively because of lesion location. No seizure history was documented at presentation.

reference_conclusion: Following gross total resection of the right temporal high-grade glioma, molecular profiling established glioblastoma, WHO grade 4, IDH-wildtype with MGMT hypermethylation. The agreed postoperative management is standard chemoradiation with daily radiation therapy over six weeks administered with concurrent daily oral temozolomide, initiated within 6 to 8 weeks after surgery if no clinical trial is pursued. After a 3- to 4-week recovery interval following radiation, adjuvant temozolomide is to be started on a 5-days-per-month schedule for 6 months, with discussion of Optune/tumor treating fields at that time. Subsequent imaging changes in this case were interpreted as pseudoprogression, and the plan is continued close observation with serial MRI rather than immediate change in therapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 32-year-old left-handed woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive right superior visual field deficit. Jerking of the right arm was also reported.

[ diagnosis ]: Left temporal/insular glioma, molecularly classified as IDH-mutant lower-grade astrocytoma, molecular grade 2.

[ histopathology results ]: Tumor pathology was consistent with an IDH-mutant lower-grade glioma. Immunohistochemistry and molecular testing were performed, including assessment of IDH1 R132H, ATRX, and p53. DNA methylation classification identified the tumor as an IDH-mutant lower-grade neoplasm. Copy number profile was described as significantly less genomically complex than that of an IDH-wildtype high-grade glioma and as a calm copy number profile. No concerning molecular biomarkers suggesting a more aggressive variant were identified. MGMT promoter was unmethylated.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative MRI demonstrated a large left temporal insular lesion with T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and expansion/mass-like growth of the left temporal lobe. The lesion was heterogeneous internally, with dark foci interpreted as vascular structures. The lesion was described as non-enhancing. No additional sites of disease were described. Postoperative MRI demonstrated resection of the majority of the tumor, with residual T2 hyperintensity along the posterior aspect and possibly along the medial/central aspect, consistent with residual abnormal tissue in the postoperative bed.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH-mutant tumor. Molecular testing included DNA/RNA next-generation sequencing and whole-genome DNA methylation profiling. DNA methylation classifier categorized the tumor as IDH-mutant lower grade. Copy number profile was calm/less genomically complex. MGMT promoter was unmethylated.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Surgical resection was performed. Postoperative imaging showed that the majority of the tumor had been resected, with residual T2-hyperintense abnormality remaining posteriorly and medially.

[ current disease status ]: Status post subtotal resection of a left temporal/insular IDH-mutant molecular grade 2 glioma, with residual postoperative T2-hyperintense abnormality.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included hypothyroidism. The patient had been previously healthy and active. She was recently engaged and worked as an attorney. She was in the adolescent and young adult age range. Potential need for laboratory monitoring of liver enzymes was referenced in the context of systemic therapy considerations, but no baseline laboratory values were provided.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 69-year-old man. Comorbid hypertension. Reformed smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Cough for 2 years. Loss of appetite for 6 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Non-small cell lung carcinoma, adenocarcinoma of the left lung. Final recorded clinical stage was T4N3M0.

[ histopathology results ]: CT-guided biopsy from the left lung showed non-small cell lung carcinoma, adenocarcinoma type.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT chest showed an area of consolidation in the left lung involving the apicoposterior segment of the left upper lobe, left perihilar region, and superior basal segment of the left lower lobe. The consolidation extended toward the hilum and encased the left descending pulmonary artery. A left pretracheal lymph node measured 16 x 10 mm. An enlarged subcarinal lymph node measured 2.0 x 1.4 cm.

PET-CT performed after tissue diagnosis showed a mildly FDG-avid ill-defined area of consolidation in the left upper lobe with SUV 3.4. There was an FDG-avid right paratracheal lymph node with SUV 5.3. A tiny nodule in the apical segment of the right upper lobe was non-FDG-avid. An additional subcentimeter left lung nodule was non-FDG-avid. No distant metastases were identified on the reported PET-CT.

Follow-up PET-CT after completion of chemoradiotherapy showed persistent lesion in the left lower lobe with adjoining left upper lobe involvement and significant perilesional lymphangitis. FDG-avid right paratracheal and subcarinal lymph nodes were present and had increased in size; the right paratracheal node had increased from 1.1 cm previously to 1.9 cm. The study was interpreted as showing residual disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Molecular testing had not been performed. The patient declined molecular analysis. EGFR, ALK, and PD-L1 results were not available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available. Echocardiography was normal. Performance status was 1.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent CT-guided biopsy for diagnosis. He subsequently received concurrent chemoradiotherapy, completed on 25 August 2023. Post-treatment PET-CT demonstrated residual/progressive intrathoracic disease.

[ current disease status ]: Residual/progressive disease after completion of concurrent chemoradiotherapy, with persistent left lung lesion and enlarging FDG-avid mediastinal lymphadenopathy. No documented distant metastatic disease was reported on the available imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: MRI brain was normal. EBUS-guided nodal sampling was not performed because EBUS was not available locally and the patient was unwilling to travel outside the city for the procedure.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old male farmer. Heavy smoker with approximately 50 pack-year smoking history.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive dyspnea over 2 months (reported as mMRC grade 1 progressing to grade 3), cough with scant sputum for 1 month, low-grade fever, anorexia, and weight loss for 1 month.

[ diagnosis ]: Lung adenocarcinoma with concurrent left pleural effusion/hemorrhagic pleural fluid and coexistent isoniazid-monoresistant pleural tuberculosis.

[ histopathology results ]: Pleural biopsy obtained after stabilization and thoracoscopic evaluation was reported as malignancy consistent with adenocarcinoma of lung.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial chest radiograph showed homogeneous left hemithoracic opacity.  
- Ultrasound confirmed pleural effusion; subsequently described as large/massive left pleural effusion.  
- CT chest dated 07 October showed left hemothorax, collapsed left lung with pleural effusion, significant pneumomediastinum, marked paraseptal emphysema, chest tube in situ, and areas of ground-glass opacity on the left.  
- Repeat CT chest dated 17 October showed interval resolution of pneumomediastinum with persistent pleural effusion.  
- Abdomen was reported as normal apart from a renal cyst described as simple cyst.  
- Clinical respiratory examination had shown findings of left pleural effusion with collapse.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Pleural fluid CBNAAT/GeneXpert for tuberculosis was negative.  
- Line probe assay on pleural fluid detected Mycobacterium tuberculosis with isoniazid resistance.  
- Resistance-associated genes reported included katG and inhA.  
- No second-line LPA result was available.  
- No mycobacterial culture result was available; MGIT culture was not performed/reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Oxygen saturation was 90% on room air at presentation.  
- Blood investigations were reported as normal.  
- Pleural fluid was hemorrhagic.  
- Pleural fluid total cell count was approximately 220 cells/mm3.  
- Pleural fluid differential was lymphocyte predominant.  
- Pleural fluid LDH was 874 U/L.  
- Pleural fluid ADA was 22 U/L.  
- Pleural fluid cytology was negative for malignant cells.  
- Sputum culture grew Acinetobacter.  
- Arterial/ventilatory assessment showed type 2 respiratory failure with pCO2 around 100 mmHg.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- The patient was admitted because of hypoxemia and large pleural effusion.  
- Diagnostic pleural tap was performed.  
- Intercostal chest drain was inserted; large-volume hemorrhagic fluid was drained, with symptomatic relief.  
- The patient required BiPAP/NIV support during acute respiratory failure.  
- Following BiPAP, pneumomediastinum and pneumothorax were documented on CT, considered in the setting of ruptured emphysematous bullae.  
- The patient was managed for Acinetobacter respiratory infection.  
- After approximately 10 days, clinical status and ECOG performance status had improved sufficiently to permit further diagnostic procedures including pleural biopsy/thoracoscopy.

[ current disease status ]:  
- After stabilization, the patient was clinically improved compared with presentation.  
- Pneumomediastinum had resolved on repeat CT.  
- Pleural malignancy had been confirmed on biopsy, and concurrent pleural tuberculosis with isoniazid resistance had been identified microbiologically.  
- Persistent pleural effusion remained present on follow-up imaging.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past history included cerebrovascular accident in 2017, managed medically.  
- On initial examination, vital signs were stable.  
- Mild pedal edema and clubbing were present.  
- Emphysema was present on CT imaging.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 72-year-old man; smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Cough for 3 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Left lower lobe lung squamous cell carcinoma, clinical stage T2N0M0.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- CT-guided biopsy from the left lower lobe lesion showed squamous cell carcinoma.  
- Endobronchial ultrasound-guided nodal sampling from N2/N3 stations was negative for malignancy.  
- Lymph node biopsy showed granulomatous pathology.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Chest radiograph showed left lower zone haziness.  
- PET-CT showed a fibrocavitary lesion in the left lower lobe with SUV 23.6, extending to the costal pleura.  
- PET-CT also showed tracer uptake in bilateral hilar and a few mediastinal lymph nodes.  
- CT imaging demonstrated a peripheral cavitary lesion in the left lower lobe with eccentric cavitation and associated emphysematous changes.  
- Brain MRI was performed; no abnormal findings were specified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- GeneXpert from an EBUS-sampled lymph node was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, reported as medium signal intensity.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- EBUS and CT-guided biopsy were performed during diagnostic workup.  
- Antitubercular therapy was started after EBUS GeneXpert positivity.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Clinical stage T2N0M0 left lower lobe squamous cell carcinoma.  
- Endobronchial ultrasound-guided nodal sampling from N2/N3 stations was negative for malignancy.  
- Granulomatous lymph node pathology in the setting of MTB GeneXpert positivity, with antitubercular therapy started.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Preoperative fitness assessment included cardiac evaluation, pulmonary function testing, DLCO, and stair-climbing assessment; the patient was considered fit for surgery.

[ chief complaint ]: Right hilar mass with bronchial cutoff.

[ diagnosis ]: Poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the right lung with infiltration of the right main bronchus. Initial nodal staging by EBUS-FNAC showed station 4R positivity with stations 7 and 10 negative, consistent with cT3N2 disease.

The patient subsequently underwent sleeve lobectomy because of upper lobe bronchus involvement. Intraoperative frozen section of the bronchial margin was negative. R0 resection was achieved.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status after R0 sleeve lobectomy with negative margins and no residual nodal disease identified in approximately 24 resected lymph nodes.

[ other clinical data ]: EBUS-FNAC findings were: station 7 negative, station 10 negative, station 4R positive. Upper lobe bronchus involvement was present.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 34-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Chronic cough.

[ diagnosis ]: Left upper lobe lung squamous cell carcinoma, initially staged cT4N0M0; postoperative pathologic stage pT4N0. Subsequent isolated endotracheal recurrence was identified approximately 1 year after initial treatment.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- CT-guided biopsy from the left lung lesion showed squamous cell carcinoma.  
- EBUS-FNAC of mediastinal nodal stations sampled for N2/N3 disease was negative.  
- Resection specimen showed poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.  
- Pathologic stage was pT4 pN0.  
- All resection margins were clear (R0 resection).  
- All dissected lymph nodes were negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT chest showed a left lung lesion.  
- Initial PET-CT showed a multilobulated soft tissue density in the left upper lobe with transfissural extension.  
- PET-CT also showed involvement of the left fifth rib region.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Systematic mediastinal lymph node dissection was performed.  
- Surveillance imaging after initial treatment had been performed at approximately 3 months, 6 months, and 1 year.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 4-year-old male child. Neurodevelopmental history included autism spectrum disorder.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidentally detected abdominal mass noted by the mother approximately 1 month prior to presentation, with rapid increase in size and progressive abdominal distension.

[ diagnosis ]: Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma) arising in a horseshoe kidney, centered in the isthmic/interpolar region. The case had been managed as stage V/bilateral Wilms tumor for treatment planning purposes. No distant metastases were identified on available imaging.

[ histopathology results ]: Ultrasound-guided core-cut biopsy was performed. Histopathology was suggestive of triphasic nephroblastoma. WT1 was positive. IRC status was reported positive.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Ultrasound abdomen/pelvis showed a horseshoe kidney with fusion at the lower poles and a large solid-cystic lesion measuring 11.6 × 6.6 cm arising from the isthmus, with mild internal vascularity; nephroblastoma was queried.  
- Initial outside CECT had described a crossed fused right ectopic kidney in the midline at L3-L5 level with upper pole fusion to the lower pole of the left kidney, and a multiseptated solid-cystic lesion measuring 7.7 × 7.8 × 9.1 cm arising from the interpolar region of the ectopic kidney and extending to the left renal pelvis.  
- Review of CT imaging favored a horseshoe kidney with lower pole fusion rather than crossed fused ectopia. The mass appeared to arise from the isthmus and right renal hilar/interpolar region, extending into the left renal hilum.  
- Initial CT showed complete encasement of the renal arterial structures, described as involving both left and right renal arteries.  
- Bilateral lungs were clear on CT, with no evidence of pulmonary metastasis.  
- Associated skeletal anomalies on CT included multiple rib and spinal deformities, hemivertebrae, partial fusion of D4-D5 vertebrae, and levoscoliosis.  
- Post 6 weeks of vincristine/dactinomycin, repeat CECT abdomen/pelvis with CT angiography showed reduction in tumor size. The lesion remained centered in the interpolar region of the horseshoe kidney and extended into the left renal hilum. A left accessory renal artery arising from the distal aorta was identified; the right renal artery, left renal artery, and accessory left renal artery were all described as encased. The IVC was compressed without infiltration. No significant lymphadenopathy was seen. No renal vein thrombus or IVC thrombus was identified. Ureters and suprarenals were normal.  
- After 2 cycles of etoposide/carboplatin, repeat CECT abdomen/pelvis showed significant further reduction in tumor size. The tumor remained centered in the interpolar region of the right renal moiety, extending into the left pararenal space and left renal hilum. A single accessory renal artery supplying the upper pole of the left kidney was free from encasement. The right renal artery coursed along the periphery of the mass but was encased near the hilum. The right renal vein was encased. The left main renal artery was encased. A tributary from the left renal vein to the upper pole was free.  
- Delayed phase assessment reportedly showed no ureteric encasement; tumor infiltration into the left renal pelvicalyceal system was described without extension into the ureter.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Clinical exome sequencing showed heterozygous carrier status for Fanconi anemia.

[ laboratory results ]: Hematological and biochemical parameters were reported within normal limits at presentation. Urinary VMA was normal/negative. Estimated GFR after chemotherapy had not yet been obtained at the time of documentation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Ultrasound-guided core-cut biopsy was attempted via retroperitoneal approach but required a partially transperitoneal route to obtain tissue.  
- Neoadjuvant chemotherapy was administered per SIOP Umbrella-based institutional protocol.  
- First-line preoperative chemotherapy consisted of 6 weeks of vincristine and dactinomycin.  
- Clinical response after 6 weeks: abdominal mass was no longer well palpable on examination.  
- Radiologic response after 6 weeks: reduction in tumor size on CECT/CT angiography.  
- Because nephron-sparing surgery was not considered feasible at that stage, treatment was escalated to 2 cycles of etoposide and carboplatin, given 3 weeks apart.  
- Radiologic response after etoposide/carboplatin: significant further reduction in tumor size.

[ current disease status ]: Residual Wilms tumor persisted in the horseshoe kidney after 8 total chemotherapy cycles, centered in the interpolar/isthmic region with extension into the left renal hilum/pararenal space. Persistent vascular involvement remained, including encasement of the right renal artery near the hilum, right renal vein, and left main renal artery; one accessory artery to the left upper pole remained free. No pulmonary metastases, renal vein thrombus, IVC thrombus, or significant lymphadenopathy were identified on the latest reported imaging.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past surgical history included surgery in infancy for right knee flexion deformity; records were unavailable.  
- Family history was non-significant.  
- Antenatal history was reportedly unremarkable.  
- Examination at presentation showed abdominal distension with inferior displacement of the umbilicus and a firm-to-hard, lobulated, non-tender abdominal mass approximately 6 × 5 cm, extending from the right lumbar region across the umbilical/epigastric/suprapubic region to the left lumbar region; margins were well defined. The mass was bimanually palpable on the left.  
- External genitalia and testes were normal.  
- Spine examination showed dorsolumbar scoliosis/abnormal curvature with suspected vertebral defect at the lumbosacral junction; no cutaneous stigmata of spinal dysraphism were described.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female child, aged 4.5 years.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in June 2024 with abdominal distension.

[ diagnosis ]: Bilateral multifocal Wilms tumor involving both kidneys.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial ultrasound-guided core biopsy from a right renal lesion showed triphasic Wilms tumor with anaplasia reported on biopsy.  
- Ultrasound-guided core biopsy from a left renal lesion after 6 weeks of chemotherapy was inconclusive.  
- Right robotic radical nephrectomy specimen showed multifocal Wilms tumor with two distinct lesions. Sections showed triphasic tumor morphology. No anaplastic features were identified in the nephrectomy specimen.  
- No evidence of tumor disruption, renal sinus involvement, renal vein involvement, extension beyond the renal capsule by viable tumor, or direct extension to adjacent organs.  
- Surgical margins were negative for viable and non-viable tumor.  
- Viable tumor was >33%, with blastemal component >66% of viable tumor.  
- One sampled lymph node was uninvolved.  
- Pathology was reported as local stage I high-risk histology.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Baseline abdominal imaging demonstrated:  
  - Right kidney: heterogeneous lesion measuring 12 × 10 cm in the interpolar region/lower pole with heterogeneous post-contrast enhancement; additional upper pole lesion measuring 4.3 × 3.9 cm.  
  - Left kidney: three lesions, including one measuring 3.7 × 3.3 cm in the posterior interpolar cortex, another interpolar cortical lesion laterally, and one lesion in the lower pole.  
- HRCT chest at presentation was normal.  
- Reassessment CT abdomen after 6 weeks of neoadjuvant chemotherapy showed reduction in size of all renal lesions.  
- Whole-body PET-CT showed uptake only in the right lower pole lesion.  
- CT was repeated approximately 1 month later during a period off chemotherapy.  
- After completion of 27 weeks of chemotherapy, residual disease persisted in the left kidney as three subcentimetric lesions: posterior interpolar, lateral interpolar, and lower pole lesions. The largest residual lesion measured 14 × 6 mm in the lateral interpolar region.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]: Not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Received 3-drug neoadjuvant chemotherapy for 6 weeks prior to surgery; regimen included vincristine, dactinomycin, and doxorubicin.  
- Post-neoadjuvant imaging showed reduction in size of all bilateral renal lesions.  
- Underwent right robotic radical nephrectomy. There was no capsular breach or intraoperative tumor spillage.  
- Following nephrectomy pathology reported as local stage I high-risk histology, the patient started adjuvant chemotherapy for 26–27 weeks as per SIOP-based protocol with vincristine, dactinomycin, and doxorubicin.  
- After 7 weeks of adjuvant therapy, referral for nephron-sparing surgery of the left kidney was made, but surgery was deferred until completion of chemotherapy.  
- Interventional radiology assessed for radiofrequency ablation of residual left renal lesions; this was considered unsuitable because of multiple small lesions and anticipated loss of surrounding normal renal parenchyma.  
- Chemotherapy was continued to completion.  
- Despite completion of 27 weeks of chemotherapy, three residual left renal lesions remained.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Status post right radical nephrectomy for multifocal Wilms tumor.  
- Persistent residual disease in the left kidney after completion of systemic therapy, with three subcentimetric lesions remaining; largest 14 × 6 mm.  
- No pulmonary metastases were identified on chest HRCT at presentation.  
- PET-CT demonstrated metabolic uptake confined to the right lower pole lesion at the time of that study.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The child was referred after initial management at another institution.  
- During right nephrectomy, only one lymph node was sampled.  
- The left kidney was not surgically addressed at the time of right nephrectomy.

The procedure should be performed as enucleation of the three residual lesions with intraoperative frozen section assessment. Radiofrequency ablation is not considered appropriate for Wilms tumor in this setting.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 6-year-old female child.

[ chief complaint ]: Abdominal distension and abdominal lump for 1.5 months, associated with loss of appetite, weight loss, nausea, and constipation.

[ diagnosis ]: Abdominal neuroblastoma, staged as L2 disease after evaluation. Primary mass was located in the left upper quadrant/upper abdomen.

[ histopathology results ]: Ultrasound-guided FNAC from the abdominal mass showed features of a small round cell tumor, with neuroblastoma considered. Immunohistochemistry was positive for neuron-specific enolase, and the diagnosis of neuroblastoma was made. No core biopsy histology, Shimada classification, or favorable/unfavorable histology was available.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Ultrasound abdomen showed a tumor encasing major vessels including the celiac axis, superior mesenteric artery, and inferior mesenteric artery, without documented vascular invasion.  
- Left kidney was visualized separately from the mass.  
- Inferior vena cava was compressed but remained patent, with no thrombus.  
- Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen/pelvis demonstrated a large left upper quadrant abdominal mass with calcifications.  
- Descending aorta was displaced by the mass.  
- Left kidney was separate from the mass, and the mass did not appear to arise from the kidney.  
- Mild left hydronephrosis and minimal ascites were present on initial CT.  
- CT chest showed no evidence of metastatic disease.  
- After 6 cycles of chemotherapy, repeat CT abdomen/pelvis showed good interval response; clinically the mass was no longer palpable, but persistent encasement of the celiac axis, superior mesenteric artery branches, and bilateral renal pedicles remained.  
- After 1 additional cycle of chemotherapy, repeat CT showed persistent encasement of the superior mesenteric artery, celiac axis, bilateral renal arteries, and portal vein by more than 180 degrees.  
- Inferior vena cava remained compressed but patent on venous phase imaging.  
- No skeletal lesions were identified on bone scan.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: N-MYC amplification testing was not performed. No MLPA or segmented chromosomal aberration analysis was available. MIBG scan was not performed due to unavailability.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Child was not anemic.  
- Renal function tests were normal.  
- Electrolytes were normal.  
- 24-hour urinary VMA was negative.  
- 24-hour urinary HVA was negative.  
- LDH was elevated; value reported at approximately 1600.  
- Other tumor markers were within normal range.  
- Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy were negative for malignancy.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- The patient received neoadjuvant chemotherapy planned as 6 cycles of a 4-drug regimen: cyclophosphamide, etoposide, cisplatin, and adriamycin.  
- Following 6 cycles, general condition improved and the abdominal mass was no longer palpable clinically; however, residual tumor with persistent major vascular encasement remained on CT.  
- One additional cycle of neoadjuvant chemotherapy was administered.  
- After the additional cycle, imaging continued to show persistent encasement of major abdominal vessels.

[ current disease status ]: Residual abdominal neuroblastoma persisted after 7 cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, with ongoing encasement of the celiac axis, superior mesenteric artery, bilateral renal arteries/pedicles, portal vein, and compression of the inferior vena cava without thrombosis. No documented distant metastatic disease was identified on CT chest, bone marrow evaluation, or bone scan. Clinically, the child had improved after chemotherapy.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- On general examination at presentation, the child appeared cachectic.  
- Abdominal examination showed a 22 × 18 cm large non-tender nodular mass involving the entire upper abdomen with well-defined margins; it was not possible to insinuate between the costal margin and the mass.  
- Per-rectal examination was normal.  
- External genitalia examination was normal.  
- Rapid progression of abdominal distension with onset of respiratory distress had been documented prior to initiation of treatment.  
- The child was not hypertensive at presentation.

reference_conclusion: Following neoadjuvant chemotherapy, the consensus was to proceed with operative debulking rather than further observation or metabolic imaging. Surgical management should aim for at least 50% tumor resection, with piecemeal excision as feasible and acceptance of residual disease along major vessels if required to preserve critical structures; nephrectomy should be avoided unless necessitated by a life-saving intraoperative circumstance. Resected tissue should be submitted for histology and MYCN amplification or other feasible molecular studies to clarify tumor biology and guide subsequent management.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 2.5-year-old male child.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive, asymptomatic upper abdominal mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Hepatoblastoma involving both lobes of the liver; staged as PRETEXT III, standard risk.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Ultrasound demonstrated a heterogeneous liver mass measuring 8.6 × 7.6 cm involving both hepatic lobes.  
- Initial CT angiography showed a heterogeneous hepatic mass involving segments 4A, 4B, 5, and part of segment 8. The left and right hepatic veins were splayed over the mass; the middle hepatic vein was not visible. The left portal vein was not visible. The main portal vein and arterial phase vessels were visualized.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Jaundice was present at presentation.  
- Gamma-glutamyl transferase was raised.  
- Alpha-fetoprotein was >180,000.  
- LDH was 1545.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed hepatoblastoma involving both lobes of the liver, staged as PRETEXT III, standard risk, with a heterogeneous hepatic mass involving segments 4A, 4B, 5, and part of segment 8, and alpha-fetoprotein >180,000. The child was otherwise asymptomatic apart from the progressively enlarging upper abdominal mass.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Examination at presentation showed generalized abdominal distension, with liver palpable approximately 10 cm below the costal margin; the mass was firm and dull on percussion and was continuous with the liver.  
- Left inguinal hernia was present.

reference_conclusion: The patient was managed as standard-risk PRETEXT III hepatoblastoma with four cycles of cisplatin monotherapy, followed by surgical resection after interval imaging demonstrated tumor shrinkage and apparent resectability. A non-anatomical resection of segments 5, 8, 4A, and 4B was performed with complete excision and negative margins. Two cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy were administered postoperatively. Ongoing surveillance has shown no residual or recurrent disease on postoperative imaging, with normalization of AFP and continued regular follow-up.

[...] After the 4th cycle, we again did a CT NGO to look for the response of the tumor. The tumor shrink in size and as you can see all the hepatic veins are visible. So, it seems resectable. So, we have gone ahead with planning the resection. [...] And we have done the non-anatomical resection of segment 5 and part of segment 8, 4A, 4B. And post-surgery, two cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy were given. [...] margins were free of tumor. [...] This was a CT angio done in postoperative period after 6 months. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult patient with prostate cancer. No further demographic data were available.

[ chief complaint ]: Rising prostate-specific antigen (PSA) following focal treatment of an extreme apical prostate tumour.

[ diagnosis ]: Localised prostate adenocarcinoma, initially staged as clinical T2a, with Gleason score 4+3. Subsequent adjacent/in-field recurrence at the prostatic apex was identified on follow-up imaging after focal irreversible electroporation (IRE).

[ histopathology results ]: Initial tumour histology showed Gleason 4+3 adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Post-treatment T2-weighted MRI performed shortly after initial IRE showed haemorrhagic change in the treated area.  
- MRI at 1 year after initial treatment showed good resolution without concerning findings.  
- PSMA PET performed in 2019 for PSA rise demonstrated uptake in the treated region.  
- MRI in early 2020 demonstrated an abnormal area on ADC imaging adjacent to the prior treatment zone, consistent with adjacent/in-field recurrence and incomplete prior treatment coverage.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- PSA was approximately 10 ng/mL in 2017 at initial diagnosis.  
- PSA rose again to approximately 10 ng/mL in 2019 after initial focal treatment.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- The patient underwent focal irreversible electroporation for an extreme apical prostate tumour in 2017.  
- Biochemical recurrence was observed by 2019 with PSA rise, and imaging subsequently demonstrated adjacent/in-field recurrence.

[ current disease status ]: Adjacent/in-field recurrence at the prostatic apex after focal IRE, with biochemical recurrence and imaging evidence of incomplete prior treatment coverage.

[ other clinical data ]: The recurrent lesion was located at the extreme prostatic apex, adjacent to the original treatment field. No additional comorbidity, age, family history, or performance status data were available.

reference_discussion.text: Thanks. I presented the results of our patients on the NanoKnife Masterclass two days ago, and so this is a denominator of about 600 cases up to date, with about 11-year follow-up. But what I thought I'd do is just share with you a couple of cases and some particular points with using irreversible electroporation. So the first one is a person who had an apical tumour, an extreme apical tumour, who then got a recurrence. The second one is a more typical extreme apical tumour that we treated. And the third one was just a tricky case in the anterior zone. So this patient had a PSA of about 10 in 2017, had a clinical T2A lesion and was a Gleason 4 plus 3 actually. After our treatment, we always do a T2 MRI image, which shows hemorrhage. I know Mark Emberton does a gadolinium at this point to look for perfusion, and having spoken to him, I think that might be a good idea. PSA dropped. One year MRI showed good resolution and nothing much to worry about. 2019, PSA went up to about 10. And then as a result of that, we did a PET scan and the PET scan did show some activity in that area. We have had a couple of people after IRE where you'll form a cavity and you'll get a false positive with the PSMA PET scan. So just a caution that when you see something bright there, you just have to look at the MRI as well. As a result of that, an MRI in early 2020 showed, as you can see, let me see here. It showed on the ADC an area just here which was adjacent to the area, so clearly I didn't treat that area completely. So that was an adjacent or infield recurrence. And so we retreated that, and the principles of treating the apex, I always put four needles into the apex. I know some people use three at the apex, but I always use four, just for a reliable ablation. And I always make sure that the distance of the active electrode is at least three millimetres from the edge. So that way I'm going to treat two millimetres outside of the capsule. One of the advantages of IRE that you can treat extracapsular disease. And this was the MRI at the two day mark afterwards showing the hemorrhage again. and PSA started to drop down to 3.7. The one year MRI showed retraction of that area and no perfusion, and biopsies of that area in 2022 was all clear, and the PSA up to today has stayed very stable. We then looked at our redo treatments, and the redo treatments, We've had 26 of the patients have had redos, and of those 26, 15 of them have had a durable response with biopsy-proven clearance. Overall, over time, that dropped down to 12. So there was some late recurrences as well. So overall, we actually ended up with half of the patients on a redo got a durable response. And again, there's treatment afterwards with either radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy. I thought I'd just share, I got one of our fellows just to look at exactly what's happened to the redos, because I think the redos are interesting. Over 344 primary RREs with a minimum of 18 months follow-up, the recurrence rate was 62 of them, as defined as any Gleason 4 pattern. Those recurrences had a redo and some had some active surveillance and just monitored a tiny little microscopic spot. Some were just Gleason 6 low-grade stuff. This was all recurrences. This is including Gleason 6. and we did redo IREs in 19 patients. And in those 19 patients, 10 of them ended up having a radical prostatectomy, two had more than two IREs, one's just been monitored and seven of them are clear from significant tumour. But what was interesting was This, when you look at the infield and outfield, the infield ones seem to do better with redo focal therapy, tiny numbers, four and two clear, although a lot of them decided that forget about it, I'm gonna actually have my prostate out. But the outfield, we had an extremely high 73% recurrence rate after redo in the outfield. which is different to what other people have presented. As a result of my general philosophy about infield tumours, if you get any biopsy recurrence on the infield, we are aggressive by doing a repeat treatment immediately, as opposed to outfield, which I think is more a disease phenomena. This is a more standard case. This is an anterior apical tumour. PSA was about 9.7. And then we treated that with, this is the PSMA PET scan. We treated that with a nanoknife. This was the MRI six months down the track. PSA fell down and biopsies were clear. This particular, was an anterior case, and the reason I'm showing you- It creates echo, literally covering my area. It is because- So that's unacceptable. We could probably turn the sound down. The reason I was showing it is, this is a biggish prostate, and so we put one needle in, and then I was trying to get the second needle in to treat this anterior zone. So what we do, we just re-angle the ultrasound probe. I suppose it's like precision point. and just go back in and it's much, much easier to place the electrodes in that extreme anterior zone. And you can see I'm placing them very, very close to the edge of the prostate, probably only three millimetres away is my preferred area. That's the fourth one that we put in, and this is the longitudinal plan, just to make sure that we're in the correct plane. We decide on the length of the electrode, and then the ablation is performed. One thing we've observed with IRE, in terms of feedback, the cancer itself tends to stay black, and you get the hydrolysis all around it, which is white. And it's one feedback that you get, not only the hydrolysis, which tells you about the tumour, but the black area which is often surrounded. So this was the black area here and as we placed it, as we electrocuted it, I showed this overall picture mainly because you'll see there's some movement of the patient when we're doing it. And when you're doing extreme anterior tumour, that amount of movement is still acceptable because we're getting direct obturator contraction. So you just need to be aware of the movement of the electrodes at the time when you're actually doing that type of movement there. And you can see the hydrolysis which is occurring there. So I thought I'd stop with that.

reference_conclusion: For biopsy-confirmed in-field recurrence after irreversible electroporation, repeat focal treatment is undertaken promptly, as in-field lesions appear to have better outcomes with redo focal therapy. Outfield recurrence is regarded as more reflective of underlying disease biology, with a high recurrence rate after redo treatment; subsequent management may include surveillance for minimal low-grade disease or definitive salvage therapy with radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy. Redo treatment outcomes should be interpreted with the understanding that approximately half of patients may achieve a durable biopsy-proven response.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 33-year-old female. Gravida 5, para 2, abortion 3. Never smoker. No family history of cancer. Obesity with body mass index 34 kg/m².

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for management after incidental identification of invasive cervical squamous cell carcinoma following prior excisional procedure and subsequent hysterectomy. The patient had been asymptomatic.

[ diagnosis ]: Cervical squamous cell carcinoma, FIGO 2018 stage IA2.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial Papanicolaou smear was suspicious for high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (CIN 2/3). Subsequent colposcopy-directed cervical biopsy confirmed high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion without suspicious invasion. Excisional procedure (LEEP/conization) demonstrated squamous cell carcinoma in situ measuring 1 cm, with glandular involvement; the endocervical margin was positive for high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion/CIN 2/3. Pathology review at the receiving institution confirmed the same findings in the excisional specimen. Review of the hysterectomy specimen by two pathologists demonstrated invasive squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix with 2.5 mm horizontal spread and 5 mm stromal invasion, no lymphovascular space invasion, and negative surgical margins.

[ imaging findings ]: Pelvic MRI showed no evidence of disease.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial evaluation and treatment were performed at another institution. After abnormal cervical cytology and confirmatory biopsy, the patient underwent LEEP/conization. Two months later, she underwent total laparoscopic extrafascial hysterectomy. Following referral, physical examination showed no evidence of residual disease, and pelvic MRI showed no evidence of disease.

[ current disease status ]: No clinical or radiologic evidence of residual disease after hysterectomy. Physical examination was normal.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 41-year-old Hispanic woman. No family history of cancer was reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Six-month history of vaginal discharge and vaginal bleeding in June 2014. No other symptoms were reported at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IIB cervical cancer diagnosed in 2014. Subsequent brain metastasis to the cerebellum was diagnosed in October 2014.

[ histopathology results ]: Cervical biopsy demonstrated moderately differentiated ulcerated squamous cell carcinoma. Histopathology from resected cerebellar lesion confirmed metastatic squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Gynecologic examination demonstrated a 7 cm bleeding exophytic cervical mass with necrotic center and parametrial involvement. Post-treatment imaging after chemoradiation showed no evidence of disease. Brain MRI in October 2014 demonstrated a cerebellar expansive lesion consistent with metastasis.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: In July 2014, the patient received concurrent chemoradiation consisting of weekly cisplatin for 8 weeks and radiotherapy for 10 weeks. At completion of treatment, imaging showed no evidence of disease. After identification of the cerebellar metastasis, she underwent suboccipital craniotomy with wide tumor resection. She then started whole-brain radiotherapy as palliative treatment in November 2014.

[ current disease status ]: Resected solitary cerebellar metastasis from stage IIB cervical squamous cell carcinoma, with no evidence of disease at the primary site after chemoradiation, receiving palliative whole-brain radiotherapy.
