reference_discussion.text: Okay, thank you. This case is about a 41-year-old Hispanic woman without family history of cancer. In June 2014, the patient comes to the institution with a six-month history of vaginal discharge. and bleeding and no other symptoms. The gynecological examination revealed a seven centimeter bleeding exophytic cervical mass with necrotic center and dry paramedial involvement. A cervical biopsy was performed showing moderately differentiated ulcerated squamous cell carcinoma. Next please. and the patient was diagnosed with stage 2b cervical cancer. In July, she received concurrent chemo-radiation with weekly c-studying for 8 weeks and 10 weeks of radiotherapy. At the end of the treatment, there was no evidence of disease in the imagined studies. And in October 2014, with a history of headache for one month, a brain MRI was performed showing a cerebellar expansive process assisted with metastasis. She underwent a suboccipital craniotomy, a wide resection of the tumor, and confirmed the diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma brain metastasis. She started olocranial radiotherapy as a palliative treatment in November 2014. And she was taken to the emergency room with severe neurological impairment in December, five days after her family reported her death. The first question is, cervix cancer in young women have different behavior and response to treatment?

So maybe we take that question first, if you don't mind. So the real question about this very full presentation and tragic ending with the patient's death is, does this disease behave differently in young women? And is the response to treatment different in young women?

I don't know of any data. I mean, I think we tend to think that these cancers, in general, that age is a prognostic indicator with older women doing worse. But that may be confounded by ability to complete all intended treatment, cycles of treatment, And then I think there may be some data that we tend to be less aggressive with older patients, even if you factor in medical comorbidities. I don't know of any data that would, in a non-immunocompromised patient, that would support that younger women have a different disease course. I don't know if Mike wants to weigh in.

Yeah, I would agree on that. If anything, in the States, the age relationship is inverse, which is the older patients with cervical cancer tend to do poorer, and I think for the reasons that Dr. DelCorno mentioned.
Is there any biological subtype that's confined to young women that makes it worse, like triple negative in breast cancer, young women with breast cancer? Is there something like that?

I would wonder if the histology here is different. I mean, I don't know if it's read as squamous, but certainly we see a more aggressive biology, some of the more rare types of cervical cancer, but it's not a I don't think brain methasis are that common.

The histologic distribution is really roughly the same in terms of squamous and adeno. I think we all think adeno tends to be a little more aggressive. In this case, it was a moderately differentiated squamous.
Is it common for these, you just said, no. Do you concur that it's not common to get brain mints from this particular cancer?

Yeah, so the interesting point here is you can certainly rest assured you had brain mints at the time the whole diagnosis was made. It was only three months between the radiation. And then once you became down with neurologic symptoms, it's a rare enough event for us that we would never recommend, you know, head CTs or MRIs as a screening issue at the time that you treat these patients. In an asymptomatic patient, we would go only with neurologic symptoms. So the way this played out is actually, I think, was handled reasonably well. It's just in this particular patient appeared to be a very aggressive tumor.

And the management of the brain meds? Kathleen, if you want to chime in, please feel free. The management of the brain meds in this young patient, she's got cerebellar metastasis from a squamous cell crossing over the cervix. What's the best management for that?

Just to take a step back, I agree with Mike and Marcella that I think when we see these cases, we usually go back and review the pathology. I mean, I just wonder if it's a neuroendocrine tumor or some other very aggressive pathology. When we have brain mats, usually we work with a radiation oncologist and the neurosurgeons. Sometimes if it's an isolated brain mat, our neurosurgeons are very aggressive. We do a lot of surgery. If it's multiple brain mats, then usually it's whole brain radiation and sometimes stereotactic radiotherapy as well.

Can I just say, Kathleen, thank you, can I just say, very often We have cases presented on these tumor boards from South America where the patient coming into a tertiary care cancer center from a peripheral center, and the management to date from the peripheral center has been suboptimal. But just to give you a reality check here, at Massachusetts General Hospital, when we get a breast cancer patient arrive for a second opinion or for a referral from an outside community hospital, it's standard practice to review the pathology in every single patient like that. So rather than sort of insulting the pathology expertise of the referring center, we just routinely redo the pathology, we routinely do the biomarkers, and it is really remarkable how often we have a change in the pathology and a change in the biomarkers by reviewing it. I don't know what the practice is like in South America, but that's what we do here. We review all cases. We have all the x-rays reviewed by our radiologists, re-read, sometimes we repeat the x-rays, we even sometimes repeat the biopsy, but we make sure that the information we're getting on the patient is accurate. And unfortunately, it very often isn't accurate from a referring center. So that might be a good idea for a patient like this who presents with a very atypical presentation of brain metastasis before accepting the pathology diagnosis, perhaps reviewing the path or repeating the biopsy would be appropriate. Do you want to make any comment about the case from INEN? Oh, they're still asking what's the treatment. treatment and management of—I don't know that we've got a brain radiotherapist yet, but— Well, I would just say, Leon— Yes, Leon.

So I do—I agree with the comments that were made. Here at Mass General, we're remarkably aggressive with neurosurgery for these patients. And as was pointed out before, if it's a solitary med, that's a clear indication of surgery. It seems to me most of what was done was quite reasonable.

If it's an isolated med that is amenable to surgery, they'll resect and then will radiate the brain. We're lucky that we have protons, and that spares some toxicity of the brain. Could be, it could be sort of, for lack of better terminology, neuronal degeneration from the radiation. It could be edema, it could be bleed. Okay. Yeah.

For brain metastasis, pathology review or repeat biopsy was advised given the atypical presentation, and management should involve multidisciplinary evaluation with neurosurgery and radiation oncology. In the setting of a solitary or surgically amenable dominant lesion, resection followed by brain radiotherapy was supported; for multiple brain metastases, whole-brain radiation, with consideration of stereotactic radiotherapy in selected cases, was described as standard management.

In an asymptomatic patient, we would go only with neurologic symptoms. So the way this played out is actually, I think, was handled reasonably well. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old woman with hypertension and diabetes mellitus. No family history of cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: In the first quarter of 2015, she presented with anorexia, weight loss, and abdominal distention.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade serous ovarian adenocarcinoma, FIGO stage IV.

[ histopathology results ]: Preoperative biopsy showed serous adenocarcinoma, grade 3. Immunohistochemistry was estrogen receptor positive and WT1 positive, consistent with serous ovarian adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Abdominal ultrasound showed ascites and peritoneal carcinomatosis. PET-CT demonstrated a 2 cm hepatic lesion with increased FDG uptake, increased uptake at the lower diaphragm, ascites, and increased uptake in the parametrial region and left ovary.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic testing results were reported.

[ laboratory results ]: CA-125 was 345 at presentation. Hemoglobin was 9 g/dL, consistent with anemia.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: She underwent suboptimal cytoreductive surgery with resection of the hepatic lesion; residual disease greater than 1 cm remained postoperatively.

[ current disease status ]: Stage IV high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma after suboptimal primary cytoreduction, with residual postoperative disease greater than 1 cm.

[ other clinical data ]: Hepatic involvement was surgically resected at cytoreduction. Residual postoperative disease burden was greater than 1 cm.

In first quarter of 2015, the patient started with anorexia, weight loss, and abdominal distention. The laboratory findings show an increased CA 125 of 345 and anemia with an hemoglobin of 9. And the abdominal ultrasound revealed ascites and peritoneal carcinomatosis. Next, please. She continued the investigation and she did a PET-CT that revealed one node in liver of two centimeters with an increased glucose uptake. There's also an increased glucose uptake in lower level of the diaphragm and ascites. Next one. Showing increased uptake in the parameter and left ovarian. Next one. The patient did a pre-autonomous biopsy that revealed a serous adenocarcinoma grade 3. And the immunohistochemistry revealed ER positive and GWT1 positive. Consist with a serous ovarian adenocarcinoma stage 4. So after that, the patient was submitted to a sub-automal cytoreduction. and resection of hepatic lesion. And after that, it was more than one centimeter in the disease, in the surgery. And after that, the patient start with chemotherapy with carbopatin, paclitexel, and bevacizumab every three weeks for six cycles. The patient had a good tolerance and no grade three or four toxicities. After that, the patient had clinical, serologic, and radiologic response. And it started with Montana's Bevacizumab, 15 milligrams per kilo every three weeks. And in the end of 2015, she did another PET-CT that revealed no evidence of disease and a normal CA 125 or 33. So the question from a primary cytoreduction stage 4 disease, what would be the best adjuvant treatment for this patient? And in the case of a complete response, when should we stop Bevacizumab maintenance treatment?
So in addition to addressing some of the questions, some general comments about the case, just general comments.

Yeah, so I think as a general comment, you know, even though there are data from two randomized studies, GOG-218 and ICOM-7, with regards to using metastasomab concurrently with chemotherapy and then as many as therapy, that regimen has not been approved in the United States, and so we don't use it very often. I would say in our practice we don't use it, I don't think, at all. Basically, primarily because there were no data to support an overall survival advantage. The data show a, I would say, a modest progression-free survival advantage at the expense of taking Avastin concurrently with chemo that has made necessary a year or 15 months, depending on which of the two trials you look at. So as a general statement, I would say that we don't use that, and maybe Mike can speak a little more to that, we don't use the combination with Avastin that was used in this case.

So can I just clarify, you use COBA, Platinum, and Paxil-Tex, or without? Because it's very expensive, and you're saying there's very little evidence of benefit. Maybe a small progression-free survival?
There's a small advantage with regards to progression-free survival interval, but no advantage with regards to overall survival. So I think based on that, we just will use it.
And this is all the treatment of stage 4 disease you're talking about?
Not as adjuvant therapy. GFG-218 was the large randomized phase 3 trial, showed 4.6 months. PFS prolongation with no overall survival.
In stage 3 and 4? Yes, that only allowed stage 3. And so of course, if you don't use it in stage 3 and 4 patients, you don't use it adjuvantly either. Correct.

And IPON-7 was a European study, same kind of design, showed about 2.1. So it's statistically significant, but about 2.1 PFS improvement, 2.1 months with no overall survival events. Ironically, in Europe, they used the GOG218 data and got approval. So they use it up front. It didn't even go to the FDA here, because the FDA made it clear that without an overall survival event, they would never approve it.

So just make that clear to our listeners, Mike. Dr. Barrett is saying that it is approved for stage 3 or 4 disease, in Europe based on American data, but didn't get approved in America based on American data. So that's where we stand. But we've had this discussion previously on these tumor boards about Bevacizumab with these results available, and we've concluded, we're all in agreement, at least in this location, that the costs for the sake of a 2 point something month, or even at best 4 point something month, progression-free survival without any overall survival advantage is probably beyond the scope of cost-effectiveness in South America and probably should not be used for that reason.

I'm surprised that actually it was used and I assume made for it. It's expensive. It's about $12,000 $14,000 per injection. So 15 months is a, at least in the States, would be about $150,000 to $200,000 investment for four months.

So I think we and others have written papers about HPV, cervix cancer, and the use of expensive drugs. And we are busy working on a publication of the rising cost of drugs and how it should be handled. So we will be publishing soon, actually, that paper. And I think that it's really, I would say that the cost of that, we were just discussing informally, just imagine how many leaps or how many pap smears or how many HPV immunizations could be performed for the cost of $100,000. And when you're only buying a few months of progression-free survival, it seems not a useful way to spend your resources actually.

The other way to look at it, I think, is that there's really no apiary evidence that you're curing anybody else by adding it to the regimen. That doesn't mean it's not an active agent. You can get that activity if the tumor comes back later in the course. with less cycles in a more cost-benefit advantage.
So you talk, are you talking, is the UCI talking about adjuvant therapy, or stage three and four, being stage, like advanced disease already?

So we call this, in stage three and four patients where they get resection and chemo, and they get bed through that, we would call that adjuvant therapy. It's a little different than the breast. I see, okay, I see.

We probably have a bigger burden. So what Dr. Burry is saying is, at very, at most, perhaps the drug should be saved for salvage of a patient who's progressing beyond the so-called post-operative chemotherapy. But to use it in a post-operative setting up front, almost in an adjuvant setting, is really cost ineffective probably for the activity of the drug. So that's an important point for this tumor board, I think. And I don't know if you want to respond or argue back with us, because it's We're not trying to be unkind when we make this comment. That's our opinion.

And then I think the other issue here is the issue of primary surgery versus neoadjuvant chemo with an interval cytoreductive surgery. I think, you know, we struggled a little bit in trying to decide who's a candidate for optimal surgery up front. I think that where we are today, we have data from Europe through a phase three randomized study, essentially looking at the role of neoadjuvant chemotherapy versus up-front debulking. And certainly in women, where we think that we're not going to reach an optimal heteroductive surgical effort with up-front surgery, we would recommend neoadjuvant chemo based on the Virgo trial from Europe, and give three cycles of platinum and taxol re-imaged, and then if the patient's tumor responded to the three cycles of upfront chemo, we would then proceed with intervals and reduction, hoping that by then we can achieve either a complete resection or nothing, or at least, or an optimal surgical effort to less than a centimeter In this case, I think given the imaging, I'm not sure that we would, I think we would have offered this patient neoadjuvant chemo, so three cycles of carboplatinum and Taxol, so that we would be able to afford an optimal surgery after three cycles of chemo and then three more cycles of chemotherapy. Kathleen, if you want to maybe comment on the trial that you are doing at MD Anderson, where you look at these patients through a laparoscopy and then assess susceptibility.

Just to go back, this is a question. We do exactly the same as you do at Mild and General. We do not give Bev a standard of care for ovarian cancer due to the, you know, the no evidence of improved overall survival. And then as far as the surgery, so we, you know, two years ago now, changed our practice, because it was all over the place of who was operating up front and who was giving neoadjuvant chemo. So we standardized it across, we have 20 G1 oncologists, so we standardized our practice, that every patient who comes in has imaging or their outside imaging reviewed, and if they have liver meds, parenchymal liver meds, or lung meds, they actually automatically go to neoadjuvant chemotherapy. unless we really think it's a liver met, we can resect. And then for all the others where they have a lot of peritoneal disease and liver surface disease and things like that, we do laparoscopy on all of them and they get scored using the Fogotti score from Dr. Fogotti in Italy. And they're scored independently by two oncologists. So if it's my case, I start the case and then I do a score And then a second GYN oncologist comes in for the other one. They do an independent score, not knowing what my score is. And if we disagree, we actually get a third person to come in. Now that's not real world because there are a few places around where there are three gynecologists hanging around the OR. But I think we're just trying to do it to sort of standardize what we're doing. And if the score is eight or above, the patient gets neoadjuvant chemotherapy. If it's less than that, then they go on to a tumor-reductive surgery. So we're trying to really standardize who we think can be optimally assessed.

So, Kathleen, thank you. Can I just say a few follow-up words in the few remaining minutes? Part of the reason for these tumor boards, apart from getting the auspicious opinions of our faculty in the U.S., is also to introduce the concept of multidisciplinary tumor boards. So what Dr. Schmiller just described is something that's widely practiced both in Canada and the United States, which is that I was joking with Dr. Barrow, who's a famous medical oncologist, that he's not a surgeon, but he should be able to answer rudimentary surgical questions. I think one of the things that we've had complaints with over the years, of course, with patients and their families, is for patients to get different opinions between disciplines on a critical part of their care, or between doctors. So when these patients with solitary malignancy traverse the system and go from a medical oncologist, the following day they see the surgeon, etc., etc., You like to think that the big questions, like do you need your breast off, yes or no, and do you need radiation, yes or no, should be within the domain of all breast cancer specialists. It shouldn't just be a surgical question that the medical oncologist cannot answer. The fine detail, it's not possible for fine detail, but broadly speaking, it's very disconcerting for a patient to hear a radically different opinion from two doctors within the same hospital or even between hospitals. And the NCI in the US and the NCI in Canada stipulated that to be classified as a tertiary care cancer center, it was mandatory to see a certain proportion of cases in the case of Canada in a multidisciplinary setting to establish harmonization of practice opinions. So I want you all to think about that. When you are a surgeon, you should know about the broad indications of neoadjuvant or adjuvant systemic chemotherapy. The same with the radiation, and so on and so forth. And I think, for example, the example that Kathleen gave, which is to harmonize the opinion about where the treatment is given, it's not that one's wrong or one's right, but within your center, many doctors, you should speak with a single voice. So if you're going to make a decision for neoadjuvant, Establish a pathway to make that your standard of practice or give it adjuvantly and make sure that you all do that. Try to avoid different, radically different treatment approaches within the same cancer center and between doctors. I think that's a really, and it tends to be, please don't take this as a criticism in South America because everybody used to practice like this in the world and still does often. And what we found in When I worked in England and in Canada, the busier clinically the doctors are, the less able they are to standardize their care. So you doctors in South America who see a hundred patients a day kind of thing, obviously you don't have time to go to multidisciplinary tumor boards, but you should make it a habit to attend these tumor boards and to have one in-house of your own where you see patients and discuss the broad management of cases Even if it's one in every 10 patients that you discuss, but you should see a proportion. In Canada, you had to see, I think, 10% of all cases at a cancer center in a multidisciplinary setting in order to achieve tertiary care cancer status, you know, like a center of excellence, like we are here from the NCI. So I think that was a very good point, Kathy. Thank you.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 52-year-old postmenopausal woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Painful right breast lump of 2 months’ duration in the first quarter of 2013.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- Initial diagnosis in 2013: right breast invasive ductal carcinoma with extensive high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), triple-negative phenotype; pathologic stage I, pT1bN0M0.  
- Subsequent ipsilateral right breast recurrence/new lesion in 2015: DCIS with multiple foci of microinvasive/invasive ductal carcinoma, triple-negative phenotype.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial core biopsy: high-grade DCIS.  
- Initial lumpectomy pathology: infiltrating ductal carcinoma with extensive DCIS; invasive component represented 5% of the tumor; invasive carcinoma size 2 mm; high nuclear grade; surgical margins were in contact with DCIS.  
- Re-excision performed 2 weeks later: no residual carcinoma.  
- 2015 biopsy of right breast lesion: DCIS with foci of microinvasive carcinoma.  
- Mastectomy pathology in 2015: DCIS with multiple foci of invasive ductal carcinoma; largest invasive focus 2 mm; DCIS comprised >90% of the tumor; stromal fibrosis present; sentinel lymph nodes negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial mammogram and breast ultrasound in 2013: upper outer quadrant right breast lesion measuring 2.5 × 3 cm, described as high density with pleomorphic microcalcifications.  
- Surveillance mammogram and ultrasound in the third quarter of 2015: pleomorphic microcalcifications below the scar in the right breast measuring 19 × 4 mm; these findings had not been present on the prior year’s study.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Initial tumor immunohistochemistry: triple-negative breast cancer.  
- 2015 recurrent/right breast tumor immunohistochemistry: triple-negative; Ki-67 20%.  
- Family history: aunt and cousin with breast cancer.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2013: lumpectomy performed for right breast lesion.  
- 2 weeks later: re-excision performed; no residual carcinoma identified.  
- Adjuvant chemotherapy: weekly paclitaxel for 12 doses followed by FAC for 4 cycles.  
- Adjuvant radiotherapy administered after chemotherapy.  
- Follow-up surveillance thereafter.  
- 2015: right mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy and breast reconstruction with tissue expander performed for ipsilateral recurrence/new lesion.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Post-mastectomy pathology in 2015 demonstrated DCIS with multiple small invasive ductal carcinoma foci, largest 2 mm, with negative sentinel lymph nodes.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Right-sided breast primary.

Well, I think that, I guess, to me it's not such a strong family history. Sure. I mean, I think that could be... Because that's an inexpensive thing, right? Yeah, it could be inexpensive, and who knows what you can get paid for.

Can I add something? But Cynthia, I think you're raising a different issue, if I may say. I know the other people, thank you very much Jack. I think you've expressed the opinion of most people online. I'm going to take the prerogative of saying so. Michelle, can we go back to you?

I just want to be clear. You know, I think that originally this tumor was excised. It was 7 millimeters. It could have been multifocal in that nature, but I think even in that setting, a priority, we would have not offered neoadjuvant chemotherapy, because remember, the original core biopsy was high-grade DCIS. And we certainly, for a seven millimeter tumor, wouldn't have included a platinum-based agent. Our neoadjuvant protocol that's open right now is for tumors that are greater than two centimeters. If they're carriers, they get randomized to receive AC or a platinum-based chemotherapy on the informed trial. So this is pretty small.
So I think we might have mixed up two thoughts. I wasn't implying she should get it. I was saying when we get a neoadjuvant.
No, but Sophie was talking about this.

Oh, okay, right. So, okay, I think we've got consensus on that. Do you want to go back to after the recurrence in this that's being performed. Is now bilateral mastectomy an option or the option of choice?

It's not the option. It's always an option. We know the contralateral prophylactic mastectomy doesn't afford any increase in overall survival. Many women choose it because they don't want to go through the screening, but we carefully caution them that, you know, if there was an infection in the contralateral breast, if there was something that could delay her systemic therapy, if that's what she needed, That's a problem. So it's always an option, but we certainly don't force it upon anyone, because there's no survival benefit.
Shaila, I can see you nodding your head. Do you want to add something surgically to this?

What we do know is that the oncologic principles take first hand. So getting a tumor out, negative margins, orients in the margin, we all know that. But if you can do that, you have to keep in mind their cosmetic outcome. And so we know that women that have a unilateral mastectomy with implant reconstruction, their satisfaction long-term is very, very low. So sometimes if you're in a community where all you can get is implant-based reconstruction, you have to consider a contralateral mastectomy for symmetry procedures and their bras fitting properly and their clothes fitting. It's not for survival, but their quality of life is significantly impacted by how they look and their sexual life.
Alfonso, are there any radiation issues?

Yeah, a couple of comments. Just in general, and there is quite a bit of data on that, the risk of local failure for triple negative patients is significantly higher than luminal A or luminal B. So when you look at the data, you will see, let's say, at 5, 10, or 7 years of follow-up, luminal A will have 2% local failure is almost three and a half times the luminal age. Compared to her two positive patients before her septum, it used to be 11 after her septum, it's much less than that. So we still struggle with the local failure rate for triple negative. We'd like to bring it down to be close to 2 or 3 percent And there are some trials here and there, like actually giving concomitant cisplatin with radiation. And this is a trial from the Brigham that we also accrue for it here. But they include only 2 centimeter triple negative. So triple negative is an issue with local failure. I don't know how to overcome this, whether by adding something concomitant to this or including And what worries me here is that she had the local failure right away, within a year or two. And I don't know if this might reflect that maybe some DCIS was left behind. The radiation was absolutely fine. It was a British hypofractionation, which gave very good results. But it's just surprising that it came rather quickly. And then just the only treatment for this patient is mastectomy.

reference_conclusion: Following ipsilateral breast recurrence characterized by predominantly DCIS with multiple microinvasive foci and negative sentinel lymph nodes, mastectomy is the indicated local treatment. Contralateral prophylactic mastectomy may be discussed as an option for symmetry or patient preference, but it is not the preferred approach and does not confer an overall survival benefit. Platinum-based systemic therapy is not recommended routinely for this small node-negative triple-negative tumor and would generally be reserved for patients with a proven BRCA1/2 mutation; genetic counseling and BRCA assessment are appropriate if available.
reference_conclusion_quote: But the NCCN guidelines now state that anyone diagnosed with a triple negative cancer under the age of 65, I think, either 60 or 65, we do routine testing for BRCA1 or 2 [...] So theoretically, she would have fallen in that category with her family history and the triple negative nature of her tumor. [...] In this case, I would think somewhat carefully about that and the possibility of retreatment with adjuvant therapy with, for example, a non-anthracycline combination of docetaxel and cyclophosphamide would not be out of the question for me. I believe activity has been established. I would not be enthusiastic about a platinum-based regimen without more information about family or genetics [...] we certainly, for a seven millimeter tumor, wouldn't have included a platinum-based agent. [...] It's not the option. It's always an option. We know the contralateral prophylactic mastectomy doesn't afford any increase in overall survival. [...] And then just the only treatment for this patient is mastectomy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 47-year-old premenopausal woman. Previously healthy. No comorbidities. No family history of breast cancer. Past surgical history included myomectomy in 2009.

[ chief complaint ]: Suspicious left breast mass detected on screening mammography at the end of 2014.

[ diagnosis ]: Left breast invasive lobular carcinoma, stage IB, pT1c pN1mi M0.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial surgery consisted of quadrantectomy with axillary lymph node dissection. Pathology showed invasive lobular carcinoma measuring 1.1 cm, grade 2, with multiple foci of lobular carcinoma in situ. Surgical margin showed atypical lobular hyperplasia with one focus of lobular carcinoma in situ. Fourteen axillary lymph nodes were removed; 2/14 contained metastatic disease, each with diameter 0.1 cm, consistent with micrometastatic nodal involvement. Hormone receptor testing showed estrogen receptor positive and progesterone receptor positive disease. HER2 was negative. Ki-67 was 10%.

[ imaging findings ]: Screening mammogram demonstrated a suspicious mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast, BI-RADS 4. Diagnostic ultrasound and breast MRI confirmed a 1.2 cm spiculated nodule at the 2 o’clock position in the left breast, 4 cm from the nipple. No suspicious axillary lymph nodes were identified on imaging. Staging workup showed no metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No genomic assay results were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the breast lesion was positive for malignancy.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent quadrantectomy with axillary lymph node dissection.

[ current disease status ]: After breast-conserving surgery and axillary dissection with staging evaluation, there was no evidence of distant metastatic disease. Lobular carcinoma in situ was present at the surgical margin.

[ other clinical data ]: None.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, thank you for the opportunity to participate in this Tumor Board and good morning to everyone. So I'm going to present the case about 47-year-old premenopausal woman, previously healthy, with no comorbidities and no family history of breast cancer. She experienced a myomectomy in the past in 2009. Next, please. In the end of 2014, her screening mammogram showed suspicious mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast by rats 4. The diagnostic ultrasound and MRI confirmed 1.2 cm speculated nodule at 2 o'clock left breast, 4 cm from the nipple, with no suspicious taxillary lymph nodes. Fine needle aspiration was positive. The staging workup showed no metastasis and the patient proceeded to surgery. Quadrantectomy and taxillary lymph node dissection was performed. The pathology report showed invasive lobular carcinoma, 1.1 centimeters, grade 2, with multiple foci of lobular carcinoma incitum. The margin showed atypical lobular hyperplasia with one focus of lobular carcinoma incitum. 14 axillary lymph nodes were removed, and two of them were positive for metastasis with a diameter of 0.1 centimeter. The patient is ERPR positive, CUR2 negative and Ki67 is 10%. So it was discussed with the patient in another hospital and she decided to proceed with bilateral skin-spanning mastectomy and immediate breast reconstruction. After the surgery, the pathology was negative and the post-surgical MR showed normal position of the silicone implants but a significant amount of residual breast tissue bilaterally. The diagnosis is breast cancer, stage 1B, PT1C, PN1MI, M0, invasive lobular carcinoma. The patient underwent six cycles of adjuvant chemo with AC. Radiation therapy was performed to the left breast and the regional lymph nodes to a total dose of 46 grays in 23 fraction. And three months after the radiotherapy, the cosmetic result is excellent. And Tamoxifen was prescribed as endocrine therapy. So our fourth question is, is there any role of prophylactic contralateral skin-spanning mastectomy for invasive level or carcinoma?
If you just stop there, we'll discuss that before. Michelle, do you want to comment on that?
Well, I mean, Alphonse, why don't you comment on our data looking at LCIS at the margin. I might have stopped at lumpectomy.

Yeah, LCIS at the margin does not increase the risk of local failure. That's different than DCIS. And we've published a paper about this maybe like a few months ago on more than 1,000 patients. When we have DCIS at the margin we try to achieve negative margin. which is per the new guidelines, not tumor on egg. But when we have LCIS at the margin, we do not try to achieve negative margin, because there is no evidence that LCIS at the margin increase the risk of local failure.
Male Speaker 1 Does it influence your subsequent boost? Male Speaker 2 Absolutely not.
It's as if it doesn't exist for some reason. I think we rely more on tamoxifen or hormonal therapy. So that's important. Do you want to continue with the original information, or do you want to…
skin-sparing mastectomy.

Yeah, I mean so honestly as a surgeon I probably would have cautioned her to stop at lumpectomy. We know that there's probably, and this is a bit controversial, a role for radiation therapy after a mastectomy. But certainly I would have felt better knowing she had stopped at lumbectomy with the two positive notes and just irradiated her. Sure, you can do a prophylactic contralateral mastectomy. I think that some of the ideas that were historic where people would have mirror image biopsies of the contralateral breast looking for lobular cancer have been debunked. And I think that's just because we're increasingly relying on adjuvant endocrine therapy in an extended fashion, you know, beyond five years. that helps control that disease. So for me, just because someone has lobular cancer does not mean that they're going to automatically get a bilateral mastectomy.
Shailaja, would you want to comment, or do you agree with that?
I agree completely.
OK. So maybe, Alphonse, there's a question here, if I may just jump in, Nelly, forgive me. Radiation after skin-sparing mastectomy and breast reconstruction, as a general point, how about that?

Yeah, I mean, if it is indicated, I mean, I would argue in this situation here, you had a small tumor, which is ERPR positive, she didn't even need any chemotherapy, and she had a mastectomy. I would have a question whether this patient actually needs post-mastectomy radiation. The issue with post-mastectomy radiation is basically the data is based on the over-guard did lymph node dissection for everybody, although there is some question of the number of lymph nodes removed. But they didn't really break down into micro metastases or micro metastases. This could be in a gray zone area, should we give post-mastectomy radiation or not. But assume we give post-mastectomy radiation after reconstruction. There are quite a bit of side effects which can impact the reconstruction. And the rate of concoction with radiation can go up to 20 or 30 percent. It goes from reasons to remove the implant all the way into encapsulation, into retraction, into hardness, into tenderness, into like the implant moves upward and then this requires some correction from the plastic surgeon So we don't, we take it very seriously when we give radiation after implant, but when it is necessary I think having a local control has a lot of, like more benefit than having a poor cosmetic products. So that's the impact of radiation on reconstruction.

Maybe I can jump in with another point and I'm going to pick on Susan. Can you hear me Susan? I'm just curious about being a 47-year-old woman with a small tumor, this is a small point, but what is the role of staging investigations? This patient was fully staged at diagnosis. Is that a routine for such an age patient with an ER-positive tumor that is so small? And secondly, do you agree with the adjuvant AC times 6 chemotherapy?

So in terms of staging, assuming she didn't have any systemic symptoms, you know, bone pain, anything like that, normally we would not do a full staging evaluation in early stage disease. Regarding, what was the second question, Paul?
About your adjuvant AC times 6.

So given that this is a left-sided tumor, I guess my preference would have been to give less adriamycin. So our standard here would be to offer her AC times 4 cycles and then on to Taxol. I think with the modern radiation techniques, there's less risk of cardiac toxicity, but I'm an old-fashioned practitioner. I still worry about small risk long-term with the higher dose of adriamycin as well as the radiation therapy.
Jack, what about TC? Do you want to just comment about TC or alternative chemotherapy approaches to this patient?

Yes, thank you. I would agree with Susan. I think the CA-LGB looked at four and six cycles of Adriamycin and showed there was no advantage to six. And TC for four treatments compared to AC for four treatments has clearly been shown to be superior in terms of efficacy for node zero to three node positive in particular. I think there's good data for that. I do also think it has the advantage of eliminating the cardiotoxicity issues and so I would find that to be a positive option for a patient like this. Thank you, Jack.
Could anyone send an Oncotype and not give chemo?
Send an Oncotype and not give chemotherapy is one suggestion by Michelle.

Right, I would be not as enthused because she's not really in an age where the oncotype has really looked at node-positive women. If you consider her node-negative by virtue of micrometastatic disease perhaps, but classically I think the data only really extends to post-menopausal women at this point for node-positive disease.

So staying with you Jack, there's a question here about, if I may just ask the question for you. nearly, prognostic significance of metastatic lymph nodes, less than two mesos, after ALND and the indication for atrial chemo and regional lymph node radiation. Go ahead, Joe.

I was impressed with the paper in the New England Journal a few years ago where ITCs, at least, or minimal disease in the nose really wasn't prognostic so long as the patient received the proper adjuvant therapy. In other words, adjuvant therapy sort of neutralized any finding in the notes. I don't know if it really extends to micrometastatic disease, but I would say that it is meaningful, but I think it's probably largely neutralized by modern adjuvant treatment.
Anybody want to comment on that point? Susan, do you have any extra comments? No, okay. Ed, what about radiation?

Yeah, I would certainly not give reasonable radiation for this situation. Actually, we have the Z11 study, which did just sentinel node, not even leaf node detection, just sentinel node. And when the node was positive, we just gave high tangents, a radiation oncologist, and we don't do lymph node dissection, and we don't do original lymph node radiation, just bear in mind that lymph node dissection will cause 18% risk of lymphedema. And then if you add original lymph node radiation to that, the risk of lymphedema will be 24%. So that's a lot of complication for two tiny positive lymph nodes. So in retrospect, what I would have done, I don't know if fentanyl node is being done or not in this place. But if it is, you could stop. You don't need to do a neutron dissection after a small, tiny positive neutrons like that. And you just give the treatment of the axilla to radiation, because she will get radiation anyhow. And I would just do high tensions, which will cover the level 1 and 2 in the axilla.

Now, I need a medical, like Susan, I'm going to hand you the question of, what are you doing in the era of post-text, post-soft data? This is a perimenopausal, declared premenopausal, 47-year-old patient with neopositive breast cancer, and the question is, what is the choice of optimal adjuvant endocrine therapy, and what is the duration? What is the duration? So, if you could just address this whole point, that'd be good.

Well, I guess the most important thing is to develop a regimen that a patient's going to be compliant with long term. So I think based on the soft and text study, the ideal treatment in my mind for someone who's a higher risk that you've given chemotherapy to would be to offer them ovarian suppression with an aromatase inhibitor. Having said that, many women cannot tolerate that. So this patient, I would view, is not in the highest risk category to really say, dogmatically, this is what I would prefer. But that would be the best therapy available. But in this particular case, I think I would have an honest discussion with her about various side effects, comparing ovarian suppression, starting that with first month, and then maybe adding in the aromatase inhibitor at month two. and she didn't tolerate ovarian suppression, then you could back off and think about extended tamoxifen or starting with tamoxifen and switching to an aromatase inhibitor once she's clearly post-menopausal.

So I think, Susan, you're saying that I think a trial of endocrine therapy is always the appropriate way to address patients. Anything we give, tamoxifen, ovarian suppression, or anything, it's always a trial. And I think in the first three months, patients sort of know how they're going to be on a treatment. I think patients between 45 and 55 are most vulnerable to side effects from endocrine therapy, more so than younger women and older women. So I think those are the problematic patients. She's in a problematic age and may not tolerate. But the good thing is these days we can reverse any kind of endocrine therapy decision. So that's good. And then I think that in my own mind, actually, it doesn't matter what kind of endocrine therapy you give, It's so much better than none. And any kind of endocrine therapy is a lot better than none. When you're talking about what kind of chemotherapy, you're talking about a difference between last year's model of a motor car and this year's model. But the difference between having a motor car or not is the big difference. And having some form of endocrine therapy, I think, is important. And in 2016, we are hoping to present data on MA17R, which we'll talk about five, ten years of aromatase inhibitor rather than five, as is the NSABP B42 trial going to present. So a lot of patients are asking after five years, should I continue my aromatase inhibitor or not? For the time being, I'm continuing because we're on the brink of a result. So for those patients where there's indecision, why not just continue if they're tolerating it well and have no financial duress or anything. Continue it until the results are available. But at the end of the day, longer endocrine therapy seems to be better than shorter. That's what all the data is pointing to. So some form of endocrine option is probably preferable to, and longer, is probably preferable to not. So that's my overall opinion about that subject. And then there's a question here about the best imaging modality for follow-up? I don't know quite what the question is. Michelle, can you comment on an invasive lobular that's been excised or had a mastectomy?

So with a lumpectomy, if she had completed the lumpectomy, it would be yearly screening mammography. We don't necessarily add breast MRI to one screening and follow-up. if they've had a lobular without a family history of breast cancer. In fact, I would argue that their risk of creating a new cancer in the contralateral breast is improved because the hormonal therapy they're on for the treatment of their known breast cancer. After bilateral mastectomy, I know that in this situation, you had noted some residual breast parenchyma, so it's kind of an interesting different situation, but we would, you know, not do any imaging Even our plastic surgeons feel like imaging the implants is not a have to and really any issues that we have with regards to implants are things that we can detect clinically. So it would be a yearly clinical exam by a surgeon and a yearly clinical chest wall exam with the other physicians involved in their care, the medical oncologist and the radiation oncologist.

reference_conclusion: The panel concluded that prophylactic contralateral skin-sparing mastectomy is not indicated solely on the basis of invasive lobular carcinoma, and that LCIS at the margin does not warrant re-excision because it does not increase local failure risk. For adjuvant systemic therapy, endocrine treatment was considered essential; for this premenopausal patient who received chemotherapy, ovarian suppression plus an aromatase inhibitor was identified as the preferred option, with tamoxifen or extended tamoxifen as acceptable alternatives based on tolerability and menopausal status. For follow-up after bilateral mastectomy, routine imaging was not recommended; surveillance should consist of annual clinical examination of the chest wall and surgical follow-up.

[...] So for me, just because someone has lobular cancer does not mean that they're going to automatically get a bilateral mastectomy. [...] So I think based on the soft and text study, the ideal treatment in my mind for someone who's a higher risk that you've given chemotherapy to would be to offer them ovarian suppression with an aromatase inhibitor. [...] if she didn't tolerate ovarian suppression, then you could back off and think about extended tamoxifen or starting with tamoxifen and switching to an aromatase inhibitor once she's clearly post-menopausal. [...] After bilateral mastectomy, I know that in this situation, you had noted some residual breast parenchyma, so it's kind of an interesting different situation, but we would, you know, not do any imaging [...] So it would be a yearly clinical exam by a surgeon and a yearly clinical chest wall exam with the other physicians involved in their care, the medical oncologist and the radiation oncologist.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 38-year-old premenopausal woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Self-palpated right breast nodule during the third trimester of pregnancy in 2015.

[ diagnosis ]: Right breast invasive ductal carcinoma, pathologic stage IIB (T2N1).

[ histopathology results ]: Mastectomy and axillary lymph node dissection specimen showed invasive ductal carcinoma measuring 2.5 cm. Scarff-Bloom-Richardson score was 7 (grade 2). Lymphovascular invasion was present. Surgical margins were negative. One axillary lymph node was positive for metastatic carcinoma, with metastatic deposit measuring 7 mm.

[ imaging findings ]: Mammography was performed following detection of the right breast nodule. No further imaging details were available.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Immunohistochemistry showed estrogen receptor positive (reported as R7), progesterone receptor negative, and Ki-67 approximately 50%. Genetic risk assessment was pending.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent right mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection. One month later she presented for adjuvant treatment planning. Adjuvant chemotherapy with doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel was initiated. The first cycle was administered on 5 November. No treatment response or toxicity data were available.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative early-stage breast cancer after mastectomy and axillary dissection, receiving adjuvant chemotherapy. No documented evidence of recurrent or metastatic disease was provided.

[ other clinical data ]: The breast cancer was hormone receptor-positive/HER2-negative by available data. The patient was pregnant at the time of initial presentation, in the third trimester.

reference_discussion.text: Our case is a 38-year-old premenopausal woman and now with breast cancer at age 50. and all the risk factors. In the third trimester of 2015, she self-pulpated a right breast nodule. A mammogram was performed and after that, a mastectomy plus axodialytic nodule dissection was performed. In the pathologic report, an invasive ductal carcinoma, well documented, of 2.5 centimeters, with SBR of 7, lymph vascular invasion positive, negative surgical margins, and one lymph node positive for a metastasis of 7 millimeters. The immunochemistry report, estrogen receptors positive, with R7, progesterone receptor negative, to negative and the CAI 57 off 50%. One month later, the patient presented to our center to advise adjuvant treatment. Next, please. So we have a patient with breast cancer, stage 2B, and we indicated adjuvant chemotherapy with dog bends of AC followed by paclitaxel. And the first cycle was on November 5th. A genetic risk assessment was pending. It's pending. Next.

So we have several questions regarding this case. So the first one is, what would be the optimal active and hormonal therapy for her being a 38-year-old woman with an N1 grade 2? And we would consider extended therapy or ovarian suppression. And we would like to know your opinion about we should consider for all premenopausal patients the combination of OFS plus adjuvant aromatase inhibitors.

So that's a very clear question. Jack, could you tell us your view after soft and text, what do you do with premenopausal patients who are already receiving adjuvant chemotherapy for perceived risk? How do you manage the endocrine therapy?

So this patient clearly does have major risk issues. She's 38. I would consider her probably closer to 35 than 40. She's requiring chemotherapy. She's PR negative. There's a whole host of factors that make one want to be concerned about her prognosis. But it's important to remember that the patients who entered SOFT were really premenopausal, if you will, by virtue of their estradiol levels or continuing to have menstrual function. And so I think it shouldn't be yet, in my opinion, and Paula would certainly be the expert, certainly yet wouldn't be my practice to put all patients on therapy. Going back to ECOG years ago, the addition of Lupron without Tamoxifen did not add to chemotherapy in the premenopausal woman who had just completed chemotherapy unselected. So I would follow the standards of SOFT. I would want to know what her estradiol was before committing her to ovarian suppression.

think that not all hospitals attaining this tumor board will have an easy estradiol assessment available. And particularly as the levels decline toward menopause and into menopause, most hospitals don't have that technology. But the question really, Jack, I'm going to push you on this a bit. The question from Montserrat, from Mexico City is, if you've already decided the patient is justified to give chemotherapy, I think you've answered this, does the administration of chemotherapy mandate a soft text approach because they were considered requiring chemotherapy? I think that's the question.

So if I could make it a little bit cleaner and make her just a little bit younger and I would have to say that I think the evidence is compelling that a very young woman in her 30s with no positive requiring chemotherapy, hormone sensitive, probably should have additional combined therapy. And the question of the aromatase inhibitor versus tamoxifen I think deserves a second discussion and in some cases will be correct. So I think yes, ovarian suppression should be considered.
Okay. Any agreement or disagreement with that, Susan?

Yeah, so I think if you look at the published data, I mean, the patients who received chemotherapy and who were part of these studies were a group, regardless of age, that benefited from ovarian suppression. So looking at the data of tamoxifen versus ovarian suppression with eczemastine, the difference at five years was like 7%. Yeah, so if you don't have access to hormonal levels, you could start with tamoxifen, and then if she gets a period, add in ovarian suppression, or take a different approach and say that the majority of women treated with ACT at this age will resume menstrual function within a year and just be aggressive with the treatment of her breast cancer.

I must say I'm inclined to be in that camp of thought. I agree that she's going to be premenopausal at 38 regardless of what happens, I think. So I think that at least here, I know several of my respective medical oncologists would agree with that opinion that Jack and Susan have just given. If anybody disagrees, please say so. But I think you're hearing that a soft text approach should be given to patients with chemotherapy, adjuvant chemotherapy.

I would just add one that I think the B30 trial was very informative as to who would or wouldn't become menopausal based on chemotherapy and by age I think you can get some very nice data as to what that outcome is going to be.
Okay, I'd like to ask Cynthia to give a second question, the next question.
Can you put the presentation, please, again, Jessica?
Or I can see it over here.
The second question is, what is the role of adjuvant bisphosphonates in premenopausal patients that receive ovarian suppression, and if there are any other features that guide us on this decision?

Another very good controversial issue, and I'm going to turf the ball to, let me give it to Susan first. Susan, do you routinely give bisphosphonates? There are two questions buried here, I think. The first one is, is bisphosphonate desirable for a young person getting ovarian suppression? for bone metabolism reasons, and I think the answer to that is yes. For one year at least, definitely. But the deeper question is, with the presentations that have been given at the major meetings, is adjuvant bisphosphonate now a routine anti-breast cancer five-year adjuvant therapy in all patients? In whom should it be given? When should it be given? That's the question.

Yeah, so I think, again, this is a controversial issue. In my young patients who I'm offering ovarian suppression as their primary endocrine therapy, particularly with an aromatase inhibitor, those are the patients that I'm normally recommending bisphosphonate for. Based on the SWOG study, I think you have your option right now, whether you use an oral versus an IV bisphosphonate. But I would consider, in this population, that would be standard. For me, although I think the national guidelines and NCCN are still not quite certain who to give bisphosphonates to.
Susan, can I interrupt you? Are you influenced if the patient expresses interest in subsequent pregnancy by the use of bisphosphonates or not?
You know, I honestly don't know that data, Paul. My guess is that would make me nervous, but I have not researched that. Does anyone else who's listening know that answer?

Yeah, hi. I would be very nervous. I think the evidence, at least in clinical studies I'm aware of, is that you can measure terminal half-life of excretion of the drug even a year out from a dose. There is drug that is stored and slowly released over time and so I think it would be, in my practice, an absolute contraindication if somebody were considering future pregnancy.
And for either oral or IV bisphosphonate?
Yes, I would avoid that because of the long half-life in the patient.
And then the question that I should probably answer, but I'll let others answer. What about denosumab? Would you consider denosumab differently or the same?
That's a great question. I actually don't know the evidence for the terminal half-life, but I would say any drug that could exist in the body for a long period of time, I'd be nervous about.

I think donosumab's got a long half-life like most antibodies, but not as long as the meto or those other agents. But I think that in patients wanting children or pregnancy after treatment, I think bisphosphonates currently are still contraindicated, actually, and probably donosumab as well, because of possible teratogenicity.
So Paul, I just researched that quickly as we were talking and both of those agents are contraindicated with pregnancy.
Right. Thank you, Susan. That's great. So Cynthia, is that the answer you were looking for or did you want to probe deeper on this question?
No, it was that because then in the meta-analysis, even the patients that were deemed postmenopausal were the ones that benefited.

And I realize I've got two experts on the line that I haven't asked a question of. So the radiation question, that's next. Perhaps Dr. Carol Marquez can address. And as well, the last question. So Dr. Chu, maybe you'd like to say something as well about the post-mastectomy radiation for this young patient. So you ask the question, Cynthia, please. The last two questions.

The question is, the third one, what is the role of post-mastectomy radiotherapy for this young patient with a T1N1, with a one-node positive, HIV-positive hormone, we said, to deposit her to negative breast cancer, and if should all young women with one, two, three positive nodes should receive adjuvant radiotherapy?
So...
It's Julia.
Julia, yes, please.

Yes, hi. So the question is always debated at our own tumor board at Penn. So because of your young age and her having one positive lymph node, we would err on the side of being more aggressive and will most likely recommend post-mastectomy radiation at our institution.
Maybe Alphonse, you want to add something to that? Dr. Marquez, would you like to say something, please?

I agree with that, and I'd agree with it also because of her other negative features, which would include the LVSI and the size of the tumor. I think all of those features together would make me recommend radiation for her.

And Alphonse is nodding his head. Absolutely right. It's beyond the age. It's beyond one positive lymph node. will bring her risk a little bit higher. So I fully agree with you. We look now at multiple risk factors. We look at the big picture. And instead of being cornered into one positive lymph node, she should have post-mastectomy radiation. So she has LVI. She's young. She didn't have enough lymph nodes removed. And the tumor was large. So she had multiple risk factors. I agree with you.
Can I add something about it? Otherwise, we would have positive features. Illuminal A of breast cancer with a grade one. But with one to three notes, H would guide you towards giving radiotherapy.

I mean, in regards to your last question, so like what you're saying is, just because she's young and just because she has one to three positive nodes, would you always give radiation? I don't think that's the case, because I think, as we discussed in, you know, the previous case, I think it depends on the amount of the nodal burden, how involved the node is. I think it does depend on the pathologic subtype, and I think the presence or absence of LVSI is really an important feature. in determining local regional recurrence after a mastectomy. So I think it is, as Dr. Takian says, kind of looking at the whole picture, at the whole combination of factors, not just age and positive notes.

reference_conclusion: Adjuvant chemotherapy with doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide followed by paclitaxel has been initiated. Given the patient’s young age, node-positive hormone receptor–positive disease, and receipt of adjuvant chemotherapy, endocrine therapy should follow a SOFT/TEXT-type approach with consideration of ovarian suppression; tamoxifen may be started initially if hormonal assessment is not available, with ovarian suppression added if menses resume. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistently detectable and rising PSA following radical prostatectomy.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma previously treated with robotic radical prostatectomy in 2020. Post-prostatectomy biochemical persistence/recurrence was present, with PSA never becoming undetectable. Subsequent evaluation identified a large bladder neck/prostate bed mass on multiparametric MRI; biopsies of this tissue showed benign prostatic hyperplasia and inflammation without carcinoma. PSMA PET demonstrated focal uptake in the prostate bed, a right iliac bone lesion, and low-level rib uptake. Axumin PET demonstrated focal uptake in the prostate bed mass without corresponding uptake in the right ilium or ribs.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial prostate biopsy before prostatectomy showed bilateral Gleason grade group 2 and 3 disease in 4 of 12 cores. Biopsy of the right iliac lesion was negative for malignancy. Biopsy of residual prostate/bladder neck tissue showed benign prostatic hyperplasia and inflammation, with no prostate cancer identified. Seminal vesicle tissue was also present in the biopsy specimen and was negative for malignancy.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- PSMA PET dated 2023-02-06 showed:
  - low-level uptake in a right rib lesion (described as right second or third rib), SUVmax 1.9;
  - a more intense focal lesion in the right iliac bone;
  - subtle focal uptake in the left aspect of the prostate bed/prostate region, concerning for local recurrence.  
- Multiparametric MRI demonstrated a 12 cm mass at the bladder neck/prostate bed.  
- Axumin PET showed no uptake in the right ilium and no uptake in the ribs, with focal/homogeneous uptake in the prostate/prostate bed mass.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Preoperative PSA: 6.2 ng/mL.  
- Post-radical prostatectomy PSA in 2021: 0.8 ng/mL.  
- PSA in November 2022: 1.54 ng/mL.  
- Repeat PSA: 1.52 ng/mL.  
- PSA nadir after prostatectomy never became undetectable and did not fall below 0.1 ng/mL.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Robotic radical prostatectomy was performed in 2020.  
- No prior radiation therapy was given.  
- Diagnostic workup after biochemical persistence/recurrence included PSMA PET, multiparametric MRI, Axumin PET, right iliac bone biopsy, digital rectal examination, and biopsy of residual prostate/bladder neck tissue.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent biochemical disease after prostatectomy, with PSA 1.52 ng/mL at most recent reported measurement. Imaging and biopsy findings did not confirm metastatic disease. Residual tissue/mass at the bladder neck/prostate bed was present on MRI and PET imaging, but biopsy showed benign tissue and inflammation without carcinoma.

[ other clinical data ]: Digital rectal examination identified palpable tissue that did not feel like a hard mass and was described as resembling normal prostate tissue. The original prostatectomy pathology report was not available. Concern was raised for residual benign prostate tissue remaining after prostatectomy.
