reference_discussion.text: Hi everyone, my name is E. David Crawford from the University of California in San Diego and welcome to our PET Tumor Board. PET imaging, especially PSMA PET, in my opinion, is one of the most significant advances in prostate cancer management in the last decade. It has created a lot of opportunities and also challenges. I have observed that in many tumor or second opinion boards, Almost half of the cases now are focused around PET scanning, particularly PSMA PET. We recently published our latest Radar 6 and 7 guidelines, which goes through in detail a lot of the indications for PET, the pitfalls and the ups and downs. We have a lot to learn, and we hope that these monthly tumor boards will broaden your knowledge in this area. I would like to thank Blue Earth Diagnostics who recently developed and launched a PSMA pet product called RH-PSMA or PASLUMA for this educational grant. We have gathered for this tumor board panel, three international experts in this field. They have not seen these cases beforehand, and so they are as blinded as you are to what's gonna happen in these cases. First panel member is Dr. Phil Koo. Phil is at MD Anderson Banner in Phoenix, Arizona. He is a nuclear medicine physician. Also, Dr. Daniel Petrulak, a medical oncologist from Yale, well-known in the field of prostate cancer, is joining us. And a radiation oncologist, Dr. Paul Nguyen from Harvard Brigham in Boston, Massachusetts. So gentlemen, let's go ahead and get started. This is a 68-year-old male who had a PSA of 6.2. He had bilateral Gleason break group two and three and four of 12 cores. He underwent a radical prostatectomy in a small town north of San Diego in 2020, okay? And this was a robotic prostatectomy. His NADER PSA really never got down to undetectable. And it was in fact 0.8 in 2021. It continued to rise and his PSA in November of 22 was 1.54. Another repeat was 1.52. And so he came to see me in January of 23. So the The issue is, what's next? Let me ask Dr. Petrelak, what's next with this guy?

Clearly, we want to image this patient since, number one, there's a very high chance of him having micrometastatic disease or actually obvious metastatic disease since his PSA never went to less than 0.1. He's now got a PSA of 1.52. My next step would be to image this patient with a PSMA PET scan.
Okay. Paul?
Yes, I agree. I think if you have access to a PSMA PET, that'd be the way to go here.
All right. Well, you guys are right on. We did that. And this is a PSMA PET, and now we're going to have to call on Dr. Koo to help us out here. What's going on? This was done on 2-6.

So on February 6th, we have several axial images of the fused images that overlay the PET image with the CT image. And these are sort of snapshots taken from that. The first image that we see on the left has that circle or region of interest around a rib lesion in one of the right, maybe second or third ribs. You know, looking at the semi-quantitative parameters, it shows an SUV max of 1.9, which is relatively low. And I presume this is the only rib lesion that was seen. Otherwise I assume- I don't have them both here, but- So if he had two, if he had one, I would look at the CT carefully, make sure we're not seeing anything abnormal and ignore it as benign. If we have two and they're all kind of this low level and there's nothing on CT, I still will be a little bit more inclined to call this benign and not metastatic disease for the time being. And then I often like to synthesize the clinical information before I come to my final diagnosis. Then we have the middle image. We have something focal in that right iliac bone that's much more intense. I'd want to look at the CT carefully to see if we're seeing anything on the CT. But this in and of itself is a little bit more suspicious for metastatic disease. And then the image on the right, screen right, we have a subtle focus of activity, presumably in the left aspect of the prostate gland, which might be an area of recurrence.

So just for our audience to know, the faculty have not seen these cases or heard them before we started. So Phil is looking at this cold and that you got it, you nailed it. Rib lesions, the iliac, and then something in his prostate. That's not the whole story, but why don't you comment on the rib lesions? Because I see that all the time. Somebody who's got something and then they get nervous Ribs aren't, positive rib lesions seem to be seen quite a bit.

Yeah, I think rib lesions have really been confounding. I think those who are sort of earlier in their learning curve often call these mets just because they see activity. But what we're learning is that solitary foci of activity, focus of activity in a solitary rib lesion, more often than not, almost 100% are benign. But the more you have and the more intense they are, I think the suspicion goes up. You also want to make sure you're looking at the CT carefully, because oftentimes a prostate med, if it has more destruction or if it's sclerotic or something like that, might push you towards calling that a metastatic lesion versus a benign lesion. But we know the ribs often have very often benign fibrosis-type lesions.
Okay. Paul, what are your thoughts?

Yeah, so now we have a patient with oligo recurrent metastatic prostate cancer he's got at least two or maybe three metastases but he also has now this lesion in the prostate bed so that complicates things a little bit. The memories had a radical right right and you're right he's got he's had his radical so. It complicates things a little bit. So one option is we do SBRT to these oligometastatic lesions. And the basis for that is the STOMP trial and the ORIL trial that says you can delay ADT so Dan doesn't have to start his drugs. So that's one option. Another way to look at it is the COMET trial. looked at these kinds of patients and said, if you do SBRT to those bone metastases, as long as they have a controlled primary, you might even be able to make them live longer. In this case, the tough thing is he's still got that prostate bed lesion. And I'm a little bit hesitant to treat that because that's going to cause more side effects. So to be consistent with the COMET trial, I might have to actually If he was super young and wanted to be super aggressive, I could actually treat the prostate bed like the prostate fossa and then do SBRT to those bone lesions. But in that case, we're really doing comprehensive treatment. So I would want to talk to Dan about maybe doing some ADT with that. So many different possibilities here from minimal radiation to maximal radiation with ADT.
Dan?

Yeah, I mean, one of the things that concerns me about this patient is the fact that this patient never went to less than 0.1. And that to me would indicate that there may be more micrometastatic disease present than what we see on these particular scans. So I would definitely consider focal radiation therapy to all three of these particular spots, but I would also go along with ADT as well. The question would be how much ADT you want to give this particular patient. How intense should it be? I probably would give a next-generation antiandrogen along with the ADT. Then perhaps at a year, re-image this patient and see what's happened. Does he have these lesions? Have these lesions improved? Are these the only lesions present? Has he developed new lesions over that time?

Well, I presented this case at the tumor board earlier in the year. They said the same thing you all said, radiate ADT, radiate the prostate bed, and radiate the right ileum and the pelvic lymph nodes. And so the discussion is, your opinion, you would, sounds like everybody pretty much do the same thing, right?

I would do this for a select patient, a young, healthy patient that really wanted to be super aggressive, partially because we are kind of extrapolating from data a little bit. We don't technically have data to fully support this in the post-op setting like we do in the upfront setting, where if you have micrometastatic disease, you can radiate the prostate and get a survival benefit. You can radiate the bones and get a survival benefit. And Dan can add a special ADT and get a survival benefit. So there's a little extrapolation here, but I would support this for the right kind of patient.

Well, everybody sort of felt that they would try to use ADT or. and radiate the areas and that. And I think it makes sense. Well, this patient and I were somewhat curious about things. So we discussed with him getting a MRI, maybe biopsy that ilium bone. And I did something that we don't do much anymore. I did a rectal exam on him. And one could feel not a hard mass, but some sort of tissue that was there just felt like normal prostate to me. So the multi-parametric MRI shows, and you can't see very well here, a 12 centimeter mass at the bladder neck, and the ileum biopsies were negative. Now what? Paul?

Wow. So that mass is way bigger than I would have expected given what we saw in the PSMA PET. And I guess if he doesn't have the ileum mass now and we're not sure about the ribs, maybe he just has purely local disease. So in that case, you know, I'd talk to Phil first and kind of get his opinion of whether there's any metastatic disease to be worried about. But if not, then I would do, um, consider doing pelvic nodal radiation and then very aggressive local radiation to this area.
Okay.

You know, this is interesting because they were aggressive and tried to get a tissue sample of that ileum lesion. Um, but I imagine on CT it wasn't visible. And most places in IR when they're doing these biopsies, it's under CT guidance for a lesion like that. And if you don't really know what the target is, you're doing more cognitive fusion. And whether or not you actually targeted lesion, it's hard to confirm. So I think we have to question whether or not we were able to get that lesion or not.

Yeah, that's that's always the question. Yeah, I didn't show I have the videos of it and everything. And it looked like they did everything they can to get that and so forth. But so anyway, um, I knew he did that. And I said, Well, what next? So I said, Why don't we get an oximum scan on this guy? So he's had a pet. Let's go back and see what that shows. And in fact, what we see here right now is there is nothing in the ileum that lights up on the oximum scan, nothing in the ribs. And now you can see this mass in the prostate. So there's more focal uptake And you want to comment on that at all, Phil? Sure.

You know, this is really interesting. And I think we're still learning a lot more about how these different radio tracers are complementary, how they're the same and how they're different. There was that study from Jeremy that did a head-to-head study between Axumin and PSMA that did show that for local recurrence, perhaps Axumin performed better than PSMA. So you get a study like this, you're seeing clearly more robust activity in that prostate bed, And now that we have the MRI, I think this really shows a nice picture of that recurrence in that prostate bed. And that ileolesion, yeah, I think it's hard to explain.
Okay. Paul, any comments or Dan?

I mean, the ileolesion is hard to explain. Also, again, when you look at all these scans, you've got to take the history into consideration. And I'm still very concerned about the fact that this patient never had a PSA that had reached less than 0.1. And that would lend me to be a little bit more aggressive. So in this situation, six months of ADT plus radiation, I think is appropriate. And then you certainly could watch the patient afterwards and then reinstitute ADT if this patient does have some evidence of biochemical redox. We had a case almost like this, except that the, the duration of time from the prostatectomy to the time the patient had a PSA relapse was much, much longer. He also had a rib lesion. We just simply focused on the bed and he wound up having an undetectable PSA. His testosterone level is now normal and his PSA has not risen. So you've got to use the history.

So what happened was I decided to biopsy the prostate or whatever was there, which was pretty easy to do. A guy had not had any radiation and the biopsies all came back as BPH and inflammation and no prostate cancer. And the other funny thing was I could never get his path report from the doctor that did it. And being a urologist, I've done a lot of radical prostatectomies and I've seen a lot. I've seen a number of cases in my career where, particularly with robots, where they left behind half of the prostate. And so this guy is a guy who had these biopsies I'm showing you right here. So I think what we're dealing with here is that all of this stuff. I mean, we had, I mean, the lesson here is the scans are not perfect. You have false positives. The tumor board wanted to rate everything. And Paul, you know, Paul Siebert, right? radiation oncologist here. He was just all over radiating this.
I was ready to light him up as well.

You have it, David. We had a nice discussion about that. I think you got to sometimes think outside the box and that there are false positives with the test. There's still a role for oximum. The oximum had a homogeneous uptake. It didn't look like it was a scattered cancer thing. And it did not show. And I was looking for a different thing. But we've got a lot of tools, and I think we had to use them. And this guy, I just kind of smelled a rat with this guy from the beginning. And it turned out. We don't know. So what am I going to do with him now?
Dave, how do you plan to re-image him? What radiotracer would you use?

I'd probably go back and using, and if this PSA was really going up, I'd probably use a pet PSMA, but I think I could use this. The question is, I mean, there are people, I talked to some of my friends at MD Anderson and other about, would you go in and try to take this out or leave it in? And that's sort of all over the place what people say, but you know what I'm doing, I'm putting them on finasteride, and to see what it does to his PSA if it cuts it in half for a while, and he's all for that. I think going in there and trying to take this thing out right now, the guy's going to have some risk. But I feel comfortable that there could be some cancer in there. I got seminal vesicle in the biopsy too, so there was nothing in there. Interesting case, huh?
That was a great case, David. I was really surprised. I did not expect that at all.

You used to use finasteride and then re-biopsy them after that, or at least use finasteride to potentially bring out a lesion. Would you consider re-biopsy at some point, even though the PSA may be going down?

Yeah, I think so. I mean, if this is BPH, his PSA ought to cut in half pretty quickly, or benign tissue. But doesn't, you know, he could have cancer hidden there. I'm like, come on. I think you're right, Dan. You were right. Everybody's right on it. There's something wrong with that nadir. And we always think microscopic disease, you have a learning curve here as you got, you got to really think, you know, these are great. The PSMA tests and oxima are all great tests, but we got to, we got to look at the clinical picture. So thank you all as a great discussion.

reference_conclusion: PSMA PET imaging was obtained for biochemical persistence after prostatectomy. Following clarification with multiparametric MRI, negative iliac biopsy, Axumin imaging demonstrating no uptake in the ilium or ribs, and biopsy of the prostate bed mass showing benign prostatic hyperplasia and inflammation without carcinoma, the consensus shifted away from immediate radiation or systemic therapy. The agreed next step was observation with finasteride and PSA monitoring, with repeat imaging using PSMA PET if the PSA rises and consideration of repeat biopsy if clinically indicated.
reference_conclusion_quote: My next step would be to image this patient with a PSMA PET scan. [...] what I'm doing, I'm putting them on finasteride, and to see what it does to his PSA if it cuts it in half for a while, and he's all for that. [...] I'd probably go back and using, and if this PSA was really going up, I'd probably use a pet PSMA [...] Yeah, I think so. I mean, if this is BPH, his PSA ought to cut in half pretty quickly, or benign tissue. But doesn't, you know, he could have cancer hidden there.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Stage IV breast cancer with spinal metastatic disease; assessment required for possible spinal cord or epidural involvement.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic breast carcinoma, stage IV, described in an oligometastatic setting with a spinal metastasis.

[ imaging findings ]: Spinal lesion was described with concern for possible cord involvement versus epidural space involvement. Determination of the extent of spinal canal involvement remained clinically relevant to radiation planning.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No prior completed cancer-directed treatment was documented. Front-line systemic therapy discussed for this disease setting consisted of a CDK4/6 inhibitor (examples cited: palbociclib or ribociclib) plus an aromatase inhibitor (letrozole/Femara). Commercially available oral therapy examples referenced for stage IV breast cancer included palbociclib (Ibrance) and letrozole (Femara). Subsequent-line therapy at relapse was described as fulvestrant-based treatment in clinical trial settings.

[ current disease status ]: Active stage IV breast cancer with known spinal metastatic involvement. Disease was described as potentially oligometastatic. Relapse after CDK4/6 inhibitor plus aromatase inhibitor therapy was referenced as a future management scenario, but no actual relapse event was documented.

[ other clinical data ]: Clinical trial options referenced for relapse settings included fulvestrant with or without venetoclax; fulvestrant combined with immunotherapy with or without a CDK4/6 inhibitor; and fulvestrant combined with agents targeting the PI3 kinase and mTOR pathways.

reference_discussion.text: of survival, both progression-free and overall, for a multitude of pathologies, breast cancer, prostate cancer, rectal cancer, et cetera, by ablating all known disease in a situation like this, oligometastatic. So let's address that first. Now it's gonna be complicated by a cohort involvement, so let's do this and then from a learning point of view, so what we need to know in this case is that your standard radiation, first of all, the patient needs to be sent to a radiation doctor, right? Pain or not, this patient must be seen by a radiation doctor. Overall survival difference is on the line. When they are seen by a radiation doctor, they must be treated with ablative techniques. And you guys all know what the difference is. When a woman has her breast irradiated, the goal is for 99% of those cells to live, right? You're not trying to destroy the cells. You're not trying to destroy that breast. That's radiotherapy. It's in little tiny pieces, day after day, right? Sometimes when a radiation doctor is treating someone, they're trying to ablate the target, destroy it, like a brain metastasis. So three, four millimeter target, we're not trying to have anything inside that target survive. We want it all to die. We're only targeting the problem. So when you look at this spine, it's a little somewhere in between. We need to use ablative doses. We need to sterilize that colony because that was what was done in the research that showed an extension of life. So if your radiation doctor isn't involved in the case immediately, you lose that opportunity. And if they just use palliative techniques from the last 30 years, you've lost that opportunity. It may help. We don't have that research study. What we do know is if your radiation oncologist gets involved early and uses ablative, aggressive doses, sometimes called radiosurgery, if they use those types of doses in this patient, they should be able to make a very significant impact on survival. Now, to complicate that is your astute observation that there may be cord involvement. You cannot use destructive doses in the spinal cord, obviously. So this is a case that would actually, in a real hospital, this case would go right to tumor board because the radiation doctor and radiologist are gonna have to hash this out. Is this court involvement or epidural space involvement, in which case the radiation doctor has to back off a little bit. And it may be that they have to give traditional palliative doses to prevent a neurologic event. Or is this an opportunity to do oligometastatic stereotactic ablative therapy, in which case we may be able to assist the medical oncologist in the extension of life.

And just to break that down just a little bit more, you know, when I'm meeting that patient with this type of stage four disease, you know, I just want to kind of relate it to them. There's that commercial on TV with the woman walking around the kitchen. They said, I have stage four disease and she's on Ibrancin, Femar. So those are the drugs that we're talking about just to give you, so you're a little bit more familiar. And that is what we call oral chemotherapy. I was going to add one other thing.

I think that's why I like these tumor boards. I mean, even this kind of set up tumor board is, he's exactly right. The first question we should always ask ourselves, even if it's stage four, is how do I cure this person? Is there a curable option? And even just you kind of saw where I was saying, oh, we're going to do this, and he's kind of readdressing us to say, hey, think about it. And that should be the first thing. The second thing would be, as far as the front line, and I think clinical trials is up there, too, and I don't know how much time we have. The frontline therapy is pretty much standardized for most people now, which is a CDK4-6, something like palbociclib or ribociclib or bambociclib, plus an aromatase inhibitor like Filmora, which is the one used in the trials. For the second line, if she relapses, if we cannot cure this person and she relapses, then I think clinical and trial enrollment becomes very critical and very crucial. At Wellstar, Northwest Georgia Oncology, we have two different clinical trials looking at full vesturant. And then they get randomized in a one-to-one fashion to either Fulvestrin or something called Venetoclax, which is a BCL2 inhibitor, which is FDA approved in other different diseases. And we also have another one called the Morpheus trial, which is looking at Fulvestrin, which is the standard of care, adding in immunotherapy, plus or minus either an AKT inhibitor, or an HDAC inhibitor. But there are clinical trial options for these women really in the second line that should be standard. I'm sure Emery has different ones that she's going to talk about too.

I'm in complete agreement with that as well. And we do in fact have also clinical trials at Emory that address the question of what happens at the time of relapse in women who have relapsed on a CDK4 inhibitor plus a bromatase inhibitor. And we have similar trials to what Dr. French was talking about. One trial is actually the combination of an immunotherapy with fulvestrand and perhaps with a CDK4 inhibitor as well if the patient had previously not had a CDK4 inhibitor. The other trial that we have is actually utilizing another targeted approach. It's a target towards two other pathways that have been proven to be involved in cell growth, cancer cell growth, proliferation, and metastases. And that is the PI3 kinase and mTOR inhibitor pathways. So it's a combination of actually a target that targets both the PI3 kinase pathway and the mTOR inhibitor pathway along with Fazlodex as well. So we have that option.

reference_conclusion: The patient should be referred promptly to radiation oncology for multidisciplinary review of the spinal lesion, with radiology input to determine whether there is spinal cord or epidural involvement. If anatomically feasible, treatment should consist of stereotactic ablative radiation using ablative doses to all known oligometastatic disease; if cord involvement precludes this, conventional palliative radiation may be required to prevent neurologic compromise. Standard first-line systemic therapy is a CDK4/6 inhibitor such as palbociclib or ribociclib in combination with an aromatase inhibitor. At relapse, clinical trial enrollment should be prioritized, including fulvestrant-based studies with targeted therapy or immunotherapy combinations.
reference_conclusion_quote: the patient needs to be sent to a radiation doctor, right? Pain or not, this patient must be seen by a radiation doctor. [...] When they are seen by a radiation doctor, they must be treated with ablative techniques. [...] We need to use ablative doses. We need to sterilize that colony because that was what was done in the research that showed an extension of life. [...] Is this court involvement or epidural space involvement, in which case the radiation doctor has to back off a little bit. And it may be that they have to give traditional palliative doses to prevent a neurologic event. Or is this an opportunity to do oligometastatic stereotactic ablative therapy, in which case we may be able to assist the medical oncologist in the extension of life. [...] The frontline therapy is pretty much standardized for most people now, which is a CDK4-6, something like palbociclib or ribociclib or bambociclib, plus an aromatase inhibitor like Filmora, which is the one used in the trials. [...] For the second line, if she relapses, if we cannot cure this person and she relapses, then I think clinical and trial enrollment becomes very critical and very crucial. [...] But there are clinical trial options for these women really in the second line that should be standard.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Abdominal swelling two years after treatment for breast cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Triple-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast, initially diagnosed two years earlier as stage III disease with axillary nodal involvement; subsequent metastatic recurrence involving liver and lung.

[ histopathology results ]: Invasive ductal carcinoma. Receptor status was triple negative: estrogen receptor negative, progesterone receptor negative, and HER2 negative. Initial primary tumor measured approximately 4 cm. Following neoadjuvant chemotherapy, residual invasive tumor measured approximately 1 cm at surgery. Residual nodal disease was present in 2 of 18 axillary lymph nodes removed.

[ imaging findings ]: Metastatic workup performed for abdominal swelling demonstrated a pulmonary lesion and liver metastasis. The liver lesion(s) were described as large.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No genetic testing had been performed at the time of initial diagnosis. No tumor genomic sequencing results were available. No PD-L1 testing results were available. No germline BRCA or other inherited cancer predisposition testing results were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy was administered with doxorubicin (Adriamycin), cyclophosphamide (Cytoxan), and paclitaxel (Taxol). The breast tumor decreased in size from approximately 4 cm to approximately 1 cm. The patient subsequently underwent bilateral mastectomies and axillary lymph node dissection. Surgical pathology demonstrated residual breast tumor and persistent nodal disease in 2/18 lymph nodes. Capecitabine (Xeloda) was offered postoperatively in the setting of residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent metastatic triple-negative breast cancer identified two years after initial diagnosis, with documented liver and pulmonary metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]: At initial presentation, axillary nodes were described as fixed. Residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy was present; a pathologic complete response was not achieved.

reference_discussion.text: Well, great. We're going to move on to the next case and we'll take a few questions at the end. Next case, she's 56 years old, most common type of breast cancer as well, invasive ductal carcinoma. She's what we call triple negative. No estrogen, no progesterone, and no HER2 new. She was diagnosed two years ago. At that time, the facility that she was treated at, they did not do genetic testing. At that stage, at that time, she was stage three. Tumor was significant, had fixed nodes in the axilla, Chemotherapy was given prior to surgery, which is a good thing. She had adriamycin, citoxin, and taxol. She opted to have, although she had disease in only one part of her breast, she chose to have bilateral mastectomies, and she had all the lymph nodes removed. And the initial tumor size was about four centimeters. It shrank down to one, and she had two out of 18 lymph nodes after chemotherapy. Her provider offered her Zolota, which is often done with triple negative breast cancer after neoadjuvant chemotherapy and residual disease is found. So she comes back in two years, has some abdominal swelling, and she has a metastatic workup. And on the right to you guys, that's actually the heart in the center. At the bottom there, there's a little round lesion right at the spine, and that is a pulmonary lesion. On the next slide to the left, the figure to your right, that's your liver. And the dark gray areas, that's a liver metastasis. So we're going to talk about what we would offer her. Want to get started, Dr. Bobby?
Sure. I think Dr. French is supposed to go first. Oh, he's supposed to go first. No, no, no. I didn't want to.
It's easier if you go first, right?

All right. So first of all, unfortunately, this is a more common situation that we'd like to see with triple negative breast cancers. Triple negative breast cancers do, unfortunately, account for a smaller subset of women, but they tend to have more aggressive disease. And oftentimes, we do see recurrence after we've attempted curative intent therapy. The first thing that I would recommend for a patient like her is, again, to get a biopsy of a metastatic site. Not so much to prove what the receptors are, but also to send the tumor for genomic sequencing to identify potentially any targeted options available for the patient. Also to send the tumor for a certain protein expression in the immune cells called PD-L1, for which we now have an FDA-approved immunotherapy to offer women that are PD-L1 positive in the metastatic setting for triple negative breast cancer. So that's the first thing that I would do. There's a number of genomic sequencing modalities that can be used, Foundation One, Tempest, Keras, so a lot of different companies that are offering genomic sequencing. It makes it very easy for patients and potentially, again, offers them targeted therapies or clinical trial options in the future down the road. In terms of our current standard of care, if a woman does have PD-L1 positive triple negative breast cancer, then we can actually offer them immunotherapy, which is an exciting new therapy for breast cancer patients that was previously not approved. So it's a combination of atezolizumab, again, which is an immunotherapy in combination with chemotherapy that has improved both how long we can control a woman's cancer and also overall survival in women that are PD-L1 positive. So that is something that I would strongly consider in this woman if she does have a PD-L1 positive breast cancer. If it's PD-L1 negative, then we do start talking about standard of care chemotherapy options versus potentially clinical trial if we are able to identify a matched clinical trial or a clinical trial that the patient would be eligible for.

That's a tough one. The other thing that she is, if she hasn't had genetics already, she needs genetic testing. You know, you're looking for, again, as we're going to talk, she'll probably talk about kind of the BRCA1 and 2 mutations because that does, you might not start with these drugs looking at Olaparib or some of these BRCA inhibitors or these drugs that work on these pathways, but the name of the game at this point is to try to open up your armament to say how many options can I have in my back pocket when I need them. If you look at the data with the Impassion 130 trial, that was with the addition of the tezolizumab, you know, it does increase progression-free survival and at the last, I think it was AACR update, they actually had an overall survival update. So it does add more toxicities to the regimen now because now you're adding immunotherapy. But with the survival advantage, it is FDA approved and that's probably the new standard of care that is as of just in the last 12 months or so. It's actually probably less than that, less than six months ago. You want to talk about that? I do. Yeah.
Thank you.

Yeah, so as Dr. French said, this patient clearly meets the criteria for genetic testing because any woman diagnosed with triple negative breast cancer under 60, regardless of her family history, her stage, anything else, is recommended to have genetic counseling and testing. And given that we've brought up genomic tumor sequencing, I just want to make sure everybody understands that there's, we've talked a lot about genomics and genetics already today, and a lot of that discussion is around tumor genetics and genomics. What I do in my clinic is different. We're testing inherited, your DNA that a person is born with. You can do that type of genetic testing on a person with cancer, without cancer. It's not dependent on the tumor. It's talking about your genes that you were born with and whether a person is predisposed to certain types of cancer due to something that they inherited almost always from one of their parents. So sometimes in these talks and even in papers or articles online, it can get confusing to know whether they're talking about BRCA or a gene that's isolated in a tumor or whether it's inherited. So you always want to make sure if you've had a tumor genomic test, that doesn't rule out the need for inherited mutation testing because a small percentage of people could have an inherited BRCA mutation that does not show up in their tumor testing. So you always want to make sure if your doctors are talking to you about BRCA, you've had both types of testing to completely, like Dr. French said, make sure that all your eligibility is known because usually the indications are for either tumor or germline or both. And germline means inherited. That's, if you see that word, that's talking about inherited DNA versus somatic or tumor or talking about mutations in a tumor.

Okay, so one of the reasons that you do tumor board with multidisciplinary approaches is that sometimes you read the body language and the tone of voice of your colleagues. Did you guys hear how excited they are? This gene and that gene will do immunotherapy, a new standard of care. From the radiation point of view, they've got something to offer, right? Now you might say, wait a minute, didn't you just say on the last patient a few mets and only a couple of organs and you should go to the races with the radiation? Yeah, those were little mets. Those were little mets. This liver, even if you called that two, they're huge and they move every time the patient breathes, right? So that's why you can't do medicine just by algorithm. You have to have some common sense in there and you have to have some teamwork. This is just not a radiation case at the moment. They've got things they can offer that can extend life, and they may shrink targets up. And maybe you invite a radiation oncologist to review the case again down the line, but at the moment, this is a systemic therapy case.

I'm going to add one other comment in terms of the gene sequencing is that I think there is a lot of education going on both in the academic world where not all triple negative breast cancer is the same. And so I think with Foundation One testing is I think eventually what we're going to find is that triple negative breast cancer is going to be kind of what we see in lung cancer, is that we're looking for a driver mutation where we used to think, oh, you have small cell or non-small cell lung cancer. Well, now non-small cell lung cancer is broken into two different parts, and now we're actually saying, oh, well, you have a met-mutated non-small cell lung cancer. I know it's a little bit complicated, but triple negative breast cancer is not all one disease. And I think there are a lot of clinical trials looking for specific targets to say, okay, you have triple negative, but what's driving it? And whether that's something to say, oh, this is an androgen positive breast cancer, so we're using therapies like you would use in prostate, or you're using pills to target that specific mutation, is very important in our triple negative cases.

I think that's a really good point and I do think that a lot of the trials nowadays that are focused on triple negative are looking at the up to six subsets of triple negative breast cancer and how to best target each of those as perhaps different type, as Dr. French mentioned, different drivers for each subset of triple negative. We do also have clinical trials available for triple negative breast cancer at Emory, and I'm sure WellStar does as well. The one that is coming to Emory soon is actually the use of a PARP inhibitor, which has been currently FDA approved only for women that have the BRCA germline mutation. There is a trial looking at the combination of a PARP inhibitor with another type of targeted therapy, also an oral drug, that perhaps works together to better control triple negative breast cancer. And that is actually offered for all triple negative breast cancer patients who have progressed on chemotherapy, irregardless of whether they have a BRCA mutation. So again, offers an oral targeted therapy to more women with this clinical trial.

And then the last, do I have time? The last thing I want to say, because this is a community forum, is just education. In terms of, this is going to be one of the first immunotherapy drugs that is approved for breast cancer space, but we've been using immunotherapies in melanoma and lung cancer for years now. So there's this guy out of Harvard named Hal Bernstein, when this got FDA approved, he said, you know, when immunotherapy comes to breast cancer, all the doctors are now immunotherapists. And so we have to be aware of the toxicities are different than chemo, right? So, you know, when we're thinking chemo, you're thinking nausea, vomiting, I'm going to lose my hair, fatigue, diarrhea. And immunotherapy toxicities are very different. And people in the community, when you go see your primary care doctors, might not recognize those. So there needs to be an education for our community and even not just medical oncologists, but our endocrinologists, our pulmonologists, your primary care doctors to say, hey, I'm not just on chemo, I'm on immunotherapy. So if you go there and you have normal blood sugars and you go see your PCP and they say, your blood sugar is 400, you have diabetes now. Well, maybe the immunotherapy took out or injured your pancreas and now you need to be on insulin and the therapy he's prescribing is not right. So we've seen this several times, and we're going to see it more, especially as this immunotherapy comes to our breast cancer patients. And there is a revolution of this immunotherapy that there needs to be education in the community and our community doctors, because you're seeing us, but most people probably have two, three, sometimes four other doctors they're seeing. And the toxicities we're seeing are not like chemo. So if you're fatigued all the time and you're saying, oh, well, it's just chemo fatigue, well, maybe that's not true. Maybe you've developed low thyroid now. And so there are things that they need to be checking for, at least communicating with us, to say, hey, my patient's in the office, and they're having this issue. What do you think about this? And I think sometimes I'm a stickler on proper nomenclature, and I don't call it chemotherapy. I call it immunotherapy, because it helps delineate that, hey, it's a different type of therapy, and the mechanisms work differently, and that profile of toxicity is different.

All right, just to go back on that patient, the reason why I brought her up, triple negative is very important when we look at stage four disease, but I did want to bring up one point just on the surgery side. So this was a woman that had breast cancer, only one part of her breast, and she actually had chemo first. The tumor had gotten much smaller. She still had the choice to do a lumpectomy and for her lymph nodes to be removed. The reason why I bring that up, because a lot of women think that if you have bilateral mastectomies, you're cured. You have no risk of the disease coming back, and that's absolutely an untrue statement. So, if you have the opportunity to preserve your breasts, or if you need a unilateral mastectomy, in most cases, it will not change your outcome if you choose a lesser invasive procedure. As well, when she had chemo initially, and then she had surgery, and she had residual tumor noted, that's another risk factor for her to have recurrence to come back. So, as providers, we were not totally shocked because she had advanced stage disease on presentation. When she had chemo, the tumor was not totally resolved, and when it's totally resolved, that's what we call a pathological complete response. just for you to be familiar with the verbiage there.

Dr. Johnson, can I make one more comment about this case? So there are some misunderstandings out there about what choice you're really making when you choose a mastectomy or a double mastectomy, and I'm really glad Dr. Johnson brought that up. One of the misconceptions out there is in a case like this, If I have a double mastectomy or even a single mastectomy, I'll avoid radiation therapy. Absolutely not true in this case. This is advanced disease, triple negative with residual disease after neoadjuvant chemo. This is a radiation patient every single day. So we really want our breast patients to meet with their radiation oncologist early in the process because they can explain when they would and would not need radiation. One of the things we have a hard time with in the community is a radiation doctor in the community often doesn't want to see a patient unless they're sure that the patient's going to need radiation. And we need to push back on that. You need a consultation with all of your specialists whether or not it's clear you'll need their services simply because a multidisciplinary approach requires all the expertise at the table.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Left breast mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Triple-positive left breast invasive ductal carcinoma (estrogen receptor-positive, progesterone receptor-positive, HER2-positive), presenting with fixed axillary lymphadenopathy and synchronous liver metastasis, consistent with stage IV oligometastatic breast cancer.

[ histopathology results ]: Invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast. Liver lesion at presentation was biopsy-confirmed metastatic disease.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial breast evaluation demonstrated a 3 cm left breast mass. Regional lymph nodes were at least 2 cm and fixed. Metastatic workup identified a liver lesion in one lobe of the liver; both described metastatic sites were less than 2 cm in size.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Estrogen receptor positive. Progesterone receptor positive. HER2 positive.

[ current disease status ]: De novo oligometastatic, hormone receptor-positive, HER2-positive breast cancer with fixed axillary nodal disease and a single biopsy-proven liver metastasis.

[ other clinical data ]: Family history included a great-aunt with melanoma. First mammogram was performed at age 58.

<image> Slide for Case #3 summarizing a 58-year-old woman with a left breast mass, receptor status, family history, enlarged lymph nodes, and CT-noted liver lesions for tumor board review.
<image> Case 3 slide outlining discussion points on chemotherapy regimen, clinical trial options, possible surgical intervention.

reference_discussion.text: All right, we'll move on to our next case. She's 58 years old. She presented with a breast mass in the left breast. She actually had her first mammogram at 58, which we know is not good. Most common type of breast cancer as well, invasive ductal carcinoma. She's estrogen positive as well, progesterone positive, and HER2 new positive. So that's what we call triple positive breast cancer. She had a family history of a great aunt with melanoma. The breast itself, she had a three centimeter mass. Her lymph nodes were at least two centimeters in size and fixed. So the doctors did what we call a metastatic workup. She had a lesion in one lobe of the liver. Both areas were less than two centimeters in size. and we're gonna go with, start talking about the chemotherapy regimen that will be recommended and possible clinical trials and move on.

I guess I get to go first. So I haven't seen that, she had surgery, right? No. Yeah, so this is one of those kind of oligo metastatic cases again, where there's kind of these isolated liver lesions. And so I think for this case, you know, again, Yes, this is stage four disease. This is devastating. Can I cure the patient? When we say cure, is there a way to get rid of all the tumor and not leave anything behind? I think this case is yes, but this person needs treatment. The kind of way to do this is you can kind of take a neoadjuvant approach. So there's a lot of different ways to do this. I think giving her a combination of Taxotere, Carboplatin, Herceptin, and Progetta up front. So that's kind of two different chemo drugs and then two different anti-HER2 drugs, assess for a response, and then you can take that patient for surgical resection. Afterwards, then you need, and again, up front, you need a multidisciplinary approach because I need my surgeon on board and I need my radiation doctor on board because the chemo is not going to cure this person. The chemo will shrink the tumor. It will make it go away. I may even make it not detectable on scans, but unless you can either cut it out or burn it out, that person is going to have a relapse. So I need buy-in from these two, and we're going to hear from them in a second about getting it out afterwards. Once that is finished, if there's any residual tumor, and maybe we can kind of come back and circle back and we'll talk about this, is what do you do afterwards? Because typically for HER2-positive disease, you need anti-HER2 therapy to complete one year total of therapy, and she's going to need an anti-estrogen because of the ERPR positivity. So once she gets through chemo and surgery and radiation, we'll hear from our colleagues there, she still needs more stuff for a whole nother year.

There's a little bit of uncertainty here based on response, but let me just generally speak. So in some centers, because the chemotherapists are so outstanding at their job, Keeping track of the liver lesion is going to be a little bit of a trick, because if you didn't put anything there, you don't know where it is anymore. And image fusion with pre- and post-therapy is tricky. It's not as accurate as, say, putting a fiducia in or marking the tumor somehow. The reality is that if you're talking about post-upfront, what we call neoadjuvant chemotherapy, or post-surgical radiation in the adjuvant setting, we're fighting an invisible disease, right? So a woman has a lumpectomy or a mastectomy, and there's a statistical risk. Technically, that patient is no evidence of disease, but the radiation doctor doesn't believe it because we're professional pessimists, and so we treat the area despite there being no detectable disease. In this case, you have a patient who presented oligometastatic, And there is a little bit of a question right now in the radiation oncology literature, how do we help the most? Because if the lesions disappear, you can't really do, we talked about the difference a little while ago about ablative versus radiotherapy. Am I destroying the target or am I scrubbing and cleansing the target? This woman can have the area of the breast or chest wall cleansed by fractionated radiation. But if the targets have disappeared, you cannot ablate a target you can't define. You can't destroy the entire contents of a volume you can't draw. So in a very good way, the radiation doctor may have been booted out of this case in terms of the metastatic disease. And that's good. We're fine with that. and in a complete response. In an incomplete response, then we would be back in that oligometastatic setting and we'd probably go to tumor board and come up with a way to treat this. The last thing I'd like to say about this case is let's pretend the liver lesion was there and we wanted it out. Although, It is true that the first prospective randomized trial was using a technology from my department. That doesn't mean you can't extrapolate from the data. There is a real role for surgical oncology to address liver metastases. There's an absolute real role for interventional radiology. So we don't want to get caught up too much in this. For your radiation oncologist to address a liver lesion, they're often going to want a fiducial marker placed. But if the interventional radiologist is sitting with a needle in the middle of the lesion, it's pretty easy to use energy at that time to destroy that lesion. Why go through the extra effort of having radiation afterwards? So these are the things that you work out in a multidisciplinary tumor board. And I'm sorry I couldn't give more specific advice, but again, the response kind of boots me out for a minute. Yeah. All right.

All right. OK. So Dr. French brought up the role of surgery in stage 4 disease. So in most cases, there is a questionable benefit, but the data is changing. So at our facility, patients who present with stage four disease, the best patients who do well are patients that have bone metastasis fibrillates sites. It's changing now for her to new positive patients. The reason being is because once you get that treatment, a lot of times when we go to surgery, particularly if they're not stage four, we see very little disease there. So, there's some current literature out now, say for instance, this is that particular patient with liver metastasis. You know, the study is not all the way conclusive, but I will tell you there are some patients who would offer her surgical intervention. The latest literature, based on what I know, is about 27 percent increase in survival. And so she would be given that choice. And I will tell you, when I talk to patients and they have stage four disease, a lot of them want it out because their goal is to get this out. But what I tell them is that in some cases we can't get that out, what's already spread. The best treatment for stage four patients is usually what we call systemic treatment radiation therapy. So in some cases we would offer it to them, but like I said, we would present this case in tumor board and see how she did after chemotherapy.

I agree. I also just want to reiterate, these are challenging cases in women who have oligometastatic disease, and I do think that it requires an upfront multidisciplinary discussion. The only reason why we're able to even offer potentially a multidisciplinary approach is because we do have very good, now systemic agents that offer prolonged survival in these women, even with oligometastatic disease. So, but I do think that these are case-by-case discussions and unfortunately it doesn't apply to every woman. And so, in some women we do solely offer systemic therapy with actually very good survival and very good quality of life and control of their symptoms related to their breast cancer. And in other women we may offer a more aggressive approach with a combination of surgery, radiation, and systemic therapy.

So, she did have surgery on this patient, so we're still, this is going to be quick for the medical oncologist. So she had residual tumor, 1.5 centimeters, 4 out of 18 positive lymph nodes. What would you offer at this point?

So for this woman, we have gone with a more aggressive approach with upfront neoadjuvant chemotherapy with a very good response of her cancer, and then the woman has gone for surgical resection at this point. So now we're at a point where we have no evidence of disease in the woman, but we still are looking for treatment to prevent the recurrence of her breast cancer in the future. There is actually some newer data that just came out in December of 2018 that utilizes a new drug called Kedsilo, which was previously used only in the metastatic setting for HER2-positive disease. We're now looking to use that in women who have residual HER2-positive breast cancer at the time of their breast surgery. And that has actually offered an improvement in both in invasive breast cancer survival. And shortly, I think we will get some survival data on this as well that will show overall survival benefit. Kedsila is given similarly to Herceptin, which was used previously in these women, IV every three weeks. So the options that we would have would be Kedsila, IV every three weeks to complete a full year of HER2-directed therapy versus Herceptin with or without Progetta to complete a full year of therapy. For this woman, given the aggressive nature of her disease with liver metastases, I would offer her KEDSILA, although she does not perfectly fit the patients that were studied in the KEDSILA, in the Catherine trial for KEDSILA. I would still offer her KEDSILA, given the improvement that we've seen in invasive breast cancer recurrence with the use of that drug.

Yeah, I would agree with that. I think if you look at the Catherine data that was published in the New England Journal of Medicine, you know, the hazard ratio is like 50%. So that basically means there's a 50% reduction in someone's invasive disease-free survival or invasive disease-free survival from their breast cancer. So you can take someone who's, you know, 77% and bump them up to 88% chance that maybe those people are cured. You're extrapolating that data because this person had a liver lesion So you're kind of extrapolating that data to say, yes, this drug works better if there is residual tumor left behind. If the person had a pathologic complete response, meaning at the time of surgery, yes, we know we marked those tumors, we cut them out, and there's just scar tissue, it might be reasonable to continue the Herceptin or even just the Herceptin Progetta and not switch the drug. But because there was a little bit of tumor left behind with this new data that came out in December, we would probably switch her. She also has one other option, which is after, now we're oncologists, so we keep doing things to patients, right? Is after she finishes that anti-HER2 therapy, she does have the option to take a pill, which is called neratinib, which is an anti-HER2 directed pill. Again, this is being extrapolated from adjuvant therapy, meaning these are not stage four patients, but there was an invasive disease survival increase by about 2% if you add this pill for another year after you've already done the year of anti-HER2 therapies. Now we're talking, after surgical resection, two more years, one of IV and one of pills, to add to this woman for about maybe a 2% to 4% benefit. This is a little tough because on the pill, I don't think there's a lot of people that are prescribing this for a 2% benefit. Now, obviously, if it's stage four and you're trying to cure these people, maybe there's some data there. But, you know, the cost is an issue. You want to talk about that?

Yeah, I totally agree, Dr. French, with what you're saying, and I do think it is worth a discussion to talk about the use of Neurotinib after CAD-SILA. The one thing I will say about it is there are specificities seen with the Neurotinib, the primary one being pretty severe diarrhea. And so if it does end up being a quality of life issue, I think at that point you do have to weigh the risks and the benefits of how much survival improvement do we get with what are we doing with the quality of life for our patient. The other thing I would also like to mention is that women was triple positive, so we would add hormonal therapy in addition to any HER2-directed therapy that we would do after surgery. And so I do think that there is a chance potentially for what we call cure for this patient, although she would need very close follow-up given still a higher risk of recurrence with the fact that she had liver metastases at the time of her diagnosis.

So she comes back now, she comes back a year later, and just has some memory loss, just doesn't feel like herself. And so we do a metastatic workup, including brain MRI, and she does have a single foci. Dr. Cavanaugh, you want to address that?

I'm glad that we've moved on to a brain metastasis because the post-mastectomy radiation question in this case is impossibly tough, and I don't have a study. So let's move on to the brain, Matt. So in this case, I believe we have a biopsy-confirmed lesion in the liver at presentation. OK, so we have evidence of hematogenous spread, right? Cancer can spread three ways. It can invade what's next. Next to it, it can go through lymph nodes. It can go through the blood. This one already learned how to go through the blood. That's really important. Because if the brain lesion is the first presentation, you've got a real trick on your hands. Do you blast away as if you know what you're doing, or do you require some proof? In this case, we can probably just go ahead and take care of the problem. So you would have a neurosurgery consult, and you'd have a radiation oncology consult. And you deserve both. And most patients, unless the neurosurgery is going to be very easy, it's a place that's going to induce very little deficit, most patients in this situation are going to lean towards stereotactic radiosurgery. And the reason is, if you have the lesion resected, you're still going to need radiation. And so why not just take care of it with a single shot of radiation? A lesion under two cm, what did we say the size was? I'm sorry. In the brain?
Two centimeters.

Okay, so your radiation doctor is probably going to be on the fence between a single shot and a few shots, but that should be a lesion they should be able to control fairly readily. Under no circumstances in 2019 would a woman in that situation receive whole brain radiotherapy. because we would want to treat again. We're not going to use radiotherapy, which is scrubbing something clean with repeated daily treatments. We're going to use radio ablation or radiosurgery, which is let's destroy the target in a very, very thin rind around the target. In this case, your margin on the target would be about 1.5 millimeters. So if you can imagine that, it's a very, very tight situation. You're just destroying everything inside because there's no functional brain tissue in there. That's all disease. And so that's how that would be managed. From that point onward, your radiation oncologist is likely to be your brain manager going forward. So yes, you're going to see your medical oncologist just as much. We're not taking anything away from them. But the radon could be expected to continue to follow indefinitely. And we actually aren't able to tell you right now what the survival data are for repeated SRS, SRT, as we call it. in situations like this because they're changing so rapidly. I have many patients who have had a half a dozen or more stereotactic interventions in the brain over several years. And if you'd have told me that 15 or 20 years ago when I was a resident, I would have laughed because those patients don't live long enough for that. But they do now. And we can get control in the brain and maintain control for quite some time. My last comment would be radiation oncologists are qualified to tell you if you can't have any more radiation. And even they often have to build a 3D model and put an hour of work in before they can give you a yes or a no. Nobody should be telling you you can't have radiation if it's not what they do. Your radiation doctor better not be telling you whether you're an immunotherapy candidate either, right? It's really important in this arena of changing data that we stay in our lanes and respect our colleagues' expertise.
All right. Any quick questions?

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 32-year-old woman; gravida 1. No family history of cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred with cervical squamous carcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Cervical squamous carcinoma, clinically staged as stage IIB. Extension studies were negative.

[ histopathology results ]: Post-radical hysterectomy pathology showed squamous carcinoma in situ. Residual tumor size was 3 mm. Parametria were free of tumor. Internal iliac nodes were reported as negative.

[ imaging findings ]: Extension studies were negative for metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy was administered with paclitaxel, cisplatin, and fluorouracil for 3 cycles. After 3 cycles, tumor size was reported as 1 cm, and pelvic examination was negative for parametrial involvement. One additional chemotherapy cycle was scheduled, followed by radical hysterectomy. Surgical pathology after hysterectomy demonstrated squamous carcinoma in situ with 3 mm residual disease, negative parametria, and negative internal iliac nodes.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status after radical hysterectomy with minimal residual in situ squamous carcinoma (3 mm), negative parametria, and negative nodal assessment as reported.

[ other clinical data ]: None.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 38-year-old Hispanic woman. Menarche occurred at age 13. No family history of cancer was reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Two-year history of intermittent vaginal bleeding associated with chronic moderate-intensity pelvic pain.

[ diagnosis ]: Cervical carcinoma, FIGO stage IIIB. Clinical examination identified an 8 cm ulcerated cervical mass with parametrial involvement. CT demonstrated extension to the lower third of the vagina and nodal disease in the common iliac and retroperitoneal regions.

[ histopathology results ]: Cervical biopsy demonstrated poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma associated with high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry was positive for pancytokeratin and synaptophysin. Ki-67 was 84% in both components. Post-radical hysterectomy pathology showed chronic cervicitis, no malignant neoplasm identified in the uterus, and metastatic involvement in 1 of 24 pelvic lymph nodes; the positive node was pancytokeratin-positive.

[ imaging findings ]: Abdominopelvic CT showed cervical malignancy extending to the lower third of the vagina, with positive lymph nodes in the common iliac and retroperitoneal areas. A subsequent abdominopelvic CT performed later showed no radiologically positive lymph nodes.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No numerical laboratory values were provided. Hematologic toxicity developed during chemoradiation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: In December 2015, concurrent chemoradiation was initiated with carboplatin plus etoposide and pelvic-field radiotherapy. Radiotherapy was discontinued after 15 fractions because of hematologic toxicity. Chemotherapy was then continued, completing a total of five cycles of cisplatin plus etoposide, with partial response achieved. The patient subsequently underwent radical hysterectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy.

[ current disease status ]: After surgery, no malignant neoplasm was identified in the uterus/cervix specimen, but residual metastatic disease was present in 1 of 24 pelvic lymph nodes. The most recent abdominopelvic CT showed no radiologically positive lymph nodes.

[ other clinical data ]: Gynecologic examination at presentation demonstrated an 8 cm ulcerated cervical mass. Parametrial involvement was present.

And I think cis is also a little bit lower dose. It's a Memorial Sloan-Kettering regimen with the radiation that is actually very feasible.

Can I just say that it wouldn't be common in the United States for a woman intermittent vaginal bleeding for two years with pain before she seeks medical attention. I mean, this patient presents with an eight centimeter. That's a very large tumor already, clinically. And I think that was the problem in this case, is that she didn't get medical attention earlier, and biopsies earlier. I think, unfortunately, it's an awareness, a public awareness issue, or an education issue, but this patient obviously sat on two years of intermittent vaginal bleeding and pelvic pain before she went for attention and showed up with an eight centimeter mass in her cervix. So if one really were to rewrite this case, my prayer would be for an earlier intervention and diagnosis at a lower stage. I think she's unfortunately, unwittingly allowed herself to get into rather a fatal prognosis situation by delaying for two years. That's my view of this. And I'm sure this is something you see very often. And this is exactly why it's less common in the United States for us to see this advanced stage of disease. Because it's uncommon for a patient to go two years with vaginal bleeding and pain before seeking medical attention. Anyway, does that answer the case? It's a very difficult case. So thank you, Dr. Morante. Dr. Salmon, are you there for the third case, please? We'd like you to present the third case. Are you there? in Santiago.

reference_conclusion: Given residual nodal disease after surgery and the high-risk neuroendocrine histology, additional systemic therapy was recommended in the adjuvant setting. Postoperative radiotherapy was not advised because prior radiation had already been administered and the interval was too prolonged for a meaningful dose. Restaging imaging, including chest evaluation, should be obtained before initiating adjuvant treatment, and adjuvant carboplatin plus paclitaxel for three cycles followed by close surveillance was favored.
reference_conclusion_quote: I personally think this patient probably needs more chemo. [...] I agree with Anuja that I think she needs further treatment. [...] I think it's going to be important that you read the pager after the surgery and include the chest in that before you embark on an adjuvant treatment. [...] The problem is that she's already gotten—she got some radiation, and now we're so far away from it. To get any dose that would be meaningful, it's too late. Really, how do we add it after she's gotten something, and now we're six months later? The question is, could you deliver a dose that was meaningful now? Probably not. [...] Yeah, so maybe, I think it would be a better part of valor to give her three cycles of carboplatin and Taxol in the adjuvant setting, and then follow her very closely. What do you think? Sure. [...] If the question is whether to give more treatment, I would definitely give her more treatments. What treatments? Carboplatin sounds reasonable. [...] Yeah, I mean, at this point, you're treated with the intent of cure. So you might as well finish that pathway and then observe.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old female. No relevant comorbidities were reported.

[ chief complaint ]: In 2012, she presented with progressive abdominal enlargement, bloating, abdominal pain, approximately 1 year of vaginal bleeding, weight loss, ascites, pleural effusion, and enlarged uterus with vaginal involvement on gynecologic examination. Performance status was reported as ECOG 2.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic endometrial adenocarcinoma, initially misclassified on biopsy as cervical carcinoma. At presentation in 2012, metastatic disease was documented with supraclavicular nodal involvement and thoracic/abdominopelvic metastatic disease. Final surgical pathology after hysterectomy demonstrated endometrioid adenocarcinoma of the endometrium, grade 3, with myometrial invasion and bilateral ovarian infiltration.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial biopsy in 2012: solid carcinoma with clear cell components; initially interpreted as cervical primary.  
- Left supraclavicular lymph node biopsy at presentation: positive for metastatic carcinoma.  
- Post-chemotherapy surgical specimen following total hysterectomy with bilateral adnexectomy: endometrioid adenocarcinoma, grade 3, arising in the endometrium, with myometrial involvement and infiltration of both ovaries.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT chest in 2012: left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, pleural effusion, and para-aortic/mediastinal lymphadenopathy.  
- Initial CT abdomen/pelvis in 2012: large uterine-associated mass, multiple retroperitoneal and pelvic lymph nodes, ascites, and peritoneal invasion involving the uterus, rectum, and pelvis.  
- Post-chemotherapy imaging after 3 cycles and after 6 cycles of carboplatin/paclitaxel: marked response with only a small residual uterine mass.  
- Laparoscopy after chemotherapy: no carcinomatosis identified.  
- Imaging in 2015: pelvic mass, supraclavicular lymph node recurrence, iliac lymph node involvement, and a 5 cm pelvic mass.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- CA-125 at initial presentation: 485.  
- CA-125 after 6 cycles of first-line carboplatin/paclitaxel: 14.  
- CA-125 at recurrence in 2015: 265.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- First-line systemic chemotherapy in 2012: carboplatin plus paclitaxel for 6 cycles.  
- Outcome of first-line chemotherapy: major clinical and radiologic response; post-treatment imaging showed only a small residual uterine mass, and CA-125 decreased from 485 to 14.  
- Surgical treatment after response to chemotherapy: laparoscopy followed by total hysterectomy with bilateral adnexectomy. No lymph node sampling was performed at surgery.  
- Postoperative management: observation without further treatment.  
- At recurrence in 2015: rechallenge with carboplatin plus paclitaxel for 2 cycles.  
- Outcome of rechallenge chemotherapy: clinical and radiologic progression.

[ current disease status ]: Recurrent progressive metastatic disease as of 2015, with pelvic mass, iliac nodal disease, and supraclavicular nodal recurrence after 2 cycles of platinum-taxane rechallenge.

[ other clinical data ]: Colonoscopy at initial presentation was normal.
