reference_discussion.text: Okay, this is a 56-year-old female with no relevant comorbidities. She was a very healthy woman But as many of our patients come in very late, she came in in 2012 with an increased abdominal size, bloating, abdominal pain. She had been for a year with vaginal bleeding. She had weight loss and a kneecog that went up to two. In the physical examination, she had ascites, pleural effusion, we didn't assess, and her gynecology exam viewed an enlarged uterus with vaginal involvement. Their images at that time, the CT of the chest, showed left supraclavicular lymph nodes, the pleural fusion, the periortic and mediastinal lymph nodes, and the abdominal and pelvis CT showed a large mass associated with her uterus, multiple lymph nodes in the retroperitoneum and the pelvic areas, a situs, and invasion of the peritoneum surrounded the uterus, the rectum, and all the pelvic area. Her colonoscopy was normal and her CA125 was 485. The biopsy that was performed showed a solid carcinoma with clear cell components and everybody diagnosed at that moment and thought that it was of the cervix. So we decided to go on with chemo and we started chemotherapy, Cargoplatin and Paclitaxel and we went in on doing six cycles of this and the images and the imaging post the three cycles and after the sixth cycle, only showed a small mass in the uterus. She had a great, great effective response to the chemotherapy. And her CA, 125, went down to 14. So, the surgeons decided they wanted to see what was going on. And finally, after performing a laparoscopy, they saw that there was no carcinomatosis. So, they went on and performing a total hysterectomy with bilateral anexectomy. and the biopsy showed that this was not a cervix carcinoma, but it was an adenocarcinoma of the endometrium. It was an endometroid adenocarcinoma, grade three, with myometrial involvement and infiltration of both ovaries. So, she went on with no more... treatment, she was just on observation, and on 2015, her images showed that there was a pelvic mass and, again, a supraclavicular lymph node. The CD scan showed iliac lymph node involvement and a 5-centimeter pelvic mass. And her CA, 125, went up again to 265. So we challenged the chemotherapy again, the same scheme, and she went on with two cycles of that, but she had now clinical and radiological progression. So the questions are, what other treatments can we offer this patient if there's a second and a third line chemotherapy for this endometrial carcinoma, and if there's a role for the radiotherapy?

And dare I say, a role for palliative therapy as well. This is a different topic that I'll cover in another tumor board. But there's been a large increase in palliative services over the past years in South America. There's also been the introduction of signed patient directives for end-of-life care legislatively in many countries, led by Mexico, I think, first in the continent, but there's a very low utilization of palliative services and signing of patient directives by patients. So this is something that's radically different from the United States. This is the kind of patient who will probably show up in an emergency room and slow down the pace of clinic resources and beds and things for her care, which could be avoided, perhaps, by involving palliative care earlier. But I'm interested in general comments from Dr. Dazon, first of all.
Yeah, I guess the biggest question I have is what was the rationale to proceed with hysterectomy in this patient?

Well, the surgeons wanted to see how much involvement was there. that there was no carcinomatosis, so they just decided to go on and do the surgery, the total hysterectomy, because they saw very little disease that was left over after the chemo.
But there was no biopsies ever done of the supraclavicular nodes that she presented with in 2012 to prove stage 4?
Yes, absolutely. But she had a complete response as images were, she had a complete response everywhere. So you did biopsy the nodes in the supercloth? At the beginning, yes.
Oh, and it was proven to be?
And it was positive.
Ah, okay.
Yes. Okay.

I agree completely with the treatment that she has received so far. I think, to me, if she had a beautiful response to chemotherapy after six cycles, I have no problem taking her back to the OR and do a hysterectomy. For what purpose? What is your intent of the surgery? I don't think there's any paradigm that shows any benefit here. To me, I would offer her surgery, no doubt if she has a nice response, and I'm extrapolating Fair amount from ovarian cancer.
You're extrapolating hugely from ovarian cancer. I would not be able to even justify that on the board.

When I worked in Toronto, there were patients operated on with diagnosis of stage 4 cancer. for 20, 30 years, for many decades, and it was finally abandoned. We used to refer to this as heroic surgery. It has no hope of curative intent.

I would say that. I mean, she got—I mean, stage 4 individual cancer has a horrible prognosis, right? I mean, this patient had two extra years of life without cancer. And you think it's because of the surgery? I mean, I don't know if it's chemotherapy or surgery, the combination of both. There's no way to know. But are stage 4 individual cancer patients ever cured with chemotherapy? No. I don't think so. I think all of them have poor prognosis. They're not cured with surgery either? No, no. I'm not saying that she's going to cure.

I'm just saying that you have to allow me to assert. So this woman was having a supraclavicular nodal involvement from carcinoma, had a phenomenal response to chemotherapy. The role for surgery of removing the uterus is what? Curative? Palliative? Control? None of the above. There was no reason to do surgery.
I think, can I talk now? I think it's for curative intent. Oh, really?
Stage four was supraclav nodes.
That's what you're hoping for. I will still offer her surgery despite Don's disagreement.

That's my personal opinion. I just think that this is a critical question in solid tumor malignancies. And we have to come down to what's out there. You're not listening to the biology. The surgeons do this all the time. All today in breast cancer. And there has never been shown an advantage of surgery other than for local reasons. If a patient has a flungating breast tumor, a bleeding And for pelvic bleeding or severe pelvic pain, fine. But no way can you ever convince me there is not a shred of literature to suggest that you can cure a patient with stage four disease surgically. No.

So you have to have an intent. Well, not only that. You did a THBSO in this patient. I'm going to have to go over it. I'll be in a couple of weeks. Well, no, no. But my point is you had a THBSO in this patient who also had nodes throughout the entire abdominal cavity.
Well, she had a response, right?
I know, but you wouldn't even bother to sample the nodes? Yeah, absolutely. Did you sample the nodes?
No, they did not sample the nodes.

Then I don't understand the intent of surgery. I think that's what we're—but here's the point. In the United States, this would be the discussion of this case even in our tumor board. People saying you should absolutely do surgery, some of us saying There is no, I don't understand the intent of the surgery, and you're talking about a palliative procedure, the woman has stage four cancer. It's a continental difference. It's a complete, yeah. It's a disciplinary difference. Yeah, oh yeah, yeah.
And I think medical oncologists, Anuja, you say what you say. And we've always got a radiation oncologist to like broker the decision.
I have to say, at MD Anderson, we would have done the surgery as well. It is based on the ovarian data. Dr. Pompa But cervix is so different. Oh my gosh.
You didn't even know it at the time. It was cervix. That's why they did the surgery, not uterine.
I know, but I have to say, at MD Anderson, that would have been—even though there is no data, and I totally agree, but it is based on the ovarian data where the debulking is important.

Actually, you can extrapolate from ovary to endometrial, because I do think endometrial—stage 4 endometrial with carcinomatosis, we do see some of those women cured with an aggressive surgical approach and chemotherapy. You can cure stage—but this wasn't endometrial. You did the surgery for stage 4. cervical cancer.
And that's what they thought. We thought it was cervical.
If they thought it was cervical cancer, I would never have done the surgery. That's the truth. I think Dawn has a point there. That's true.
I agree.

If my thought was a cervical cancer, I would never have done a surgery. If I thought that there was a concern whether there was endometrial, I would definitely have offered a surgery. But you're absolutely right. If it's cervical, then there's no room for surgery. Right? And that's a good point.

Yeah, so all of us are starting to say, you know, endometrial, we do apply an ovarian cancer algorithm with advanced endometrial. I am more comfortable with someone who has uterine cancer and carcinomatosis going to surgery than getting chemotherapy alone. This is not endometrial cancer. At least you didn't think it was endometrial cancer when you started. and you guys did surgery for stage 4 cervix cancer. That's a totally different thing.
Yes, absolutely.
Brittany, you haven't said anything. Do you want to make a comment?

Sorry, I joined late today. But I agree. I think, you know, I'm a medical oncologist, too. And I think probably my opinion would align with Don's in regards to the fact that I think this patient with stage 4 cervical cancer probably shouldn't have had a surgery. You know, it'd be one thing if there was an indication where she was having severe abdominal pain or they were trying to control bleeding and they couldn't do radiation, but that wasn't the situation it sounds like. It sounds like she wasn't very symptomatic and she was doing well after chemotherapy that I think, you know, I think here, we probably would not have done surgery.
Does chemotherapy prolong survival? For cervical cancer? Either, endometrial or cervical?

Well, we do. We do. Yes. Yes, it does. I think for metastatic disease, compared to historical controls, chemotherapy does have a role in prolonged survival. That's in the first line setting, like most solid tumors. So first line, you have a bigger benefit than second, third, and fourth line therapies. But we tend to continue to give treatments with the hope that we're extending survival. The problem with endometrial and for the large extent of cervical cancer, after you progress on one line of therapy, median survival across the board for any drug you give is less than a year. Yeah. And that's based on phase two trials, really. And, you know, the attempts at getting a US approval for a second line agent, say, after platinum taxane and endometrial cancer, I can think of two randomized trials, both of which were negative for a new agent. One was Nixabethalone versus Agent.

Just to go back to non-sexy chemotherapy individuals, I'm intrigued by the literature showing that ambulatory patterns of care for patients end-stage cancer improves survival a little bit. So I think for a resource-constrained environment, an aggressive move towards palliative services and ambulatory palliative services is a mandatory part of stage 4 solitary malignancy and should be focused on a lot, I think. Because it would free resources to treat earlier stage disease better.

I think this is a case that this is a patient that you know that you're not going to be able to cure. And chemotherapy, the response rates in chemotherapy in someone with recurrence in the middle of cancer after going through a second line of carbotaxel, I mean, there is very limited data. I mean, I would offer her a single agent that has low toxicity. I would think about Doxil. I think the response rates with Doxil in this setting is 8% to 10%. So that's an agent that it has low toxicity. It's easy to administer. And other than that, you know, I don't see any other, you know, you can use single-pane taxol, but she already kind of progressed to carbon taxol. Yeah.

Yeah, so an anthracycline, like Ali mentioned, would be our probably a second, is what we would offer her now. If I needed the response, I'd use Adriamycin rather than Doxil, but if she was doing okay and not, didn't have a lot of symptoms, I think doxil does make a lot of sense, and it's better tolerated than adriamycin. It can keep things stable, not as high of a response rate perhaps, but again, this is not a curative situation. And if she did maybe six months of adriamycin or doxil and then had progression, I would probably try taxol again. If she got it weekly, then try the every-three-week dose.

And I think the other question about radiation, I'll let Anish respond to that, but my sense widespread metastasis, there is little role for radiation. Especially with humans, she has multiple sites of metastasis.
I'm sorry, I didn't get that.
So with multiple cytometastases, if she has a lymph node, positive pelvic mass, I don't think radiation has a role, but I'll let Anuja respond to that.
I think it's only palliative. I totally 100% agree. If she needs palliative radiation, I would do it, but otherwise, I agree. She does not have a role for radiation right now. Definitive.

So Anuja, here in Boston, it's becoming more frequent that our preferred second line choice is Taxolabastin. And we're using that quite frequently on our patients here. And it's producing disease control that we don't have any phase 2 data saying how how durable the response is. But what are you guys using second line over there? You know?
I know it's Bev, but I don't know if it's with Taxol if it is with something else. But I can find out, Don, and I can email you.

OK. I know we're using Bev. I did a calculation on the back of an envelope. But for something like a 2.4-month or 2.5-month prolongation of survival, it costs about $100,000, for which you can do about 100,000 pepsimums. Yes. So I think for a resource, constrained environment, the use of invested in surface cancer is really not fully justified.
Right, right. And I totally agree with that. It's hard to justify it here in the U.S. even. But, you know, where it's accessed, that tends to be our go-to in the second line.
Well, Dr. Salmon, you've managed to do what I hope with tuberculosis. You've created a fist fight in Boston and I'm sure across the world. This was a great case, so thank you very much.

reference_conclusion: For recurrent metastatic endometrial carcinoma progressing after rechallenge with carboplatin and paclitaxel, the recommended next systemic therapy is a low-toxicity single-agent anthracycline, with pegylated liposomal doxorubicin favored if the patient is minimally symptomatic and conventional doxorubicin considered if a higher response is required. On subsequent progression after approximately six months of anthracycline-based therapy, paclitaxel rechallenge may be considered. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 71-year-old postmenopausal woman.

[ chief complaint ]: One month of pelvic pain, with subsequent worsening abdominal pain over the following two weeks.

[ diagnosis ]: Right adnexal mass highly suspicious for ovarian malignancy with omental involvement and small-volume ascites; advanced-stage intra-abdominal malignancy was suspected clinically. Pathologic confirmation had not been obtained.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathologic diagnosis was available. Omental biopsy had been planned but was not performed.

[ imaging findings ]: CT demonstrated a complex 9 cm right adnexal mass with omental nodularity and small-volume ascites. The lesion was reported as not amenable to ultrasound-guided drainage. Imaging appearance was considered highly suspicious for malignancy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: CA-125 was elevated at 579 initially and subsequently increased to 1,253 over approximately two weeks. CEA was slightly elevated at 8.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for three cycles followed by interval surgery had been planned because of concern regarding surgical tolerance. Chemotherapy was not initiated. Omental biopsy was scheduled for diagnostic confirmation but was not performed. Endoscopic evaluation for elevated CEA was not performed.

[ current disease status ]: Symptomatic untreated pelvic/adnexal malignancy was suspected, with worsening pain and rising CA-125. No tissue diagnosis had been established, and no systemic therapy or surgery had been delivered.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus, chronic hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism. BMI was 42. ECOG performance status was 2. Family history was unremarkable. Physical examination demonstrated obesity and a slightly tender 9 cm right adnexal mass; no other abnormal examination findings were described.

reference_discussion.text: So, please note that this case consultations do not create or otherwise establish a provider-patient relationship between any IGCS volunteer, clinician, and any patient whose case is being presented. Responsibility for the patient remains with the medical team who cares for the patient at the presenting institution. So we have for our case presentation a 71-year-old woman who is postmenopausal and has had about one month of pelvic pain. Her past medical history includes type 2 diabetes, chronic hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and hypothyroidism. Her family history is relatively unremarkable. The CT scan shows a complex 9-centimeter right adnexal mass with omental nodularity and small volume ascites, which is not amenable to ultrasound drainage. Abnormal labs include an elevated CA125 at 579 and a slightly elevated CEA at 8. Physical exam, patient is obese with a BMI of 42. She is somewhat limited in her mobility with an ECOG score of 2. And on physical exam, the only finding is a nine centimeter, slightly tender, right adnexal mass. CT scan has shown the mass looks highly suspicious for malignancy. So the plan of treatment was because the patient was somewhat frail and, um, We were a little bit worried about the ability for her to tolerate surgery. We were going to get a biopsy of the omentum to confirm the diagnosis. And we had planned to treat her with three cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, followed by surgery, possibly minimally invasive, after three cycles. This was scheduled, but CT scan called and informed us that we could not do a biopsy as the case was considered nonessential due to the COVID-19 epidemic. I called the radiology department and they still refused to do the biopsy because they were so busy. We were informed that all surgeries that are not immediately life-threatening are on hold due to increased surge in our hospital. And I could not get an endoscopy scheduled for the same reason to evaluate her elevated CEA. So our options at this point were to give chemotherapy without pathologic confirmation or to wait until she was symptomatic. So over the next two weeks, the symptoms got worse with increasing abdominal pain. Her CO125 increased to 1,253. After discussion, the patient opted for chemotherapy without a biopsy, but now the infusion unit is closed. due to the need for additional hospital bed space. So I think this highlights the rapidly changing situation that we have in many places. I think the situation is different for everybody, but we have to remember that this doubles every three to five days, depending on where you are. And so short-term plans will change rapidly. And I just wanted to discuss this in terms of deviations from standard of care and see what our panelists had to say about this.

We can open it up to the panel to make a couple of comments on situations that they've experienced regarding delay of care, particularly diagnostics. Daniella, being in Italy, I'd like to start with you.

Yeah, and it's a very interesting case that could occur in each of our hospitals. So I agree with the choice to postpone the big surgery in this moment in patients with ovarian cancer in advanced stage, like this case with a mental involvement with peritoneal carcinomatosis in favor of neoadjuvant chemotherapy and later surgery. In fact, in this particular moment, when we're planning a treatment for our patients, it's mandatory to consider multiple factors, such as comorbidities, age, immunostatus, because first of all, we should prevent the patients becoming infected, but also we should preserve the hospital resources for COVID-19 patients. For example, the intensive care unit beds or ventilators or blood products. So the risk to start a treatment without a specific diagnosis could lead to an incorrect diagnosis. Thinking about, for example, a Krugenberg tumor or breast metastasis or specific histotype like the low grade, that as we know, the low grade can respond very well to the chemotherapy. So in Italy, for example, we try to centralize oncological patients to the referred center. So it's very difficult that a patient can have a surgical biopsy by laparoscopy or by CT scan. But I have a question for Wendell, is it possible? And do you think that a possibility, Wendell, it could be have a cytology, for example, from oxidase by ultrasound to have more information?

Yes, certainly that would be my choice if she had fluid that was amenable to biopsy. But I do, and I have been fooled before in this situation by cytology where the, as you pointed out, the cancer might be a low grade and that's difficult to call on the cytology diagnosis. Okay. And I know you've experienced this in Italy in terms of just closing down all care. Is this a situation that you run into?
Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes, it's the same.
And Jun, from China, you probably have experience also. Do you have any comments?

Yeah. I do agree to give this patient maybe the new agent of chemotherapy first. but it's hard to get the biopsy, get the pathology results. This is a big question, so I agree with Dr. Roper's comments. We need some identification of diagnosis. So at this time, maybe we can more often to use some non-invasive methods to make a more clear diagnosis. Sometimes, such as for this lady, maybe we can test HE4, another tumor mark. If HE4 increased, obviously, maybe just indicate there's a malignancy and also high-grade malignancies, I think there's another way. Also, I think, could we just give the patients a new adjuvant chemotherapy for the cycle if she had a good response to the chemo, maybe to help us to make the right diagnosis?

Thank you. So what we're going to do next is a couple of poll questions. If we can move to the next slide. So we clearly know that there's lots of delays. I just want to see how it's assessing you. So the first question is, are you anticipating significant delays in surgery, radiation, imaging, or chemotherapy as a result of the pandemic compared to a normal schedule? And you can just click on whichever time frame you're experiencing. And then the second question, which you may need to scroll down for, how have these changes impacted cancer care? from no changes to care to currently cannot deliver cancer care, as you heard in this case. And while you're voting, I'd like to ask Dr. Pereja if he has any comments on these questions that we just posed to the group before we get to the didactic. Renee, any comments?

And according to the presented case, the only option now for this lady is surgery. And even during COVID-19 pandemic, you will have to perform some surgeries. So you need to be assured that this patient is not a COVID patient right now by asking for a rapid test, CAT scan, and then take her to the OR. taking all the preventive measures, PPE for all the equipment, because we will have to operate some patients. And this patient is getting worse. She's right now in pain. So you need to operate some patients under special circumstances.
Thank you. And I'd now like to introduce Dr. Emma Rossi, who's going to present delays in gynecologic cancer surgery.

reference_conclusion: Given advanced ovarian malignancy with worsening abdominal pain and inability to obtain biopsy or administer chemotherapy during pandemic-related resource restrictions, the board supported deferring extensive primary surgery in favor of neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by interval surgery when feasible. However, under the current circumstances, surgery was identified as the only available immediate management option. Preoperative COVID-19 assessment with rapid testing and CT imaging, followed by operative management using full preventive measures and PPE, was recommended.

We were going to get a biopsy of the omentum to confirm the diagnosis. And we had planned to treat her with three cycles of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, followed by surgery, possibly minimally invasive, after three cycles. [...] So I agree with the choice to postpone the big surgery in this moment in patients with ovarian cancer in advanced stage, like this case with a mental involvement with peritoneal carcinomatosis in favor of neoadjuvant chemotherapy and later surgery. [...] And according to the presented case, the only option now for this lady is surgery. And even during COVID-19 pandemic, you will have to perform some surgeries. So you need to be assured that this patient is not a COVID patient right now by asking for a rapid test, CAT scan, and then take her to the OR. taking all the preventive measures, PPE for all the equipment, because we will have to operate some patients. And this patient is getting worse. She's right now in pain. So you need to operate some patients under special circumstances.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 58-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Liver lesions detected on surveillance ultrasound in November 2019 in the setting of known cirrhosis.

[ diagnosis ]: Hepatocellular carcinoma arising in a cirrhotic liver. Initial disease involved a dominant left hepatic lobe lesion with several additional subcentimeter hepatic lesions. Disease later progressed to multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology data were provided.

[ imaging findings ]: Surveillance ultrasound in November 2019 demonstrated liver lesions. CT on 11 December 2019 demonstrated a hepatocellular carcinoma in the left lobe of the liver and several subcentimeter lesions throughout the remainder of the liver. The CT images also demonstrated varices. Staging arteriography on 20 February 2020 demonstrated a large hypervascular left lobe tumor supplied independently by segments II and III. Post-radioembolization PET demonstrated good targeting of the dominant tumor and an adjacent smaller posterior lesion. Follow-up imaging after radioembolization showed that the largest tumor had decreased in diameter and was no longer vascular. Multiple hypervascular subcentimeter nodules in the right lobe remained unchanged at that time. Approximately 7 months later, imaging remained stable overall. On more recent follow-up imaging, the previously treated radioembolized tumor was no longer visible, but the subcentimeter nodules had increased in diameter, consistent with multifocal disease progression.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: Platelet count 107. INR 1.1. Creatinine 1.03. Alkaline phosphatase 289. ALT 49. AST 69. Total bilirubin 1.7. Albumin 3.1. AFP 334 at diagnosis. ALBI score -1.67. Child-Pugh class B7. AFP decreased after treatment and did not exceed 150; approximately 7 months later AFP was 107. On subsequent follow-up, AFP increased to 701.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Cirrhosis had been present for several years. The patient had required one prior paracentesis for ascites a few years earlier; ascites was subsequently managed with diuretics. No known varices had been identified before cancer workup; varices were later seen on CT. The patient underwent radioembolization of the dominant left lobe tumor, with treatment delivered to segment II and segment III arterial supply. Post-treatment course was clinically well tolerated. The dominant treated lesion decreased in size and lost vascularity. The adjacent smaller treated lesion was also targeted. The patient underwent transplant evaluation and was placed on the transplant list. No systemic therapy had been administered up to the time multifocal progression was identified.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive intrahepatic disease with enlargement of previously subcentimeter nodules and AFP rise to 701, consistent with multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma. The previously radioembolized dominant lesion had resolved on follow-up imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: Cirrhosis with ascites controlled on diuretics. No known varices had been documented before diagnosis, but varices were subsequently identified on CT.

reference_discussion.text: Thanks Rich, and it is a pleasure to be here with you and Laura, and a pleasure to talk about the treatment of patients with liver cancer. This slide is fairly basic, but shows the treatments for people as they move through the BCLC staging and treatment algorithm. We in IR have had a preeminent role for years, decades, and for a long time, we provided the only therapy beyond resection and transplant, because systemic agents weren't terribly effective. That changed with serafinib, and we then were trying to figure out ways that we could work with people providing serafinib to provide good care to patients. It changed a lot in the last couple of years when really good systemic agents came on and they're supported by really good studies. So we have now a very changing environment in the management of patients with hepatocellular cancer and it's important that we figure out how to treat our patients well within that environment because Even though we're doing a good job, the mortality of patients with liver cancer is increasing. The incidence is increasing and the mortality is increasing. So we can do a better job. And our goal would be to treat patients earlier and get them toward curative therapies. Or in optimally, people take people who are further along to the right in the algorithm and move them toward the left or stage transition and prevent stage migration. The way to do that is working together. And so that's what this symposium is all about, is optimizing our care of patients by working with every member of the team and trying to figure out the best synergies between what we can provide. And so with that, I will move on to the first patient to discuss. And both of the patients we'll discuss are mine, and they're real. And the first patient is 58 years old. She had cirrhosis for several years and required her first paracentesis only a few years ago, after which her ascites was treated with diuretics. So she had one paracentesis, now has ascites, treated with diuretics. And at the time of her diagnosis and up until this point, she had no known varices. Her labs are as stated with a platelet count of 107, INR of 1.1, creatinine of 1.03, ALKFOS-289, ALT-49, AST-69, bilirubin 1.7, albumin 3.1, and AFP-334. Her ALB score is negative 1.67. So together, she's a child Pugh B7. and being followed, and surveillance ultrasound in November of 2019 showed liver lesions, so she was sent to us for further evaluation. The December 11, 19 CT scan demonstrated clearly a hepatocellular cancer in the left lobe of the liver and several subcentimeter lesions throughout the rest of the liver. The smaller slides also show the presence of varices on the bottom right of your screen, unknown up to that point. We went to multidisciplinary conference and decided that she would hopefully make it to transplant. And we wanted to try to stabilize her largest tumor, keep her within Milan, and then work toward getting her transplanted. So this is from the staging arteriogram on February 20th. She delayed because of COVID to come into us. And we eventually did get her in. And you can see the large hypervascular tumor in the left lobe. It was actually fed independently by segments two and three. So I treated both of them. And this is the post-radioembolization PET scan, and you can see good targeting of that tumor, and it actually hit the smaller tumor that was coddled to it and posterior. And the smaller slide just shows the correlation between the post-itrium PET and the CT prior. She did very well with that and her largest tumor decreased in diameter and no longer was vascular after that. And you can see multiple hypervascular nodules in the right lobe of the liver, all sub-centimeter and not changed from prior to her radioembolization. So we thought that was great. We started her evaluation for transplant and December, seven months later, everything looked about the same and her AFP was still 107. It hadn't ever been above 150 after treatment. So at this point she's on the list and she just came back for a follow-up study about a few weeks ago and unfortunately even though the tumor that we treated with radioembolization is gone, those subcentimeter nodules have increased in diameter, and her AFP is up to 701. So she has developed multifocal hepatocellular cancer that is now diagnostic of that. So we, up to this point, did not have her on systemic therapy. It was discussed, and we didn't have her on systemic therapy. But before I get to that, I should probably have asked a more important question, or at least a question of a more general nature, and that is, if she were child Pu-A at diagnosis, would that have changed any of your treatment options? What would it have changed for this patient? And I'll ask that of Laura.

So given that she is young and her AFP was relatively low when she was diagnosed and she'd already had some complications of liver disease requiring a paracentesis, I think the goal would be to get this woman to transplant. So I think I would have probably done similar to what you guys had performed with the goal of bridging her to transplant, regardless if she was an A or a B.

Thanks. And the reason I asked that one first is that the next three are best answered, I think, by Rich. So the first question is, would you have decided earlier to move on to systemic therapy for this patient?

So I think to Laura's point and how you guys manage her, our goal is cure and if we could get the patient a transplant, that's great. But as patients are waiting, their tumor biology will declare themselves. And I think as this patient advances, and what I've often said is patients who have intermediate liver cancer, if they don't get cured or die of some other comorbidity, they will stage progress to advance disease. And I think when we start seeing multifocal disease in the liver, in both lobes, we start to get concerned that local regional treatment won't be enough. And now, as you alluded to, we do have very good medical treatments available, not only frontline, but second line, and potentially even third line. Given all of these have been studied only in patients who are Child Pue A, and so the safety and efficacy of some of these regimens has not firmly been established. For patients who are candidates, atezolizumab and bevacizumab has clearly established a new standard of care for frontline liver cancer. One of the things we do get concerned about is this risk of bleeding. And in the Mbrave 150 study, all patients were required to have an endoscopy within six months of starting. And many patients did have varices. Some of them had to have them treated. But as long as they were not high risk for bleeding, then they were allowed to come on study. And we can't forget that there's a whole lot of regimens on the horizon, new combinations and ongoing clinical studies, which we should always consider how to get patients into these clinical trials to do better. But again, most of them do require patients to have good performance status in child PUA liver disease.
Well, what are the considerations for treating the varices before starting on atezolizumab and bevacizumab?

So not all varices need to be treated. Obviously, we would defer to the endoscopist if they're at high risk for bleeding. Small varices probably do not need to be treated. But if there are varices that are at high risk for bleeding based on the endoscopist assessment, then those should be banded. And then probably it's prudent to wait a week or two before starting the BEV. But this is a minor procedure. In reality, unless they're, again, high-risk for bleeding, a tezobev should be considered a treatment of choice for advanced liver cancer. You know, there's been a lot of advances in liver cancer treatment, and this slide comes from the NCCN, which highlights the role of a tezolizumab as a new option for patients, as well as what we have is the established TKIs of saraftib and lenvantinib. Interestingly, they maintained a potential recommendation for nivolumab, even though there was a phase 3 study of nevo versus serafinib that did not meet its statistical endpoint. But we did see nivolumab had a response rate of 15%, was well tolerated, and a survival of over 16 months. It just was not statistically different than serafinib. And that would be for patients who can't tolerate any anti-angiogenics. But for the large majority of patients, they will probably be candidates for a tezobev if they're candidates for systemic treatment. And this study was published in the New England Journal of Medicine last year, where it met both its primary endpoints of improving overall survival and progression-free survival. And at the time of the initial analysis, we did not reach the true median in the treatment arm. We did have a hazard ratio of about 0.58. That was stable and significant. And at GI-ASCO now, with an additional 12 months of follow-up, we see that the new frontline survival for advanced liver cancer is over 19 months. 19.2 months with a Tez-O-Bev, and the soraphin arm did not change. That was 13.4 months. The PFS data was very stable, because we had reached those medians at the time of the primary analysis. And what was very striking is that with longer follow-up, we've actually seen the response rate go up. At the time of the primary analysis, the response rate with the tezobev by conventional resist was 27%. And now, with longer follow-up, we see that response rate is 30%, including 8% complete responses with systemic treatment. And this regimen is pretty well tolerated, I would say. We don't see any new safety concerns with longer follow-up. Obviously, the autoimmune phenomena, which we are familiar with PD-1 or PD-L1 inhibitors like atezolizumab, can be seen, but generally they're low grade. Really, a lot of the side effects we've seen were related to Bevacizumab. And we see that here on this slide, where looking at the safety of Bev versus Serafinib, you can see the most common side effects with Atezobev were hypertension and protonuria. And in this slide, all grades are lighter, high grades are darker. But things that the patient really notices, such as diarrhea, hand-foot skin syndrome, anorexia, are really more common with seraphinib. And this type of data was very much supported by improved quality of life assessments with a tezobev over seraphinib. There is similar bleeding risks with both drugs. Most of it is low-grade, such as epistaxis. There are worse, more higher-grade bleeding events with the Tez-O-Bev, but again, this can be mitigated by patient selection, good performance status, child PUA, and doing your pre-operative endoscopies, or pre-treatment endoscopies, I should say. Now, You know, single agent PD-1 inhibitors have had challenges in phase three studies. Both nivolumab and pembrolizumab have accelerated approval for progression after serafinib. Now that we've seen IO move to the frontline space, the number of patients getting this beyond progression I think will be fewer because the patients who will get this will be the ones who get TKIs in the frontline. And again, a Tez-O-Bev is not gonna be for every frontline patient, but I think it'll be the majority. Maybe some of us estimate around 15, 20% of patients might not get a Tez-O-Bev frontline for various reasons. And if they get a frontline TKI, a progression, both Pembro and Nevo would be appropriate, as both of them gave response rates of about 15 to 20% that were very durable. The thing is, as you see here in Checkmate 459, nivolumab did not reach its primary endpoint of improving PFS statistically in the Checkmate 459 study. And interesting enough, at GI-ASCO, we saw data from the single arm Keynote 224 data a subset of patients who had got pembrolizumab frontline. Again, an uncontrolled study. And again, similarly, the survival was 17 months. So very similar data that single agent checkpoint inhibitors are active, we just don't have level one evidence. And there's ongoing studies, a lot of exciting combinations. Those include dual inhibitors of two checkpoints together, such as Dervalumab and Tremulumab, which is PD-L1 and CTLA-4 combinations, or CheckMate 90W, which is NEVO and IPI, and that's PD-1 and Tremulumab. CTLA-4 combo, and some combinations of immunotherapy and TKIs, such as atezolizumab and cabizantinib, which is already approved in second line CABO, and LEAP-002, which is pembrolizumab and linvantinib. So we've seen some early phase data with these combinations. This study from ASCO of last year looked at tremilumab and dervalumab in various arms looking at different dosing strategies or single agents versus combinations. What's very interesting is this dosing here with a single dose of TREMIE at 300 plus DERVALUMAB gave an overall response rate of 24% in second line with a duration of response that still had not been reached and a median survival of just under 19 months in the second line population with a tolerable safety profile. And this regimen is being compared to Seraftib in the Himalayas study, and we're waiting for those results. There's also several early stage studies with this combination, in combination with TACE or after resection or curative RFA. Looking at the study designs here, you see Himalaya with Derva versus Derva-Treme and Serafnib, and Checkmate 90W with Nevo-IPPE versus Serafnib or Lenvantinib. And we should comment that Nevo-IPPE itself is approved now in the United States for second line. It has accelerated approval, and it is based on response rates of about 30%, and that is what's driving this confirmatory study front line. Also in front line, we have the combination of Linvantinib and Pembro. Now Linvantinib is a multikinase inhibitor. It's approved front line based on non-inferiority to serafinib. And in this study published in JCO last year, we saw response rates, if you look at conventional resist of 36%, median duration of response is over a year. And disease control rate of 88%. And this is very exciting data, I would argue. Median survival was 22 months. And again, this is a single-arm frontline study, but not too similar from the single-arm IAMBRAVE-150 data or a TezOBev data that led to IAMBRAVE-150. And this study has completed accrual and we're waiting for results. And here you see the design of LEAP-002, which is LEN and PEMRO versus LEN. This is a placebo-controlled study for the Pemrolizumab component. And COSMIC-312 is looking at cabizantinib, the VEGF receptor inhibitor, Met and Axel inhibitor, in combination with the tezolizumab versus CABO or serafinib, which is really the control arm here. We don't have a lot of data on this combination in the public domain, but needless to say, many of the TKIs in combination with PD-L1 inhibitors or PD-1 inhibitors are showing very exciting responses. Now, we can't ignore the fact that we have several drugs available at progression. If we look at the I.O. approvals, as mentioned, NEVO and Pembro have approval, accelerated approval, as single agents. And NEVO and IPPE now has an approval as of last year, 2020. for accelerated approval after prior serafinib. And you see the response rates go up with the combination. There is more toxicity with the combination, about 50% in the combination in the phase 1b study actually needed steroids for immune-related adverse events. But needless to say, these are options for patients, and I think specifically for patients who do not get IO in the frontline setting. And also looking at second line approved TKIs. Regorafnib was the first drug approved since serafinib, and it was approved for patients who had tolerated serafinib. It was approved in second line based on an overall survival benefit versus placebo, a hazard ratio of 0.63. Similarly, cabizantinib was looked at versus serafinib or after serafinib progression. And interestingly, the Celestial study also had about 25% of patients who were third line. And again, an improvement in overall survival with a hazard ratio that's consistent, I would say, with the other drugs in the space, which also includes ramucirumab. the anti-VEGF antibody. So this is a monoclonal antibody to the VEGF receptor. This differs from Bevacizumab, which is to the VEGF ligand. And in this study, patients had to have an elevated alpha-beta protein in order to be enrolled. So this is a biomarker-selected cohort where we saw has a ratio of 0.69 for this cohort. So a risk reduction for death in this population of patients who have a worse prognosis based on the high AFP. And certainly the AE profiles of the TKIs are fairly similar. hypertension, Hanford Skin Syndrome, diarrhea, and anorexia. Ramicerumab, as a monoclonal antibody, has a little cleaner side-of-the-heck profile and really is related to its VEGF receptor engagement. And we've seen things such as hypertension, proteinuria, and some fluid retention. So before we go on to the next case, I see there's some questions coming in from the audience. And Matt, maybe this is a good one for you. As we talk about these newer combinations that are more active, how do you see them affecting where we stop LRT? You commented that before we had serafinib, LRT kind of filled a void. Then we had Serafinib, which improved survival, but not a high response rate. And now we have a new generation of drugs that seem more active.

And it's a great question. But I think it's not really stopping LRT because local regional therapy has occurred. It's whether you do it again. It's a different metric now. It's a different equation because if there wasn't anything else, then you would do the same thing. You'd pound your head against the wall again because it's the only wall you could pound on. Now it's not. Now if you've done something and it either it wasn't completely successful or it recurred afterward, you have to evaluate the patient at that moment and determine what's the best thing to do at that time. We don't know always what that is, but these drugs work. And so they should be actively considered rather than doing the same thing you already did that didn't work, that may have worked at one point, but isn't working now.

Yeah, I think that's a good way to put it. And I would also remind the audience that, you know, to have advanced liver cancer or liver cancer that's a candidate for systemic treatment, you don't necessarily need to have extra hepatic disease, right? Bulky progressive disease in the liver post-local regional therapy would be something to consider for systemic treatment. Laura, you're a hepatologist. You're very involved in the management of liver cancer and this idea of transplant. What about this idea of IO agents and downstaging? What are your thoughts and concerns?

So it's something we have started thinking about. Certainly there are people who will have a very robust response and a sustained response and should those patients be considered for transplant in the context that there's never been concern for extra hepatic spread. I think we need some more safety data. There have been case reports of patients undergoing transplant after receiving an IO and subsequently losing their graft very quickly. There is a recent publication, which was a letter to the editor that comes from the Mount Sinai group where they had a total of nine patients of which eight had received transplant within four weeks of their last IO. And they've only had one patient with mild rejection and no one has lost their graft. So I think we need to start thinking about it, but we need to do it safely. These grafts are very precious and we need to make sure that we are not putting patients at at risk of a more quicker demise as a result of graft failure due to a severe rejection.

Yeah, and I think we need to characterize who those patients are, right? I mean, I'm at a large transplant center, all of us are, and my sense is most patients can be controlled with local regional treatment, right? And who are those patients, to the discussion before, but here we're looking at curative intent, who are those patients who we stop LRT pre-transplant and say, look, you're still a transplant candidate, but now you need systemic treatment, right? What's their... clinical course look like? That I think we need to clearly define in order to target them. And it relates to our next question about safety. How does post-transplant status affect choice of drug? And I think this is referring to patients who have recurrent liver cancer after transplant. And I think many of us think that the TKIs are probably the first choice. Certainly the most safety data is with Seraphinib. Whether or not these drugs work the same post-transplant, we don't have those data sets. you know, assuming they're not going to die of liver failure, we would offer these patients some treatment. And to Laura's point, I think now in the post-transplant setting, we need to be very careful with IO because, you know, You know, the question is, are we hitting the brakes and the accelerator at the same time? Meaning, you know, patients are on immunosuppression, and then we want to give them drugs that activate their immune system, right? So maybe one of the first things is just to decrease the immunosuppression, see how they do. But I think IO in this setting is right now contraindicated. So for the sake of time, and there are good questions coming in, I think we will transition back to you, Matt, with your second case.

reference_conclusion: Following initial radioembolization as bridge therapy with the goal of transplantation, interval progression to multifocal bilobar hepatocellular carcinoma with rising AFP was recognized as advanced disease for which repeat locoregional therapy was not favored if prior treatment was no longer effective. Systemic therapy should be actively considered, with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab regarded as the preferred first-line regimen for eligible patients. Endoscopic evaluation for varices is required before initiation of bevacizumab; high-risk varices should be banded, with bevacizumab started after an interval of approximately 1–2 weeks.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 61-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Liver nodules identified on surveillance ultrasound in the setting of cirrhosis.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal infiltrative hepatocellular carcinoma involving the right hepatic lobe and lower liver, in the setting of cirrhosis secondary to previously treated hepatitis C virus infection with sustained virologic response. Child-Pugh class A6 liver function.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology data were available.

[ imaging findings ]: Surveillance ultrasound demonstrated liver nodules. Contrast-enhanced CT showed diagnostic imaging appearance of hepatocellular carcinoma with two measurable nodules in the right lobe. Additional lower hepatic lesions included nodules and confluent irregular infiltrative disease; the dominant infiltrative mass measured slightly greater than 5 cm. No portal vein tumor involvement was identified; the main portal vein, right portal vein, and segmental branches were patent and free of disease. Extensive gastroesophageal varices were present. No extrahepatic spread was described.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Platelet count 106. INR normal. Sodium normal. Creatinine normal. Alkaline phosphatase 99. ALT 35. AST 63. Bilirubin at the upper limit of normal. Albumin 3.5 g/dL. Iron deficiency anemia was present.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Hepatitis C virus infection had been treated successfully, with sustained virologic response. The patient had been taking iron supplementation for iron deficiency anemia. No prior cancer-directed therapy was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Untreated multifocal intrahepatic disease without documented vascular invasion or extrahepatic metastases. Preserved liver function with Child-Pugh A6 cirrhosis.

[ other clinical data ]: Cirrhosis was present. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable apart from obesity and mild hypertension. Past medical history was otherwise not significant.

reference_discussion.text: Thanks, Rich, and be interested to hear what people have to say sincerely, given that this gentleman just presented to me last week, and so his treatment plan isn't immediately set upon. He's a 61-year-old man with cirrhosis. His HCV is cured. He has a sustained viral response. He's otherwise totally healthy, save for iron deficiency anemia, for which he takes iron supplements. No significant past medical history. He's heavy, but other than that, and mildly hypertensive, but otherwise fine on physical exam. He has a platelet count of 106, his INR is normal, his sodium is normal, his creatinine is normal, his ALKFOS is 99, AST, excuse me, ALT35, AST63, bilirubin at the upper end of normal, and his albumin at the just below normal. So with an albumin of 3.5, he has a Child's Pew A6. If it were 3.6, he'd be a Child's Pew A5. So with that presentation as normal, he was found on surveillance ultrasound again to have liver nodules. So we obtained a CT and he has a diagnostic appearance. Here are two measurable nodules in his right lobe. But unfortunately for him, he also has varices and more nodules and Down lower in his liver, he has not only nodules, but confluent disease, irregular infiltrative. So the mass there is measured a little over five centimeters. And I think it's best shown on this coronal scan, showing a nodule up in the top of his liver, and then that irregular confluent infiltrative stuff at the bottom. Of note, his portal vein is completely free of disease. I show one picture with the main portal, but his right and segmental branches looked clear as well. But he does have extensive varices, as we have seen previously. This time, gastroesophageal varices. So as I said, we've discussed what we plan to do with him, but I'd be interested to know what you guys think is the appropriate next step for him.

So I'll take a stab at that. For one, he's iron deficient, and we want to know why, right? Hopefully, he doesn't have varices, but he'd have to have an endoscopy. Because to me, this patient is like the patient we talked about before. They don't have extrapatic spread. They have an ugly-looking, infiltrative, multifocal tumor in the liver. And I think this would be a great candidate for systemic treatment if they didn't have varices, a tezobev, but obviously a clinical trial might be appropriate as well if their physiology otherwise allows.
Thanks, Rich. Laura, how would you handle it? What do you suggest is the next step?

So similarly, I would want to get this patient scheduled for an endoscopy in a timely fashion, because if you are considering vasocizumab, you're going to potentially need to scope this person more than once, especially if they have large varices, which may be the case based on what we're seeing on the imaging, but not necessarily when you may not see that he's not risen to the surface of the esophagus yet. And also would want to consider, does this person meet a clinical trial that's available, given that they have preserved liver function?

Thanks. And both of you mentioned clinical trials, and I'll tell you that that's what we're hoping to get him into, a trial of looking at taste plus or minus systemic therapy. But that's just one of many trials. Any of you consider any other trials that you might want to enroll in?

Yeah, like there's studies now that are building on Atezobev as frontline, right? Atezobev plus a new drug. You know, The benchmark of 19.2 months now in advanced disease is quite high. And if you look at this patient who does not have extropatic spread, does not have vascular invasion, that subgroup of patients with a tezobev even has a survival beyond that as a subgroup. you know, systemic treatments alone would be a very reasonable option for this patient. Again, if you have a trial with LRT, that's great. I would say if they're not in the study, I throw it back at you, Matt, would you still give them LRT and systemic treatment or outside of a study?

We're gonna look at trials first, and then it is a question. It's about his preferences and ours. Local regional therapy is pretty well tolerated. So I don't think we'd be putting him at risk, and it might be helpful. I can't state that it would. The combination is better. That's why we need to study it. But I think we've got pretty great responses with radioembolization, even with infiltrative disease. So I think that is not an unreasonable thing to consider.
And I think, Laura, you're gonna take us through some of the combination stuff, building on that case.

reference_conclusion: The agreed next step is prompt upper endoscopic evaluation to assess the cause of iron deficiency and to evaluate for gastroesophageal varices, particularly if bevacizumab-containing therapy is being considered. The patient is considered an appropriate candidate for frontline systemic therapy with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab if variceal assessment permits, and clinical trial enrollment is preferred if eligible. If no suitable trial is available, locoregional therapy such as radioembolization may be considered in conjunction with systemic treatment, given preserved liver function and liver-confined multifocal infiltrative disease without vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread.

Because to me, this patient is like the patient we talked about before. They don't have extrapatic spread. They have an ugly-looking, infiltrative, multifocal tumor in the liver. And I think this would be a great candidate for systemic treatment if they didn't have varices, a tezobev, but obviously a clinical trial might be appropriate as well if their physiology otherwise allows. [...] So similarly, I would want to get this patient scheduled for an endoscopy in a timely fashion, because if you are considering vasocizumab, you're going to potentially need to scope this person more than once, especially if they have large varices [...] And also would want to consider, does this person meet a clinical trial that's available, given that they have preserved liver function? case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 26-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Four weeks of right neck swelling.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with bulky locoregional nodal metastases. Structural distant metastatic disease to the lungs was present.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial needle biopsy was positive for papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Core biopsy identified a RET fusion–positive papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Outside ultrasound demonstrated a 3.3 cm right thyroid nodule and an approximately 11.5 cm right neck mass described as a group of matted nodes.  
- Physical examination showed right thyroid bed fullness and a large oblong right neck mass extending from just below the ear inferiorly into the neck.  
- Flexible fiberoptic endoscopy showed normal voice and normal vocal cord motion.  
- CT neck showed diffuse calcifications in the enlarged thyroid; an approximately 12 cm group of matted right cervical lymph nodes; additional left neck nodes; and bilateral central compartment nodes.  
- CT demonstrated nodal disease extending from the lateral neck into the central neck, with tumor abutting the vertebral artery; additional potential interfaces involved the sternocleidomastoid muscle and jugular vein.  
- Chest CT demonstrated pulmonary metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Core biopsy molecular testing identified CCDC6-RET fusion (RET-PTC1).

[ current disease status ]:  
- Papillary thyroid carcinoma with bulky right cervical nodal disease extending from the lateral neck into the central neck.  
- Tumor abutted the vertebral artery, with additional potential interfaces involving the sternocleidomastoid muscle and jugular vein.  
- Structural distant pulmonary metastatic disease was present on chest CT.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The patient had otherwise been healthy.  
- Examination outside the neck was negative.
