reference_discussion.text: Yes, hi, I'm Greg Randolph. I'm an otolaryngologist at Mass Eye and Ear and Mass General, and I'm very honored. I want to thank Mark and thank Mike for putting this wonderful program together. And so this will be a thyroid tumor board. I appreciate also Peter Sadow, our expert pathologist. He really helped a lot with many of the slides here relating to pathology. And it's really my honor to be here with such a elite group of panelists. So we're going to do three cases, and I'm going to just kind of present the case and then Mike will take it and moderate through the panel. So the first one is a case number one, which is a case of local regionally advanced DTC. I wanna first think that when I say these are my cases, they're really our cases. We have a very, very large group of people. And I think all of us would admit that all of our activity research and otherwise is really multi-pronged and based on all of our colleagues that we work together. This is a sampling of all of the people that help to treat these patients and research the problems that these patients present. So this is a lovely 26 year old woman who came up from North I think from New Hampshire or so and she had a four weeks of right neck swelling, otherwise completely healthy. She had a outside ultrasound when she came down that showed a 3.3 centimeter right thyroid nodule and an 11.5 centimeter something or other in her neck, a group of matted nodes, they thought perhaps, and she had a needle biopsy that was positive for PTC, and then it was referred to our practice. So, Mike?

Yeah, so when we have these, we'll start with Eric, and then we'll go to Mark. Eric, sort of, what initial thoughts when you're seeing this and sort of, you know, what are you thinking about as we're sort of thinking out loud here a little bit?

I didn't have the ultrasound. I mean, I'd say, you know, acute onset of enlargement of the anterior neck. And I'd be wondering, is there a cyst that bled? Is there some maybe even de Quervin's thyroiditis that's showing kind of a mass? Those are more common issues that would kind of acutely grow. I will say the ultrasound here, you know, that shows a very large lymph node. So that is not a subtle, a small thing. And that kind of changes everything. And I would try and get a handle on whether the patient really feels there's been that rapid of growth, and that would lead to really concern for a very aggressive process.

Yeah. Now, Mark, this, you know, it's a tumor board. So, we all know this is going to be thyroid, but you don't always know that when people walk in your door, right? So, are there, what else is going through your mind when you're looking at this beyond just the sort of typical thyroid cancer stuff, Mark?

Thanks, Mike. So, yeah, I think, as Eric mentioned, I mean, I think if you didn't have the, you know, the ultrasound and the biopsy, you would be looking at the possibility of some type of benign you know, thyroiditis, of course, once you see sort of the enlargement of the significant enlargement of these lymph nodes, you're not thinking that anymore. But the other thing in this age group, I mean, lymphoma, of course, would be in your differential. So, you'd be asking the patient if they have had fevers, night sweats, weight loss, those types of things.
Okay. And Greg, tell us about your physical exam now when they got to you.

Yeah, so we have a right thyroid bed fullness, she's a fairly thin person and you can feel it feel felt like I remember it felt like a banana in her neck, there was this oblong ovoid. mass that started just below her ear and extended downward into the neck. There was some lobulation to it, but it felt like one large mass. We examined her otherwise negative, and her voice and vocal cord motion were normal on flexible fibro-optic endoscopy. And so then the next question is, what sort of imaging would you get? She had had an outside ultrasound, but In these sorts of patients, I really never ever rely on outside imaging, especially when the findings are quite extreme on exam. I worry about the accuracy and cuts of the CAT scan and so forth. So these are usually people who get, you know, clean slate new imaging here. But what would everyone, Mike, what would you think about imaging ultrasound alone? What else? Anything?

Yeah. So, I mean, I think when you, there's very little question when we have these big, lots of lymph nodes in the neck and big masses, we're going to go to imaging beyond ultrasound, right? So, we've all seen ultrasound underrepresented that. To Dr. Ghassandi, in some patients, some centers go to MRI with contrast, other folks do CT with contrast. It seems to be very kind of center and physician specific. Is there any reason to pick one versus the other when we're looking at neck and lymph nodes in the neck?

I prefer CT. It's quicker. most patients cannot stay in the scanner for that long. MRI scanners are longer. The second thing is that most of the lymph nodes for thyroid disease are lower in the neck. So that's when patients are breathing and you get a lot of artifact, particularly from shoulders and breathing by the thoracic inlet. So evaluation of central compartment is much harder, evaluation of level five and four, lateral compartment, neck nodes are much harder. I prefer CT. In addition, the biggest challenge with ultrasound is that you will never be able to evaluate a lateral retrofringal lymph node. So that's why, especially with someone with such bulky disease, which if you don't know the first diagnosis without a biopsy in this age group with lymphoma, you have to consider lateral retrofringal nodal disease. I would go to a CT. Easy, low radiation these days with the new equipment.

Yeah. Dr. Erkin, Dr. Shaha, the young surgeon that I work with over here, he loves CT scans with contrast. That's generally what we do. It seems like you order a lot of MRIs in this setting. Am I sort of dreaming that up or do you have a preference there, Mark?

No, I would agree with Dr. Versandi. Obviously, this question of an iodine load from the contrast, but that really is not something that we pay much attention. The value added is significantly outweighs the delay in RAI.

Dr. Alexander, should we be thinking about anything beyond the neck? We're all focused on the neck with cross-sectional imaging in the neck to guide the surgery. Chest, anything else that you'd be doing? I think so.

I mean just putting this in perspective, if we are dealing with thyroid cancer, I think we had a biopsy or we certainly would get one if we didn't. When you have this amount of disease, you'd be worried about distant disease as well. So you're kind of thinking to yourself, you have to address, diagnose what's going on in the neck. You'd be worried at the rapidity of growth potentially, but you do want to look at the lungs.

Dr. Zeferio, you know, a lot of times I'll see people just operate off the neck and they'll miss these upper mediastinal lymph nodes when somebody has a ton of disease in the neck like this. So, in your cross-sexual imaging, do you do neck and chest or does your neck CT see far enough down to the upper mediastinum? How do you think about that, Mark?

Thanks, Mike. So, yeah, typically the neck CTs do go down and get the superior mediastinum anyway, but we would definitely get a CT neck and chest on this patient as described, just because this demographic of patient would suggest she's in her mid-20s, that this is probably like a pediatric thyroid cancer almost that may have been there for years and even decades and grown over that time. Those patients, in addition to bulky lymph node disease, often have tiny little lung nodules, you know, representing metastasis, and these aren't particularly threatening. They grow, you know, slowly over the years, but they're typically there, and it's a good baseline to have for the patient.

I just want to mention something, emphasize something that Dr. Khorsandi said, which I think is really important, that there's always this debate, MR versus CAT scan. It's all about, you know, cross-sectional imaging is what we want, but that blurring, that MR artifact from breathing in the neck base, that's a very big ticket item, as is the readability and speed of CT scan to quickly have that information, have it read by the surgeons who are going to be bringing the patient to the OR. Those are really good points that are subtle, but I think trump the MRI scan in the setting of getting a quick and easily read CAT scan were very good points. Yeah.

Dr. Rossley, before we move on to look at the imaging, 26-year-old papillary thyroid cancer at some point, is there any role for other nuclear medicine imaging here, or we're just starting down the pathway with the CT scans as you're thinking about this one, Monica?

I don't think a preoperative assessment with nuclear medicine is necessary. You might change your mind after the operation when you've got the surgeon's findings in the operation and the histology, but we don't do any preoperative scanning.
Awesome. Thanks. All right, Greg, let's go ahead and look at it.

We got, I'll show you the image in a second, the CT scan showed diffuse calcifications in the enlarged thyroid, the 12 centimeter a group of matted nodes on the right, some left neck nodes and bilateral central compartment nodes. And the way we're thinking about this now, and I'd be interested in both Mark's commentary on this, is with neoadjuvant trials now, we think of like, where is this tumor going to beat me? That is, what is a potential R2 interface based on this imaging. And so that is where might I leave gross disease if I don't take something outside of the thyroid. That's very helpful for me as I summarize the CAT scan findings and so here, it looked to me like the right RLN, the right trachea, right straps, and that was in terms of potential R2 interfaces relative to the primary in the right thyroid? And then where might this large nodal mass give me problems with an R2 interface? And that was SCM, jugular, and vertebral artery. And so SCM, no problem at all. Jugular vein, no problem at all. Vertebral artery, that's an issue. So I think this is a helpful way of looking at it. I'll show you the images in a second. In terms of ultrasound, I was trying to force the discussion that we've already had, and we obtained it, and it added nothing. Chest CT scan Y, we did get that. And as Mark outlined, I mean, the mediastinum, I think, is well evaluated by our NET-CAT scan. Mary Beth Kinane does a great job with that. But it's really, you want to get more of a robust local regional evaluation. Lori always appreciates this information with the patient coming in. Maybe she can comment on what is this information important for her to have right out of the gate.

But before you move on, I really like this concept of R2 interface. Now, most of the endocrinologists and most of us deal with, we know TNM, but we don't know the R. Can you say just in a second what you mean by that R2?

Yeah, R0, these are the three types of surgical resections. R0 means all tumor macroscopic and microscopic has been resected. R1 means all gross disease has been resected, but there's a microscopic positive margin. And R2 means you cut across gross disease. There's gross disease left in the neck.
So, you're trying to make that decision up front.

These are areas that you would potentially have to leave gross disease, which would be... Or configure a surgery that would encompass that R2 interface. Like, where are the extrathyroidal extension frontiers? Possibly, based on imaging. And, you know, with a good forensic evaluation of your imaging, you can do this.

Okay, so let's, let's look at his imaging, and then look at the molecular testing, because somebody's already mentioned sort of neoadjuvant stuff. And then let's go from there. So what are we looking at?

So this is this is the lateral neck node. So you know, in general, and I'd be interested in Mark, Erkin and Zeferio commenting on, you know, generally, these are pushing nodes, they're keeping everything away, you can often dissect them away from even a jugular vein that's strapped, splayed over them. But you see, in the coronal images, you see, this is not the simple straightforward set of nodes, there's a finger of this group of matted nodes that is extending lateral to the subclavian common carotid bifurcation, and then a finger of disease that is extending into the central neck, and that's where I thought the vertebral artery was being abutted by this tumor. This is not a typical pattern of extension, but when tumor starts to extend dorsally in the neck base, you have to think about things like phrenic and vertebral artery that you typically don't have to worry about for routine thyroid nodal distribution. This also kind of helps to confuse the nomenclature of the neck locations, central versus lateral, because the nodal disease is not in any way respecting that. It's jumping the fence and extending. This is all one group of nodes that will bring you from the lateral neck into the central neck. I'll show these are the other sets of images here with the pulmonary images. And so then we did not automatically bring her to surgery because of that long list of potential R2 interfaces. And so a test was ordered and that would be the next step, but I'll stop for discussion of imaging.

Dr. Wirth, come in here for me for a second. So normally, we're thinking about molecular testing and somatic testing. Normally, it's a long ways down the road to get you involved in it. But now, what's the setting in this pre-op thing we should be thinking about the molecular testing, Lori?

Well, exactly a case like this, although this case is so dramatic. It's kind of a no brainer, but I think that idea of, you know, when the when the surgeon is going to be leaving our to disease behind. I think we're getting to the point where we might want to begin doing something about that in the neoadjuvant setting. Then also, this woman is only 26 years old. I'd be jumping all over Greg to do a core needle biopsy so that we could do molecular testing. I'd be particularly excited about the potential for finding an actionable fusion in this young adult. The pediatric and young adult patients with PTC are much more likely to harbor RET fusions, ENTREC fusions. We even see ALK fusions and rarely ROS1 fusions. You can't do that molecular testing well off of an FNA. A core needle biopsy in this patient would be quite easy to do. It's definitely the right next step to see if we can identify something actionable.

I just want to comment on something subtly that Lori said, which relates in part to something that Mark Zufferio implied, that as you get a multidisciplinary evaluation of this, like I've learned from Peter, learned from Lori, so we're dealing with a young patient, you know, you think about solid variant, you think about pediatric kind of areas like Mark was implying, and so then With Peter and Lori's input, you start to think about this could be a fusion patient, you know, like this is something that you kind of seeing the headlights come down you on the road, but this is really an idea that is generated by a group of people really focused on this a multidisciplinary group.
All right, let's show Lori the somatic testing, and then we'll come to Mark to see where he's going to use that.

And that is exactly what we did. We brought together the group in our Mass General Mass Eye Near Advanced Thyroid Cancer Clinic that Lori and Peter participate in, and a core biopsy was done. And this is the fusion. What I know about this fusion, you could fit on the head of a pin comfortably. And so I'll let Peter or Lori comment on this.
If in doubt, always go to Lori. Lori, you ordered the test. Is this what you were looking for?

I told you so. Actually, I mean, obviously, I know the patient, but this is exactly what we'd be thinking about. This is a RET-PTC1 in the older nomenclature fusion or a CCDC6 RET gene fusion. This is the most common RET gene fusion that we see. The CCDC6 is the five prime fusion partner to the RET part of the gene that contains the intracellular business end or kinase domain of RET. And this fusion leads to constitutive activation of the RET kinase. So that's a driver alteration. And because it's an oncogenic kinase, it should be druggable. Several years ago, there were a couple of drugs that were designed to potently and specifically inhibit the activated Rett kinases that can be activated by these gene fusions in papillary thyroid cancer, also in a small subset of non-small cell lung carcinomas, and then also the drugs were designed to inhibit the Rett mutations that we see in medullary thyroid cancer.
Perfect. Okay, Greg, in the interest of time, take me through the clinical course and then stop once you get the surgery done. And then we'll have Mark comment on his experience with this as well.

Very good. So patient was started on selprocatenib, one of the two new RET inhibitor agents. She basically tolerated this one pill a day incredibly well. In fact, when I said, so how was the medicine? She goes, well, the minute I took it, it started shrinking down my neck disease. And I said, so What about the complications? Were there problems with this? She goes, well, to be honest with you, I didn't know I was on the medicine. They told me right before surgery that my liver function tests went up a little bit, but I didn't really know that I was on the medicine. So this was incredibly well tolerated. This is the before and after coronal images that she had after four months on neoadjuvant cell percatenib, no more R2 interface in the SCM, just in terms of the nodal mass, no more R2 interface with the jugular vein, no more R2 interface with the vertebral artery. This improves my mood considerably as I bring this young woman to the OR. Again, you still have nodal disease, but this is the result. We divide sometimes for more complicated patients, we'll stage the surgery. She had initially a right lateral neck dissection. These are the images that you see there, and then followed by a total thyroidectomy. The right neck dissection showed 10 of 37 nodes. Peter will talk about the path in just a second. We have some images. Then the total thyroidectomy showed this to be right lobe about five centimeters, diffuse sclerosing. Eight of 46 nodes in the central and left lateral neck. And these nodes, just at surgery the and Mark and probably Mark so Pharaoh can comment on this, but these nodes, when we dissected them look like someone had taken a baseball back to them. They were shrunken and hemorrhagic, and they looked beat up. There was some mild desmoplastic reaction around them, but not ponderous. But they had clearly shrunken. There was this rind of desmoplastic reaction around them, but not too, too difficult to dissect. But the nodes themselves looked hemorrhagic and beat up. And so again, the pathology confirmed what we knew based on the core. And Peter, I'll go through these slides as you tell me to here.

Yep. Hold on a second for me. Before we do the path. Dr. Cefario, give me sort of some 30,000 feet observations here. So this is cell per cat nib, it's a red fusion. How long do you generally leave these folks on before you take them to surgery? How much shrinkage do you want to see before you take them to surgery just from a, you know, practical standpoint, Mark?

Thanks, Mike. So yeah, this is a classic, great example of a very, I think, wise use of neoadjuvant RET-specific inhibitors, sulfurcatinib in this case. And yeah, we do have a trial looking at this where ret-altered thyroid cancers, and we've enrolled about 14 patients on that trial, most of which are medullaries, but there's been about four ret-fusion patients we've enrolled in that trial, and they've all been patients like this who were essentially patients in their 20s, have a pediatric-type thyroid cancer presentation with bulky lymphadenopathy. often little lung nodules and they end up having a ret fusion. I completely agree with Greg. From that imaging, it appears that certainly neoadjuvant therapy could help with the R2 interfaces especially. Often, as I think Dr. Randolph mentioned, often these are pushing margins in these types of patients, but you really don't know until you get in there. The last thing you want is to be in a situation where you have to leave gross disease on the recurrent nerve or the vertebral artery or somewhere like that. And so I think this is a great. example of how the R2 interfaces can dictate neoadjuvant therapy. In terms of the timing, in the trial, we typically leave patients on for a maximum of six months. I don't think we have any good data. As Dr. Randolph mentioned, in this case, you typically do see responses in the first month or two. What I've noticed is that the responses are the most dramatic in the first couple of months and then they tend to level off, you know, after that in months three, four, five, and six in terms of the trial. So I think you're at least going to want to leave patients on for two or three months. And, you know, we leave them on up to six months. The other minor point to make is we've had quite a few patients, although these drugs are pretty well tolerated, The issues that we've typically seen and had to dose reduce is due to a lot of patients do have fatigue. That's a very common complaint on the RET inhibitor. Certainly, the increased LFTs were mentioned. Then the other thing that we've seen in a couple of patients is some pancytopenia that we've had to dose reduce for. Those are a few highlights.

Can I just make a comment because I've spoken a lot to Mark and also to your colleague, Rich Wong, both of whom I respect quite a bit about neoadjuvant and how we think about it. And I think for the endocrinologists and oncologists, we're thinking like, so we can shrink the tumor down. So what, what would be the outcomes of this? Like, what are we really trying to do? You know, one would be to say, We will do the same surgery we would have otherwise done but with neoadjuvant therapy, we may get a better margin. That's goal number one. this is an aspirational goal, we may or may not see this, that we may not need to resect that thing that is representing the R2 interface, trachea, esophagus, and I think that will be borne out. Nerve, I'm not so sure about nerve, is linear and gets gummed up in the tumor and that often will still need to come. But trachea and esophagus, I got a feeling we may end up resecting less of those in some circumstances, depending on the degree of invasion that the patient presents with. surface adherence, transmural invasion, there are different degrees.

One quick word of caution. I've had two cases now with neoadjuvant therapy where I had a great response and on treatment, I missed a window and the patient started to progress on treatment. We're still in the nascent stage of this, but just a word of caution.
Very good. Okay, so we're running a little bit long here. I want to look at the slides from Peter, because we're going to talk about adjuvant therapy at several journal clubs going ahead.

I'll pop right through them, Mike. So this is a lymph node. I just wanted to give people a relative lay of the land that where you see those arrows, those blue circles with the purple in the middle, those are germinal centers, which allows us to know it's a lymph node. The asterisk represents where you have viable carcinoma. You'll see some fluffy stuff in the bottom right in white, which those are papillae of metastatic capillary thyroid carcinoma, or you can see architecturally. And then the giant end in the middle is necrosis, and this is actually a response to the drug. Next slide, Greg. This is higher power, and you can just see those areas more closely. Next one, Greg. This is what I wanted to show you. This is actually in the thyroid proper. This is diffuse sclerosing variant of capillary thyroid carcinoma. And I wanted to point out to everyone, just so you can get a great, perfect view of it, those pink bands are what is called sclerosis. Oftentimes there's actually no nodule seen at all in the thyroid because the thyroid's diffusely involved, you don't see a mass. So you could look and see a normal thyroid and then actually see lymphadenopathy, especially in young patients. So the one thing that actually, we could diagnose the fusion based on looking at the slide without actually even needing molecular diagnostics, And the reason we can do that is all those tiny little microcalcifications that you see, which are represented here by me before I became exhausted, the yellow arrowheads, are all pointing toward the calcifications, but there's many, many more. And so that's these microsomoma bodies, tiny little calcifications, are diagnostic of diffuse sclerosing variant and further CCDC6 RET fusion. So this is actually a diagnostic look at this. So next slide, Greg. And this is one sort of small papillary area that's left over. And then next slide. This is what I wanted to point out is that you have these areas that are kind of interspersed within normal thyroid. So that's why I say it's sometimes very difficult to even see a proper mass because it is spread evenly throughout the thyroid. And then next slide. And the other thing I want to point out, this is not typical changes that you see in papillary thyroid carcinoma in terms of the nuclei. They're more round, there are fewer grooves, there are barely any intranuclear pseudo-inclusions. This has a different morphology to the tumor. And so although we call them papillary thyroid carcinomas, it really isn't. And in some ways, it's a very specific tumor that's very distinct from what your classic papillary thyroid carcinoma would look like. And like I said, as we learn more about the genetics, as well as the morphology of these tumors, we're able to actually say, by the way, the genetics are going to be this, because this is what the morphology of the tumor looks like, this is the architecture of the tumor, and although it's still currently classified as we speak as a papillary thyroid carcinoma, I honestly feel by the next edition of WHO, we're going to be classifying these tumors in a different way. Okay, I think that should be it for me, Greg.

Awesome. Thanks, Peter. Laurie, finish this one out for me and Monica. I'll go to Monica first. So, we've used the suppercat neb as neoadjuvant, they've done the surgery. Should we leave them on the suppercat neb to try to do the radioactive iodine scan as a re-differentiation thing? way out there. But Monica, what are you sort of thinking about that if you see one of these that has been treated this way?

Well, I haven't actually seen any treated this way, but because I would have thought diffuse sclerosing variant, you don't need to continue re-differentiation, but I see that you guys did. And that's interesting. I have I mean, I've had cases where we didn't have uptake in known mets and then we have done the re-differentiation in a lot older patients. And then we retreated when the scan showed uptake following re-differentiation. So I thought it was interesting that you kept her on the cell percatinib.

Okay. Laurie, talk about that just a little bit, because I'm going to see this exact patient, honest to God, at 10 o'clock this morning. Same case, same mutation, same diffuse sclerosing, cell percatinib, Dr. Shaha whining about the surgery, and I'm going to have to decide whether or not to leave him on for the radioactive iodine. So what do I do, Laurie?

Well, so I think Monica makes a good point that a young patient like this should be responsive to radioiodine. So why do you need it? One of the reasons that we did it was because we knew that she had the structural distant metastases, and because she tolerated sulprocatenib so well, it was a known entity, and we knew that she wouldn't have any difficulty if we gave her sulprocatenib leading into the radioactive iodine treatment. That fusion does activate the MAP kinase cascade, and so it may indeed downregulate the thyroid differentiation genes, TIPO, the sodium iodine symporter expression. There have been a couple of case reports published now in patients with retfusion positive iodine refractory disease, showing that pretreatment with selprocatinib does bring about uptake of radioactive iodine. So that was the rationale for her treatment and so far she's doing quite well.

That's good for her. So I mean, I think that the teaching points in this case is the imaging when we have all that bulky disease up front, making sure we're doing the adduct surgery, recognizing that you do, that this may not be an easy surgery and shrinkage would help with that, which will lead us down the molecular testing, the ideas of using a neoadjuvant and then still that opening if they're on the drug already, can you just go ahead and do the radioactive iodine while they're on drugs? I think those are good. Greg, how about if I do a player trade for you? Let's do case number three. Because I want to be able to talk about case number three. Can I just have you pop ahead?

reference_conclusion: Cross-sectional staging with contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest was obtained, and preoperative nuclear medicine imaging was not pursued. Given the extensive locoregional disease with concern for potential gross residual disease at critical interfaces, a core needle biopsy was performed for molecular profiling and identified a CCDC6-RET fusion. Neoadjuvant selpercatinib was initiated and continued for four months with marked reduction in disease burden, followed by staged surgical management consisting of right lateral neck dissection and subsequent total thyroidectomy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 66-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent Hürthle cell carcinoma in the neck following prior right thyroid lobectomy.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent/metastatic Hürthle cell carcinoma involving the right thyroid bed/central neck, central neck lymph nodes, and multiple intramuscular/subplatysmal soft-tissue nodules in the neck.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial outside pathology after right thyroid lobectomy had been described as Hürthle cell adenoma with microcarcinoma.  
- Needle biopsy of a new right ipsilateral paratracheal mass demonstrated Hürthle cells.  
- Pathology from revision right central neck dissection demonstrated metastatic Hürthle cell carcinoma with several foci in the central neck.  
- Additional excised subcutaneous/intramuscular nodules were identified at revision surgery.  
- Subsequent pathology review described a multinodular remaining thyroid lobe without particularly Hürthle-appearing nodules.  
- Central neck specimen showed a true nodal metastasis with lymphoid rim.  
- Soft-tissue/subcutaneous nodules showed Hürthle cell lesion morphology.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Follow-up imaging identified a new right ipsilateral paratracheal mass.  
- CT at Johns Hopkins demonstrated a 5.3 cm mass with associated nodes.  
- Preoperative ultrasound later showed scattered cervical nodes, including right central neck and left central neck nodes, multiple subcutaneous nodules, and an intact left thyroid lobe.  
- Imaging demonstrated several soft-tissue nodules along the strap muscle/platysma region of the neck.  
- One right neck nodule was described as fairly small.  
- A central neck node on coronal imaging was enlarged and clinically suspicious.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- No patient-specific molecular testing results were reported.  
- Hürthle cell carcinoma biology was described as distinct from other thyroid cancers, with possible HRAS mutations reported in some tumors generally, mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation abnormalities, characteristic mitochondrial DNA mutations involving complex I of the electron transport chain, and widespread chromosomal loss; these were not reported as confirmed findings in this individual patient.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent right thyroid lobectomy at an outside institution; pathology was reported as Hürthle cell adenoma with microcarcinoma.  
- After ipsilateral bed recurrence, underwent revision right central neck dissection at Johns Hopkins.  
- Planned surgery was limited to the right side because of loss of signal from the right recurrent laryngeal nerve intraoperatively.  
- Revision surgery was complicated by right vocal cord paralysis and pneumothorax.  
- Returned to the operating room the following day for bronchoscopy and neck exploration related to pneumothorax; additional excision of soft-tissue/subcutaneous nodules was performed at that time.  
- Disease recurrence had continued over time in the neck, with nodules recurring every 2-3 years by history provided in the case.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Persistent/recurrent locoregional disease was present in the neck.  
- Disease sites included central neck nodal disease and multiple palpable soft-tissue/intramuscular nodules involving the platysma/strap muscle region and sternocleidomastoid region.  
- Left thyroid lobe remained in situ and was nodular.  
- At the time summarized, no confirmed distant metastatic disease had been documented.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history was otherwise reported as unremarkable.  
- Right vocal cord paralysis was present following revision neck surgery.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, so this is a case of peripheral cell carcinoma recurrence. And so a 66-year-old who presented here with recurrent Hercules cell carcinoma. Her initial history started back at Hopkins, and this was no other past medical history. Right lobectomy at an outside institution. This was described as a right lobectomy. It was described as a Hercules cell adenoma and a microcarcinoma. In follow up then, a number of years later, a new right ipsilateral paratracheal mass was identified needle biopsy was done of that recurrent ipsilateral mass and it showed purple cells and so the patient went. from that outside right lobectomy with ipsilateral bed recurrence to Hopkins had CT scanning there. The mass was then 5.3 centimeters with nodes. Again, a little disconnect, the past history was benign herthal cell adenoma, at least by history. Now at Hopkins with recurrence.
Peter, help me out here. This is metastatic herthal cell adenoma or what's going on here? That's hilarious. I'm giving the pathologist the benefit of the doubt. Come on, you know.
Peter, it's a leading question. Don't you get it?

Yes. So, so, so no. In some ways it is. And we actually talk about this in other diseases in the head and neck. We talk about benign metastasizing, for instance, in women, benign metastasizing leiomyoma. We talk about benign metastasizing pleomorphic adenoma. These are tumors that have a very bland appearance that look exactly like the original lesion in the, in the, in the organ. but they metastasize and they look like for all intents and purposes, you're taking it out of the thigh of the skin and it looks like a thyroid nodule. So, you know, this is what we get. This is what we get with a really well-differentiated tumor. So I think the answer to your question is yes, and yet no. Okay, go ahead, Greg.
Well, that's helpful.
We didn't give him the slides and he didn't charge for that. So you get what you get.

All right, go for it, Greg. So this is the continued history at Hopkins. So now the patient, right lobectomy, right bed recurrence. And so then at Hopkins had a revision right central neck dissection. What they planned wasn't exactly clear, but They did have loss of signal, LOS, on the right from the recurrent laryngeal nerve, and so they only did the right side. Pathology from that right central neck dissection with vocal cord paralysis was metastatic peripheral cell carcinoma, several foci in the central neck, and they also actually found several at that time subcutaneous nodules at that time. There were some problems with the surgery, there was vocal cord paralysis, there was a pneumothorax that occurred. And so the patient was taken back for bronchoscopy and neck exploration. Turns out at that exploration, the next day, there were for pneumothorax, there was an additional excision of subcutaneous nodules. The bottom line is complex surgery with proven recurrence in the right bed, and at that time, at least two subcutaneous nodules identified at that revision surgery.

Dr. Erkin, help me think through this just a little bit. We've presented her at those cells at these tumor boards, it's usually Dr. Wirth involved with distant mets and lung mets and bone mets, and sometimes, you know, big recurrences in the TE. This subcutaneous nodule stuff, help me sort of, what is that, Mark? And how does that sort of frame how you think about the case?

Yeah, I'm sort of remembering a case that we talked about in this forum several tumor boards ago. And I think it's just, we have to think about this as most likely metastatic disease rather than some surgical implant. I have to believe that that's entirely unlikely. And so I think the fact that it says presented in this way has to be a consideration of local metastatic disease.

Monica, let me come to you. On the first case, we weren't doing a lot of upfront or nuclear medicine imaging in the world. In this hurtful cell cancer setting, where are you with like nuclear medicine imaging and PET scan? And how's that going to help us here, Monica?

Well, in an aggressive case like this, PET scan may be useful in assessing extent of disease because this has been proven to be an aggressive disease in this particular patient. So I think it may be useful in this patient.

Lori, a question came up on the last case, I think it's pertinent this case is, in these ones that look are more aggressive or growing more rapidly, when do we need to think about imaging the brain or imaging bones, and you know, not just the neck and chest, right? So what, how do you sort of think about that, Lori?

No, as Monica was speaking about the PET CT, I was thinking, yeah, I would definitely want to do that. With this unusual distribution of disease, then, you know, anything is fair game. and so you could pick up unexpected sites of disease with a PET CT, no problem. And the brain MRI question is a great one. In patients that have been enrolled in the drug cancer treatment clinical trials with advanced DTC, in the last decade, we're seeing about a 10% rate of brain metastasis in these patients. And so that I think is an underappreciated fact. And I think that really doing brain MRIs in patients with iodine refractory DTC should be more of a default in our initial workup of these patients.

Yeah, I agree completely. I was, I was embarrassed many times when we first got these TKs and you guys would image and we'd find asymptomatic that I knew were there for a long time. So I routinely doing these aggressive ones, the bone mats, the lung mats one, you know, not, I don't know what sequence interval I do it, but as part of that initial staging, Eric, Eric, how are you sort of In this case, what are you thinking about now? It's a heart-throat-cell cancer. We're still in the neck. It's coming back. If you're talking to the family, what do you think is going to happen here sequence-wise?

You know, I guess I'm thinking to myself, it's still local right now we don't have evidence of distant disease, I think, from best I've seen, though I'd be worried about that. And you're kind of getting into a scenario here where it continues to come back, locally at least, but repeatedly. And so you're going to be thinking, how can you stop that? What would be the process to try and abate that? You know, maybe a question to Monica as well, which is, is there always, is there any utility in ever thinking about radioactive iodine, acknowledging that for those cell carcinomas are felt to be iodine resistant, but, you know, there's probably a little harm also to a single dose. I would be curious how you think about that, Monica.

Well, I agree. In general, hurdle cell is said not to be great in getting a response to radioactive iodine, but we would give it. We would give at least one dose, but she's still got her left lobe of thyroid in. I know Dr. Randolph has written about giving radioactive iodine with half the thyroid in, but we prefer to have the whole thyroid out before we gave radioactive iodine.

Dr. Zeferio, somebody taught me one time thyroid cancer was always a surgical disease, and we should always let you guys have the chance to cure it and that sort of stuff. When do you start thinking about maybe the role for external beam radiation, somebody like this, you know, how many recurrences, you know, you didn't do the first surgery, so maybe you do a better surgery. So where are you sort of thinking about the role for external beam radiation as we're thinking about a difficult case like this?

Yeah, thanks, Dr. Tuttle. So I think just broadly speaking, and a lot of these ideas have already been mentioned, but you know, this type of, this is a particular pattern of sort of metastatic local regionally aggressive hercules cell cancer that we see biologically aggressive disease, whether it's, you know, related to, you know, metastasis through the blood, the lymphatics, whether it's some type of seeding, but they get these sort of little tiny little tumor nodules that are diffuse in the soft tissues of the neck. And I always counsel patients, you know, when I see this, that it's not really a surgically curable disease. It does not mean that surgery does not have a role. I definitely think surgery has a very important role here. but it's very important to counsel the patients up front that this, I can take out all these little spots that I can see. And oftentimes you get in there and you'll see other little tiny little one to two millimeter nodules in there in the soft tissues that you couldn't even appreciate on a CT or a PET. I do think the PET is very important here because I think that with all this scar tissue in the neck, sometimes the PET can help you appreciate little small nodules. But I think, I think it's very important in these cases, in these patients to look at the long-term gain. So this patient has had this disease for a long time. She's 66 years old. So your goal is really to get her to 76, 86, 90 with the least amount of morbidity. And I think you start to look at, you know, how often you're having to do surgery. So, you know, last surgery was in 2017, you know, perhaps you're about to do another surgery in 2022. That's a five-year interval. So I wouldn't pull the trigger on radiation at this point. I would say I would do it. I would do a surgery. I would clean her out and then I would wait and see. I mean, she's going to have disease that pops up elsewhere in the coming years, but your goal is to get her to sort of outlive the disease and with, with the minimum amount of morbidity. And I would, I would not pull the trigger on radiation at this point.

Can I just ask a question of the view in the group is that one of the reasons I thought this case would be interesting is this is a unique as Mark described, kind of a. a type of pattern of recurrence. It's really within the platysma muscle. These are really strapped. It's not really subcutaneous. It's in the platysma. It's in the SCM. It's intramuscular is really what it is. It happens to be subcutaneous when it's affecting the platysma, but it's a really muscle tropic kind of thing. And I struggle with the idea because you brought up brain metastasis. I think probably the reason you thought about that is that That's a normal thought to think whenever you have a subdermal met, a true subdermal met, because then hematologic lymphatic trains have jumped the tracks. It could be on the tip of your nose, great toe, brain, whatever. But this is an intramuscular local regional, very strange recurrence. I haven't seen any muscular recurrences in other parts of the body. I wanted to have discussion of is this or isn't this different than what we typically regard as a subdermal MET, which is a really bad prognostic thing for most entities.

Yeah. Anecdotally, because I've never let the lack of data slow me down whatsoever. Anecdotally on ones like these, I haven't generally seen them explode out into lungs and bones, even though I've followed some of these guys for five or 10 years, which made me wonder whether it's I don't know whether it's a metastasis or direct invasion, maybe it's lymphatic. Some of these are like, you know, right. You just don't see them in other parts of the skin. It's the area where we were operating and where the tumor was. So I think it's a local phenomenon. I always worry about these guys. I image them all over. And I mean, I've only seen half a dozen of these, so it's not a bunch of them. But, you know, they haven't done that explosive two year, five year course where they met out all over the body. I don't know, Laurie, have you guys seen these? I mean, we may as well do anecdotes while we're here since we don't have a thousand cases. What are you thinking, Laurie?
Oh, I really don't have anything further to add. I think it is such a rare situation.

And the ones you've seen, Mark, I mean, the general pattern has been local control and then recurrence back in other areas in the muscle and the skin three years later, five years later, but not like widespread distant mats, at least early on.

Yeah, I think, yeah, I agree exactly with what you're saying. I think typically, you see the continued local regional recurrence. Eventually, some of these patients do often have distant disease, but it doesn't tend to be this fast growing distant disease that, you know, is immediately life threatening. So I think, again, I don't think surgery is curative here, but I think surgery has a role in sort of just controlling the disease and delaying, you know, the treatment with other, you know, therapies such as systemic therapy and radiation.

Yeah. And I think you can see why we're going to look for distant mets. We probably don't expect to find it. And that's why we're so focused on this local control. So go ahead and Greg, tell us where we are on the case now.
So basically, I'm sorry, go ahead.

Two quick questions. Once that left lobe is out and she goes on to get her next recurrence, would Monica want to do a test whole body scan to assess radioactive iodine sensitivity before addressing recurrent disease? And a follow-up question to Mark Zeferio, what would he need to see in order to pull the trigger on external beam? Where would this lady need to get to to make that decision?

I think having been operated on by expert thyroid surgeon, I'd be happy to give an empiric dose of radioactive iodine in this setting and not do a pretreatment iodine scan because I think it's reasonable to offer her one dose of radioactive iodine. It may or may not work. And I don't think a pretreatment scan would alter my decision to give it or not.

So before we come to Marcus, Greg Randolph, what if I made the case that doing that left lobectomy is more likely to harm this lady than the effectiveness of radioactive iodine? She's got a right cord out already. Right cord's already out, right? So we're talking about, you know, I guess it's probably different if you do this every day of your life and you're the king of recurrent ringer nerves. but if this is being operated on in a regular place where most of these people get operated on, what you're trying to balance is not radioactive iodine is not harmful, but a lobectomy could either damage this lady's nerve or she doesn't really get a lobectomy because everybody's so afraid of the nerve. How do you balance that in this sort of situation?

Yeah, absolutely. That is a very significant concern. And so that's why I took comfort in the multidisciplinary decision-making that we took Part of the driver here was this patient that even though we explained to her look, this is not a subdermal met the your disease is not exploding. That was a hard argument to proffer towards this patient, because her eyes were getting wider and wider every time she felt another nodule in her neck. She wasn't liking that, and she's fairly healthy 60 year old and she did want as Mark had said to get to 80 or 90. And so she was fairly motivated, and we did feel that our AI was something that should be offered to her. And in this setting the morbidity of. completion thyroidectomy was stated as potentially the source of a tracheotomy tube, and she knew that. But we discussed altogether that we thought that having the information, interrogating it from the molecular point of view, and then offering her potentially RAI afterwards was a potential endgame that would allow her to get back on the road and stop having recurrences every two to three years.
Dr. Alexander, this is a nice discussion, but there's no way on this planet radioactivity is going to help this lady, right?

Well, so to put out there, frankly, there's no prospective comparative trial, right? And there's also kind of no clear data saying that it's negative as well. We know it has a low yield. And you just always are asking yourself, what's the smallest fraction of meaningful uptake that could perhaps make a meaningful clinical, you know, next step important? And we don't know, but But we've had seven, I mean, just to kind of put the radiobacterium back on the table, I'm not saying I'm advocating for it in any way in all hercocell carcinomas. I totally get that. But you do have a track record of 70 years of use. And you know it's actually quite a safe thing. And it's likely not going to slow down anything else. So it still is out there in the kind of clinical opportunity landscape.

Also, there were two, in addition to the subcutaneous nodules, there were two central neck nodes that were macroscopic, clinically apparent disease. So there was, we felt a need for surgery because of that reason.

And I think, I mean what we're talking about here is a risk benefit ratio right, what are the risk of the surgery. We understand it's unlikely for this tumor to grab on radioactivity, but if it did, that would potentially be a game changer right so so sometimes yeah and this is to the surgeons in the audience, this is something

We don't take lightly and I never operate on anyone like this unless I've met them for at least three separate appointments at length, one of which was this multidisciplinary visit so that they know like I'm not really crazy about doing this either. There are some problems there's definitely some brick walls here, and we got to think about that. The reason for doing it is this this and this. The downside is this, and let's think about it, but this is not the sort of patient that you push a consent format when you first meet them, you build a relationship, and then generally with time they see that you're thinking carefully and in a sober way about them, and they reach out to you and say, I want to have the surgery.

Great. And I'll come to Mark Pacifico here. I mean, I mean, that's really the key, right? The key is when we have that discussion is radioactive iodine, it's not just no big deal, or that, you know, we give you a little more dry mouth that they need external beam radiation, but no big deal. It's like, but for us to say that, that means that lobe has to be something done with it. So Mark, Mark, we're sort of think through this with me as we're sort of thinking out loud about this risk benefit ratio, and how you, you know, honestly, just present that to the patient.
So I think is the question with regard to external beam radiation therapy?
Yeah. So where do you draw the line at some point?

Yeah. So I really look at two factors primarily, and it's really the rapidity of the recurrence. So when was their last surgery? Was it a year ago or was it five years ago? So that's the first question. How fast is this disease growing? And then the location of the disease. Okay. Is this disease that's, you know, just in the SCM and the platysma and subcutaneous where, you know, I feel like I can go back with another surgery and get that out pretty quickly. Or is this like disease that's in the soft tissues at the bilateral, you know, cricothyroid joints where the nerve is going into the joint where that would be a situation where you may be more likely to consider, you know, radiation therapy if you didn't think you could do another surgery. I think the other, you know, reason why, you know, we don't always pull the trigger, we don't generally pull the trigger with radiation therapy for these is because there's other options. I mean, in addition to surgery, you know, if, especially if the tumor is slow growing enough, you know, this patient's 66, There's also drug therapy options down the road, you know, that could be tried. So these patients typically don't have really targetable mutations, but there's certainly sort of the general Linbatinib and those types of drugs could be used in the future to sort of keep disease at bay and, you know, avoiding sort of the acute toxicity of radiation therapy. So those are a couple of thoughts.

Awesome. Greg let's show do the yes we'll move through the surgery so ultrasound again showed basically some scattered nodes in the neck, including in the right central neck and left central neck, the subcutaneous nodules and then an intact left lobe. This was the right neck nodule, fairly small. This is in the side that is paralyzed. I thought if everything went well with the left, I can go to the right. The bridge is already burnt, no problem. That was not easy to get to, actually. It was quite scarred and under the carotid. But we were able to get that. And then this is showing the coronal left images show several of the subcutaneous nodules. These were really, you look at them, they look like they are on the strap muscles. They were basically in the platysma. They could be felt. And as Mike, you said these were like a string of pearls right along the scar. It's why that happens. You know, I mean, well, you know, if you manipulate tumors, so do you seed the body? Is there some stickiness of the Herthal cell hematologic metastasis that we create by doing a surgery and squeezing the tumor that somehow sticks to the musculature local regionally? But that's what's happening. And here are a couple of other pictures. Here, the left coronal panel is the one of the central neck nodes. And Mark Zaffario and Mark Erkin, I know you look at a lot of CAT scans with a lot of neck nodes. This looks a little peculiar for thyroid cancer, right? It looks a little roundish. It looks a little fluffy. It doesn't look so angry, but it's too big, right? And that's exactly the morphology at surgery. It was this maroon colored, beefy, fleshy, like liver, but more fried.
We have about two minutes left, so get to me.
Okay, yeah.

Here we go. So I just wanted to show you, this is what the thyroid looks like. It's a multinodular thyroid to begin with. And none of these nodules are particularly hurtful. I have a high power view here where you see these dark navy blue nuclei and small micro follicles. All right, next slide. This is the central neck. And I just wanted to show you this central neck because what you can see is on the top left is a metastasis, because you can see a lymphoid rim around it, and then the other negative lymph nodes that are there. So this is a legit metastasis of the central neck. Next. These are the subcutaneous nodules that are present there. This high-power view just shows you normal hurtle cells. This is a normal hurtle cell lesion, which brings back the tautoloid question of the subcutaneous things. Is it a benign adenoma there? And this is the issue that will then bring in Laurie as the go-to, is like, what the hell do you do with this? The reason why Laurie is the hurtle cell professor of oncology is because of the fact that here and at Memorial, we're trying very, very hard to understand the molecular genetics of these hurtful cell tumors, because they're not the classic genetics of other thyroid cancers that we can think about targeting for drugs. They're very, very rich in mitochondria, which is the reason why they're particularly hypoxia sensitive. So the idea that these benign nodules appear in other parts of the body is absolutely curious to me, because if you put a needle in it, it can completely die because of the hypoxia that you're inducing. So they're really, really strange nodules. Sometimes they have HRAS mutations, but the truth is we start seeing they have the oxidative phosphorylation issues. They've got all sorts of things, and they're completely different than any other tumor, which is reminiscent of the fact that My colleague, who Bill Fagwin is sitting next door to me, had a case that he saw in 2011. And then six years later, the patient had a contralateral hurtle cell lesion that metastasized to lymph nodes and got a call from our good friends in Philadelphia who said, oh, I looked at your case from 2011, and that's hurtle cell cancer, too. But it's not. They all these benign appearing things that don't look like anything. No necrosis, no nothing. So, you know, how do we even say, so that's the reason why you want to know your pathologists are completely paranoid about misdiagnosing a hurtful cell carcinoma because they look like these benign things that you're finding underneath the skin. So how do you actually make the diagnosis of cancer? We need molecular markers that we don't have, and we need molecular therapies that we don't have. So Laurie, why don't you close us out and tell us what the hell to do.

Well, I'd consider external radiation because we don't have good drugs for these herthal cell carcinomas yet, but I think we will be getting there. As you mentioned, Peter, you know, it's a very unique entity. These are not subsets of follicular thyroid cancers. There's really unique molecular biology. The Memorial Group and our group took a look at what drives herthocell carcinomas, and we found characteristic mitochondrial DNA mutations in a large proportion of these cancers that are all concentrated in the complex one of the electron transport chain of the mitochondria. There are other mutations that have been found as well. Another really interesting thing is that we found widespread chromosomal loss in herthal cell thyroid cancers. We've been able to develop now some cell lines and animal models. Also, David McFadden at UT Southwestern is working on on these models, and we're working on developing drugs that can leverage these unique molecular drivers of herthal cell carcinoma. Not quite there yet, though.

reference_conclusion: Staging with PET/CT was recommended to define the extent of disease, with brain MRI included in the initial workup given the aggressive, iodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer phenotype and unusual distribution of recurrence. The panel favored operative management for local-regional control, including completion thyroidectomy and resection of clinically apparent recurrent neck disease, recognizing that surgery is not curative but has an important role in disease control. After expert thyroid surgery, an empiric dose of radioactive iodine may be offered without a pretreatment iodine scan. External beam radiation therapy was not recommended at this time and would be reserved for more rapid recurrence or unresectable disease in critical locations.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 26-year-old female; pregnant with second child at time of thyroid cancer diagnosis. She was 10 weeks pregnant at initial specialty evaluation.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable goitre and bilateral palpable thyroid nodules.

[ diagnosis ]: Bilateral papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of both thyroid nodules was malignant (Bethesda category VI).

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Thyroid ultrasound in September 2019 showed bilateral thyroid nodules with thyromegaly.  
- Right thyroid nodule measured 1.7 cm, solid with hypoechoic areas and smooth margins; categorized as TI-RADS 4.  
- Left thyroid nodule measured 3.7 cm, heterogeneous, slightly hypoechoic, with lobulated margins and possible microcalcifications; categorized as TI-RADS 5.  
- Repeat thyroid and neck ultrasound at 10 weeks’ gestation showed grossly stable thyroid nodules and no suspicious cervical lymphadenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Genomic classifier testing performed externally showed BRAF V600E mutation positivity in both nodules.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed bilateral papillary thyroid carcinoma (Bethesda category VI, BRAF V600E positive) in a woman 10 weeks pregnant at initial specialty evaluation, where repeat thyroid and neck ultrasound showed grossly stable thyroid nodules and no suspicious cervical lymphadenopathy.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No symptoms of hoarseness, dysphagia, or shortness of breath were reported at presentation.  
- No history of radiation exposure was reported.  
- Family history was notable for a maternal aunt with papillary thyroid cancer.

reference_conclusion: During pregnancy, the patient was managed with active surveillance rather than immediate surgery, with serial thyroid and neck ultrasonography demonstrating overall stability and no new lymphadenopathy. Following delivery, total thyroidectomy was performed without lymph node dissection because no nodal disease was identified. Postoperatively, thyroid hormone replacement was adjusted to achieve TSH goals, and radioactive iodine was not recommended. Ongoing surveillance with thyroglobulin monitoring and follow-up neck ultrasonography was planned, with reassessment in six months.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 38-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive goiter; persistent elevation of thyroglobulin following thyroid surgery and radioactive iodine therapy.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the thyroid, classical variant, well differentiated.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- October 2017: Subtotal left hemithyroidectomy/lobectomy specimen showed a 6.0 cm encapsulated well-differentiated classical variant papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Capsular invasion was present.  
- Vascular invasion was present in more than four vessels.  
- No lymphatic invasion was identified.  
- No minor extrathyroidal extension was identified.  
- Completion thyroidectomy specimen showed no carcinoma in the remaining lobe.  
- Biopsy of indeterminate cervical lymph nodes showed no lymph node involvement.  
- Biopsy of a left level II lymph node in 2020 was benign.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Thyroid/neck ultrasound after initial surgery showed multiple nodules in the right thyroid lobe and indeterminate level V lymph nodes.  
- CT neck showed small indeterminate lymph nodes.  
- Preoperative CT chest showed no pathologically enlarged mediastinal or hilar lymph nodes; two subcentimeter pulmonary nodules measuring 4 mm and 3 mm were present.  
- CT chest also showed soft tissue attenuation in the anterior mediastinum, favored to represent thymus.  
- CT identified an indeterminate enhancing 1.8 cm hepatic lesion and a lesion in the abdominal wall.  
- MRI abdomen characterized the 1.8 cm hepatic lesion as most consistent with focal nodular hyperplasia; this lesion remained stable on follow-up MRI.  
- Post-therapy radioactive iodine scan after first treatment showed residual uptake in the neck and no radioactive iodine-avid metastatic disease in the lungs or bones.  
- Follow-up neck ultrasound after radioactive iodine showed no worrisome findings in the thyroid bed and no suspicious lymph nodes.  
- Follow-up CT neck and chest with contrast showed no metastatic lymphadenopathy.  
- CT chest demonstrated patchy ground-glass opacities in the right upper lobe; the previously noted small pulmonary nodules were not significantly characterized on that study.  
- Follow-up MRI abdomen showed a stable T2-hyperintense lesion at T11, considered possibly a hemangioma.  
- Subsequent neck ultrasound showed bilateral upper neck level II lymph nodes that were not highly suspicious initially; later, left level II lymph nodes became more prominent.  
- Bone scan showed no evidence of metastatic disease and demonstrated degenerative changes only.  
- A subsequent radioactive iodine treatment was followed by a scan that again showed no evident metastatic uptake.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Preoperative TSH: 1.5.  
- Thyroglobulin before completion thyroidectomy: 158.  
- Thyroglobulin after completion thyroidectomy: 37.  
- August 2019 TSH: 130.  
- Six months after first radioactive iodine therapy, thyroglobulin remained elevated at 26.9.  
- Thyroglobulin values subsequently fluctuated, including values around 70 and 46, without clear correlation to TSH stimulation or suppression.  
- Thyroglobulin was described as not clearly TSH responsive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- October 2017: Subtotal left hemithyroidectomy/lobectomy performed for progressive goiter; surgery had not included total thyroidectomy at that time.  
- Completion thyroidectomy was subsequently performed; no residual carcinoma was found in the remaining lobe.  
- First radioactive iodine therapy: 200 mCi, prepared by thyroid hormone withdrawal. Preparation was described as suboptimal with incomplete adherence to a low-iodine diet, although TSH elevation was adequate for treatment. Post-therapy scan showed residual neck uptake without iodine-avid distant metastatic disease.  
- Second radioactive iodine therapy: 150 mCi. Subsequent scan again did not identify metastatic radioactive iodine uptake.  
- Serial imaging and biopsies did not identify structural metastatic disease.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Persistent biochemical abnormality with elevated thyroglobulin after surgery and two courses of radioactive iodine.  
- No confirmed structural disease in the neck, lungs, bones, liver, or lymph nodes on available imaging and biopsies.  
- Current status was consistent with persistent biochemical evidence of disease without localized structural correlate on available studies.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Initial surgery was complicated by recurrent laryngeal nerve injury/tear during traction on the goiter.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 29-year-old woman. Occupation: attorney. No significant past medical history. No family history of thyroid disease or malignancy was reported. No history of radiation exposure. She lived with her husband and 7-month-old child.

[ chief complaint ]: Asymptomatic neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with bilateral thyroid involvement and bilateral cervical nodal metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Cytology was consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma, with bilateral proven metastatic disease.

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a heavily calcified lesion in the upper pole of the left thyroid lobe, echogenic with marked posterior shadowing. In the right thyroid lobe mid-pole, there was an 8 x 8 mm mixed-echogenicity lesion with an anterior hypoechoic component, posterior echogenic component, and punctate echogenic foci. Ultrasound assessment assigned TI-RADS 4 to the left lobe lesion and TI-RADS 5 to the right lobe lesion. Cystic and septated lymph nodes were present in the central compartment and level IV neck.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck demonstrated a heavily calcified left thyroid lobe nodule and an 8 mm hypodense right thyroid lobe lesion. No vocal cord paralysis was present on imaging, and no definite extrathyroidal extension was initially identified radiographically. Metastatic cervical adenopathy was present in the left central compartment and left lateral neck, including levels II, III, and IV. A central compartment nodal mass extended inferiorly into the superior mediastinum to the level of the aortic arch. On the right, there was a calcified and cystic metastatic right level IV lymph node. Retrospective review described an irregular medial border of the left thyroid lesion, raising concern for extrathyroidal extension.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Fiberoptic laryngoscopic examination before surgery showed normal vocal cord mobility.

[ current disease status ]: Bilateral papillary thyroid carcinoma with bilateral cervical nodal metastases and central compartment nodal extension into the superior mediastinum, with radiographic concern for extrathyroidal extension at the left medial border.

[ other clinical data ]: Physical examination showed diffuse thyroid enlargement, greater on the left than the right, with palpable cervical disease bilaterally. She denied voice change and dysphagia. Preoperative fiberoptic examination confirmed normal vocal cord mobility.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary panel supported definitive surgical management with total thyroidectomy, central neck dissection, and bilateral lateral neck dissections performed in a single operation, with intraoperative neuromonitoring. For the mediastinal extension, resection through a cervical approach was favored, with possible manubrial swing if additional exposure were required; thoracic surgery involvement was not considered necessary. If tumor were found inseparable from a functioning recurrent laryngeal nerve at the cricothyroid joint, the panel discussed prioritizing preservation of the nerve by leaving a small volume of gross residual disease rather than sacrificing the nerve, recognizing the uncertainty of this decision and the anticipated role of postoperative radioactive iodine for classic papillary thyroid carcinoma.

Putting somebody back to sleep again to do this, I don't think serves them well. [...] I would probably try to get rid of it all at once in one sitting. [...] definitely neuromonitoring for this case. [...] Maybe I'm wrong, but I actually wouldn't get a thoracic surgeon in there. If sometimes I do use, I would say, you know, maybe we'll do a manubriatomy. I use a manubrial swing. You can take out the upper part of the manubrium with the clavicular joint and the clavicle, and you can sort of swing the clavicle up and get a little bit more space and get a little bit further down. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 43-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistent cough from September of the preceding year, followed by a rapidly enlarging left posterior cervical neck mass noted by December. She later developed exertional dyspnea and discomfort/pressure from bulky neck disease.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma, hobnail subtype, with extensive cervical and mediastinal nodal metastases, diffuse left lung involvement with a lymphangitic pattern, and subsequent osseous metastasis in the right ninth rib. Disease was metastatic and clinically aggressive at presentation.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsies were obtained from left level III cervical lymphadenopathy and the left thyroid lobe. EBUS-guided biopsy was obtained from mediastinal nodal disease at station 4. Pathology was reported as hobnail subtype of papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- February PET-CT demonstrated extensive bilateral FDG-avid cervical lymphadenopathy, FDG uptake within the thyroid gland, mediastinal nodal involvement, and diffuse left lung involvement described as a lymphangitic pattern. Overall disease burden was large at presentation.  
- MRI was also performed at baseline.  
- Repeat PET-CT approximately 4 weeks later, obtained before systemic therapy because of clinical progression, showed interval progression, including slight increase in neck disease and a newly reported lesion in the right ninth rib. Lung disease had not changed substantially.  
- MRI brain performed before systemic therapy was negative for intracranial metastases.  
- Early response-assessment CT after 6 weeks of systemic therapy showed radiologic stable disease by RECIST.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: ROS1 fusion identified on urgent molecular profiling of tumor tissue.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Entrectinib was started as systemic therapy.  
- Within the first 6 weeks of treatment, she developed a change in baseline cardiac findings requiring cardiology assessment.  
- Symptomatic improvement occurred on treatment: cough resolved and neck pressure reduced significantly.  
- First imaging assessment after 6 weeks showed stable disease by RECIST rather than partial response.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma with persistent but symptomatically improved bulky cervical, mediastinal, pulmonary, and osseous disease while receiving entrectinib. At first on-treatment assessment, disease was radiologically stable.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Performance status was effectively near 0, limited by cough and exertional shortness of breath.  
- On examination at initial oncology review, there was a visible bulky left neck mass with palpable smaller right-sided cervical nodes in levels II-IV.  
- Past medical history was otherwise unremarkable except for COVID-19 infection in January of the same year.  
- She was undergoing IVF treatment when symptoms began.  
- She was taking no regular medications.  
- Family history was not significant.  
- Smoking history was less than 10 pack-years.  
- There was no prior radiation exposure.
