reference_discussion.text: Brilliant. Thank you so much. And again, thank you very much for the invitation to present some cases on this tumor board. It's such a helpful forum and brilliant that we can access it at convenient times around the world as well. So thank you for that. So my name's Kate Newbold and I'm an oncologist in London, UK, and I'm a clinical oncologist, which in our country means that we do both the radiation and systemic therapies and isotope therapies. So that's the background for how I get my patient referrals. So we have three cases to discuss today and I hope they're interesting and I hope they spark some good discussions for everybody. So the first case we'll launch into it. This is a 43 year old lady who previously very well undergoing IVF treatment when she noticed a cough in September of last year. She didn't really take much notice of it as you wouldn't she didn't have any past medical history. But by Christmas she then noticed a lump in the left side of the neck quite posterior on the left side, but this increased over size quite rapidly over the next few months, and so she was referred to a respiratory physician. in view of this palpable lump within the neck, but also the persistent cough. And she underwent a CT scan and a PET-CT scan with them. So these are the images that she had. So she actually was looking at an MRI as well, obviously, and PET CT here. And this was in February of this year. And shall I just talk through them? So the main thing, obvious is on the MIP I think that you just get this big overall picture of what's going on so a huge amount of bilateral lymphadenopathy uptake within the thyroid gland as well but also this mediastinal involvement and a diffuse process of sort of lymphangitis picture going into the left lung as well. So pretty large volume disease at the outset. So she went on to have core biopsies. This was all before she was referred to us. So this is from reports that we had received. So she had core biopsies from the left level three lymphadenopathy and also from the left thyroid lobe. She also had EBUS for the medicinal disease and had a biopsy a biopsy at Station 4 as well. So we had pathology from both the neck and from the midostinum chest.

Let's pause there for just a second, Kate. Zubair, this hobnail thing popped on our radar screen a few years ago. Can you tell us a little bit about what this hobnail variant is and from the pathology standpoint, how you think about these tumors?

So just to make something clear, in the new WHO, which will be coming out for the classification of endocrine organ neoplasms, the word variant is going to disappear because the word variant is used for a lot of molecular stuff. So we're going to call them subtypes of papillary thyroid carcinoma. So let's make that clear. So this actually, the first cases were reported from Mayo Clinic by Dr. Lloyd in 2010. And this was really a seminal article, which did get a lot of press, but also a lot of pushback because everybody thought it's just a little growth pattern that is, you know, just caught an eye of a pathologist who's probably just wants to make another entity. But what we also realized that when the tumor has the small structures and it almost looks like a tiny flowers with a lot of petals. If you can consider, you know, thinking of in a layman terms and if you do not do pathology every day. We have recognized these type of structures and other organ systems like in urinary bladder. which have these micro papillary type carcinomas, and ovary, and even in the breast, and lung. And what we recognize that when these tumors have these small papillary structures, they tend to be more aggressive, because you can just imagine mechanically they can easily snip off, can go into the lymph nodes and blood vessels. And this tumor, when it was described, some of these cases were already associated with other aggressive subtypes, like tall cell subtype is the most common where you see these tumors. And as you can see on the high power, which is the bottom right picture, my screen, the right, there is these very smaller structures, but if you see the nucleus, it is kind of pushed to the edge of the cell. And that what is known as the hobnail appearance. And as you know, if what is hobnail is, if you go back into the Western times, you can see the, how the nails were, or sometimes what the cowboys kind of wear on their boots. And that's what comes out, the term comes out from. So what we see these tumors that they can have multiple molecular alterations, which will be talked about later in there, they tend to have increased lymph node metastases recurrences. Now you make the diagnosis, you call something all hobnail subtype of papillary carcinoma, when 30% or greater of the tumor mass that is examined on the slide shows hobnail features. And these tumors can be a little bit cystic also sometimes, but they are, what I have seen mostly, that they are very much associated with other aggressive subtypes. So you kind of have a mixture. You can have a classic variant as a nidus, you have a tall cell, and then you have a hobnail and lymphatic spread or angioinvasion, you can very easily, and even perineural invasion, you can easily see in these tumors. but they are tyroglobulin positive, they are TTF1 positive, and they are also Pax8 positive, which we use markers to confirm the follicular derivation.
Fantastic. And in the new WHO, Hobnail is going to be its own subtype and it'll be clearly defined.
Yes, it is. Yeah.
Yes. Okay. Awesome. Okay. So we're a little worried about this, not only from the PET scan to begin with, but from this pathology. All right, Kate, tell us some more about the story.

So in herself, as I said, she was pretty well. The only thing that takes her off a performance status of zero is that she has this persistent cough and some shortness of breath on exertion. And remember, she's only in her forties. She was also then starting to get quite a lot of discomfort from the bulk of the disease within the neck. And when I first met her, she obviously had a visible bulky mass. I mean, she looked worryingly like an anaplastic when you first looked at her. And then, so not only could you see the big bulk within the left side of the neck but then on palpation you could feel smaller lymph nodes throughout the right neck levels two to four as well. As I said, past medical history was fairly uninteresting other than COVID in January of this year. She wasn't on any medication. She had no significant family history. She had smoked but had a less than 10 pack year history of smoking and no radiation exposure in the past. So we went on to send the tissue for urgent molecular profiling as well. Do you want to discuss that?

Pause here for me just a second before we talk about this ROS1 fusion. Eyal and then probably Lori, what are the cases that we should be thinking about first as an endocrinologist and then as an oncologist where we should do this fancy molecular testing? We've all seen people that have big lymph nodes and lymph nodes in the test. Eyal, where do you draw that line to say in the perfect world, if you could, you know, if this was all paid for for everybody, when would you be thinking about doing this fancy sort of somatic molecular testing?

So first, it's really important to state that this is a paradigm shift, at least for endocrinologists. So oncologists are used to doing NGS and giving targeted therapies, but endocrinologists that follow thyroid cancer patients know how to give radioactive iodine and send them to surgery, but NGS, genetic assessment, is a new thing for them. So when we see someone with an aggressive disease, with a static disease, that we can envision that in the near future would need systemic therapy, either for a neck disease that is progressing or distance metastasis, or this case, which is obviously an aggressive disease, that's the time to send a tissue for NGS. And it's important for endocrinologists to send it on time, not to wait until like we waited for lymphadenine. Today we have better options.

So, Lori, let me ask you, you know, a lot of these are going to start with the surgeons, they're going to start with the endocrinologist, and then eventually get to you. Where in that pathway and which patients do you think we should really be thinking about up front molecular testing that's going to make a difference up front as opposed to five years from now?

I think that there's an increasing role for thinking about biomarker testing up front. Clearly for a patient like this, it's a no-brainer. But also for patients who are presenting with very bulky disease, we're now doing clinical trials looking at neoadjuvant therapy in order to improve the surgical outcome and minimize the surgical morbidity. And so if the patient didn't have metastatic disease, but this kind of bulky disease in the neck, there's a good chance that you can find a druggable alteration. And if you find a druggable alteration, there's a good chance that you can improve on the surgical outcomes. So we still need to complete those neoadjuvant studies, but so far I think we're seeing a lot of promise.

Yeah, so the biomarker testing is not just for a drug for distant meds down the road, but now potentially even in the, can we shrink things and make Cary's surgery easier? We'll come to that in just a minute. Let's talk about this specific mutation, Kate, because this is a little bit of an unusual one. So tell us about this specific mutation.

Yes, so just to also just to add to Laurie's comments there, I mean, we don't, we don't have neoadjuvant therapies funded here. So it was a little bit of a Because of this particular case, because it's behaving badly, I sent the molecular at the same time as I sent the review of pathology, just in case this was anaplastic, where we do have the opportunity of giving some targeted therapies, but also I think we do have the opportunity to put a case forward for individual cases. So that's one of the reasons for sending for molecular. So this fusion, yes, so this is the first ROS1 fusion that I've come across within my thyroid practice. And this particular fusion is more commonly seen in gliomas, I think, and also, well, we see them in non-small cell lung cancers as well. And although even in non-small cell lung, it's still only one to 2% that have a ROS1 fusion. That in lung cancer, when you're talking about a common cancer, it still equates to a lot of patients. And I think one of the papers was suggesting 20,000 patients globally a year would have these fusions. So not so uncommon to our lung colleagues. But in thyroid, I think, Laurie's group published a patient with a fusion such as this, but there's very little else within the literature, certainly when I looked when this lady was first diagnosed. So in lung, patients do, you know, have more aggressive disease as well. They have, you know, more nodal involvement, perhaps more distant metastases as well. So here we were faced with an unusual fusion, and I actually discussed her case with our lung colleagues because of their experience with this particular, sorry, let me just, and Currently, the first line of treatment for lung cancers with this particular alteration is with n-trectinib. And with n-trectinib, and I'll come on to explain a bit more about n-trectinib itself, the overall response rates in lung were around 70% with a median progression-free survival of around 16 months, so this sounded promising for this lady whose disease was progressing pretty quickly in front of us. So, Entrectinib is a TRK inhibitor. It inhibits specifically ROS1, but also TRKA, BNC, and ALK. It's an oral preparation taken once daily. One of the main cautions with it is ensuring there's no baseline QTc prolongation And this was just taken from Google, basically, just to show the pathway of this particular drug.

Perfect. Yeah, pause here for just a second. So we've found a target, and as Lori talked about, maybe in a neoadjuvant setting, maybe in a therapeutic setting. Take me to the next slide. Then I want David to talk about the difference in these two PET scans. So talk us through these real quickly here, Kate.
Kate or David?
So this is the February 2022.

Yeah, so February was the scan that she arrived with and then because clinically things were moving, her cough was getting worse, I obviously did a new baseline before starting systemic therapy and I also did a brain just to make sure there was no disease there. So the MRI of the brain was negative but the repeat PET-CT scan did show some degree of progression, even within that four weeks, with a new lesion commented in the ninth rib, although maybe we might have seen it looking retrospectively. But the lung disease hadn't changed very much, although that's quite difficult to quantify, but the neck disease had increased also slightly as well. So quite a rapidly growing tumour.

David, when I compare these PET scans, I mean, the oncologists have taught us we can use resist, we can do structural stuff, but you know, sometimes the SUVs vary a little bit and I can't tell if they're changing. I mean, how do you compare these PET scans that we know there's a real change there, David?

Yeah, certainly. That's a good question. Good question, Mike. There's a variety of ways to variety of things to look at. I mean, first of all, just looking from the MIP as we can see this maximum intensity projection that gives a really good snapshot and overview of the extent of the disease and the intensity and distribution of the FDG uptake. So that's one guide. Obviously, then we've also got cross-sectional imaging associated with that. And so we can actually look for the size on the CT, which is an important marker of change. But then particularly with the PET characteristics, there's the SUVmax, which as you pointed out, there is some variability based on things like blood sugar level, and also uptake time and other variables. So we tend to think if there's more than, you know, certainly more than a 20 or 30% increase, that's definitely significant on the FDG. There's other different markers we can look at, not just SUVmax alone. We can look at things like, you know, glycolytic volumes and more of a volumetric analysis as well. But in this case, you know, the snapshot certainly looks worse. And the key finding is actually finding new lesions as identified, rather than just sort of minor changes in morbidity.
I'm Kate I want to get to the decision about the thyroid surgery so so show the next slide really quickly and then let's get to the CT scans and get carry on to see what we should do.

So the reason for putting in the cardiology slide was just to say that within the first six weeks of being on the Entrexanib, she did, you know, fit 40 odd year old lady, did have a change in her basic cardiology. And that was just because that might help us decide whether we're going to keep her on this drug for a prolonged period of time or whether we should be thinking of other options. So she had her first response assessment after six weeks, which is quite early, but I think we just wanted to, because of the cardiology changes, we just wanted to have an idea of where we were going. And she'd had a favorable response, certainly symptomatically. Her cough had stopped, the pressure in her neck had reduced significantly, but the CT in my mind was a little bit disappointing, because I thought clinically she was going to have a nice partial response, but in fact, still by resist, She remains within the stable disease, however, early stage and continuing clinical response.
Go ahead, David, you were going to say?

I was just going to make a quick comment that, you know, in this situation, occasionally there can be a benefit of PET in that sometimes you can see those changes on the FDG avidity before you can see the structural changes on CT. Yeah.

Carrie think through this a little bit it's not totally fair, you just get started with an easy one. I say, I'm sorry. I mean, how much were you sort of thinking of this new adjuvant how much shrinking would you have to sort of think throughout loud for this type of case.

I mean, I think for this case, you know, we actually looked at a group of pop now, you know, I don't know it was about seven, seven years ago now, but in addition to the distant metastatic disease they also have a high risk of really invasive disease as well. When I look at this, I'm looking at the scan, the axial over on the right of the screen or anatomic left, as I like to say. I'm concerned about the invasion of the trachea and esophagus there as well, especially given her symptoms. I would consider just in terms of imaging, if I'm going to take this patient to the operating room, potentially getting an MRI. which sometimes helps with looking at invasion of those other important structures that I'll be looking at. During the procedure, I'll place an NG tube so I can feel the esophagus and exactly where it is. I would 100% get a laryngeal exam to assess the vocal folds before. Sometimes patients can not have any symptoms, although you know, vocal changes but looking at the function of those cords so you can have a very informed conversation with the patient prior to taking them in the operating room. I would take any help I could get with this patient with neoadjuvant. That lung disease is very frightening. You're in there and where do you cut off your levels? Normally with a modified radical neck dissection, we take levels 2, 3, 4, and 5. Then 6 is obviously around the trachea. Then what is your 7 here? Where do you cut it off once you're heading into the chest? It's arbitrary at this point, especially if they have bulky nodal disease like that. This is clearly more of a palliative and debulking procedure than a curative procedure. given the extent of disease in the lungs and elsewhere? I'm not sure I answered the question, but this would be a, let's buckle down, the only case for the day, total thyroidectomy, bilateral, central, bilateral, modified radical neck dissection, if all goes well.

Hey, let me ask you any as they're sort of thinking about surgery because sometimes it comes up we're going to take out half we're going to take out whole first comments about radioactive iodine and then Laurie finish the case for me was sort of your thoughts about where we are in general in terms of some learning points from this. the radioactive iodine possibility.

Okay, so this is still a differentiated type of cancer, so we need to think about radioactive iodine. On the other hand, it's an aggressive disease. We see this uptake on the PET scan, so the chances of significant response is extremely low. If we could do a thyroidectomy, give radioactive iodine, get whatever we can from that, we would, but we wouldn't risk the patient doing a massive surgery just for that because the chances are really low that she's going to respond.
Yeah. Lori, finish this up for us and sort of summarize here and give us some final thoughts here.

Let me just make one more comment about the radioactive iodine. So ROS1, like the other fusions, entrec fusions and ret fusions, does upregulate the NAP kinase pathway, and we know from other settings like BRAF mutant disease or RAS, driven disease that that MAP kinase upregulation downregulates sodium iodine symporter expression, TIPO, etc. So it could be that with ROS1 inhibition, you could actually help stimulate radioiodine uptake. So in a case like this here, we would try to give the n-trectinib along with radioactive iodine to try to enhance any possibility for uptake. But just to take the case home, I'm so glad that you showed this case because this is a great example of oncogenic kinase fusion differentiated but bad actor thyroid cancer. And when we think about oncogenic kinase fusion-driven malignancies, we want to think about thyroid cancer. Thyroid cancer actually has the highest rate of oncogenic kinase fusions of any solid tumor. And so if we think about Ntrek targeting, ROS1 targeting, RET targeting, ALK targeting in non-small cell lung cancer, we should be thinking about it in thyroid cancer as well. And using a good assay that can detect those fusions is so important in patients who need systemic treatment.

Awesome. Right before we go to the next case, I can't resist. David, give us a couple words about re-differentiation therapy. I know you guys are using it and thinking about it. Where do you see that in sort of three or four sentences here?

Yeah, sure, certainly. So the first thing is, I think there has been a case series with larotrectinib with providing re-differentiation therapy for thyroid cancer. We really view it as a good effective treatment. It's just a very neat approach that you can have one month of a TKI leading to re-differentiation. The way that we do it, we'll do an I124 PET before and then after, and then we'll quantify. know that change in uptake and we'll ensure that we get you know adequate uptake to deliver more than 20 gray before proceeding to therapy and so it's just a neat approach that you can can limit the duration of systemic therapy and then have a durable response and those benefits of radioactive iodine.
Would you recommend a diagnostic iodine or a PATI-124 pets in this situation in the first instance, or? Well, I think that I'd go with the thyroid. We've got the thyroid.

Yes, I'd go with the thyroidectomy first, but then I think I'd be hopeful. I mean, without the entrectinib, you know, I think I'd be pretty cautious and be relatively unlikely to get a good response. But I think you just have to hope and see and continue the entrectinib.
Yeah. Thank you. That's really, really interesting. Thanks.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary consensus was to proceed with thyroidectomy first, with surgery undertaken only if feasible as a palliative debulking procedure rather than with curative intent given the extent of pulmonary and nodal disease. If operable, the proposed procedure would be total thyroidectomy with bilateral central and bilateral modified radical neck dissection, with preoperative laryngeal examination and consideration of MRI to better assess tracheal and esophageal invasion. Entrectinib should be continued, and radioactive iodine may be administered in conjunction with ROS1 inhibition to maximize the possibility of iodine uptake, while recognizing that the likelihood of meaningful response to radioactive iodine alone is low in this aggressive PET-avid disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapidly enlarging left neck mass in April 2019, with pain radiating from the left neck posteriorly to the occiput and dysphagia to solids without aspiration symptoms.

[ diagnosis ]: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, clinically staged cT1b cN1b cM0, stage IVB, with no distant metastatic disease at presentation.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsy of the neck mass confirmed anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. No differentiated thyroid cancer component was identified on the biopsy specimen.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging demonstrated a large left-sided thyroid/neck mass extending posteriorly, marked deviation of the airway to the contralateral side, contralateral cervical lymphadenopathy, and retropharyngeal FDG uptake on PET imaging.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF V600E mutation detected on tumour molecular testing.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Previously diagnosed with a benign thyroid mass approximately 2 years before presentation. Enrolled in an international tissue bank. Initially treated on a phase I study of intralesional STING agonist with pembrolizumab; an initial clinical and radiological response was observed, followed by disease progression with ulceration. Received palliative radiotherapy to the neck for pain and ulcerating local disease, with good symptom control.

[ current disease status ]: BRAF V600E-mutant anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, stage IVB, with local disease that progressed with ulceration after intralesional STING agonist plus pembrolizumab and was subsequently treated with palliative radiotherapy to the neck with good symptom control. No distant metastatic disease had been identified.

[ other clinical data ]: Examination at presentation showed a large left neck mass with posterior extension and minimal palpable abnormality on the right.

reference_discussion.text: So let's, so let's move on. Let's do case two. We're going to aim for 15 minutes here for case two. So let's do case two. And I see Dr. Kim signed on. Dave, if you want to turn your camera on, just sign on and join in here with us. And we'll let Kate introduce Dr. Kim.

There we go. So Prof Kim is here. Prof Kim is a thyroid and head and neck surgeon who works with us here at the Royal Marsden. And his particular interest really is thyroid cancer, but also the preclinical and the molecular side of thyroid cancer is looking into some circulating tumour DNA studies with us as well, which is All very exciting. So I'm moving on. Thank you for joining day and moving on now to our second case. This is a 64 year old lady who presented back in April 2019, which is important because at that period we did have limited treatment options, and I'll talk about that in a moment. But she presented with a rapidly enlarging left neck mass, associated pain radiating from the left neck posteriorly to occiput, and she also had some dysphagia to solids, but no symptoms specifically of aspiration. She'd previously been diagnosed with a benign thyroid mass two years prior to this and this was the appearance clinically. She had a large mass which was extending posteriorly on the left side particularly, not a lot to feel on the right side and this was the imaging at the time and I think the sagittal PET is quite helpful here and also highlights this retropharyngeal uptake as well. You can see she had a lot of deviation of the airway to the contralateral side but also had contralateral lymphadenopathy as well. She had a core biopsy which was confirmed as the clinical picture suggested of anaplastic thyroid cancer. Unfortunately, no areas on the biopsy have differentiated thyroid cancer. We sent her tissue for molecular pathology. At that time, it was slow, but we did get a result eventually which showed us that she had a BRAF V600E mutation present. She was staged clinically as a T1B, N1B with no distant disease, so stage 4B anaplastic thyroid. So at that stage she actually, we enrolled her in the International Tissue Bank that Dr Laura Moss was chairing at the time, so her tissue went off to that. She had no, we didn't have access to targeted therapies at that time but there was a phase one study of intralesional sting agonist with pembrolizumab which she enrolled in under my colleague Professor Kevin Harrington and she had an initial response to this both clinically and radiologically but not long afterwards her disease started to progress again and you can see the ulceration that was associated with this disease. We made an application for Dibrafenib and Tremetanib at that stage, as we had the early data then available, but there was no predefined pathway for this. I think we were the first to apply for this in the UK at the time. So in the meantime, we gave her some palliative radiotherapy as she was getting a lot of pain and this was ulcerating. So very old-fashioned, simple, Maltese cross arrangement of radiotherapy, anterior-posterior beam, just so that we could get her on treatment within a day and treat for some palliation. And actually that did give her quite good symptom control. So we did then get approval through expanded access program it's now set up for the graph and it's been tremendous nib based on the mutation to be roughly 600 D, and you can see that very rapidly. she got remarkable clinical response which we are now thankfully all getting accustomed to seeing which is such a brilliant move forward for anaplastic. But she did have some of the toxicities so not uncommonly we see nausea and she actually also had vomiting requiring admission to her local hospital unfortunately. However, just the first dose reduction of her drometinib improved that significantly and she was able to continue to tolerate this. So we can see radiologically, sorry, another mix of modalities, but we had a reduction quite significantly in the tumour. with the dibrafinib and trimetanib, and this MRI also at 10 weeks was done because we were considering heading towards surgery.

Okay, let's pause there for just a second, Kate. Go back one for me. Lori, this dibrafinib, trimetanib thing has really been on our radar screen the last two or three years, and we've seen some really remarkable responses. Now that more have been done, do you get a feel for, like, how many of them get this traumatic response and kind of what duration this response is now? I know there's not a ton of data, but anecdotally, what are you sort of feeling about that right now?

So I originally was skeptical of the data from that small group of 15 patients from the dibrafinib basket trial. But as these patients do trickle into clinic and we get more and more experience, I've actually had several patients have incredible responses to Dibrafinib and Trematinib, quite durable responses. So I think that there is, you know, real activity. And then there was an updated publication with a number of more patients that were treated in the study that, again, showed very high response rates for anaplastic thyroid cancer with good durability as well. It's important, though, to note that not everybody achieves responses, and sometimes you can see a response but have it be very short-lived, and I don't think that we really quite understand what the mechanism of resistance is yet in these patients.
And Kate, your experience, have you had many with on Dabtram? Nobody's had a ton, but that same sort of field that Laurie has there?

Yes, so within the expanded access in the UK, I think we've had approaching 30 patients now. And in fact, we're just publishing the outcomes for UK wide for the first 18 patients. And the results are not as good as the single center publication in term, but they're still, you know, they're still pretty good. And we've, my personal experience is, has been very impressive results, although I have had a primary resistance. And as Laurie says, you know, it's, it's not the complete answer. Unfortunately, not everyone, all of our anaplastics have, have this mutation. And so we've still got a lot of work to do with the BRAF wild type tumors as well. but yes our experience has been generally positive and generally well tolerated but most patients I have need a dose reduction quite often due to nausea and we'll talk about another toxicity with this lady.
Okay so let's go ahead and talk about the toxicities and then we'll pause next when it comes to the surgical decision making.

So quite early on in her treatment with this, she developed blurred vision and described floaters. So she had an urgent ophthalmic review and she was diagnosed with bilateral granulomatous uveitis, which is reported, but not as very common. She was advised to stop her diprafenib at that time. She continued the trimetanib and started some dexamethasone topically. and the uveitis improved and we restarted at a dibrafinib dose reduction and she seemed to be okay for that. She had a continued response as we've seen on the imaging and she was assessed for surgical resection including EUA and esophagoscopy at that time. She, however, declined surgery at that point, and she wanted to continue. She was feeling much better. She didn't want to go for a big op, and so she continued on the medical treatment for a bit longer, in fact, until 16 months post her diagnosis. At that stage, we did opt to go for surgery, and Day, I don't know if you were able to or wish to chip in at this point to discuss the surgical approach.
Should I do that now, Mike, or do you want to?

Yeah, go ahead. I was going to ask you, Dave. So tell us, A, sort of the way you think about, you know, when is it time for you to do your surgery? And then, interesting for us non-surgeons, what do you actually find when you get in there?

Yeah, so I think that's a key question, and it'd be great to learn from other surgeons and other units. It's the timing, How long can you take the drug off for? Because it often has antigenic properties. It's individual, it's for that patient. What are we trying to achieve for each drug? What is the window period? How are they responding? All those things I think factor in. So I think for myself, I'm there to offer Kate support, knowing that these patients will develop resistance and it may be too late then. um to try and agree when a reasonable time to intervene with surgery if we both feel that that has a role both either temporarily for salvage reasons locally or possibly to to provide more long-term progression free survival so so that's what we're always thinking and therefore there's no exact timings so for this lady we we had numerous discussions but So when I assess this patient, I'm thinking, you know, what problem will I cause? Will I be able to excise most of this tumor? Can I actually provide some material benefit for this patient and therefore give Kate a reasonable chance for other treatments or continue the treatments? and get more robust results. And when I examined this patient, everything was rock hard. She's had radiotherapy. She's had everything. She's had injectables. And so it was challenging, but at the same time, we saw a fantastic response. So it was really radiologically made the decision for this patient. So when I looked at it, I thought, look, this is really doable now. And so we did the oesophagoscopy. I was convinced that there was no gross invasion of the oesophagus. Although having said that, we did consent her for reconstruction. We consented her for PET major because we had to take some of the skin. Really, really didn't know what we were expecting, but we went in there. And as expected, it was very much easier than normal. Everything stuck down. So we started from first principles about preserving the carotid artery. We had to take the vagus because it was part of the tumor, but she had a left vocal cord palsy anyway. We managed to save the esophagus. We did a myomectomy, but we preserved the mucosa. We left an NG tube just in case, but she didn't have any perforation issues. And so it was a learning case, it was a challenging case, but she didn't need a PET major reconstruction, we closed primarily, and she did very well. So we don't have much experience, but we're building that with one or two other patients. So I don't know if that gives you some insight, but it is certainly challenging.

It does. And there was a question in the chat. Laurie, maybe you can take this one. Out of everybody that gets down the neoadjuvant therapy pathway of all of these target agents, how many of them really get surgery? I know we don't have an exact number, but what's your gut on that right now?

We definitely don't have any data yet from the studies that have been done. But anecdotally, I can say that we're using therapies that have very high response rates in the range of 65, And those response rates really do translate, I think, into a better opportunity to do resection. So we've we're so far with our clinical trials that are underway. We're fairly pleased with what we're seeing.
Dr. Lubitz.

Yeah, I just want to make one for the comment I agree with Dr. Kim's approach at minimizing harm when you know you're not going to completely entirely, you know, this is not going to be an R0 resection and just want to be careful about and involve the patient. The one thing actually, Dr. Wirth and I had a patient. that after this treatment where the tumor sort of melts away, you actually have to be concerned about the absence of tumor. If you remember, Laurie, we had a patient who had a tracheal, basically a hole in the trachea from the absence of the tumor or the treatment of the tumor. So that's something also to consider that the wall of the trachea and other surrounding structures may be weakened by the actual treatment itself. So consideration of a tracheostomy in certain cases is something we need to think about.
That's great. Kate, show me the next, yep, where was that?
Yep. Yeah, quick question for Kerry and Dr. Kim. Does frozen section play any role intraoperatively during these delayed resections here?

Sorry, go ahead, Dr. Kim. So as in this case, sometimes when you reset this tumor, actually you don't find any anaplastic and you find the differential component it may have developed. But I don't think that would change the decision to perform the surgery, nor the way we perform the surgery. So in my opinion, I don't think so. I don't know if Dr. Lubitz has a different opinion, but not really.

No, I agree with that. It's pretty obvious when you're in there where the tumor is. It's pretty sticky, either tumor or the effects of radiation and treatment. So it's hard to differentiate even on frozen section between those things, between the changes from radiation and involvement directly with the tumor. So no, I don't normally send frozen sections during them.

Okay, take me to the next slide, then I'm gonna come to Zuber. Zuber, the path reports I see on some of these are like this one, no anaplastic, but there's almost always some residual well differentiated. How do we make sense out of those path reports? I mean, Dabtram is pretty magic, but it made the anaplastic go away and leave some papillary behind. How do you think about that?

I mean, to be honest, I have seen only one case like this, depending upon how much the anaplastic component was there. You know, when the whole tumor is anaplastic carcinoma, greater than, I mean, I call them like a blind man's tumor. I mean, anybody can look at it and say, that looks bad, right? So that is not the problem. The problem is to really look at the cases where the anaplastic is only present at the invasive edge, or there are cases of this small anaplastic carcinomas arising de novo in the background of multinodular goiter, and that's when really the problem starts. And then there's a lot of bleeding of the stains when you're doing these differentiated stains, so-called anaplastic should be thyroglobulin stain positive, but if they're in the mix of all this other benign thyroid disease or papillary carcinomas, you're going to get some bleed over. For me, those are the hardest cases, depending upon how much the anaplastic component was there and where it was located in the surgery. Was it in the middle of the tumor or was it situated at the invasive edge? I mean, this case, to me, looking at the amino profile, it looks pretty clear. But I mean, I have only seen one case where the anaplastic disappeared, but there was a tall cell and hobnail, which was sitting. And that was not, there was nothing happened. So that nidus was still there of a well differentiated, but I mean, you know, these are not such common tumors. So, you know, I, I have only seen one where there was no anaplastic on there, but the core biopsy and FNA did show the anaplastic carcinoma completely.

So Eyal, we need to move on to the next case. But teaching points for this one are things that endocrinologists and regular thyroid folks need to think about as you're listening to this complicated case.

Yeah, there was a question in the chat about the original nodule that this patient had. Now, today we're treating less, we're doing active surveillance. People are afraid maybe it's going to turn into anaplastic. So it doesn't happen. It's extremely rare. We can't prevent that. many patients with people without cancer don't know that they have thyroid cancer. So I think it's not something we need to consider when we treated differentiated low, not intermediate, not poorly. So it happens, but it's not, we can't prevent it and it's unexpected.

This has been an exciting field to see how this Dab Tram has changed what we do, but as Dave mentioned, I think it's given us more questions than answers. When do you intervene? When do you stop the Dab Tram? When do you restart it? Is it different if they have distant METs? Is it different if they don't have distant METs? I think we're still doing these very much as a one-off. as individual cases within the disease management team but I think for the for the general audience knowing that anaplastic cancer we actually have options now for beyond the standard treatment things that were so disastrous and things to think about in terms of this test and get these folks in a rapid fashion to people that can deal with these because you know hardly anybody does a bunch of these except at specialized centers so these are great cases and so tell me the last couple of sentences on her Kate how's she doing now just to round out.

So we did start restart the debriefing of a tremetinoid because she had residual thyroid tissue because we didn't really know. whether to or not but she got a reappearance of the uveitis and in spite of further dose reductions this continued to be a problem so we stopped and actually she wanted to stop and she's been off treatment now for over a year and fingers crossed everything is stable as post-op appearances so you know she is doing well and we just keep our fingers crossed now we're in unknown territory.

reference_conclusion: Following an initial response to intralesional STING agonist plus pembrolizumab and subsequent progression, palliative radiotherapy was delivered for pain and ulceration, after which dabrafenib plus trametinib was initiated via expanded access for BRAF V600E-mutant anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Treatment-related nausea, vomiting, and bilateral granulomatous uveitis were managed with dose reduction, temporary interruption of dabrafenib, continuation of trametinib, and topical dexamethasone, with maintained radiologic response. After initial deferral, surgical resection was performed at 16 months from diagnosis following favorable response assessment; postoperatively, dabrafenib and trametinib were restarted because of residual thyroid tissue but were ultimately discontinued because of recurrent uveitis, and the patient has remained clinically and radiographically stable off treatment.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in 2018 with mild hypercalcemia and osteoporosis identified on routine medical assessment, followed by a rapid rise in serum calcium over approximately 1 month.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic parathyroid carcinoma with liver metastases and subsequent pulmonary metastases; associated refractory hypercalcemia due to hyperparathyroidism.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial left parathyroidectomy had been performed for presumed benign parathyroid adenoma. Subsequent clinical course and identification of metastatic liver disease established the diagnosis of parathyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Further investigations in 2018 demonstrated liver metastases. Restaging CT later showed progression in multiple liver metastases. Subsequent CT confirmed progression in both liver and lungs. Disease had initially been confined to the liver before later development of lung metastases. Gallium DOTATATE PET imaging in parathyroid carcinoma had shown only low-level uptake and had not supported peptide receptor radionuclide therapy; no patient-specific positive somatostatin receptor imaging result was documented.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Molecular profiling identified a TERT promoter mutation and a SMARCE1 variant. PD-L1 testing showed CPS >20.

[ laboratory results ]: At the time of marked biochemical progression, serum calcium was 3.9 mmol/L and PTH was 85 pmol/L. Hypercalcemia persisted after initial parathyroidectomy. During later progression, calcium rose to approximately 3.3-3.5 mmol/L. Renal function remained preserved during the documented course.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Left parathyroidectomy was performed in 2018; calcium and PTH did not normalize postoperatively. Medical therapy included cinacalcet and pamidronate without adequate biochemical control. Liver metastases were resected later in 2018, after which calcium and PTH normalized, but both rose again approximately 6 months later. Bisphosphonate therapy was continued during this period. Owing to symptomatic and difficult-to-control hypercalcemia, bisphosphonate was changed to denosumab. Bland embolization/trans-arterial embolization of liver metastases was performed when disease was confined to the liver, with good initial effect; calcium remained only mildly elevated for most of the following year. With later hepatic progression and new lung metastases, repeat trans-arterial embolization was performed just over a year later, with virtually no improvement in calcium. Systemic chemotherapy with ECX (epirubicin, cisplatin, capecitabine) was administered for 6 cycles; this stabilized disease temporarily and reduced calcium to below 3.0 mmol/L, but progression recurred soon after completion, predominantly in the liver. Further liver embolization produced no significant improvement. The patient alternated supportive calcium-lowering therapy with cinacalcet, bisphosphonate, and denosumab. Weekly paclitaxel was given as interim systemic therapy and produced limited temporary disease control but caused toxicity.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic parathyroid carcinoma involving the liver and lungs, with refractory hypercalcemia despite calcium-lowering therapy, repeat liver-directed embolization, and prior systemic chemotherapy. The patient remained clinically well despite marked hypercalcemia.

[ other clinical data ]: Hypercalcemia had become symptomatic during the disease course, although the patient was later described as remarkably well clinically despite elevated calcium levels. He was not eligible for phase I studies because of hypercalcemia.

reference_discussion.text: I was hoping that Dr Morgenstein would also be on online for this one but this is a 50 year old gentleman. Brilliant, brilliant. Daniel, would you like me to, you can chip in at any point. So this is a 50 year old chap who presented with mild hypercalcemia and osteoporosis to another centre back in 2018 just on a routine medical. But his calcium levels then suddenly dramatically rose over just a short period of just over a month. So his calcium was 3.9 millimoles and his PTH at that point was 85 picomoles per litre. I don't know whether that's your units.
No, we don't speak the Queen's English despite the anniversary. So that's a calcium level around 15 and a PTH probably in the 800-ish range, right Dan?
Yeah, so our upper limit of normal on most assays is 2.6 millimoles per liter. So that's, yeah, anything above three we would consider life-threatening.

Yeah, so these are sky high, I mean high calcium numbers that would be around 15 and a half in our range and a PTH in our assay that goes to 65, this would be around 800 or something in our assay. So clearly way above the range, okay.

So he had a left parathyroidectomy for what was thought at the time to be a benign parathyroid adenoma, but his calcium and his PTH levels didn't fall. all despite sinicalcid and pomidronate and further investigations led to what looked like liver metastases and he was in fact diagnosed with metastatic parathyroid carcinoma. So he actually had resection of those liver metastases later that year and his calcium and PTH normalized but rose again about six months later. and all this time he was receiving bisphosphonate. Restaging CT scan revealed progression within multiple liver metastases. Daniel, would you like to take over the story from here, because I think you know it very well.

Yeah, so this was when he came to see me, and he essentially was not struggling to control his hypercalcemia. He was becoming symptomatic. We switched him from bisphosphonate to denosumab, and there was a case series suggesting that there's a greater response rate in parathyroid carcinoma. and we restaged him to look to see if we could pursue any local ablative treatment. At that stage he only had disease within the liver and we proceeded to a bland embolization of the liver metastasis which worked very well. Calcium was controlled only mildly elevated for the best part of a year. after that, but then started to rise with progression within the liver and development of some lung metastases. We did repeat the trans-arterial embolization almost just over a year later and unfortunately saw virtually no improvement in his calcium after the second embolization. And that's, so after those were so gradual rise despite monthly denosumab and high dose Sinocalcet, that's a point at which we got Kate involved to see him.

Yes, so then, when I saw him, his calcium was rising again, his CT scan confirmed progression, both within the liver and the lungs. I mean, when I saw him, I thought, crumbs, you're going to be ill, you're going to feel terrible, but actually he was symptomatically remarkably well. Clearly, he was used to tolerating these high levels of calcium. and remarkably his renal function remained pretty good. So what were we going to do? We had progressing cancer and our experience for these within our unit is that we end up treating them as a generic carcinoma because there's very little evidence evidence for specific therapies for this situation.

Let me ask, let me ask David, is there anything from like the neuroendocrine land, you know, there's this peptide receptor therapies, lutetium, I don't know what dotatate is, or gallium or that, so I mean, this is kind of a neuroendocrine thing, is there, is there anything you guys could leverage from that?

Yeah, look, it is. I mean, we've had two patients like this in probably the last couple of years. And we tried imaging them with gallium dilatate PET scans. So with a view to potentially treating them with a radionuclide therapy, which is what we do for our new endocrine tumors. So if they express somatostatin receptors, then we get uptake and we can then treat them with lutetium bound to that. But unfortunately, in the cases we've tried this, it just hasn't been very successful. So unfortunately, but yeah, it's something we try.
Laurie, I mean, who was that? Daniel. We've done gallium dosatate PETs on three or four patients now and have seen only low-level uptake and never sufficient PRRT.
Laurie, any sort of high-level thoughts in your vast experience of parathyroid persona? Sorry, you're the oncologist. Tag, you're it. What are you sort of thinking here, Laurie?

Well, I was really deeply appreciative of the comment on the bullet down on the bottom, generic chemotherapy for carcinoma, which is what my high level approach to as well. And I've been raked over the coals for trying generic chemotherapy in these cases because it quote unquote doesn't work. And, you know, the alternative is doing nothing. And that doesn't work very well either. So it's perfectly fine in the world of oncology when you're treating a rare, rare disease that you extrapolate from other cancers and use your best judgment to try to do something to help a patient.

I was going to say, Dan, any information on molecular biology of these parathyroid cancers that can inform us or help us or still just a black box? Do I get you, Dan? Just, you know, the next-gen sequencing or anything?
Yeah. So, Raj Vakha has published a paper looking at mutation mapping, suggesting mutations in the mTOR pathway, but there's no therapeutic data to date.

And we always have a sort of window of opportunity with these patients with renal function, because at some point their renal function is going to go off and that will limit from an oncology point of view what we can give. So we actually gave ECX chemotherapy, which is a combination that we've given in this situation before. So epirubicin, cisplatin and capecitabine, so like a sort of sledgehammer for a carcinoma. And he showed, it sort of stabilised his disease for a period of time and his calcium came down below three on our measurements. and he proceeded to six cycles, which is the limit which we normally stop at, but actually pretty quickly after that, his disease started to progress once again in the liver and he was referred for further liver embolization. Unfortunately, he had no significant improvement with this. He's not eligible for any phase one studies because of the hypercalcemia. And we did do some molecular profiling and we identified TERT promoter mutation and a SMARCE1 variant, but nothing that we had drugs to target. So he switched to sinicalcid backwards and forwards with bisphosphonate and denosumab. And at the same time, we requested a PDL-1 status because I read a case report about this and his CPS came back as greater than 20. Now, there's no significant data on immunotherapy in parathyroid, but based on his fitness, he's very well. we'd exhausted our options as calcium continued to climb. We were sort of at 3.3, 3.5 levels on our assay, so creeping up to the highest it had been. We requested permission. In the meantime, we gave some weekly paclitaxel just while we waited, and that held things a little bit, but he obviously started to get toxicity from that. And actually, we then did get permission for pembrolizumab, and he started at the end of April, he's tolerating this well, his calcium has come down from around 3.5 on our assay to 2.7 and Daniel nicely summarised his levels for us at the moment. So we are in again unknown territory but it's you know it's interesting and we will see how he does with immunotherapy but you know this is not something that we have lots of data on from a teaching point of view or any data sorry.

Dan, from just the teaching point for this regular endocrinologists that don't see this stuff, what are the flags that the once in your lifetime you're going to see a parathyroid carcinoma out of all of the hyperparathyroid you guys see? Can you help us understand what were the flags maybe in this case or other case that would make you say, hey, I need to go look for something else?

So, the pre-op calcium is the big clue. I mean, all the aggressive paraphyroid carcinomas we've seen all had presented with pre-op calcium as well, well above 3 millimoles per litre in SI units. They all had high calciums, they all had short histories. I think that is crucial because clearly the best chance of cure is the right surgery up front and an on block resection with a hemiphyroidectomy. And so I think recognition of the unusual cases which present with much higher calciums than standard primary hyperthyroidism. And then I think the other group is patients like this whose calcium does not return to normal despite appropriate upfront surgery.

Yeah, let me do day and then super day. Anything special about a parathyroid cancer when you're doing the operation or does it look like a parathyroid adenoma is there anything that's like signals you if you're in there doing the surgery.

So, unfortunately, Most of the parathyroid cancers that I've been involved with, we diagnose afterwards. There's nothing obvious sometimes. But if you have an indication like this, I'd like to say that we didn't operate on this, something like this where you have a high suspicion, then you're going in for wide local excision and doing the lobectomy and trying to clear as much as you can. And clearly the classical teaching is that there is invasion, there is adhesion, and it just feels hard and different. But last week, I had a case where I thought this must be parathyroid carcinoma and turned out to be just adenoma, just very inflamed and very active. So it's challenging. But, you know, I think it's challenging. It's just trying to be upfront, just to be aware, certainly high, very high calciums like these cases. Maybe we should be thinking more wider resection.

Yeah. Zubair, finish me up, Zubair, with pathologically differentiating an adenoma from a cancer. If we're not going to give you the labs and we're not going to tell you anything else, we just put you in a room and give you the slides, how are you going to do?

First of all, very difficult diagnosis to make because you don't see them every day. Mostly you see adenomas. You really have to rely on few features and they have to be very clear cut to really differentiate them from parathyroid adenomas. or some of those parathyroid adenomas which have been needled mistakenly for thyroid nodules and caused a lot of reactive changes. You have to have a clear-cut invasion either in the blood vessels, which includes in the angio-invasion or in the lymphatics, or there has to be perineural or intra-neural invasion. Infiltrative growth is in the eyes of beholder, but it has to be clear-cut infiltrative growth into the surrounding. There are other features, but that's why they really overlap with a lot of adenomas. So that's why the diagnosis of parathyroid carcinoma now is on a spectrum. So according to the new WHO, there's going to be three types of parathyroid tumors. One is going to be your run-of-the-mill parathyroid adenoma. The one which sits in the middle is going to be called as atypical parathyroid tumor, which used to be called as atypical parathyroid adenomas. Clinically behave like adenomas, but have some really kind of iffy invasive features, and then you have parathyroid carcinoma. This is a case that is still, if I'm going to make a parathyroid carcinoma case, a diagnosis on histology, I personally will show it to somebody else just to make sure that I'm making this, because I think there's so much overlap that you can really mistakenly call something which is just fibrosis in a parathyroid adenoma as a carcinoma.

reference_conclusion: For progressive metastatic parathyroid carcinoma involving the liver and lungs with refractory hypercalcemia, systemic therapy was administered with ECX chemotherapy, resulting in temporary disease stabilization and reduction in serum calcium, followed by further liver embolization without significant benefit. Molecular profiling identified a TERT promoter mutation and a SMARCE1 variant without actionable targets, and the patient was not eligible for phase I studies because of hypercalcemia. Given PD-L1 CPS greater than 20, preserved performance status, and exhaustion of other options, pembrolizumab was approved and initiated; treatment has been well tolerated with improvement in hypercalcemia.
reference_conclusion_quote: So we actually gave ECX chemotherapy, which is a combination that we've given in this situation before. So epirubicin, cisplatin and capecitabine, so like a sort of sledgehammer for a carcinoma. And he showed, it sort of stabilised his disease for a period of time and his calcium came down below three on our measurements. and he proceeded to six cycles, which is the limit which we normally stop at, but actually pretty quickly after that, his disease started to progress once again in the liver and he was referred for further liver embolization. Unfortunately, he had no significant improvement with this. He's not eligible for any phase one studies because of the hypercalcemia. And we did do some molecular profiling and we identified TERT promoter mutation and a SMARCE1 variant, but nothing that we had drugs to target. [...] And at the same time, we requested a PDL-1 status because I read a case report about this and his CPS came back as greater than 20. Now, there's no significant data on immunotherapy in parathyroid, but based on his fitness, he's very well. we'd exhausted our options as calcium continued to climb. We were sort of at 3.3, 3.5 levels on our assay, so creeping up to the highest it had been. We requested permission. In the meantime, we gave some weekly paclitaxel just while we waited, and that held things a little bit, but he obviously started to get toxicity from that. And actually, we then did get permission for pembrolizumab, and he started at the end of April, he's tolerating this well, his calcium has come down from around 3.5 on our assay to 2.7

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented to the emergency department with worsening chest pain over 3 days.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma, papillary thyroid carcinoma follicular variant, with extensive distant metastatic disease involving chest wall/ribs, right atrium/superior vena cava, pleural/posterior cul-de-sac region, multiple vertebral bodies, left humeral head, spine, and iliac crest.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Core biopsy of the chest wall mass was consistent with metastatic well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma.  
- Thyroid ultrasound-guided biopsy of a 3.5 cm solid thyroid nodule (TI-RADS 4) showed papillary thyroid carcinoma, follicular variant.  
- Histology of metastatic and thyroid lesions showed follicular architecture consistent with well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT demonstrated a 6.5 cm mass at the right manubriocostal junction protruding through the chest wall.  
- CT showed tracheal narrowing to 7 mm associated with thyroid goiter.  
- CT demonstrated a mass in the right atrium/superior vena cava region.  
- CT demonstrated a large left posterior cul-de-sac mass.  
- Multiple lytic lesions were present in the vertebral bodies.  
- A lytic lesion was present in the left humeral head.  
- Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a 3.5 cm solid thyroid nodule.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- BRAF immunostain on chest wall biopsy was negative.  
- Molecular testing of the thyroid lesion showed no BRAF mutation.  
- NRAS mutation was detected.  
- TERT mutation was detected.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Ki-67 proliferation index was reported on pathology assessment; exact percentage was not provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Anticoagulation was started after development of pulmonary emboli during workup.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Newly diagnosed widely metastatic well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma at initial presentation, with disease involving the chest wall/ribs, right atrium/superior vena cava, pleural/posterior cul-de-sac region, multiple vertebral bodies, left humeral head, spine, and iliac crest, and tracheal narrowing associated with thyroid goiter.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No notable past medical history was reported at presentation.  
- Physical examination showed an obvious protruding mass over the right chest.  
- Pulmonary emboli developed during diagnostic workup.
