reference_discussion.text: Yeah, thank you. I'm Rick Payne. I'm from McGill University in Montreal, Canada. I work in the Department of Otolaryngology and Head and Neck Surgery. And before getting started, I'd like to say I have no conflicts of interest to report. I'd like to thank the Thank Foundation for inviting me to present these cases today. It's also a privilege to work with all of you, specialists, world experts on this topic. And so thank you. I hope that we have a great session together. And last but not least, I want to thank these individuals for helping put this together. As you all know, everything we do is collaborative. And especially at our center, McGill, this is how we do it. And so let's jump into the first case, if everyone's ready. Please cut me off at any time if you have any questions or comments. It's a 53-year-old male who presented to the emergency department with chest pain that had been getting worse over three days. There was no notable past medical history, and he had no other complaints. On exam, there was a very obvious protruding mass over the right chest. The emergency physicians worked him up, and they did a CT scan, and then they called my team, and this is what we found. Does anyone want to comment on this, or should I go through this?
Go ahead and go through it first Rick and then then we'll talk about it once we get the initial presentation.

Perfect. So this is, as you see here there's a mass coming through the chest wall and that's what was protruding through the end and lower down, there's a cut here you see the part of the thyroid, you see the trachea being narrowed somewhat. And then we have this and me as a thyroid surgeon, I don't know this part of the body so well. I just had our radiologist tell us that this was in the right atrium or superior vena cava. And so on the reports. They tell us that there's a six and a half centimeter right manubial costal junction mass, as I showed before, something in the right atrium, and a big left posterior cul-de-sac mass. And of note, the trachea was narrowed at seven millimeters at thyroid goiter. In the vertebral bodies, there were many lytic lesions and lytic lesions in the left humeral head. And our expert radiologists we worked closely with had their impression of this being either sarcoma, renal cell carcinoma, and possibly an aggressive thyroid cancer. And so the team came down and did a core biopsy of the chest wall. And this is what we got. And this is just on higher power. It doesn't look like chest wall to me. It looks like something that I actually know what it looks like.
Let me pause for just a second. Go back for me. Margie, it's totally not fair to ask you to read slides off a video, but initial impression looking at this?
Well, so I know that's well-differentiated thyroid carcinoma. And I know from experience this could be a widely invasive follicular carcinoma, or it could be follicular variant of PTC.
And why did those two things come to the top of your mind, Marty?

Well, you know, this is, it's okay. It's a very extreme, but yet classic example if it is follicular carcinoma, widely invasive follicular carcinoma. People, you know, even though this is part of a well-differentiated thyroid cancer family, it's, you know, a thing that follicular carcinoma comes to diagnosis with a bone metastasis, maybe not a metastasis protruding from the chest, but this is a known thing. And it's also a known thing that PTC follicular variant can behave like a widely invasive follicular carcinoma.

Yeah, so this is this is you're guessing from this presentation lots of bone mass that sort of stuff we're going to have some sort of follicular lesion probably with widespread vascular invasion and that's what this is going to turn out to be. Okay, so that's what we're thinking. All right, where are we going.

All right, let's see. So we have our bodies of the chest wall. This is the actual pathology report from Dr. Pustateri. He's one of our thyroid and head and neck pathologists at McGill. And you see here in red highlighted consistent with metastatic well-differentiated thyroid cancer, as Marge was saying. And we do IHC, or we've been doing it for a couple of years now, just looking with a BRAF stain. and it was negative for BRAF. We also do a KI-67. I don't know if all institutions are doing that right now. We do that fairly regularly now, just to have an idea of how aggressive it is. And for us, a KI-67 less than 5%, we're happy with that. 10 to 15% is a little bit aggressive, nothing crazy, but a little bit.
It's beyond what's normally expected.

So, um, if following on what Margie was talking about, are you surprised this is not BRAF or what, what mutation would, would you be guessing here? I mean, I thought all of these bad cancers were BRAF and tall cells. Does this surprise you here? Are you okay with this?

What's interesting is how we change our mind as things go along. So at first, if we've known it's thyroid cancer beforehand, we would have thought about anaplastic thyroid cancer, about poorly differentiated thyroid cancer, because it's so aggressive. We would need some more information about the history, how fast everything happened, if we could get some information. But then, we saw the biopsy. And on the biopsy, we saw follicles. We didn't see solid pattern. We didn't see anaplastic cells. We saw follicles. It looks like a thyroid. And this is when you, like Margaret said, it looks like a well-differentiated thyroid cancer. And then you think about other mutations, especially RAS mutation, which is typical to to follicular or follicular variant. And it causes us to be slightly optimistic about the chances of radioactive iodine, because if we see follicles, there's some production of thyroid hormones. So maybe, maybe we can be optimistic about some efficacy of radioactive iodine.

Okay. Mike. Yeah, so I just also want to add something like this, you'll have to think about, you know, Pax8 PPR gamma rearrangement. Because, you know, that's what you see in follicular carcinomas with angioinvasion. And you can see it in these tumors.
So I assume, Rick, you biopsied thyroid. Let's let's go ahead and see what that looks like.

Wow, you knew it. So, next thing we do we brought our old sound machine down and we did the no sound guided biopsy of the thyroid and we saw three and a half centimeter solid thyroid nodule, we use tirad scoring regularly and as a tirads for in the thyroid. And the biopsy showed papillary heart cancer, follicular variants, same as what was on the chest wall. We're routinely starting to rely more and more on molecular. It's been a few years now, and we're starting to get somewhat accustomed to it. And as expected, the BRAF stain was negative, or the BRAF, there was no BRAF mutation, but there was an NRAS and a TERT mutation that was uncovered.

Which is not surprising, right? This is following along what Margie was talking about before, and Eyal was talking about follicular lesions, RAS base with the TERT. Bruce, you know, traditionally oncologists always had to wait last in line, and, you know, everybody else took care of them, and then we gradually came to you guys. This guy's got disease everywhere. And, you know, I'm going to come to Dr. Shah and let him tell me about the surgery, but is there a role for oncology up front in anything like this, Bruce?

Well, I think it can always be discussed. I think the mainstay generally would be surgery if that's an option. I think for well-differentiated tumors, we do have options with kinase inhibitor therapy that may shrink the tumor or give some benefit, but I still think that You know, and often if surgery is in the plan or is feasible, you know, it doesn't often make surgery less. And that's, you know, that's really a concern. I think if there was any issues where surgery was, you know, need to be delayed or something, it's something that could be considered, you know, for buying time. But I'm not sure that, you know, we can say that it often leads to less of a surgery. So I think it always has to be decided surgery feasible at this point.

George, part of the decision making in what we do or don't do always is what's the likelihood that radioactive iodine is going to be helpful, right? He's got big disease that needs to be taken care of. But from what you know right now, do you think there's going to be a role for radioactive iodine and part of the process somewhere?

Well, I think maybe if you consider removing the thyroid, I think radioactive iodine would be considered. But I think at the present time, maybe an FDG PET-CT upfront would be interesting also to evaluate how active the glucose metabolism is and to predict poor prognosis.

Right, and it would help you understand likelihood of RAI-avidity and likelihood of Bruce having to be involved. Because if we had 1,000 places with SUVs of 30 that were really high, that may rethink, right? Ashok, obviously, everybody's thinking about surgery on this one. But before you talk about the surgery, he's got meds everywhere. I mean, when you look at that big picture, how do you think about getting him started and then headed towards surgery?

I think that's a great question. And one of the things we need to see and decide is, number one, He's young man, he's 54. So we cannot just say, you know, it is a big, big difference between 84 and 54, number one. Number two, probably this disease has been there for a long time. That's why you've got sternal met. For some reasons, follicular cancer with a vascular invasion or a capsular invasion, I don't know what is the link, but we, that sternal mets are not uncommon in thyroid cancer. They are rare, but you do see two or three cases a year And, you know, when I saw this picture, first CT scan, I knew this was thyroid cancer. Yes, you do need to distinguish between renal cell or sarcoma. But when I saw the details of the CAT scan with a big mass in the thyroid, there was no doubt in my mind, this is thyroid cancer. So the first important question is, number one, can I resect this satisfactorily? That is number one. Number two, am I going to give more morbidity to the patient, which may be postoperatively difficult to manage. Three, can I take out all the tumor? And the other thing which is very important, and Mike, you mentioned he has diffused metastases, but those diffused metastases are unlikely to be detrimental at this time, unlikely to be lethal. What is going to be lethal in this patient's care is the growing of the thyroid tumor and the sternal mass, which will fungate through the skin in future, and the thyroid tumor invading the trachea, at which time airway will become a catastrophe. So should the surgery be considered? Absolutely, yes. Obviously, you will need multidisciplinary group, especially with the superior vena cava metastatic disease, and you need to get a thoracic consultation. What can they do to do the best surgical procedure? So my recommendation is do a wide and handsome surgery, do the appropriate reconstruction, be prepared with the family to understand the risk and complications of the operation.
Okay, Rick, take us through your treatments and then let's get up to radioactivity and we'll pause and talk a little bit there.

All right. Mike, just a quick thing from the audience. We have a question circling back on KI-67. I think this probably goes to Margie. With respect to the aggressiveness of tumor mitosis or the KI-67 in terms of whether or not this is pointing towards poorly differentiated.

Yeah. Yeah, I routinely do K, excuse me, K67 and P53, although I don't, you know, rely on it as like religion, but if both are elevated, then it may be below, you know, the threshold for poorly diff, but it still points to like the possibility of grade progression or, as Rick said, more aggressive within the category of well-differentiated thyroid cancer.

Awesome. Thanks, Martin. Rick, go ahead. All right. Thank you. Great discussion. During the workup, the patients start to develop pulmonary emboli. That's not so uncommon as we read, as we learned when you have cardiac METs. And so we started him on anticoagulation and. Pretty quick, we brought them up at our tumor board, which is, as I said before, the one thing that I hope everyone out there picks up is treating thyroid cancer patients is really, really, truly multidisciplinary. Our endocrinologists, our thyroid surgeons, our pathologists, endocrine med physicians, oncologists, as you said before, more and more, everyone. And so we discussed the treatments. As we said before, we could go palliative, With radio therapy he's got met all over the place. I think survival cardiac matches very very low. And there's also for us we didn't feel that there was a molecular mutation that we could target with targeted therapy because it's it's interest. On the other hand, we discuss because, as Ashok was saying, the patient's young, so consider surgery with radioactive iodine and possibly external beam, because this is, in fact, seems to be well-differentiated thyroid cancer. And we know, at least in our experience, we look at TERT not as an aggressive mutation locally, But as a mutation that allows, it's an open passport to the body. So it opens up everywhere. And that's what we've seen with our turd. And we have a fair amount of experience with that. So that's how we look at it, an open passport to go wherever it wants. But it's the NRAS that's going to drive the tumor. And so we opted for surgery. And the patient opted for surgery after the long discussion with the family and expectations were discussed. and this is August 2020. We did a total thyroidectomy, neck dissection, excise, the metastasis, and we decided that we'd follow with external beam radiation and I-131. And this is what the thyroid tumor looked like. It looks like well-differentiated thyroid cancer. Marge, just correct me if I'm wrong.
You're doing well. You're doing well.

Oh, what this is clear vascular invasion I'm not sure who mentioned that before but this is the type of tumor as you can predict it's in the chest wall so there's going to be somewhat vascular invasion and this. And look at the radiation mets. This looks like well-differentiated thyroid cancer. A medical student not long ago bought me a pair of socks, and they are histology slide of thyroid cancer. And this is what it looks like, the follicles. That's what it is.
Looks like socks.

And here's a chest wall metastasis as well. So in final pathology, there was a large papillothoid cancer follicular variant with extensive angioinvasion, not many lymph nodes and as we know with RAS, RAS doesn't tend to spread to lymph nodes at least in my experience. The right atrium and SVC masses were large. It was the cardiac surgeon who removed that. We started our surgery with the cardiac surgeon on pump, and then the thoracic surgeon, and then I did my hour thyroid. I tried to be the quarterback here, but it was really the cardiac surgeon and the thoracic surgeon who did all the hard work. and a 13 and a half centimeter met to the ribs and one or two lymph nodes positive. And following that, we immediately gave external beam to the spine and iliac crest for those mets. And we do, I don't know how others do it, for the radioactive iodine, in these kinds of cases, we like to give three doses, a fairly good amount, every three to six months. And so that's what we did. And here's some pictures.

Pause there for just a second. So George, they did the surgery. The tumor came back exactly as Margie predicted 15 minutes ago, right? This is an NRAS, TERT positive vascular invasion. So no surprises here at all. These often do concentrate radioactive iodine, as Eyal said. So we're on the right page. So we still have Bruce on the sideline here for a little bit in this one. There's always a question about how much of the big stuff do we need to resect? How much can you kill with radioactive iodine? Can you talk about sort of how much surgery needs to be done before you do radioactive iodine in these distant meths, or what you're thinking about that?

Well, I think whenever you can do mostly the excision of the larger messes, it's better to, because you expect a better response to radioactive iodine when you have a smaller lesion. We know that very large lesions, especially those larger lesions that do not concentrate very well can have a decreased response. Or if they have an extreme uptake, they can still uptake from the other lesions. So whenever possible, we try to remove surgically the larger masses. And in this case, I think it was very well done. We've seen the post-therapy scan that the size of the mats are the usual many bone mats spread through the skeleton. Not all of them concentrate radioactive iodine very well, some of them have mild to discrete uptake, so we have to keep an eye on these lesions. What we do here in the Cancer Institute in the University of Sao Paulo, we do an upfront larger radio-IF initial treatment with 200 millicuries of radioactive iodine for bone mass. But we do not follow a schedule of subsequent doses. We always try to evaluate how well the patient responded before deciding for new radioactive doses.
I'm a oh what's what's your approach to is when do you retreat these guys because obviously we're unlikely to cure him, but you will get shrinking so what's your what's your sort of plan for retreat.

So first, looking at the images that we're seeing now, it's amazing to see in such an aggressive disease, to see such a strong uptake in some of the metastases will drive us to give significant dosing, do doses of radioiodine until we don't see any uptake. Now, there are two approaches. There's the approach of giving the maximum the first time and then evaluating. And there's the French approach. They give 100 millikiri. Repeatedly until there's no update. So we usually try to give a large dose to begin with 200 millikere. And if we see response we give it again. And this patient is probably going to need high chances is going to need systemic therapy. And then in the future, we want to get every bit of efficacy we can from radioactive iodine, which is much easier, much safer treatment. So at least twice with 200 mini curie, and then we'll see how we responded and the type globally. And, and during fallout, we'll decide if we give more.

Perfect. OK, I need a couple of one-sentence answers. There's a few things that come from the crowd before we come off this case. George, there's a question about this guy obviously got external beam radiation and radioactive iodine. Efficacy, who goes first? Would you rather give radioactive iodine first? Do you do external beam radiation? How do you sort of sequence that in about two sentences?
Well, there was a myth that external beam radiotherapy would decrease uptake from radioactive iodine. In my experience, the cases I used EBT before did not decrease, so I have no preference.
Okay. Ashok, very quickly, you talked about wide and handsome, and I thought you were talking about me. There's a question about clear margins.

Not wide. I heard the wide part. Somebody asked a question in the chat box about the positive margins. Remember, this patient is going to have positive margins everywhere. You know, there is a myth between, there is a big difference between squamous cell carcinoma and thyroid. Thyroid positive margins mean very little. What is more important is, can the surgeon tell you, I took out all the tumor? There is no surgeon who is not going to have a positive margin in thyroid. One margin is the muscle. One margin is the air in the operating room. So don't worry about it. What you need to know from the surgeon is, did I leave any gross tumor behind?

I'm going to answer two quick questions and we're going to move on to the next case. One was, does the molecular signature drive the extent of surgery and I'm going to say no that was driven by all these other decisions that we talked about. And Dr. Coburn asked about maybe using dosimetry in cases like this because sometimes you get this diffuse lung uptake that you can hurt the lungs. We can either do dosimetry like we do or just use your initial diagnostic scan. If that initial tracer diagnostic scan doesn't show that diffuse uptake like you see in kids, then I don't really worry about too much to the lungs.

Rick, let's jump ahead to the next case. Mike, just one point about molecular signature. I think we're not using this today in the clinical practice except an aplastic BRAF and a red PTC. I think we have some data now that the red PTC may make the tumor shrink a little bit and the surgeon may feel a little better to do the surgery. But otherwise, I don't think we are using that. Our clinical factors are so strong that the molecular signatures are not going to make any decision today. But I think we are in the right track to learn more about it. Okay, I'm moving on.

reference_conclusion: Multidisciplinary review favored aggressive multimodality treatment rather than palliation. The patient proceeded with total thyroidectomy, neck dissection, and resection of metastatic disease including the right atrial/SVC and chest wall lesions, with planned adjuvant external beam radiation and radioactive iodine therapy. External beam radiation was delivered immediately to the spine and iliac crest metastases, and radioactive iodine was administered in repeated therapeutic doses at 3- to 6-month intervals.

[...] And following that, we immediately gave external beam to the spine and iliac crest for those mets. And we do, I don't know how others do it, for the radioactive iodine, in these kinds of cases, we like to give three doses, a fairly good amount, every three to six months. And so that's what we did.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old female. Past medical history was reported as non-significant.

[ chief complaint ]: Left thyroid nodule under surveillance with interval growth.

[ diagnosis ]: Follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe, with central compartment lymph node metastasis showing extranodal extension. Additional papillary thyroid microcarcinomas were identified in the right thyroid lobe after completion thyroidectomy.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- 2019 biopsy of a 1.5 cm left thyroid nodule was Bethesda II.  
- Repeat FNA in March after interval growth to 1.9 cm was Bethesda III.  
- Left hemithyroidectomy in July demonstrated follicular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- A central compartment lymph node removed at the time of surgery measured 4 mm and contained metastatic carcinoma with extranodal extension.  
- Completion right thyroidectomy demonstrated papillary microcarcinomas; at least one focus was BRAF-positive.  
- No extrathyroidal extension of the primary tumor was described.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Thyroid ultrasound in 2019 showed a 1.5 cm left thyroid nodule.  
- Follow-up ultrasound 1–2 years later showed modest increase in size to 1.9 cm.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Molecular testing on the Bethesda III left thyroid nodule identified an NRAS mutation with low allele frequency; the report estimated an approximately 50% likelihood of malignancy.  
- Immunostaining/molecular assessment of the metastatic lymph node was BRAF-positive.  
- At least one right-sided papillary microcarcinoma was BRAF-positive.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Postoperative thyroglobulin decreased from 61 to <0.1.  
- Thyroglobulin antibodies were absent.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Initial surveillance was undertaken after Bethesda II cytology of the left thyroid nodule.  
- Repeat ultrasound-guided FNA was performed after interval growth and yielded Bethesda III cytology.  
- Left hemithyroidectomy with central compartment lymph node biopsy was performed in July. Pathology showed follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma with a 4 mm metastatic central lymph node demonstrating extranodal extension.  
- Right completion thyroidectomy was subsequently performed. Pathology showed papillary microcarcinomas in the right lobe.  
- Biochemical response after surgery was favorable, with thyroglobulin falling to <0.1 and negative antibodies.

[ current disease status ]:  
Post-completion thyroidectomy status with no biochemical evidence of persistent disease based on thyroglobulin <0.1 and negative thyroglobulin antibodies.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- The metastatic central compartment lymph node was identified intraoperatively using methylene blue dye.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapidly progressive very hard left neck mass involving levels III and IV over 3–4 weeks. No signs of infection.

[ diagnosis ]: Thyroid malignancy consisting of tall-cell variant papillary thyroid carcinoma in the thyroid with metastatic anaplastic thyroid carcinoma in a left cervical lymph node. BRAF-positive disease. Suspected bilateral pulmonary metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Ultrasound-guided FNA of the thyroid nodule was consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma; pathology comment indicated possible tall-cell or columnar features. Biopsy/FNA of a left level III/IV cervical lymph node showed anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Final surgical pathology demonstrated tall-cell carcinoma in the thyroid with metastatic anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Tumor was PAX8 positive and strongly PD-L1 positive. Four of 23 lymph nodes were positive. The anaplastic component was described as massively invading muscle. Resection was considered grossly substantial, with suspected residual microscopic disease and possible small-volume gross residual disease.

[ imaging findings ]: Office ultrasound demonstrated a thyroid mass and a separate irregular fixed lateral neck mass/lymph node lateral to the carotid artery. Thyroid nodule was categorized as TI-RADS 5. Pathologic left level III lymph node measured 4.4 cm on ultrasound. CT neck showed a 1.5 cm left superior thyroid mass and a large necrotic left neck mass/lymph node. The left internal jugular vein was not visualized. The left common carotid artery was not encased. CT chest demonstrated tiny pulmonary nodules suspicious for metastases. PET imaging showed bilateral pulmonary lesions/nodules, concerning for bilateral lung metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF positive in the involved level IV lymph node/final tumor. Ki-67 was 25–30% in the lymph node specimen. p53 was negative. PAX8 was positive. PD-L1 was strongly expressed.

[ laboratory results ]: Preoperative thyroglobulin was not markedly elevated.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Past surgical history included right hemithyroidectomy and left parathyroidectomy years earlier; prior thyroid pathology had been benign. Flexible laryngeal assessment showed mobile vocal cords preoperatively. Surgical resection of the thyroid and neck disease was performed; disease was considered resectable based on imaging and operative assessment. Postoperatively, substantial tumor removal was achieved, but residual microscopic disease and possible minimal gross residual disease were suspected.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status after resection of tall-cell papillary thyroid carcinoma with metastatic anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. Bilateral pulmonary metastases were suspected on PET/CT. Thyroglobulin was considered unreliable for surveillance because of dedifferentiated/aggressive disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Neck mass was clinically hard and fixed. No evidence of infection was present at presentation.

And the final pathology showed a BRAF positive tumor, PAX8 positive as well, PD-L1 strongly expressed. Only four to 23 lymph nodes positive. The ATC, as was mentioned before, it was fixed. It was massively invading the muscle everywhere. We got a pretty good resection. We think we got most of it out, but there's for sure some microscopic, probably a little bit of gross disease. And so then we go to the next point and the final point, and the TG. Interestingly, but not so surprisingly pre op wasn't very high the thyroid globulin, because it was so aggressive it forgot how to express the thyroid globulin obviously. And so post up we can't rely on it too much. We suspect that there's something in the lungs. right now, which we see on PET scan on the right and left side. So bilateral lung metastases. And so our current plan right now, and this is all fresh, right to the original, our discussion was, do we give radiation, radioactive iodine, or go straight to targeted therapy? And that was a big discussion after the surgery, knowing what we dealt with. And after a long discussion, we figured we'd treat the primary site with IMRT because we can really ensure that any gross or microscopic disease is taken care of. Our plan right now is to follow with I-131 as per protocol, starting with 150 and then going once everything is gone. But if it doesn't respond to the I-131, if we don't see any take up, then to go straight to targeted therapy so we don't miss that window in the lungs.

Yeah, so Bruce helped me out here a little bit. So I'm trying to figure out when to get you involved and when do we go with systemic therapy, right? Because you're going to have six weeks of IMRT, then they're not going to feel like swallowing for a month or two after that. Now, they'll get the radioactive iodine. We're going to be three, four, or five months down the road before we figure out whether these lung things concentrate. So how do you integrate into all that?

Well, I mean, I'm concerned, you know, with this case, it's an anaplastic. So we know that this patient could be in trouble sooner than later. So I do think, I agree totally, radiation with doxorubicin is very reasonable. And that's what we would do for most of our patients after surgery for anaplastic. So that shouldn't change. I'm not sure how, again, I leave that to the team, but as far as the, you know, radioactive iodine, yes or no, I don't think it's unreasonable to consider targeted therapy now, you know, as soon as that is done, as soon as possible, even included, because this patient has a very high chance of recurrence and death from anaplastic thyroid cancer, I think. So I think targeted therapy, even considering with immunotherapy, Pembro, you know, which seems to give you a longer progression-free survival is a reasonable approach. I would say as soon as possible, I would consider it. I would discuss it for sure.
Yeah, I would too. George, what do you think in terms of timing? Because he's got a well-differentiated component as well.

Yeah, I think timing as planned is quite OK. I think the main concern is local recurrence from the anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. So radioactive iodine can be in a second plan. there was small landmass and sometimes we see CT that does not even show the nodules and have radioactive iodine concentration. So in this case, before planning radioactive iodine therapy, maybe I would consider pre-therapy scan and maybe if it does not show any uptake, I would consider treating focused only in the anaplastic thyroid cancer.

Yeah, so we're winding down the end. I think our approach would be when we start the IMRT, they almost always get a repeat FTG PET scan as part of that staging. So that's going to give you a two-month gap, right? December to February. If the lung things are rapidly progressing, then Bruce is on and we're not doing radioactive iodine. If they're stable, we do CT scans again when IMRT ends. And again, if they're progressive, Bruce is on. If not, it's radioactive iodine. So this is not somebody that you just sit back and watch for a long time. because if those lung mets are anaplastic, they're likely to change in just a few weeks. And I think there could be some good logic, as Bruce said, for just upfront Pembro or targeted therapy. So that would definitely be on the arranged form there. So let's answer a few questions from the audience before we finally down. Mark, was there a couple more on there from the audience about any topic that's still out there?

Yeah. I actually am not seeing anything that is terribly significant that we haven't covered in some form or not here. I think we are good. I have one quick question for George. George, the SUVs on those lung nodules was not very high. Can we take any comfort in that or is that irrelevant?

Well, I think one problem is the size of the nodules. We can have an effect of partial volume, and we are measuring lower than it really is due to the small size. So I would not take comfort relying only in SUVs.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 59-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Hoarseness beginning in November 2019.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma involving bilateral thyroid lobes with cervical lymph node metastases, multiple liver metastases, and pheochromocytoma. Left vocal cord paralysis was present. No parathyroid disease was identified.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration cytology of thyroid tumors and cervical lymph nodes was suspicious for medullary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial evaluation showed masses in both thyroid lobes and multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the bilateral neck. Abdominal CT demonstrated multiple liver metastases and bilateral adrenal nodules. CT findings at first visit to the treating department showed left upper neck and left middle neck lymphadenopathy, bilateral thyroid tumors, apparent invasion of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve by the left thyroid lobe tumor, multiple liver metastases, and left adrenal enlargement.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline RET exon 11 codon 634 mutation was confirmed. The patient’s mother and two children were also found to carry the same RET mutation.

[ laboratory results ]: Serum CEA was 295.9. Serum calcitonin was 7,260. Urinary metanephrine and normetanephrine were elevated.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: In June 2020, right laparoscopic adrenalectomy was performed for pheochromocytoma.

[ current disease status ]: Advanced medullary thyroid carcinoma with bilateral thyroid tumours, bilateral cervical nodal disease, and documented liver metastases, following resection of the pheochromocytoma.

[ other clinical data ]: No significant past medical history was reported. There was no family history of thyroid disease. Left vocal cord paralysis was present at initial presentation.

reference_discussion.text: So let's go ahead and start the first case.

Thank you very much again for the invitation, and let me get started with case one. Case one, a 59-year-old woman noticed hoarseness in November 2019 and visited a local ENT doctor. There, she was shown to have left vocal cord paralysis from masses in bilateral lobes of the thyroid, and multiple lymph nodes swelling in the bilateral neck. She did not have any particular past illness or family history of thyroid disease. One month later, she was referred to the Oncology Difference Center for neck surgery. They conducted fine needle aspiration cytology on thyroid tumors and lymph nodes. The results showed a suspicion of medullary thyroid carcinoma. As for tumor markers, the serum CEA level was 295.9, and castonin level was 7,260, both of which were very high. In addition, abdominal CT scan revealed that she had multiple liver metastases and bilateral adrenal nodules. Both urinary metanephrine and non-metanephrine levels were also high. There was no parathyroid disease.
So let me have you pause there for just a second go back one, Dr. Patel, what do you think in this far we've got this information sort of top line, what do you think in here.

Well, I would say that for us it's not as frequent to have a fine needle aspiration showing a medullary or suspicious medullary thyroid carcinoma. So we probably will have a category 6, but not typified or subtypified what kind of tumor we are seeing. And sometimes we do not ask for calcitonin as a first measurement, and sometimes we need to repeat the five-needle biopsy. So what we see in our real-life scenario, not, I mean, in my hospital, but we can see that perhaps we have a delay in the diagnosis of these kind of tumors for some time until somebody asks for the calcitonin, as it is not a routine measurement here in Argentina.
Zubair, I think Carmen's right. We often don't think about medullary cancer on the FNA, but what are the descriptors that come up on that that should at least make us think about medullary, Zubair?

The classic teaching is that if you have something which does not look like your regular run of a mill, FNA, like papillary carcinoma or follicular neoplasm, you should always think of medullary. In the old teachings, medullary was almost called melanoma of the thyroid. That means it mimics other tumors like melanoma does. So even that suspicion raised by FNA is enough to really think of medullary. And the most confirmatory test that is available is doing serum calcitonin, or you can even use the FNA rinse to do calcitonin level to confirm that suspicion that was raised on FNA. So to me, even that suspicious of our medullary carcinoma is almost equal that it is compatible. Now, it is a rare tumor, so some cytopathologists see it in reference centers more than the others. But I think it's very much indicative, even when somebody calls it suspicious rheumatoid thyroid carcinoma.
Three of these calcitonin numbers of 7,000, CEA 295, is this in the neck? Is it helping you sort of get a picture already before the imaging? What are you thinking here?

Yeah, I mean, when you have a calcitonin and CA that are that high, you should always suspect that the patient has distant metastatic disease. And so you should do cross-sectional imaging, basically of the axial spine and the body. because medullary likes to go to the liver, it likes to go to the bones, we see lung metastases. The other thing is that with this particular patient, you want to look at the adrenal glands, of course. I'm sure you're going to touch upon that in a moment. But this calcitonin is very suspicious for distant metastatic disease. The guidelines, I think, go a little bit too low in terms of what they recommend the ATA guidelines, which I believe is 250. We see calcitonins in the thousands, even with just localized disease. But you should still always check before you go to surgery.
Okay, let's keep going through the case. Hiroko?

Yes. Okay, subsequently, Late germline genetic testing was conducted, and X11, codon 634 point mutation was confirmed. Afterwards, her mother and two children were revealed to have the same late mutation, but no one has developed medullary-sided cancer or related diseases as of now. She was deferred to a university hospital to have adrenal surgery first. In June 2020, she underwent right laparoscopic adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma. Then she was referred to our department to consult regarding the treatment plan for midway thyroid carcinoma.

Okay, let's pause just a second. I can't go past this, Maria, without at least saying a couple of words. We always say do the germline testing. So what do you, this 634, what's it mean? How does it help you?

Yeah, so this patient is very suspicious for hereditary disease, and so you need to rule out. you need to at least rule out pheochromocytoma before you take a patient to surgery because the surgery could be disastrous for the patient if they have a pheo. This patient had bilateral disease in the thyroid and has adrenal nodules. The biochemical testing is suspicious for pheochromocytoma. The patient was tested for germline RET, which every single patient, whether they have a family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or not, a diagnosis they need to be tested for hereditary disease. Because, for example, this patient was the first one identified in the family. you know, if you can't wait for the genetic testing, which oftentimes can take weeks because partially because of insurance clearance, then you can always just check for pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism before they go to surgery. Hyperparathyroidism because you want to be able to remove parathyroids at surgery while if you're in the neck already and pheochromocytoma because you need to address the pheos prior to going for thyroid surgery.

Fantastic. There's lots for you to talk about this case, but what I want to focus on is sort of the initial surgery, because Dr. Kazusaka's question for us is this initial surgery. So let's go ahead and look at the imaging and take us through that, Hiroko.

Next, please. So these are the CT scan findings from her first visit with us. You can see left upper neck lymph node and left middle neck lymph node. The bilateral thyroid tumors are remarkable, and the tumor in the left lobe seems to invade the recurrent laryngeal nerve. And multiple liver metastases like this were also evident. And you can see left adrenal swelling here.

Okay, take me, take me backwards one slide. I'm better for Sunday incredibly unfair to ask you to say anything about true images on a PowerPoint but that's not going to stop me whatsoever. Initial thoughts when you're looking at this or help us understand when you're looking at this, what are you looking for knowing that marks going to be thinking about a surgery, what are the things you're thinking about here.

So I can't make a diagnosis based on CT. I make that very clear. You know, we see thyroid cancers and you have to go to FNA. The things that I would give to the surgeon is their tracheal invasion. I think they already know if there is vocal cord paralysis or not. You see the lesion at the tracheoesophageal groove, which they already talked about. You also talk about if there is substernal extension, most important, extrathyroidal extension. So the surgeon is aware of, I do talk about central compartment nodes, and I do talk about specifically lateral compartment node, up to what levels. And then I stop and lower my head. go away.

That's perfect. Dr. Corafilo, there's like nuclear medicine studies that you guys use for the medullary cancers, you know, where do we kind of stand with that right now? Because, you know, we're thinking this is probably distant medicine. What role of nuclear medicine helping us imaging medullary here, George?

Yeah, since the advent of PET-CT, we've been studying several radial tracers to do a one-stop shop. It's a dream to stage the whole body in a single examination. But at the present time, we haven't found something that is as good as separate individual examinations like neck ultrasound, a dedicated chest tomography or a magnetic resonance of the liver. We, a couple of years ago in our group, we've published a paper in JCM studying somatostatin analogs receptors. When we look in separate every compartment of the body, the PET-CT had an improved diagnosis only for bone disease. But if you think that you can use a contrast-enhanced CT and separated lung-chest CT, with the PET-CT, you can have a good examination. In this case that has a germline mutation, also PET-CT is very good for philchromocytomas and paragangliomas with somatostatin analogues. So we can use these. The trick is to choose which analog you are going to use, since you have a variety of affinities for each kind of receptors, if you are using DOTATATE, DOTATALK, DOTANOC, DOTALAS, DOTABAS, DOTALAN. So in nuclear medicine, the trick is to choose the better radio tracer to do the imaging. And nowadays, we are having some studies using some other biomarkers like fluorocholine to track cell proliferation. And we also have F-DOPA, which is an amino acid analog that seems to have an improved value to evaluate medullary thyroid carcinoma. But one thing we have always to keep in mind is that they all have a complementary role to FDG, because when things go sour, FDG seems to be the best radial tracer to evaluate very aggressive disease.

Yeah, Mark and then Maria, let's go to the heart of this. The heart of this is, Mark, are you just going to do a surgery and clean things out? Or we notice as a rep mutation, because it's germline, are you going to involve Maria to say, can we shrink things before? So where are we in this sort of surgery versus neoadjuvant space? Mark first and then Maria. Mark?

Yeah, I would be thinking about doing some DOTA surgery. But if you go back to the previous slide of the neck, I would agree with what one more slide back with what Azita was commenting on. You know, right there. You know, I think the fundamental question is really, first of all, can this surgery be done safely? and should it be done at the outset here. And so, obviously, our antenna goes up that the left vocal cord is out. And I think it's most likely, based on this imaging, to be due to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, even though that level four disease appears to be involving the carotid sheath with compression of the jugular vein anteriorly. It appears to be fairly well circumscribed. So I think the essence of this is that the left thyroid disease has knocked out the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and therefore the pressure on the surgeon is to make sure that right nerve is preserved. I think because of that, and certainly I would certainly want a multidisciplinary input here, and I would look to Maria to agree with the plan, but I think saving that right nerve and going in at this time makes the most sense.

Where are we on this? I mean, these neoadjuvant things, it just makes such sense to do it. But, you know, sometimes what makes sense isn't always the right thing to do. From a research setting and from a real, you know, patient care setting, where are you on that sort of neoadjuvant in this RET-specific area here, Maria?

Yeah, with RET-specific, it's experimental. So we have clinical trials for neoadjuvant therapy for different diseases, but we have one specifically for RET mutation and RET fusions. And I think, you know, it's helpful in other, more helpful like in anaplastic thyroid cancer. where you can really change the surgery that the patient's going to have. I'm not sure that this patient would gain much from neoadjuvant. And so, you know, I would consider putting them on the trial. If the surgeon was on board with that, but I probably wouldn't offer it outside of a trial. I'm not sure it's going to save that left vocal cord. And that's really the reason why we would do it. For example, if it were encasing the carotid, then that's a good reason to try that. But again, it's still experimental.

Dr. Patoya, every month or two, I get an email from somewhere around the world that says, the patient has distant metastasis. Should I even really still be doing a surgery? Should we just be going to systemic therapy? I mean, we're assuming this is distant meds. So talk a little bit about, are you still going to do a neck surgery in somebody that has presumed liver meds? How you think about that, Fabio? Sorry.
I would like if you could speak a bit slower to understand.
So, in the setting of the distant metastasis. Yeah. Are we really going to do a thyroid surgery. That's, that's the email I get from a lot of people.

So what do you think. Sure, there's no doubt that you continue with the local treatment, then to be able to do systemic treatment with the progression is observed in this group of patients. But we have to understand also that the different facts from around the world make this discussion very different. Because we in Argentina, we do not have salpercatinib, and we had it for a couple of months as an expanded use program, but now these companies saw that the number of patients were really very, very high. They stopped the compassionate use program. So now we do not have any of these alternatives. We have to think only in bandana because we also do not have cables Anthony approved in Argentina and in many regions of our countries in Latin America to be in medullary thyroid cancer so this is a completely different fact from. U.S., for example. Absolutely. Well said.

Mike, I'd like to just also, because I'd like to just mention that these drugs, when these targeted therapies, they all eventually stop working, right? So even if you treated the patient up front, if you had sulfurcatinib or palsatinib, you know, access to these drugs, eventually you're going to be back where you're where we are, find ourselves now, which is we need to operate because the airway is at risk.
And the goal here is local control. Okay, so go ahead, Dr. Katsusaka.

Yes, so we thought that the patient had two options for treatment plan. However, the specific infectors were only available by clinical trial at that time in Japan. And based on our surgical experience, So, primary MTC is not so invasive compared to papillary thyroid carcinoma. So, we presume that we could perform R0 rejection on her neck. And we also expected that reduction of tumor burden may enhance the effect of drug therapy. In July 2020, we conducted total thyroidectomy with bilateral neck dissection for advanced MCC. We accomplished R0 dissection and were able to preserve right recurrent laryngeal nerve with complete function. And here are the pathological findings. It was a medullary-thyroidal carcinoma with 14 pathological lymph nodal metastases. Necrosis was not seen. Stomal deposits of amyloid can be identified. They were positive for Congo vet. the tumor cells were immunoreactive for Calcitonin, and the KI-67 labeling index was 5 to 10 percent.

I was going to say, let's pause there. Zuber, there's been sort of a change in how you guys are describing these medullaries. We weren't used to high-grade medullaries before. Can you talk a little bit about, so we understand what those reports are going to look like now?

I mean, it's not like we're talking about it now, we are bringing it to the front because we always realize that the tumor which follow neuroendocrine patterns, that means they have nested growth like in carcinoids or other neuroendocrine neoplasms throughout the bodies and even pheochromocytomas, that when you saw mitosis And even in thyroid cancers, which are non-medullary, it was something to be really careful about because that means that the tumor proliferation rate or it's kind of has features which are going towards being an aggressive tumor. And I think then the era came and we got all tuned to looking at tumor necrosis. And most of these tumors do not have necrosis, but when you submit a good amount of tumor, you realize there are areas when the tumor goes under what is called the comedonecrosis. That means it's a true tumor necrosis, not because of FNA or because it's just an area of edema or hemorrhage. And I think two major studies that came from, one of them is from your institution from Memorial, Rani Ghosen and Ben Zhu were part of it, where they described certain features to look for in medullary carcinoma, which were associated with higher recurrence rate or poor prognosis. And most studies which follow up also showed that up to 25% of the medullaries can be classified as such. So again, those similar findings that you see in other neuroendocrine tumors, mitosis and the mitotic count of greater than five and two millimeter squares, KI67 proliferation index, because the mitosis is in the eyes of beholder, my mitosis may not be somebody else's mitosis, and then necrosis. Then I think all of those authors got together on an international scheme and they found that if you have even any one of those features present in a medullary thyroid carcinoma, as was pointed out by the I'm going to, I'm sorry, Dr. Kotsuka, that, you know, most of these medullaries are going to be non-invasive tumors like we see in PTC or follicular. So I think these things are very, very helpful. Now, there has been some validation studies to look, even if the pathologist agree on those features when they are reviewing this, what is the variability? And they found that when you have these three features, most pathologists are able to identify it and come to an agreement. Now, there's a recent study from Italy which showed that the necrosis far more succeeded being a top-level variable to really identify these high-grade carcinomas. So still, it's a process, but WHO has recommended this because I think this is one of the major findings that we can focus on, and I sign off my cases now saying low-grade and high-grade. Like I have a case that it is low grade, and Dr. Lavolsi also shared that case with me. And also we discussed it in the tumor board. It is a low grade tumor, but it has multiple, multiple foci of angioinvasion. Now, where do you put that tumor in? case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Enlarging neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma involving the left thyroid lobe with cervical nodal disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration was diagnostic of anaplastic carcinoma. No differentiated thyroid cancer component was identified.

[ imaging findings ]: CT of the neck demonstrated a tumor in the left thyroid lobe and left cervical lymph node enlargement, both with central necrosis. The trachea was distorted. Esophageal muscular layer invasion was considered possible. The carotid artery appeared intact on imaging. Internal jugular vein invasion was suspected. FDG-PET showed no evidence of distant metastasis.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing identified NRAS and TP53 mutations and a promoter mutation. No actionable mutation was identified. Microsatellite instability was stable. Tumor mutational burden was low.

[ laboratory results ]: White blood cell count was >10,000/µL. Neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio was 3.7.

[ current disease status ]: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe with cervical nodal disease and no distant metastasis on FDG-PET.

[ other clinical data ]: On presentation, there was an approximately 8 cm large, firm neck mass with slight mobility. There was no hoarseness, dyspnea, or dysphagia. Prognostic index for anaplastic thyroid carcinoma was 3.

reference_discussion.text: Next slide. There we go. Case two. So let's move on to case two. Dr. Kazusaka.

Well, from here, I'll talk about the cases. A 64-year-old lady visited our department complaining of the enlarging neck mass. From the fine needle aspiration, it revealed that it was anaphylaxis-style carcinoma. There was an 8-centimeter large and firm tumor on her neck. It moved slightly when touched. She had no hoarseness, no dyspnea, and no dysphagia. White blood cell count was over 10,000, and neutrophil lymphocyte ratio was 3.7. This CT scan shows left neck lymph node swelling and a tumor in the left lobe of the thyroid. Both seem to have necrosis in the center of the tumor. The trachea was a bit distorted and the muscle layer of the esophagus might be invaded by the tumor, but the carotid artery seemed to be intact. There is no evidence of this metastasis on FDG PET.

Dr. Cassandra, you reminded me occasionally that you don't make diagnosis off the CT scans. We know you guys have a pretty good feel. When you look at anything about this that makes you think this is more than a run of the mill, poorly differentiated capillary, what are you thinking here?

The jugular vein, I never see the jugular vein. I think, I don't have enough images, but I think the jugular vein is probably invaded by tumor, more than compressed. I think that's what concerns me the most about this case. Besides all the other stuff that I talked about in the last case, you know.
Yeah. Mark, resectable, not resectable? I mean, I guess technically everything's resectable. It just means what you're going to have to take out with it. So how do you kind of make that decision?

Yeah, so it's, as Dr. Sugitani mentioned, the artery, carotid artery appears to be clear. I'm worried about that adenopathy that looks very onerous and worry about the interface between that tumor and the trachea. I think that's probably where this will be lost. in terms of doing a complete resection. So I think at best, my expectation going in would be to do, that I would come out with an R1 resection here. I don't think that one could get an R0. And certainly in this setting, doing more aggressive surgery to remove the trachea, which I think would be necessary, just wouldn't be warranted here. So we can only do BRAF in this patient provided by the laboratory who sell the drugs. So it is covered, reimbursed by the laboratory. It is fast, and we can have it in two or three days. really important point to just don't lose them for six weeks while they're getting the radiation and see what happens on the other side, right, then knowing what's going on there. who would go with our oncologists to do traditional chemotherapy. We can do anything else at this moment.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 39-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Right thyroid nodules detected on screening ultrasound during a health checkup.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal papillary thyroid microcarcinoma of the right thyroid lobe; low-risk disease without extrathyroidal extension or lymph node metastasis.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration performed at the referring hospital was diagnostic of papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Ultrasound demonstrated two right-lobe thyroid tumors. The index lesion was located in the mid right lobe and measured 9 mm in maximal diameter. A second ipsilateral lesion measured 10 mm. No extrathyroidal extension was identified. No cervical lymph node metastasis was identified.

[ current disease status ]: Multifocal papillary thyroid microcarcinoma of the right thyroid lobe, with two tumors measuring 9 mm and 10 mm, without extrathyroidal extension or cervical lymph node metastasis.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient’s wife persistently encouraged operative management.

reference_discussion.text: Very good. Well, after two challenging cases, we all knew we were not going to let Dr. Sugitani do this tumor board without presenting at least somebody to do active surveillance on since I started active surveillance.

A bit of a tricky case with a very low risk side of cancer, actually. A 39-year-old gentleman was referred to our department due to the right side nodules, which were detected by ultrasound examination on the health checkup. At the previous hospital, FNA was done and the diagnosis was papillocyte carcinoma. The tumor was located in the middle of the right lobe and was 9 mm in the maximal diameter. He also had another small tumor in the same lobe, measuring 10 mm. There was no extracellular extension or lymph node metastasis.
So, it's also in the vehicle man. Get this echo so I have to keep turning on and off.
That's what we do in Argentina, so this is multifocal capillary microcarcinoma in a clearly a young man, we would both agree with that.

Yeah, we probably will talk with the patient and to understand exactly what is the mentality of this patient. We won't oppose directly to active surveillance, although this person has a multifocal disease, we could do that. But we will explain that the published experience is not much with active surveillance. It's multifocal disease, and probably we will feel more comfortable with surgery. But if the patient would choose to do the active surveillance, we would go with him doing it and going with him with this decision.

Kevin is this is the opposite end of the spectrum that you play on so I assume there's no neoadjuvant you're not going to ask for next generation sequencing so absolutely not. In Texas, what are you guys going to do with these.

Yeah, I mean, we would do the same. We would encourage surgery, but if the patient wanted active surveillance, we could watch them for a time because it's young, especially if the patient had something they needed to get done, like finish, you know, whatever, their dissertation, then we can always delay surgery.

You've had some of these with active surveillance with me. How do you make that decision? And you know, he's young, it's a guy, it's multifocal. Yeah, well, the first thing I carved out about four hours of time in my office to have this discussion. It's disproportionate to the size of the primary tumor. But having gotten through that part of it, we look at a number of things that have been widely published. One is the location of this tumor in the thyroid lobe, and whether it's in a favorable or an unfavorable location. I also go back and look and see if there's any prior ultrasounds that might give me a hint as to what the rate of change has been in the past. And that's often helpful. Obviously the absence of nodal disease is extremely important. I'm less decided about the multifocal nature of this as to whether that really plays a role as long as that So I sort of put that on the back burner, but it's one more factor. I think the biggest, really the biggest issue is what comes down to the psychological effect of impact of living with disease in the neck or having it removed. And we've talked about this extensively, but I think that's where probably two thirds of the discussion will come down to. Perfect. Dr. Sugatani?

Okay. According to our conservative way of thinking, Japanese consensus statements say younger patients and patients with multiple regions still can be candidates for active surveillance. After shared discussion, he made the decision to undergo active surveillance, actually. However, One year later, he changed his mind and decided to have surgery, although the tumor status had not changed. You can imagine what made him change his mind.
Dr. Batoya, you've got a series of some active surveillance in Argentina. Talk about a little bit why they change their mind or don't change their mind or the decision making there.

I think that the mainly other physicians has a lot to do with the change of mind of patients undergoing active surveillance. We have seen it like in 10% of our series this situation where what the worst thing a doctor can say if I would have these I would have removed my thyroid gland in one second and so the patient came back very nervous and sometimes even we see the patient when they came back operated on with no asking us what they would do. So this is something that continues happening. So I advise my patients under active surveillance not to talk to anybody about this issue and continue with this only with us, only with the doctors we are following them.

You're absolutely right. We have about the same number as Dr. Sigatani in terms of changing their mind. It's not very many. Most people stay in there. Sometimes it's because there's benign changes on the other lobe or nonspecific lymph nodes. I've had two patients that needed organ transplants, but they couldn't be transplanted until their cancer was treated. A couple patients that needed parathyroid surgery on the same side, so we just dealt with the thyroid at the same time. And then the other ones have been pressure from family members or pressures from other stuff. In the United States, I've had a couple people have to change their mind because they couldn't get long term health insurance. because you had to be cancer-free for five years. So there's a lot of reasons beyond just the tumor that made us do that. So in his case, that was the story here.

OK. Here, I would like to briefly review the Japanese medical care system. And the universal public health insurance program everybody in Japan can receive the same medical care with the same inexpensive price. However, more than 40% of people in Japan take out private cancer insurance. Indeed, it covers a good amount of expense for cancer care. But the coverage does not reach the person without histological diagnosis and More importantly, people are not allowed to join private cancer insurance when they have even a minute cancer. As a matter of fact, his wife persistently persuaded him to have surgery. Yep. So we have appealed to insurance companies on the basis of our consensus statements and position paper. Eventually, one company has admitted patients with low-risk thyroid cancer under surveillance to join the cancer insurance plan, excluding compensation for thyroid cancer.

Yeah, it's a challenge, right? Even in the United States, I've had one or two patients choose to have their surgery at Memorial, even though they were stable for eight years, because they were retiring to a different part of the country, and they didn't know the medical team. I've had other people on purpose choose to watch for a set period of time. We call this our bridge program. They want to watch until they get married in nine months, or they want to watch until that a couple of policemen are going to retire or professional voice users. They have no intention of watching forever, but it just takes the pressure off them and gives them that release. So I don't see somebody changing their mind as a failure of active surveillance. I see that as success. That means we're still having the conversation. I routinely tell the patients, I can change my mind once a year. You can change your mind whenever you want to. And I think that's the success of active surveillance is operating at a time when it's still effective, regardless of the reason, whether it's slight progression or whether it's patients changing their mind. So I think we're just being honest about what really happens when you follow these people. And I think being sensitive to that when you first meet them, right, if they're One person in the room and their six family members are all rushing to get to Dr. Erkin before he finishes on Friday night. It's a different sort of conversation. Mark, how much do you really sort of, you know, like in multifold, I'm the same way, I don't worry about that too much. How do you sort of gauge what the patient wants or doesn't want? I mean, you know, sometimes you're just really quiet and listen to your talk. How do you sort of have that conversation to sort of figure out whether they're kind of a minimalist or a maximalist? There's sort of an art to that. How do you sort of, advice on having that conversation?

Yeah, it's really challenging and you sort of have to be able to read the room. I'm carefully, I kind of like the idea of the cone of silence that seems like interesting. Those of you who remember get smart that. you sort of put your blinders on and once you make that decision and move forward. But, you know, now in the pandemic era, you have to read their eyes, and they're very revealing. Having a discussion with somebody who's got thyroid cancer or any cancer and say we're going to watch it, often that look of in the eyes tells you you can pretty much give short shrift to active surveillance. And so it's both the patient and the significant other that really give you the clue. So usually try to be as giving equal shrift to each of these two options, but oftentimes that patient will declare themselves very early on here.

reference_conclusion: For this low-risk multifocal papillary thyroid microcarcinoma without extrathyroidal extension or nodal metastasis, management should be individualized through detailed shared decision-making that incorporates tumor location, interval imaging history, absence of nodal disease, and the patient’s psychological tolerance for observation. Active surveillance is an acceptable option despite multifocal disease, although surgery is the preferred recommendation given the limited published experience in this setting. If active surveillance is selected, close follow-up is appropriate, with the understanding that delayed surgery remains feasible if the patient later elects operative management.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 18-year-old female; senior in high school; previously healthy and active.

[ chief complaint ]: Thyroid nodule identified on routine physical examination/wellness check by pediatrician.

[ diagnosis ]: Cribriform morular thyroid carcinoma, initially identified on fine-needle aspiration as papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid nodule was positive for papillary carcinoma. Surgical pathology demonstrated a 1.4 cm cribriform morular thyroid carcinoma. Histologic description included absence of colloid, cribriform architecture, morular formations, and papillary structures. The tumor was intrathyroidal. No lymph node involvement was identified. No other high-risk pathologic features were reported.

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated several small thyroid nodules measuring approximately 10-15 mm, generally classified as TI-RADS 3 and 4. A suspicious hypoechoic solid isthmus nodule was described. No abnormal cervical lymph nodes were identified on ultrasound.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Prior parental whole-genome sequencing reportedly showed no abnormal FAP-associated mutation in either parent.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy was performed and was positive for papillary carcinoma. Surgical resection of the thyroid lesion was performed. Postoperative thyroglobulin was reported as very low/less than 1.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status after thyroid surgery for a 1.4 cm intrathyroidal cribriform morular thyroid carcinoma, without documented nodal disease and without reported high-risk features.

[ other clinical data ]: No family history of thyroid disease or thyroid cancer. No childhood radiation exposure. No symptoms concerning for thyroid malignancy were reported. No family history of colorectal cancer was reported. The presentation included multiple thyroid nodules.

I'm an endocrinologist at the Brigham and Women's Hospital up in Boston, and happy to start on the first case here. Excellent. I'm going to keep us on time as well. I know we've got two other great cases ahead and time moves quickly. It's a pleasure to present to you a case that I thought taught me a lot and had me reflect on a few things, share it with all of you. This is an 18-year-old female who's referred for a thyroid nodule. She's completely healthy, active. She's a senior in high school and it was just a routine physical exam, a wellness check where her pediatrician actually noticed the nodule, and she has no family history of thyroid problems, let alone thyroid cancer, and also the usual questions, no childhood radiation or symptoms of concern. She was completely healthy and not worried about this at all. To keep us moving, obviously, I think most people when you would have a nodule suspected would pursue an ultrasound. And I'm just going to cut to the chase on that. This is the report of the ultrasound, which, as you see, shows several small nodules, roughly 10 to 15 millimeters, and generally classified tirads three and four, and notably no abnormal lymph nodes. And the first teaching point for me a little bit was the questions I posed at the bottom of the slide, which Increasingly, I've been a bit more tuned to this question of how to think about age as a risk factor for thyroid cancer, but I'll throw that out to Eyal maybe a little bit, which is, is there really a meaningful difference in overall risk when you think of a nodule in a younger person than an older person, however you want to define those terms? And then also, do we think about cancer risk at all differently, whether it's one or whether it's multiple? So maybe Eyal, I'll toss it to you for a second.

Yeah, so I think the answer is yes and yes. With age people, healthy people, have more and more nodules and the risk per nodule decreases. So most patients after the age, most people after the age of 60 or 70 have nodules. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable thyroid nodule identified incidentally on examination. No compressive or local thyroid nodule symptoms were reported.

[ diagnosis ]: Medullary thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe with multifocal disease and central compartment nodal metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration cytology of the left thyroid nodule was reported as follicular neoplasm of undetermined significance, with mention of some peripheral cells. Surgical pathology after total thyroidectomy demonstrated two foci of medullary thyroid carcinoma in the left lobe, including a left upper lobe lesion measuring 1.8 cm and an additional small focus in the lower pole of the same lobe. No C-cell hyperplasia was identified. Twenty-two central compartment lymph nodes were examined; 3 were positive for metastatic carcinoma. One involved lymph node measured 1.4 cm, with metastatic deposit measuring 0.4 cm. No extranodal extension was identified.

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a TI-RADS 3 nodule in the right lobe and a TI-RADS 4 nodule in the left lobe. The left-sided lesion met biopsy criteria. Intraoperative ultrasound identified an abnormal left paratracheal lymph node. No lateral compartment lymphadenopathy was identified on intraoperative ultrasound.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Afirma testing on the biopsied thyroid nodule was suspicious and positive for medullary thyroid carcinoma. Germline RET sequencing was negative.

[ laboratory results ]: Calcitonin was elevated preoperatively. CEA was 32. Serum calcium was normal. Plasma metanephrines were obtained. Parathyroid hormone was slightly elevated preoperatively. Immediate postoperative PACU PTH was within acceptable range and was neither elevated nor low.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent total thyroidectomy with bilateral central lymph node dissection. Nerve monitoring was used intraoperatively. Pathology confirmed multifocal medullary thyroid carcinoma with 3/22 positive central lymph nodes.

[ current disease status ]: Status post recent total thyroidectomy and bilateral central lymph node dissection for multifocal medullary thyroid carcinoma with central nodal metastases. No lateral compartment lymphadenopathy was identified intraoperatively.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included hypothyroidism, primary hypertension, and diabetes mellitus requiring intermittent insulin use. Medications included liothyronine (Cytomel), levothyroxine, semaglutide (Ozempic), amlodipine, metformin, and intermittent insulin. Blood pressure had been reported in the 140s to 160s. Family history was notable for paternal grandmother with breast cancer; no family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN syndrome was reported. Married, with one healthy son.

And I believe this was not just medullary, this is all different types of thyroid cancer, but just something to keep in mind when your patients are on that.

Eyal, what's your take on that literature? So I looked at many of these studies, not all of them. I think most of it is detection bias. Because you go see an endocrinologist, and they worry about your thyroid. They do an ultrasound, and then you have thyroid cancer. So I think it's mostly detection bias. And it's almost impossible to tell apart detection bias than real. Sure.
How long does a pandemic develop? Yeah, how long has it been on the market? I mean, we'd have to come up with some kind of latency period before we need to talk about, you know.

Yeah, the class of drugs has been on for about 10 years. There's been a couple of papers now that suggested there was an increase in thyroid cancer. It was significant enough that the EMA, you know, the European group, like the FDA, looked at this back in October and said, there's no signal here, that you can't rule one out. But because of selection bias, that's why they were seeing not only an increase in medullary, but an increase in the papillary. So the paper was published in the diabetes literature, so you'll hear that a lot. But right now, at least the main organizations say probably no direct effect that we can pull apart from just screening and detection. OK. I'm going to move us along. I'm going to carry those. Those were great topics to talk about. Laurie, you've got a couple of topics and a very interesting case in a young lady. So take us through that.

reference_conclusion: Following diagnosis of medullary thyroid carcinoma, the patient underwent total thyroidectomy with bilateral central lymph node dissection after intraoperative identification of an abnormal left paratracheal node and no lateral compartment lymphadenopathy on ultrasound. Pathology demonstrated multifocal medullary thyroid carcinoma in the left lobe with metastases in 3 of 22 central lymph nodes and no extranodal extension. The panel indicated postoperative management should focus on biochemical surveillance, specifically assessment of calcitonin and its doubling time, with consideration of lateral neck dissection only if biomarkers warrant further intervention.
reference_conclusion_quote: So my usual strategy is to do the central and the total and see where the biomarkers come down to. And then if needed later on to do the lateral compartments. [...] So this patient underwent, I always do an on-table ultrasound. And I did note, unfortunately, abnormal left paratracheal node. [...] I did not note any lateral compartment lymphadenopathy. So she underwent a total thyroidectomy, bilateral central lymph node dissection [...] Three of those nodes were involved. [...] And no extra nodal extension was identified. [...] In medullary, we really look at calcitonin and doubling time. So, we can have the same pathology like this, and then it's going to have low calcitonin and stable forever, and we can have the same pathology and calcitonin doubling time of like six or eight months, and then it goes badly. So, it gives us just the first step, but we need to wait for calcitonin and for the dynamics.
