case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult female treated at Massachusetts General Hospital.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent right neck masses following initial treatment for medullary thyroid carcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Sporadic medullary thyroid carcinoma, initially diagnosed in 2016. Initial surgical stage was pT3N1bM0. Recurrent locoregional nodal disease developed postoperatively. Somatic RET-mutant disease with later oligoprogression in a right supraclavicular lymph node while on selpercatinib.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial thyroidectomy pathology demonstrated a 2.5 cm medullary thyroid carcinoma with extrathyroidal extension, lymphovascular invasion, and positive margins. Immunohistochemistry was positive for calcitonin and CEA. Numerous lymph nodes were involved. Several additional microscopic medullary thyroid carcinoma foci were present in the remaining thyroid gland. Revision neck dissection in January 2017 showed metastatic disease in 4 of 9 lymph nodes; the largest metastatic node measured 3.2 cm and showed extranodal extension.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial staging evaluation after January 2017 revision neck surgery showed no evidence of distant metastases. PET/CT performed after development of four new palpable right neck masses over subsequent months demonstrated uptake in multiple nodal stations; the largest node measured 1.6 cm. Restaging CT after 2 months of cabozantinib showed a mixed response, with regression of some cervical lymph nodes but a new 1.0 cm right supraclavicular node. CT after 8 months of cabozantinib showed significant progression. On selpercatinib, serial imaging showed a partial response within the first few months, with a 51% decrease in sum of target lesion diameters, followed by a durable response and eventual radiographic complete response by 2022. In February 2024, evaluation identified a solitary recurrent right supraclavicular lymph node measuring 1.4 cm, radiographically concerning for extranodal extension.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline RET testing was negative. Tumor next-generation sequencing identified a somatic RET M918T mutation.

[ laboratory results ]: Postoperative calcitonin was 181 and CEA was 15.7. After subsequent nodal recurrence, calcitonin was 270 and CEA was 17.1. During cabozantinib treatment, calcitonin and CEA initially decreased, then rose again at progression after 8 months. During selpercatinib treatment, calcitonin and CEA decreased markedly and subsequently normalized for a prolonged interval. With the February 2024 recurrence, calcitonin increased slightly from previously normal levels.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial surgery for medullary thyroid carcinoma was performed in 2016. Revision neck surgery was performed in January 2017 for a new right upper neck mass. Cabozantinib was started in April 2017 for recurrent locoregional disease. Adverse effects on cabozantinib included hypertension, mild diarrhea, mild nausea, hoarseness, hair depigmentation, and later hand-foot syndrome. Best early radiographic assessment on cabozantinib showed mixed response at 2 months; disease progressed significantly by 8 months. Selpercatinib was started in March 2018 on LIBRETTO-001 at 240 mg twice daily. Early treatment response was a partial response with 51% reduction in target lesion measurements. No adverse events were reported on selpercatinib. Treatment produced a long durable response, with radiographic complete response achieved by 2022.

[ current disease status ]: As of February 2024, there was isolated oligoprogressive locoregional recurrence consisting of a solitary 1.4 cm right supraclavicular lymph node. No other active disease sites were described. Selpercatinib treatment was ongoing.

[ other clinical data ]: Four new palpable right neck masses, including one in the right supraclavicular fossa, developed within months after the January 2017 revision surgery.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 54-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidentally detected thyroid nodule on annual physical examination in 2020. The patient had been asymptomatic, with no voice change and no dysphagia.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma diagnosed by fine-needle aspiration of an isthmic thyroid nodule (Bethesda VI).

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration cytology was Bethesda category VI, consistent with papillary thyroid carcinoma. No surgical pathology was available, as no operation had been performed.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Neck ultrasound in 2020 demonstrated a 1.4 × 0.9 × 1.2 cm solid isoechoic nodule in the thyroid isthmus with well-defined borders and no calcifications.  
- No additional nodules were identified in the right or left thyroid lobes.  
- No cervical lymphadenopathy was identified on ultrasound.  
- Serial ultrasound surveillance from 2020 through 2024 showed no significant interval growth of the isthmic tumor over 4 years.

[ laboratory results ]: Thyroid function testing was unremarkable at presentation and remained stable from 2020 through 2024.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Isthmusectomy had been offered because the lesion was confined to the isthmus and there were no bilateral thyroid nodules.  
- The patient did not undergo surgery.  
- The lesion had been managed with surveillance, with stable thyroid function and no significant tumor growth over 4 years.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent biopsy-proven papillary thyroid carcinoma in the thyroid isthmus under nonoperative surveillance. As of 2024, the lesion had shown no significant growth on serial ultrasound. No cervical nodal disease had been identified on available ultrasound imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: No additional objective clinical data were available.

reference_discussion.text: Good morning, everyone. Thank you so much for being here. So we have a first case. This is a 54-year-old man who was found to have a thyroid nodule on an annual physical exam that was back in 2020. The neck ultrasound showed the presence of a 1.4 by 0.9 by 1.2 centimeter solid isoechoic nodule in the isthmus with well defined borders and didn't have any calcification. He did not have any other nodules on the right or the left lobe and did not have any cervical lymphadenopathy. The patient was completely asymptomatic. He didn't have any changes in his voice or any difficulty swallowing. His blood test, his thyroid function test was also completely unremarkable. So he had an FNA that revealed Betesda 6-PTC.

OK, hold right there for me. Go backwards one. Jeff, when you're doing this ultrasound, I check off a box that says ultrasound. But in the community, do I order ultrasound? Do I order lymph nodes? From a practical standpoint, what do you want to see from us when we ask that question?

Well, standard at Memorial, we do a full survey of the thyroid, central neck, and lateral neck for obvious reasons. Unfortunately, for many, many years in the community, that was just not being done. People would just simply get the dimensions of the lobes, report on some of the nodules, and that would be the end of it. That, of course, is not the standard of care, and I think the community is catching on more and more, although we still do plenty of foreign interpretations where we just get the, imaging and thyroid, and we have no idea what the nodal status is, and that's extremely important for every single reason. So, yes, we do that as standard, and it should be done.

Gotcha. Ashok, just initial thoughts. This is a 50-year-old. Even I can probably fill this nodule in the estimates at one and a half centimeters. Sort of, what are you thinking about this case at this point?

Well, you know, the evaluation is very appropriate. I think Jeff mentioned at Memorial, we always look for the central and lateral nodes. That's our practice. You know, you go to Florida, you'd order two separate ultrasounds. So it is a little different, but it's a practice of the institution because Jeff and his colleagues, they know we're interested in the lymph nodes more also in the primary tumor. Now, if you look at this primary tumor, it's well encapsulated. It's involving the isthmus only, not going on either side of the thyroid lobes, which is very important to appreciate. Now, the nodules in the isthmus, which are mobile, and you can practically pull it up from the trachea, I think those are very favorable nodules. We try to avoid them on active surveillance as best as possible. Could they be actively surveyed for a while? Yes. Eventually, he's 54, he's going to come to surgery. in next 45 years his tumor is going to grow probably go in the either side of the thyroid lobe. So I think this is what we think all the time. This surgery is pretty simple. We'll talk a little more when you come to surgical intervention. I just want to add one more thing. As a surgeon, this ultrasound is very nice. It gives you the whole idea, but the CAT scan is something that is quite helpful. The three-dimensional view of the whole thyroid nodule, extend into the surrounding areas, how close it is to the trachea, and is there a plane of cleavage between the thyroid and the trachea? I think that is very important. The one last thing I just want to add, The isthmus is a very small organ, three centimeter thickness. So anything more than that is going to come out of the thyroid. So don't be surprised to find there is extra thyroidal extension in these tumors. That's almost a given in all isthmic thyroid tumors.

Jeff, let me come back to you for a second because you do ultrasounds and you do radiology. Help me understand what the CT scan tells us that maybe we don't see as well in the ultrasound and vice versa.

But with respect to nodal status, as we've discussed many times in DMT, it is extremely helpful to get a CT scan, especially, you know, as a baseline preoperatively. We've had over the last 15 years or so adopted that more and more, and I'm happy to see it. The reason is ultrasound is operated dependent, and depending on, you know, how meticulous the sonographer is going to be, how meticulous the attending, and how often they go into the room, depending on how busy the day is, Things can be missed and even recently we had a case that was scanned where unfortunately an operation was done six months later, came back for the normal surveillance. And lo and behold, there's all this lateral disease. Obviously, the lateral disease was there preoperatively. We just failed to recognize it. And that's one of the failures of ultrasound. So, you know, we used to worry about the radiation dose. Oh, my God, you know, should we? Radiate all these people. It's not that big of a deal. Let's do it. And I find that it helps a lot with nodal status. And, of course, the things that are hidden, like, retrofringal adenopathy, we're never going to see on all the time. Regarding thyroid, you can capture extension with both modality and ultrasound. You know, again, it's operating dependent on ultrasound, how meticulous you want to be. And also, you can create extra tapestry extension just by moving your hand a little bit, and you can hide it that way, too. With CT, you see ill-defined borders. It's sort of a hazy look, and you can find that to be very helpful. So they're complementary, and they're not perfect, but I'm glad that we're getting more and more CT imaging for patients.

Superior on a related question, the biopsy is Bethesda rheumatoid number six. And I always thought that was like 100% thyroid cancer. And we saw a case a couple of weeks ago that it was Bethesda six read by our team. And when we took it out, it wasn't thyroid cancer. But does that happen? Or, you know, should I be worried about that? Trade my cytologist in? Help me with that.

So, Mike, you can hear me clearly, right? Gotcha. Yeah. So, I mean, when you look at the studies, the risk of malignancy for apoptosis sex is between 98 and 100 plus percent. So naturally, some of the cases are going to be very rarely 1% or so that the Bethesda-6 call is going to lead to either a neoplasm or commonly the oncocytic nodules, because the oncocytic cells, which we used to call heart cell cells, can have very atypical nuclei. And sometimes these patients also have chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, which we know can cause horrific reactive change in the nuclei because they are being bombarded by all these inflammatory cytokines. So yes, it does happen, but very rarely it does. And I have seen also cases in which, and I'm sure the search path was also read by the same pathology group, but sometimes there are very small capillary carcinomas that are sitting very close to the main focus that is being biopsied, and that may show a few cells. And depending upon one's threshold, one may call it Bethesda 5 or Bethesda 6.
Okay. So Lena, let's go to the next slide. Give us a little more information. We'll bring Dr. Alexandra and Dr. Newbold into the discussion here. Go ahead.

So, given the location of the nodule that was in the isthmus and he did not have any additional nodules bilaterally, we offer him the possibility of isthmusectomy, but the patient didn't go through any surgical procedure. And as you can see here on the table, his thyroid function has remained stable since 2020 when we started to see him. So the next ultrasound, you will see that since 2020 to 2024, basically the tumor has not grown in the last four years.

So Jeff, I know it's not fair to have you look at two isolated ultrasound pictures without your hand. What's your initial thought when you look at this, understanding different planes and all that stuff?

Yeah, I was surprised that it didn't grow just based on these static images. On the left, wasn't very impressive. I'd give it a TIRADS 3 at most, only based on the fact that it's solid and it's isochoic. I wouldn't give it anything else. The lobularity, and it looks bigger to me on that side, but the lobularity is worrisome. That's something I would push it more into category 4. And given the size, it's 1.4, 1.5, we would definitely, we would buy it. On ATA, same thing. you know, low and intermediate there. We don't have calcifications, but the lobularity is worrisome, and that always pushes my hand into a biopsy.

So Eric, this is a real case. You run into these. How do you deal with this? I mean, we told him years ago to do a surgery. He hasn't. The ultrasound report is saying really no change in size. How do you deal with this and follow with this?

I mean, I think you meet the patient where they're at, and every patient certainly deserves their own autonomy and whatnot. I think, you know, as we all have gone through clinical medicine, you try and find the ability to keep the conversation going, and you certainly don't want to lose the patient knowing that you're dealing here with a malignancy. And certainly you can acknowledge there's some data that we can follow some malignancies conservatively, non-operatively, and they do fine, but there certainly are others. That do not. And the only thing I would share, and maybe this comes up in conversation two or conversation three, is there is some intriguing new data that isthmic nodules are not only higher risk, but molecularly different. And I've never understood why that is, but it is some new data that has caught the attention of many of us. So I would follow him at least every four to six months or so and keep the conversation going.

This seems to be a discussion I'm having more and more because we can never get the pendulum in the middle, right? It was like everybody needs surgery. Now people come to me and say, well, we heard you two never do surgery. In England, are you having this same sort of situation?

Yes, absolutely. And actually, the lower the risk, the more complicated the discussions are becoming, I think, almost. Because obviously, if there is a higher risk, the decision is more black and white. And I absolutely agree. We're having more of these discussions. And so, you know, with a case like this, again, it does very much, as Eric says, come down to the discussion of the individual patient. You know, some patients can live with a little bit of uncertainty. Some patients find they can't, and often that opinion changes for them as well as they go through. And, you know, if they get very anxious before each ultrasound scan, then, you know, you kind of tend towards to move towards some definitive surgical treatment. And I think with this picture, as Jeff said, even though the size may not have changed greatly, the features of it, I mean, just on that one image starts to look a little bit more concerning, and we may have that discussion.

Yeah, and this is one in particular, the three-dimensional volume helps you. Sometimes you get fooled by you're saying they're only changing a millimeter or two, but when you do the volume, you go, holy cow. Dr. Shah, you and I follow a bunch of these. Yeah, if you look at the, you know, I mean, the four years is a good time to say, hey, it's time to do something. He bought four years without surgery. But if you look at the current ultrasound, if I can use the word funky looking, I don't like it, you know. And that is a new classification, you know, Shahad's classification, funky or non-funky. I don't like it. The lobulation that bothers me, it is swinging on one side rather than staying dead in the midline. Maybe this is one picture. So I would definitely push him for surgery. I would tell him that, look, you are going to come to surgery sooner or later. You want to buy another six months? Fine with me. So the surgery, which would have been just the isthmusectomy, may end up with left thyroid lobectomy and isthmusectomy, because we may not be able to get a good margin beyond that. Eric, most of us are pretty comfortable following papillary microcarcinomas now with observation, and now patients are coming in at 1.4, 1.5, 1.6. How does your sort of feel on observation change as you get up in that one and a half centimeters, sometimes almost two centimeters?

I think that's a little bit of the unknown, and I always lead with most well-differentiated thyroid cancer does well, and I was always also reassured by the data out of the, you know, Asian teams that rescue surgery, so to speak. So, you know, finding something that's worse than six, 12 months down the road seems to not impact overall endpoints. And that was always the reassuring that if you were the 1%, 10%, whatever that number is that were to change, you could catch up. To what Ashok was kind of getting at, I do think you look at some and you're just like, I don't really feel that comfortable with this one though. And there is something a little unique about what's growing here in the isthmus. So I would use my best persuasive abilities to talk them into seeing one of our good surgeons.

Yeah. As somebody that tries to develop risk stratification systems, you guys kill me with that funky stuff and I just don't like it. and happy surgeon. Those are all great. They're important prognostic features, but really hard to put in AJCC and ATA risk. Subir, you put the reference up there for the molecular assessment. Can you make any sense out of that for me?

No, I have to read the article first. So, I mean, I think they're high, the BDF or BDF score is high. Also, and I think it's also, as Dr. Shah was saying, it's the location. I mean, on the slide, when I look at it, the nodules in the isthmus, there's not much tissue. to pull them in, you know, and they invade. I see that extension, and I sometimes worry I'm probably over-calling that because there's not much left there. So, you know, but they do have high, it has been shown previously also, they do have a high BRAF-like score. So then, you know, they can be radioactive iodine resistant or more aggressive tumors.

Yeah, interesting. This is sort of their And a few papers talk about how the biologic behavior may be different if it's in the isthmus or lobes or that sort of stuff. And even in those small tumors, at least to me, it feels like they preferentially live sort of subcapsular. I mean, it doesn't seem like they are evenly distributed through the thyroid. So I wonder if It may not be the lobe, but it may be that location relative.
I think it's a real state, to be honest.
I do, too.
And Dr. LaVolze always said, be careful with isthmus nodules.

Yeah, I do, too. I think it's that microenvironment stuff. Okay, let's see. Do the next slide for me there, Dr. Pedraza. And let's see what, so we talked about the location. We talked about the growth rate. Oh, this is a great question. So, uh, we'll do this to Kate, Kate. So the good Dr. Shahad does an isthmus and a hemithyroidectomy and six weeks after the surgery, the TSH is 4.5. Uh, we'll present, we'll pretend this is a 1.3 centimeter papillary thyroid cancer confined to the thyroid. Nothing else special about it at all. Um, what do you do with that TSH?

Well, I would say that the practice in the UK is pretty varied on this. Some of the guidelines now do recommend that we bring the TSH down to the lower end of the normal range. And so I think we've probably moved towards that. For a while, we didn't suppress because, you know, one of the benefits of not having a total thyroidectomy is the patient isn't having to take the thyroxine. But our national guidance has changed to suggest that we do try to bring that TSH down to the lower end of the normal, which for us would be kind of 0.3 to 2, 0.5 to 2 in the US guidelines. So yeah, I think we probably would in that instance.
Gotcha. Eric, what do you really do? Real practice, your practice?

You know, I think there is kind of a graded impact of a lower TSH, meaning a beneficial impact. With lower TSH, the worse your tumor is. And it's probably kind of a linear process. You know, having said that, the pendulum has absolutely shifted and we're doing much less suppression. And there was some recent data that I guess I read the other day that, you know, in low-risk disease, and I guess that's what we're assuming maybe we hypothesized here, Maybe there's not much benefit. So, you know, to me, I don't like a TSH of 4.5 initially. I think the bigger factor to consider clinically is certainly as you deal with someone over the age of 50, long term, I don't like at all the idea of a TSH that's truly suppressed, less than 0.5, because I do think the data as you get older, and the association with AFib is real, and that's a bigger, harder endpoint I don't like. So if you're going to do it, is what I'm getting at, I probably would do it for a year or two, and then I'd loosen it into the normal range. Yeah.

So just from a practical standpoint, we try not to usually bother Erickson and these guys. The first TSH that comes back about six weeks after surgery is often four or five or six. And if you don't do anything for another month or two, they'll often come back at two or three, which makes you feel a little bit better. So in a guy like this, obviously one of the reasons he didn't want surgery was going thyroid hormone. We will give him the option. But it is a graded thing. The more I worry about them, because we do lobectomies on stuff that's not low risk, I will push their TSH down sort of the one to two, recognizing the ATA guidelines completely made up less than 2.5, because we were trying to move everybody away from undetectable TSHs, and we thought people would accept a 2.5 as a baby step. Okay, last question on this one, Eric. What about one of the thermal ablation options for somebody that doesn't want a surgery?

You know, the majority of data, of course, relate to RFA and other non-surgical options in benign nodules and showing the reduction in the structural disease and lack of growth. But really, the data as to treating malignant processes, I think, is a lot less certain. And in this case, where it's right there on the isthmus, not a good location, I don't think. I would not be a fan of RFA for this one.
OK. Dr. Pedraza, any questions that you wanted clarified or that we missed on this one?
No, I think we covered everything.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidental neck lump.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe, tall cell variant, with extrathyroidal extension and metastatic cervical lymph node involvement (right central and right lateral neck).

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid lesion was Bethesda VI papillary thyroid carcinoma. Surgical pathology after total thyroidectomy with right central and right lateral lymph node dissection showed a 1.7 cm papillary thyroid carcinoma, tall cell variant. Vascular invasion was absent. Extrathyroidal extension was present. Right central compartment nodes: 2/3 positive for metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma; largest metastatic focus 1.3 cm; no extranodal extension. Right lateral neck nodes: 4/35 positive for metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma; largest metastatic focus 0.6 cm; no extranodal extension.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial neck ultrasound showed a 1.9 x 1.5 x 1.9 cm solid hypoechoic right thyroid nodule with extension beyond the capsule/posterior capsule involvement, and suspicious right-sided cervical lymph nodes. Post-radioiodine SPECT/CT showed uptake in the thyroid bed and intense uptake in a right level III lymph node. Ultrasound in January 2024 showed a right level IV lymph node measuring 1.2 x 0.7 x 0.6 cm. Follow-up ultrasound approximately 1 year later showed the same right level IV lymph node measuring 1.4 x 0.8 x 0.9 cm with microcalcifications.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Postoperative laboratory studies showed normal TSH, free T4 1.7, thyroglobulin 0.9, and negative thyroglobulin antibodies. After radioactive iodine, thyroglobulin was suppressed. Subsequent thyroid function tests were reported as normal.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent total thyroidectomy with right central and right lateral lymph node dissection. She subsequently received radioactive iodine, 150 mCi, at another hospital. Post-treatment SPECT/CT demonstrated uptake in the thyroid bed and a right level III lymph node. On follow-up, a persistent right level IV cervical lymph node remained detectable on ultrasound and increased from 1.2 x 0.7 x 0.6 cm to 1.4 x 0.8 x 0.9 cm over approximately 1 year, with microcalcifications.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent structural cervical nodal disease was present on surveillance ultrasound in the right lateral neck (level IV), with suppressed thyroglobulin and normal thyroid function tests.

[ other clinical data ]: Thyroglobulin antibodies were negative. No extranodal extension was identified in either the central or lateral neck nodal specimens.

reference_discussion.text: Beautiful. Let's do case number two.

Okay, so we have a 50-year-old woman with an incidental finding of a neck lump and the ultrasound showed a 1.9 by 1.5 by 1.9 centimeter solid hypoechoic right by the nodule extending beyond the capsule and also avoiding the posterior capsule. You can see it here on the a transverse and the sagittal view. She was having some right side lymph nodes also suspicious. And she had an FNA that revealed that it is the 6PTC.

So Jeff, Jeff, help me out with this sort of the ability of ultrasound to detect that, you know, small extra thyroid extension. Sometimes it seems like it does. Other times I don't see it. Help me with that.

Sure. So here you can see it. It's coming up over and it's going to give you the scrap musculature. We still have plenty of room here for the recurrent laryngeal nerve issue. I wouldn't call this a budding, there's plenty of space here. I'm not worried about it and we'd be more worried about this than that anyway. But the fact that it's got extra capsular extension, there are nodes, we're looking for a total thyroidectomy of this. But again, meticulous detail and just literally moving your hand this much, you can hide the extra capsular extension or you can show it.

Yeah, it's been a challenge. I think particularly on the small papillary microcarcinomas we've been following and trying to tell if there's minor extra thyroid extension. It's been a challenge. I mean, sometimes we call it, it's there. Sometimes we don't see it on the path report. What is it about the ultrasound features itself, Jeff, that tells you it's into the capsule or through the capsule, just sort of in general? How do you look at that? It's difficult.

you know, listen, you can have micro extension out that you'll never see. I don't trust the contrast resolution thing. You're bounded by the physics of it. But, you know, if it's something like this, it's easier to tell. You could just see it butting out. It's lively. It's coming in. It has mass effect. And what we do now is when we worry about it, we just have the sonographers take clips so we could, you know, look through all of it. So it's not as operating dependent. We don't rely on the static imaging. And, you know, sometimes that CT will help. It'll show that haziness. sort of a little bit of, not necessarily gross disease, but just a little bit there where you don't see that nice fat plane. And that's when you know that it's extra capsular.

Kate, in a case like this, so we got a papillary cancer, two centimeter, assume there's no other lymph nodes, nothing in the other side of the thyroid. This is all you have on the ultrasound there. Your initial surgical recommendation as you point them to the surgeon is going to be lobe or total, or what are you going to tell these guys?

Well we have a trial running in the UK between hemothyroidectomy and total thyroidectomy so we would see if they fit the eligibility for that and then because we haven't got the results of that trial yet we may be, and if it's going out extra capsule, um, extra thyroidal extension, um, we would probably still lean towards a total, um, in, in this situation, but it is variable.

So, so Eric, um, Asiak often consents these guys for either a lobe or a total, uh, what, what happens if he gets in there and he takes out that, right lobe and there's no gross extra thyroid extension. Strap muscle's not attached to it. It's just a clean right lobectomy. Do you tell him to stop or go ahead and do the total thyroidectomy?

You know, I kind of respected a surgeon's choice in the moment, obviously. And I think the harder one is the patient comes back after hemithyroidectomy. That was the best surgical option despite being consented for both. And then you find something that's kind of in the gray area a little bit. Though I will say increasingly, if you go back 10 years or more, we routinely did completions and now we just don't. And certainly there hasn't been a big uptick death from thyroid cancer. So, you know, I think increasingly it's harder to have the informed discussion with the patient, but then for them to choose to go back for a second surgery. I'll just end by saying the one thing you do get with a completion, with a near total, is you just on the endocrine side of things, you do get much more sensitivity to follow up and detecting recurrence, which certainly can happen.

Yeah. Yeah. And the more we rely on that, the higher risk on that post-op thing. Dr. Shah, for the non-surgeons in the audience, You're looking at this, obviously you're going to be worried about strap muscle. How do you sort of step through that interoperative decision making for me?

You know, I just want to go back. There is an extraterritorial extension which is divided into minor, which is fairly common, and the gross extraterritorial extension. The surgeon's responsibility is to take out all the tumor that he can feel and see. And don't be too surprised, the final pathology report in this patient comes minor pericapsular adipose tissue involvement. And I have a strong feeling, I do this myself. I take out the inner strap muscle, sternothyroid. It has no function, it is a vestigial muscle, but it gives you a sense of security that I have done an oncologically sound operation. Keep in mind, the thickness of the thyroid is barely one centimeter. 3 cm by 2 cm by 1 cm. 1.9 cm thyroid tumor has to be under the capsule of the thyroid. The only time I would consider going back and completing the total thyroidectomy is major vascular invasion which you don't appreciate clinically, radiologically, till you get the final pathology report. And another time I would consider doing total is at the time of surgery, I see a bundle of large lymph nodes. There are 10 lymph nodes. Then I know this patient will be benefited by radioactive iodine. What we need to appreciate, and I think the question was brought both by Eric and Kate, When do we consider completion thyroidectomy? When we feel that this patient would be benefited by addition of radioactive iodine. And that can happen only if there is a major vascular invasion or 10 lymph nodes positive, there is a 11th one which we are not appreciated. Otherwise, there is hardly any reason, no matter what the final pathology report shows, to go back and do a completion. We also have to put in perspective the quality of life difference between lobectomy and total thyroidectomy. I think we have never paid attention to that. We have been having a reflux phenomenon about lobectomy at Memorial and total thyroidectomy at other institutions. And I think we need to get away with that, with the understanding of the quality of life and the long-term outcome.
So, Dr. Pedrasa, tell me what happened with this patient.

So this patient underwent a total thyroidectomy with right central and right lateral lymph node dissection. And as you can see here in the pathology, it was basically a 1.7 PTC, a tall cell variant. There was no vascular invasion, but there was extra thyroidal extension. She had two of three central lymph nodes that were metastatic for PTC, and the largest was 1.3 centimeters. no extranodal extension, and then she had four of 35 right lateral lymph nodes that also showed metastatic papillary thyroid cancer, and the largest one, 0.6, with no extranodal extension. Her labs, post-surgical, showed a normal TCH, free T4 of 1.7, and TG of 0.9, and negative antibodies.
And Sue Barry, help me understand. I mean, I see this report that says tall cells all the time. Help me understand what this tumor is and sort of how do you understand it?

So this is basically based upon morphology, where the cell size, so cell length is two to three times the width, and they tend to have more pinkier and onchocytic cytoplasm, and their nuclear features are readily identified. So if you take all tall cell subtypes of papillary carcinomas and do FNAs on those, they are going to be, I will say greater than 90 plus percent will be outright callable as Bethesda 6. And then you need to have 30% of the tumor that you're examining under glass to have those features to be classified as tall cell subtype of papillary thyroid carcinoma. But the recommendations are, and which the literature also shows, that even if you see a minor component You should mention it, that it is a classic subtype of papillary cancer, but it has features and which is less than 30% given whatever the ratio you calculate, because it has shown those tumors also behave differently than a classic subtype.

Yeah. Eric, I'm trying to sort of re-stratify this tumor in my head based on all these things. The number of lymph nodes, the size of lymph nodes, the percentage of lymph nodes, how do you factor that into how you think about the risk? Not necessarily whether you're going to treat him, but the risk.

Yeah, I think a little bit depends on the extent of dissection, but assuming they looked and they found everything they could find when they removed, you know, I think if you're in particular, the size of the lymph node is important to me. And when you get down to millimeter sized metastatic nodes, meaning, you know, two, three millimeters or smaller, I think you're dealing with no impact there on kind of your risk assessment. Consider those almost irrelevant. When you get into, you know, one to two centimeter nodes, it's certainly real. Here we're dealing with like six nodes. I think this is substantial disease and hence N1B. I also will just say I look at for extranodal extension as a particularly bad adverse finding on path that can sometimes tip me over on next step decision making, and it's good that this patient did not have it.

Good. Kate, help me understand in this 1.5 to 2.5 centimeter range, How that specific tall cell variant versus classic versus solid versus poorly differentiated, everything else remaining the same. How does that aggressive, potentially aggressive histology think about how you think about risk stratification or how you're going to move with your treatments?

So we still use it as a factor that tips us towards considering radioiodine ablation. And that's because those factors, so tall cell variant, columnar variant, and N1B disease were excluded from our trials, the HILO trial and the estimable trial in reducing your ablation activity that you administer. So we still use this as a factor that informs our decision about whether to give iodine ablation and then subsequently which activity we're going to administer.

Dr. Shahab, if I don't know you and I'm looking at op report of somebody from the outside, as an endocrinologist, what's the things I need to look at in your op report on a case like this that, you know, I've got this extra thyroid extension on the pathology report, but what are the stuff you're going to put in the op report that would be critical for us to know after surgery?

First of all, before the pathology report, you need to know the surgeon. because I think that does make a difference. And what's the philosophy of the surgeon? I think that is one important thing. In this case, if you see the lateral nodes, there must be something. We don't do prophylactic lateral node dissection. So they did the lateral node dissection, they found 35 nodes. So this is something more that they were prepared for. So what are you looking for? Number one, the surgeon should describe in his operative report what he felt at the end of the surgery. Did all the tumor come out? Was there gross extraterritorial extension? I'm not talking about minor, that he won't be able to tell. Was the tumor stuck to the muscle? Probably yes. So he should describe that. The other thing he should describe is, were there clinically apparent lymph nodes that he removed? Now Eric made a very good comment on this, 1.3 centimeter metastatic focus, that's not good. that's pretty large. That node was very obvious at the time of surgery. We don't hesitate to get frozen section at the time of surgery primarily because Hashimoto's is so common and the Hashi lymph nodes are so common that the more we dissect the more we're likely to hurt the patients. So I think in the clinical picture, the surgeon should describe about the primary tumor, the lymph node metastasis, gross exothermic extension, and then what is happening to the posterior border of the tumor. Was it stuck to the nerve? Did he have trouble dissecting the nerve? Was it adherent to the trachea or esophagus? I think those are the important points, which probably we don't write in the operative report, but a good surgeon should communicate that with the endocrinologist that, look, I did a good operation, but I'm not happy at the end of the operation. I'm concerned. That's a good indication for doing something more on radioactive iodine.

Awesome. All right, we're gonna put a vote out here and see what we really do. Don't give me any platitudes, don't tell me about guidelines, don't tell me patient preference. It's one of those patients that says, doc, I paid you a lot of money, just tell me what to do. There's a reason I flew all the way to London to get this opinion. So radioactive iodine, yes or no? London, Dr. Newbold? Yes. Boston?
Yes.
Oh my Lord. Dr. Shah?
Yes. I would kiss your hand, Mike.
Dr. Pedraza?
No.

It's because Lena's rotating with me. So I know I'm probably the only person in the country that would tell this guy he probably does not need radioactive iodine. I'll agree with you guys 100%. What you identified was risk factors. No question about it. This guy is at high risk of recurrence. The qualm that I would have is whether radioactive iodine is going to impact that risk of recurrence, right? So I think in the ATA guidelines before, we had sort of really talked about risk and treating because of risk. But in oncology, you have to take the second step, right? Instead, what's the benefit? If this was a medullary, we wouldn't treat with radioactive iodine, right? We all agree that high risk, but there's no benefit. So over the years, I've really come, particularly in these tall cells, to give the patients the option, in fact, lean toward not doing it. It's a long discussion where I got to say, I'm not going to give it to you, and you're still likely to recur. That's a difficult discussion to have. But because this was not one of my patients, Dr. Pedraza, what happened to this patient at Memorial?

So, I have a little bit of this slide for discussion, but I think we cover. So, what happened was this patient in another hospital received 150 milligrams of radioactive iodine. And as you can see here on the spec, it confirmed the uptake on the thyroid bed and the intense uptake on the right level three lymph node.

So help me here, Kate. You know this is a trick case, and you know I'm going to show you one that radioactive iodine didn't work, to prove my point. But in a lesion like this on spec CT, no question, this place grabbed onto radioactive iodine, and almost probably the same as sort of pyramidal lobe there. What would you tell the person the likelihood that destroying this lymph node on ultrasound, it was about a centimeter, a little bit bigger, something like that?

So generally, we would suggest that radioiodine has most of its effect with microscopic disease, obviously, so a sub-centimeter. And, you know, if in follow-up we identify a lymph node that's a centimeter or more, then we would usually go towards surgery before we would consider radioactive iodine, because the chances of iodine, certainly in a one-off administration, in getting rid of that, they're low. In this situation, the patients had it, we would then monitor and see what the effect has been. And that would be with ultrasound to see what the anatomical effect is and also biochemically as well.

Dr. Shah, help me here. This, the, I read the op report from the surgeon and it said he did a totally, he did a right, he did, he took 35 lymph nodes out on the right hand side. That's a respectable number. And yet we have a leftover one centimeter lymph node. How's that happen?

This is a commonality. This is a missed lymph node. This is a, most probably the surgeon had not done the CT scan, most probably, because he would have seen that lymph node and he would have been more kind of inclined to, even though he cleaned up very well, this lymph node was missed. Now, I completely agree whether the radioactive iodine is going to help or not, we don't know. Could he buy time and not rush into second operation? I think I would. Because it is quite likely that this is the fifth node, there is a sixth and seventh node, which will bring him to the second, third and fourth operation. I would rather avoid that and conglomerate that into one nice operation at a best time when the lymph node has increased in size or there is some concern.

So Eric, from a real practical standpoint, what do you tell this guy? How do you do his follow-up? You know, radioactive item apparently did what we wanted to do to start with. What do you set these expectations?

Yeah, I usually tell them, you know, after the kind of shared decision making that we walked through and decided to do it. And I might just make one editorial. 150 millicuries is beyond probably what nine out of 10 people would give. So I just want to make sure that that wasn't the Boston recommended dose. That would be 30, OK?
It was probably Philadelphia, you know, you can't, I totally made that up.

But I think, you know, the way I approach it now is I say, look, there's kind of a standard upfront treatment, which is surgical removal. And if you consider it radio iodine ablation, and you've done that now. And so now it really is about following you over time. And let's see if it did the job, right.
Perfect. Sounds good. And so we're going to follow and where did we go from there, Lena?

So here at this table, what I want to show is the trending of her thyroid function and the thyroglobulin. As you can see, after the radioactive iodine that was on this date, she has suppressed thyroglobulin. But on January 2024, we had an ultrasound that shows a right level IV lymph node that was measuring 1.2 by 0.7 by 0.6. And a year later, with a normal TFTs and suprasterial groaning, we had an ultrasound that showed this in the lymph node that was increasing size to 1.4 by 0.8 by 0.9 with the presence of microcalcifications.
Hey, Jeff, help me understand these, these repeated ultrasound measurements, but what, what, what's the variation I can expect, you know, from, from, you know, experienced ultrasonographers.

So Memorial, we use three millimeters in short axis as our standard for through increase and You know, at the lateral neck, seven millimeters of the short axis is what our cutoff is. However, size is irrelevant when you have concerning features like cystic change and microcalcifications. There are two microcalcifications that are cortical, and that's just a little perivascular stat that's often mistaken for microcalcifications. So three millimeter and any concerning features and or change in reniform shape, more rounded in appearance, peripheral vascularity because the tumor does hit the cortex first before it invades centrally But these little size variations, to me, I would have reported this as really no change, 1.4, 1.2. Again, you can scan it five minutes later and give you a different thing. So really, three millimeters is our threshold. This, I would just say, is stable. The microcalcifications, if they truly are, well, that's, of course, it's not a disease, and it probably is. And, by the way, many lymph nodes that harbor micrometastases show absolutely nothing, but on PATH, we know that they were positive for disease, and we see that all the time.

Kate, in terms of response to radioactivity and the timeline, we have a pretty good feel from external beam radiation, but We'll call this lymph node the same or maybe slightly bigger is what we'll call it for right now. If I wait longer, are we still going to get effective radioactive iodine?

I think, so my experience with macroscopic nodes following iodine uptake is that they won't go away. It's just a question, you know, you'll probably always be able to see them and they probably will always look abnormal structurally. But the question is whether they're active. And so that monitoring is key with the ultrasound is to see if there's any significant growth. I think you don't want to put a needle in it too early because it will be positive and then you're kind of thrown as to whether it's viable or not. But yes, certainly you can still see effect of iodine up to a year afterwards. We know that from our ablation and why we don't do the dynamic risk stratification too early. So I wouldn't rush into anything.
Eric, any role for another dose of radioactive iodine now or at some point in the future? This was RAI Abbott.

No, I rarely, in the last decade, I can't even think on one hand how many times I've double-dosed. I mean, other than the setting of re-differentiated disease for advanced, not this scenario, so no. The only other thing I would note though is in the era, just as we're all clinicians here, in the era of patient-facing notes online, The loaded concern that an ultrasound reads bigger and microcalcification leads to a Google search, and quickly, it's very hard to stop the train sometimes to not do something, right? I agree with everything, but it's worth noting that, right? So how we word all of our notes, not to, you know, in any way take away the real data, but it can be so impactful on the patient decision.

It totally does. Even words like five millimeter thyroid bed mass, because mass has to be huge, right? So that wording and stuff. All right, Ashok, we follow a bunch of these. We've talked about detectable versus actionable. What's going to drive you to actually do something here?

I think this is where the judgment comes. I like to get a CAT scan to see what we're looking for in the CAT scan is the location of the tumor. Remember, when the radiologist reports level four, it's a very big area. It's an entire Siberia. You need to know where the problem is. Is it next to the trachea? Is it adherent to the trachea? That's very important. Is it adherent to the jugular vein? Is it causing indentation on the jugular vein? Is it between the jugular and the carotid artery where the vagus nerve is? I think this is very important and when you talk about detectable versus actionable, I think these are the points that go through our mind. The slight increase doesn't bother me. He is going to need surgery. He is 54. One day he will come to surgery. What is the best time for surgery? Probably we could monitor him and rather than repeating the ultrasound in one year, I would do it in six months. and maybe in a year and a half I would repeat a CAT scan and compare the two CAT scans. So I think those are the important issues when we think about it. The one thing I need to be absolutely sure that in the next six months he doesn't come up with one more node at another level three or level two, which will push me into surgery. The last thing I want to describe is If you are thinking about not doing surgery, don't put a needle in it. Because once you put the needle and that is positive, there is no way, Jose, you're going to stop operating on the patient.

Yeah. And in my own defense, since we gave him radioactive iodine and he had persistent disease, nobody feels bad about it. If I wouldn't have given him radioactive iodine and we were looking at that exact same lymph node right now, we'd feel bad about it. When in fact, we probably didn't make much difference at all. So that's where we're at. Okay, Selena, what questions did you want to finish with us on this one?
I think we covered most of them.

Okay, so no second dose radioactive iodine. We talked about surgery. And I really do think active surveillance in these guys. I don't follow these alone. I follow these either with usually a surgeon or a really good ultrasonographer because it's all about location. All those details you heard Dr. Shah talk about, yeah, I know where level four is, but where is it within level four relative to the nerves and the vessels and that sort of stuff. And every once in a while it'll look to me, it'd be lateral and he'll call me back and he'll go, no, this is really sitting right on in a bad location to take a look at. So having, our surgical colleagues that really understand the anatomy of those. I often tell patients, if I ask the surgeons, if it got bigger, is it going to grow into anything? And if it got bigger, is it going to make your surgery harder? Those two questions would help us kind of know to move in the right direction. All right, Dr. Pedraza, you're on a roll. Let's do some more practical. Let's try one more and see what we get on number three here.

The persistent right level IV nodal abnormality should be managed with active surveillance using serial neck ultrasound, with repeat imaging in approximately 6 months and consideration of interval CT to define anatomic relationships and assess for additional nodal disease. Fine-needle aspiration should be deferred while observation is ongoing, and surgical intervention should be reserved for clinically meaningful progression or the appearance of additional concerning nodal disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 27-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for further management following total thyroidectomy for thyroid carcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma of the left thyroid lobe.

[ histopathology results ]: Total thyroidectomy specimen reviewed at MSK showed a 3.5 cm left-sided poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma. The tumor was completely encapsulated with extensive capsular invasion and marked mitotic activity. Necrosis was absent. Extensive vascular invasion was present in 7 foci. There was no extrathyroidal extension. Tumor was present at the surgical margins. Three perithyroidal lymph nodes were benign.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic test results were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: Approximately 3 months after surgery, serum thyroglobulin was 5.9.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had a history of hyperthyroidism/Graves disease prior to surgery and was prepared preoperatively with methimazole and beta-blockade. He underwent total thyroidectomy in October 2024.

[ current disease status ]: Status post total thyroidectomy for poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma with extensive vascular invasion and positive surgical margins, with a thyroglobulin of 5.9 approximately 3 months after surgery.

[ other clinical data ]: History of hyperthyroidism/Graves disease. A possible consideration of vocal cord paralysis was mentioned, but no confirmed clinical finding was documented.

reference_discussion.text: Yes, so we have a 27-year-old man who underwent a total tyroidectomy in October 2024. He had a history of hyperthyroidism, and prior to surgery, he was prepared with methimazole and metabloccus for the procedure. He came to MSK for further treatment, and then the pathology review here showed a left 3.5-centimeter poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma. completely encapsulated with extensive capsular invasion with marked and methodic activity. There was no necrosis, and there was extensive vascular invasion of seven foci. No extraterritorial extension, and the tumor was present at the surgical margins. Three periterital lymph nodes were benign. And at the time of the visit, we have this a viral panel that showed that three months after the surgery, his seroglobulin was 5.9.
Zuber, take a couple minutes and help me understand this. Your guys' new terminology of poorly differentiated versus high-grade differentiated, where do we sort of put this in that sort of spectrum?

So, I mean, not much has changed. I mean, if you really look into it from the earlier classification, but what we have done, we have created an umbrella term of high-grade follicular drive, that means follicular cell drive carcinomas, and that includes the classic poorly differentiated which was based upon the criteria from what we call as Turin criteria. And now we have brought in also these well-differentiated carcinomas. They look like papillary, they look like tall cell, or they look like columnar cells, but have necrosis and mitosis, which is greater than five by two millimeters square. But the criteria for the poorly differentiated, for diagnosing it stays the same, but it is under that term of high grade. because these have that intermediate to high, you know, the prognostic on the risk of stratification.
And they signal RAS-like, BRAF-like? Do you get a feel for it?

So if it's a papillary thyroid carcinoma, which is high grade, they are BRAF or BRAF-like. but they can have additional like a tart promoter and stuff. Whereas the poorly differentiated carcinoma, depending upon which tumor it's coming from. So most of them are RAS and then they have a layering of other additional mutations or fusions.

Perfect. So Eric, I'll come to you on this, this thyroglobin level here. I mean, we were, we're already thinking this is potentially a higher risk. We're worried about distant metastasis, all that vascular invasion. What do you expect the Firework Goblin to be afterwards? And this one came back at that 5.9. Happy? Not happy? What do you think about that?

You know, as Ashok kind of mentioned, you get to know your team and your surgeons and you kind of fit within kind of the remnant that's normal for each surgeon. Everyone operates a little different. This is a little higher than we would typically see post-operatively, but it's not 40, you know, or something like that. So it's kind of in that middle ground. I find poorly differentiated carcinoma to be worrisome that sometimes it can go bad. Other times it does just fine. It's, it's kind of a very wide range, large standard deviation around this, this pathology in my opinion.

So Eric, I don't know anything about Graves' disease other than how to spell it usually. He had Graves' disease before surgery, No data whatsoever. Do you factor that in as maybe that's why the thyroid goblin's a little bit higher? He probably still has TSIs in whatever remnant tissue, or am I just making that up?

You know, if you're stimulating the TSH receptor, which is a natural growth factor for the cells, I think the clinical reality that that's ever shown to be a negative prognostic factor or a causative problem is nil, really. So I don't lead into that or kind of blame it. I find it a curiosity.

Yeah, me too. Kate, where do you go with this? So, clearly, high-risk guy with all this extensive vascular invasion, young, 27, TGF 5.9, and they're sent to you to consider radioactive iodine, obviously, because this is probably going to be a RAS-driven tumor. Do you do more staging? Do you do a post-op ultrasound? What do you do with that 5.9, Kate?

So if there was any gap from the surgery or the patient was coming from another center then I would do an ultrasound just to make sure that there's no macroscopic disease that's residual that would benefit from further surgery or consideration of further surgery. We wouldn't particularly do any more distant imaging at this point because we would recommend radioiodine and then we would use the post iodine SPECT to fully staged and more sensitively staged. I would probably also do a PET CT at the same time as my iodine with the poorly differentiated components so that I would have both the post iodine scan and an FTG image to look at in just because of my suspicion that you know we may have some iodine non iodine avid disease present and I would want to make sure we weren't missing anything.
And you could do your PET-CT without iodinated contrast, Kate?

Yes, yes, absolutely, yeah. So that if you wanted to go ahead and give the radioactive iodine... Yeah, we kind of make the most of the raised TSH and do it just after they've had their thorogen. We do the FDG, then give the iodine, and so you just maybe increase the sensitivity a little bit by piggybacking onto that.

So Jeff, uh, we're about to run up against the hour here that, you know, traditionally I was taught not to do ultrasounds in the first few months after surgery. And that yet my European colleagues frequently, as Kate said, if there's been a couple three month gap and they haven't seen somebody, uh, can, can you use the ultrasound in that first two or three months after if I'm just looking for golf balls?

Yeah. I mean, if you're looking for golf balls, I mean, we, we wait longer than that usually, but, um, you know, we don't expect to find anything postoperative. Our surgeons are excellent in what they do. And, you know, we, they don't leave macroscopic disease. Except for that one caveat that we said earlier, where the patient came back six months and because of a failed ultrasound, that wasn't all that lateral disease. And I was a very, uh, you know, the, the surgeon was extremely upset. There was a lot of problems with that case, obviously. So, you know, we wait, we, we don't, if there's, you know, there's not going to be macroscopic disease in it. it, you know, we would just follow as you often dealt on DMT. And if it was rising, then we'd have to do some cross-sectional imaging. We've, of course, would start with the ultrasound, but then we'd have to, you have to go beyond that.
Perfect.

So I'm going to stop us there. It turns out that this gentleman had like 25% uptake in the neck and got radioactivated and no distant METs or anything like that. But the discussion about where we cut off that thyrogum in a five, when you do additional imaging, Certainly, the higher it gets, the more we have to be concerned that maybe you don't go straight to radioactive iodine and look and make sure you're not missing just a metastasis or structural disease in that setting. Dr. Shahan, last comments on this. 27-year-old guy, poorly differentiated. As Eric was saying, there's a large spectrum. What's your feel about how this guy's going to do?

In my judgment, he will do quite well because he is young, he has an encapsulated lesion, but what is not good is a major vascular foci of invasion, and he needs to be monitored very closely. If next year his thyroglobulin jumps to 20, that's almost a sign that he had a distant disease. And I would be very careful monitoring his thyroclobin every six months. And this is one patient where I would try to keep the TSH below one with no data, as long as I don't hurt him too much. And I would definitely get endocrinologists directly involved. It's not a one-man show.
Yeah.
I think I would, if it was my patient, I would have you come and see the patient or follow with me.
Yeah. Yeah. This, you're going to need lots of members of the team, potentially on this one. Dr. Pedraza, any last questions on this one before I sign off for everybody?

No, I don't know. I think we covered everything. These are the images of the remnant. And then, um, I think there was a discussion. Uh, we were like a hypothetically said that it, Alternative if there was a vocal cord paralysis, but Yeah, in terms of watching and going back in.

Radioiodine therapy is recommended, with post-treatment iodine SPECT used for staging; FDG PET/CT without iodinated contrast should also be performed around the time of thyrotropin stimulation to assess for possible non-iodine-avid disease. Ongoing surveillance should include close thyroglobulin monitoring every six months, maintenance of TSH below 1 if tolerated, and direct endocrinology involvement in follow-up.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 66-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Compressive thyroid symptoms in late 2023, including dysphagia predominantly for solids, fatigue, constipation, depression, and cognitive symptoms described as “brain fog.”

[ diagnosis ]: Graves disease diagnosed in 2003. Right thyroid lobe neoplasm resected in April 2023, reported as thyroid tumor of uncertain malignant potential. Post-thyroidectomy left thyroid bed hypoechoic lesion identified on surveillance ultrasound in 2024.

[ histopathology results ]: Thyroidectomy specimen from April 2023 showed a 1.7 × 1.1 × 1.2 cm well-circumscribed nodule in the mid portion of the right lobe. No other focal lesions were identified. Surgical margins were negative. Two lymph nodes were negative for malignancy. Background thyroid tissue showed hyperplasia consistent with Graves disease. Pathology was reviewed at the treating institution and by Mayo Clinic, with final interpretation reported as tumor of uncertain malignant potential.

Fine-needle aspiration of the left thyroid bed lesion in 2024 yielded scant cellularity with few follicular cells and a background of mixed lymphocytes and histiocytes, interpreted as consistent with lymphoid tissue. TTF-1 was non-contributory. LCA highlighted lymphocytes. Molecular testing submission was insufficient for analysis.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI cervical spine in 2022 reportedly demonstrated a left thyroid lobe abnormality; outside records were unavailable. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated an approximately 1.5 cm solid isoechoic-to-hypoechoic right lobe nodule. The gland was described as heterogeneous. Follow-up ultrasound in 2024 showed an empty right thyroid bed, a small remnant in the left thyroid bed, and a suspicious hypoechoic lesion in the left thyroid bed.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No contributory molecular/genomic result was available. Specimen submitted for molecular analysis from the thyroid bed lesion was insufficient.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- 2022: Laboratory findings were consistent with active Graves disease, with suppressed TSH, elevated free T4/T3, positive thyroid antibodies, and elevated TSI/TSHR antibodies.  
- Late 2023 preoperatively: Developed hypothyroidism with elevated TSH and low free T4.  
- Immediate postoperative period: TSH 0.1.  
- August 2023: TSH 7.3; thyroglobulin undetectable; thyroglobulin antibodies positive.  
- November 2023: TSH 4.9; thyroglobulin antibodies remained positive.  
- September 2024: TSH 1.2; free T4 1.6; thyroglobulin 2; thyroglobulin antibodies positive.  
- At time of thyroid bed lesion evaluation: TSH 6.6; free T4 1.1; thyroglobulin negative; anti-thyroglobulin result unavailable at that draw, although prior positivity was documented.  
- FNA washout studies from thyroid bed lesion: calcitonin negative; thyroglobulin negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Methimazole therapy had been administered for Graves disease since 2003 with long-term control of hyperthyroidism. Thyroidectomy was performed in April 2023 for compressive symptoms and goiter. Postoperatively, levothyroxine replacement was required and titrated according to TSH. Compressive and hypothyroid symptoms reportedly resolved after surgery.

[ current disease status ]: As of 2024, there were no palpable neck masses. Surveillance ultrasound demonstrated a small left thyroid bed remnant and a suspicious hypoechoic lesion in the left thyroid bed. FNA of this lesion was non-diagnostic for malignancy and favored lymphoid tissue. No confirmed recurrent or metastatic malignancy had been demonstrated.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included Graves disease. Family history included a cousin with thyroid cancer and a mother with thyroid disease of unspecified etiology. The patient was an active smoker at presentation.

reference_discussion.text: Perfect. OK, let's go ahead and get started with the first case.

OK. So yeah, I'll be presenting three interesting thyroid cases and I'm looking forward for that panel's input. So the first case here is 66 year old female, past medical history of Graves disease. And she was diagnosed like long time ago in 2003. She has been treated with methimazole. She has history of thyroid cancer in her cousin and thyroid disease, unknown like etiology in her mom. She was current a smoker when she was presented to the clinic. Just a brief story about her. In 2003, she was having hyperthyroid symptoms. She was treated with methimazole for many years and she was controlled. But in 2022, she had an MRI of cervical spine that showed left thyroid loop in another hospital and the outside records were not available. And 2022 labs showed active Graves' disease, suppressed TSH, and elevated 3T4 and positive antibodies, and also elevated TSR.
And go ahead and show us the ultrasound there.
Yeah. Yeah, the ultrasound showed like around 1.5 centimeter solid isotohypoechoic right lobe nodule.
Catherine, can I put you on the spot here? And it's just two pictures of the ultrasound. What are you seeing on the ultrasound here, Catherine?

And it's a fairly well circumscribed nodule. It's abutting the capsule of the thyroid. No really obvious extra thyroid extension. There's maybe a little blurring of margins in the longitudinal craniocordial view, but I think that's more just artifact than anything else. Fairly heterogeneous gland as well, which would be consistent with thyroiditis, but nothing greatly impressive there.

Dr. Guan, let me bring you on this. So we've got a longstanding Graves person and now a nodule in the setting of the Graves' gland. Do you treat that any differently because of the Graves' disease or you treat it the same way? How do you sort of think about that?

Yeah, actually I think we are treating the same way. Yeah, but if the nodule, if the nodule is suspicious, usually we are trying to, how to say, differentiated diagnosis of seroneodule, benign or malignant. If it's malignant, we are going to send the patients to surgery.

And let me bring Dr. Demirtas in here. She had a family history of a cousin with thyroid cancer. My patients are always worried if they have another family member with thyroid cancer to nodule. Does the presence of a cousin with thyroid cancer bother you or change anything you do about it?
No, it does not bother me that much. But if patient is persisting to get an ultrasound, I do it, to be honest, just for relief of the patient. But yeah, it does not.
Yeah, we try to reassure him. Okay, so keep going, Ibrahim, and let's see what we see.

Sure. So yeah, as part of her course, she developed hypothyroidism in late 2023, TSH was elevated, free T4 was low, and also she started to have some symptoms, like compressive symptoms, dysphagia, mainly for solids, fatigue, constipation, depression, and also brain fog. So just for the compression symptoms and for the goiter, patient had a thyroidectomy in 2023, like in April. and the pathology came back as a tumor of uncertain malignant potential. The pathology was read in our institution and also we sent a specimen to May Clinic for a second opinion and review. And then within like this is like I just copied the report it said like within the mid portion of the right loop there was like 1.7 by 1.1 by 1.2 centimeter of well circumscribed nodule And also no focal lesions were identified. And the surgical margins were negative. There was like two lymph nodes negative for malignancy. And the other cells were like hyperplasia consistent with Graves' disease. And also have a copy of the formal pathology here.
All right, Margie. The first time I heard about this tumor of uncertain malignant potential is in the early Chernobyl days, right? Right, right, right. Tell me what the heck this thing is.

Well, you know, this is a term that, you know, we've heard this said at this forum many a time. It's a term that pathologists should try to avoid if at all possible, because it sounds more ominous than it usually is. You know, if you say unknown potential, just, you know, in the void, it sounds like, well, it could be okay, it could be a disaster, right? We don't know, right? Where in reality, it might be benign or it might be a tumor of low-grade malignant, you know, a low-risk tumor. So, you know, I really can't say anything more than that because there's nothing to look at, right? It's not big. It's 1.7. That decreases my suspicion. The bigger something is, the more likely it is to be malignant. Of course, you could see something that's highly malignant, that's 1.7. But then, you know, it wouldn't be of uncertain malignant potential. We'd have a handle on it. We would see invasion, whatever, you know. So I like to avoid that term.
Dr. Duong, practically when you get this, how do you treat this? Is this benign? Is it cancer? How do you sort of think about this from the endocrine perspective?
You know, for me, I will treat this as a benign because it doesn't show any malignant thing. So I will treat this as benign.

And Catherine, you're the one that gets to talk to the patient first because they see you a week after surgery to look at the scar and you've got the path report. What do you tell the patient with this report, Catherine?

I think the main thing is to reassure them that when the word uncertain appears on a pathology report, it actually makes the patient pretty concerned usually. the first thing is to kind of reassure them that, you know, that we're not uncertain about the diagnosis here and that this is, you know, consistent with benign, it's not invading anywhere, there's no evidence of lymph nodes, and to go through all of the positive factors of that histology report rather than focusing on that one word of uncertain, I think. And then malignant as well, when you get uncertain malignant patients sort of panic, so I agree with And Dr. Brown, you know this is not a great term to have on a pathology report because it usually breeds panic by the time they come in to see you. So reassurance and explanation of what it is and why it's called that as opposed to a malignant tumor.

So Margie, is it fair for me to think about this as somewhere between a follicular adenoma and worst case scenario, like a minimally invasive low risk follicular thyroid cancer that's likely cured with lobectomy or am I on a different path?

Bingo. I think that it's probably something that, you know, maybe has invasion, maybe a capsular invasion, maybe not. Maybe has vascular, maybe not. But, you know, I don't want to say these are highly subjective. That's not true. But they're not, sometimes capsular invasion is not easy, right? So it's probably around that realm.

Yeah, I think so. I mean, we don't see this very often, as Margie said. I mean, this was really brought to us by some really, really expert pathologists that sometimes you just can't tell. But we see this a handful of times. This is not a common diagnosis that we get handed. I do measure one thyroid globulin a few weeks after surgery, the same I would do for a minimally invasive follicular thyroid cancer, and then I follow it. I tell the patient, I think it's benign. If I'm wrong, it's a really low risk thyroid cancer that you're probably cured with lobectomy. So that's how we set kind of the follow-up. All right. So where did we go from there? Go ahead, Dr. Ibrahim.

Thank you. So yeah, post-op labs, we have like the immediately post-op like TSH was 0.1 and then it increased 7.3 by August. Thyroglobulin was undetected but also they have like the antibodies was positive also limiting the TG interpretation as well. Post-op course she required levothyroxine and was titrated according to the TSH. Last one was or like November 2023 her TSH was 4.9, TG antibodies again positive with symptoms completely improved. She does not have any palpable neck masses. Fast forward in September of 2024, TSH is 1.2, 3T4 1.6, TG is 2, again, TG is positive. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 57-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Rapidly enlarging neck mass over approximately 4–6 weeks with dysphagia and compressive symptoms.

[ diagnosis ]: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid mass was reported as malignant and interpreted as consistent with medullary thyroid carcinoma on immunostaining, with calcitonin positive and TTF, PAX, and A103 negative.  
- Definitive surgical pathology after operation in August 2018 showed anaplastic thyroid carcinoma.  
- Tumor size was 8.9 cm.  
- Extensive necrosis was present.  
- Ki-67 proliferation index was 80%.  
- Extrathyroidal extension was present.  
- Surgical margins were positive.  
- Six lymph nodes were examined and were negative for malignancy.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- CT neck in 2018 showed a large relatively hypodense mass replacing the right thyroid lobe.  
- The mass circumferentially involved the right common carotid artery.  
- There was significant mass effect on the trachea with tracheal narrowing, without tracheal invasion identified on the reviewed images.  
- The mass extended into the tracheoesophageal groove.  
- Retrosternal extension was present.  
- Cervical lymph nodes were described on imaging.  
- PET/CT performed 8 days after surgery showed increased FDG avidity in the resection bed and superior mediastinum, with FDG-avid level II lymph nodes.  
- PET/CT performed 65 days after surgery again showed increased avidity in the right thyroid bed and superior mediastinum.  
- PET/CT in October 2021 showed no suspicious lesions.  
- Subsequent CT showed stable postsurgical changes with no recurrent mass in the surgical bed.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- BRAF testing was negative.  
- FoundationOne testing identified NRAS as a potential target for off-label trametinib therapy.  
- PD-L1 status was not provided.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Serum calcitonin was negative.  
- CEA was not elevated.  
- TSH was 3.4 initially.  
- Free T4 was 0.99 initially.  
- TPO antibody was 1.5.  
- Postoperatively, TSH remained within normal range.  
- Postoperative free T4 was 1.4.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent right thyroid lobectomy and right central neck dissection in August 2018. The operation was described as technically difficult because of involvement of multiple adjacent structures.  
- Received aggressive adjuvant chemoradiation consisting of 33 fractions of radiation therapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin.  
- Subsequently received trametinib 2 mg daily as consolidation treatment; dose was reduced to 1.5 mg daily because of severe rash/eruption requiring antibiotic treatment.  
- Remained on trametinib from 2019 until June 2021.  
- Trametinib was discontinued in June 2021.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Off trametinib since June 2021.  
- No evidence of recurrence since discontinuation.  
- Imaging through October 2021 showed no evidence of recurrent disease.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Physical examination at presentation was notable for marked non-tender thyromegaly.  
- Family history included lung cancer in both maternal grandparents and prostate cancer in the father.

reference_conclusion: Postoperative PET/CT demonstrated persistent FDG-avid disease in the right thyroid bed, superior mediastinum, and level II lymph nodes after right thyroid lobectomy and central neck dissection for BRAF-negative anaplastic thyroid carcinoma. The patient was treated with adjuvant concurrent chemoradiation consisting of 33 fractions of radiation therapy with paclitaxel and carboplatin. FoundationOne testing identified NRAS as a potential target, and trametinib was initiated as off-label consolidation therapy, subsequently dose-reduced to 1.5 mg daily because of rash. No completion thyroidectomy or further surgical intervention is indicated at this time; ongoing surveillance is appropriate given the absence of recurrent disease.
reference_conclusion_quote: the patient was referred or like we were managing also the patient with colleagues from oncology and they started an aggressive chemo protocol. He got 33 radiation therapy, fractions of chemotherapy using like Paxil and Carboplatin. And then we did the BRAF, and the BRAF was negative. So we send it to Foundation 1, and they suggested to use an off-label use of trimetanib for targeting the NRAS for the consolidation treatment. [...] So trimetanib was started at 2 mg daily. The patient had very bad eruption after that, so we had to deal with it with antibiotics and then we reduced the dose to 1.5 mg. [...] No, I mean, initially, if you're planning surgery, you may plan a total thyroidectomy. But I think at this point, the bed will be fairly scarred from the radiation as well. It's not going to be a pleasant surgery, a pleasant thyroid lobe to take out. And I think this far out, really, it's probably not under consideration giving any radioactive iodine for potentially differentiated components. So I don't really see any need to touch that lobe, given it looks completely normal in that single ultrasound image. [...] so yeah, I don't see any reason here to do, just take your win and go with it and sit back and watch here.
