case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old female. Past medical history included congenital optic atrophy, reported as probably bilateral.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred in early 2019 after resection of a 12 cm parieto-occipital scalp mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma (FVPTC/FBPTC reported in record), with osseous and orbital metastatic disease. Documented metastatic sites included parieto-occipital scalp/calvarial lesion, temporal bone involvement, and right orbital metastasis with intracranial extension.

[ histopathology results ]:
- Outside pathology from a 4.8 cm right thyroid nodule resected approximately 2 years earlier had initially been reported as benign after right thyroidectomy/lobectomy.
- Following diagnosis of metastatic thyroid carcinoma, outside thyroid pathology was reviewed for second opinion and amended to metastatic follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma.
- Pathology from the resected 12 cm parieto-occipital scalp mass showed metastatic FVPTC.
- Pathology from urgent anterior orbitotomy specimen again showed follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma, with a small amount of background necrosis.

[ imaging findings ]:
- In 2019, CT head and MRI demonstrated metastasis involving the temporal bones and right orbit.
- Post-radioactive iodine treatment scan after 175 mCi showed only small uptake in the right thyroid bed and occipital region.
- Whole-body scan and PET imaging performed in late 2022 with levothyroxine withdrawal showed no metastasis.
- Repeat PET-CT in mid-2024 showed no abnormalities despite rising thyroglobulin.
- After recombinant TSH stimulation, scan demonstrated intense right orbital uptake.
- CT showed right orbital disease with intracranial extension.
- Imaging of the orbital mass showed proptosis, significant mass effect on the right globe, and areas of flow void consistent with marked vascularity.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]:
- At initial detection of metastatic disease, serum thyroglobulin was 778.
- After surgical resection of the scalp mass, thyroglobulin became undetectable.
- Thyroglobulin remained completely undetectable until late 2022.
- In late 2022, thyroglobulin rose to 10 over 6 months.
- Thyroglobulin then remained detectable but below 10 until mid-2024.
- In mid-2024, thyroglobulin increased to 64.
- Five months later, thyroglobulin increased to 181.
- After recombinant TSH stimulation (0.9 mg IM twice), stimulated thyroglobulin was 1300 and TSH was approximately 80.
- Thyroglobulin antibodies were negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:
- Approximately 2 years before referral, the patient underwent right thyroidectomy/lobectomy for a 4.8 cm thyroid nodule; original outside pathology had been reported as benign.
- In early 2019, the patient underwent surgical resection of a 12 cm parieto-occipital scalp mass; pathology showed metastatic FVPTC. Postoperatively, thyroglobulin became undetectable.
- In 2019, the patient underwent completion thyroidectomy.
- Following identification of temporal bone/right orbital metastatic disease, the patient underwent additional surgical resection of this mass.
- The patient received radioactive iodine, 175 mCi. Post-treatment scan showed only small uptake in the right thyroid bed and occipital region.
- After development of right eye proptosis and edema following recombinant TSH stimulation, high-dose corticosteroids were administered.
- The patient subsequently underwent urgent anterior orbitotomy; pathology again showed follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma with small background necrosis.

[ current disease status ]: Rising thyroglobulin in 2024 was followed by clinically and radiographically evident progressive right orbital metastatic disease with intracranial extension.

[ other clinical data ]:
- The patient had poor tolerance to levothyroxine withdrawal, prompting use of recombinant TSH for subsequent stimulated evaluation.
- Right orbital disease developed with right eye proptosis and edema.
- Vision preservation was a significant clinical consideration because of pre-existing optic nerve atrophy.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, so this is a long story, but I will try to summarize it. So this patient was referred to us in early 2019. She's a 70-year-old female, past medical history of congenital optic atrophy. She came in after a removal of a 12-centimeter parieto-occipital scalp mass, and the pathology was metastatic FBPTC. The patient had two years prior to that. She had a right thyroidectomy or lobectomy, for a 4.8 centimeter nodule. The final pathology was in an outside hospital that showed as benign, but then when we received the diagnosis of the FVPTC, we send it again for a second opinion and it was amended to be metastatic. So at the time of initial detection of the metastasis, the serum thyroglobulin was 778, which was consistent with active metastatic disease. The patient had a surgical resection of the scalp mass, her thyroglobulin was undetected, reflecting the reduction of the tumor burden. Then afterwards, she'd had a completion thyroidectomy in 2019 and a CAT scan of her head showed, an MRI as well, showed a metastasis in the temporal bones in the right orbit. Then the patient had another surgery and we resected this mass and she received 175 microcurie of the radioactive iodine. The post-treatment scan showed only small uptake in the right thyroid bit and the occipital region.

Laurie, help me with this sort of natural history here. Somebody presenting with this big tumor and then a bone mat. What are you sort of thinking about natural histories likely to happen here, Laurie?

Well, so, you know, that big 12 centimeter calvarial lesion probably had been there for a long time. And so, I think that this seems like a very rapidly aggressive, progressive cancer, but it may not be. However, with this lesion here on the CT scan invading the right orbit, it makes you wonder because with the calvarial lesion, the patient would have had good head imaging and a lesion there should have been appreciated even if it was a little bit smaller. So I am a little bit worried about this being a more aggressive variant than a typical follicular variant PTC. And you can see disease that's been around for a long time becoming more more de-differentiated and have one area in particular becoming more de-differentiated than disease elsewhere. So, I'm a little bit concerned about what the histology of that particular orbital lesion is.
Azita, any comments on that imaging other than there's a big blob there?

No, well, the mass, if you look at it, has areas of flow void, which means it's very vascular, which you typically see. It has proptosis. It has significant mass effect against the right globe. And there is one thing that's very important that was in the histories. The patient already has optic nerve atrophy, and it's probably bilateral. So in terms of, you know, vision preservation is very important in this patient.
Very good. Okay, and where do we go from here, Dr. Imer?

Yeah, so the patient had like the completion thyroidectomy in 2019 and she has been following up with us. She had like a completely undetectable thyroglobulin until late 2022, which like subsequently it rose to 10 over six months. We did an i9 whole body scan and also PET scanning with levothyroxine withdrawal that showed no metastasis. Thyroglobulin was like stabilized, was below 10. It was detectable but was below 10 until mid of 2024. Then suddenly the thyroglobulin increased to 64 and then we were thinking about like possible de-differentiation like given the prior negative scanning. So we repeated again like the PET-CT that showed like no abnormalities. But five months later, the thyroglobulin increased to 181. And then during that time, we decided to do the precombinant TSH with the scanning because the patient had poor tolerance to the levothyroxine withdrawal. So the protocol that we used was like 0.9 IM twice and the patient had like a stimulated thyroglobin of 1300, TSH was around 80 and the thyroglobin level was antibody was negative. Suddenly after the recombinant TSH patient started to have right eye proptosis, edema, and then the scan showed intense right orbital uptake with intracranial extension on the CAT scan. I have a video here, hopefully you can detect a little bit of the uptakes.

All right, so David, help me here. We always were, when we got thyrogen years ago, we were always worried that we were going to see big swelling either in the spine or in the brain. How often does that happen and if you do, how do you deal with it, David?

Yeah, so it's rare. It is very rare when it occurs. Clearly it is a concern. I mean, I haven't personally had this, you know, happen to me in this scenario, but really, you know, the key is in those patients that are at particular risk, you know, it's worthwhile doing, you know, appropriate staging beforehand when you are suspecting either clinically metastases or otherwise, if there is a significant likelihood, particularly of cerebral or spinal mets to do imaging, to confirm that before you know, treatment, but then really if it does occur, you know, that key step is giving things like steroids to try to reduce that, you know, edema and swelling and inflammation and, you know, manage accordingly on spec in this case.

Yeah, because our usual approach in the setting of these widespread distant meds is to treat any of them that we know about before we give the thyrogen. Like we radiate before, we give them steroids and stuff before, but every once in a while you get surprised because you didn't know one was there. Okay and so you guys had some swelling with the thyrogen and then where did you go from there?

Correct, so we gave her a high dose of corticosteroids but then the patient unfortunately she went for another surgery which was an urgent anterior orbitotomy and then the specimen again showed a follicular barium PTC. was a small amount of background necrosis and this was the CAT scan after the MRI. The tumor board in our institution recommended orbital inoculation with limited craniotomy. because of the progressive orbital metastasis invading the intracranial space. The patient underwent the surgery in late 2024. It was a big surgery. We have people from ophthalmology, neurosurgery, ENT, and this is the pathology. Also, the patient got external beam radiation and the surgical pathology confirmed the follicular variant BTC.
I mean, this just seems like way out of control for a follicular variant.

Sure. So, you know, like, this is not the typical story. You know, I have seen, unfortunately, you know, a benign thyroidectomy and then a bone mat. So this is not the first time I've seen this. And then go back to the original benign histology and find out something that is not benign. But even then, you know, it's not the typical story for for PPC follicular variant. So I would put money down that, you know, if they go back and they look at the original thyroid lesion, that they're going to find the high mitotic rate or some necrosis, you know. And so I think from the get go, this is acting like high grade differentiated thyroid carcinoma. And so from here, all I could see is, well, this is thyroid and, you know, I'm sure it's TTF1. And then, you know, you have to look at the overall picture for four prognostic. You know, it's not the picture of, as you say, a usual follicular variant PTC.

Yeah. Laurie, thoughts about this one for me? I mean, this is, it's a weird pattern. I suspect Margie's probably right. If we looked into it, it'd be. some molecular combination? How are you thinking about this, Laurie?

So I think, you know, we don't quite know the extent of disease elsewhere, but this is bad disease and in bad places. And so even if there's not a large tumor burden elsewhere, if there is some residual disease, my interest in starting an effective systemic therapy is a sooner rather than later thing. For the tyrosine kinase inhibitors, the word on the street used to be that they don't work in bone. But we actually, when we took a look at the select patients from the lenbatin and phase three trial who had bony disease, they had the same progression-free survival benefit that patients with other METs like lung METs had. So I do actually think that there is a role for Linvatinib offering benefit when patients biggest problems are bone metastases. So that's one thing, you know, we definitely want to know the genotype. What I'd really like to know is, you know, in addition to a driver alteration here, Are there additional alterations that are suggesting this is a much more aggressive disease, like an ARID1A commutation or a P53 commutation? Again, those aren't drugable, but they can give us an idea of what to expect going down the road.
Dr. Wang, what are you thinking here to help them out?

You know, first of all, we didn't have a research until end of last year in China. So, so we only do withdraw of ILT4 in China. But right now, we do have a recombination TSH now in China, so we are hearing what kind of thing will happen. Especially this is a very special case, but it's very interesting case and I noticed this case was published already, so I will introduce this case to my to my colleagues. And the second for this patient. So why do we should put further therapy or treatment. So, I will discuss with my oncologist and not endocrinologist. So, in China, most endocrinologists actually do not treat cell cancer at this late stage.

Yeah, same way in the United States. Laurie, the role for bisphosphonates or zoledronic acid in people with bone meds, it seems to wax and wane. We use it some years and we don't. Where are we sort of, I mean, this patient's going to have other bone meds because it's coming up in the bone. Do you use the zoledronic acid or one of the other ones? How do you do that, Laurie?

Yeah we do. So you know unfortunately we don't have randomized phase 3 trials in people with thyroid cancer with bone modifying agents and bone metastases but there have been studies done across other solid tumors that have shown both with zoledronic acid as well as denosumab that the bone modifying agents do decrease the risk of complications related to bone metastases, including things that are really meaningful like pain, need for surgery, pathologic fracture. So we use them. I think one of the things that's different about the thyroid cancer patient population is that they tend to live for a long time. And so what's the right frequency of using those drugs and for how long do we use them? We don't have great data, but I usually give the bone-modifying agents every three months, and I might stop after two or three years. The other thing is, you know, with this patient population with radioactive iodine, they have xerostomia. Our patients may be at a slightly higher risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw on bone-modifying agents, so you definitely want to make sure that the patient's dental health is in good shape.

Dr. Demers, let me bring you back in. Just from the practical clinical aspects of taking somebody like that. I mean, we endocrinologists do thyroid cancer and people do well, and we send them back for surgery. We're not usually sending them back for big eye surgeries or, you know, even taking tracheas out and that sort of stuff. How do you sort of think through that discussion with the patient? I know the discussion happens at the disease management team, but how does that get translated back to this individual patient at your Geist Center?

So I think it's a hard discussion. It's going to be a hard discussion because it's going to be compromising the eye. It's going to be a tough discussion. That would be a tough one. I don't have a real answer, but I would probably put it out in a way that here is the disease, and this is what we are kind of Making a decision as a team, we think this is a better idea to do and I would probably bring up to the patient and we'll kind of, you know, get the patient's output and see what the patient thinks about the, because some patients don't want to do anything, you know, they will just say, I'm fine, I don't want to lose my eye. Yeah, it depends on the patient, yeah. So I would try to do with the patient like, we'll try to be on the same page with the patient, yeah.

David, can you speak to sort of how your disease management team communicates this information with the patient? Is there one person that's the lead of everything or is it the person that's known them the longest or is it different? How does that really work on these difficult discussions, David?

Yeah, I think it really depends on which clinician has had the most, you know, contact and has the best rapport with the patient. So, you know, some patients will have, you know, been predominantly followed in nuclear medicine or within radiation oncology or endocrinology. So it really depends on who has that best rapport with the patient and their family. or a medical oncologist. I mean, in this case, I think it would be a discussion with the surgeon, who's really that key decision maker. But yeah, I think it really depends on who has that best rapport, and also, in this case, who's actually gonna be delivering the intervention as the best.

Exactly, yeah, that everybody's on the same page, somebody's not being too optimistic, too pessimistic, we're giving the same message, and then we do the same thing. Whoever's really delivering that, aggressive treatment, whether it's the oncologist or the radiation oncologist. They're making the final decisions, but all of us are supporting that in the background. Difficult things that we're not traditionally trained to do as endocrinologists, part of that. Fantastic. Well, let me say thank you very much to our team from Missouri. These were great cases. They were some wonderful discussions. Oh, perfect. And that's the publication that we were talking about. Beautiful. That's there. Perfect. All right. Thank you again for doing that. So coming up will be Dr. Nair, an interesting discussion next week, and then you can see the other ones coming. And then just a reminder about the Voices of Wisdom. I got it right this time. Wonderful podcast, great things to listen to. Thanks again to our panelists. We stuck to the landing right on time. Wonderful cases. Thanks, team. Bye-bye.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 69-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for evaluation of primary hyperparathyroidism. Reported musculoskeletal pain. No history of nephrolithiasis or pathologic fractures.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- Primary hyperparathyroidism.  
- Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe, tall cell subtype, multifocal, with nodal metastasis.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Fine-needle aspiration of the thyroid nodule was diagnostic of papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Thyroidectomy pathology demonstrated papillary thyroid carcinoma, tall cell subtype.  
- Multifocal disease was present.  
- Metastatic carcinoma was identified in a lymph node deposit measuring approximately 0.2 cm.  
- Two parathyroid glands were excised: right upper parathyroid gland and intrathymic left lower parathyroid gland.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Neck ultrasound demonstrated a highly suspicious right thyroid nodule, 1.8 cm in greatest dimension, described as solid, hypoechoic, with infiltrative ill-defined margins; categorized as ATA highly suspicious / ACR TI-RADS 5.  
- Ultrasound also demonstrated an enlarged right upper parathyroid gland.  
- Post-radioiodine imaging showed uptake including a focus above the left clavicle consistent with a supraclavicular lymph node; a right-sided focus could represent residual thyroid bed uptake.  
- Follow-up neck ultrasound demonstrated a central compartment (level VI) lymph node measuring 4 x 8 x 6 mm, indeterminate in appearance, without definite cystic change.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- No tumor molecular testing results were reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Hypercalcemia was present.  
- Parathyroid hormone: 122.  
- Vitamin D: normal.  
- 24-hour urinary calcium: increased.  
- Postoperative thyroglobulin became undetectable.  
- TSH was suppressed postoperatively.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent total thyroidectomy.  
- Underwent excision of the right upper parathyroid gland and an intrathymic left lower parathyroid gland.  
- Received radioactive iodine therapy, 80 mCi, approximately 5 years before the current review.  
- A small central neck lesion was biopsied after treatment.

[ current disease status ]:  
- No biochemical evidence of persistent thyroid carcinoma was documented, with undetectable thyroglobulin after treatment.  
- Persistent small-volume structural disease was present in the central neck as a level VI lymph node measuring 4 x 8 x 6 mm.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past medical history: hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation.  
- Family, social, and surgical history were otherwise unremarkable.  
- The patient had been anticoagulated for atrial fibrillation.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you. Thank you for allowing us to present today. I wanted to bring this case up because it was actually after Dr. Tuttle visited us that my management of this patient really changed. So this is a 69 year old female who was actually referred for primary hyperparathyroidism. Her biochemical profile is pretty consistent with primary parathyroidism, elevated calcium, PTH of 122, and a setting of normal vitamin D and an increased 24-hour urinary calcium. Her medical history, just hypertension, hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation, otherwise unremarkable family, social, or surgical history. Her presenting symptom, she felt overwhelmed except for some musculoskeletal pain, otherwise no kidney stones or pathologic fractures. And with all of our patients, we started examining her and obviously doing a neck ultrasound.
All right, Jill, let's take a look at the ultrasound. What do you see in there?

Yeah, so we do see a very highly suspicious nodule using ATA lingo, a TYRAT5 nodule using American ACR. So this almost certainly would be a neoplasm. It's solid, it's hypoechoic, it has infiltrating ill-defined margins, highly suspect for a papillary cancer.
So this was a, you know, greatest dementia 1.8 centimeters, exactly what you said, and also very obvious right upper parathyroid gland.

So Jill, help me out here a little bit. This is obvious to surgeons and you guys that look at that, but help me understand why is that not a lymph node? Why is that a parathyroid gland? How do you sort of think through that, Jill?

Yeah, that's a very good question. And certainly there's overlap. So for a classic enlarged parathyroid gland, the color Doppler is actually really helpful. It'll have rim or arc-like flow as opposed to a lymph node, which would have sort of central arborizing flow or no flow. Of course, not all parathyroids read the book. And if I were to see cystic change or echogenic foci calcifications, that would favor that it's a metastatic lymph node. In some patients, particularly the renal failure patients, however, that have secondary tertiary hyperpara, they can have those more atypical findings. But when all is said and done, this does look like it favors a enlarged parathyroid gland.
Okay. Joyce? I'm trying to find my cursor. Okay. So we did an FNA, pretty classic, PTC, and cytology.

Pause there for me for a second. So normally when we're having this discussion, we're having the argument of 1.8 centimeter, do we do a lobectomy, do a total thyroidectomy? Now that you've got this parathyroid thing going on the same side, I mean, it's the nodules on the right side, the parathyroid gland looks on the right side. How does that dealing with the parathyroid change how you think about total versus low from a practical standpoint, Mark? Thanks, Mike.

I think it's a good question. I mean, I think every once in a while, a couple times a year, we'll get a case that's got a concurrent type of parathyroidism plus a capillary thyroid cancer. In this case, it's incidental. So yeah, if it's on the same side, it makes it more straightforward. Most of us who do parathyroid surgery We'll still use intraoperative PTHs to confirm that we have successfully helped the patient by reducing their PTH according to the Miami criteria, at least 50% drop at 10 minutes. But I think when I'm thinking about lobe versus total, I'm typically even more likely to do a lobe in somebody who as primary hair parathyroidism if the parathyroid adenoma, suspected adenoma, is on the same cell side. It's a little bit trickier. You have to think about what are the risks that you have to go back to in the future. I still, in most cases, do a low, but it's a little bit more discussion.
Perfect. All right. So it'd be one or the other. And Joyce, what did you guys choose to do?

So with the discussion with the patient, this is my patient, so I remember she was a little bit nervous going off of her anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation. Here at the Cleveland Clinic, we always do a four-gallon expiration, so they will be scarring on both sides if we ever needed to go back for a completion. So all those discussions were had and she opted for a total thyroidectomy. although the cancer is small enough to potentially undergo a lobectomy. We also did excise two glands, the right upper as we've seen, and there was an intrathemic left lower parathyroid gland as well.
Perfect.
Alrighty, and let's look at the pathology. Dr. Golosh, this is my favorite thing to do, show you two pictures and have you give us a formal opinion. What do you see, Zuber?

OK, so on the left hand side, as you can see, that's like a medium to high power picture of papillary thyroid carcinoma. And if you look at the right, my right, actually, at the edge of that picture here, the cells, if you take an individual cells, they are actually tall. So they are about almost two to three times the width of the cell. And the nuclei you can see in the middle where there's a lot of blood is actually the papillary core is. You can see beautiful intranuclear holes, and there's many of those. Now, if you go to the, almost again to the right side, you see the cells are kind of lining up what is called the tram track appearance. So they are very parallel to each other, the way cells are lining up. So those are the typical features of a papillary thyroid carcinoma tall cell subtype. And on the right hand side, you see a lymph node metastatic deposit in a lymph node, and which, you know, from even the screen looks like about 0.2 centimeter or a little less, almost to 0.2 centimeters. I mean, that has to be measured. So this is a classic case of a tall cell subtype of PTC with a lymph node met.

Perfect. Nicole, what are you thinking now? We'll assume the parathyroid gland is all taken care of. We've got It looks like a little multifocal. It's a tall cell subtype. What's the prognosis here? Help me risk, and then I'll come to JP and Monica, and we'll talk about maybe the role of radioactive iodine. risk and sort of prognosis? What are we thinking here?

Well, we're thinking it's incidental, so the presentation would be low itself. The tall cell variant does make it a probable BRF-driven thyroid cancer, but it's small, it's two centimeters, and so I would think this would be a low-risk thyroid.
And at your center in Mexico, Nicole, would you normally give radioactive iodine here or talk about it with the patient or normally don't give?
We talk about it with the patient. In the past it was given like almost to everybody but now we're trying to selectively give the radioactive iodine.

I got you. JP, a lot of discussion over the last sort of five or ten years about radioactive iodine responsiveness and tall cell and whether to use it or not use it. Where are you and the team at the Mayo on this right now?

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 36-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Right thyroid nodule with bulky cervical lymphadenopathy.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma, infiltrative follicular subtype, involving the right thyroid with metastatic cervical lymph node disease. Residual/recurrent cervical nodal disease and suspected contralateral thyroid involvement were subsequently identified.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration of the right thyroid nodule at an outside hospital showed atypia of undetermined significance and was suspicious for ETV6::NTRK3 fusion. Surgical pathology from the outside operation showed papillary thyroid carcinoma, infiltrative follicular subtype. Skeletal muscle was present in the specimen without microscopic skeletal muscle invasion. A right cricothyroid mass specimen contained positive papillary thyroid carcinoma, submitted in the context of margin assessment. Multiple lymph nodes were positive for papillary thyroid carcinoma in both the central and lateral neck. Histology demonstrated an infiltrative follicular-pattern papillary carcinoma with papillary-type nuclear features and colloid-containing follicles. Subsequent biopsy of abnormal bilateral level II lymph nodes showed papillary thyroid carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial presentation included a right thyroid nodule and bulky lymphadenopathy. Postoperative neck ultrasound demonstrated a remaining left thyroid lobe containing multiple tiny foci without a discrete nodule, concerning for infiltrative intrathyroidal disease. Ultrasound also showed two abnormal level VI lymph nodes with hyperechoic foci, irregular margins, and enlargement, suspicious for metastatic disease. Bilateral lateral cervical lymphadenopathy was present, including abnormal level II nodes with cystic change and echogenic foci. Neck CT demonstrated medialization of the right vocal cord, consistent with right recurrent laryngeal nerve sacrifice, bilateral abnormal enhancing lymph nodes at the level of the carotid bifurcation, and a small enhancing abnormal lymph node in the lower neck at level VI/VII. Radioiodine whole-body scan/SPECT showed avid uptake throughout the left thyroid lobe and uptake in lymph nodes adjacent to the clavicles.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Cytology/molecular assessment of the right thyroid nodule was suspicious for ETV6::NTRK3 fusion.

[ laboratory results ]: Serum thyroglobulin was 39. Thyroglobulin in lymph node aspirates was markedly elevated.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: At an outside institution, the patient underwent right thyroidectomy, excision of a right cricothyroid mass, right central neck dissection, and right modified radical neck dissection. Left thyroidectomy was not performed. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve was sacrificed intraoperatively because of tumor encasement. After referral, abnormal bilateral level II lymph nodes were biopsied and confirmed metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma. The patient subsequently underwent left modified radical neck dissection and revision/selective right lymph node dissection. Left thyroidectomy was not performed at that operation because of concern regarding the only remaining recurrent laryngeal nerve. A diagnostic radioiodine scan was then obtained and demonstrated avid uptake in the residual left thyroid lobe and nodal uptake near the clavicles.

[ current disease status ]: Residual left thyroid lobe remained in situ with imaging findings concerning for infiltrative thyroid carcinoma. Persistent metastatic cervical nodal disease had been documented by ultrasound, CT, biopsy, and radioiodine imaging. The patient had right vocal cord paralysis following sacrifice of the right recurrent laryngeal nerve.

[ other clinical data ]: Operative findings from the outside surgery documented tumor encasement of the right recurrent laryngeal nerve. The residual left thyroid lobe was described on palpation as very firm. The patient had expressed strong concern about any intervention that might risk loss of the remaining recurrent laryngeal nerve and possible tracheostomy.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, so this is a patient, a young patient, 36-year-old male. An outside hospital was found to have a right thyroid nodule and bulky lymphadenopathy. According to the operative report, obviously it was an ugly cancer. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve was sacrificed due to tumor encasement, very detailed in the fact that it just was not able to be saved. But before we go to the pathology, Zuber, these names of these genes just keep getting longer and longer with more initials. So help me with this one, this NTRK fusion.

So, I mean, I think this is a very interesting part that, you know, the molecular pathology has really helped us understand. And it kind of, I think, also relates to how these tumors present, their pathologic features, as well as their clinical follow-up. So if you look at the three main food groups of papillary thyroid carcinomas, you know, you have BRAF-associated tumors, which is your classic and tall cell. Then there are follicular pattern tumors, which are mainly RAS-associated tumors, NRAS, KRAS, and HRAS, along with other mutations or stuff. Now, this is a third food group, which is actually the translocation or fusion associated carcinomas, which are two main genes and they fuse. Basically, there is a exchange of genetic material and it fuses. And in most cases, there is over activation of the tyrosine kinase pathway and it leads to these tumors. The classic poster child for this is diffuse sclerosing subtype that we saw with RADPTC, especially after the nuclear accidents that happened around the world and in those databases, we came across these tumors. So these are bulky infiltrative tumors. They are very heterogeneous in morphology. Sometimes they can have just papillary carcinoma features. or they can have mixture of like follicle formations, solid growth, multiple somoma bodies, and papillary carcinomas. They tend to be infiltrative tumors with a very bulky lymphadenopathy. And as we know, the NTRK3 is not just for papillary carcinoma. It's the same translocations or fusion you can find in salivary gland and other carcinomas. So we do have targeted therapies for this. So this is actually, for me, this is like not good for the patients, but this is really a fantastic way of looking at these tumors and now it really explains why some of these tumors are the way they present and stuff and it kind of we see the same scenario in other other tumors throughout the body also.

Mark let me bring you in here so when we see we've got a 36 year old guy we've got big bulky disease let's pretend like we knew that it was invading nerve that sort of stuff before the surgery. Zubair mentioned this is a targetable mutation where are we with like Tell us about neoadjuvant therapy, what that really means, and should we be thinking about something like that with a known fusion like this, Mark?

Yeah, it's a great question. I mean, the short answer is yes, we should be thinking about it. I mean, this patient, I'm assuming that on a patient like this that's got bulky thyroid disease as well as lymphadenopathy, you're going to get a preoperative CT neck with contrast, and you're going to be able to see sort of the degree of extramural extension here. And if there is significant extension into the tracheoesophageal groove, which I'm assuming there may have been here, or, you know, significant extranodal extension, you can appreciate on the scan, you know, you would think about the possibility of neoadjuvant, you know, in this case. inhibitor, which is very effective. You can get 40, 50, 60% shrinkage of this tumor and it may help you. I mean, in this case, in hindsight, I mean, the nerve was sacrificed. So you don't have a lot to lose with the neoadjuvant approach here in terms of maybe the possibility of saving that nerve.
Yeah, it's kind of sort of what the newer things we're thinking about. All right, Joyce, let's look at the pathology and see what this tumor actually looks like. Zuber?

Yeah, so I mean, if you see on the, which is a beautiful shot of this tumor on the leftmost side, and I've been on the low power, you can see it's an infiltrative process. It's not a nodule, main nodule of tumor. And you have these small groups, irregular shapes kind of infiltrating and it also causing tumor associated fibrosis, which is the host response. On the high power, it has nuclear cytology of papillary carcinoma. It's forming follicles with colloid in it. So it's an infiltrative follicular pattern papillary carcinoma, which is the infiltrative follicular subtype. I do want to pitch in that we do not use the term variant anymore. Why is this infiltrative tucked under the papillary thyroid cancer as opposed to under those encapsulated follicular variants? Make sure we're in two different areas here.

So remember, great question. Remember we talked about this. So here you can see that this is an infiltrated process, even if it's follicular pattern. That's why we call them infiltrated follicular subtype, according to the new WHO. and that's why they are undercome under pulmonary carcinoma. Fantastic. Fantastic. All right. And how did you guys read this one, Joyce?

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 75-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidentally detected thyroid nodule.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade differentiated thyroid carcinoma, pT2N0, arising in the thyroid isthmus.

[ histopathology results ]: Preoperative biopsy was suspicious for papillary thyroid carcinoma. Thyroidectomy specimen showed high-grade differentiated thyroid carcinoma measuring 2.8 cm with widely invasive growth pattern and extensive angioinvasion. Histologic description included follicular-pattern infiltrative tumor with fibrosis, increased mitotic activity, and a focus of vascular invasion. Three lymph nodes were negative for neoplasm.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial thyroid nodule measured 2.5 cm in the isthmus.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: NRAS mutation and TERT promoter mutation were identified on molecular profiling.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent total thyroidectomy. Surgical pathology demonstrated pT2N0 disease with 3 negative lymph nodes.

[ current disease status ]: Post-thyroidectomy status following resection of pT2N0 high-grade differentiated thyroid carcinoma. No nodal metastasis was identified in the resected lymph nodes.

[ other clinical data ]: None.

[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic carcinoma of the lung with disease progression on prior EGFR-targeted therapy.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV lung carcinoma, initially diagnosed in July 2023 as metastatic lung cancer with EGFR-mutated disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Histologic subtype was not documented.

[ imaging findings ]: PET scan performed in July 2025 showed progressive disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- NGS panel at initial diagnosis in 2023 showed EGFR exon 19 deletion.  
- Liquid biopsy performed in October 2025 showed acquired EGFR T790M mutation and TP53 mutation.  
- Additional report details indicated EGFR exon 19 deletion remained detectable and dominant, with variant allele fraction 27.6%.  
- EGFR T790M was detected with variant allele fraction 12.9%.  
- Two additional low-level variants were reported at 0.12% and 0.25%; one TP53 alteration was described as TP53 R175 mutation.  
- An EGFR exon 20 variant was also referenced in the report material, but the exact alteration was inconsistently documented.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Afatinib was started in 2023 following identification of EGFR exon 19 deletion.  
- Afatinib was continued from 2023 to 2025.  
- Best documented response on afatinib was partial response.  
- Disease progression was subsequently documented on PET scan in July 2025.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic EGFR-mutated lung cancer after prior afatinib, with acquired EGFR T790M resistance mutation and TP53 co-mutation.

[ other clinical data ]: No laboratory values were provided.

[ chief complaint ]: Follow-up after treatment for right breast cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Carcinoma right breast, triple-negative breast cancer, stage II at diagnosis in January 2024. ECOG performance status was 1 at diagnosis.

Received postoperative radiotherapy. Received maintenance capecitabine for 1 year, continued until August 2025. Last imaging showed complete response.

[ current disease status ]: Complete response on last imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: Comorbidities included diabetes mellitus and hypertension. Family history was significant for carcinoma endometrium in an elder sister.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 49-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Progressive breast cancer with increasing breast lump and axillary disease despite systemic therapy; breast lump was painful.

[ diagnosis ]: Initially diagnosed with locally advanced triple-negative breast cancer, clinical stage T3N2. Subsequent disease progression with extensive bone and nodal metastases. Performance status was 1. No known comorbidities.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial diagnosis: ductal carcinoma of the breast, triple-negative subtype.  
- Repeat biopsy in July after neoadjuvant chemotherapy: ductal carcinoma, triple-negative subtype.  
- Subsequent repeat biopsy after metastatic progression: infiltrative ductal carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial imaging had included contrast-enhanced CT chest.  
- Post-chemotherapy PET scan demonstrated extensive bone metastases and nodal metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Next-generation sequencing showed low tumor mutational burden.  
- Microsatellite status: stable.  
- HRD score/genomic aberration score: 44, reported as positive/borderline positive.  
- TP53 mutation detected.  
- MCL1 copy number gain detected; copy number reported as 16.  
- RICTOR copy number gain detected; copy number reported as 8.  
- TERT copy number gain detected; copy number reported as 8.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- PD-L1 by immunohistochemistry: 0.  
- HER2 status from prior outside testing: 0.  
- ER/PR/HER2 were not repeated locally on the latest biopsy.  
- No other laboratory values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for locally advanced disease:  
  - 4 cycles of doxorubicin/cyclophosphamide (AC).  
  - 2 cycles of nab-paclitaxel.  
  - Followed by 2 cycles of nab-paclitaxel plus carboplatin.  
- Clinical response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy was poor.  
- After 8 cycles of chemotherapy, PET scan showed metastatic progression with extensive bone and nodal disease.  
- Subsequently treated with eribulin.  
- After 2 cycles of eribulin, there was no clinical response; breast and axillary lesions increased in size.  
- Additional prior systemic exposure was described as including anthracyclines, taxanes, carboplatin, capecitabine, and eribulin.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Progressive metastatic triple-negative breast cancer.  
- Clinical progression continued on eribulin, with enlarging breast lump, enlarging axillary disease, and a small additional nodule.  
- Pain was present in the breast lesion.  
- Performance status remained 1.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No known comorbidities.  
- Family history: doubtful/unclear history of malignancy in grandmother.

reference_conclusion: The panel recommended repeat biomarker assessment on the current specimen, specifically reassessment of HER2 status to determine whether HER2-low or ultra-low expression is present, and evaluation of androgen receptor status. If HER2-low or ultra-low expression is identified, trastuzumab deruxtecan may be considered; if not, sacituzumab govitecan was preferred, with datopotamab deruxtecan as another option where available. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 41-year-old female.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent/metastatic HER2-positive breast carcinoma with progression after multiple lines of systemic therapy; history of left breast lump in 2021.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic breast carcinoma, HER2-positive, hormone receptor-negative/low-positive on serial biopsies, with skeletal metastases, nodal disease, skin recurrence, right axillary nodal involvement, and brain metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial details from bilateral lumpectomies performed in 2009 were not available. Following left breast recurrence in 2021, post-mastectomy tumor biomarkers were ER negative, PR negative, HER2 3+, Ki-67 25–30%, and androgen receptor strongly positive at >90%. Right axillary node biopsy at progression in November 2024 showed ER 0, PR 3, HER2 3+, and Ki-67 30%. Re-biopsy in October 2025 showed ER Allred score 2, PR 4, and HER2 3+.

[ imaging findings ]: Disease progression during maintenance trastuzumab was associated with skeletal metastases. After T-DM1, there was local progression with nodal disease, skin recurrence, and skeletal metastases. On lapatinib/capecitabine, there was partial response at some disease sites with new right axillary lesions. Interim PET after 6 cycles of docetaxel and 11 doses of PHESGO showed good response. PET in November 2024 showed disease progression with brain metastases. Subsequent PET after initiation of trastuzumab deruxtecan showed good response. PET in October 2025 showed disease progression.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: NGS identified MSH6 positivity as a variant of uncertain significance. This testing was described as germline testing. Family history was positive for endometrial carcinoma in the patient’s mother and maternal grandmother.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Bilateral lumpectomies were performed in 2009; operative/pathology details were unavailable. In 2021, after presentation with a left breast lump, the patient underwent modified radical mastectomy. She then received adjuvant treatment with 8 cycles of AC and docetaxel with trastuzumab, followed by adjuvant radiotherapy and maintenance trastuzumab for 16 doses. During maintenance trastuzumab, after an approximately 3-month delay, metastatic progression with skeletal metastases occurred. She received T-DM1 from July 2023 to August 2023, followed by progression with local, nodal, skin, and skeletal disease. Treatment was changed to lapatinib plus capecitabine, with partial response at some sites but new right axillary lesions. She then received docetaxel plus PHESGO; after 6 cycles of docetaxel and 11 doses of PHESGO, interim PET showed good response, and maintenance PHESGO was continued. In November 2024, PET demonstrated progression with brain metastases. She was then treated with gemcitabine, carboplatin, pertuzumab, and trastuzumab, with progression again by February after approximately 2–3 months. Treatment was changed to trastuzumab deruxtecan, with good PET response, and this was continued for 8 cycles. PET in October 2025 showed progression. She was then started on tucatinib, capecitabine, and trastuzumab.

[ current disease status ]: Progressive metastatic HER2-positive breast carcinoma after multiple prior lines of HER2-directed and cytotoxic therapy. At the time of reporting, the patient had completed 2 cycles of tucatinib, capecitabine, and trastuzumab, started on 27 October 2025. Brain metastases had been documented by November 2024. Performance status was described as clinically good apart from radiologic disease progression.

[ other clinical data ]: No comorbidities were reported. Family history was significant for endometrial carcinoma in the mother and maternal grandmother.

[ chief complaint ]: Right lung carcinoma with progressive disease and right pleural effusion.

[ diagnosis ]: Right lower lobe lung adenocarcinoma with metastatic disease involving bone and paraesophageal lymph node. ECOG performance status was 1. Comorbidity: hypertension.

Pleural drainage was being performed via pigtail catheter; the drained fluid was hemorrhagic, and cell block yield was limited due to low malignant cell number.

[ other clinical data ]: Repeat biopsy had not yet been completed and was being planned after pleural fluid drainage and repeat CT imaging.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 33-year-old female. Non-smoker. No prior comorbidities were reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Severe breathlessness with hypoxia requiring supplemental oxygen at presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: Poorly differentiated neoplasm/carcinoma, treated clinically as probable non-small cell lung carcinoma with suspected lung primary. Radiologic pattern was considered consistent with lymphangitic carcinomatosis.

[ histopathology results ]: EBUS-guided biopsy of a subcarinal lymph node was performed. Initial pathology impression was non-small cell lung carcinoma. After extensive immunohistochemistry, the specimen was reported as a poorly differentiated neoplasm. TTF-1 positivity was reported.

[ imaging findings ]: Chest radiograph showed diffuse bilateral haziness. HRCT thorax showed bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities and multiple lymph nodes above and below the diaphragm. Multiple lytic bone lesions were also described.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Limited NGS panel reported MET amplification at a borderline threshold and stated it was not commentable. ALK point mutation was reported as a variant of uncertain significance. No ALK fusion was documented. The panel was described as covering major mutations including EGFR and ALK.

[ laboratory results ]: PD-L1 tumor proportion score was reported as approximately 8–10%.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received carboplatin and paclitaxel. Clinical improvement was observed after treatment, including improvement in breathlessness and hypoxia; oxygen dependence resolved. A second cycle of paclitaxel/carboplatin was being planned.

[ current disease status ]: Marked symptomatic improvement after paclitaxel/carboplatin. Performance status improved from poor functional status at presentation to approximately ECOG PS 1 at the time of review.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had initially been admitted under pulmonology. Lymphoma had been considered initially because of thoracic and infradiaphragmatic lymphadenopathy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Dizziness; increased cough with sputum.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic colon cancer diagnosed in October 2024, described as upper-end metastatic colon cancer. Metastatic sites documented in lung, liver, sigmoid colon, and brain.

[ histopathology results ]: Endobronchial/lung biopsy had been obtained via bronchoscopy by pulmonology. No formal histopathology description was available.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging demonstrated a new single hemorrhagic brain metastasis. A lung mass previously measuring approximately 10 cm had increased to 14 cm and subsequently occupied essentially the entire left lung. Concomitant infectious/inflammatory pulmonary changes were present. A 2 cm right lung lesion had disappeared after initiation of trifluridine/tipiracil. Sigmoid colon lesion and liver lesion had also disappeared after initiation of trifluridine/tipiracil. Overall imaging pattern was of mixed response, with progression of the dominant left lung lesion and new brain metastasis despite regression/disappearance of other lesions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Next-generation sequencing reported KRAS mutation, GATA mutation, APC mutation, mTOR mutations, and PIK3CG mutation. MET exon 14 skipping was reported. HRD was reported as positive/high. Microsatellite instability was not detected. Tumor mutational burden was low.

[ laboratory results ]: Hemoglobin was approximately 9 g/dL and had been falling. No overt bleeding was reported by history.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- First-line XELOX had been administered after diagnosis; subsequent repeat imaging showed progression. Exact number of cycles was not available.  
- Second-line XELIRI had then been administered; disease progressed.  
- Trifluridine/tipiracil (Lonsurf) had subsequently been started; the patient presented while on cycle 2. After starting trifluridine/tipiracil, the small right lung lesion, sigmoid lesion, and liver lesion disappeared, but the previously 10 cm lung lesion enlarged to 14 cm and a new brain metastasis developed.

[ current disease status ]: ECOG performance status was 2. Ongoing cough persisted, with recent brown-colored sputum. Weight loss was ongoing; body weight was 40 kg. The patient had a concomitant fungal pulmonary infection and remained on oral antifungal therapy. She was described as systemically stable.

[ other clinical data ]: No peripheral neuropathy was reported. No hemoptysis was reported. The left lung was described as entirely occupied by tumor mass.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 65-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic right lung malignancy with diffuse skeletal metastases.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic adenocarcinoma of the right lung with diffuse bone metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial tumor tissue biopsy from the lung showed adenocarcinoma. Tissue was inadequate for next-generation sequencing.

[ imaging findings ]: PET-CT after 6 cycles of chemotherapy showed partial response, with reduction in size of disease and previously lytic bone lesions becoming sclerotic. Follow-up scan also showed partial response.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Liquid biopsy demonstrated an EGFR compound mutation comprising exon 19 deletion and T790M mutation. Reported variant allele frequency was approximately 14% for the exon 19 deletion and 53.5% for T790M. The exon 19 deletion was described as atypical, starting at codon 747 rather than the more typical codon 746.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received 6 cycles of pemetrexed plus carboplatin-based chemotherapy. No prior EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy had been given. Chemotherapy resulted in partial radiologic response, including reduction in tumor burden and sclerosis of bone lesions.

[ current disease status ]: Partial response following pemetrexed-carboplatin chemotherapy. EGFR TKI-naive. Solid repeat biopsy had not been performed because the patient declined repeat tissue biopsy; liquid biopsy had been performed instead.

[ other clinical data ]: Molecular testing was not performed upfront on tumor tissue because of inadequate sample for NGS. The patient declined repeat solid biopsy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 52-year-old male; never smoker.

[ chief complaint ]: Severe breathlessness at presentation to the emergency department.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IV non-small cell lung carcinoma, adenocarcinoma subtype, with disease localized to the left pleura and malignant left pleural effusion.

[ histopathology results ]: Pleural fluid cytology was positive for malignancy. Cell block from pleural fluid and pleural-based lesion showed adenocarcinoma with TTF-1 positivity. Tumor cellularity in available tissue/cell block material was approximately 5%.

[ imaging findings ]: PET scan showed pleural-based nodules and left pleural effusion, with no disease identified elsewhere. Disease was described as localized to the left pleura. Brain imaging was normal.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tissue was sent for next-generation sequencing, but testing could not be performed. Liquid biopsy obtained after the first cycle of chemotherapy showed no targetable mutation. A PD-L1-positive result was reported from blood-based testing; no tumor proportion score was available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient was initially admitted under pulmonology. An intercostal drain had been placed and was subsequently removed. Pleurodesis was performed. Systemic chemotherapy with pemetrexed and carboplatin was started because of symptomatic disease. Liquid biopsy was performed after the first chemotherapy cycle. At the time of reporting, the patient had received two cycles of pemetrexed and carboplatin.

[ current disease status ]: Symptomatic malignant left pleural effusion and pleural-based disease at diagnosis; no extrathoracic disease identified on PET imaging and brain imaging was normal. Ongoing treatment with pemetrexed/carboplatin after two cycles.

[ other clinical data ]: Multiple tissue fragments from pleural fluid cell block and pleural-based lesion were combined for molecular testing because of low tumor cellularity.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 59-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Persistent upper abdominal pain for 6 months, associated with loss of appetite, weight loss of approximately 10-15 kg over 4-5 months, and low backache.

[ diagnosis ]: Carcinoma of unknown primary at presentation, based on metastatic poorly differentiated carcinoma identified on left supraclavicular lymph node biopsy. Subsequent imaging demonstrated a pancreatic mass with metastatic disease involving liver, retroperitoneal lymph nodes, and left supraclavicular lymph node.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from the left supraclavicular lymph node showed metastatic poorly differentiated carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry showed strong positivity for MUC1, patchy nuclear positivity for NKX3.1, and occasional cells positive for PAX8. Tumor cells were negative for CK7, CK20, glypican, CD10, p40, and Hepar-1. The outside pathology interpretation reported the findings as most compatible with prostatic primary adenocarcinoma, with clinicoradiologic correlation advised. A repeat biopsy had been performed and additional immunohistochemical workup, including neuroendocrine markers, had been sent; results were not available.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial outside CECT showed a well-defined heterogeneous abdominal lesion measuring approximately 7-8 cm near the liver, involving hepatic segments V, VII, and VIII, without venous washout. Multiple enlarged lesser omental and retroperitoneal lymph nodes were present, along with an enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node measuring approximately 2.8 cm. Prostate and bladder were reported as normal. Whole-body PET imaging, including FAPI PET and PSMA PET, showed a FAPI-expressing soft tissue mass involving the proximal body/head region of the pancreas, with additional uptake in liver lesions, retroperitoneal lymph nodes, and left supraclavicular lymph node. Prostate was reported as normal, with only mild prostatomegaly and no abnormal prostate uptake on PET.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tissue NGS showed TERT positivity, CREBBP positivity, and TP53 mutation. Tumor mutational burden was low. Microsatellite status was stable. Genomic instability metric was low.

[ laboratory results ]: Tumor markers were within normal limits, including CA 19-9, CEA, AFP, and PSA. ECOG performance status was 1. BAC was documented as 1.7.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had been started on gemcitabine plus carboplatin on a day 1/day 8 schedule for carcinoma of unknown primary. After 2 cycles, he had symptomatic improvement.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic poorly differentiated carcinoma with pancreatic mass and metastatic involvement of liver, retroperitoneal lymph nodes, and left supraclavicular lymph node. The patient had symptomatic response after 2 cycles of gemcitabine/carboplatin.

[ other clinical data ]: Past history included diabetes mellitus. He had a history of tobacco chewing for more than 30 years, alcohol intake for approximately 10 years at 7-8 drinks per week, and no smoking history. On examination, ECOG performance status was 1. A hard left supraclavicular lymph node measuring approximately 2.5-3 cm was palpable. Abdominal examination showed epigastric fullness. Upper GI endoscopy and colonoscopy were normal.

[ current disease status ]: No residual lesion was seen in the esophagus on post-treatment PET imaging. A lung lesion had been identified and treated with SBRT. Disease status following SBRT and before planned irinotecan-based palliative chemotherapy was consistent with treated metastatic disease.

[ other clinical data ]: PD-L1 testing had not been documented. Tumor mutational burden and MSI status had not been reported.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Sex was male. Performance/fitness was described as fit.

[ chief complaint ]: Symptomatic local pelvic disease with hematuria and requirement for Foley catheter at the time of recent progression.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic high-risk, high-volume prostate carcinoma diagnosed in March 2023, with subsequent neuroendocrine transformation. Disease progression occurred in the prostate and iliac lymph nodes after platinum-based chemotherapy plus immunotherapy.

[ histopathology results ]: Neuroendocrine transformation was documented. Ki-67 proliferation index was 80%.

[ imaging findings ]: PSMA PET was normal at the time of neuroendocrine progression. FDG PET demonstrated disease in the prostate and iliac nodal region. After 3 cycles of etoposide/carboplatin plus toripalimab, iliac nodal disease increased in size and new nodal disease appeared. No disease was identified outside the prostate and iliac nodal sites on the available imaging before radiotherapy. No post-radiotherapy imaging had yet been performed; reassessment imaging was planned after 12 weeks from radiotherapy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No patient-specific molecular/genomic alteration was reported.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA was normal at the time FDG PET identified recurrent/progressive disease.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Orchiectomy was performed after diagnosis. The patient received docetaxel with abiraterone for high-risk, high-volume disease, followed by abiraterone maintenance for approximately 2.5 years. On subsequent progression with neuroendocrine-transformed disease, the patient received 3 cycles of etoposide/carboplatin plus toripalimab. Disease progressed on this regimen, with increase in iliac nodal size and appearance of new nodes. Curative-dose radiotherapy was then delivered to the involved sites for symptomatic progression. Following radiotherapy, symptoms improved; the patient was off Foley catheter and hematuria had resolved.

[ current disease status ]: Following radiotherapy, the patient was clinically improved and somewhat better symptomatically, with no hematuria and no Foley catheter requirement. Biological/radiological post-radiotherapy response had not yet been assessed. The last documented disease distribution before radiotherapy remained confined to the prostate and iliac lymph nodes.

[ other clinical data ]: Platinum plus immunotherapy had already been administered before the latest local radiotherapy. No other metastatic sites were reported on the available pre-radiotherapy imaging.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 52-year-old postmenopausal woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic recurrence of left breast carcinoma with lung, liver, nodal, skeletal, and central nervous system involvement after prior curative-intent treatment.

[ diagnosis ]: Left breast carcinoma, initially staged clinically as cT3N1M0. Metastatic recurrent disease was identified in March 2025, involving bilateral lungs, liver, mediastinal/sternal nodal disease, skeleton, and brain/pituitary-sellar region.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial breast malignancy was reported as invasive ductal carcinoma. Following left modified radical mastectomy, pathological stage was ypT1bN1a. No biopsy of metastatic lesions was performed at recurrence.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- During surveillance after completion of adjuvant therapy, PET-CT had been performed at 3-month intervals.  
- After a disease-free interval of approximately 1 year and 3 months, metastatic recurrence was detected in March 2025.  
- PET-CT/imaging at recurrence showed multiple bilateral lung nodules, including a right lower lobe lung lesion measuring 5 × 4 cm; metastatic lesions in both lobes of the liver; mediastinal/sternal lymph node involvement; skeletal lesions; a nodular suprasellar lesion; and bulky pituitary gland.  
- MRI brain demonstrated an enhancing sellar mass involving the hypothalamus and contacting the optic chiasm; radiologic impression favored metastasis rather than pituitary adenoma.  
- Repeat MRI after 1 cycle of ado-trastuzumab emtansine showed a new lesion in the right cerebellar hemisphere, in addition to the sellar lesion.  
- Stereotactic radiosurgery was delivered to the sellar and right cerebellar lesions in 5 fractions to 25 Gy.  
- After 6 cycles of trastuzumab deruxtecan, response PET-CT showed complete metabolic response of all lesions, including brain lesions.  
- After 10 cycles of trastuzumab deruxtecan, MRI performed following seizure episodes showed multiple new small nodular lesions in the cerebellum, brainstem, cerebral hemispheres, and thalamus.  
- At the time of reporting, repeat PET-CT and MRI for response assessment after 12 cycles of trastuzumab deruxtecan had been planned but not yet performed.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No next-generation sequencing had been performed. No liquid biopsy results were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Marked hyperglycemia was documented at the time of seizure episodes after cycle 10 of trastuzumab deruxtecan. No other laboratory values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Neoadjuvant systemic therapy: 4 cycles of TCHP (docetaxel, carboplatin, trastuzumab, pertuzumab), with clinical partial response.  
- Surgery: Left modified radical mastectomy.  
- Adjuvant systemic therapy: 2 additional cycles of TCHP, followed by 1 year of adjuvant trastuzumab. Adjuvant trastuzumab emtansine was not administered.  
- Surveillance: Follow-up with PET-CT every 3 months.  
- At metastatic recurrence: ado-trastuzumab emtansine was started as first-line therapy for metastatic disease; treatment was discontinued after 1 cycle because of severe oral mucositis/mycositis and odynophagia.  
- CNS-directed therapy: Stereotactic radiosurgery to sellar and right cerebellar lesions, 25 Gy in 5 fractions.  
- Subsequent systemic therapy: trastuzumab deruxtecan was started at 300 mg; 6 cycles were administered, followed by complete metabolic response on PET-CT. Treatment was then continued for 4 additional cycles at 200 mg. After MRI-documented new CNS lesions following cycle 10, 2 further cycles were administered, for a total of 12 cycles completed.  
- Supportive treatment after seizures included antiepileptic therapy and blood glucose control.

[ current disease status ]: After 6 cycles of trastuzumab deruxtecan, there had been complete metabolic response of systemic and intracranial lesions on PET-CT. After 10 cycles, MRI demonstrated new multifocal intracranial lesions in the cerebellum, brainstem, cerebral hemispheres, and thalamus, with no contemporaneous extracranial response assessment available. The patient had completed 12 cycles of trastuzumab deruxtecan, and repeat PET-CT and MRI were pending.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Two seizure episodes occurred the day after cycle 10 of trastuzumab deruxtecan.  
- Apart from seizures, no other neurologic symptoms were reported at that time.  
- Reduction of trastuzumab deruxtecan dose from 300 mg to 200 mg was due to financial constraints.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 55-year-old female; postmenopausal. No comorbid conditions were reported. No family history of breast cancer or ovarian cancer was reported.

[ chief complaint ]: Left breast carcinoma with metastatic disease to the lungs.

[ diagnosis ]: Triple-negative carcinoma of the left breast, staged as T4b N2 M1, with multiple pulmonary metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Triple-negative breast carcinoma. Ki-67 was 12%.

[ imaging findings ]: Baseline disease included multiple lung secondaries. After completion of six cycles of paclitaxel-carboplatin, PET-CT showed an almost near-complete response in both the breast primary and the lung nodules.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline BRCA variant of uncertain significance (VUS) was identified on germline testing. Variant allele fraction was reported as 44%.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received six cycles of paclitaxel plus carboplatin. Carboplatin was added in the context of the germline BRCA VUS. Following six cycles, PET-CT demonstrated an almost near-complete response in the primary breast lesion and pulmonary metastases.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic triple-negative breast cancer with radiologic near-complete response after six cycles of systemic chemotherapy.

[ other clinical data ]: None.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 54-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Hepatic mass identified on surveillance imaging after cure of hepatitis C.

[ diagnosis ]: Hepatocellular carcinoma diagnosed radiographically in the setting of cirrhosis and prior hepatitis C infection; solitary lesion.

[ histopathology results ]: No biopsy was performed.

[ imaging findings ]: Contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a single hepatic lesion measuring approximately 3.5 cm. The lesion showed arterial phase hyperenhancement and washout on delayed phase imaging, with imaging features categorized as LI-RADS 5.

[ laboratory results ]: Liver-related laboratory studies were reported as normal. Platelet count was relatively preserved. Liver function was described as good.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had previously been treated for hepatitis C and was cured.

[ current disease status ]: Early-stage disease at presentation, with a single small hepatic tumor and preserved liver function in the setting of cirrhosis.

[ other clinical data ]: Underlying cirrhosis persisted despite hepatitis C cure. No evidence of impaired hepatic synthetic function was described.

Good. Well, thank you very much for having me. So what we see here are two slices for CT scan and basically, you know, for lack of a better word, I always tell my patients, it's like we're looking into your body from the feet towards your head. So normal liver on these scans and these CTs are done we give contrast or x-ray dye in the IV and then we wait for a few seconds and then image them in a subsequent sequence and you know the way we find this tumor is one if you see the entire liver has a different shade, and then right under the first image, under the arrow, there is a lot of white deposition. That basically shows that it is an abnormal focus of tissue that is taking up contrast, that has a lot of blood supply. And then over like decades of research, we've learned that liver tumors have a very particular way of taking up contrast. So what we see in most of the tumors is in the first sequence, we see they take up a lot of contrast. So we call them hypervascular. Vascular means blood. They take a lot of blood. And in the second phase, we see that you see how now it is actually darker than the surrounding liver. So when the tumors form, they form leaky blood vessels. So they make a lot of blood vessels and they're leaky. So these two image characteristics kind of make us very confident in calling this as a liver tumor. Now, over time, we've developed a grading system where we would say that this is something and we've kind of read them based on probability. It's called LIRADS, right? So, LIRADS 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, which basically gives us a probability of how sure we are that this is true or not. So in somebody who has underlying risk factors, that's an important thing. Somebody with underlying risk factors, with a new mass, massless tumor, with arterial phase enhancement, which is the white uptake of contrast I spoke about, and washout, these characteristics make us, make this allowance five. And so we treat this actually without needing to do a biopsy because of this characteristic appearance. Not all liver cancers have this appearance, but when it's present in the right clinical setting, once again, we treat accordingly. So it's a very unique aspect of liver cancer compared to other cancers. So this patient, because they were treated for their hepatitis C, fortunately continues to have good liver function. They still have cirrhosis, but their liver is functioning well. So we have grading scores for cirrhosis, and this patient has good labs. Yeah. So that's exactly right. So the nice thing here is that this person's liver is working well. This is a patient who was found early. We have curative therapies available. And so this patient should be eligible for surgical resection, where you go in, you cut out that part of the liver with the tumor, and this patient once again can continue to do fine with their underlying liver intact. So there are a few that are more commonly used. Dr. Benjamin went over them. One of them is ablation, where we put an antenna and kind of burn the tumor under anesthesia, of course. What that means is therapies that we deliver to the blood vessels. And as I discussed previously, these tumors have a lot of blood vessels. So we go into those teeny tiny blood vessels that supply the tumor very close to them under x-ray, and then we can inject two options. We can inject chemotherapy, or we can inject beads, which are reabsorbable beads that are coated with radiation, which is known as trans-arterial radioembolization, and the first one I mentioned was trans-arterial chemoembolization. Historically, before the radiation therapy came, we used to treat them with chemoembolization, and that has good results. But more and more, as our research progresses, we're getting more data that show that when we actually inject radioembolization or we inject radiation-coated beads, they have a longer response rate and more curative. By curative, I mean they can treat the tumor. So we have three options. I think given the size of this, we can either talk about trans-arterial radioembolization, or Y90, or trans-arterial chemoembolization, based on where the patient is, what facilities are available.

Yeah, so I think that this is like a common situation that we'll see in our tumor boards. So once again, with the idea that we try to do surgical therapies if possible. And if somebody isn't eligible for surgical therapies, then the next thing that we often think about is what local therapies are possible. Like Dr. Chowdhury was saying, that you basically have multiple different local regional therapies available. You have these therapies where you can inject beads with either chemotherapy or radiation directly into the tumor. And we heard from Dr. Benjamin that this is nice because it spares the patient from lots of other side effects. It gives local therapy. You're able to really shrink the tumor in the vast majority of cases. We have an ablation where you can try to burn it. The other therapy that we didn't talk about very much, unfortunately, our radiation oncologist wasn't able to be here today, is external beam radiation therapy. So, you know, we talked about the internal delivery, but you can also do external radiation therapy to this where you deliver high doses of radiation, also, once again, are able to typically shrink these cancers well. We talked about this. So this patient underwent a robotic resection. This is also an interesting phenomenon where we can now do this in a minimally invasive manner, laparoscopically essentially, where you can have it so the patient is able to recover quicker and go home in a very quick period of time after the surgery. So given time, I'm going to skip that. I want to talk about one other aspect here. So Nicole, I'm going to obviously send this one your way in terms of what do you think here. So this is somewhat of a similar case in the sense that we have a 62-year-old male with alcohol-associated cirrhosis has stopped drinking. But this patient has liver dysfunction, meaning that their liver is not working well. They've had complications of their cirrhosis, including ascites. And we haven't gone through these in detail, but this is the fact that the liver is not functioning well. You have an accumulation of fluid in the abdomen because of the liver not being able to operate perfectly. So this patient was found to have a small tumor, a small cancer of 2.1 centimeters. So similar to the last patient, this patient was found early. But in contrast, the liver is not functioning well in this case. So Nicole, can you talk through like what your thoughts here are? You know, before we went to surgical resection, would you recommend surgical resection in this case?

reference_conclusion: The hepatic lesion demonstrates classic imaging features of hepatocellular carcinoma in the appropriate clinical setting and may be managed without biopsy. Given preserved liver function, compensated cirrhosis, and a solitary 3.5 cm tumor, the patient is considered eligible for curative surgical resection. If the patient is not a surgical candidate, liver-directed therapy with transarterial radioembolization (Y90) or transarterial chemoembolization would be appropriate alternatives.
reference_conclusion_quote: "we treat this actually without needing to do a biopsy because of this characteristic appearance." [...] "So I think the first thing we would want to do is see is the patient a candidate for surgery to have it removed or resected while they keep their own liver." [...] "And so this patient should be eligible for surgical resection" [...] "I think given the size of this, we can either talk about trans-arterial radioembolization, or Y90, or trans-arterial chemoembolization"

[ imaging findings ]: Hepatic tumor was present; size and segmental location were not documented. Ascites was present.

[ laboratory results ]: Liver-related laboratory studies were reported as acceptable/okay; specific values were not provided.
