reference_discussion.text: Yeah, so you highlighted the difference in this case, which is that the patient already has symptoms of their cirrhosis. They have the fluid in their belly. And, you know, We talked about during my talk that when we try to cut out part of the liver, yes, it can regenerate, but not immediately. It can take time. So of course, we always try to consider resection in everybody. One of the things that the surgeon will actually do is they'll calculate something called FLR, which is how much liver will be left after a surgery and try to calculate, is that enough for the patient to survive or do well? When somebody's at this point where they've already developed symptoms of cirrhosis, they're not going to have enough liver remaining to be able to survive the surgery. And so in this case, you would need to replace the whole liver with a transplant. And so for in this patient, I would recommend that they, you know, go to a transplant center, get referred there, have a transplant evaluation and kind of be checked out head to toe. And then in the interim see, you know, Dr. Chaudhry, Dr. Benjamin, to see if we can try to burn the tumor or embolize the tumor while we wait on the transplant list, knowing that from the time they meet me till when they actually get a transplant can be up to a year. So that would be my recommendation is urgent evaluation for transplant and then to see what are these two folks.

Yeah, so the analogy that I use here is it's almost like a car towing on an edge where it hasn't fallen off that cliff. But if you just remove more of that liver, there wouldn't be enough liver there to function. And so thereby, this patient who's actually doing okay right now, the complications are controlled, the labs look okay. But if you cut out any of the liver that's there, they wouldn't have enough left to thereby function. And this patient could thereby get sicker from their underlying liver disease. And this really highlights the complexity of this cancer, because we talked about this happening in the setting of liver disease and cirrhosis. And so whenever we think through the treatments, the tolerability, the outcomes, it's not just treating the cancer. It's also not upsetting or worsening the underlying liver disease. And so it really comes into all of our decision making of what's the stage of cancer, how well is the liver working or not working, and how strong is the patient. I always tell my patients the easiest way, the worst way to kill off a cancer is to kill the entire liver or to kill the patient, right? And this is one thing that we need to make sure that we don't do, that we treat the cancer effectively while preserving the patient and their liver function. And so this is one of the key things that always comes into our tumor board and highlights the importance of us getting together to discuss these things. So this patient, to Dr. Richard's point, was referred and enlisted for liver transplantation, underwent bridging therapy to Dr. Chaudhry's discussion, underwent bridging therapy with a local ablation, actually underwent a living donor liver transplantation. And I would argue this is the other thing that we need to think through as a group here. is that unfortunately for as many people who need a liver transplant, we don't have enough organs available. And so we need to make sure that we continue doing our part to get the word out that for those that are able to do so, that they consider donating if and when possible. And so living donation saves a lot of lives. Okay. Final case, and then I'm going to leave time for questions. I know we cut this short, but I think it's important to do so, so we have some time for questions before lunch. So 57-year-old female here with cirrhosis related to metabolic dysfunction. And conversely to like our last couple of patients, this patient unfortunately was not undergoing screening. and was found to have an eight-centimeter mass that was consistent with liver cancer and disease outside the liver. So also has a lymph node that's two centimeters in size. So liver's functioning well, but unfortunately, large tumor and metastatic spread, disease spread outside the liver. So I'm going to start just, Nicole, Moaz, would you guys consider this patient for a surgical therapy or local therapy? And you can be brief here.

reference_conclusion: The patient is not an appropriate candidate for hepatic resection because symptomatic cirrhosis indicates insufficient future liver remnant to tolerate surgery. Urgent referral to a transplant center for comprehensive liver transplant evaluation is recommended. While awaiting transplantation, bridging locoregional therapy with tumor ablation or embolization should be pursued.

And so in this case, you would need to replace the whole liver with a transplant. And so for in this patient, I would recommend that they, you know, go to a transplant center, get referred there, have a transplant evaluation and kind of be checked out head to toe. And then in the interim see, you know, Dr. Chaudhry, Dr. Benjamin, to see if we can try to burn the tumor or embolize the tumor while we wait on the transplant list [...] So that would be my recommendation is urgent evaluation for transplant

reference_discussion.text: I guess at this point I wouldn't consider surgery right now because we know it's involving the lymph node. Presuming we've proven that and, you know, removing the whole liver, removing part of the liver won't take the cancer out of the lymph node. So I think we'd have to address that first and could consider in the future.

So, and same idea for me. Yeah, same idea. I think like we spoke with Dr. Benjamin's talk, we do a liver directed therapy, which is therapy inside the liver. Once it's outside, then I think we need to think of what, where else the tumor is, and then have a discussion of the multidisciplinary with all the different specialties involved.

Yeah, so, David, what kind of, how would you think through systemic therapies here? Like, what would you recommend? You talked about immunotherapy, you talked about TKIs, and you don't have to say specific regimen, but just sort of like the classes of immunotherapy, TKIs.

Yeah, so I think To me, this patient is very appropriate for systemic therapy, because as I mentioned, you know, the advantage of systemic therapy is that it can attack the cancer where it is and where we don't see it. So it's not that, you know, the lymph node is something that's dangerous to have. But the problem is that all the lymph nodes in our body are in some way connected. It's like a highway, right? And it tells us, and we have a lot of historic data to tell us this, is that you could try to kill the cancer where it is right now, but it's almost certain to come back. So, you know, again, there might be caveats to this, you know, and patients may, there are possibilities, you know, patients may only have one lymph node involved. I mean, you could, you know, treat it and may not see it back, but statistically that's just going to be unexpected. So in this case, you know, the assumption is that this cancer is already spread outside the liver, it's spread to the lymph node, and it could be in other places that we don't see yet on the scans. So to me, this patient is healthy. They don't have any contraindications that I can see for immunotherapies. And so using one of our immunotherapy combinations would be a good first place to start. Their liver also is very functional. So this patient is ideal for that reason.

Yeah, I mean, this is a perfect patient to start with systemic therapy. So one of the immunotherapy combinations, you know, to David's earlier point, there are proven immunotherapy combinations, which have changed our perspective on this. So whereas we used to have an average survival of only a year before, we now have patients, 20 to 30% of patients are having incredible responses. We've seen data where patients can survive five years. We see one in five patients surviving five years despite presenting with metastatic spread. I mean, it's a completely different era for our systemic therapy options. And so we have hope, even when patients present at a more advanced stage. And so it's important for patients to not just say, oh, I have advanced disease. I should just give up. Patients should be referred for therapy. We have fantastic therapies available. And to David's other point, we have clinical trials where we're now not only just sort of staying with what we have, there's many other therapies that are coming around that are also promising, both in terms of improving tolerability and efficacy. And so this patient was treated with systemic therapy and has done well. The final case was more so a case of somebody who did not have liver disease who was found to have a liver mass. I think the only thing that I wanted to point out there, once again, was that in the absence of liver disease, it's uncommon, it's possible, but uncommon to have cancer. There are many liver masses that are found in the absence of liver disease. adenomas, FNHs, you don't have to remember the name, but there are many benign liver masses that are found in the absence of liver disease. So I see, like Dr. Rich and I see these commonly in our sort of practices, and it's actually, it's the best visit that I have, right? I get to go in and I get to tell this like typically young person, you don't have cancer, you have a benign condition, Like you don't need further follow up. You don't need anything done. It's a fantastic and like invariably they're just super happy. Like they hug me like or whatever and they walk out the door and like, you know what I mean? Like it's the best visit. But like once again, I think it's important for like these people to go to sort of somebody who understands the evaluation of this because not every mass is cancer. We spent a lot of time talking about cancer. But there are other non-cancerous liver lesions that are important to differentiate. So we'll go to Q&A. I just want to highlight, once again, you've heard a ton of information. If I were you, I'd be like, what do I even take away here? So I would say there are several key takeaways. One, liver disease is common. Liver disease is the main risk factor for liver cancer. So we need to do a good job of treating, of diagnosing and treating liver disease, right? So these simple steps, remember. Be healthy, so exercise. And it doesn't mean you've got to go on a marathon. This can simply be 10,000 steps a day. Eat healthy. So I know there's a bunch of cookies, which I also looked at every cookie there. Don't necessarily take four cookies. There's a lot of healthy options. Try to eat healthy. Okay? So, not, no, like, heavy alcohol. Like, it's okay to have a drink here and there, but do not drink heavily. Okay? Get screened for viral hepatitis. Hepatitis B, hepatitis C. If you're not vaccinated, get vaccinated for hepatitis B. We don't have a hepatitis C vaccine, but you can get, if you get screened for it. There's a simple blood test, and they're treatable. Okay? If you know somebody who has cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B, get screened for liver cancer. Finding it early is the key. The other unfortunate thing is we do see people who are found early, and they get treated with some rando therapy. Not a bad therapy, but not a curative therapy. So if you're found early, get referred to a center that considers surgical therapies. You heard from Dr. Rich that the cures are local ablation, surgical resection, liver transplantation. I have to say the saddest thing that I see is somebody who went through all the initial steps right, got found early, they got started on a non-curative therapy. And the only time that somebody asked about something like liver transplant was when the cancer progressed. It was bigger. And we're like, you missed your window. The window was two years ago. And this happens often. And it's so sad. So if you're found early, surgical therapies are your friend. If you're not found early, but it's liver localized, there's a lot of very well-tolerated and efficacious or effective local regional therapies. And finally, if you're found more advanced, it doesn't mean all hope is lost. There are really great systemic therapies. The immunotherapies are fantastic. They can actually shrink tumors. Sometimes people are found not transplantable or resectable. These immunotherapies are able to shrink it and bring it into sort of criteria. So not all hope is lost anymore. So we have very effective therapies, clinical trials. And one thing that we didn't explicitly say, but sort of referenced in this tumor board, the most important thing that I would say is if somebody is found to have liver cancer is to go to a multidisciplinary center. Not all doctors, not all practices are the same. Go to a center that has a setup where you have all of the doctors that are talking to each other to figure out your best therapy, not only at diagnosis, but as you go through your course. Once again, the time that I typically see people who aren't treated with surgical therapies if they're found early is if they just go to whoever down the street. And if you're a hammer, everything in life is a nail. But you want to have a toolbox where you have all the therapies that are being considered and weighed.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 74-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for management of newly diagnosed high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer following outside transurethral resection of bladder tumor.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal high-grade T1 urothelial carcinoma of the bladder with concomitant carcinoma in situ (CIS); high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.

[ histopathology results ]: Outside TURBT demonstrated multifocal T1 disease and CIS. Tumor volume was not clearly documented in the operative note. Presence or absence of muscularis propria in the specimen was not provided.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed high-risk NMIBC after initial outside TURBT, with extent of residual disease not yet fully characterized in the available record.

reference_discussion.text: So non-muscle invasive bladder cancer is getting more complex every day. We have more and more agents. It's a good problem to have, but it's complicated to manage. So I wanted to pick your brain on some cases and see how you think through these situations. So let's say we have a pretty standard patient, 74-year-old male, average age for bladder cancer. Referring urologist does a TRBT. He finds multifocal T1 and CIS. Not really clear what the volume of disease is based on his op note. Patient comes to see you in the office. Can you walk us through what your first steps are?

Yeah so I think first things first when you hear high volume T1 plus CIS all of the bells go off that this is a patient who very much needs to have a thorough staging and evaluation so you really have characterized that disease and you make sure this is one of those moments where making the right decision at this point is critical because it will change that patient's clinical trajectory. So I think at this point the first thing is we do a path 3 review and I think I talk to patients to say at this point we need to look back in your bladder and make sure that all of the disease that can be resected has been resected and fully understand everything, especially if there's not muscle in the specimen. But I actually re-resect all high-grade T1 irrespective of muscularis propria in the first specimen. I just think it's rude. I call it a quality check. I tell the patients before I take them to the OR if I find high-grade T1 Even when I'm doing your first resection, four to six weeks later we're going back and that's to make sure that we didn't miss anything because of that historic data that 25% of people are upstaged. But I think also I want to be thinking about the prostatic urethra and I want to make sure that the upper tracts are staged. I do get a chest CT even though the likelihood of pulmonary metastases is low. It's more because I want to have a baseline so that I have something to compare to in the future if and when we get further CTs down the line. So I think at this point it's kind of start from scratch, do all the work, make sure you fully understand that tumor.

Yeah, I think most of us will have a low threshold to do a repeat evaluation. Let's say the patient did not have T1 disease. Do you do an office systole sometimes or are you still taking that patient to the operating room?
I think it depends on, I don't know what you think, Mark, but I think the volume of high-grade TA, I think high-grade TA, if it's a larger tumor, I will still often re-resect those.
And are you doing those with blue light?
If there's carcinoma in situ in that first biopsy, absolutely, I do.

Any other thoughts, Mark? No, I think Sarah and I see it pretty much the same. I don't routinely re-resect TA. So I'll read the op note if the outside urologist, and they're somebody I know and trust especially, they've done a complete TUR, it's a smaller tumor, then I might not re-resect that because there is some data in the BCG immunoablation setting where BCG can ablate residual disease. So if we think there's some residual high-grade TA, that's probably not a big deal, just give them induction BCG. I'm not sure you have to totally clear it. But high grade T1, obviously we're worried about the potential for muscle invasive disease. And so that obviously changes the trajectory for the patient. So I think resection is very important, like Sarah said, for all high grade T1s.

Yeah. Let's go through some different potential scenarios once you're in the operating room. And to be honest, I don't know the best answer for this. Let's say bladder looks really good. You see the prior scar from the site where presumed T1 disease was. Are you doing a biopsy of that area? Are you doing a full loop resection? Are you re-resecting the entire scar? Walk us through that.

So I honestly will usually re-resect the whole scar, especially if there wasn't muscle. If it looks like sometimes you have those sort of little dystrophic calcifications and you sort of have one area where it looks like that was truly where the stalk was and I'll cold cup that just to make sure I don't get cautery artifact because I do think a lot of times you resect the scar and you just get that sort of denuded epithelium and you don't get anything definitive. But I otherwise just like taking the loop and doing the sort of staccato method and basically I tell my residents it's like Mohs surgery and just shave it down until we see some muscle fibers. Personally that's my preference. And then I will often take like a satellite biopsy sort of right next to it because I think sometimes you get that sort of halo of CIS and I kind of want to make sure that I fully understand that.

Yeah, I think it's tough because we want to sample muscle, we want to make sure we're not missing occult muscle invasive disease, but a lot of the time these scars come back benign and we'll see a rim of CIS, but I think it still seems to help these patients. Let's say we find a lot of CIS in the bladder, you know, with or without blue light, do you think it's important to resect all of the disease or just sample some and let the intravascular therapy handle the rest?

I generally try to resect all of it. I'm not sure how important it is for CIS, but I think it's an assumption when you see something light up on blue light that it's CIS. It could be invasive disease. So in general, I try to resect everything that we see. Now there are those patients that have very high volume disease and they're heading towards a cystectomy anyway. I may not in those situations. I may just get a representative sample and the patient's really not going to go for intravascular therapy anyway because they have symptoms or they can't tolerate it or they've been through a lot already and now it's time for a cystectomy. So in those cases, I may not, but generally I try to.

Philosophically to me, it kind of makes sense to try to get rid of as much cancer as we can so that the intravascular therapy works, but there's definitely no answer. I don't think a trial has actually assessed that rigorously. Now, I have seen this, sometimes it can be a little frustrating. Let's say we didn't do an office cysto, you go to the operating room, you see a rim of tumor around the ureteral orifice. You're not totally sure if there's more going inside. What do you do then?

I think that's a really challenging situation because the way that you manage the UO has implications for that patient's bladder and upper tract health. My practice has been to resect on cut and not cauterize and basically just take the UO. I was having a conversation with somebody this morning actually about this about do you stent or not stent and my practice has been to try to avoid stenting but then if it looks like it's really narrow I will sometimes put a stent up just to try to avoid that stenotic UO situation because that can be a really tough problem later on if that scars down and you end up threatening the function of the upper tract and the drainage and then you're in there trying to sort of resect to find the UO. That can be really hard. But in general, I know the level of the evidence for sort of the risk of upper tract seeding with a stent after an immediate resection. It's low, it's retrospective data, but I still try to avoid seeding the upper tract if I can.
I cringe a little bit at putting a ureter scope in there, but that would be a definitive way to rule out the extent of upper tract involvement.

If there is tumor coming out of the ureter, I generally will scope them just to understand what's going on. But it's tricky. And so the upper tract guidelines do say that though if we have concomitant upper tract and lower tract disease, generally what I do is I will take care of everything. I like to take care of the lower tract first and then I will rinse the bladder a couple of times just on continuous flows. I mean you hope that there isn't anything floating around. and then I'll do my upper tract work. In general, that's how I've approached it. But I know that some people say, no, you should do the upper tract first and then clear the lower tracts and you avoid the bleeding. So I think there's really not a perfect answer. You sort of have to do what you're most comfortable with.

Definitely case by case. The stent issue is a tough one because I've had stenotic ureters with stenting or without stenting. I don't think there's one right answer. I've asked some of my recon colleagues and there's no consensus on that.

And I think that the intravascular therapy probably causes also a fair amount of irritation and I worry sometimes that that actually exacerbates if a ureter is going to become stenotic that can sometimes make it worse. I've seen that. So it's tricky.

Now let's say you left a stent and you're planning on giving intravascular therapy. Are you going to leave that stent in through the induction course to try to get a little bit of treatment up there or not an important consideration?

I wanted to hear what you think about this, but my personal reading of the literature is that that doesn't really work terribly well. I think that in training we did that, but based on some of the animal studies that have looked at sort of transfer of like dyed intravascular therapy, we just don't get the kind of treatment in the upper tract that we would like to think we get with reflux from the bladder. So, especially if, I mean, if there's upper tract disease, I'm going to treat that upper tract disease according to what it needs. If the upper tract is not involved, then that stent is in there just usually for five days and I'll leave it on a tether so that they can take it out at home and avoid another procedure in the office.

My thought process is sometimes there's some low-volume papillary disease or CIS that kind of retrograde ascends up the ureter and maybe that stent will let some treatment affect that, but it's definitely a soft call. All right, Mark, so this patient comes to the office, you've done the full restaging, let's say maybe just find a little bit of CIS. Are you using any biomarkers to help guide the next steps, or are you just going based on the PATH report?

Going just based upon the PATH report. Saw the data at the AUA for the Vesta, I think the Valor Labs, data for GEMDOSI versus BCG. In the biomarker-selected population, GEMDOSI did better than BCG, which, you know, I think we were joking about this yesterday, that might be the first time GEMDOSI took down BCG. in any setting, you know? I am trying to get that process up and running, that workflow up and running at Mayo and Arizona, but I'm not routinely using any biomarkers at this stage, primarily because I'm not convinced that at this stage there's like enough diversity in therapeutics to really make a difference. I mean, we're going to be putting most of these patients on BCG if we haven't, if we don't, Tymdosy. So, no, not typically.
Well, good segue there. What treatment options are there? Do you think that's true, that we only have BCG, or are there other treatments you're talking about?

For a high-grade T1 with CIS? Yes, newly diagnosed. Newly diagnosed. I mean, so, I mean, we just, the BRIDGE trial just finished accrual, so we were very enthusiastic about trying to put people on that trial, I think, especially for a lot of reasons. One, I think that question needs to be answered, whether or not gemdose should be used in the frontline setting. But also in the setting of the BCG shortage, it was a way of getting more people treatment. You know, kudos to Max Cates and everyone who did that and ran that study. But in general, if it's a high-grade T1 with carcinoma in situ, I'm having the conversation about afferent cystectomy versus BCG. And at this point, I don't think we have anything else that I would consider in the frontline setting.
Do you think about clinical trials or, you know, the new CREST data is interesting as well?

Yeah. I mean, well, and we'll see, you know, once that's ready for primetime, I think that's going to be a conversation we will be having. Yeah, it's interesting. I think we preferentially start with GEMDOSY for a couple of reasons. Interesting. But I also, and maybe this is just the Canadian in me, the cost piece comes into play. I have a really hard time with how expensive those drugs are. But it's interesting, I do think at this point in the absence of comparative data, it's the logistics that end up oftentimes driving patients towards one decision versus another. So I'm a heavy believer in enrollment to clinical trials if I have them available. We are also opening the Credo EAP and there's going to be a TAR 200 sort of further registry that will open up if and when we get the registration on that. But I think that right now, I guess what I'm seeing is that most patients are definitely starting with gemdosy and then we're gonna sort of ratchet up as we go.

Yeah, I think really great points. I personally find the GEMDOSI data to be pretty compelling. There's multiple large retrospective multi-institutional series that are consistently showing one-year complete response in the 60 to 70 percent range. There was recently a study in Europe also where they reproduced this as well, so I find that interesting. I totally agree with your point that it's not prospective data, and it's tough to do these cross trial comparisons. Sometimes that's going to end up shifting the decision considerably too.

reference_conclusion: The panel recommended comprehensive restaging for newly diagnosed high-grade T1 bladder cancer with concomitant CIS, including pathology review, repeat transurethral resection of all high-grade T1 disease, assessment of the prostatic urethra and upper tracts, and baseline chest CT imaging. Following restaging, management should consist of a discussion of upfront radical cystectomy versus intravesical BCG as frontline therapy. If BCG is unavailable, enrollment in a clinical trial is preferred; if trial participation is not feasible and cystectomy is declined or not appropriate, intravesical gemcitabine/docetaxel is a reasonable alternative.
reference_conclusion_quote: the first thing is we do a path 3 review [...] we need to look back in your bladder and make sure that all of the disease that can be resected has been resected and fully understand everything, especially if there's not muscle in the specimen. But I actually re-resect all high-grade T1 irrespective of muscularis propria in the first specimen. [...] But I think also I want to be thinking about the prostatic urethra and I want to make sure that the upper tracts are staged. I do get a chest CT even though the likelihood of pulmonary metastases is low. It's more because I want to have a baseline [...] But in general, if it's a high-grade T1 with carcinoma in situ, I'm having the conversation about afferent cystectomy versus BCG. And at this point, I don't think we have anything else that I would consider in the frontline setting. [...] Like Sarah said, usually a trial. [...] that would probably be where I would ultimately land if they weren't a candidate for cystectomy, if they declined a clinical trial and there's no BCG available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 75-year-old woman. Never smoker. No alcohol use. Prior treated breast malignancy. Reported comorbidities were present. Functional status was described as good; she had still been working at presentation.

[ chief complaint ]: New dyspnea.

[ diagnosis ]: Squamous cell carcinoma of the left lower lobe lung. Clinical stage before brain MRI was described as T4N1 non-small cell lung cancer. A small brain lesion concerning for solitary metastasis was subsequently identified on MRI; stage designation under consideration included stage IIIA versus stage IVA.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy confirmed squamous carcinoma. Diagnostic tissue was obtained from a level 11 lymph node. Other sampled lymph nodes were negative aside from the involved level 11 node.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial thoracic imaging showed a large left lower lobe mass. The mass obliterated the inferior pulmonary vein and abutted the airway and undersurface of the pulmonary artery. PET imaging showed the primary lesion to be metabolically active with probable central necrosis. An FDG-avid lymph node was present at the bifurcation/hilar region. No other mediastinal nodes were described as significantly FDG-avid. Brain MRI showed a small lesion concerning for metastasis.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Liquid biopsy was performed. Next-generation sequencing was also sent. Comprehensive molecular testing could not be completed on the biopsy specimen because of insufficient tissue. PD-L1 status was not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had a prior breast malignancy that had been treated. For the current lung cancer, invasive mediastinal staging with biopsy was completed.

[ current disease status ]: Left lower lobe squamous non-small cell lung cancer with level 11 nodal involvement and an equivocal small brain lesion of uncertain significance. The patient was considered appropriate for resection, with possible need for complex left lower lobectomy with airway reconstruction/sleeve procedure based on local extent.

[ other clinical data ]: Mediastinal staging was completed by interventional pulmonology. Surgical local therapy, if pursued, was described as lobectomy rather than pneumonectomy if feasible.

Yeah, 100%. I think even if it's radiographically negative, I think that the chance, there's a reasonable chance of radiographically occult N1, N2, potentially even N3 disease. And so doing invasive mediastinal staging is absolutely imperative here.

Yeah, this was actually a great case from our side in the sense that this came back to what we started talking about, came from a pulmonologist who then immediately said, look, I've got this individual, I have this imaging, why don't we just see them in the multidisciplinary clinic right up front? And so that way, even before a diagnosis, they saw our interventional pulmonologist, they spoke with our medical oncologist, and they saw me. So we immediately were able to say, well, yeah, the staging plan we're going to need is to go this direction. And so they started out in that multidisciplinary format, and then I think it helped us make the best choices to get a diagnosis, a stage, and then move forward with them. Right. And so we're always thinking about TNM staging regardless of the M part of it, you know, because we often get the patients when the metastasis has happened. And we would want them to get the treatment they would get for the rest of the lung disease first, you know, unless it was widely metastatic. So yeah, I mean, so I mean, if there's an adrenal, you know, anything that's kind of oligo, even a local bone lesion, if it's if it's one, the bone is a little tricky, often on subsequent imaging. Once they start getting treated, they become many. But again, we're looking toward. curing a patient if we can. And so that's kind of where our starting point is. I see this as metastatic. Because we always, as surgeons, are kind of on the fence where if I see nodal disease, and yeah, we've got an isolated brain met, you know, you start to question, should we undergo surgical resection, which comes with a lot more morbidity, or is this someone we shift over to chemoradiation, immuno? and then can treat the brain with CyberKnife, still treat them that way, but take the surgical morbidity away when we start seeing nodal disease. So, I mean, I think an N1 nodal disease is different than N2 or multistation N2 disease. So, I think with N1, I would still proceed. Also squamous cell. The agreed plan was neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy followed by reassessment after completion of systemic therapy and, if still appropriate, definitive surgical resection with lobectomy-based local control rather than upfront chemoradiation. Interval imaging during neoadjuvant treatment was not planned unless there were specific clinical concerns; restaging imaging would be obtained after completion of systemic therapy before definitive local therapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Abnormal screening mammogram leading to recall diagnostic breast imaging for a left breast mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Left breast invasive ductal carcinoma, grade 2, estrogen receptor-positive, HER2-negative, clinically early stage; final pathologic tumor size 1.8 cm; sentinel lymph nodes negative.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsy of the left breast mass demonstrated ductal breast carcinoma, grade 2, estrogen receptor-positive. Final surgical pathology showed a 1.8 cm tumor with clear margins. Sentinel lymph node biopsy was negative for nodal involvement.

[ imaging findings ]: Diagnostic mammography identified a mass in the left breast upper inner quadrant, near the chest wall. Ultrasound demonstrated a corresponding left breast mass close to the pectoralis/chest wall muscle. Physical examination identified a very small palpable mass in the upper inner left breast without clinically concerning lymphadenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Oncotype DX 21-gene recurrence score was 23. The reported estimated 9- to 10-year recurrence risk with endocrine therapy alone was 9%, with estimated chemotherapy benefit less than 1%. Family history met NCCN criteria for consideration of hereditary cancer genetic testing. Genes specifically identified as relevant to assessment included BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, and ATM. No germline test result was reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent breast-conserving surgery for the upper inner quadrant left breast cancer with excision of the lesion and bilateral breast reshaping/breast-lift type oncoplastic procedure. Sentinel lymph node biopsy was performed. Surgical outcome showed complete excision with clear margins and no nodal metastases.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status after breast-conserving surgery for left breast cancer; primary tumor resected with negative margins and node-negative disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included osteoporosis. Medications were reported only for osteoporosis treatment. Family history included mother with breast cancer at age 68 and maternal uncle with pancreatic cancer at age 60. Physical examination was otherwise normal.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you, Dr. Westberg. So this team gets to work together every week, which is the best part of my job. So I'm glad we get to share this tumor board with you tonight. Our first patient is a 62 year old woman who has an abnormal screening mammogram. She was called back and had diagnostic imaging that identified a mass in the left breast, the upper inner part of the breast near the chest wall. She's otherwise very healthy with only osteoporosis, and the only medications she takes is for the treatment of her osteoporosis. Next slide. Her family history is interesting. Her mother had breast cancer at the age of 68, and her mother's brother, her maternal uncle, had pancreatic cancer at the age of 60. She has a very normal physical exam, except for a very small mass that can be felt in the upper inner part of the left breast, and she has no concerning lymph nodes on physical exam. So here's a representative. These cases are also representative cases. specific patients. But here's an example of a mass that would be concerning on a mammogram. Mammograms are taken in two views. And so the first view looks at the breast from side to side. So you can see that the mass is in the inner part of the breast. And the second image shows the breast from top to bottom. So you can see that the mass is in the top of the breast as well, and very close to the muscle of the chest wall. The ultrasound showed this mass. And as you look at the ultrasound, you see the stripes on the bottom of the screen, that's the muscle of the chest wall. So you can see again that this tumor mass is close to the muscle. So she had a biopsy and the biopsy demonstrated that this area was a breast cancer. It's a ductal cancer, grade two, and it's estrogen receptor positive, which is a favorable tumor biology. So this is where patients will usually see a surgeon as first course of treatment. And so we'll review medical history, surgical history, her social and her family history. And then we'll make, surgeons will make the referral to the tumor board for discussion of the primary team. In general, someone with a good early stage and favorable biology cancer will be referred for surgery as the first course of treatment. So I'd like to turn it over to Pam Fitzgerald, who is our patient navigator, who will sit with patients at this initial consultation and will start the process of helping patients work their way through the system.

Hi, can you see me? Yeah, I'm Pam Fitzgerald and I am one of the navigators at Smilow, Trumbull and Fairfield. I am a social worker and what I would do is sit with the patient at initial consultation with Dr. Lynch and get to understand a little bit about their social history and their family history, who their supports are. We would also review the distress screening tool at this time and see what in particular this woman generally speaking, would indicate we're her stressors, and we would try to help problem solve those issues. So for example, in a 62-year-old woman, we would talk sometimes about loss of loved ones. She may have recently had a family member pass away. Her children may be moving away. She may still be working and worried about financial stressors. So in that period of time, would talk about what supports are available to her in the community. We do have financial grants that we can help with. We can also help her with paperwork for work, whether it be FMLA or short-term disability. We also can refer her to counseling. if it's felt that she would benefit from that. The integrative medicine services that we have available are numerous. We have support groups, dietary counseling. We, you know, we have acupuncture and also massage someone very helpful throughout their course of treatment. But what's kind of unique to navigation is that we can travel, so to speak, with the woman throughout her continuum of care. So we can meet with her to discuss her options for treatment, but also explain why things are happening in a certain way, sort of in layman's terms. We're available. We tell them as soon as they walk out of the office, if they have a question, please call us. Call us tomorrow, call us next week, whatever we can do to alleviate stress. We can also meet with them, with the medical oncologist and the radiation oncologist. And again, assess at that time, oftentimes in radiation oncology, people have problems with transportation, we have resources for that as well. So again, we're here to eliminate barriers to care and to also help you from diagnosis through till survivorship. And, you know, we're just like to say we're, you know, a new sort of friend that you would make and please call us if you need us. And with that, I'll turn over to Amanda.

All right, we can go to the next slide. I'm Amanda Ganczak. I'm one of the genetic counselors. We have several who are staffed in the Bridgeport Trumbull location. And basically what we do is help to review an individual's personal and family history of cancer to determine the likelihood that the cancers are hereditary, meaning a gene is running in the family, placing them and their family members at high risk for particular types of cancers. And with that information, we can then target and help the providers plan how to attack those increased risks, how to offer different surgical approaches, how to discuss various chemo prevention or other risk reducing options that might be available based on those increased risks. So if we take this case one as our example, some of the factors that I would be looking at in terms of assessing for the likelihood of a hereditary risk for cancer is the patient's own breast cancer diagnosis, although she was diagnosed after the age of 50. So that alone is not something that would highly be concerning for a hereditary risk. However, she has a family history of both breast cancer in her mother and pancreatic cancer in her maternal uncle. So we see two affected relatives on the same side of the family, combining both breast and pancreatic cancer, which for me are all red flags to see, you know, to further assess this family for a potential hereditary risk. Next slide. So we utilize the NCCN guidelines, which are published on an annual basis out of the National Comprehensive Cancer Network. These are ever-changing and involving as new data and information is collected from our hereditary cancer families. So it can certainly be difficult to keep a bridge to these year to year, but that's what we hope to be there for, and particularly in tumor boards. We help to review these guidelines and all the cases that are presented to determine how eligible someone may be for referral to cancer genetics for an evaluation and discussion of genetic testing. And so, if you just hit next for me, please. In looking at this, this particular patient was diagnosed with breast cancer over the age of 50, and she has a close relative with breast cancer and a close relative with pancreatic cancer. So using these guidelines, we see that she does meet criteria for consideration of genetic testing. Next. And so historically, BRCA1 and BRCA2 are the genes that we see most often associated with hereditary breast cancer. But these genes cause other cancers like ovarian and pancreatic cancer. So for me, kind of top on my radar of assessment for this patient would be BRCA1 and 2. Although they are not the only genes that link breast and pancreatic cancer. The other genes that we might think about in this particular case are PALB2 and ATM. And so in the kind of world of genetic testing nowadays, we do what's called a multi-gene panel where we can test multiple genes for hereditary cancer risk. And I think that would be the best test suited for this patient. And she does meet NCCN guidelines. And so more than likely, she would also meet her insurance guidelines for genetic testing. And that test would help us determine, does she have a hereditary risk? Does she have future risk for other cancers that are higher than we would expect in the general population and our other family members at risk. That testing comes back in a couple of weeks and we can help facilitate that, disclose those results and help facilitate next steps as needed. I'll pass it along to Dr. Mastroni.

It comes back to surgery. Okay. So our breast surgery is certainly continuing to evolve as we develop new techniques to make sure that we are both curing the cancer and also providing patients with a good result and minimizing the morbidity or complications of our operations or symptoms associated with them. And we've moved from mastectomy to being able to offer breast conservation or lumpectomy to more patients and the Pictures in the bottom show the difference between axillary dissection, which was the standard of care when I was a medical student, to now sentinel lymph node biopsy, removing only one or two lymph nodes at each operation, as you see in the picture in the lower corner. Next slide. And so now we've moved into the area of oncoplastic breast surgery, which is providing the best possible operation for patients to achieve a good cosmetic and functional outcome, as well as ensuring that we are providing the best oncologic outcome, that we are contributing to the cure of a cancer. Oncoplastic surgery as often requires teamwork from a breast surgeon and a plastic surgeon working together to come up with the best operation for a patient, and also making sure that we understand what the patient's goals are. Next slide. This is Dr. Mastriani's slide.

Now I'll jump in. So oncoplastic breast surgery is not a cookie cutter operation. And as you can imagine, based on your tumor size and the ratio of that tumor size to the rest of the breast size, breasts come in all shapes and sizes in many different patients and women. So typically we're looking at a ratio of the tumor and the tissue that we need to remove in relation to the rest of the breast. simple slam dunks or smaller tumors in larger breasts. Patients will hardly notice the difference if we remove that lump and we may not necessarily have to do anything very complicated to yield you with a normal looking breast at the end of your operation. However, as you approach the 20 and 40 percent range where you're going to be removing a significant portion of the breast. Oftentimes, and the literature shows this too, it's important to consult with a plastic surgeon because there are options that don't involve more surgery or implants or anything that's going to cause more scars on your body besides that lumpectomy scar. Occasionally we can do things to match the other breast too. So this is our sort of basic guidelines where if you have less than 20% of breast tissue being needed to be removed, you oftentimes can close very simply and you're not going to have a very cosmetically noticeable difference. As you approach the 20 to 40% range, there are a variety of different techniques that we can use to essentially squish tissue from one area into the area that is now a hole where the cancer used to be. Once we go beyond that, then you need to think about volume replacement or removing tissue from somewhere else outside the breast to help fill in that volume and to make sure that you're in your own skin look normal. Next slide, please. And as you can imagine, there are nearly limitless possibilities. So this is one of the fun parts of my job, where I get to talk closely and work with Dr. Lynch, where we figure out exactly where that tumor is, and how can we best design an incision that's going to be cosmetically sensitive. It's not going to be right in the middle of your face every time you look at yourself. And that can easily be hidden in clothing. And also, how can we make this look nicer for you? Sometimes this often requires an operation on the other breast too to help it match. So these are just some examples of what we can do. Next.

So this patient had a cancer in the upper inner quadrant of the breast. And so we planned an operation to excise that to remove underlying tissue and to reshape both breasts in a breast lift type operation. Next slide. And so many studies have been done to demonstrate that this kind of approach to breast surgery is both safe from a surgical standpoint and provides a good oncologic outcome that we can ensure that we are also curing the cancer in the same way that we would be doing it with a simple lumpectomy. So two large trials have shown that they're both safe and effective. And next slide. This is kind of a busy slide, but if those two last columns, oncoplastic breast surgery and therapeutic mammoplasty, the type of operation that we just showed you, also have the best patient-reported outcomes, including sexual well-being, appearance, emotional well-being, and physical well-being. Next slide. So this was the outcome of the case for this patient where the final tumor was 1.8 centimeters in size. We achieved clear margins. We did a sentinel lymph node biopsy, a limited axillary surgery, and the lymph nodes were not involved. Next slide. We sent a test called an oncotype, and we'll move from here to the next slide and to Dr. Phan.

So hi. So as a medical oncologist, I typically will see patients such as this one who have small lymph node negative tumors that are hormone receptor positive, HER2 negative, to discuss treatments that we can offer to reduce the risk of recurrence. long-term. And as a medical oncologist, I'm particularly interested at reducing the risk of distant recurrence. That means cancer outside of the breast and the lymph nodes, lungs, you know, liver to reduce or increase the chance that patients will survive long-term cancer-free. And so for this type of breast cancer, one tool that we have to assess whether a patient needs chemotherapy is called the oncotype. And we'll move to the next slide, and I might go back to this one. So historically, many patients with this profile were offered chemotherapy, but we now know that many patients, in fact, most patients with node negative hormone receptor positive breast cancer actually don't benefit from post-operative or what we call adjuvant chemotherapy, though there is a subset of patients that do benefit in reducing their risk by receiving chemotherapy. So our goal is to identify the patients who will benefit and offer them chemotherapy and then, you know, reassure the patients who won't benefit that chemotherapy is not necessary and the side effects that potentially could come thereof are, you know, we can avoid them by avoiding chemotherapy. So this Oncotype DX test is what we call 21-gene recurrence score. This is a test that was developed by researchers by looking at a whole array of genes that are involved in breast cancer biology and identifying 16 genes that are very strongly associated with breast cancer recurrence, as well as five reference genes. So when we send this test, this test is a test sent on the tumor tissue. It's sent out to a lab. And the levels of those 21 genes are assessed. And then using a mathematical model, a recurrence score that ranges from zero to 100 is resulted as in that report that you just saw on the previous slide. So this test is what we call both prognostic and predictive. It can allow us to estimate the chance that cancer comes back in nine to 10 years with endocrine therapy, which I'll talk about in the next slide alone. And then it can also predict, you know, how much can we lower that risk by adding on chemotherapy to that pill that I'll discuss. So when this test was developed, you know, it was shown when they looked at patients treated on previous clinical trials that there's a subset of patients with a high recurrence score who really do benefit from chemotherapy, whereas patients who have lower scores, you know, the benefit's less clear. So with this oncotype score result from zero to 100, we consider up to 10 to be low risk, 11 to 25 to be intermediate risk, and 26 and above to be high risk. And so this, you know, is validated in a clinical trial called Taylor X, in which patients who had low recurrence scores did not receive chemotherapy and did quite well long term, whereas those patients who had high recurrence scores did because we knew that already that these patients are at high risk of recurrence. And then patients with an intermediate score between 11 and 25 were randomized. a flip of a coin to receive chemotherapy and followed by a pill, endocrine therapy, or endocrine therapy alone. And the results of this study show that for patients with a recurrence score of 25 and below, these patients did not, in general, benefit from additional chemotherapy after surgery. And so, you know, I say here postmenopausal women, but really women who are over 50, like our patient here, with a recurrence score at or under 25, really, we don't think benefit from chemotherapy. And you can see that on the report on the previous slide, they give an estimate of recurrence risk at nine to 10 years as patients was 9%. and they estimated that really we can't lower it any further by giving chemotherapy. That was less than 1% benefit. For those patients, unlike our patient who are younger, under 50 years old, there might be some benefit from chemotherapy in the high intermediate range. And often we take into account other features such as the size of the tumor and the grade. But again, for this patient with a recurrence score of 23, I would not recommend adjuvant chemotherapy. So that brings us to a quick discussion about endocrine therapy. So certainly, though chemotherapy is not needed, adjuvant endocrine therapy will be a really important part of this patient's care. So by this, I mean a pill that's taken once a day for we say at least five years or five to 10 years, which yields a really significant reduction in the risk of recurrence by about half and death from breast cancer, and then has a secondary benefit of reducing the risk of a second breast cancer. So for postmenopausal women, just a really brief overview. A class of pills called aromatase inhibitors, really the preferred therapy to reduce breast cancer recurrence risk. Pills that many of you may have heard of in this class include anastrozole, letrozole, eczema stain. These pills reduce estrogen levels. And in general, these pills can be quite tolerable in many patients with no to few side effects. And side effects are often very manageable with various strategies. But it's important to know that they can carry some side effects. For these particular aromatase inhibitors, joint stiffness and pain may occur. as well as some hormonal like symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. We also look out for bone loss on vermicase inhibitors. This patient had osteoporosis. which is not in and of itself a reason not to offer an aromatase inhibitor, but we would want to make sure that we are working with her primary doctor or endocrinologist to make sure that we're reversing any other causes of osteoporosis, make sure that her vitamin D levels are optimized, and then also potentially offer an IV medication to enhance, you know, bone strength and reduce bone loss. The alternative endocrine therapy is called tamoxifen. This can be offered to either pre or postmenopausal women. But in studies comparing aromatase inhibitors and tamoxifen is slightly less effective in postmenopausal women. These pills can have similar hormonal-like symptoms and also carry a small but increased risk of side effects such as blood clots and uterine cancer. So really, this is a kind of personalized discussion with the oncologist and the patient to decide on endocrine therapy. But for this patient, I would potentially discuss with her an aromatase inhibitor. Then really briefly, in terms of how long do we treat patients for, you know, our standard is at least five years, though there are studies, many studies that are looking at or have looked at extending this treatment to seven to 10 years. And in general, it's an area of controversy. You know, these studies generally show that there's a increased reduction in the risk of recurrence by extending therapy. But this benefit might be more significant in patients who have higher risk disease. This includes patients with larger size or lymph node positive disease who we really might strongly feel to extend to 10 years. For this patient with a small node negative tumor, it's an individualized decision depending on how well the patient's tolerating treatment at five years. I will mention briefly there is a test called the breast cancer index that is also a gene expression assay similar in concept to the Oncotype DX. a score, which can sometimes allow or help for patients who are on the fence, predict, you know, the risk of recurrence in the years five to 10 after treatment, you know, treatment, and also predict benefit of extending treatment. And so this is something that is not right for every patient, but it's something that, you know, potentially might be right for this patient if she's on the fence and continuing endocrine therapy at year five.

OK, I think I'm up. My name is Kevin Du. I'm the radiation oncologist here at Smilo Cancer Care Centers in Trumbull. And I actually really liked what Pam said up at the beginning of this session about being a friend. I think that Really, the best thing about treating patients who are going through a difficult time is really trying to learn what the priorities are, what you hope for, and really being there to help you to try to get there. And I think that's exactly what friends do. So thank you for joining us here, for all the attendings for joining us here and joining the panelists. The radiation therapy is used in combination with surgery in order to reduce the risk of the cancer returning after surgery. It's really enabled what Dr. Lynch referred to earlier, which is an approach called breast conservation therapy. That is, instead of larger surgeries like mastectomy, enabling patients to preserve their breasts and to still maintain the same cure rates as larger surgeries. It's been really a big advance in terms of combination therapy between modern surgeries, chemotherapy, systemic therapies, and radiation therapies. That's been a huge advance in breast cancer care in recent years. As I'm showing here on the slide, we use radiation to reduce the risk of recurrence and to help cure cancer. But in addition, and very importantly for radiation treatment as well as all our treatments, we also want to reduce the risk of side effects from treatment. This is very important. In my earlier comment about understanding patient priority, It's a very important thing to understand the priorities and what a patient is hoping for out of treatment. This is very important to tailor treatment around the relative benefits and the relative toxicities of treatment. For radiation treatment, what we do typically is after surgery, after systemic therapies, we treat the breast with x-rays, and we use x-rays to clean up any possible remaining cancer cells. It may be just a few cells that no one can really see, but we use radiation to clean up those cells. And what you're seeing here is actually a a patient similar to the patient that Dr. Lynch presented with a left-sided breast cancer. What we're looking at here is a CT scan of the patient laying down on my radiation table, my treatment table. We're looking at a CT scan where the patient is laying down on their back, and we're looking from the feet up through to the head in kind of bread loaf slices. And in the front, at the top of this image are the patient's breasts, and on the back, the patient's spine, and in the red contours, the patient's heart, and these black areas to both sides of the heart are the lungs. just to orient you to what we're looking at. You can see that close to the breast on the left side where the heart is, the breast is actually very close to the lungs and the heart. These are very important things that we pay attention to when we're thinking about how to aim the radiation. and things that we worry about when we worry about the side effects of radiation. There's some things that we can do that are very simple conceptually. Of course, we need to make sure that we execute them correctly in order to reduce the side effects of radiation. This is one technique where very simply we ask the patient to take a deep breath when we treat them with radiation. You can see, that by taking a deep breath, your chest expands, and during the breath hold here on the right-hand side of the screen, you can see that, and I had arrows here, I apologize, I don't know where the arrows went, but you can see in the space between the breast, which is in pink, and the heart, which is in red, that that black area, the lung, expands out and puts more space between the heart and the lungs and the breast where I'm aiming the radiation. And so this pink line is actually an actual dose of radiation that I've delivered to a patient. And you can see that it very nicely avoids the lung, maybe just a little bit of catching the lung here and in the along the, where you can see a little bit of black area encompassed by the pink, and entirely avoids the heart. And so this is one technique that we can use to reduce the toxicities of radiation while still maintaining cure rates. Next slide. And then another technique that we use commonly to reduce side effects of radiation is to simply have the patient lay down on their stomachs instead of laying on their back. And you can see in this pink foam board here, which this simulated patient is laying on, is called a prone breast board. And there's an opening here where the breast will fall into that opening and away from the patient's body. And you can see on the, again, on the right side of the screen where I have my radiation doses on, again, this CT scan, that treating a patient supine really, while we're treating the breast well, really captures a lot of this black area, the lung. And we don't want that. So, and you can see that by simply repositioning the patient the breast falls away from the body in the lower panel away from the body and, and you can actually avoid entirely long exposure by simple techniques like this so. Next slide. So, I. Traditionally, a radiation therapy would be delivered by over six to seven weeks of daily radiation. And in recent, probably the last 10 years or so, because of advances in radiation, how we deliver radiation, better improved techniques, improved technologies, improved understanding of breast cancer biology, that we've been able to actually shorten that down to most commonly four weeks of daily radiation. Each treatment of radiation is only about 10 minutes, but Even so, with this reduction from six, seven weeks to four weeks, you know, every day when I talk to my patients I can still tell that four weeks is a lot of visits for them. And in recent, just the last few years there have been more of a data, more of a push, more clinical trial results, which support, in fact, perhaps even shorter treatments than that, potentially even as short as five treatments for radiation treatments. And I think the, the discussion here that I have with my patients is that probably the most standard treatment is the rather lengthy four weeks of daily treatment. However, in selected patients and if it's right for them. You know that. potentially shorter courses of treatment would be appropriate and safe for them to choose. I think the point here, as the slide alludes to, it's not a one-size-fit-all approach for radiation. A lot of it is really just with the surgical approaches and the chemotherapy, the medical oncology approaches. that it does depend a lot on the biology, you know, the discussion between all the folks on this panel, the medical oncologists, the surgeons, in order to come up with a tailored approach and most importantly, the patients. And this again goes back to what I was first saying, which is it is very important to understand what the patient hopes for, what they're looking for out of treatment, and to be able to help them meet what they need. That's my take on the radiation. I think in terms of all these different approaches, probably the four-week regimen is what I would recommend for this patient.

reference_conclusion: The patient underwent breast-conserving surgery with excision of the upper inner quadrant lesion, bilateral reshaping in a breast-lift type oncoplastic procedure, and sentinel lymph node biopsy; final pathology demonstrated a 1.8 cm tumor with clear margins and no nodal involvement. Multigene germline testing is indicated based on the family history and NCCN criteria. The Oncotype recurrence score of 23 does not support adjuvant chemotherapy in this postmenopausal, node-negative, hormone receptor-positive case. Adjuvant endocrine therapy is recommended, with discussion of an aromatase inhibitor, and adjuvant whole-breast radiation is recommended, with a four-week regimen favored for this patient.
reference_conclusion_quote: So this patient had a cancer in the upper inner quadrant of the breast. And so we planned an operation to excise that to remove underlying tissue and to reshape both breasts in a breast lift type operation. [...] So this was the outcome of the case for this patient where the final tumor was 1.8 centimeters in size. We achieved clear margins. We did a sentinel lymph node biopsy, a limited axillary surgery, and the lymph nodes were not involved. [...] In looking at this, this particular patient was diagnosed with breast cancer over the age of 50, and she has a close relative with breast cancer and a close relative with pancreatic cancer. So using these guidelines, we see that she does meet criteria for consideration of genetic testing. [...] And I think that would be the best test suited for this patient. [...] But again, for this patient with a recurrence score of 23, I would not recommend adjuvant chemotherapy. [...] But for this patient, I would potentially discuss with her an aromatase inhibitor. [...] I think in terms of all these different approaches, probably the four-week regimen is what I would recommend for this patient.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 38-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Self-detected palpable breast mass on breast self-examination.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage I triple-negative breast cancer of the breast.

[ histopathology results ]: Core biopsy demonstrated invasive breast carcinoma, grade 3. Estrogen receptor was negative. Tumor was triple negative. Ki-67 was elevated, consistent with rapidly proliferating tumor cells.

[ imaging findings ]: Mammography was abnormal at the site of the palpable lesion. Breast ultrasound demonstrated a small breast mass with an adjacent nearby lesion. Breast MRI demonstrated the enhancing primary tumor with biopsy clip visible centrally and showed no evidence of additional disease elsewhere in the breast; the lesion was near the central breast but not involving the nipple. On clinical examination, the palpable mass was located at the edge of the areola without skin or nipple retraction. No palpable lymphadenopathy was present.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline BRCA1 mutation was identified on genetic testing.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed stage I triple-negative breast cancer in a BRCA1 carrier, with no additional disease in the breast on MRI and no palpable lymphadenopathy. She was a candidate for nipple-sparing mastectomy.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included anxiety and depression. Family history included paternal grandmother with breast cancer and grandfather with prostate cancer. Fertility preservation was a relevant consideration given age.
