reference_discussion.text: We can go one more ahead. We'll catch up to our next case. So in summary, this lady was treated with oncoplastic surgery, sentinel node biopsy. She got whole breast radiotherapy. She had an oncotype test and then was treated with endocrine therapy with a high expectation of cure. And then we can move along to the next case. We'll come back to survivorship at the end. So the second case is a young woman. She's 38 years old who presented with a mass that she identified on her own breast self-exam. And she had abnormal imaging and a biopsy. And her only medical history is anxiety and depression. Next slide. Her family history includes a paternal grandmother with breast cancer, grandfather with prostate cancer and she had a palpable mass at the edge of the areola, the pigmented area of the breast, but it wasn't pulling on the skin or the nipple and she had no lymph nodes. Next slide. The mammogram is done with, you can see the triangle on the skin there that seems to overlie, you can almost see a little triangle underneath there in the breast tissue. Next slide. And on ultrasound, there was a small mass and then another one right nearby. Next slide. She had a biopsy that showed that this was a breast cancer, but this was a different biology breast cancer. This was a higher grade. It was grade three. And it was estrogen receptor negative. In fact, it was what we call triple negative breast cancer. There were no receptors that were found on the cell surface that regulating the cell growth. And the KI67 shows that this is a cancer where the cells are dividing very rapidly. Next slide. A breast MRI was done to make sure that there was no sign of disease elsewhere. And you can see, I see your question. I'll jump in in a minute. You can see the tumor there that lights up. It's kind of whitish, and you can see the dark area in the middle, which is the biopsy clip. The other slide shows that this tumor is not close to the nipple, though. Even though it's near the center of the breast, the MRI is very helpful in very finely mapping the tumor extent, which can help us in surgical planning down the road. And I saw the question in the chat box about grade three versus stage three. which is a great question. And you notice that we talk about the stage quite a bit in both of these cases. The stage of the cancer is determined by the tumor size, the involvement of local lymph nodes, any sign of metastatic disease, and then we take into account the receptors on the cell surface. The grade is how the cells look under the microscope and how big are the nuclei, the middle of the cells, and how rapidly are the cells dividing? Do we see things like mitoses and how are the cells organized next to each other? So the stage takes into account all of these factors and the grade is just how it looks under the microscope. Thanks for that question. Next slide. So this patient is still early stage cancer, like the other one was also stage one. This is stage one, but it's a different tumor biology. And so she then was brought to tumor board for discussion and the discussion leaned towards chemotherapy as first course of treatment. Next slide. Back to Pam. When we meet this type of a patient, what are some of the issues involved in navigation?

So younger ladies have a little bit other issues going on as a little bit different than our first case. She may have issues with finances and working just like the other lady did. But given her age, we would talk to her about fertility preservation if she's thinking about having more children in the future. And if she is, we would refer her to our endocrine a reproductive endocrinology clinic. We would also talk to her about if she has children, how do you tell your kids you have cancer? And depending on the age of the child, we have different resources to help her to do that. But we also noticed that this lady has a history of anxiety and depression. So while we're always assessing for that, we would really be keeping a close eye on her, making sure that her depression or her anxiety aren't a barrier to her care. And if her depression was getting worse, we would make sure we would put the appropriate referrals in, whether it be to social work or psychiatry. We would also refer her to the psychologist. We also have different support groups for younger ladies. We have triple negative support groups. And we also know that our percentage of our triple negative ladies do tend to be African-American. And there are support groups that are specific to African-American ladies. So again, we would follow this woman very closely. We would meet with her with Dr. Fenn, most likely in a multidisciplinary clinic. And just make sure she gets to the right doctors at the right time and meet any of her needs that may come up. With both ladies, we would also be talking to them about sexuality and intimacy and how does breast cancer and the treatment of it affect them. So next slide, please. Thank you.

All right, so I want to take us into considerations for this case and whether or not she has a high chance to have a hereditary cancer risk. And so first let's start with the fact that she has a triple negative breast cancer, which is definitely a more rare type of breast cancer and can be more highly associated with genes that cause a hereditary breast cancer risk. And she's 38. So that alone are two factors independent of any other factors in her family history that would qualify her for an evaluation and genetic testing. But she also has a family history of breast cancer in her grandmother on her paternal side, as well as prostate cancer in her grandfather. Next. And with triple negative cancers in particular, as much as 20% of these women, regardless of family history, will have a hereditary cause for that triple negative type breast cancer. So that is one reason which just within the last month or two, the NCCN guidelines have changed and now recommend that all women with triple negative type breast cancer regardless of when they were diagnosed and regardless of what their family history might look like, should be referred and considered genetic testing. So that is certainly something that has changed based on our recognition of how, what high percentage of these women have a genetic cause. Next. And so she would meet criteria and we would definitely recommend that she come and see us and consider genetic testing. Next. And so in this particular case, my suspicion for a hereditary risk is really high. And so this patient undergoes genetic testing before she has surgery, let's say, and she's found to have a BRCA1 mutation, which is just a fancy way of saying she has a genetic risk. And BRCA1 is the gene in which that defect was identified. And so for this woman who has this new diagnosis of a triple negative breast cancer, these genetic test results now tell us that she has an additional risk to get a new primary cancer. So separate then from this new triple negative breast cancer. And that lifetime risk for her is 20 to 40% that she'd get a second breast cancer. Given how young she is, she's probably on the higher end of that risk range. So maybe even closer to the 40% risk. And so her options based on this risk might include increased screening of remaining breast tissue, depending on what surgical option is decided, or she might meet with Dr. Lynch and the plastic surgeon to decide that the best approach is to undergo a bilateral mastectomy where removing both breasts, including the cancer that's there, removing the rest of the healthy breast tissue to reduce as much as possible that risk for the second primary breast cancer. BRCA1 is also associated with ovarian cancer and that risk ranges between a 40 to 60 percent chance. The hard part is that there's no effective screening to identify ovarian cancer at an early stage, meaning we caught it where we can easily treat it and have long-term survival for that woman. In the absence of effective ovarian cancer screening, We strongly encourage and recommend that women with a BRCA1 mutation elect to have their ovaries and both of their fallopian tubes surgically removed between the ages of 35 to 40 or whenever they're done with their family planning. And so certainly the breast cancer diagnosis is first and foremost in our priority in her care right now at this time. But this is information for future planning for us to think about after we get her through this stage, that ovarian cancer risk is the next thing that we should be focusing our attention on. And then with BRCA1, you can see a less than 5% risk for individuals to be diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in their lifetime, although it's still rather low in all. Most individuals with a BRCA1 mutation will not go on to be diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. And so pancreatic cancer screening has its limitations. It has its risks. We're still trying to prove benefit. And so we really reserve pancreatic cancer screening in individuals who have a BRCA1 mutation, but whom also have a family history of pancreatic cancer in a close relative. So in this case, since she did not have a family history of pancreatic cancer, we would not strongly encourage consideration of pancreatic cancer screening in her case. And next slide for the next.

So this is someone who in medical oncology, I would meet, you know, before surgery and with an eye on time, I'll go through, you know, how we treat systemically triple negative breast cancer and our thoughts about, you know, timing of chemotherapy. So as we had mentioned, you know, triple negative breast cancer is a subtype of breast cancer that can have a particularly aggressive biology. and have a propensity to spread elsewhere in the body quickly. So this is something, a diagnosis where unfortunately because it's not expressing the estrogen receptors or another protein called HER2, we don't have traditionally targeted therapy such as endocrine therapy that I mentioned in the last case to treat these patients with. And so what we think of as traditional quote unquote cytotoxic chemotherapy So traditional IV chemotherapy is really the mainstay of systemic treatment for triple negative breast cancer and the vast majority of patients with triple negative breast cancer will need chemotherapy as part of their treatment. When we know that someone is going to need chemotherapy, we think about whether they would benefit from chemotherapy before surgery, which is called neoadjuvant therapy, versus going to surgery first and doing chemotherapy afterwards. But for patients with triple negative breast cancer, there are particular advantages of giving chemotherapy upfront prior to surgery. So these advantages include for certain patients, especially those who have more advanced tumors, we can shrink the tumor with chemotherapy and may allow for less extensive surgery and improved surgical and cosmetic outcomes. But from my perspective in medical oncology, and more relevant to this case in this woman who has a relatively small tumor, is that giving chemotherapy before surgery allows us to assess the response to chemotherapy at the time of surgery. We know a proportion of patients will have what we call a pathologic complete response or no active viable cancer cells in the pathology tissue at the time of surgery. Those patients generally have a good prognosis. For patients who have residual disease or active tumor still left over after preoperative chemotherapy, we know those patients may benefit from additional therapy after surgery. But we wouldn't be able to identify those patients unless we gave the chemotherapy up front and assess the response. So when we think about who should receive neoadjuvant chemotherapy for triple negative breast cancer, certainly this is the standard of care for more advanced early stage breast cancer, such as stage two and three. But when we know patients are going to need chemotherapy, we will certainly consider it preoperatively for patients who have slightly smaller tumors, including this patient who has a tumor between one and two centimeters. Certainly, she's young, she has aggressive biology, she's a candidate for chemotherapy. I would advocate for her to receive chemotherapy before surgery so we can assess response. And in my next slide, I'll explain potential options for her after chemotherapy if she doesn't have the optimal response at the time of surgery. So when we think of post-operative therapies for residual disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy, You know, I wanted to mention, you know, two options just to make aware of, you know, options that would be available to her if she did have a suboptimal response at the time of surgery. This includes briefly oral chemotherapy called Zolota, which we know improves disease-free and overall survival in triple negative patients with residual disease. But for her situation in particular where she has a germline BRCA1 mutation that she inherited, from her family members. There is a drug called Olaparib, or brand name Lymparza, that's in the class called a PARP inhibitor, which prevents, in general terms, prevents cancer cells from repairing DNA damage leading to cell death. And the patients with BRCA mutations are particularly susceptible, their tumors are susceptible to this drug. And so we have a recent study that came out just over the summer called the Olympia trial that notes that adjuvant olaparib can improve disease-free survival in patients with high-risk early breast cancer and BRCA1 mutation. And so if she had residual disease at the time of surgery, she could potentially benefit from this drug. And that's a pretty new development. And that's all I'll say to preserve time.

It's very exciting, those changes. I mean, thinking about it in the course of my career, how treatment of women with triple negative breast cancer has improved is really, really thrilling. So this patient, because she has a BRCA mutation elected to have a bilateral mastectomy, I just wanted to comment briefly on nipple sparing mastectomy, which she is a candidate for. This is a technique for both treating breast cancer and for doing prophylactic surgeries. And it allows us to preserve the entire skin of the breast, including the nipple. This picture, which is from a research publication, I think really gives a wonderful picture because patients often don't understand how we do the operation through a very small incision underneath the breast, where we're able to remove all of the breast tissue and maintain all of the skin and provide exposure. So the plastic surgeon, my partner, Dr. Mastriani, who have done a few of these cases with can then place an implant or can even use the patient's own tissue to create a reconstruction. These really require, the breast can't be too large. So we have to choose the right patient for the right operation. And it's also better for patients that are not smokers. Next slide. And the outcomes are safe. And so there is both a registry and a large review of multiple studies with multiple patients that show that these are both safe from a surgical perspective and from a cancer perspective and that we can still achieve a cure using these new operations. Next slide. Dr. Mastriani.

I forgot I was on mute. So in general, when we remove the whole gland, what you're left with is a skin skeleton or a shell, basically. So we have two different options currently available to fill up that skin envelope. One is with using an implant, and that's something that we make synthetically. It is made of silicone. All of them have silicone shells. Some of them can be filled with silicone gel itself, or they can also be filled with saline, but all of the shells have silicone on the outside. And it's something that we've studied for the past 50 years and we know that it's safe. The other option is that we can fill in your skin envelope with your own tissue. And this is not an implant. You don't have to take any rejection medications for this. It's your body. It's going to feel the most natural. Next slide, please. The two different kinds of implants that we can do, you'll notice on that former slide, there was a one stage and a two stage. The two stages where I have to put in a tissue expander, which is the device you see on the left, that is an inflatable expander. It allows me to add more volume or take it away as we need to based on how your wounds heal. When we do remove most of the breast, you're removing about 80 to 90% of the blood flow to that skin. So I wanna make sure that you heal well. So this, I guess, adjustable implant allows me to tailor make your reconstruction for you. It also gives you an opportunity to try on the size and you can walk around with that size in your body and decide if that's what you really like. Oftentimes, and more and more often, we're able to go directly to the implant, which is what you see on the right. And as you'll notice, it's not a round sphere like a water balloon. We've also come a long way as far as implant technology to make it more breast shaped and to help it move more fluidly with you and to feel more natural under the skin. Next slide. And then finally, I just wanted to talk briefly about using your own skin. This is probably your own tissue to reconstruct. This is probably the most popular option and it's been around for more than a decade, but we're now becoming more facile and it's becoming more mainstream. More people are training to do this kind of procedure. It is a bit more involved. We can't just move up skin and fat from anywhere. It actually has to come with a blood supply to it. We need to nourish that area. So one common place that we take this extra tissue from is the lower abdomen. Oftentimes women have a little bit of extra fat down there. Perhaps they've had pregnancies and they have a little extra skin down there that is hard to exercise away. So those kinds of patients are ideal candidates for this. Even if you've had a cesarean section, you're still a candidate for this. So we are able to trace all of the blood vessels down into your groin and reconnect them up in your chest using a microscope and we use sutures as fine as hair. So this is an intensive operation. It does require special training, but a place like Yale, we can offer services like this. We can offer a whole range of reconstruction options. And then the beauty of this kind of reconstruction is you don't need any long-term follow-up. With implants, I tell my patients it's a lot like getting an oil change. You're going to come in every 10 to 15 years to get the implant switched out. And while that's an outpatient surgery, it's still another surgery. Whereas if you undergo this option, you're done with reconstruction for the rest of your life. You don't need to come in for oil changes or anything like that.

So our patient had that operation. She had an implant-based reconstruction. Next slide. And she had a complete pathologic response. So she had a tumor there. She received her chemotherapy. And then at the time of the surgery, the tumor was gone, which tells us that she'll have a very good prognosis and that Dr. Fenn saved her life. So next slide. So we're at the end of our time. And so maybe let's make sure we've answered any questions and then we can talk about issues in cancer survivorship. Were there any other questions in the Q and A or in the chat box or any questions you'd like to ask us now?

reference_conclusion: For this stage I triple-negative breast cancer, the multidisciplinary recommendation was to proceed with neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy prior to surgery in order to assess treatment response. Given the identified germline BRCA1 mutation, the patient elected bilateral mastectomy with implant-based reconstruction. Postoperative management would depend on pathologic response, with consideration of additional therapy for residual disease, including olaparib in the setting of BRCA1-associated residual disease.

[...] So this patient, because she has a BRCA mutation elected to have a bilateral mastectomy [...] So our patient had that operation. She had an implant-based reconstruction. [...] And so if she had residual disease at the time of surgery, she could potentially benefit from this drug.

reference_discussion.text: Fantastic. Thanks, Michael, for that. So we will just push on with the cases. And if, Michael, you can advance those slides, that would be great. Thanks. Good. OK. So case one is actually a case of a 58-year-old man with a PSA of 16 who had a Gleason 9 biopsy-proven cancer. and he was referred for consideration of curative intent treatment, and an external staging PSMA PET was done, and it came in with the report of bilateral pelvic nodal metastases, left axillary metastases, bone metastases in the right iliac bone and L3, and multiple lung metastases. This was accompanied by some safe screens that were sent in with the report. So the question for the MDT panel actually, firstly, is What would you guys do as the referring clinicians of this patient and you got this report, what would your first step be? I guess we'll start with Shankar or Declan actually, we'll start with Declan.

Yeah, so we showed in the Pro PSMA trial that the use of PSMA PET-CT provided greater accuracy compared to conventional imaging. And that's been well borne out in other data. However, it's still very important that we scrutinize these images. There is variability in the quality of PSMA PET-CT, although again within Pro PSMA. We did do central review from the 10 sites and did show the concordance was very high, especially compared to MRI, for example. But nonetheless, it's still very important to review these images. So that's the first point I think I'd made to Yiting is that we do like to review all these images ourselves because it's a big call. Does this patient have distant metastatic disease? Does he have high volume distant metastatic disease? It's very important that we have confidence in the findings before we make a management recommendation.
Excellent. OK, well, we might actually move on to the next slide and actually get James to present the case for us.

All right, thank you. So we did get the images imported and had a look. You can see that this is the MIP to the right, and it's quite saturated. So I think that if we have a look down here, you do see the prostate cancer very highly avid, just below the bladder. There is quite a bit of noise, as you'd expect for BSMA PET, but it's very, very saturated. So usually Peter Mac will window it with 15 upper windows, so it looks a little bit more like this when you're interpreting and you have a little bit less of that noise that isn't actually significant. And if we have a look at those screen caps, you actually just had a lot of noise down here in the lower lobes of the lungs. So it wasn't actually, there weren't actually metastases, nothing on CT there. And you just look at the PET image itself, it doesn't look like there's anything that actually stands out. Same for the nodes down here in the pelvis. So again, it does look a little bit more alarming. But then when you look at it in a more appropriate window, there isn't anything suspicious. And same for those bone metastases. So windowing is quite important. It does change how you interpret. It's OK to change it. So you can adjust the windowing. As you see, we say 15. So anything above 15 is very red or very dark. Here, anything that was above 4 had that same appearance, so it's good to have it more around 0 to 15. You can change it just to increase sensitivity while you're reporting, so it's good to change that windowing, especially if you're looking for little pelvic nodes and you just want to have a higher sensitivity.

Thanks for describing that and the importance of windowing. So my question for the panel would actually be, does every PSMA PET that you get from an external site or even internally need to be presented at a MDT? Any one of you?

Yeah, I think at the moment, definitely yes. Because outside of clinical trials, we're doing PSMA PET scans either to aid in diagnosis or to assess whether a patient's suitable for radionuclide therapy. And I think those are decisions that really need to be made in the multidisciplinary setting. But this case also really highlights the danger of not doing an expert review of the PSMA PET scan because obviously in centers that aren't used to reporting PSMA PET scans, there can be variability in the quality of the reports. And also emphasizes the importance of doing PSMA PET scans in the appropriate setting. In this case, it was appropriate because the patient had high-risk disease. I think it was grade group five. So according to the PRO-PSMA trial, it's appropriate. But for example, in a patient with lower risk disease, having this particular PSMA pair report could have caused them a lot of danger, particularly if it wasn't reviewed in an MDT. Fantastic.

[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for consideration of curative-intent treatment for newly diagnosed prostate cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostatic adenocarcinoma, Gleason score 3+4=7, ISUP grade group 2.

[ histopathology results ]: Prostate biopsy confirmed Gleason 3+4=7 prostate cancer, grade group 2.

[ imaging findings ]: Multiparametric prostate MRI demonstrated a PI-RADS 4 lesion. No pelvic lymphadenopathy was identified on MRI. PSMA PET/CT demonstrated a highly PSMA-avid lesion in the left mid prostate with SUVmax 14. No suspicious pelvic nodal disease was identified on PSMA PET/CT. A retroperitoneal focus of uptake with SUVmax 6 corresponded to a small elongated soft tissue structure measuring approximately 0.5 mm by 1.2 cm; this was bilateral and linear in morphology.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA 6.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed Gleason 3+4=7, grade group 2 prostate cancer referred for consideration of curative-intent treatment, with no pelvic lymphadenopathy on MRI or PSMA PET/CT and a retroperitoneal focus of PSMA uptake.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had been referred for possible surgery as curative-intent treatment. An external PET report had described the retroperitoneal finding as a nodal metastasis.

reference_discussion.text: We might move on to case two. 62-year-old man, PSA of six. MRI shows a PIRADS 4 lesion with no pelvic nodes. Biopsy confirms a Gleason grade group 3 plus 4 equals 7, grade group 2 prostate cancer. And he is referred for consideration of curative intent treatment, perhaps surgery. And a PSMA PET CT was done. James, do you want to show us what it shows?

Yes, so you can see the PSMA PET right here, the prostate cancer, left mid prostate, highly avid, SVMAX of 14, and effectively there's nothing in the pelvis. You don't see any node metastases as you carefully scroll through. You can increase the windowing just to have a little bit more sensitivity, but nothing is suspicious. The only finding is up here in the retroperitoneum. So you do have one focus here with the SVP max of 6 and a little bit of a nodular, a little bit elongated soft tissue finding at 0.5 millimeters by about 1.2 centimeters. Otherwise no metastases other than this finding.

Yeah, and that little nodule on the outside PET report was reported as a retroperitoneal nodal metastasis. So that actually makes it M1A disease because it's outside the pelvis. What do you think about that, Declan?

Well, you know, Tom's talk earlier about appropriate criteria is very, very important because, of course, this patient shouldn't have had a PSMA PET CT in the first place. It's like looking for directions in Ireland. If you drive up to a crossroads and ask a farmer, how do I get to Tipperary? And they say, well, I wouldn't start from here if I were you. And that's exactly the case here. We shouldn't start from here. This is favorable intermediate risk prostate cancer. And actually, EAU, NCCN guidelines don't recommend any form of cross-sectional imaging here. So that's very important that when we consider an indication for a PET scan, we make sure that we're following some sort of appropriate criteria. And look, these are expensive. You know, when you made the announcement about funding, the loudest yelps in the audience were from the chief executive. Did you notice? She wears the cost of all these thousands of scans. And so it's still very important that we have some sort of correct criteria. And I think the criteria are going to say intermediate and high risk, Michael, if I recall from the the expert advice that we were given. So that was quite generous. So in fact, this sort of patient will be able to get a funded PSMA PET CT. But I think it's very important that we clinicians recognize there's no data to support the use of an expensive scan like this in this sort of patient, who in actual fact, guidelines don't recommend any form of cross-sectional imaging. It only leads to confusion and delay.
And what do you think about this periodic note?
I'm not looking at it. It should never have been done. It's a crack on. This man should have surgery or radiotherapy and, you know, I will unsee it.
You want to unsee it. James, what do you think about the periodic note?

Well, you do see up in the cervical thoracic junction. You also see some other spots where you do expect to see some ganglia. And when you come back to that node, it is a little prominent. However, you have one on the other side, and it is a typical location where you do find these celiac ganglia. So it wouldn't be of any concern. I'd consider it benign, and this patient does not have any metastatic disease.

Yeah, so it's actually physiologic ganglion uptake. It's not actually a lymph node. And this was a little bit of a trap early on. We might go back to the slides. When we started doing PSMA PET, we saw some physiologic uptake in sites that we just don't see with other traces. And a classic trap are these ganglions that do have PSMA uptake. Here is some histopathology of ganglion. This was first described by German groups as well. Cervical, celiac, sacral ganglia. The key is on the CT, they're linear rather than round. And they're often bilateral, as we saw. So it's really important to be aware of the normal distribution of PSMA PET. and all too often we see new centres starting PSMA PET with inexperienced reporters that just kind of learn as they're going along. If you come here to learn how to do PSMA PET, you really need to do a little bit of literature review, reading, spend a few weeks at a centre doing high-volume PSMA PET, go to a course like this, upskill, because we don't want you reporting normal findings as physiologic. or as pathologic rather. And as Tom Hope alluded earlier, we do want to really improve the quality of PSMA PET-CT reporting around Australia. And we've now trying to do systematic reports using a template. We're currently using the ePSMA template at Peter Mac. It means everyone's using the same criteria, makes the things easy for our referrers to find. And for the audience, go off and have a read of this EANM PSMA position paper. It's really quite handy, helps us all report in the same way. James, do you want to add anything else about standardised reporting and teaching and templates?

No, I think it's just good to think clinicians are watching. They do use this information, even what could seem seemingly unimportant, like what kind of tracer was used, what dose. It can have implications, for example, for the referrals to any research projects. They do pay attention. They do expect a certain quality. So I think it's good to keep that in mind. It's the only idea they have of the case.

And looking on earlier, George showed a couple of reports that were quite drastically different, and making it in a way that's easy for the clinician to actually understand without spending 15 minutes on it, that would be, I'm sure you'd appreciate that in the safety of time.

I guess, I don't know, Shankar, do you have any thoughts about? I think from a clinician point of view, as Declan had mentioned, you don't want to steer away this patient from having potentially curative local therapy for their prostate cancer. But even for myself, I've been saved a few times by nuclear medicine colleagues who've reported what has been uptaken, sacral ganglia or celiac ganglia, which are really an ask. And the question is, can I give sabre to these oligometastatic nodal disease? And clearly I shouldn't be because they're not actually nodes, but they can be reported externally and you can be led down the wrong pathway.

reference_conclusion: PSMA PET/CT findings were interpreted as physiologic ganglion uptake rather than nodal metastasis, with no evidence of metastatic disease. The patient should proceed with definitive curative-intent local therapy for favorable intermediate-risk prostate cancer, with either radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy.
reference_conclusion_quote: I'd consider it benign, and this patient does not have any metastatic disease. [...] Yeah, so it's actually physiologic ganglion uptake. It's not actually a lymph node. [...] This man should have surgery or radiotherapy [...] you don't want to steer away this patient from having potentially curative local therapy for their prostate cancer.

[ other clinical data ]: COVID vaccination had been administered in the right arm 10 days before the PSMA PET scan.

reference_discussion.text: Great. Okay, we might move on to the next case then, which is that of a 53-year-old who presented in 2019 with metastatic prostate cancer with a grade group 5, Gleason 10 cancer, and multiple lines of treatment had been given, including ADT, docetaxel, Abbey, and Pred. And a restaging PSMA PET was requested upon disease progression in a clinical trial, and of notice that a COVID vaccination was given in the right arm 10 days prior to this scan.

So this is the PSMA PET. You can see that the patient has predominantly osseous metastases. You can see some here in the scapula, going down to the spine, here in L5 in the sacrum, and some local recurrence, some local disease in the prostate bed. And you do have these nodes right here. So in the right axilla, they're quite small. They have very intense uptake though. So SVMAX are almost 17, probably just a millimeter or two. So the question is, and the injection was on the left side, so it wasn't an explanation for that. So are there any thoughts about if this is actually metastatic disease, could it be related to COVID?

I think this is really timely because ATAGI, which for our international guests is the Australian immunisation group that creates our vaccine guidelines, they just released another recommendation last week that certain patient groups should go ahead and have a fourth dose for winter. So we are going to be seeing imaging changes quite soon when patients start having that fourth vaccine dose. I remember last year when the COVID vaccines first came out, there were concerns with women having mammograms because of auxiliary lymphadenopathy. And I certainly saw changes in my patients with FDG PETs and even DOTATATE PET scans as well. But I haven't actually seen any changes on a PSMA PET scan that's been attributed to just reactive changes.

And I think- Can I just pause you, Louise, because we want to take a vote while you're talking. Voting is going to take 20, 30 seconds. We want to vote on this question, if everyone can open their app. And the question is, do you think these nodes are benign due to COVID and you don't need to do anything? Would you report them as equivocal? I don't know. Maybe you should biopsy them. Or are they definitely just malignant because they're a PSMA avid and after all, it's prostate-specific membrane antigen? So interested in people's thoughts and sorry to interrupt you Louise, you can continue.

No, that's all right. So I think we heard very nicely this morning about PSMA expression and it is quite specific to prostate cancer. There is uptake in other cancers as we heard and in some normal tissues like salivary glands, but it really isn't expressed in normal lymph nodes. So my opinion would be that it's malignant. Particularly looking at that SEV, which was quite high at 17, you could see that lymph node was quite hot on the PET scan.

You're in the minority. Only 7.4% of people agree with you. Less than 1 in 10, Louise. But the PhD students, they're always the smartest in the room. Always. Declan, what do you think? Does prostate cancer spread to auxiliary nodes?

Well, I voted with Louise on that one, I must say. And one of the things that I think PSMA PET CT has taught us is the quite extraordinary distribution of prostate cancer in the body, even in patients you think have localized disease or local regional. And we usually think that the lymph nodes are in certain templates, but guess what? They're not. They're in the mesorectin, they're in the presacral region. So I think PET-CT has shown us the extraordinary ability that prostate cancer has to metastasize to odd places. And because the specificity is so high, when these things light up like that, not like a celiac ganglion, this is, you know, In a guy with metastatic cancer, I'm usually very, very convinced. We published a big systematic review like this, about this in European Urology, and that was one of our big findings is the specificity is very high. When they light up like that, you know, you got to presume it's prostate cancer in that type of location in a guy with metastatic disease.
Michael, was that 7% from the panellists voting for that number there?

Oh, no, that's the audience. And I was told there were 300 people online, virtually, in addition to what we see in the audience. So we've got a lot of people voting. So that's statistically significant, the p-value for that was 0.01. I'm told. But of course, you know, this lymph node, this is the follow-up PET. You can see that it progressed and it's had an SUV of max of 54 a few weeks later. So these were clearly malignant. And do you want to talk us through this paper seating? Someone's off. There's a study on COVID for everything.

Everything. You name the tracer and it's got a COVID slant to it because that's how you get published these days, you know. Internal medicine, anything with COVID will get published. So this paper quite nicely showed, and that was in PSMA 1007 that you all heard about before and saw that there was actually quite a bit of I can't see that. It was metastasis, I think, in that far right graph. Yes.

Yeah, that's right. So on the y-axis is the SVMAX, so it's a lot higher, whereas the other three boxes are for the nodal react... Anyway, essentially there was a group of patients with COVID vaccines. Some of them had none, so you had controls. And there was a slighter increase in those who had a vaccine, but only around 2 to 3 SVMAX. So it can be mildly increased, but nothing in the order of 17. Once you get above 4 or 5 SVMAX, it's already getting a lot more suspicious than that low-grade uptake.

And I think once you get an SUV, I mean, there's no rule, but it increases with higher intensity. Once you've got an SUV max over 10, it's extremely likely to be prostate cancer and nothing else in that two to three range. That's when you need to think, could it be reactive?
That's right. And we might move on to the next case, because I think that's where the SUVs get a little bit more interesting.

[ chief complaint ]: Slowly rising prostate-specific antigen (PSA) following prior treatment for prostate cancer.

No definite corresponding lesion was visible on CT, although there may have been very subtle sclerosis at that site.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA had risen slowly to 5.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had been managed with active surveillance for low-risk prostate cancer. Low-dose brachytherapy was performed in 2008. Subsequent course was notable for slowly rising PSA.

[ current disease status ]: Persistent/recurrent PSMA-avid disease was present within the prostate after prior brachytherapy. No nodal metastatic disease was seen on PSMA PET. A solitary PSMA-avid lesion in the left inferior pubic ramus was present and was regarded as likely metastatic disease.

reference_discussion.text: Case 4, a 67-year-old who presented with slowly rising PSA, up to 5. And previously, Gleason score 3 plus 3 equals 6. So a grade group 1 cancer, has been on active surveillance, had low-dose brachytherapy in 2008, and was referred for slowly rising PSA. Is this an appropriate indication for PSMA PET, Shankar?

So yeah, I think this is not the kind of patient you would normally be looking at for PSMA PET in general. We'd be using conventional imaging. But in this modern era, when you have a patient who's been previously treated and having a rising PSMA, I think it's very reasonable to be using this tracer.
James, do you want to show us the images? Yes, it's a pleasure.

So you can see the PSMA PET here, essentially very high, moderate to high uptake. So 13 within the prostate. So you can see the seeds are there, the brachy seeds, and there is in bed recurrence. And interestingly, there's no evidence of any nodal metastases. You do go down into the inferior pubic ramus to the left. There is a mild uptake, so SVMAX 4.5 approximately. There isn't anything visible on the CT, though it is perhaps slightly more sclerotic, but quite subtle. So that's the only finding. It's mild degree, so that's a known metastasis elsewhere.

Yes, I guess we could debate whether this is a metastasis or not. If we follow the rule from the previous slide, it's low grade, maybe it's benign, but it's got an SUV of 4.5, it's getting up there. Declan, what do you think?

We do review these cases in MDT all the time, Michael, don't we? And two comments. The first is that we'll usually give a patient like this the benefit of the doubt because the likelihood of metastatic disease is extremely low based on his clinical background, and we would definitely If he was someone suitable for curative intent salvage treatment, we would offer him a biopsy of the prostate. But I think the bone thing, we would give him the benefit of doubt on. But the second comment that just struck me watching these beautiful images that James is presenting is, again, it's an important reason why we need to look at these images together. And using this type of software, MIM, which you all use, which we don't normally get access to. When we log into the hospital system, we see the more straightforward PACS system. And in most of our private providers, it's a very good PACS system, good for MR. But you don't get this degree of separation and being able to separate out the contrast sequences, which is fantastic for looking at the ureters, et cetera. So it just strikes me that that's certainly worth talking about, is the way you folks can show us these images using very advanced software is incredibly valuable for how we make these calls. Because if this was just described as metastatic thing and there was a screen grab, you might just treat it as such. But when you review them in an MDT with expert teams, we would give that patient the benefit of the doubt, I think.

James, do you just want to wind this up and down just so we can see, you know, we can wind these heads up and down and it looks like a metastasis, right? Or we can wind it down and it looks faint and not like a metastasis.

And Michael, you know, we still do see a lot of that, you know, and the whole bowel is glowing green on the fused images, overwinded and so on. But I think because there's now a lot of experience of PSMAT PET-CT in Australia as people have gained experience, we see less of that. But I think for the US in particular, where there's going to be a lot of early experience of PSMAT PET-CT rolling out, I think this is a really big pitfall people need to be very careful about. the wild west of PSMA PET imaging when if you don't have, as Tom said earlier, appropriate acquisitions, appropriate protocols for reporting, then there will be some misleading guidance, misleading interpretation.

to know the distribution of prostate cancer metastases. And if it's in a spot that's very likely to be prostate cancer, then you need to sort of wind up your suspicion and lower the intensity of uptake. So what about this location, Declan? Do you think this is a typical location for a metastasis?

For sure it is. However, I suppose if we think of the initial disease, it's actually a type of cancer we wouldn't even treat nowadays, a low-grade cancer. And I didn't see his PSA, but it's like two or three or something slowly rising. You've got a focal hotspot there. Could that have transformed into a high-grade cancer that could metastasize? Yes, that's why we would biopsy the primary. And if it turned out to be a four plus five grade group five cancer, it probably would be a different way we might interpret this. But generally speaking, we'd be inclined to give someone the benefit of the doubt, I think, if all he had was a little bit of recurrent great group 2 cancer.
We might go back to the slides. Are we going to do an audience poll?
I think George has a question. Yeah. Can you just show us the C distribution on the CT?
Rearrangement.

So George is just making the point to look at the CT and where are those seeds? Is there a bit of a gap there? I think we do see a local recurrence on the PET. Maybe the metastasis is more likely in that setting. Most people think this is definitely a bone metastasis, which actually we agree with. And that's because it's a common site. Prostate cancer likes spreading to bones in the pelvis. And we've done some research on this. I might let James talk about that.
Yeah, can we flip? Go back to the slides, please. Yeah, just go back to the slides for George. There's the...
Sorry, to MIM.
Oh, yeah, to MIM. So, yeah, we do see there were... Yep.
Thanks.

So you'd almost describe it as local persistence of a cancer from 10 years ago. It was a low grade cancer that's now probably a higher grade cancer rather than a local recurrence per se. And the rest of the cancer, the rest of the prostate's well treated.
Could you re-biopsy it to confirm high grade?

Yeah, definitely. Because the specificity is very high, but we've definitely seen one or two that we've biopsied these and it's such a big deal because salvage treatment, even focal re-irradiation can be morbid, but certainly prostatectomy or cryotherapy, whatever, can be very morbid. So I think you need to know for sure.
Michael, back to the slides.

Yes, so there had been the first inhuman nanocoloid injections done at Peter Mac, so for sentinel node imaging for patients with prostate cancer. So there were injections directly into the prostate and quite an interesting series of patients where you do see many typical sites where you do expect to have some drainage, but also many atypical ones. In the image here, you can see some up in the thoracic duct. There were some up in the supraclavicular nodes, in the virchinos, as well as one patient who had direct drainage into the left inferior iliac. So just good reference. Yes.

So I think what we saw in this study was some drainage via venous plexuses in the pelvis from the prostate into that exact location in the inferior pubic ramus. And we see that as a site of metastasis quite frequently. And it's not hematogenous. It's probably a local regional pattern, even though it's in bone.

Great. We'll go on to our next case now, which is a 63-year-old with a recent diagnosis of prostate cancer, PSA of 24. Biopsy showed Gleason 4 plus 3 equals 7, great group 3 disease. And he was referred for consideration of local definitive treatment and had a PSMA PET scan done. Next slide. Yep, so James.

The case should be managed with curative-intent salvage treatment assessment, including prostate biopsy to confirm intraprostatic disease grade before any salvage intervention, given the morbidity of salvage therapy and the need for diagnostic certainty.

Because the specificity is very high, but we've definitely seen one or two that we've biopsied these and it's such a big deal because salvage treatment, even focal re-irradiation can be morbid, but certainly prostatectomy or cryotherapy, whatever, can be very morbid. [ current disease status ]: De novo metastatic prostate cancer with discordant staging between PSMA PET/CT and conventional imaging: extensive osseous metastatic burden on PSMA PET/CT and low-volume metastatic burden on bone scan.

[ other clinical data ]: Conventional imaging was available in addition to PSMA PET/CT. The case illustrated marked discordance between PSMA PET/CT and bone scan assessment of metastatic volume.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, so this one, I just have the screen cap. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Biochemical recurrence after radical prostatectomy, with rising PSA.

[ diagnosis ]: High-risk prostate adenocarcinoma status post radical prostatectomy in 2012, followed by nodal metastatic recurrence involving pelvic and retroperitoneal lymph nodes, consistent with nodal metastatic disease (N1 and M1a).

[ histopathology results ]: Prostate cancer with Gleason score 9, ISUP grade group 5.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- PSMA PET in March 2015 demonstrated moderately to highly PSMA-avid left pelvic nodal disease involving internal iliac, external iliac, and common iliac chains, with extension into the retroperitoneum including interaortocaval/periaortic nodal stations.  
- Disease extended to approximately the level of L3.  
- No bone metastases or visceral metastases were identified on that scan.  
- Largest involved node was subcentimeter, approximately 8 mm.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- PSA was undetectable for 3 years after radical prostatectomy.  
- PSA subsequently rose to 3.5.  
- PSA doubling time was 2 months.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Radical prostatectomy was performed in 2012.

[ current disease status ]: Nodal metastatic prostate cancer involving pelvic and retroperitoneal chains without bone or visceral metastases, with rapid PSA doubling time of 2 months.

[ other clinical data ]: No additional objective clinical data were available.

<image> Slide summarizing Case 6: a 64-year-old man with prior radical prostatectomy for high-grade prostate cancer, now referred for evaluation of rapidly rising PSA after three years of undetectable levels.

reference_discussion.text: This is a 64-year-old man who's had a radical prostatectomy in 2012.

Gleason's score of 9, grade group 5. And for those who aren't familiar with what grade group means, you need to go off and do some reading after this, because the nomenclature's moved from GleasonScore across to this ISIP, International Grade Group Scoring System, so you'll quite frequently see that on your referrals, and you really need to know what that means, because it helps you adjust your sensitivity. Is this a low-risk prostate cancer or a high-risk prostate cancer? So pro-PSMA included grade group 3, 4, 5. So 3 is sort of your intermediate high risk and 4 and 5 is high risk. This patient had undetectable PSA for three years. So the surgeons were seeing the patient every six months saying it's great news, we've cured you. But then the PSA was starting to rise, 3.5, with a doubling time of two months, meaning the PSA is doubling every two months, and that's quite a rapid doubling time. For those who aren't familiar with PSA doubling times, we kind of divide that into less than 10 months, which is rapid, or greater than 10 months, which is slow. So two months suggests this is definitely disease, and that it's probably fairly aggressive disease. Now, I guess the PSMA PETs requested to localize where this recurrence is, which is an entirely appropriate indication, and James will show us the scan results.

All right, so you can see here the PSMA PET. The pelvis right here, there are multiple clips. So this patient, just to remind, did have radical prostatectomy in the past. And you do see moderately avid nodes, moderately to highly avid nodes in the left-sided pelvic chains. So you do see some internal iliac, external going up into the common iliac over here. They do extend all the way up into the retroperitoneum. So you have some inter aortic a periodic sorry as well, so it is a disease with there is n1 disease, but also m1a so there is There are metastases However, there are no metastases past that point. So approximately the height of l3 and no bone visceral metastases So how big is the largest node? The largest one, I think they're all sub-centimeter. So if you just take this one, it's around eight millimeters.
So they kind of look bigger than that on the MIP images. They look really chunky.
Yeah, this one would probably be the largest.

But they are pretty small. So we get a light bulb effect with PET scanning. If the tumours are very PSMA avid, they'll take up a lot of tracer and they look really big, a bit like looking into an old-fashioned light globe, one millimetre filament, but you look straight at the globe and it looks big. So it allows us to really identify very small volume disease. Now the really observant people in the audience have noted the date on that scan. March 2015, so seven years ago. So this was a very early use of PSMA PET. And when we saw these in our MDT seven, eight years ago, it created a lot of confusion because what do you do with this patient? Is it even real? Do I want to maybe confirm? These are tiny nodes. They're three millimeters. Is it really disease? So the question seven years ago would have been, should we histopathologically confirm this? And if I was a surgeon at the MDT, I'd be saying, Renu, I think we should do a pelvic node dissection for two purposes. One, to confirm these PSMA PET findings, because I don't really believe it. And two, maybe we can improve the outcome by cutting out all the tumour that's now left behind.

Yeah, this is, you know, this is the classic Pokemon phenomenon that you're kind of alluding to here. And Declan wrote the paper on this in, was it 2017, Declan? In European Neurology. And, you know, this concept of cutting out Mets as they come up. And I guess the question is, are we really making a difference in terms of their disease recurrence and recurrence-free survival. And I don't think we have enough evidence to really suggest that that helps. Although this is kind of high-volume nodal disease, you know, the kind of pokey met phenomenon is sort of when you have low-volume or oligometastatic disease and you sort of hit them over the head and wait for the next one to pop up and hit that one. But this, you know, this is a man with a short PSA doubling time. There's nodes that are up high, so this is indicative of a systemic relapse.
So you wouldn't be recommending a retroperitoneal nodal dissection?
I would not be recommending a retroperitoneal nodal dissection.
Genevieve, would you irradiate all this tumour? We can just do a little extended field of radiation, get rid of all the disease, try and cure the patient.
We've made a lot of progress for irradiation. I wouldn't go for that because it's going far too much higher in the fields.

So one of the themes that our MDTs, you know, five or six, seven years ago was just because you can see it on a PSMA PET doesn't mean you need to treat it. You don't need to cut it out or sabre it. I mean, this patient may need systemic therapy, but a sort of local regional approach. It's probably not worth it. So we said, just because you can see it, you don't need to treat it. And then in 2016, we hosted the Theranostics World Congress in Melbourne. It was at Peter Mac. And the theme of the Congress was, can you remember what it was, Declan? It was? If you see it, you can treat it. If you see it, you can treat it. And Declan was like, at the NDT, you're telling me just because you can see it doesn't mean you have to treat it. And then you're running a conference, and the theme is see it, treat it.
You're confusing me. You can treat it, you just shouldn't.
And look where we've come seven years on.
Maybe we can go back to the slides.
Slides, please.

I think we do have follow-up on this patient. I can tell you, for whatever reason, this patient was subjected to an extended retroperitoneal nodal dissection. That was deemed the appropriate treatment at the time. And four months later, you can see the result of that. Do you want to take us through the results, James?

Yes, you can see, we can flip back if you want back to the MIMS screen actually, but you do see there were, there was an extensive retroperitoneal and pelvic nodal dissection. And unfortunately you do see it was quite rapidly progressive disease. So you do see nodes. There was one node that was still in the pelvis, but you also see some coming up in the retrocrural Sorry, I'll just back this up. So there is one also, a retrocrural. It did creep all the way up into the mediastinum. There are two bone metastases as well. So it did spread quite quickly and it went all the way up into the left cervical chains. So just a few months later, it did spread quite quickly.
Back to the slides.

Back to the slides. Yes, so Declan wrote an editorial in European Urology titled, Pokermats, got to catch them all. And the message here was that salvage lymph node dissection or stereotactic radiotherapy, you may be feasible for that, but is it worthwhile? And you do need to select patients carefully. Do we really need to ablate all these lesions? And the long-term outcomes may not be any different. And in that short time frame, systemic therapies has evolved. Louise Costos, what would be the appropriate medical oncology treatment in a patient like this with a PSA doubling time of two months?

Yeah, I think in a patient with a short doubling time and relatively high volume nodal disease, systemic therapy is definitely warranted and we can no longer say androgen deprivation therapy is enough. We do have to have a discussion about chemotherapy with docetaxel or one of the novel anti-androgens. There's now even an argument for triplet therapy in some patients. We are limited in Australia, though, as the antiandrogens, so enzalutamide and abiraterone, are not subsidised on the PBS yet, so it is a bit of a nuanced discussion with the patient, but it would definitely be ADT plus one of those agents. And I think I agree with Renu and Genevieve in that with the doubling time that quickly, local regional treatment I think would be inappropriate because the concern is micrometastatic disease that's being missed on the PET scan, which is clearly what happened and recurred.

reference_conclusion: PSMA PET demonstrated pelvic and retroperitoneal nodal recurrence consistent with systemic relapse (N1/M1a) without bone or visceral metastases. The multidisciplinary consensus was against retroperitoneal nodal dissection or extended-field radiotherapy, as local-regional treatment was considered inappropriate in the setting of rapid PSA doubling time and high-volume nodal disease. Systemic therapy was recommended, consisting of androgen deprivation therapy combined with treatment intensification using either docetaxel or a novel anti-androgen; triplet therapy may be considered in selected patients.

I wouldn't go for that because it's going far too much higher in the fields. [...] [medical oncologist] Yeah, I think in a patient with a short doubling time and relatively high volume nodal disease, systemic therapy is definitely warranted and we can no longer say androgen deprivation therapy is enough. We do have to have a discussion about chemotherapy with docetaxel or one of the novel anti-androgens. There's now even an argument for triplet therapy in some patients. [...] but it would definitely be ADT plus one of those agents. And I think I agree with Renu and Genevieve in that with the doubling time that quickly, local regional treatment I think would be inappropriate because the concern is micrometastatic disease that's being missed on the PET scan

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 81-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: De novo metastatic prostate cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic prostate cancer; Grade Group 3 disease.

[ imaging findings ]: PSMA PET was performed before and after enzalutamide treatment. Post-treatment imaging showed increased PSMA uptake in most lesions, with approximately 50% increase in SUVmax in multiple sites. A lesion in the proximal right femur increased in SUVmax from 30 to 45. A lesion in the lower dorsal spine increased in SUVmax from 40 to 60. The number of PSMA-avid lesions also appeared to have increased on the post-treatment scan.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA declined from 390 to 210 during enzalutamide treatment.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient was enrolled in a clinical trial and received enzalutamide. PSA decreased from 390 to 210. PSMA PET after enzalutamide demonstrated increased uptake intensity in existing lesions and an apparent increase in lesion number.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic disease remained present on post-enzalutamide PSMA PET, with increased tracer uptake and apparent increase in lesion burden.

[ other clinical data ]: None documented.

reference_discussion.text: Great, thanks for that, Louise. And so we might move on to the next case now, which is that of an 81-year-old gentleman who presented with de novo metastatic prostate cancer, had great group three disease. He was on a trial, and he had a PSMA PET done pre and post enzalutamide, and the PSA did decline quite a little bit from 390 to 210, but the SEV max was rising. And we might go on to the next slide, please. And so the MDT discussion was whether this was actually progression on PSMA PET.
Yeah, we could show the images.
We might have to get Louise back up to the panel to mic up.
I think the audience is already an expert now in this domain, right?
Exactly, I think so too.

So we do, this was a patient with, who was treated with ANZI, you see the, to the left it was pre and then post to the right with the fused images in the middle. And overall, there was an upregulation. You see an increase in SVMAX in most of the lesions, around at least 50%. You have this one, for example, in the proximal right femur. It went from 30 all the way up to 45. In the lower dorsal spine as well, from 40 to 60. And even the number of lesions does seem to have increased. A lot of them just are a lot brighter, probably some that just were below resolution as well previously.

So knowing that Enza does upregulate, like what we've heard before in the previous session, and now seeing the proof for yourself, How would you actually go about treating this patient? What would you actually do?

I think that's a really good question. And I don't think we have the evidence just yet to say that we can give enzalutamide prior to each dose of lutetium PSMA or continue it concurrently. But I think potentially that will be standard of care in the future. As Louise mentioned, we do await the final results of the ENZAP study. But in the VISION trial, which we'll hear about later today, in the arm of patients who received lutetium PSMA, I think about half of those patients, about 52%, were receiving concurrent antiandrogen therapy as well. And they actually did better compared to the group that weren't receiving the antiandrogen therapy. So it does seem to be synergistic, and I think potentially in the future, but not just yet.

As you mentioned, it's not funded, so that always comes into the picture as well. So we might go on to the next. Back to the slides, please. So actually, we might look at some of these response criteria that Tom talked about earlier, and particularly this proposal for the therapy response assessment criteria, the PSMA-PEP progression criteria. Michael, would you like to comment on this that was released?

Yeah, the PPP criteria. So this essentially defines sort of one or two new lesions. So you're not, you know, a change of intensity of uptake alone does not define progression. Even if your SUV's gone from 30 to 60, that's not progression. You've got to have new sites of disease. That's the key here. And I think that is an important differentiator. If you do the same PET scan on a patient every day for seven days, the SUV does have some natural variability. And that has been looked at. Here's a study of Gallium PSMA-11, where they took the same patients, intra-patient variability, 14 days apart, repeated the PET, and there was a variability in SUV, which was quite consistent with FDG. And there's also a study of DCFPYL showing exactly the same. So these are, you know, the SUVs are quite reproducible, but you will have a variation as much as kind of plus or minus, maybe even up to 30% at the extremes. Just routinely. Just routinely. The same with FDG. So you do need to have a big difference for it to be significant. Throw in a drug like enzalutamide that's not actually causing progression, but just up-regulation of a receptor expression, then you may get a doubling of SUV and it's not progression at all, it could be response. So we really do need to be seeing new sites of disease. I think throwing in CT is very useful if it's a lymph node. Is it getting bigger? If it's not getting bigger, it's not progression. Bone is more difficult because you can't really measure it. Whole body MR, which is not really done in Australia, is useful for measuring these bone lesions. It may be useful.
Thank you. Good. We'll move on to the next one.

reference_conclusion: PSMA PET findings were not considered sufficient to establish progression in this case. Increased PSMA uptake intensity alone, including substantial SUV rise after enzalutamide, should not be interpreted as progression without new sites of disease; correlation with CT was considered useful for nodal lesions to assess interval enlargement.

That's the key here. [...] Throw in a drug like enzalutamide that's not actually causing progression, but just up-regulation of a receptor expression, then you may get a doubling of SUV and it's not progression at all, it could be response. So we really do need to be seeing new sites of disease. I think throwing in CT is very useful if it's a lymph node. Is it getting bigger? If it's not getting bigger, it's not progression.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Male patient. Age was not documented.

[ chief complaint ]: Biochemical recurrence after radical prostatectomy, with slowly rising PSA.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma, status post robotic radical prostatectomy, with subsequent biochemical recurrence and suspected solitary osseous metastatic recurrence.

[ histopathology results ]: Prostatectomy specimen showed Gleason score 9 disease, corresponding to ISUP Grade Group 5.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Preoperative prostate MRI showed a PI-RADS 5 lesion.  
- Initial PSMA PET at staging demonstrated localized disease only, with no nodal involvement.  
- Follow-up gallium-68 PSMA PET performed approximately 18 months after prostatectomy showed no abnormal uptake in the prostate bed and no pelvic nodal uptake.  
- The same scan demonstrated a single mild focal PSMA-avid lesion in the left side of the T2 vertebral body, SUVmax approximately 3.  
- No corresponding abnormality was identified on CT at the T2 lesion site.  
- Comparison with prior gallium-68 PSMA PET from approximately 9 months earlier showed no uptake or CT abnormality at T2 at that time.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- PSA at recurrence was 0.7.  
- PSA doubling time was approximately 12 months.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Robotic radical prostatectomy had been performed for high-risk localized prostate cancer.  
- At approximately 18 months post-prostatectomy, PSA had risen slowly to 0.7, consistent with biochemical recurrence.

[ current disease status ]: Approximately 1.5 years after prostatectomy, the patient had low-volume recurrent disease with a slowly rising PSA and a new solitary PSMA-avid T2 vertebral body lesion suspicious for metastasis. No local recurrence in the prostate bed and no nodal disease were identified on the most recent PSMA PET.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Both the prior and current PSMA PET scans were gallium-68 PSMA studies performed on the same scanner with similar acquisition conditions, including uptake time of 60 minutes.

Only 0.7, so quite low, below 1, doubling time of 12 months, that's a little bit unusual, but that's this patient, so they've got kind of a lower kinetic recurrence, even though they did have aggressive disease initially, and we're now one and a half years after the prostatectomy. We do see sort of slightly higher incidence of ganglion, maybe benign reactive nodal uptake between these traces. So when we look at them, we do want to know what tracer it is, and it makes some very minor nuanced difference, but we agree that there are both equivalent and in fact that that rumor I shared recently about funding you know that in Australia the funding will be tracer agnostic so it will apply for gallium psma-11 or the fluorinated dcft oils or even 1007.

So I think from our perspective as nuclear medicine physicians is to make sure that we know of these pitfalls and actually apply that in our clinical practice when we're actually reporting it to make sure that we're not over calling things because that obviously does make a difference to our referring team. Yeah, thank you. So you can see this patient had the radical prostatectomy, a little bit of an elongated bladder there. There's nothing in the prostate bed. best test is waiting and seeing. That was the answer I was looking for. Oh really? I didn't think you were going to come up with it. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old patient with prostate cancer.

[ chief complaint ]: Referred for curative-intent treatment of prostate cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma, Grade Group 4.

[ imaging findings ]: Conventional staging imaging was normal. PSMA PET using DCFPyL demonstrated mildly to moderately PSMA-avid primary tumor in the left peripheral zone of the mid prostate, with SUVmax approximately 7. No suspicious nodal metastases were identified in the pelvic chains. A solitary focus of mild PSMA uptake was present in a rib, with SUVmax 2.2, corresponding on CT to very subtle, well-circumscribed mild sclerotic change. Physiologic/benign tracer uptake was also seen in the tracheal/submucosal region, ganglia, and bronchociliary activity.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA 23.

[ current disease status ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma, Grade Group 4, with normal conventional staging imaging and PSMA PET demonstrating a mildly to moderately avid primary tumor in the left peripheral zone of the mid prostate, no suspicious pelvic nodal metastases, and a solitary mildly avid rib focus.

All right, so you can see the prostate cancer in the peripheral zone, left twister mid-prostate. Mildly avid, so mild to moderate, seven SV max. It isn't quite striking. We don't see any nodal metastases, so we go through quite the higher intensity in the prostate. those pelvic chains just to increase our sensitivity. There's nothing suspicious that stands out. Have another look in that SUV15 window and looking at the MIP, so the only thing that does stand out, just increase the intensity a bit, but you do see one focus of mild uptake in a rib right here. So again, it's something that depends how you window. If you bring it up a lot, it does stand out quite a bit. Could be alarming if this is like the fused image in the packs, for example. When you window it a little more appropriately, it's quite mild. And then on CT, there are some mild sclerotic changes. Very subtle, though. It looks well circumscribed, though.
And what's going on in the trachea? I kind of see the trachea out like on the skin.

Yeah, we do see trachea and also a lot of, you see those ganglia that stand out, sorry. So these are two common normal findings that we see quite frequently. And you see the ganglia right here as well. And then bronchociliary activity.

Yes, a little bit like the salivary glands, the submucosa that tracks along the trachea that kind of makes your mucus, has some PSMA expression, so you often see that, particularly a little bit more with DCF-PYL than the gallium, that tracheal pattern of uptake. So, who thinks this is a ribmetastasis? I don't know that we have an audience vote on this. Do we or not? Do we have a poll? I believe so. We have a poll. We want to know, is this a ribmetastasis? It could be a benign finding, it could be equivocal. Should we tell what tracer we're using? It could be intense. It is DCFPYL.
Have you said the SUVmax of that?

Or is it PSMA1007? So you can see a little bit of a theme of this MDT has been these tricky cases. If it's really intense it's easy. If it's got an SUVF20, it's prostate cancer, it doesn't matter what tracer you're using, it's really easy. These are the ones that you need to get a better feel for, low intensity uptake, low SUV, then you need to know where is it, which tracer is it, what's the grade group, what's the likelihood of metastases, then you need to put all those things together to try to guide you, is it malignant, equivocal or benign.
So this apparently was a SUV of 2.2?
SUV of 2.2.
Can we have a look at the audience poll please?
There is no audience poll. That's okay. We'll have a panel poll instead. Renew.
Met or no met?
Three choices.
You can tell time is...
If you don't know, just pick C. I think it could be a met. Could be a met. Louise.
I think because of the location and the low SUV, I'm going to say equivocal.
I would say quite the same and give the benefit to say it's not I'd say it's equivocal as well.
Probably not I probably thought this is not probably benign. Yes. James, what did you report it as?

Yeah, probably benign also, quite frequent But were you right? Do we have a follow-up? Do we have the best test? We don't have the best test We do have time, we've got 5 minutes left Not as in time on this patient We just have to change. No, we don't have a follow-up for this one. So this was reported as probably benign. Quite frequently see these, very mild uptake, very well-defined slight sclerosis, but nothing concerning. If we go back to the slides.
There is a great paper on this. James, tell us about it.

Yeah, so BGUI, so solitary rib lesions, how frequently they're malignant or benign. And the key message here is that it's very, very unlikely metastases. In 2% of the time with gallium, we did find malignancy within those. And so 98% of those were actually benign. And if we looked at the median of the false positives, it was SCV max of 3. So it's quite low, quite similar to this case, where when you have that SCV max around 2 and 3, solitary rib lesion, it's very probably benign.

And can I actually make a point here? I think from my learning experience over the years, so five years ago, I would have definitely been much more suspicious of that, saying that, you know, likely solitary metastasis. But obviously, repeat it again and see whether it's progressed. But these days, right, I would completely actually go more towards the benign side of things because we know how uncommon it is to actually have a solitary rib metastasis. I mean, we knew that from the bone scan days as well, where a solitary rib lesion as well was very unlikely to be a solitary rib metastasis. So I guess, you know, that really tells us how important having the follow-up is for these patients and also time when we actually learn in terms of a new technology that comes into place where we need to know the pitfalls again of what we are seeing and what we're reporting.
Yeah, I agree completely.

I think part of the problem was his PSA was so high. You know, that always causes a bit of discomfort, but when a young patient, when it's equivocal like that, you would give him the benefit of the doubt.
Correct.
Lucky last case. We're going to move on to an experimental pet indication.

reference_conclusion: PSMA PET demonstrated uptake confined to the primary prostate lesion, with no suspicious nodal metastases. The solitary mildly avid rib focus was interpreted as probably benign rather than metastatic disease. Management should therefore proceed as for non-metastatic prostate cancer with curative-intent treatment.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old patient with a family history of prostate cancer in the father and brother.

[ chief complaint ]: Elevated prostate-specific antigen.

[ diagnosis ]: Elevated prostate-specific antigen with PI-RADS 2 multiparametric MRI and a focal PSMA-avid lesion in the left transition zone.

[ imaging findings ]: Multiparametric MRI demonstrated PI-RADS 2 findings. Pelvic PSMA PET/CT using gallium-68 PSMA-11 demonstrated an obvious focal area of increased uptake in the left transition zone with SUVmax 12. Mild diffuse uptake was present throughout the remainder of the transition zone. No other focal abnormal uptake within the prostate was described.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None available.

[ laboratory results ]: PSA 8. PSA density 0.2.

[ current disease status ]: Elevated prostate-specific antigen under evaluation, with discordant multiparametric MRI (PI-RADS 2) and PSMA PET/CT findings.

[ other clinical data ]: PSMA PET pattern was described as focal transition zone uptake with SUVmax above 12.

Just some people have 100cc prostates with a PSA of 5, and in the context of such a large prostate, that PSA is less significant.
And the Pirates was only 2. So I guess the question is, how would you manage this patient? Surveillance, biopsy, or other? But we'll have a look at the scan first, actually, James, if you could.

All right, so obviously this is a patient from primary, primary one. So it's a pelvic only scan, PSMA PET scan. It's with gallium PSMA 11. And it's a beautiful case. You can see here, it's quite clear. There is an obvious focus right here. within the left transition zone SVMax of 12, so it is quite high. And then you can notice that there's a little bit of diffuse uptake within the rest of the transition zone, so it's quite mild. If you have a look at the MIP right here. You see the bladder here. There's a little bit of diffuse uptake here, which isn't really concerning. And then that focus that is very suspicious. This is a great example I find because you do see the peripheral zone around.
