case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old male; right-handed; Karnofsky Performance Status 90.

[ chief complaint ]: Forgetfulness and generalized weakness.

[ diagnosis ]: WHO grade 4 astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, involving the left temporal lobe with multifocal disease.

[ histopathology results ]: Histopathology from left temporal lesion after resection showed astrocytoma grade IV, IDH-mutant. Ki-67 proliferation index was reported as 20–30%.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial MRI brain showed a multifocal left temporal lobe lesion with cystic and necrotic components and heterogeneous infiltrative enhancement. There was surrounding vasogenic edema extending into the left insular cortex and ipsilateral basal ganglia. Abnormal T2/FLAIR hyperintense signal was also present in the contralateral medial temporal lobe without significant enhancement. Imaging described bilateral temporal lobe abnormal signal, with edema appearing to cross the midline. The lesion demonstrated multifocal/nodular enhancement along the cyst wall. Descending transtentorial herniation and effacement of the basal cisterns were described on preoperative imaging. Postoperative MRI performed within 24 hours of surgery showed postsurgical changes and near-total resection of the enhancing lesion, with decreased size of the cystic component and a few residual enhancing foci along the superior aspect of the operative region.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH-mutant. MGMT methylation status had not been performed/reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent neuronavigation-guided left temporal craniotomy with maximal safe resection. Postoperative imaging demonstrated near-total resection.

[ current disease status ]: Status post left temporal craniotomy and maximal safe resection, with residual enhancing disease on early postoperative MRI. Multifocal/bilateral temporal lobe signal abnormality remained evident on imaging.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 26-year-old man; ECOG performance status 1.

[ chief complaint ]: Severe headache and rapid blurring/deterioration of vision.

[ diagnosis ]: Astrocytoma, WHO grade 3.

[ histopathology results ]: Stereotactic/open biopsy via right frontal mini-craniotomy showed astrocytoma grade 3.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative MRI brain showed a diffuse, ill-defined infiltrative lesion centered in the corpus callosum, crossing the midline and infiltrating the adjacent cerebral hemispheres. T2-weighted imaging demonstrated hyperintense infiltrative signal involving predominantly the corpus callosum with extension into subcortical white matter and cortex, posterior extension into the corona radiata, involvement of the frontal and parietal lobes, and inferior extension into the temporal lobes. The lesion involved more than three lobes bilaterally. Post-contrast T1-weighted imaging showed no discrete enhancement, no cystic component, and no necrosis. Postoperative MRI showed a right frontal surgical tract/post-surgical changes after biopsy; the lesion size was reported as more or less unchanged, with interval increase in the infiltrative component also described on postoperative imaging.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: 1p/19q codeletion not detected. IDH1 and IDH2 alterations not detected. MGMT promoter methylation not detected.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent biopsy only; extensive resection was not performed because of diffuse lesion extent. Postoperative imaging demonstrated post-surgical changes in the right frontal lobe without meaningful reduction in tumor burden.

[ current disease status ]: Diffuse non-enhancing infiltrative supratentorial astrocytoma involving the corpus callosum and bilateral frontal, parietal, and temporal regions, symptomatic with headache and visual blurring, status post biopsy.

[ other clinical data ]: No additional laboratory results were available.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 39-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in 2021 with frontal lobe symptoms and seizures/fits.

[ diagnosis ]: Right frontal diffuse astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 2.

[ histopathology results ]: Histopathology from February 2022 neuro-navigation-guided craniotomy/debulking showed diffuse astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, grade 2. GFAP was positive. p53 was positive. ATRX loss was present. Ki-67 proliferation index was up to 5%.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Pre-operative MRI dated December 2021 showed a large right frontal lobe lesion crossing the genu of the corpus callosum, with a central cystic component, heterogeneous signal characteristics, vasogenic edema crossing the midline, subfalcine herniation, marked mass effect on the ipsilateral lateral ventricle and frontal horn of the contralateral lateral ventricle, and small subarachnoid seepage along the occipital horn of the left lateral ventricle. There were internal T1 hyperintense/T2 low-signal foci consistent with hemorrhagic areas. The lesion showed irregular peripheral/nodular enhancement of the cystic component.  
- Early post-operative MRI, approximately 6 weeks after surgery and before radiotherapy, showed reduction in bulk of the right frontal lesion with decreased mass effect and reduced subfalcine herniation. A new/enlarged enhancing lesion was seen contralaterally in the left frontal region, in an area that had previously shown edema. Post-surgical changes were confined to the right frontal side.  
- MRI from July 2022, approximately 5 months after completion of radiotherapy while temozolomide was ongoing, showed encephalomalacic/gliotic change in the right frontal resection bed with significantly reduced mass effect. The contralateral lesion had partially regressed in size, with residual enhancing component near the genu of the corpus callosum.  
- MRI from July 2024 showed no enhancement at the site of the prior contralateral lesion.  
- MRI from May 2025 showed recurrent enhancement in the contralateral frontal region.  
- MRI from August 2025 showed interval increase in enhancement in the left frontal lesion and also enhancement on the right side along the inferior/medial aspect of the lesion, anterior to the frontal horn.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH mutation was present. ATRX loss was present. p53 was positive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent neuro-navigation-guided craniotomy/debulking of the right frontal lesion in February 2022. The left-sided lesion was not surgically approached.  
- Received chemoradiotherapy after surgery, including concurrent temozolomide and whole-brain radiation.  
- Received temozolomide for 7 cycles (5 days per month).  
- Serial imaging showed initial reduction in the right frontal lesion and subsequent regression of the contralateral lesion, with no enhancement seen on July 2024 imaging.  
- Imaging in 2025 demonstrated recurrent/progressive enhancing disease.

[ current disease status ]: As of August 2025, there was radiologic progression with increasing enhancement in the left frontal region and additional enhancing abnormality on the right frontal side. Functional status was reported as class I. She had returned to work as a school teacher. She was neurologically and behaviorally well apart from urinary incontinence.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Examination at presentation showed subtle cognitive impairment and papilledema; otherwise no major abnormality was described.  
- The patient had shown significant clinical improvement over time after initial treatment.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 26-year-old female. Performance status was documented as APS 90; KPS 100.

[ chief complaint ]: Right nasal blockage and progressive right eye proptosis for 2 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Olfactory neuroblastoma involving the right nasal cavity with extension into the right orbit and intracranial parasagittal/right gyrus rectus region.

[ histopathology results ]: Endoscopic biopsy of the lesion performed on 12 November 2024 showed olfactory neuroblastoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative MRI brain with contrast dated 27 October 2024 demonstrated a contrast-enhancing lesion extending from the right nasal cavity into the right orbit and intracranially to the right parasagittal region. Imaging review described a mass filling the right nasal cavity, causing mild right proptosis, with remodeling of the medial orbital wall. The lesion had an intracranial component in the region of the right gyrus rectus near the midline/parasagittal location. The lesion was T2 hyperintense. Post-contrast imaging showed significant enhancement, with intense enhancement of the intracranial component and heterogeneous enhancement of the nasal cavity component. Coronal and sagittal images demonstrated continuity between the intranasal and intracranial components through the olfactory groove region. There was extension into the right orbit up to the right optic nerve. The right medial rectus was not appreciable, and portions of the right superior and inferior rectus muscles appeared infiltrated. No abnormal signal intensity was described within the brain parenchyma. Postoperative MRI brain with contrast dated 11 December 2024 showed near-complete resection; residual enhancing tissue along the surgical tract was questioned on imaging review. PET scan showed pulmonary lesions suspicious for metastases.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available. CT-guided biopsy of pulmonary lesions had been performed, and pathology results were pending.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient initially presented to ENT clinic. Endoscopic biopsy was performed on 12 November 2024 and established the diagnosis. Open craniofacial resection was performed on 10 December 2024 using a combined surgical approach involving neurosurgery, ENT, and plastic surgery; the operative approach was described as craniotomy extended to lateral rhinotomy. Postoperative MRI on 11 December 2024 demonstrated near-complete resection.

[ current disease status ]: Status post open craniofacial resection with near-complete resection on postoperative MRI. Pulmonary lesions remained under evaluation for possible metastatic disease; CT-guided biopsy results were awaited. Vision was intact.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had initially presented to the ENT clinic. Orbit involvement was present radiologically on the right side.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 33-year-old male; Karnofsky Performance Status 90.

[ chief complaint ]: Multiple cranial nerve palsies. Left hemiparesis and facial weakness developed in 2019.

[ diagnosis ]: Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma in the sellar/suprasellar region with residual/recurrent disease after surgery and CyberKnife treatment.

[ histopathology results ]: Histopathology from resection performed on 05 December 2017 showed adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- MRI brain dated 02 August 2017 showed a heterogeneous midline sellar/suprasellar lesion posterior to the optic chiasm, with a large T2 hypointense component in the midline likely at or inferior to the third ventricle.  
- The lesion extended into the right cavernous sinus/paracavernous region and inferiorly into the sphenoid sinus.  
- It caused significant mass effect with compression of the midbrain and upward displacement/lifting of the third ventricle.  
- Temporal horns appeared mildly prominent, suggesting possible hydrocephalus.  
- The lesion demonstrated heterogeneous enhancement with both enhancing and non-enhancing components.  
- The optic chiasm was not separately visualized on the provided images.  
- Postoperative MRI in November 2017 showed significant residual disease/large residual lesion with persistent heterogeneous enhancement, residual suprasellar component along the floor of the third ventricle, and right paracavernous involvement.  
- MRI in 2021 showed reduction in tumor size compared with prior studies.  
- Comparative imaging through December 2021 demonstrated decreased enhancing component after radiotherapy, with persistent residual mass effect.  
- MRI dated 18 December 2024 showed mild progression of the lesion, with multiple internal non-enhancing areas/necrotic change, persistent residual mass, involvement of the right cavernous sinus, and mass effect on the pons/brainstem.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Not available.

[ laboratory results ]: Not available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Right craniotomy and resection of sellar/suprasellar tumor performed on 05 December 2017.  
- Postoperative MRI showed significant residual disease.  
- CyberKnife treatment was administered in March 2018.  
- Follow-up MRI in 2021 showed reduction in tumor size after treatment.

[ current disease status ]: Residual/recurrent sellar-suprasellar craniopharyngioma with mild radiologic progression on MRI dated 18 December 2024 and ongoing multiple cranial nerve palsies.

[ other clinical data ]: The lesion had longstanding mass effect on adjacent critical structures including the midbrain/brainstem and third ventricle, with right cavernous sinus involvement.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 41-year-old male; Karnofsky Performance Status 90.

[ chief complaint ]: Coccygeal pain and increasing urinary hesitancy for 6 months.

[ diagnosis ]: Sacrococcygeal mesenchymal chondrosarcoma.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Sacrococcygeal lesion biopsy was performed on 27 October 2024.  
- Intraoperative frozen section showed malignant pathology and was inconsistent with chordoma.  
- Final pathology favored mesenchymal chondrosarcoma.  
- Immunomarkers reported included CD99 and NKX2.2.  
- Tumor grade was not reported.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- MRI lumbosacral spine with contrast dated 22 October 2024 showed a contrast-enhancing sacrococcygeal midline mass.  
- MRI review described a large sacral mass with intrapelvic and extrapelvic components, with the intrapelvic component larger. The lesion was hypointense on T1, heterogeneous on T2, showed internal necrotic areas, and demonstrated significant post-contrast enhancement. The distal sacrum and probably coccyx were involved. There was infiltration/surrounding of cauda equina/sacral nerve roots. The urinary bladder was markedly distended, consistent with neurogenic bladder. No lymphadenopathy was appreciated on the limited images reviewed.  
- CT chest/abdomen dated 31 October 2024 showed a sacroiliac/sacral midline mass with suspicion of a deposit in the left parapholic/left hypochondrial region and suspected peritoneal metastases.  
- PET scan dated 14 November 2024 showed a large hypermetabolic destructive mass arising from the distal sacrum with dense calcification and central necrosis. A morphologically stable subcentimeter nodule in the left hypochondrium was reported as most likely a splenule rather than metastatic disease. PET review showed FDG uptake confined to the primary lesion, with no abnormal FDG-avid lesion elsewhere.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]: None reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Surgery was initially undertaken with intent for maximal safe resection; biopsy of the sacrococcygeal lesion was performed on 27 October 2024.  
- The initial resection procedure was abandoned because of significant intraoperative bleeding.  
- Preoperative angioembolization was subsequently performed.  
- Maximal safe resection was performed on 26 November 2024.  
- Operative assessment documented gross complete resection; no rectal resection was required, although the tumor was very close to the rectum.  
- No postoperative imaging had been performed at the time of documentation.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Post-resection status following gross complete excision of sacrococcygeal mesenchymal chondrosarcoma.  
- Significant microscopic residual disease could not be excluded on operative assessment because of close proximity to the rectum.  
- No confirmed distant metastatic disease was identified on PET imaging prior to surgery.  
- Postoperative radiologic disease status had not yet been assessed.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Initial radiologic differential diagnosis included chordoma and chondrosarcoma.  
- CT-guided biopsy of the intra-abdominal/left hypochondrial lesion had been considered but was deferred because it was assessed as high risk.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 34-year-old woman. Karnofsky Performance Status was 80. No comorbidities were documented. No significant smoking history was reported. Family history was significant for multiple cancers on both paternal and maternal sides, predominantly hematologic and gastrointestinal malignancies.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache, vomiting, left-sided weakness, and disorientation.

[ diagnosis ]: Stage IVB metastatic lung carcinoma, suspected right lung primary, with brain, pulmonary, mediastinal nodal, left adrenal, and T8 vertebral metastases. Intracranial disease was symptomatic with mass effect from dominant right frontal and right parietal lesions.

[ histopathology results ]: Resection specimens from the right frontal and right parietal brain lesions showed metastatic adenocarcinoma with cribriform pattern, reported as likely lung in origin / metastatic lung carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI brain demonstrated multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the gray-white matter junction in both supratentorial and infratentorial compartments. Approximately 8-9 intracranial lesions were appreciated. Dominant lesions were located in the right frontal and right parietal regions and caused mass effect and midline shift. Additional lesions were present in the left and right cerebellum.

CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis with intravenous contrast demonstrated a large necrotic right upper lobe mass closely abutting the mediastinum, encasing the right upper lobe bronchus and right pulmonary artery. There was a large necrotic right hilar lymph node and necrotic subcarinal mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Subsegmental atelectatic change was present in the right upper lobe. Adjacent pulmonary soft tissue nodules/satellite lesions were seen in the surrounding parenchyma. No discrete contralateral pulmonary nodule suggestive of contralateral metastasis was described. A metastatic deposit was present in the T8 vertebra. A large necrotic metastatic deposit was present in the left adrenal gland. Overall imaging was consistent with bronchogenic carcinoma with metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic test results were documented.

[ laboratory results ]: Tumor markers were reported elevated, including CA-125, CA 19-9, and LDH.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent neuronavigation-guided right frontal craniotomy and right parietal craniotomy with maximal safe resection of the dominant intracranial lesions using two separate incisions. Postoperatively, no new neurological deficits were documented.

[ current disease status ]: Residual multifocal intracranial metastatic disease remained, including supratentorial and infratentorial lesions. Systemic metastatic disease involved the lungs, mediastinal lymph nodes, left adrenal gland, and T8 vertebra. Preoperatively, left upper limb power was 4+/5. No lower limb weakness was present. After surgery, no new neurological deficit was documented.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient presented through the emergency department. The dominant intracranial lesions were resected because of severe mass effect.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 21-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache for 2 years and left-sided weakness for 6 months at presentation in October 2023.

[ diagnosis ]: Right temporal/basal ganglia/insular pilocytic astrocytoma, low-grade, with residual tumor after subtotal resection and subsequent radiologic regrowth.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from October 2023 showed a low-grade tumor consistent with pilocytic astrocytoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Historical imaging from 2014 reportedly showed an enhancing lesion in the right temporal region; digital subtraction angiography was unremarkable for vascular anomaly.  
- CT brain in October 2023 showed a heterogeneous lesion in the right temporal region involving the insula, with compression of the third ventricle.  
- Radiologic review described a mass lesion in the right basal ganglia region extending into the temporal region with extensive vasogenic edema, central hyperdensity, and peripheral hypodensity.  
- MRI demonstrated a solitary lobulated lesion with marked mass effect, associated vasogenic edema, and right-sided descending transtentorial herniation with distortion of the midbrain and effacement of the basal cisterns.  
- The lesion had mixed components: a central T1-hyperintense component interpreted as probable hemorrhagic component, surrounding soft-tissue component, and peripheral cystic component with CSF signal intensity.  
- Post-contrast MRI showed significant enhancement of the soft-tissue component with multiple enhancing nodules along the inferior aspect of the lesion in the temporal region.  
- No additional intracranial lesions were identified.  
- First postoperative CT showed subtotal resection/biopsy changes with persistent mass effect.  
- Follow-up imaging in the second week of May showed residual tumor with regrowth; mass effect and descending transtentorial herniation were reduced relative to preoperative imaging but not completely resolved.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- In 2014, the patient had sudden-onset left-sided weakness that gradually improved with symptomatic treatment/steroids; she regained ability to walk.  
- Surgical treatment/biopsy was offered in 2014 but declined by family.  
- In October 2023, she underwent subtotal resection and biopsy of the lesion. Approximately two-thirds of the tumor was reported to have been removed.  
- No new postoperative neurological deficit was reported after surgery.  
- Radiation therapy was deferred after histopathologic diagnosis of pilocytic astrocytoma.  
- On follow-up after surgery, the patient was symptom-free and family declined further surgery at that time.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Residual right-sided tumor remained present on follow-up imaging with interval regrowth by May after subtotal resection.  
- At latest clinical status described, left-sided weakness had improved; the patient was mobile and otherwise symptom-free.  
- No headache or other new neurological change was reported.  
- No signs of raised intracranial pressure were reported.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- On examination in October 2023, Glasgow Coma Scale was 15/15. Higher mental functions were intact.  
- Left-sided weakness was present with increased tone. Plantar responses were bilaterally extensor.  
- The patient was able to walk with support and had preserved mentation and sphincter control.  
- The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Recent clinic presentation following a single episode of altered level of consciousness.

[ diagnosis ]: Pineal region/posterior tectal plate extra-axial lesion; radiologic impression favored epidermoid cyst. History of obstructive hydrocephalus requiring VP shunt insertion in 2005.

[ histopathology results ]: No histopathology was available. No biopsy had been performed.

[ imaging findings ]: Recent MRI brain demonstrated a well-defined non-enhancing lesion in the pineal region/posterior tectal plate region. The lesion was described as extra-axial, with CSF-like but slightly heterogeneous/“dirty” signal characteristics, insinuating between the basal cisterns. It was hyperintense on FLAIR, hypointense on T1-weighted imaging, and showed no significant pathological post-contrast enhancement on axial or sagittal post-contrast T1 imaging. It caused mild mass effect on the posterior aspect of the midbrain. No associated vasogenic edema or other abnormal signal intensity areas were described. A VP shunt was visible with the tip in the lateral ventricle. Comparison with prior imaging dating back to 2005 showed long-term stability over approximately 19–20 years.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: VP shunt insertion was performed in 2005 outside AQH for hydrocephalus associated with a brain lesion. No other prior oncologic or surgical treatment was documented. Disease remained radiologically stable for approximately 19–20 years after shunt placement.

[ current disease status ]: At recent presentation, the patient was neurologically intact with no focal deficits. The intracranial lesion remained radiologically stable and non-enhancing, with persistent mild mass effect on the posterior midbrain.

[ other clinical data ]: Initial presentation in 2005 included a brain lesion with hydrocephalus. Diffusion-weighted imaging was referenced but no definitive diffusion result was documented.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 33-year-old woman. Karnofsky Performance Status was approximately 70–80.

[ chief complaint ]: Seizures at initial presentation in 2021; recurrent seizures in May 2024.

[ diagnosis ]: Right frontal astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 2.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial resection specimen (September 2022): astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, grade 2.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial preoperative MRI (July 2022): non-enhancing right frontal lesion involving the superior/middle frontal gyrus; T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesion with reported T2-FLAIR mismatch pattern; no significant contrast enhancement.  
- Postoperative MRI (October 2023): postsurgical changes in the right frontal region with partial/complete resection cavity, residual surrounding T2/FLAIR hyperintensity/gliosis, mild ex vacuo dilatation of the right frontal horn of the lateral ventricle, and no other abnormal lesion identified.  
- MRI (May/June 2024): interval increase in T2/FLAIR signal and bulk adjacent to the resection cavity in the right frontal region, extending more medially than on prior imaging; no definite new enhancing disease was initially described, although patchy enhancement was also reported on post-contrast review of the June 2024 study. Findings were interpreted as disease progression.  
- Post-radiotherapy imaging (before October 2024 surgery): enhancing right frontal lesion with central necrotic/hemorrhagic component, surrounding vasogenic edema with extension toward the periventricular region, nodular enhancement, and adjacent leptomeningeal nodularity; differential included progression versus radiation necrosis.  
- Perfusion imaging performed before the second operation showed high perfusion, favoring tumor progression rather than radiation necrosis.  
- Postoperative MRI after repeat surgery (October 2024): gross total resection of the enhancing disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: IDH mutation was present. No additional molecular data were documented.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- September 2022: right frontal craniotomy with maximal safe resection at AKUH. Postoperative imaging showed no residual disease.  
- Surveillance followed; disease remained stable for approximately 1.5 years, including stable imaging in October 2023.  
- Following radiologic progression in May/June 2024, she received radiotherapy to 5400 cGy, completed in September 2024.  
- Chemotherapy was also administered with radiotherapy; six cycles of PCV were reported.  
- October 2024: repeat craniotomy with maximal safe resection for recurrent/progressive right frontal lesion. Postoperative MRI showed gross total resection of the enhancing component.  
- Intraoperatively during the second surgery, seizures occurred; postoperative weakness was present and subsequently improved.

[ current disease status ]: Status post repeat right frontal resection in October 2024 with postoperative MRI demonstrating gross total resection of the enhancing lesion.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Lesion was located near the motor cortex.  
- No residual disease was reported after the first surgery.  
- No laboratory results were provided.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Six-month history of progressive left-sided headache and painful ophthalmoplegia with diplopia, left-sided ptosis, vomiting, and unintentional weight loss of 26 pounds.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal hepatocellular carcinoma in the setting of hepatitis C-related chronic liver disease/cirrhosis. Symptomatic left skull base/sellar-region lesion involving the pituitary, sphenoid sinus, and cavernous sinus, with differential not histologically confirmed at the time of reporting.

[ histopathology results ]: No liver biopsy had been performed. No histopathologic confirmation of the skull base/sellar lesion was available at the time of reporting.

[ imaging findings ]: Abdominal imaging demonstrated a cirrhotic liver with hypertrophy of the left lateral and caudate lobes and more than 15 variable-sized hypodense/hypointense lesions involving both hepatic lobes. The largest lesions measured 37 mm in segment 3 and 27 mm in segment 5. These lesions showed arterial phase enhancement with venous and delayed phase washout, consistent with hepatocellular carcinoma. MRI of the brain and orbits demonstrated an ill-defined lesion involving the left pituitary, sphenoid sinus, and cavernous sinus with encasement of the left internal carotid artery, measuring 33 mm anteroposteriorly, 20 mm transversely, and 27 mm craniocaudally. Review of the MRI described extension into the sphenoid sinus and clivus, predominantly T2 hypointense signal, smooth appearance, complete filling of the left sphenoid sinus, preserved aeration of the right sphenoid sinus, and possible clival invasion; the epicenter was described as appearing more within the sphenoid sinus than the cavernous sinus.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Alpha-fetoprotein levels were 36.2 in February, 55.1 in April, 106.4 in June, and 167.5 on 19 September.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Trans-arterial chemoembolization was performed in February. Systemic therapy with lenvatinib and sofosbuvir was ongoing at the time of reporting.

[ current disease status ]: Multifocal hepatic disease remained present on imaging. The patient remained symptomatic from the left skull base/sellar-region lesion, with cranial neuropathies on examination including left pupil-sparing third nerve palsy and left sixth nerve palsy, with visual symptoms reported as worsening.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included diabetes mellitus and hepatitis C-related chronic liver disease. He was a non-smoker and did not consume alcohol. Family history was significant for hepatocellular carcinoma in his father; his brother had undergone liver transplantation. Examination demonstrated left pupil-sparing third cranial nerve palsy and sixth cranial nerve palsy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old man. Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS) 100.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented to the emergency department with generalized tonic-clonic seizure and behavioral changes of 6 months’ duration.

[ diagnosis ]: Bifrontal atypical meningioma, WHO grade 2, status post neurosurgical resection.

[ histopathology results ]: Histopathology from the resected lesion was consistent with atypical meningioma, WHO grade 2.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- MRI brain with contrast performed in August 2025 demonstrated homogeneously enhancing lobulated bifrontal extra-axial lesions attached to the falx and anterior meninges.  
- Lesions showed surrounding vasogenic edema and mass effect on the ventricles and corpus callosum.  
- Signal characteristics included heterogeneous T2 signal, relatively isointense to gray matter.  
- No hydrocephalus was identified.  
- Postoperative MRI demonstrated hemorrhage in the surgical bed, marginal enhancement around the resection cavity, and enhancement along the anterior bifrontal dura.  
- Post-surgical hemorrhagic change and edema were present, with some relief of mass effect after surgery.  
- Small residual disease could not be excluded on postoperative imaging; overall, good/maximum resection was described.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent neuronavigation-guided bifrontal craniotomy with maximum safe resection of the lesion in August 2025.  
- Postoperative imaging showed postoperative hemorrhagic change and edema with reduced mass effect; possible small residual enhancing tissue remained indeterminate.

[ current disease status ]: Status post maximum safe resection of bifrontal WHO grade 2 atypical meningioma. Postoperative MRI showed postoperative cavity enhancement and anterior dural enhancement; residual disease was not definitively confirmed but could not be excluded.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Large bifrontal extra-axial lesion with dural/falcine attachment.  
- Behavioral symptoms had been present for 6 months before presentation.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 30-year-old male. No known comorbidities were reported.

[ chief complaint ]: New-onset seizures and right hemiparesis.

[ diagnosis ]: Diffuse glioma, WHO grade 2, involving the left frontal region.

[ histopathology results ]: Surgical pathology reported diffuse glioma, WHO grade 2. The report did not further classify the tumor as astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma.

[ imaging findings ]: Preoperative MRI brain demonstrated a large, well-demarcated left frontal solid-cystic lesion with enhancing components and septations. The lesion extended slightly across to the right side, caused mass effect with left-to-right midline shift, and displaced the corpus callosum and ventricles. The solid component was predominantly medial and posterior, with much of the remainder appearing cystic. Imaging appearance on T1 sequences favored a low- to intermediate-grade glioma / low-grade tumor. Postoperative MRI demonstrated a large resection cavity with air-fluid level and intrinsic T1 hyperintensity consistent with blood products. No definite residual tumor was identified; postoperative imaging was interpreted as gross total resection.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular testing was performed. 1p/19q codeletion testing and IDH1/IDH2 testing were not obtained.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Dexamethasone was started for right hemiparesis, with subsequent clinical improvement. The patient underwent surgical resection of the tumor via modified unicoronal incision under general anesthesia. Postoperatively, he was reported to be doing well without neurological deficits. No adjuvant radiotherapy or chemotherapy was documented.

[ current disease status ]: Status post gross total resection of a WHO grade 2 diffuse glioma. No definite residual tumor was seen on postoperative imaging. Neurologically, no postoperative deficits were reported.

[ other clinical data ]: The lesion was located in the dominant hemisphere, in a premotor/mesial left frontal region, and extended to the ventricle intraoperatively. The case was performed as a charity case. Financial constraints limited access to molecular testing.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 37-year-old right-handed male. No known comorbidities.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in January 2023 with new-onset generalized tonic-clonic seizures.

[ diagnosis ]: Right frontal intra-axial brain lesion, radiologically consistent with glioma. Intraoperative frozen section favored low-grade glioma. Final histopathology was pending.

[ histopathology results ]: Intraoperative frozen section was reported as low-grade glioma. Limited immunohistochemistry available locally showed GFAP positive, p53 performed, and Ki-67 less than 1%. Histology also described abundant gemistocytic cells. Final permanent histopathology review had been sent to Aga Khan University and remained pending.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial MRI in January 2023 demonstrated a right frontal intra-axial lesion. Follow-up MRI approximately 6 months later showed slight interval increase in lesion size. Available MRI sequences demonstrated a right frontal FLAIR/T2 hyperintense lesion with extension toward/across the corpus callosum. The lesion was reported as non-contrast-enhancing. There was slight mass effect without significant midline shift described. Postoperative MRI demonstrated subtotal resection with residual T2/FLAIR hyperintense disease in the medial/posterior/inferior aspect near the cingulate/anterior corpus callosum region adjacent to the ipsilateral ACA territory.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Final molecular testing, including IDH status, was pending. No completed molecular/genomic result was available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: After initial presentation, the patient was treated with steroids and antiepileptic therapy and observed. Steroids were subsequently stopped. He remained on levetiracetam, with seizures reported as well controlled and no recurrent seizure until later specialist review. He subsequently underwent neuronavigation-guided craniotomy under general anesthesia with maximal safe resection. Postoperative imaging showed residual disease near the corpus callosum/cingulate region.

[ current disease status ]: Status post subtotal resection of a non-enhancing right frontal glioma with residual radiographic disease near the corpus callosum/cingulate region. Final histopathology remained pending.

[ other clinical data ]: Intraoperatively, concern was documented for risk to ipsilateral ACA branches along the medial/posterior/inferior tumor margin, contributing to intentional residual tumor left in that region.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 22-year-old woman; right-handed.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache, initially relieved with oral analgesics and symptomatic measures but subsequently persistent; longstanding left-sided weakness for approximately 12 years.

[ diagnosis ]: Right deep hemispheric intracranial mass lesion, radiologically described as a well-circumscribed solid-cystic lesion centered in the right subcortical region/basal ganglia-thalamic region, with mass effect on the ipsilateral lateral ventricle and brainstem compression. Tissue diagnosis had not yet been finalized.

[ histopathology results ]: Stereotactic/open biopsy had been performed via right temporal craniotomy. Final histopathology was pending. Frozen section was not available.

[ imaging findings ]: CT brain showed a solid-cystic lesion in the right subcortical region involving the right thalamus and right basal ganglia, with perilesional edema. MRI demonstrated a well-circumscribed mixed-intensity solid-cystic lesion extensively involving the right thalamus and compressing the right lateral ventricle. T1-weighted imaging showed intrinsic hyperintense areas consistent with hemorrhagic/proteinaceous content. T2-weighted imaging showed a hyperintense lesion with minimal to mild surrounding edema. Post-contrast MRI showed heterogeneous enhancement, extension to the anterior temporal tip, involvement of the right parahippocampal gyrus, and significant mass effect with basal cistern effacement and descending transtentorial herniation. Brainstem involvement was described radiologically as significant compression without definite macroscopic invasion. Multiple adjacent satellite nodular enhancing lesions were also described inferior to the main lesion. Postoperative imaging after biopsy was obtained.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient had experienced an initial episode of left-sided weakness in 2012 with partial improvement over 2-3 months. A further episode occurred in 2013 with incomplete recovery, leaving residual weakness. She subsequently underwent biopsy through a right temporal craniotomy. Postoperatively, she remained mobile and neurologically stable compared with baseline, with persistent pre-existing weakness.

[ current disease status ]: At latest assessment, the patient was fully conscious and oriented with GCS 15/15, ambulatory without support, and able to perform daily activities. Residual left-sided weakness persisted at the preoperative baseline. Karnofsky Performance Status was 80. Final biopsy result was still awaited.

[ other clinical data ]: Neurological examination showed left homonymous hemianopia, left spastic hemiparesis with power 4+/5, bilateral grade II papilledema, and an upgoing left plantar response. Past functional status remained relatively preserved despite residual weakness.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 40-year-old man; right-handed.

[ chief complaint ]: Headache and confusion for 10 days.

[ diagnosis ]: Multifocal high-grade glioma, with histopathologic features favoring astrocytoma, WHO grade 4.

[ histopathology results ]: Surgical tissue diagnosis from the left parietal lesion showed high-grade glioma with features favoring astrocytoma, WHO grade 4.

[ imaging findings ]: MRI brain demonstrated two contrast-enhancing intra-axial lesions in the left cerebral hemisphere: one left frontal and one left parietotemporal/parietal lesion. Both lesions were heterogeneously T2 hyperintense with significant surrounding vasogenic edema and mass effect, including effacement/replacement of the ipsilateral lateral ventricle. Subfalcine herniation was present, with possible descending transtentorial herniation. There were T1 hyperintense foci consistent with hemorrhagic component, particularly in the parietotemporal lesion. Post-contrast imaging showed thick/nodular enhancement with internal non-enhancing necrotic areas. Edema possibly extended across the corpus callosum, with corpus callosal involvement/crossing of the midline described. CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast showed no extracranial lesion.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic test results were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent neuronavigation-guided left parietal minicraniotomy with debulking/tissue biopsy. Postoperatively, the patient was reported to be doing well.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative residual multifocal intracranial high-grade glioma remained after debulking. Karnofsky Performance Status at presentation was 90.

[ other clinical data ]: Multiple intracranial lesions were confined to the left hemisphere on reported imaging.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Bleeding per rectum.

[ diagnosis ]: Rectal adenocarcinoma with metastatic disease (stage IV), with liver and lung metastases on PET-CT.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy from the rectal growth showed adenocarcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: PET-CT was suggestive of liver metastases and lung metastases. Rectal growth was identified on clinical examination.

[ current disease status ]: Newly diagnosed metastatic rectal cancer with synchronous hepatic and pulmonary metastatic disease. No treatment details were available.

reference_conclusion: For newly diagnosed stage IV rectal adenocarcinoma with liver and lung metastases, imaging should be reviewed to determine resectability and potential for later conversion, and baseline carcinoembryonic antigen with molecular profiling should be obtained. Molecular testing should include at least RAS, BRAF, and MSI, with broader next-generation sequencing considered based on logistics and affordability. Resection of the primary tumor is reserved for symptomatic indications such as obstruction, bleeding, or perforation. If metastatic disease is unresectable, systemic therapy should be initiated; if conversion to resectability is feasible, reassessment should be performed approximately every two months and surgery undertaken at the earliest point of resectability rather than prolonging preoperative chemotherapy beyond about two to three months.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 56-year-old male. Non-smoker. Occupation: mechanic.

[ chief complaint ]: Penile mass present for approximately 4–6 months, described as slightly painful with minimal bleeding. No urinary difficulty.

[ diagnosis ]: Penile squamous cell carcinoma of the glans penis, clinically node-negative at presentation. Clinical stage was reported as cT2N0, stage IIA.

[ histopathology results ]: Confirmatory biopsy demonstrated HPV-negative squamous cell carcinoma. Partial penectomy specimen showed squamous cell carcinoma measuring 2.7 cm with lymphovascular invasion. Intraoperative margins were negative. Dynamic sentinel lymph node sampling identified two left groin nodes positive for squamous cell carcinoma without extranodal extension.

[ imaging findings ]: Physical examination demonstrated a 2 cm firm red ulcerated mass of the glans penis with no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy. CT imaging showed possible invasion of the penile glans and no inguinal adenopathy. SPECT/CT following radiotracer injection to the partial penectomy scar demonstrated drainage to selected inguinal sentinel nodes; two left groin sentinel nodes were subsequently identified intraoperatively.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor was HPV negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Confirmatory biopsy was performed. The patient then underwent partial penectomy. Pathology showed a 2.7 cm squamous cell carcinoma with lymphovascular invasion and negative margins. The patient declined upfront inguinal lymph node dissection and underwent dynamic sentinel lymph node sampling instead. Two left inguinal sentinel nodes were positive for squamous cell carcinoma; no extranodal extension was present. A plan was described to proceed with superficial and deep lymph node dissection on the involved side.

[ current disease status ]: Post-partial penectomy with negative primary surgical margins. Pathologically node-positive disease was present in two left inguinal sentinel lymph nodes without extranodal extension.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical and surgical history were described as otherwise standard. No inguinal lymphadenopathy was present on examination at initial presentation.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, well, indications for brachytherapy would be, you know, a tumor that's generally under four centimeters in maximum dimension. The patient has to be circumcised first, if they have not been circumcised, and the tumor should not straddle the coronal sulcus. So, assuming we've got a patient that fits that, there are two basic ways of doing the brachytherapy. The traditional way was a low dose rate implant. Much of the historical literature was manually afterloaded implants using iridium wires. But now this can be done with a pulse dose rate machine, which treats the patient at the same dose rate. So it's still a low dose rate implant given in pulses once per hour. And the effectiveness and the radiobiology is the same. So it's usually two or three planes of needles, four to nine needles in total. The spacing is prescribed. The dose would be 60 to 65 gray. And that takes four to five days in hospital. And what you see in the top picture there is just a styrofoam slab that holds the penis separated from the other normal tissues. You can see in the lower slide that he's got the styrofoam plate under the implant just to distance it a little bit because this radiation doesn't go very far and a little bit of distance makes a big difference. And the bottom slide shows the pulse dose rate machine connected with cables to each of the needles. It's not as uncomfortable as it looks. They usually need minimal analgesia, but they are in hospital for the four to five days. Next slide. That's a result of one patient eight years after his implant. You can see the depressed white scar just proximal to the meatus. And, you know, he has excellent cosmesis, excellent function, and he's, you know, very happy with his results. Next slide. Now most of these would be done with a high-dose rate implant, and this is, you know, radiobiologically quite different. The approach is a little different. This guy was only 36 when he had his diagnosis. He had an excisional biopsy with positive margins. His urologist says it has to come off, and he said, no way. He found his way to me, and I did a HDR brachytherapy procedure. You can see the implant slide up in the top corner there. It looks like a lot of needles. There are actually only three in tissue, and the other three are just adjacent to the penis with some tissue-equivalent material in between. And that ensures that you're getting a full, even dose to the skin's surface. So it's just a way of improving the cosmesis, and the coverage without any trauma to the patient or the penis. And he's without evidence of disease 10 years later. And this is done with two treatments per day, usually over a six-day period. And again, they're usually in hospital because this is, you know, it's not that they're radioactive, but it's just, you know, they can't really be very mobile.

Next slide. Can I ask you one question there? So low dose versus high dose, the biggest thing I heard you mention is that the high dose, they're only receiving two to three treatments, whereas low dose, they're going to get more frequent treatments. Is that correct?

Yeah. It's actually low dose rate versus high dose rate. So the low dose rate implant gives a higher dose continuously over that five or six day period, whereas the high dose rate gives a lower dose, but gives it very quickly. So radiobiologically, it's more effective with a lower total number of gray delivered.

Let me break it down from my understanding as the urologist here. You know, when we looked at low dose brachytherapy for prostate cancer, you implant all the slaves and they stay there. In this case, you're putting the seeds in there, but you're not leaving the wires or whatever you're using for your radioactive source. You're not leaving them in there per se. You're providing a venue for them to stay in there and deliver radiation over a longer period, whereas the high dose is similar. You're putting in a seed or a wire that's coming out sooner. Is that correct?
That's correct. And for prostate, it's all delivered while they're under anesthetic. So it's, you know, it's delivered over 20 minutes instead of six months for prostate. Right. OK. But we diverge.
Great. Great.

This is another HDR example. This guy was 72 at an HPV positive squamous cell cancer. He'd had multiple local excisions, which left some deformity in his glands because he always refused penectomy. And the surgeon finally threw up his hands and said, we cannot take any more bits. It has to come off. And he refused. So I treated him with high-dose rate brachytherapy using, again, two templates. This gives you more flexibility than with a low-dose rate implant in that you can put the needles where they're needed. It looks like a lot of needles, but if you look at that picture in the top right corner, there's only six needles that are in tissue. And the ones in the arc around the outside are outside the penis for the same reason, as I already explained, to modulate the dose and make sure that you get full dose to the skin surface without hot spots. So it was six interstitial needles and eight that were just around the outside. And this treatment was given over seven days. Afterwards, he's disease-free. Five years later, he has the deformities from the previous excisions, but tumor-free. Next slide. This can be done in other centers without templates. Now, this means that all needles are interstitial, embedded in the penis, because you don't have any template to hold things adjacent. But this is from Jay Seesky at the Cleveland Clinic. And similar fractionation, six-day treatment, but plastic needles and no templates. Next slide. And this is from Peter Johnson's group at the Lee Moffitt Cancer Center, and they've actually turned the HDR brachytherapy into an outpatient treatment. They also see the advantage of using the template and having the needles adjacent to the penis, but the templates are very, very light. You can put the whole thing into a jockstrap and the guy can go home or stay at an adjacent lodge or hotel and just come back twice a day for his treatments. Next slide. And they do get acute moist desquamation that can take a couple of months to heal up. And it's just basically cleanliness and hygiene, which will help it heal. There are other things that can be added if necessary, such as antibiotics or steroids, whatever. But they generally heal up pretty well. Next slide. You can also get a complication called radiation necrosis or ulceration. This is more common with deeply invasive bigger tumors, which makes sense, and can be quite painful. But these will heal after hyperbaric oxygen treatments, as in this example here. Next. Oh, anyway, that's all I was going to say about this one. The radiation necrosis in those smaller tumors is extremely uncommon. You do get some ulceration, but that heals with just local hygiene. But as I said, the deeper, more invasive cancers, you can get deeper necrosis.

So Dr. Kirk, that's impressive. This is really, really good for all of us to see what you're capable of doing. I have a couple questions for you. So you mentioned that, you know, you must be circumcised and the tumor must be located to basically the glands. Is that right? So if you have a tumor that's more proximal or invasive, more into the corpora, mid-shaft or something like that, are they not necessarily a candidate?

They can be. The ABS guidelines suggest that this should be limited to tumors on the glands. But I know of colleagues who have treated mid-shaft tumors. And I mean, it works just as well. It's just a bit more complicated. It's not something you do for your first case.

Right. Well, this is really, really good information. And I think there's a lot of urologists and folks out there that don't even know that we can do this or this is possible. So really good to see. I really appreciate you enlightening us here because often, you know, we're not thinking I would ask that, do you think that a radiation oncologist community who has a specialty in brachytherapy, no matter what, would be able to do this? Or is this someone that's highly selected that's done it before? Or how would you approach that?

There are videos out there. The ABS and other Canadian societies do workshops. So we try to teach as many people as possible how to do it. I also get emails for advice. How do I do this? What do I go about? And so there's counseling that can happen as well. Technically, it's not hard to do. It's you're putting needles into an area that is very accessible. So it's not difficult and you just follow the guidelines.

reference_conclusion: For appropriately selected penile tumors, brachytherapy is an organ-preserving treatment option when the lesion is generally less than 4 cm, the patient is circumcised, and the tumor does not straddle the coronal sulcus. Treatment may be delivered as low-dose-rate or pulse-dose-rate interstitial brachytherapy to 60–65 Gy over 4–5 days in hospital, or more commonly as high-dose-rate brachytherapy administered twice daily over approximately 6–7 days. Acute moist desquamation and limited ulceration are managed primarily with local hygiene, with antibiotics or steroids if needed; deeper radiation necrosis or ulceration in more invasive tumors may heal with hyperbaric oxygen treatment.
reference_conclusion_quote: indications for brachytherapy would be, you know, a tumor that's generally under four centimeters in maximum dimension. The patient has to be circumcised first, if they have not been circumcised, and the tumor should not straddle the coronal sulcus. [...] The dose would be 60 to 65 gray. And that takes four to five days in hospital. [...] Now most of these would be done with a high-dose rate implant [...] And this is done with two treatments per day, usually over a six-day period. [...] And this treatment was given over seven days. [...] They do get acute moist desquamation that can take a couple of months to heal up. And it's just basically cleanliness and hygiene, which will help it heal. There are other things that can be added if necessary, such as antibiotics or steroids, whatever. But they generally heal up pretty well. [...] You can also get a complication called radiation necrosis or ulceration. [...] But these will heal after hyperbaric oxygen treatments

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old male. Moderately obese. Otherwise reasonably healthy, active, and working.

[ chief complaint ]: Longstanding difficulty voiding associated with a meatal lesion, splayed urinary stream, and desire to preserve normal function. At presentation in 2023, he had a tender erosive distal penile mass with urethral drainage.

[ diagnosis ]: Penile squamous cell carcinoma, HPV-independent, clinically T2N0 at initial oncologic diagnosis.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- June 2023 shave biopsy: epidermal hyperplasia with possible carcinoma in situ.  
- Subsequent wedge biopsy of the penile lesion: well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Pelvic MRI at initial workup demonstrated a mass occupying the glans penis.  
- Clinical examination and imaging were consistent with an invasive distal penile/glanular mass.  
- Post-induction chemotherapy imaging showed marked interval local improvement.  
- Follow-up MRI approximately 2 months later demonstrated rapid local recurrence.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: HPV-independent tumor.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- History from 1998 onward of meatal stenosis and lichen sclerosus with multiple prior local procedures, including meatal dilations, removal of painless lesions, circumcision with urethral meatal dilation, and circumcision revisions.  
- Initial definitive surgery was refused.  
- Initial radiation therapy was also refused.  
- Received induction TIP chemotherapy for 4 cycles. This produced substantial initial local response on post-treatment imaging and examination.  
- After a lapse in follow-up of several months, he developed worsening firmness and difficulty voiding, with rapid local recurrence within approximately 2 months.

[ current disease status ]: Rapid local recurrence of HPV-independent penile squamous cell carcinoma after 4 cycles of induction TIP chemotherapy, with worsening local firmness and difficulty voiding. He remained clinically node-negative.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Past history included meatal stenosis and lichen sclerosus.  
- Examination findings at oncologic presentation included significant scarring of the remaining glans, slight hypospadias related to prior dilations/surgeries, a lobulated tender erosive firm mass at the tip of the glans, urethral drainage, difficult examination due to discomfort, and partially buried penis related to obesity.  
- He remained clinically node-negative at initial diagnosis and at the time of first documented local recurrence.

So if the patient already got TIP, it kind of uses up the platinum. It uses up the taxols, which are active. We still have the 5-FU. We have the topal tecans, potentially. And there's been a lot of interest in using checkpoint inhibitors. In a retrospective review of over 100 patients, we do see some activity. But it's low of monotherapy checkpoint inhibitor. But it seems to be higher in combination. I did a phase one trial of cabozantinib, nivolumab. So cabozantinib is a multi-tyrosine kinase inhibitor, plus nivolumab or nivolumab and nipolimumab. And we had nine patients with penile cancer. And about five of them had tumor reduction. Three of them were in PR. So that was really exciting. So there's definitely some activity there. And we're exploring that a little bit more in a prospective study called ICONIC, where we give cabonibol ipi to patients with penile cancer. And I have a couple of trials to exploring antibody drug conjugates. There's several of them out there that are currently being used for other GU tumors. We have a study with saxituzumab global tecan, which targets trope 2 with a TOP1 payload similar to a renal tecan. We have infortumavidotant, which targets Nectin-4 with an MMAE payload. And that has been shown to be active even in patients that have gotten paclitaxel in the past. So those are being explored. I also have a study with PARP inhibitors, where I allow multiple GU tumors. And when you look at the clinical trials, they're all super small numbers. So in a way that's a little bit embarrassing to kind of, you know, present this as prospective data, but it's just such a rare tumor that doing prospective trials has been very difficult. And there's also interest in other targets like EGFR and HER2. The known expression of HER2 in penile cancer is being explored. There's been different series that really give completely different numbers. Some say it's not really expressed in penile cancer. There was a Chinese study that showed up to 50% of patients can express HER2. And there has been some activity with EGFR inhibitors, either alone or in combination. So a lot of trials are ongoing right now to try to find better treatments for patients. In the second line, which we don't really have a lot, I kind of stopped using bleomycin because it's so toxic. which is the chemotherapy. So we do have limited options as to what we can give our patients with advanced disease.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 67-year-old male; otherwise healthy.

[ chief complaint ]: Groin mass developing approximately 1 year after prior excisional biopsy of a penile lesion.

[ diagnosis ]: Recurrent penile cancer with fixed bulky groin nodal mass measuring 7 cm.

[ histopathology results ]: Prior excisional biopsy of penile lesion had clear margins. Subsequent biopsies of the groin mass ultimately confirmed recurrent penile cancer.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging demonstrated a 7 cm fixed groin mass.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Initial penile lesion had been managed in the community with excisional biopsy.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-confirmed recurrent penile carcinoma presenting as a fixed bulky 7 cm inguinal nodal mass.

reference_conclusion: For patients presenting with a penile mass and unilateral fixed bulky inguinal nodal disease greater than 4 cm, upfront surgery is not recommended. Initial management consists of either neoadjuvant TIP chemotherapy or definitive chemoradiotherapy to the nodal disease. case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult male.

[ chief complaint ]: Metastatic penile cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Unresectable metastatic penile squamous cell carcinoma.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: HPV positivity had been reported in approximately 50% of cases in some series and up to 80% in others. PD-L1 positivity and high tumor mutational burden had been described as potential biomarkers associated with immunotherapy susceptibility in penile tumors. No patient-specific molecular results were available.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: No patient-specific prior treatment history was available.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic disease was present. Morbidity described in the metastatic setting included severe lower-extremity lymphedema, scrotal edema, deep vein thromboses, hypotension with diuresis, and anasarca; no patient-specific current complications were documented.

[ other clinical data ]: A first-line systemic regimen discussed for metastatic penile cancer consisted of pembrolizumab with cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil every 3 weeks for 6 cycles, followed by pembrolizumab maintenance for up to 2 years. In a 2024 Brazilian multicenter study (11 centers, n=33) in penile cancer with unresectable metastatic disease, this regimen produced a reported response rate of 40%. TIP chemotherapy was described as a more intensive comparator regimen, but no patient-specific administration data were available.

reference_discussion.text: So this is a great case because we often just extrapolate from the neoadjuvant setting and then use TIP in this setting. But recently at ASCO last year, 2024, we saw the results of the Hercules study. This is a Brazilian study from 11 different centers enrolled 33 patients with penile cancer or unrespectable metastatic penile cancer. And they were treated with pembrolizumab plus platinum-based chemotherapy, cisplatinum and 5-FU. every three weeks for six cycles, and they received the pembrolizumab for up to two years. And they saw a response rate of 40%. So that's great for us, because that's a lot gentler than TIP chemotherapy. And one of the questions is, there wasn't a long follow-up yet for this study, but will we have durable responses if we incorporate immunotherapy up front for these patients? So we're currently working on designing a first-line trial for patients with penile cancer, and we wanted to have a randomized component to it. We don't, you know, with this new data coming out, the Hercules data, and, you know, some data that I have from my phase one CAVONEVO study that enrolled about nine penile cancer patients, and we currently have the ICONIC study open right now that's enrolling more. The question is, is there equipoise to have a non-penile immunotherapy arm in the metastatic setting now? Should we have a TIP arm and then an IO plus chemo arm, kind of like the Hercules study? But then what about the TKIIO promise there and just kind of building on some data that we have? So these are kind of questions that we're having right now as we develop the next phase of first-line trials. and really trying to find the best therapies for our patients with metastatic penile cancer. And in the second line setting, again, like I said, we're testing antibody drug conjugates. A comment by Dr. Crook in the beginning about the HPV status, and although we don't have HPV-directed therapy, Seattle, though a lot have been tested. There's vaccines out there. There's IO therapies. There's even CAR therapies that are being tested right now on penile cancer. We just don't have any specific therapies for penile cancers per se, but we do have some that are being developed for HPV-positive squamous cell tumors that can potentially be extrapolated and used in this setting. And the incidence is kind of, it depends on which series you look at. In some, it's about 50% in terms of HPV positivity, but it can be as high as 80% in some series. And there's also other markers like PD-L1 positivity and TNB high that make these tumors a little bit more susceptible, that we think make these tumors a little bit more susceptible to IL. So therein goes back to the frontline option that I would give this gentleman, I would give him the Hercules regimen at this point because, you know, it's, it's, it's easier, it's easier to give than tip. I've given a lot of tip and I never like giving it. Iphosimide is tough. The patients really struggle through it. It's, it's a, it's a, it's a tough regimen.
Tell us the regimen again, the Hercules regimen.

So the Hercules regimen is an IO chemo. So it has pembrolizumab and it has 5-FU and cisplatinum. And it's given every three weeks and for six cycles, like metastatic disease. And then the pembrolizumab is kind of given maintenance over two years.

Right. Well, that's really interesting. I will tell you that I've had a couple one-offs here and there with my medical oncologist here doing chemo-immuno or penile cancer or urethral cancer, primary squamous urethral, and actually I've been really pleasantly surprised by it.

Yeah, yeah. For urethral cancers, we've seen some really nice responses in the ICONIC study, again, the Cabo Nebo study that I have, Cabo Nebo IPI. So there's activity there. And those, the issue with urethral tumors is that they can have different histologies, but I'm really focusing right now on the squamous histology. I've seen really nice responses, which is very in line with what we see in the penile cancer patients. But not all patients respond, right? So I'm talking about a 30% response. What about the 70% that don't respond? What do we do with those? They're coming to me for other clinical trials, and we're looking for better treatments. One of the things that I wanted to comment on, I know we talked a lot about primary treatment of the lymph node, bulky lymph nodes, and initially the diagnosis of penile cancer and doing a lymph node dissection, there's a lot of morbidity. And of course, I see all of the morbidity in the metastatic setting, right? So I see these terrible lymphedemas.
You see them after we're done with them, like, terrible.

They can't walk. They get scrotoedema because their legs are so swollen. that then it becomes scrotal edema, and we try wrapping them, they get DVTs, and we try diuresing, but then they get low blood pressure because it basically becomes anasarca. It's very difficult to manage these patients at the end of life. And, you know, we're trying to find better treatments to improve upon that. But even the primary treatments, I think, need improvement in order not to deal with this morbidity that happens post-surgery and could be also post-rehabilitation.

reference_conclusion: The tumor board favored first-line systemic therapy with the Hercules regimen for metastatic penile squamous cell carcinoma. This consists of pembrolizumab combined with cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil administered every 3 weeks for 6 cycles, followed by maintenance pembrolizumab for up to 2 years. This approach was selected over TIP chemotherapy based on the discussed activity and more favorable tolerability.
