case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 64-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Incidentally detected renal mass on abdominal imaging performed during evaluation for diverticulosis.

[ diagnosis ]: Localized renal cell carcinoma of the kidney; postoperative diagnosis was clear cell renal cell carcinoma, pathologic stage pT1a.

[ histopathology results ]: Robotic retroperitoneal partial nephrectomy specimen showed clear cell renal cell carcinoma, ISUP grade 2, low grade, with negative surgical margins.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial abdominal imaging demonstrated an incidental 3 cm renal mass. The lesion was described as solid and enhancing, in a favorable posterior location. The colon was approximately 1 cm from the lesion.

[ laboratory results ]: Renal function was good at baseline. Postoperative kidney function changed minimally.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent robotic retroperitoneal partial nephrectomy. Surgical pathology confirmed clear cell renal cell carcinoma, ISUP grade 2, pT1a, with negative margins. Postoperative renal function was largely preserved.

[ current disease status ]: Status post robotic retroperitoneal partial nephrectomy for clear cell renal cell carcinoma, ISUP grade 2, pT1a, with negative surgical margins and largely preserved renal function.

[ other clinical data ]: Past surgical history included appendectomy. The patient was otherwise described as healthy.
slides:
<image> Case 1: CT image and clinical summary of a 64-year-old man with an incidentally detected 3 cm renal mass, presented for discussion of management options.
<image> Case 1 slide outlining a post-nephrectomy renal mass scenario and prompting discussion of pathology, postoperative kidney function, surveillance follow-up, and possible consideration of adjuvant therapy.
<image> Case 2 slide summarizing a 45-year-old man with bilateral renal masses, no family history of kidney cancer, relevant comorbidities, and preserved renal function.

reference_discussion.text: Fantastic. Well, I am super excited. So much like most of our listeners who participate in tumor boards at their institutions, that's what we're going to go through today. And these are real cases. Some of these are from my practice. Some of these, Brendan also provided from his practice. But no one here has seen the whole slide deck, but there are no surprises here. These are just common cases that I think that our listeners hopefully can get some insights from. And you know, what I often find at Tumor Board is that reasonable people can see the same case and come to different opinions. And sometimes that's the most interesting thing. So we might have areas of consensus and we may have some areas where we can learn from one another. So first case here, I chose this case because this is a common scenario. So this is a patient that presented. He is a 64-year-old man, and he had some abdominal imaging for a workup for diverticulosis. All that sort of resolved. It was negative, but he was incidentally found to have a 3-centimeter renal mass. otherwise healthy, just had an appendectomy in the past, and good kidney function. So I think this type of case is probably going to be referred to the urologist first. So maybe, Brandon, is this a typical case that you would see in your practice? And if it is, how do you sort of counsel a patient on what their options are?

Yeah, thanks, Mark. So, this is a pretty classic case that, you know, I think anybody who does kidney cancer sees a lot of these, you know, the incidental diagnosis, typically a smaller renal mass, under 4 centimeters. These are pretty common. So, you know, first thing that I do when I see a patient like this is try and get a sense of what the patient knows. Obviously, being at a cancer center, I may be the second, third, fourth, but sometimes I'm the first, you know, if they went to the ER. So starting by trying to get a sense of, you know, what the patient knows, what they've heard, right? A lot of information before I even say anything. So I sort of know how to frame my discussion with them. Sometimes, as we all probably know, patients come in with their own idea, mindset of what they want, right? And so it's important to get that from the get-go, because then you're sort of addressing the patient's needs on that sense. When it comes to this patient specifically for their mass, They have quite a few options. You know, this mask looks like it's solid, obviously. I'm sort of guessing, but it looks like it enhances. So, you know, statistically speaking, this is more likely than not a malignancy. One of the considerations here would be a biopsy to really prove that. I think the field has changed quite dramatically over the last several decades where we used to you know, think it was taboo to biopsy these things. But me personally, I tend to biopsy a lot of these small renal masses, especially in patients where they may not be the healthiest or if I'm worried I'm going to have to take a kidney. I really want to make sure I'm doing it for the right reasons. So that's something to consider. But I also don't think in a case like this, in a healthy patient with a pretty sizable mass and radiographic features that are pretty strongly pointing towards malignancy, proceeding with surgery or some kind of intervention is also reasonable. A little bit depends on the patient's comfort level with that. When it comes to treatment options, this patient, three centimeters is sort of the typical landmark we use when we talk about ablative versus surgical having equivalency. So at three centimeters, I think it's still within the realm. And lucky for this patient, the location of the mass is in a pretty good location for ablation. It's not really close to anything. The colon's a little close to it, but I think they could get that off with some saline or something. So They would have that as an option. I think the gold standard still in this case in an otherwise healthy patient, 3 centimeters and above, would be a partial nephrectomy. So that would be my initial recommendation. But obviously tell them I'm biased, I'm a surgeon, but I don't think they're unreasonable if they want to get some more information with a biopsy or meet with my IR colleagues. I think those would be the ones I would consider in this situation.

Excellent. I think that all that sounds similar to my practice as well. Brendan, let me ask you this. You mentioned biopsy. I think biopsy is being increasingly utilized. Is it something that you use often in your practice?

Yeah, I do. When I say often, I guess I'm comparing it to historically through my training where I saw my attendings. Rarely getting a biopsy except for sort of the more complex cases. I don't think if I were back in residency and I mentioned getting a biopsy, my attending right then and there would be like, what are you doing? And they weren't wrong. It wasn't in a lot of our guidelines. It wasn't really an established practice. So, that was the way it is. But I think the field is changing. Part of it is, As a surgeon, I really don't like it when I go in, cut something out, and find out it wasn't cancer, or the patient didn't need that operation, technically. Now, sometimes if patients are proceeding directly with intervention, I caution them on that, saying, listen, this isn't a guarantee, this is cancer, and that's an important thing. It seems a little ludicrous. I'd never go in and take somebody's prostate out without proving that they had prostate cancer or something like that. So, you know, those are the situations I try and avoid. Unfortunately, they happen to all of us. The MRI are great, but they are not perfect. And neither is a biopsy for that part too, so I caution them on that. But I do think biopsy is becoming more common. It's just an extra way to ensure that you're selecting the right patient for the right intervention. Absolutely.

So, you counsel the patient on these options and they say, you know, doc, that sounds great, but I really don't want to do surgery. You've mentioned ablation. That is not really ringing as a great option for this patient either. Is it ever appropriate to do surveillance for a tumor this size?

So, again, in this patient, how do you describe them? It's a pretty healthy person. Yeah, they had some diverticulitis hypertrophy. I think we would all agree, especially those who do surgery, this is a good surgical candidate from everything I've heard thus far. So, if that wasn't the case, then I think that definitely opens the door for watching these. In those cases for active surveillance, right, anything under two centimeters, it's well in our guidelines to monitor those. tumors, you know, obviously selection based on the patient characteristics matter a little bit too. Sometimes I'm a little more hesitant to watch a tumor that's really central in the kidney and close to the vessels where I already know it's going to be difficult making it bigger just potentially as long as I'm trying to spare the kidney. But in a case like this, in a favorable location, you know, a couple, half a centimeter here or there is probably not going to change my management. So from a surgical perspective, I'd be okay watching this, but there's a cancer perspective. And if the patient's really sick, has some comorbidities, then I think it's reasonable to entertain that option as long as the patient's on board too. And in those cases, almost for sure, I'd get a biopsy if at all possible to help sort of guide management. And again, if this is a clear cell, which this, you know, statistically speaking, most likely to be, you just have to caution, you know, there's good data from Mayo and other places, you know, historical rates for the development of metastasis based on the primary tumor size. So, something like this, about three centimeters, I think looking at that data, you'd estimate, you know, probably a one to two percent, maybe up to a three percent chance if they had some bad histology.

Excellent. Well said. I'm gonna throw things over to Rakib. Rakib, you know, this patient, after meeting with the urologist, thinks surgery sounds okay, but wants to really explore all their options. And, you know, their brother had radiation for their prostate cancer, wants to hear what's going on in 2025 with radiation for kidney cancers. You know, in my training, just a little while ago, we used to say that renal cell carcinoma, you know, there's no role for radiation. And that's really not at all where we are now. So, Can you kind of tell us what's changed? What does the up-to-date data say for treatment of primary renal masses with radiation?

Absolutely. So, renal cancer used to be considered radio-resistant, but mainly to the older form of fractionated radiation, those radiation that was delivered over five, six, seven weeks. Now at that time we did not have the technology to deliver the high dose focused radiation to a target such as kidney which as you may know moves with breathing. So it becomes much more difficult to target and focus the radiation. But now we do have the technology that is what is called the stereotactic radiation. You may often hear the abbreviation SBRT or SABR. With the application of SABR, we have seen local controls that are on the order of 95% to even 100%. So far, three trials have been reported, the Fast Track 1, Fast Track 2, and our own Phase 2 trial. And we have data that is about five to six years out. So reasonable duration data, reasonable number of patients, and we have been able to get local controls on the order of 95% to 100%. The benefits, of course, with Savor, it takes one planning session and then either a single treatment or three treatments. These are completely non-invasive. The patient is just laying on the table for about an hour on the maximum. This particular case, it's a posterior location, favorable location for us. Colon is about a centimeter away, which does not bother me as much, particularly because, again, with the advancement of technology, we are able to do adaptive radiation. We can even take into account daily motions that may be there in this colon. And we should be able to deliver and adequately offer local control for this patient.
Fantastic. Are there any locations or any type of comorbidities that takes SBRT off the table?

So comorbidities, no. I mean, comorbidities actually, those are patients that we are seeing because they are not surgical candidates typically. Location-wise, and that's a good point, you know, size, I keep saying size is not an issue, but location is more key. So if you have an exophytic anterior tumor that is up against small bowel, That's something that I would worry about and something that, you know, there will be increased risk of bowel damage or small bowel damage. So that would be the one case where I would worry about.
Got it. Excellent. And, Reina, is there any role for systemic therapy for patients with localized small renal masses? We often think about for advanced disease, but what about in this space?

You know, quite honestly, if we weren't going to do any local treatment, the patient wasn't a candidate for surgery because of comorbidities, also wasn't a candidate for focal therapy, whether that be SBRT or cryoablation or some other radiofrequency ablation, then I think we really have to think and talk about our goals of care and what do we anticipate is going to be the risk of this renal mass impacting that individual's survival if they're not a candidate for any of the above items. And generally in that situation, I'm watching expectantly as opposed to putting somebody on systemic therapy for a three centimeter mass. So I think, you know, it all depends upon the risk of the mass and competing risks in the patient that may impact the patient's life expectancy.

Well said, and I think when we're thinking about any treatment, really weighing the risk and benefits and the competing morbidity and mortality risk is we should all be doing that whether we're treating with surgery, ablative therapies, radiation, or systemic therapy. So, excellent points. So, for this case, I think we sort of hit these topics. So, what we did here is we did surgery. We did a robotic retroperitoneal partial nephrectomy and sort of what we would expect. This was a clear cell RCC, it was low grade, it was I sub grade 2, pathologic T1A with negative margins, kidney function didn't change much. So maybe back to Brandon, how do you surveil these patients post-surgery and is this a patient that you would be calling Reina about to think about adjuvant therapy or no?

Yeah, so for follow-up for these patients, so first of all, this patient has what we sort of expected, so I don't think there was any, you know, curveballs or anything in their post-op path. So hopefully the patient's sort of prepared for this. Again, this is a good prognosis. You know, I would tell the patient, based off this kind of pathology, you know, well over 90% cure rate. So that usually puts them at ease. And because of that, I probably wouldn't pick up the phone and call Dr. McKay for this specific patient. I think we're going to get into a little more of the role of adjuvant, which is obviously a big part of how we manage patients. But in this case, it's still a little classic bread and butter. And so for this one, I would just recommend surveillance. And for me, I pretty much follow the NCCN guidelines, which, you know, I'd usually get a patient imaging about six months, if that looks good, go to once a year at this point. And that's how I would follow them. Unless, of course, I had some suspicion about hereditary family genetics, something like that. But that would be the standard.

Excellent. And going back to Reina, when you see a patient post-surgery and just much like the radiation space has changed, really the adjuvant therapy space has changed over the last few years to something that was where we didn't have great options and then now with Pembro with a survival benefit to adjuvant Pembrolizumab, we're really talking about adjuvant therapy after surgery more and more. So who are your ideal candidates for to consider adjuvant therapy?

You know, I think I revert back to the Kino 564 eligibility criteria and that largely included patients who had T2 grade 4 tumors, T3, T4, N1. It also included patients who are M1 resected to NED. And there's some caveats there regarding the sites of resection that were permissible. And that did not include, which we'll get to probably later, people who were deemed NED because of SBRT as opposed to a surgical outcome. So this patient who's got a T1A grade 2 expected management, I mean, I would not offer any adjuvant treatment.

Excellent. And this patient went on to have NCCN-based surveillance and has done well. So I think we can move on to our next case. This is also a localized case, but this is a 45-year-old man who is found to have bilateral renal masses, no family history of kidney cancer, a few comorbidities that are well managed, and good kidney function. And he comes in with these scans, and I just have one cut of each, but just a single mass in each kidney. In the right kidney, a large, somewhat central mass. And in the left kidney, a completely endophytic mass, also somewhat central going into the renal sinus. We can start off with Rakib here. You kind of told us before about size doesn't really matter for SBRT and location as long as it's not abutting, you know, critical structures, which to me doesn't appear. So would this patient be a candidate, you think, for SBRT based on these imaging?

reference_conclusion: The patient underwent robotic retroperitoneal partial nephrectomy for the 3 cm renal mass. Final pathology demonstrated low-grade clear cell renal cell carcinoma, ISUP grade 2, pathologic stage pT1a, with negative margins and preserved renal function. No adjuvant systemic therapy was indicated, and surveillance was recommended in accordance with NCCN guidelines, with imaging at approximately 6 months followed by annual imaging thereafter.
reference_conclusion_quote: So, what we did here is we did surgery. We did a robotic retroperitoneal partial nephrectomy and sort of what we would expect. This was a clear cell RCC, it was low grade, it was I sub grade 2, pathologic T1A with negative margins, kidney function didn't change much. [...] And so for this one, I would just recommend surveillance. And for me, I pretty much follow the NCCN guidelines, which, you know, I'd usually get a patient imaging about six months, if that looks good, go to once a year at this point. [...] So this patient who's got a T1A grade 2 expected management, I mean, I would not offer any adjuvant treatment.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 45-year-old patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Bilateral renal masses at initial presentation. At 10-year follow-up after nephron-sparing surgery, enlarged left renal hilar/retroperitoneal lymph nodes were identified.

[ diagnosis ]: Bilateral papillary renal cell carcinoma, type 1. Pathologic stage after staged bilateral partial nephrectomies: right renal tumor pT1b; left renal tumor pT1a. Subsequent nodal recurrence/metastatic disease in the left renal hilar/retroperitoneal lymph nodes, biopsy-proven metastatic papillary type 1 renal cell carcinoma.

[ histopathology results ]: Renal biopsy demonstrated papillary type 1 kidney tumor. Following staged bilateral partial nephrectomies, both renal tumors were papillary type 1 renal cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial imaging demonstrated bilateral renal masses. The left renal mass was described as essentially entirely endophytic. Small bowel was within approximately 1.5 cm of the left renal lesion. The right renal lesion was not in close proximity to the hepatic flexure of the colon. At year 10 follow-up imaging, there was no tumor identified in either kidney, but there was a chain of enlarged lymph nodes along the left renal hilum/left renal artery in the retroperitoneum. Staging imaging demonstrated disease confined to the retroperitoneum. Brain imaging was negative. Bone scan was negative.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Germline genetic panel was negative.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent staged bilateral partial nephrectomies for bilateral renal masses. Postoperatively, surveillance imaging was performed according to guideline-based follow-up for the first 5 years, with no evidence of local recurrence. Imaging intervals were then extended to every 2 years. Imaging at year 7 was unremarkable. At year 10, nodal recurrence in the left renal hilum/retroperitoneum was detected.

[ current disease status ]: Isolated nodal recurrence along the left renal hilum/retroperitoneum after staged bilateral partial nephrectomies, biopsy-proven metastatic papillary type 1 renal cell carcinoma, with staging imaging demonstrating disease confined to the retroperitoneum.

[ other clinical data ]: Bilateral renal masses at presentation and young age prompted hereditary evaluation. Concordant histology was present bilaterally. No evidence of intracranial or osseous metastatic disease was identified on staging studies.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, based on this imaging, the left kidney mass is mostly endophytic. I mean, pretty much actually entirely endophytic. A little bit of small bowel is coming about within a centimeter and a half of it, and that is treatable. The one on the right, I believe the hepatic flexure of the colon is again not too close. So yes, both of the lesions are treatable with SBRT.

Hey, Rakib, can I ask a question, maybe an obvious or silly question? You know, obviously when it comes to radiation treatment, you know, very familiar with the sensitivity of bowel and stuff, but what about some of the other organs? Do you even worry about liver proximity or spleen? Like, in my head, I sort of figure, just radiate it, what's the worst that can happen? But that may not be true, I guess.

Yeah, very good question. And I actually hear that often. So liver, as you know, it's what we call a parallel functioning organ. You can cut out half the liver, throw it out and patient's going to do perfectly okay. There's so much reserve. So liver, we don't worry about at all. Something like that is a serial functioning organ, which is colon or small bowel we worry about because you damage one part of it, it renders the entire organ non-functional. So that's something we worry about. Spleen, as you also know, splenectomy patients do perfectly okay. So yes, spleen doesn't bother me, liver doesn't bother me, you know, lung doesn't bother me. Large bowel is a lot more radio-resistant than small bowel. So large bowel for the most part doesn't bother me too much. Small bowel is the only thing that if it comes to proximity or if it's up against the tumor, then that bothers me.
Thank you. Excellent. Going back to Brendan then, this patient comes to you, 45-year-old, multiple renal masses. What are you thinking here and how do you start to work this patient up?

Yeah, so bilateral renal masses is not an uncommon thing I see in probably you too, Mark. You know, these patients tend to, and I think appropriately so, go to tertiary centers because the level of complexity does jump up once both kidneys are involved. The first thing, you know, that I think any of us do is do a good history and physical. History means a lot. This patient's age is, you know, they have a couple red flags, sort of, that I would make sure, you know, the trainees that are with me sort of know. One is the age, right? We all know that Average age for RCC development still right now is around 64, 65 in the US, so this is considerably younger. So that should be a red flag. In addition, having bilateral renal masses, which radiographically look to be homogeneous, and we know 90% of the time, pathology should be congruent. I also tell all the trainees, when you see bilateral renal masses, the diagnosis for clear cell RCC goes down the list. right, whereas most renal masses we see that's at the top of our list. When you have bilateral, the development of hereditary syndromes, which can include all varieties of RCC, but more commonly we see the papillaries and the chromophobes and the onchocytomas show up. So that's another sort of red flag. In these cases, I almost always get a biopsy. When both kidneys are at risk, I want to know what I'm dealing with so I can counsel the patient because Sometimes, rarely, you do have to think outside the box. So, and this is the kind of case where if we get some really rare things, we may have to get, you know, Dr. McKay involved. We may need to, you know, you can't always just tackle these surgically because sometimes they're hereditary or other medical issues. So, history and physical, and then a biopsy, and then I usually try and get them to genetics if I think it's going to affect my management up front. So that's sort of the first couple of steps before I come up with a treatment plan.

Fantastic. We thought very similarly to you. So yeah, you mentioned genetics. Just my only question is, I guess you said if it affects the treatment plan, so sometimes before surgery, sometimes after surgery, depending.

Yeah, a lot of times, I'd say about one out of four cases, I need it before surgery because to be honest, most of it comes in handy after you've taken care of the tumors that are there. It's what are you going to do with the next one? How are you going to follow those patients?

In this case, we did germline genetics. Actually, the germline panel was negative. We did a renal biopsy and it was a papillary type 1 kidney tumor. You know, Dr. McKay, we talked about the use of systemic therapy for a small renal mass in a clear cell tumor. Now we have a papillary tumor, what we used to call PAP type 1, now just kind of papillary RCC. Any role for systemic therapy in the localized setting in this disease space?

No is the sinful answer. So there's no level one evidence on utilization of perioperative systemic therapy for a localized papillary RCC, whether that be pre or post treatment. Now, I think that this case is complicated, and I think sometimes patients who present with complicated bilateral renal masses, particularly renal masses where they're larger or, you know, T3 or budding other structures, and they're going to be undergoing a staged approach to target both tumors, sometimes in that context, you almost treat the individual like a locally advanced unresectable patient and give them, you know, the best upfront systemic therapy for cytoreduction to see if you can potentially convert them to a resectable status. Now, the other thing with this individual is just because one side had a papillary doesn't mean that the other side is also going to be a papillary. When I see bilateral papillary tumors, I think about hereditary screening, germline testing, looking for hereditary syndromes. So that could be considered in this context, but just because one side is a papillary doesn't mean that the other side is too.

Excellent points. Yeah, can't take it for granted. Yeah, concordance rates, 75-80%, but you can definitely see mixed histologies. In this case, they were the same, though. We ended up doing stage bilateral partial nephrectomies, and they were both papillary type 1, RCC, T1B, just based on the size for the right, T1A for the tumor on the left. And then, so going back to Brendan, similar surveillance to the last patient, you think, after surgery?

So, you know, I think all of us know here we have made a lot of strides when it comes to characterizing hereditary syndromes, but I fully don't think we've done all of it. So, there's definitely patients that I think many of us who are high volume and see that we're almost sure like based on looking at their notes, their history, there's something genetic going on, but their panel is negative. And I think that's either because we haven't found the genes or the combination of genes that are doing it. if a patient has all the other red flags, even if their pin was negative, I will treat them as a hereditary patient in essence, especially these younger patients. And, you know, for the hereditary papillary patients, right, they don't, some of these people, you know, have multiple family members, their kidneys look like, right, every other sign is telling you something's going on, they just don't have a gene to tie it to. So in these patients, you know, it sort of depends on what your level of suspicion is for that. And I think inevitably, when you start taking care of hereditary patients, you sort of just get a, I don't know how to say, a sense of that they're hereditary or something, but not always they are. But for these patients, bilateral, obviously, you're doing two surgeries, you're going to probably be following them a little closer for their kidney function the first year or so. So I usually just tie in some imaging at that point, I would probably treat this patient more like a T3 patient for the first at least couple years. And then this is a patient where I'd probably, as long as I can get their insurance to agree, I'd follow them longer than five years too as well. I try and, you know, do every other year with an MRI or something like that if I can get it for these patients. Because, again, part of it is probably just my bias because of the practice I have where I do see Patients recur long after our guidelines told them they shouldn't. And that's true for any cancer. But in a younger patient, bilateral kidneys are already exposed. You don't want to catch the next tumor that comes in that kidney when it's any bigger than it has to be, because then you're going to really start losing options for this person.

I agree 100% with your biases here. Who knows what's causing these? This patient could be a risk for developing de novo tumors in the future. I also sort of consider them lifelong risk. We imaged sort of NCCN guidelines for the first five years, no evidence of local recurrence, and then started to space out. So went kind of every two years after that just to look for new tumors. Everything looked good at year seven. Skipped a year and then at year 10 returned for follow-up and boy did we have a surprise. Nothing in the kidneys, but we saw that along the left renal hilum, along the renal artery, there are these enlarged lymph nodes, a whole chain of lymph nodes. And so I guess going back to Reina, can you kind of walk us through if you have a patient that you suspect may have either locally advanced or possibly metastatic disease, what is your sort of go-to staging scans? What do you recommend? What do you not recommend?

Oh, very good question. So I generally like to get imaging of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis. Depending on what is going on in the abdomen, sometimes MRI may be preferred over CT. You know, if patients had a nephrectomy and there's something in the nephrectomy bed and you're not really quite sure if it could be post-op changes, sometimes an MRI may be better suited. In patients who have overt metastases, sometimes brain imaging is indicated. It's not necessarily indicated for every single patient, certainly anybody who has any neurologic symptoms, of course. But in my practice, if somebody is stage 4 metastatic, I do tend to get MRI brain imaging. even in asymptomatic folks, just more so with a baseline. Now, there's a lot of interest in PET imaging in these patients. FDG-PET is really not indicated. You know, there are some tumors that are FDG-AVID, some that are not, and it's not necessarily used in the diagnosis, though there are other PET modalities that are being developed in RCC. PSMA PET imaging, because these tumors tend to have a lot of vascularization, which can be detected on a PSMA PET scan. And there's also CA9 PET imaging. We saw some really nice work presented at ASCO by Michael Hoffman and the Australian group on the advent of CA9 imaging for diagnostics. I mean, right now, my tools are CT of the chest, CT or MRI of the abdomen. If I'm suspecting a recurrence, I do generally like to biopsy. I mean, not every enlarged node or lung nodule is a recurrent disease, so I do like to do those diagnostics.

We did obtain PET here to assess for a clinical trial eligibility in addition to all of the other sort of head-to-toe staging imaging, negative brain imaging, we had a bone scan that was negative, and we just had disease that was confined to the retroperitoneum. I'm just going to go back to the CT imaging here. Back to Rakib, you know, if we're thinking about options for this patient that has locally recurrent kind of nodal disease, we'll talk about what all is on the table. Could SBRT be on the table for this, or are we in proximity to the adrenal concern? I don't see any bowel loops. Well, yeah, there are some bowel loops close to. What do you think?

So adrenal, if the patient has the contralateral intact adrenal, then it is not an issue because that will compensate for it. Yes, I agree with you, not too much bowel. So radiating and getting local control on these nodes is feasible with SVRT. The questions to answer there would be, oftentimes with other tumors, we, whenever there's node involved, we cover elective nodes. So we think, you know, maybe a little bit superior, inferior, or on the pathway, there could be micrometastasis. Whether elective nodes should be covered or not, that's something we don't know or we don't have the data for. But yes, local control with SBIRT for these would be feasible. And there is the oligometastatic paradigm, which is another perhaps separate topic. This perhaps would fit into oligometastasis if no other sites of metastasis is present.

Excellent. Biopsy was attained here too. It demonstrated what we thought it was, metastatic papillary type 1 RCC to the nodes. So Brandon, you see this patient now 10 years out, locally recurrent nodal disease. Is this a surgical candidate in your mind? And what operation would you do if he is?

Yeah, so papillary is still one of the few tumors in RCC that we can cure patients even after it leaves the kidney. And this is a case that, you know, many of us, again, who do this, this happens with the papillaries. More common in the papillary type 2 historically than the type 1. It's a little surprising to see that. Those typically are not as aggressive. Given that they tend to go to the lymph nodes much more than the other RCCs we're used to seeing, it does offer a therapeutic window if you can catch the patients, and it looks like you may have, to offer them potentially a curative option with surgery. So this patient I would counsel and probably recommend, because this patient's still only, what, 54 or something, pretty young and hopefully still healthy, a full retroperitoneal lymph node dissection. I think you could make a decent argument. They probably don't need a full one, maybe just a, you know, a templated one over on the left side. But my preference is this patient's already got a surgery on one side, a surgery on the other side of their kidney. Now you're putting a big surgery on them. I don't want to go back. Nobody wants to go back after this one. So I would clean them out just to make sure I offered them everything I could.

Fantastic. And Reina, if the surgeon doesn't feel confident that they can clean out or there's some contraindication, what can you offer from a systemic therapy perspective for someone with type 1 PAP? Are you going to a clinical trial? What are your thoughts there?

I mean, I think for all of our variant histologies, we are absolutely targeting a clinical trial. I mean, it is critically important right now. There's PapMet2 that's enrolling throughout the cooperative groups. This is a critically important trial that's testing the role of TKI-IO in patients with advanced papillary RCC. And I think we as a community need to get behind these studies. Also for the papillary tumors, there's another study being conducted through The ETCTN looking at bevrolatinib plus atezolizumab, you know, it's for both sporadic and germline HLRCC. So I think we need to get behind these trials in the absence of a trial or one may not be eligible for a trial. My go-to is an IO-TKI combination for these patients. I don't necessarily think it's wrong to consider Nevo-Ipi or single-agent TKI, but I think the best responses are going to likely be observed with that strategy. I think when we think of IO-IO for these patients, i.e. Nevo-Ipi, the primary PD rate is even higher for papillary RCC, closer to 30%, 40%, and then the objective response rate lower than what's classically seen with clear cells. So I think we need to think about that. You know, in this context, where you have somebody who's got not a large volume of disease, has retroperitoneal nodes without other sites of metastases, where there could be a possibility to kind of significantly cytoreduce them or get them into a CR or near CR, you know, leaning towards an IOTKI combination that has a pretty high response rate and low primary PD rate, where then you can potentially think about a deferred surgical strategy could be a possibility.
I have a question for Brandon on this case. Given that this patient had previous surgery, would you worry about adhesions or other difficulties in your surgery?

Yeah, you always worry about that, but the first two looks like we're done robotically, so I wouldn't expect it to be horrible. But saying that, that's why I mentioned this would be, I would go into it, and I always tell the patients that, I want this to be your last surgery, right? That means I've done everything I can do. So I would do this open, which is how I do most of my RPLNDs anyway, just to ensure it's the safest, most therapeutic, and hopefully the last operation. But the adhesions I wouldn't think would be terrible in this patient.

Excellent. In this case, we ended up doing a robotic RP-LND and we did a left-sided template. Patient had 5 out of 20 lymph nodes positive for papillary type 1 RCC. I agree with Brandon. I do almost all my RP-LNDs open, particularly if there's disease behind the vessels. Here, there was kind of good space between the aorta and the nodes, and we were thankfully able to get in with few adhesions. And afterwards, the patient is on surveillance every three months, and we wanna get them to many more years, hopefully. So with that, I think let's get on to case number three. And this is actually one of Brandon's cases. It's a 51-year-old man with new onset right testicular swelling with concern for a right-sided varicocele, I believe. And so he's getting worked up for that with an ultrasound and a CT. Actually, we just want to pause right there, Brandon. Maybe, you know, we think about this as surgeons, but kind of tell us, is that odd to have a right-sided varicose heel? Is that something that we see commonly or what?

reference_conclusion: The patient underwent staged bilateral partial nephrectomies for bilateral papillary type 1 renal cell carcinoma. For the subsequent isolated retroperitoneal nodal recurrence, biopsy confirmed metastatic papillary type 1 RCC, and the multidisciplinary recommendation was surgical management with retroperitoneal lymph node dissection as a potentially curative approach. In the documented course, a robotic left-sided template RP-LND was performed, followed by surveillance every three months.
reference_conclusion_quote: We ended up doing stage bilateral partial nephrectomies, and they were both papillary type 1, RCC [...] this patient I would counsel and probably recommend, because this patient's still only, what, 54 or something, pretty young and hopefully still healthy, a full retroperitoneal lymph node dissection. I think you could make a decent argument. They probably don't need a full one, maybe just a, you know, a templated one over on the left side. But my preference is this patient's already got a surgery on one side, a surgery on the other side of their kidney. Now you're putting a big surgery on them. I don't want to go back. Nobody wants to go back after this one. So I would clean them out just to make sure I offered them everything I could. [...] In this case, we ended up doing a robotic RP-LND and we did a left-sided template. [...] And afterwards, the patient is on surveillance every three months

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Adult male. Exact age was not provided.

[ chief complaint ]: Right testicular pain consistent with a symptomatic right-sided varicocele.

[ diagnosis ]: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma of the right kidney with extensive local involvement of the inferior vena cava (IVC), initially considered locally advanced and unresectable.

[ histopathology results ]: Percutaneous biopsy confirmed clear cell renal cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial CT demonstrated a large right renal mass with extensive involvement/encasement of the IVC. The IVC was difficult to delineate over an approximately 6 cm segment, extending from just below the renal hilum to near the inferior edge of the liver.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: No baseline laboratory values were provided.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-proven clear cell renal cell carcinoma of the right kidney with extensive local involvement of the inferior vena cava, initially considered locally advanced and unresectable.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient had comorbid health factors affecting surgical candidacy, including smoking, alcohol use, and excess weight. Surgical planning initially considered the possibility of major vascular reconstruction or leaving the IVC in discontinuity.

reference_discussion.text: Yeah, so this is a good... I just remember when I found this out, and I don't know if it happened to you, Mark, when you go through training. You know, it's like when your first year anatomy class comes back and you're like, oh my gosh, I remember. So it is not uncommon. You actually see it. I think it's on our boards. You see it in question sets from time to time. But because of the gonadal vein for most guys usually comes off the IVC. if there's an occlusion or blockage of that IVC, those patients tend to develop varicoceles on that testicle, which most guys usually complain of the varicoceles as a dull ache, pain kind of stuff. So, while it's rare, I think any person who does this long enough gets these cases where they come in with no other complaint than my ball, you know, my testicle hurts. And it's the right one as opposed to the left one, which can happen too, but you just see it less often because of the anatomy that's usually coming off the left renal vein versus the IVC itself. So it has more collateralization to work with. So it's always an interesting thing when this happens.
Excellent. So this patient comes in, gets this workup, gets a CT, and kind of walk us through. This looks like a nasty process going on in the right kidney. What do we have here?

Yeah, so this was a, you know, incidental finding, sort of surprisingly, other than the testicular pain, I guess. But, you know, it's hard to capture, I think, on a still image, but you can see pretty clearly that it's really difficult, if not impossible, to make out his IVC. And this sort of continues if you scroll up and down for a good... six centimeters along the IVC. So I realized that whatever disease process going on, you know, sometimes it can be hard. Although this patient didn't have a history that fit it, but sometimes patients will have some spontaneous bleeds or a trauma event. And that blood, that capsule, which you can sort of make out a little bit on this patient too, can sort of fool you as, is this tumor, is this blood? You know, if I wait it out, we'll go away. It's hard because if you wait it out and it's not blood, guess what? Now it's grown bigger and you sort of missed your window. But if it's blood, you can sort of maybe get a little pullback. But I was concerned in this patient because he didn't have that history. I had to assume this was all tumor that was basically encased in his IBC. So in addition, as you can see, he wasn't, well, he's not terribly old. He wasn't the healthiest patient. So, this is sort of one of those cases where I knew we had to think a little more outside the box. And so, I knew surgical resection, if I got in there, was going to be a major thing. I don't think I'd probably have to either graft his IVC or leave it in discontinuity, which, you know, if you have to do, you have to do. This patient, and I don't think we've said it yet, you know, if he had other options to try and shrink this tumor or facilitate the surgery so I don't have to do as much. In addition, we sort of use that as a time for him to get himself healthier, stop smoking, stop drinking, lose some weight. And so there was an opportunity to not only maybe shrink the tumor, but optimize him as a surgical candidate as well.

Excellent. And just some more images here. And you can really see the extent of this process involving the IVC. And like you said, you kind of really lose the IVC sort of just below the renal hilum up to the edge of the liver, hard to make out. So you talked about taking some time to try to shrink the tumor and get him optimized for surgery. So I'm assuming that you are going to ask for a lifeline from your medical oncology colleagues here. Is that correct? Correct. So Reina, The urologist has this patient with a IVC tumor thrombus and a large tumor and has the intent of hoping to downstage for surgery. I'm sure this is a type of patient you see in your practice. How do you manage these patients?

So I would basically put this individual in the category of locally advanced unresectable. These patients were actually included in all of the phase three trials that tested various IO combination strategies. I think in the context of potential receptability down the road, where you're really looking at a regimen that's gonna be associated with the highest response rate, the lowest primary PD rate, the fastest time to response, so you could potentially get them to a potentially curative surgery, I generally go with an IOTKI combination and generally Lymvetinib Pembrolizumab in this context.

Excellent. So it looks like in this case the patient had a biopsy of course, confirmed that this is clear cell RCC and then started on Axi Pembro. Marina, can you just go back a little bit and tell us a little bit about sort of the kind of anticipated speed of response with TKI I.O. versus I.O. I.O. and how you think about if you want to get quick shrinkage, it sounds like you're going TKI I.O. Is that correct?

Yeah, I mean, I think if we think about Nebo IPI, for example, like the primary PD rates about 20%, which is a high primary PD rate for somebody you're trying to get to receptability. I mean, the caveat that I would use there is unless the patient had sarcomatoid differentiation of some kind. And also, the response rate's around 40%. Now, that response rate means 30% shrinkage or more. When we look at the data, for example, in vatneprimalizumab, the primary PD rate is less than 10%. The response rate is actually close to 70%. I could see the rationale for using Exitinib. Exitinib has a short half-life and, you know, is a favorable TKI when we think about stopping the agent for a planned surgical resection. But those are kind of the considerations to be had. I think you would expect, timing-wise, to see best response within a couple of months with an IO-TKI combination.

Hey, can I ask a question real quick for Rana, too? So, you know, traditionally, and I don't know if you're still in this game, because you mentioned it, if, like, say the biopsy showed sarcomatoid elements, and we always think epinevo when we see sarcomatoid, but do we really have data that shows that it's better than any other IO-containing regimen when it comes to sarcomatoid response?

We do. I mean, it's never been compared head to head, but I think if you're actually looking at the response data, the response rate is doubled in that population. And actually, what's really striking is the durability of response. is much more pronounced in those individuals. So when I think of like IOIO, we have one in five patients that have really no response, have primary resistant disease. We have one in five patients that can have a durable response. That's just your kind of all comer population. I think if we were to apply this to sarcomatoid, we really are bumping up the tail on the curve. And we see that when we look at the PFS curves actually in the subset analyses, though they're post hoc, demonstrating, you know, sustained durable response or durable benefit in that group of patients.
Thank you.

And Rakib, is there any role for radiotherapy to treat disease that's in the IVC? Is there, I guess, is there any data for efficacy? And on the other side, is there any concern for treating disease with major vascular invasion?

Yeah, not too much data that has matured yet. And we have started getting some experience with this, mainly started with treating a few cases of refractory and patients that are not eligible for surgery. And we started seeing actually very good 70 to 80 percent radiographic measurable response with radiation. So we went around because these cases are so rare combining a case report from multiple institutions that we published a case series of 15 patients and now we are updating that and we also have completed now enrolling on a small phase 2 feasibility trial of neoadjuvant radiation followed by surgery and nephrectomy. That trial, we hope to publish in the next couple of months, and it is feasible and safe. Now, I'll go over a few indications that we explored. One of them is the neoadjuvant, one of them is adjuvant, and another would be palliative. In the neoadjuvant case that I can remember, a patient similar to this, but a little bit more, a larger level, 4 thrombus with butt carry syndrome, so venous congestion. So that patient was not a candidate for surgery up front, but after SBRD of full dose, Within three months, the patient's SITs resolved, LFTs normalized, and then we had MRI showing that the venous congestion also relieved, and then patient was a surgical candidate and underwent surgery. So that was one case. Another case was an adjuvant case. So that is something that could apply to this patient where the patient wasn't really in good shape like this patient for an extensive surgery, but the patient was a candidate for a nephrectomy, a robotic nephrectomy, which is a much less complicated surgery as you know. So in a planned way, the patient underwent robotic surgery and the thrombus we gave local control with stereotactic radiation. So both together combined, the patient overall had local control. So this is something that I would like to eventually explore on prospective trials, because in many tertiary care centers, I mean, community setting, patients don't have access to surgeons that can do extensive surgery, but they will have surgeons who are able to do nephrectomy. And combined with radiation, you could probably give local control to this patient. So an area that we are exploring and the data is maturing, but we don't have long-term data yet.

Very cool to hear and look forward to seeing that for sure, to have more options for these complicated patients. So it looks like this patient went on to receive Axipimpro, had a decrease in the size of this mass and sort of stable lymphadenopathy over the next six months, developed, had some complications, DKA, ICU admission, and then six months later sort of was reevaluated for surgery. So, Dr. Manley, now we're a few months down the road. What do you see now compared to when you started?

You can start to make out the kidney actually, which is something you couldn't do before. You can actually see part of the IVC, which you couldn't see before. So, those are all good signs. So, you know, this was early in the experience for me of giving, you know, this wasn't standard of care, still not, but this is a case I think definitely deserving of neoadjuvant treatment, although some people could argue you could have resected him up front, but I think that would have been a tall task. So, I think we had a really great response. The sad thing was he did develop lifelong diabetes, so it's not without cause, but I still think and know the patient would do it all again if they needed to. So, they had a really good response and this sort of, is an emerging problem, I would say, or situation. I'd be interested to see what your take is, Mark. You know, after these patients have a good response, right, however you want to characterize that, decrease in size, change in enhancement, whatever, when do you offer these patients surgery and when do you not? Because, you know, now that we're seeing more of these patients come through and they still have their kidney intact and it's the only area that has any disease, do we really always go in, you know, and take these out? a little bit, right, some of these patients will start getting hits to their kidney, too, with treatment, too. So now they're not the same kidney function when you first met them, too. So I'm interested, you know, I've sort of adapted, but I'm interested how you sort of triage these patients, Mark.

Yeah, it's a great question, and there's not an easy answer to it. The PT0 rate, in my experience, is on the lower side, but it's definitely not zero. There are some patients that can have a complete response in the kidney, and then others who their disease is now somewhat more quiescent. Most of these patients, I would say, probably do end up having a resection if they are otherwise, if we deem it resectable, we can do it safely, and that we think the competing risks are favorable. And we do find viable disease more often than not, but are happily surprised when we get a YPT0, right? You know, sometimes These surgeries can be very challenging, especially after IO therapy and when there are big lymph nodes around the vasculature, sometimes you get a desmoplastic reaction and then sometimes It's, you don't really have any desmoplastic reaction at all. It's not like post-chemo testis cancer, right? So it's definitely a little bit of a box of chocolates.

And Rana, I'm sort of interested in, do you just send them to surgery? Like the surgeon will tell you if you need surgery or not. Or like, because you probably see these more and maybe they don't always come to us. And when do you decide, hey, I think that kidney needs to go or not, I guess?

Yeah, it's a very interesting conversation. I think we have a multidisciplinary tumor board actually that meets every Friday afternoon where we actually bring these cases and there's an assessment by a radiation oncologist, medical oncologist and surgeon and have a weekly tumor board as well. So I think that these are dynamic discussions. I can't emphasize enough the importance of just continued communication and collaboration because there's things that that I may see or have sort of insight into that maybe one of the other multidisciplines may not. And vice versa, there may be aspects from a surgical standpoint that I'm just not aware of that I will be enlightened by sort of reaching out to colleagues. But I think in general, my rule of thumb is, you know, if they've had two serial scans where they've maintained a sustained response with no other evidence of disease progression and they're clinically doing well, that's generally when I'm pulling the trigger to say, okay, let's have you go back and see the surgeon. I don't generally jump on the first scan because I want to ensure that response is maintained. There's been so many times where you kind of jump the gun too early, and then you stop their systemic therapy, and you're getting them teed up for surgery, and they met out in the middle of that process, and that's the worst thing you could do for somebody. So I like to ensure that there's sustainability in the response before we pull the trigger on actually taking somebody to the OR.

Excellent. So, Brandon, what did you end up doing here? Did surgery. And it was stuck. It was so, which again, sorry for, I feel like it's just me and Mark complaining about being surgeons, but he was so stuck. And when he looked at that scan, it didn't, it looks so much better that I think I got tricked a little bit, but it was really, really stuck. But we did discuss some of these other options. And again, we'll talk about it probably in a little bit, but you know, he, uh, we got him through surgery and he's doing fine. And yeah. I don't know if I would do anything different in his specific case again, but it has made me question other patients I saw subsequent to this about, you know, how to handle them. And every situation is different, but we ended up doing surgery, just an open radical nephrectomy, because I knew it would probably be stuck and wanted to make sure the vessel we had good control, but it was definitely more plastered than I thought it was going to be. Because like you had mentioned, I've done several cases of patient systemic treatment before. You always hear these horror stories about don't do it if it's CABO or no, IPI's the worst or, you know, this one's the worst. But in my experience, I really haven't found one that's worse than the other. It's just that sometimes some patients it's like horrible and other patients, it's like they never had anything.
Interesting. And did you have to do anything to the to the CAVA?

Yeah, so basically we, I sort of took a side swipe of it. So oddly enough, you know, this is, and again, there was no way to know. He never had a thrombus, and that's what I was worried about. The thrombus was never in there. What had happened is basically the tumor just closed off, just, you know, and you see this sometimes in testes too, it just basically, you know, compressed the IVC and had probably been there so long it just, you know, wasn't functional. So, you know, we didn't have to do a whole graft because it was slightly less than 50% of his circumferential IVC width. And considering that he had practically had no IVC before we started systemics, it was new blood flow. And so we didn't have to do, luckily, as much vascular work as I was fearing. Fantastic.

reference_conclusion: Biopsy confirmed clear cell renal cell carcinoma, and neoadjuvant systemic therapy with axitinib plus pembrolizumab was administered to downstage the locally advanced right renal mass with extensive IVC involvement. After approximately six months, imaging demonstrated reduction in tumor burden with improved visualization of the kidney and IVC, and the case was reassessed for operative management. The patient subsequently underwent open radical nephrectomy with partial caval resection/control; no true IVC thrombus was present, and full caval grafting was not required.
reference_conclusion_quote: the patient had a biopsy of course, confirmed that this is clear cell RCC and then started on Axi Pembro. [...] it looks like this patient went on to receive Axipimpro, had a decrease in the size of this mass and sort of stable lymphadenopathy over the next six months [...] six months later sort of was reevaluated for surgery. [...] we ended up doing surgery, just an open radical nephrectomy [...] we didn't have to do a whole graft because it was slightly less than 50% of his circumferential IVC width

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 62-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Gross hematuria. Associated fatigue and weight loss over several months.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic renal malignancy with a large left renal primary tumor and metastatic disease involving bilateral adrenal glands and lung.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial cross-sectional imaging demonstrated a centrally located left renal mass measuring approximately 10 cm in maximal diameter, radiographically malignant in appearance. Bilateral adrenal nodules were present, with the right adrenal lesion larger and highly suspicious for metastasis. A lung nodule was also identified and considered suspicious for metastatic disease. No additional sites of disease were identified on staging imaging. Brain imaging was normal. No bone metastases were identified. On subsequent imaging after systemic therapy, the pulmonary lesion(s) had resolved, the left adrenal lesion was no longer visible, and persistent lesions remained in the left kidney and right adrenal gland. The residual left renal mass was described radiographically as non-enhancing/rim-enhancing, necrotic-appearing, and suggestive of treated or nonviable tumor.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient received systemic therapy with lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab. Disease was reported as fairly stable over the subsequent next couple of years. During treatment, chronic kidney disease/decline in renal function developed gradually. At later reassessment, systemic therapy had been discontinued. Residual radiographic abnormalities persisted in the left kidney and right adrenal gland, while prior lung disease had resolved and the left adrenal lesion had resolved. The patient was subsequently managed with surveillance. At approximately 1 year after this decision, he remained under observation.

[ current disease status ]: Off systemic therapy. Residual radiographic lesions persisted in the left kidney and right adrenal gland. Prior pulmonary metastatic disease had resolved, and the left adrenal lesion had resolved. Disease had been stable on surveillance. Renal dysfunction/chronic kidney disease was present.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included diabetes. Physical examination at presentation was unremarkable. No acute cause for the renal dysfunction was identified; the decline was gradual during systemic therapy, and no other associated symptoms were reported at the time treatment was stopped.

reference_discussion.text: All right then, let's move on to our last case then. Another case of Brandon's actually. 62 year old man, this time presents with gross hematuria. Looks like has some diabetes, some fatigue, some weight loss over several months, and an unremarkable physical exam. And to work up for all this, gets some scans. So Brandon, if you wouldn't mind again, tell us what you saw on these scans and

Yeah, so I think these highlight pretty much, but his primary tumor is on the left side. I think it's something around 10 centimeters was the total tumor diameter and very central, you know, looks malignant. He also had a contralateral right-sided adrenal lesion that also looked highly suspicious along with a lung nodule. And then in the left side, I think actually had bilateral adrenal nodules with the right side being the bigger. So those were the sites of disease that we identified. Everything else was negative.

So, large renal mass and suspicious areas look like metastases, bilateral adrenals, and in the lungs, you've got the, you know, no brain is normal, no bone mets. So, it looks like we've characterized the sites of disease. So, you know, this seems like the type of patient that would be presented at a multidisciplinary discussion. So, Reina, we've, the sort of the role of surgery versus upfront systemic therapy has really kind of maybe shifted over the past few years with CARMINA and SIRTIME and other trials. For this type of patient, I mean, every patient's a little different, but for this patient, what do you think the best next step would be?

Generally for patients who present like this, I am leaning towards systemic therapy first. And then it's not to say everybody's going to get resected. That's not the case, but a consideration down the road. I think it's really important to guard against patient expectations around surgery. I think a lot of times, depending on, you know, how the patients are kind of, you know, being seen or being evaluated or who sees the patient at any given time, I think that, you know, you could really do somebody a disservice if they have it in their mind that they're going to at some point in time get resected and that's just going to be an expectation. So I think I level set and say this is a systemic disease. You have a system problem. You need a system treatment, which is immunotherapy based. And then depending on what happens, we can always reassess surgical options, though that is not the primary goal here. So I try to level set that discussion up front.

Yeah, I think that level setting, the importance cannot be overstated. I would definitely agree and I think in my center, this patient would likely get systemic therapy first. Before we delve into the details here though, are there any types of patients who present with metastatic disease that you do consider maybe surgery first and that could be because of either of cause of histology or maybe because of the location or amount of metastatic disease? Do any of those things factor into your calculus?

Yeah, no, very good question. I mean, I think that, yes, it does. I think there are some individuals who are young, healthy, maybe have very low volume, minimal lung metastases, and that's really the only thing that's designating them metastatic. They've got the bulk of their disease is in their kidney as opposed to outside their kidney. They don't have poor risk features. They don't have this inflammatory phenotype of anemia, thrombocytosis, their calcium is not dysregulated. So I think their only IMDC risk factor is that they basically presented with metastatic disease at their initial diagnosis, but their other as well. So I think in that context, it makes sense. I have had patients who have had very symptomatic hematuria at the time of their presentation and otherwise had low burden disease where it made sense to treat the renal primary with a surgical resection. I think sometimes in that context we're actually embolizing to deal with the hematuria and then get them on their systemic therapy.

Excellent. So, for palliative purposes and, you know, I think it was maybe one of the European guidelines at least a couple of years ago that was if the amount of metastatic disease wouldn't warrant immediate systemic therapy, so maybe that low-volume lung-only disease, and I've carried that as a helpful heuristic for me. Okay, great. So, So it looks like this patient did go on to receive systemic therapy. Linvon Pimbrough, back to Rainer for a second. We talked in the last scenario about sort of your preferred regimens for unresectable local. Would you agree with the treatment here or what are your thoughts for a patient who presents like this?

So I think actually in this scenario, I'm a little bit shifted. In the other scenario where you had somebody who had localized disease, who maybe was borderline resectable and you're really trying to get them to a point where they could undergo a curative intent therapy, I think the goals of care are a little bit different there, where I do want to get them maximally slight or reduced with a regimen that's associated with the highest response rate and lowest primary PD rate, which is the IO of edge FTKIs. But in the context of somebody who's overtly metastatic, like in this scenario, even though they're intermediate risk, We've demonstrated long-term disease durability with IOIO that we just have not seen with the other regimens. And so while 1 in 5 progress and the response rate is numerically lower compared to the IOVEGF regimens, 1 in 5 are going to have a long, durable response. and potentially even cure. So I think that that is an important thing to consider when you're treating somebody with metastatic disease. And also the other piece to it, from a quality of life standpoint, though there are immune-related AEs that are associated with the chronicity of long-term TKI treatment, can have a negative impact on quality of life as well. So I generally favor NEVO-IPPE to give that individual the greatest chance of a long, durable remission. And then if they do progress, favor VEGF-TK monotherapy strategy.

I do have a comment here. Please. I think Raina may be too shy to mention that she is leading a trial that this patient may be eligible for, the SAMURAI trial, which is exploring the application of debulking with stereotactic radiation in the setting of metastatic diseases where primary is intact and the patient is starting an IO-based regimen. And we are trying to take advantage of both the immunogenic properties of stereotactic radiation, which is not clinically established yet, but has a lot of preclinical data, but at the same time debulking with the radiation. So again, we will not know until the trial matures. Cytoshrink, a similar trial, actually completed enrollment, but I have not seen the data for that yet either.
So that's fascinating. So I'll ask you both. So is the intent here to treat both the primary and the metastatic sites with radiation or just the primary?

Just the primary, yep. It's a trial of combination IO therapy, any standard of care combination regimen for patients presenting with de novo metastatic disease with an intact primary. And they're randomized between radiation to the renal primary versus observation with their systemic therapy of choice as deemed as selected by their investigator.

And the thought is that the radiation, there might be some immunogenic releasing antigens and maybe the, you know, the abscopal effect. Is that, am I reading too much into that or is that the, one of the thoughts?

Well, I think it's actually multifactorial. I think it's one, cytoreduction with SBRT actually, as opposed to cytoreduction with surgery. And two, could there actually be a synergistic effect with the IO therapy? So I do think it's the combination of the two. Fantastic.

So in this case, the patient went on to systemic therapy and it looks like, Brandon, like things were fairly stable over the next little while, really over the next couple of years, other than the patient developed some CKD. And then I guess a little while later, a couple of years later, we have this. So walk us through what we have now.

So in essence, the patient was on treatment I hadn't seen him for a couple years, seen one of my colleagues, but it came back to me. I don't know if they met the qualifications that Dr. McKay said, you know, they've had more than a couple scans, nothing else has shown up, the lung stuff went away, and it's left with basically two tumors. So the left adrenal one is gone, but the right one is still there, and the left renal mass is still there. And so I think this sort of probably borrows a little bit from our past conversation, What do you do with these patients now? And I think one thing maybe Dr. McKay can speak on, because I think this is also new, is historically a lot of our kidney cancer trials really were cognizant that many patients were coming into the trial probably with poor renal function, right? They already had their kidney removed, because that's used to be, I think, the early trials, the Mozart trials, 90% of patients had one kidney, right? So everything was sort of designed. But I've noticed some of the newer trials are starting to have you know, renal function qualifications for getting on trials. And in fact, this patient, because their kidney function took a pretty big hit with just the systemic therapy, this is a patient where I would feel really bad if I went and took out that left kidney and it was all dead tumor, and now he's not eligible for some trials. So I don't know if you can comment, Rana, about how that field sort of changed a little bit in having some of the inclusion-exclusion criteria around the renal function of patients, because that seems sort of new to me. I don't know, maybe it's not.

I mean, I think in the metastatic setting, I think we are a little bit more generous with our inclusion-exclusion criteria, but I think that, especially around renal function, and that varies. You know, if it's a Phase I study, it's obviously more restricted. If it's a Phase III study, it's... broader, I would pause and ask, why did this patient have renal dysfunction while on treatment? And what is the cause of this person's renal dysfunction? Did they have ridiculous sarcopenia at baseline from the disease, and they've actually been able to stabilize and gain some weight and gain some muscle, and this renal function is more reflective of their normal state? Or did this patient develop an aphritis? Like, what's going on?

There's no smoking gun, I can tell you that. You know, everyone sort of chalked it up to just cumulative IO. It sort of happened slow enough that nobody really sounded it. It's not like he came in for one lab meeting. It was like, oh my God. But when I looked back, I was like, nobody really even noticed it. I don't know. That's just because it happens a little tick here, a little tick there, and you just look. So I don't know.

So it's just kind of one of these things. I think these things can happen. Does it correspond with a parallel increase in weight? I see that all the time. Patients, they do better, they gain weight because they've lost weight and then their cramping goes up and it's because they've actually gained a ton of weight. But, you know, sometimes these patients need to get in, see a nephrologist, and actually get a biopsy and make sure they don't have nephritis, which can be reversed with steroids, actually, if that's what's going on. So that's where I was getting at.
At this point, he was already off treatment, too. So there was nothing more, and he wasn't having any other symptoms. So that was sort of the rationale, I guess. Yeah.

I mean, I think we have to think about, like, what's the ultimate goal, right? Like, what is the goal? Do we think that this person is going to have, like, Is the goal of therapy cure? What is actually our goal? So in the context of somebody kind of having been cytoreduced to this point and you're really running up against it from a GFR standpoint, I don't know that I would subject an individual like this to resection. I mean, also looking at the location of that tumor, you know, I'm not a surgeon, but that central location makes me a little nervous about how much, even though the rest of the renal parenchyma actually looks pretty good, but it's just location looks concerning. But I tend to have a more conservative strategy, I guess is what I'm saying.

Systemic therapy stopped at this point, stable disease and two locations, this mass in the left kidney and this right adrenal. So multiple options on the table here, surgery to remove everything, more systemic treatment, monitor radiation. Let's just go back to Rakhee for a second. Based on what you've taught us, these look like decent locations to consider SBRT, would you say?

Yeah, I agree. They are feasible and treatable, safely and effectively. Again, if there's no viable disease, then perhaps I would wonder why. Maybe we watch and see whether there is any activity or growth, and if there is, then we take them out with radiation. But yes, radiation is an option.
Now, do you typically require or at least want a biopsy before treatment? Or I guess it depends.

Yeah, that depends. I mean, it goes back to the earlier discussion we had. I mean, nowadays with MRIs, you're getting so much information and you're almost confirming the diagnosis. For this patient, of course, before IOT care, perhaps had a biopsy to confirm the histology. So we would not need another biopsy.

Okay, so Brandon, what did you end up doing here? So this patient I watched, and he's a year out, and I think this is an area that both for the surgeons, you know, do you operate or not, but to recoup to point two, do you radiate or not in these scenarios, it's equally same problem. One is we probably need a little more data on the radiological side. Some groups are looking at this. How can you tell if there's viable tumor there or not, you know? And I also think it's probably going to be a space where we start biopsying more of these lesions, you know, just to try and prove it. For this one, radiographically, you can sort of tell, like, it looks like a dead tumor, right? There wasn't really enhancement. It's sort of rimmed, looks necrotic. And so I sort of learned The problem with this guy is he had both adrenals involved at the beginning, and I didn't want to take both his adrenals. If you're going to go, that means both his adrenals, kidney goes, cranium goes over too, which I talked with the patient. This is, again, where I'm having to get more, you know, historically, I never had to do this. But I sort of talked with his medical oncologist and said, hey, if he progresses, what trials are you looking at? And then we looked at the inclusion and exclusion of those trials. And one of them was specifically, it was to his GFR. And so when I told him that, he was like, no, that's, That trial was his baby. He's like, I don't want to lose that trial. He really loves that trial. And so we agreed there's risks and benefits. But I think, again, how to select which ones you watch, which ones you don't, I think is still a moving target.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary consensus favored initial systemic therapy for de novo metastatic renal cell carcinoma, with counseling that this represents systemic disease requiring immunotherapy-based treatment and that surgery is not the primary objective; surgical options may be reassessed subsequently based on response. For the residual left renal mass and right adrenal lesion after prolonged disease stability off therapy, resection was not favored given renal function concerns and the central renal tumor location. Active surveillance was selected, with local radiation considered feasible if subsequent activity or growth is demonstrated.
