case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 52-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Gross hematuria and increased lower urinary tract symptoms at initial presentation.

[ diagnosis ]: High-risk localized prostate cancer. Initial biopsy demonstrated Gleason score 5+5=10, Grade Group 5 adenocarcinoma. Subsequent pathology demonstrated very high-grade adenocarcinoma with possible neuroendocrine/small cell features on re-biopsy after initiation of androgen deprivation therapy.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial prostate biopsy showed the index lesion in the left prostate with Gleason score 5+5=10, Grade Group 5 disease involving >90% of that core; right-sided biopsy cores were negative. Re-biopsy after initial androgen deprivation therapy showed a very high-grade poorly differentiated tumor with almost no glandular differentiation, sheets of poorly differentiated cells, and Ki-67 proliferation index approximately 80%. Neuroendocrine markers including synaptophysin were negative. This specimen was signed out as Gleason score 5+5=10, Grade Group 5 adenocarcinoma with a note of possible neuroendocrine differentiation/small cell features.

[ imaging findings ]: Prostate MRI demonstrated a PI-RADS 5 lesion in the left lobe of a 44 cc prostate, with suspicion for neurovascular bundle involvement and possible seminal vesicle and pelvic sidewall invasion. MRI appearance was described as involving nearly the entire left side of the gland with extraprostatic extension and aggressive diffusion characteristics. Initial metastatic workup with bone scan and CT showed no evidence of metastasis. Research PSMA PET demonstrated avid uptake in the primary prostatic lesion without definite extraprostatic disease on pelvic imaging and identified a 7 mm right upper lobe pulmonary nodule.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Genetic testing was negative.

[ laboratory results ]: Initial PSA was 3.9 ng/mL. Repeat PSA was 3.5 ng/mL. IPSS was approximately 25. SHIM score was 13.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient enrolled on protocol J1560. Planned androgen deprivation therapy consisted of leuprolide for 2 years plus bicalutamide. Androgen deprivation therapy was initiated.

[ current disease status ]: High-risk localized prostate cancer with very high-grade adenocarcinoma and possible neuroendocrine/small cell features on re-biopsy after initiation of androgen deprivation therapy. No evidence of distant metastatic disease was identified on conventional imaging with bone scan and CT.

[ other clinical data ]: Family history included uncles with prostate cancer at older age and a mother with an unspecified kidney tumor.

reference_discussion.text: We're going to get started with these three patients. Our next patients are a 52-year-old gentleman with a high-risk localized disease, a second gentleman with biochemical recurrence, and a third gentleman with focal therapy options. So in our first patient is a 52-year-old gentleman who initially presented with gross hematuria with increased lower urinary tract symptoms on his gross hematuria workup. He was noted to have a PSA at 3.9 with an abnormal digital rectal exam, which prompted a prosthetic MRI, which revealed a Pirates 5 lesion in his left lobe with suspicion for neurovascular bundle involvement, as well as potential seminal vesicle and sidewall invasion. He had a 44cc gland. He underwent a prostate biopsy, which showed a left, which that lesion showed a Gleason 5 plus 5 or gray group 5 disease greater than 90% of that core. The whole right side of his biopsy was negative. He underwent a metastatic workup given his advanced disease, including a bone scan and a CT scan, which showed no evidence of metastasis. Under a research protocol, he underwent a PSMA PET scan, which showed a primary prostatic lesion and a seven millimeter right upper lobe pulmonary nodule. Genetic testing was negative at that time. His repeat PSA was still 3.5. Of note, his family history was significant with uncles with prostate cancer at a late age and a mother with an unknown type of kidney tumor. Otherwise, his preoperative IPSS or his voiding symptoms were roughly 25, so moderate to severe lower urinary tract symptoms, and his SHIM, which is a marker for his erectile function, was 13, indicating moderate to severe erectile dysfunction. He underwent discussion at our prostate multidisciplinary clinic, and the decision was made to enroll the patient on a J1560 trial, which included androgen deprivation therapy, as well as radiation. The androgen deprivation therapy was going to include two years of Luprolide, as well as bicalutamide. He started his ADT. And on the research protocol was a re-biopsy at Hopkins, which revealed actually small cell features of his prostate cancer. He was re-discussed at our tumor board, which the tumor board consensus was recommending continuation of ADT and radiation therapy, however, chemotherapy given his small cell features. He completed four cycles of his chemotherapy from December last year to March of this year. However, he was having ongoing hematuria, his lower urinary tract symptoms persisted, as well as horrible nocturia. He underwent a restaging physical exam with his digital rectal exam, revealing a prostate that was relatively mobile, and underwent a cystoscopy, which showed no involvement of his ureral orifices or prostatic involvement of his bladder neck. And his repeat PSMA showed resolved pulmonary nodules. if we can review our pathology or the pathology and radiology review.

Great. So this is the biopsy we received following his initial course of ADT. And it's a very unusual and very high grade appearing tumor. There's almost no glandular differentiation in this tumor. You can see just sort of sheets of very blue cells here. And the blue is the nuclei of the cells, which is taking up most of the space within the cytoplasm or within the body of the cell. So the nuclei are very large. And again, no glandular differentiation whatsoever. So, given the lack of glandular differentiation, we suspected that this might have some features of neuroendocrine differentiation, which is when the prostate cells sort of lose their identity, often because we've applied some selective pressure, such as androgen deprivation therapy. And so the pathologist examining this case looked first at a proliferation marker to see what fraction of the tumor cells are proliferating. In a typical prostate tumor, it's not larger than about 5% of cells overall, so actually a very low proliferation fraction compared to other types of tumors. But you could see here in this prostate tumor, all the brown cells on the left, all the brown dots are the nuclei that are proliferating actively, meaning dividing actively within this tumor. And so the proliferation rate or the percentage of cells that are dividing is probably, you know, 80% at least, which is very, very high and unusual for a prosthetic adenocarcinoma. And that would be more typical of a neuroendocrine differentiated tumor. However, when we looked at neuroendocrine markers, these are sort of neural cell markers that prostate cancer cells can begin to express. particularly after they're put under some kind of pressure like androgen deprivation therapy or some kind of treatment, we don't see any synaptophysin or any neural marker expression. So it's a little bit of a hybrid case, the proliferation rate or the rate of cell division is suggestive of some neuroendocrine or very, very high-grade features, but we don't have a complete picture of neuroendocrine differentiation because the cells are not expressing neuroendocrine markers. So it was eventually signed out as a glucine 5 plus 5 equals 10 or grade group 5 adenocarcinoma with a note suggesting that it might have some neuroendocrine differentiation and perhaps chemotherapy could be useful in that context. So in this slide, you can see his prostatectomy sample. And at this point, we have sort of a tumor with divided features. So on the left side, you can see tumor cells that are making some glands, some sort of circular structures or glands that resemble the normal prostate. So these are cancer cells that are better differentiated. They're adenocarcinoma cells. And on the right, you can see just sheets of very poorly differentiated cells. These still have overall more features of adenocarcinoma than neuroendocrine carcinoma, but this may have been, you know, this area may be better related to that very poorly differentiated area we saw on the biopsy here. and may have differentiated after additional therapy. So this was, again, signed out as a 5 plus 4 is 9 adenocarcinoma. And then this is just an example of seminal vesicle invasion that we saw in this case. So the case was pathologic stage 3B, meaning there was invasion of the adjacent seminal vesicle glands adjacent to the prostate. On the left, you can see with some brown pigment in them, the normal seminal vesicle epithelium. And on the right, you can see the cancer cells invading in the muscle layer around the seminal vesicle there. Again, these are adenocarcinoma appearing cells. There was also a metastasis in a lymph node. And so this was stages P or pathologic stage 3B and 1 at radical prostatectomy.

All right, so we'll take a look at some imaging for this patient. He has both an MRI and a PSMA PET. And similar to the pathology, the appearance of this tumor is highly unusual on MRI. On the left-hand side of the screen is the TT-weighted or anatomic sequence, and on the right-hand side is a diffusion-weighted or more functional biological sequence of the MRI. And nearly the entire left side of the gland and extending outside of the gland is a heterogeneous tumor with a very odd growth pattern. So we don't normally see such obvious violation of the capsule around the prostate and growth of tumor in this fashion, all the way up to the sidewall of the pelvis. So a very unusual appearing tumor on MRI. And the right-hand image we're able to see is decreased signal on diffusion-weighted imaging. Admittedly, diffusion-weighted imaging is sort of the Rorschach test of radiology. You really have to sort of be honed in I'd be looking at something very specific to make anything out of all the sort of gray and white dots. But in the area where the tumor is, again, occupying the left side of the gland, there's relatively low signal, which indicates sort of tightly packed cells and is very suggestive of an aggressive tumor type. So can we move on to the PSMA PET? Perfect. So PSMA PET's a relatively new tool. The first PSMA radio tracer was FDA approved in the US in December of last year. And then an agent that's more nationally available was approved in May of this year. This was done on a research protocol. And most of what we see here is completely normal. So the lacrimal glands above the eyes, the salivary glands around the face, all have normal uptake. The liver, the spleen, the kidneys, the bowel, all normal. And then there's excreted radiotracer in the urinary bladder. And then right below that, there's this fuzzier, less well-defined area of uptake. And that's the tumor in this case. On this whole body image, there's really no evidence to suggest that there's anything outside of the prostate. There's just the primary tumor. And we'll look at a few sort of slices through the pelvis on these images. And these are the PSMA PET fused to CT for anatomic correlation. And in the upper left, the bright spot, there is actually just urine in the right ureter. And we see that again in the bottom right. There's really nothing else abnormal, or nothing actually abnormal in any of these images. That is at least suggestive of this being a tumor that's confined to the prostate. Although, as Dr. Lotan told us, there was a pathologic evidence of disease in the lymph nodes. And in spite of how great PSMA PET is and how sensitive it is for sites of prostate cancer, it doesn't replace true pathologic surgical staging in these cases. And the sensitivity is relatively marginal for pelvic lymph node involvement. However, we can see there's very bright uptake in the primary tumor in the prostate. And this is also in keeping with the pathologic findings of this still being an adenocarcinoma. Neuroendocrine differentiated prostate cancers tend to lose PSMA expression and will not appear hot on PSMA PET. So this is additional evidence that this is at least somewhat behaving as an adenocarcinoma.

So, in summary, we have a 52-year-old gentleman with initial diagnosis of gray group 5, high-risk prostate cancer, with initial decision to pursue ADT as well as radiation therapy on a research protocol. He was re-biopsied, which was significant for some evidence of small cell features. Now, sounds close, chemotherapy with persistent significant lower urinary tract symptoms with no evidence of metastatic disease and a negative cystoscopy for trigonal involvement.

So I would just comment that to give a patient this type of chemotherapy is not what we usually do for an average prostate cancer. Cisplatinamide and etoposide is reserved for patients we're very concerned about who have at least some indication of These neuro endocrine features and as you saw from the pathology that ki 67 staining with 80% of the lesion, even though there's some nap device and was negative made us concerned that this patient would have micro metastatic disease and so. We actually treat, when we worry about that, we think about using what's a regimen that's usually used for neuroendocrine lung cancer, and that's this cisplatinum etoposide regimen. And we gave four cycles of that to try and shrink everything we could, even things we couldn't see. And it's interesting for us that it was noted that the patient had a small lesion in the lung that did go away on a subsequent scan, which suggests that that might have been a metastatic foci that we treated with the chemo.

You know, we're learning so much about these PSMA scans and Dr. Rowe, you've been a leader in that, but, you know, this case is fascinating because, you know, typical prostate cancer is an adenocarcinoma, which you would expect to light up in a PSMA scan. Do we know yet, or are we still learning about variant histology within prostate cancer and how PSMAs do or do not detect that?

Yeah, great question, Max. And I would say that because these tend to be such rare tumors, there's not necessarily a big prospective clinical trial that's told us exactly how PSMA behaves in an imaging sense. Although at the pathologic level, it does seem as though most of these tumors will lose PSMA expression and I think we'd expect them to be cold on imaging. And the small sort of retrospective case series and case reports that we do have are consistent with that, where we don't necessarily reliably image these with PSMA PET. Although, again, his primary tumor was quite hot. So I do think that is suggestive of at least some some maintenance of kind of the adenocarcinoma phenotype or otherwise, again, we wouldn't have even seen it on the PET scan. As to whether potential metastases might be sort of more differentiated along a neuroendocrine phenotype and we might miss them with PSMA PET, that's certainly possible, although I don't think we know that definitively yet.

Just to add a comment from the radiation oncology perspective, I think this is also a positive plug for research and considering research trials as part of the continuum of care. In this case, we have a trial that was designed for patients with high-risk prostate cancer who were considering radiation and hormonal therapy. And prior to it becoming commercially available, we had it available just under research, wanting to detect, see if we could detect patients with, know, distant disease not being picked up on their conventional scans. But also it included this second scan and baseline biopsy and second biopsy trying to assess response to hormonal therapy and see if there are some sort of correlates with imaging and biology. And in this case, you know, I think it was helpful, you know, hopefully had a positive impact on the patient's course. And it was that research biopsy that really detected the small cell differentiation and altered the course and advising, you know, additional systemic therapy. And then later he was, you know, kind of steered towards surgery, you know, perhaps taking that into consideration and also some of his response to the treatment.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary review supported continuation of androgen deprivation therapy and radiation therapy, with the addition of platinum-etoposide chemotherapy because of the biopsy findings concerning for small cell/neuroendocrine features. Four cycles of cisplatin and etoposide were administered from December through March. Given persistent significant lower urinary tract symptoms, absence of metastatic disease, and negative cystoscopy for trigonal involvement, the subsequent course included direction toward surgical management.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 70-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Biochemical recurrence following radical prostatectomy for prostate adenocarcinoma.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma, pathologic stage pT3bN0, Gleason score 4+3=7, Grade Group 3, with seminal vesicle invasion and subsequent biochemical recurrence.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial prostate biopsy demonstrated bilateral high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia without carcinoma.  
- Subsequent transperineal saturation biopsy demonstrated 4 cores with Grade Group 4 disease and 1 core with Grade Group 3 disease.  
- Radical prostatectomy specimen demonstrated adenocarcinoma, Gleason score 4+3=7 (Grade Group 3), composed of approximately 90% pattern 4 and 10% pattern 3, with cribriform Gleason pattern 4 present.  
- Seminal vesicle involvement was present.  
- Pelvic lymph nodes were negative (pN0).  
- Surgical margins were negative.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Prostate MRI in 2015 demonstrated a 41 cc gland with no focal abnormality; PI-RADS 2.  
- Repeat prostate MRI in 2016 demonstrated no change from prior imaging.  
- Preoperative bone scan and CT scan demonstrated no evidence of metastatic disease.  
- Preoperative PSMA PET performed on a research protocol was negative.  
- Restaging CT scan and bone scan obtained at biochemical recurrence demonstrated no evidence of metastatic disease or local recurrence in the prostate bed.  
- Bone scan showed uptake consistent with degenerative change at the acromioclavicular joints and sternomanubrial joint; no findings suggestive of osseous metastatic disease.  
- CT pelvis demonstrated postoperative changes without evidence of recurrence and no pathologic pelvic adenopathy.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- PSA was in the 2 ng/mL range in 2014.  
- PSA increased to 7.8 ng/mL in July 2015; free PSA was 10%.  
- In May 2016, PSA increased to 20.2 ng/mL; free PSA was 7.6%.  
- Prostate Health Index was 96 in May 2016.  
- Postoperatively, PSA remained relatively stable initially.  
- PSA began rising approximately 31 months after surgery and reached 0.13 ng/mL at 46 months after surgery.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Underwent prostate biopsy after initial PSA rise; biopsy showed bilateral high-grade PIN only.  
- Underwent repeat MRI and then transperineal saturation biopsy after further PSA rise; biopsy confirmed prostate adenocarcinoma.  
- Underwent robotic-assisted laparoscopic radical prostatectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection in September 2016.  
- Postoperative course was characterized by initially stable ultrasensitive PSA values, followed by biochemical recurrence.  
- Restaging CT and bone scan at PSA 0.13 ng/mL were negative.

[ current disease status ]: Biochemical recurrence after radical prostatectomy, with PSA 0.13 ng/mL and no radiographic evidence of local recurrence or metastatic disease on CT and bone scan.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Digital rectal examination was small and symmetric without abnormalities at initial evaluation.  
- No urinary tract symptoms were reported prior to diagnosis.  
- Erectile function was intact preoperatively, with no erectile dysfunction reported.  
- Family history was significant for bladder cancer.  
- At recurrence evaluation, urinary tract symptoms were minimal.

reference_discussion.text: All right, thank you everyone for your comments. So the next case is a 70-year-old gentleman with biochemical occurrence. So initially presented with a rising PSA, twos in 2014, all the way up to 7.8 in July, 2015, with a 10% free value. His DRE was small and symmetric with no abnormalities. He underwent a prostate MRI, which showed a 41cc gland. Again, no focal abnormalities, which was read as a pyrites two. Given his concern, he did undergo a prostate biopsy, which showed bilateral high-grade PIN. There's no really evidence of true prostate cancer, potentially a precursor. And then, however, in May of 2016, his PSA sharply rose to 20.2, and his free PSA was down to 7.6, and his prostate health index was 96, which was pretty convincing that he potentially had some sort of clinically significant disease in his prostate. He underwent a repeat MRI, which actually revealed no change from his prior. Given the lab values, he underwent a transperineal saturated biopsy, which revealed four cores showing gray group four disease and one core of gray group three disease. Of note, he had an excellent shim with no erectile dysfunction and no urinary tract symptoms. His family history was significant for bladder cancer. He underwent a bone scan and a CT scan, which showed no evidence of metastatic disease. He underwent a PSMA PET scan on research protocol, which was negative as well. And subsequently underwent a robotic assisted laparoscopic prostatectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection. And in September, 2016, which showed a path of T3B with seminal vesicle invasion, grade group three disease. also sensitive PSAs. And you can look at this chart. His PSAs remain relatively stable postoperatively. However, around month 31 after his surgery, it started to rise to 0.13 in 46 months after surgery. He underwent restaging CT scan and both scan given his rise of his PSA, which was negative. Again, his lorinary tract symptoms were very minimal and his erectile function was actually mediocre and actually quite well at 19. We'll review his pathology and radiology right now.

Great, so this is a slide from his radical prostatectomy specimen. We're looking at a slide section through the prostate now. All of the pink is the muscle that surrounds the prostatic glands. And in the upper left-hand corner, or sorry, in the upper right-hand corner, you can see normal prostate glands with some pink secretions within them. On the left-hand side, almost all of the epithelial cells that you see are tumor, and they're forming what we call cribriform pattern, Gleason pattern 4, which is when we see not a single lumen in the center or a single hole in the center of a kind of a circle of glandular cells, but instead we see multiple back-to-back small lumens kind of punched out, appearing like a sieve. Cribiform just means sieve-like in Latin. So this is Criboform Gleason Pattern 4. and his overall grade group was grade group three. So he was mostly cribriform pattern four, 90%, and then 10% of the tumor was pattern three. So it was four plus three equals seven. This is similar to a patient that we saw in the last cases. Gentleman also had seminal vesicle involvement. On the left side, you can see the seminal vesicle epithelium and the lumen of the seminal vesicle, which is the white space you can see there. That's where all the seminal vesicle secretions end up. And then on the right side, you can see tumor just adjacent to that seminal vesicle epithelium. And again, more of this sort of cribiform pattern. So his overall pathologic grade was four plus three equals seven, 90% pattern four with some cribiform pattern. And he was on pathologic stage P, T3B because of the seminal vesicle involvement, but he had no lymph node involvement, so it was N0. And the surgical margins were actually negative.

All right, so this patient underwent a bone scan and a CT scan, which is not surprising. These have been standards of care for patients with biochemical recurrence for decades. But in a patient with a low PSA biochemical recurrence, we'd expect both of these tests to be negative in more than 90% of patients. And the few percent of patients that they may show an unexpected metastasis, that's important, as it obviously is going to impact the patient's subsequent management. But again, the vast majority of these patients will have a negative bone scan and CT. Here, we'll start with this bone scan. And this utilizes a radio tracer called methylene diphosphonate, which just adsorbs onto the surfaces of bones. And anywhere there's bone turnover, there tends to be more accumulation of this agent. And we can see this in a couple of spots that are related to degenerative arthritis. shoulders, there's these bright spots at the acromioclavicular joints, which are degenerative. And there's also a spot kind of in the middle of the sternum, which is the sternum manubrial joint, which often has degenerative change. The right elbow is sort of where the radio tracer was ejected, and that's just a little bit of contamination. But there's nothing to suggest metastatic disease. And then where the CT really can be helpful is in identifying small lymph nodes or sites of local recurrence in the prostate bed. And here are a couple of representative slices, one through the pelvis showing sort of the obturator fossa and the internal and external iliac vessels, where we would often find nodes that would be recurrent prostate cancer. And then in the right-hand image is a part of the prostate bed. which shows kind of normal post-operative changes and no evidence of recurrence there either. So again, it comes as no surprise that these two tests would be negative, but they are important to do in case they do uncover something unexpected.

So in summary, we have a 70-year-old gentleman with grade group four prostate cancer, status post prostatectomy PT3BN0 with seminal vesicle invasion negative margins with biochemical recurrence with a slow prostatectomy, PSA is 0.13 with a negative CT scan and bone scan. And really the question is whether there's the role for PSMA scan and also the role for salvage radiation.

Maybe the PSMA scans, the easier of the two. So I'll just kind of weigh in on that briefly. So most of our data with PSMA scans is in patients with PSAs at least 0.2 in the post-operative setting. And the detection efficiency of PSMA scans between a PSA of 0.2 and 0.5 is about 50%. So about half of patients will have a positive scan and about half of patients won't have a positive scan. That's much better than CT and bone scan in the same setting where, again, we're talking about detection efficiencies in the single digits. So PSMA is really a remarkable advance in identifying sites of disease in these patients. And I guess from my perspective, probably the patients it's most important in are the about 25 or 30% of patients that are gonna wind up having evidence of a disease that's outside of what would be the traditional salvage radiation field, so that that salvage radiation field can be adjusted or the patient can have alternative treatment. I think PSMA is really important. Again, at this PSA level, it's not particularly well studied, but there's a decent chance that the patient would have a positive scan that may be helpful.

Before Kurt weighs in, I would just say that to the audience that PSMA scanning has been approved for biochemical recurrence now and will be used more and more as insurance figures out approvals and sites come online to do that. And I do wanna emphasize that Dr. Rowe was one of the major drivers of PSMA scans being approved in this country and we should all thank him for that. And he also just recently published a paper showing that when you combine the rise in PSA, the speed at which it's rising, with the absolute PSA value, he can predict pretty accurately who's going to have a positive PSMA scan and who's not. I'll stop there and turn it over to Kurt.

No, I think those are all important, great comments and how we think about salvage radiation and kind of plan salvage radiation. I think often folks are thinking that, you know, if you don't have a positive scan or something visible on the skin, that means you don't treat, which, you know, I think Dr. Rowe articulated well, that really we're just looking to see if there's something that alters the management that might help us or we're often going to see something which is within the field that we were going to treat. So it's sort of somewhat reassuring from that perspective. So in this setting, it's fairly straightforward in the sense that the patient is a candidate for salvage radiation. We know that men do well when we essentially treat the prostate bed, the space where the prostate was removed or the prostatic fossa. And there's somewhat of a debate in our field, ongoing studies, whether we also include the adjacent pelvic lymph nodes, as with some of the vessel invasion, a high initial PSA, that they're still at risk for that micrometastatic disease, which is within the lymph nodes. And then there's also a question of whether we include hormonal therapy with that salvage radiation, often what we call short course, so six months of testosterone suppression overlapping with their radiation treatment. And there's a few studies that have shown some benefit to doing that, although we're still trying to refine, you know, again, what features, risk factors, Gleason score, indications for that. And then also I think an additional thing to consider, we can use genomic studies that the CIPR score is an example of one genomic classifier, which gives sort of a risk score of the tumor. And there is data that men who have a high risk genomic score, you know, do better when salvage radiation is applied earlier as opposed to a late salvage. So those are just some of the considerations when we're evaluating for salvage radiation and the timing of when to proceed.

reference_conclusion: The patient is a candidate for salvage radiotherapy for biochemical recurrence after prostatectomy. Salvage treatment would target the prostate bed/prostatic fossa, with consideration of inclusion of the adjacent pelvic lymph nodes given seminal vesicle invasion and high initial PSA as risk factors for micrometastatic nodal disease. Short-course androgen suppression for approximately 6 months overlapping with radiation may also be considered. PSMA PET may be obtained to identify disease outside the traditional salvage radiation field that could alter management.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 72-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Lower urinary tract symptoms.

[ diagnosis ]: Prostate adenocarcinoma, initially low-risk disease diagnosed in 2015; subsequently upgraded on repeat biopsy in April 2019 to Grade Group 2, Gleason score 3+4=7, favorable intermediate-risk, left-sided disease.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Initial prostate biopsy in 2015: 1/12 cores positive for prostate cancer, Grade Group 1, involving 30% of a left-sided core.  
- Confirmatory biopsy after initial diagnosis: 1/12 cores positive in the same left-sided region, Grade Group 1, involving 30% of the core.  
- Repeat biopsy in April 2019: 2/12 cores positive, both left-sided. One core from the left apex showed Grade Group 2 disease; one core from the left mid gland showed Grade Group 2 disease involving 10% of the core.  
- Biopsy pathology demonstrated Gleason pattern 3 and pattern 4, overall Gleason score 3+4=7, with pattern 3 predominating.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial prostate MRI: prostate volume 73 cc; no obvious lesions identified.  
- Repeat prostate MRI: prostate volume approximately 100 cc; PI-RADS 3 lesion on the left side.  
- MRI also showed marked benign prostatic hyperplasia with heterogeneous enlargement of the gland.  
- Left seminal vesicle appeared diminutive, darker in signal, and atrophic.  
- Tumor localization on MRI was not clearly defined.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- PSA in 2015: 4.9 ng/mL.  
- PSA in April 2019: 8.5 ng/mL.  
- Digital rectal examination at initial workup was normal.  
- IPSS: 25.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Active surveillance was elected after initial diagnosis in 2015.  
- Active surveillance continued through at least February following the April 2019 biopsy, during which PSA rose and repeat biopsy demonstrated upgrading from Grade Group 1 to Grade Group 2 disease.  
- The patient underwent consultations with radiation oncology and obtained second opinions during this interval.

[ current disease status ]: Localized unilateral prostate cancer, left-sided, Grade Group 2 in 2/12 biopsy cores, with PSA 8.5 ng/mL and enlarged prostate gland.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- No erectile dysfunction was reported.  
- No contributory family history was reported.  
- Prostate gland size increased from 73 cc to approximately 100 cc over the documented interval.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you, everyone, for your comments. We'll move on to the third case. It's a 72-year-old gentleman. Initially, in 2015, was worked up for a lower urinary tract symptoms. His PSA was 4.9 at that time with a normal digital rectal exam. He did undergo a prostate biopsy, given his elevated PSA, which showed one out of 12 cores positive for prostate cancer, low risk with prey group one disease, 30% on his left side. And he was counseled and patient elected to go on active surveillance. He underwent a confirmatory biopsy. which showed again, one out of the 12 cores, the same region on the left side, gray group one, 30% of that core. His MRI was notable for a large gland, 73 CCs, no other obvious lesions. His PSA trended, started to trend slightly up over the years. And in April of 2019, he underwent a repeat biopsy given his PSA up to 8.5. His prostate biopsy revealed two out of 12 cores. On the left side, again, left apical area with pregroup 2 disease, so upstaged, as well as left midgland pregroup 2 with 10% of the core. His IPSS score is 25, so notable for moderate to severe LUTs. However, no evidence of erectile dysfunction. He had no other familial contributory history. From April, 2019 to February of this year, he underwent a decision-making with consultations with radiation oncology, as well as second opinions given his upstaging from regroup one to regroup three disease. He underwent a repeat MRI, which showed a 100cc gland with the pyrites three and lesion on the left side. His pathology first.

Great, so this is from his second biopsy where he was upgraded to grade group two prostate cancer. And this case is actually a beautiful illustration of the pathologic differences between grade group one and grade group two prostate cancer, and it's very straightforward in that sense. So here, in contrast to the other cases we looked at, which were radical prostatectomy samples, we're looking at a prostate biopsy, a needle core biopsy. And so you can see it's a long, very narrow, small piece of tissue, just a very small sample of the prostate. Again, the pink is the smooth muscle, which is making up most of the bulk of the prostate and the blue lines and sort of circles that you see throughout are the epithelial cells. That's where we're really paying attention and trying to see if those cells are tumor. Most of the tumor in this core is on the right side at the very far right part of the core where it becomes very thin. And you could see even from low power, it looks more cellular in that region, it looks more blue. So if you go to the next slide. we'll look at a higher power view of that right-sided area. And you could see on the very far left of the slide, so the left part of the core, we see small sort of circular glands with little white spaces in between. The white spaces are the lumen. That's where a normal gland would, and even a cancer gland will secrete some secretions from the epithelium into that space. That's why it looks like a space. And these are pattern or grade group one or three plus pattern three prostate cancer. glands because they make normal lumens like normal prostates and glands do. On the very far right side, you can see areas of blue cells that are just making solid areas or cords of cells where we don't see any of those white spaces, those lumens, and that's Gleason pattern for prostate cancer. Those tumor cells are starting to de-differentiate to sort of forget how to make a lumen the way a normal prostate cell does. And that's a very signature change that we see in Gleason pattern four. The next slide is just an additional core from this patient. In this case, the cancer is predominantly on the left side, which you can see looks a little more blue and cellular. And if we go to the next slide after that, We can see a higher magnification view of an area of cancer. Again, this is a beautiful illustration of the difference between grade group one and grade group two. So on, or I should say Gleason pattern. Gleason pattern 3 and Gleason pattern 4. So on the left side, we see an area of Gleason pattern 3, again, where we're making round glands with clear lumens. And on the right side, you can see that you no longer have those lumen spaces. They're very small. The glands are forming sort of small cords of cells. So that's Gleason pattern 4. So this was overall a 3 plus 4 equals 7. tumor. So there was more pattern three than pattern four in this tumor.

All right. And here we have the patient's MRI. And as would be suggested by the pathology with a relatively low grade tumor, this is where MRI struggles a little bit to actually define exactly where the tumor is and to what extent it's affecting the gland. In the image on the left, this is an image actually up through the seminal vesicles and the right seminal vesicle, left side of the image, are these sort of bright tubular structures and that's what the seminal vesicles should look like. The patient's left seminal vesicle is is diminutive, rather darker in signal, and looks to be very atrophic. That is not in and of itself a particularly specific finding, but it might sort of draw our attention to the left side of the gland, and we'll at least pay particular attention to that to see if we can see something like a tumor at the confluence of the seminal vesicles that may be impacting one of them. The image on the right is sort of an image that's taken through the middle of the gland, and almost the entire gland is benign prostatic hyperplasia. So the gland is sort of distorted. There's this very heterogeneous look to it, and it's fairly enlarged. So this is consistent with some of the a patient's clinical presentation is to exactly where the tumor is. Quite honestly, I don't think it's very convincingly shown on the MRI. We can sort of probably squint and find something that would correlate to the pathology, but quite honestly, it's not necessarily something we would prospectively call on the MRI.

Thank you. So, in summary, we have a 72-year-old gentleman diagnosed with prostate cancer, low-risk, in 2015. We're usually on active surveillance with a PSA rise. Recent biopsy in 2019 with upstage SIGGRAP2 disease in two cores, all left-sided, who's very interested in focal therapy options. So, the question for the two awardees, focal therapy options and recommendations.

Yeah, so, so this is a, this is a common patient, that would that we see. I think it does a number of things it highlights how we approach active surveillance. This patient's been on active surveillance for more than four years. And that means that for those four years, their quality of life was not impacted by an intervention for their prostate cancer. So there was net benefit to this patient. And now there needs to be a time for shared decision making. There's a couple of factors here that play into the decision that the patient will make. Active surveillance isn't necessarily traditional for grade group two disease in two cores, but it's unilateral and it's a very reasonable approach for this patient if they're willing to understand that there's a small, unlikely, but small risk of cancer progression. And then focal options, you know, are also available to this patient. And we have several options, you know, here at Hopkins that we would discuss, but most notably focal cryotherapy or whole gland cryotherapy could be considered. And then radiation is also an option to this patient. I don't know if Dr. DeVille wants to comment on the patient's gland size as impacting sort of the decision making regarding that.

Yeah, definitely. Thanks, Dr. King. So he has a number of radiation options. And I think as we're sort of thinking through all the options, each one sort of has its pros and cons. And that can kind of make the decision making guy with favorable intermediate risk, you know, sort of just aggressive enough, but not too aggressive. And so you're trying to balance all of these risks in terms of the side effect profiles. From a radiation standpoint, if we're going to do radiation, we would usually do external beam radiation and not an internal brachytherapy. Internal radiation, given the gland size, he kind of exceeds the limits temporary radiation. And those are not good for men with very large prostates. There tends to be more local inflammation, swelling, irritation, and complications. And from the external beam standpoint, then he would have kind of conventional radiation with IMRT, with photons, or we also have proton therapy available. They're delivered the same way. Historically, it's eight weeks, you know, daily, Monday through Friday. We also have now accelerated courses of radiation have become more standard, so we can get through the treatment in usually five and a half or four weeks is kind of the fastest mild acceleration. And then there's also stereotactic body radiation treatment, which is five treatments usually every other day, which a little bit of controversy, but we tend to steer away from men with similar to the brachytherapy considerations with very large prostates, and they tend to have more local urinary symptoms. And so an aggressive dose regimen may be potentially a little bit more risky in that setting. But those would be his radiation options to consider.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 28-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Recurrent right knee pain in October 2022.

[ diagnosis ]: Osteoblastic osteosarcoma of the right distal femur, initially diagnosed in 2009. Recurrent high-grade pleomorphic spindle cell sarcoma in the right thigh/femur region in 2022, characterized as recurrent osteosarcoma. Metastatic pulmonary disease was identified on staging imaging. Segmental pulmonary embolism was diagnosed in January 2023.

[ histopathology results ]: Surgical resection of the distal right femur mass in 2009 showed 35% necrosis. Biopsy of the new right thigh mass in October 2022 showed high-grade pleomorphic spindle cell sarcoma, best characterized as recurrent osteosarcoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- October 2022 radiograph followed by CT approximately 3 weeks later demonstrated a new 8.3 cm soft tissue mass in the vastus intermedius muscle.  
- Staging imaging after biopsy demonstrated multiple pulmonary nodules, considered metastatic disease.  
- PET scan demonstrated uptake in the right femur mass and pulmonary metastases.  
- Subsequent surveillance/staging imaging showed enlargement of the femur mass, consistent with progression.  
- March 2023 imaging after total right femur replacement showed no recurrence in the femur and a mixed response in the lungs.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
Liquid biopsy performed after enrollment in the TRAC study showed:  
- TP53 splice-site mutation at approximately 0.5% variant allele frequency  
- No microsatellite instability detected  
- Tumor mutational burden not elevated  
- Tumor fraction not elevated

Tumor tissue profiling showed:  
- Microsatellite stable  
- Low tumor mutational burden  
- TP53 alteration present in tissue  
- KIT amplification  
- PDGFRA amplification  
- KDR amplification  
- TSC1 alteration  
- CDKN2A/B loss

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory values were provided.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2009: Treated on protocol with methotrexate, doxorubicin, and cisplatin.  
- Underwent surgical resection of the distal right femur mass.  
- After resection, came off study and received cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, cisplatin, etoposide, and high-dose methotrexate.  
- Developed doxorubicin-associated cardiotoxicity.  
- Followed with surveillance imaging for 4 years after resection.  
- 2014: Right femur implant placement.  
- After recurrence/metastatic disease in 2022, treated with ifosfamide and etoposide.  
- Sustained a right femur fracture.  
- January 2023: Inferior vena cava filter placed because of bleeding complications limiting anticoagulation for pulmonary embolism.  
- January 2023: Underwent total right femur replacement.  
- From March 2023 to present: Treated with gemcitabine and docetaxel.  
- May 2023: Enrolled in the TRAC study.

[ current disease status ]: As of the latest update, she remained on gemcitabine and docetaxel. Postoperative imaging in March 2023 showed no local recurrence in the femur and mixed response of pulmonary metastases. She was reported to be clinically doing well on current therapy.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Right femur fracture occurred in the setting of recurrent disease.  
- Shortness of breath in January 2023 prompted CT, which demonstrated a new segmental pulmonary embolism.  
- Age at initial sarcoma diagnosis was in adolescence.

reference_discussion.text: So I'll tell you about our patient. She's a 28-year-old lady who was first diagnosed back in 2009 with osteoblastic osteosarcoma. She was started on a trial of methotrexate, adromycin, and cisplatin. She then underwent a surgical resection of a distal right femur mass, and that showed 35% necrosis. After that resection, She came off study and was treated with cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, cisplatin, etoposide, and high-dose methotrexate, but then developed cardiotoxicity from the doxorubicin. And she had been followed. for four years with just surveillance imaging after the resection. She then in 2014 had a right femur implant placed and she continued beyond surveillance. And then about eight years later, she developed new pain. in her right knee, which was October of 22. That prompted an x-ray and then CAT scan about three weeks later that showed a new 8.3 centimeter soft tissue mass in the vastus intermedius muscle. That prompted a biopsy two days later that showed high-grade pleomorphic splendocell sarcoma, which was best characterized as a recurrent osteosarcoma from her eight years history. From that, she had a staging scan that showed multiple pulmonary nodules, believed to be metastatic disease, and a PET scan that also showed the right femur mass, and then the pulmonary mets lit up as well. She was started on a vasfomide and a topazide. She also had a fracture in her right femur as well again. And she developed shortness of breath in January, had a new CAT scan that was read as having a new segmental pulmonary embolism. And then a subsequent staging scan or surveillance scan that showed a femur mass was growing. So she was having some progression. She had an IVC filter placed because she had complications with bleeding, so she couldn't get beyond anticoagulation. She had underwent surgery in January of this year and had a total right femur replacement. And then a new scan in March showed that she continued to have this mixed response in her lungs, but no recurrence in her femur. March of this year until present, she's been on gemcitabine and docetaxel, and then May was enrolled in the TRAC study.

So thank you, Jacob. I don't know if anybody has any questions about the history. Basically, young person with a long history of osteosarcoma, which is a rare cancer, and with a lot of prior therapy, a lot of therapy of every type, surgery, and a lot of different types of chemotherapy. We will move on. And this is actually what usually happens. We get the liquid biopsy results first because all you have to do is draw a blood specimen. And for tissue biopsy, it takes longer because you have to find the tissue and ship the tissue and so forth. So Dr. Julia Albin, if you want to discuss the findings here. Thank you.

So just to orient everybody, a liquid biopsy is a peripheral blood sample that takes advantage of the fact that small amounts of DNA from both your normal cells and tumor cells are shed and are present in the plasma component. So we utilize this feature in the TRACK study to look for any information about the mutations that are present in the patient's tumor that we can make treatment decisions on. So this assay assesses over 324 different cancer-causing genes, looking for all types of alterations in those, including point mutations, insertion deletions, We can pick up fusions and copy number alterations in some of the genes. We also assess complex biomarkers such as microsatellite instability status, MSI, and can make an assessment of potentially the antigenicity of the tumor by the tumor mutation burden. So, as Dr. Kurzweil said, the patient was enrolled in May, this blood was drawn in June, and we had her results about a week later, ready to... ready to discuss at the tumor board. And so what we found was, first of all, there's another biomarker that we've come to report on and we think is very useful, which is called tumor fraction. So remember I said in the plasma, it's a mixture of DNA from normal cells and tumor cells. So if more than 10% of the DNA fragments are coming from the tumor, then we would know that the tumor fraction was elevated in this particular case. And that would give us confidence that there had been an abundance of tumor DNA to assess. Here, we didn't see it elevated. We also did not detect microsatellite instability or an elevated tumor mutation burden. What we did detect was a TP53 splice site mutation. Now, in a liquid biopsy, as we heard from Dr. Schwartz-Levine earlier about interpretation of P53 mutations, in the blood biopsy, we're thinking, is this coming from the tumor? Is this coming from CHIP, which is also one of the components that sheds DNA into the liquid biopsy, or is it potentially coming from the germline? With osteosarcoma being one of the kinds of tumors that are associated with P53 germline mutations. So in this case, the variant allele frequency of this was approximately 0.5%. So this is a very low allele fraction, and so not suggestive of it coming from the germline, and more consistent with either clonal hematopoiesis or the tumor. Luckily, in this trial, we get the tumor tissue for cases like this to help us sort out that final question about tumor-derived versus clonal hematopoiesis-derived, particularly in an osteosarcoma where P53 mutations are the most common alteration that we see in this tumor type.

So thank you. So that is one of the issues with liquid biopsies is that there is contamination by clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential that comes from the blood, not from the tumor. And as Dr. Elvin noted, The thing against this being CHIP would be the patient is young. That's usually something that occurs in older people. But you can see CHIP in younger people, too. But the tissue really helps tell the story there. So usually, as soon as we get results, we do a molecular tumor board. because we want to get something back to the patient. And we give some initial suggestions. And then those may be revised when we get the tissue results. They're often revised. So the only thing that we had here was a P53. And P53 is a tumor suppressor gene that is not considered targetable. But one thing we know about P53 is that it upregulates the VEGF, VEGFR, vascular endothelial growth factor axis. And we've published several papers showing that patients that have P53 mutations respond to inhibitors of VEGF or VEGFR. And other groups have published on this as well, including Kohler, who published specifically in P53 altered sarcomas. And including a group that was cooperative groups, Sloan Kettering, about P53 and gynecologic cancers, all showing that P53 makes tumors more susceptible to VEGF, VEGFR inhibitors. So when we had the initial discussion about this patient, the recommendation was to give pazopanib. Pazopanib is a small molecule inhibitor that is approved for sarcomas. And it does a lot of different things. But one of the things it does, it's a very potent VEGFR inhibitor. So, that was our first recommendation that went out with our first MTB. And again, if anybody has any questions, happy to entertain them. So, then, we found, And we got the tissue back. And now the tissue turned out, as it often does, not always, but often, to be very informative. And it showed, again, that the patient was microsatellite stable, tumor mutational burden low. This is important for immunotherapy. microsatellite status, unstable or high tumor mutational burden, predisposes to immunotherapy responses. But now the patient had a whole group of alterations. So the first thing that I think is very important to notice, which I tried to allude to in my previous talk. This patient has seven alterations. So, how lucky are we sometimes when we give a single drug that we actually get responses? But if people want to ask, why doesn't everybody respond? Well, the answer is sitting in front of you. It's because there's more than one driver. And probably we need to counteract as many drivers as possible. So the other thing that this tissue told us is that the p53 was not CHIP. It was there in the tissue. The same p53 mutation was there in the tissue. And so we have a scientist, Pradeep Deed, that works with us. And he's not here today, but he always prepares these beautiful diagrams of what is going on. in the patient's tumor. And he tries to put it together with what drugs can be used. So it turns out that KIT, PGFR-alpha, and KDR were amplified. And there's a good reason that they're co-amplified. They're all on the same amplicon. They're all on the same region of chromosome 4q12. That's the long arm of chromosome 4. And so there are drugs that can hit all three targets. Pazopanib is one of them, but it doesn't hit these three targets very strongly. There's another drug called oxitinib. which is approved for different cancers, like lung cancer, which actually hits all three targets very strongly with a very low IC50. And excitinib is also a VEGFR inhibitor. So even though pazopanib is still a good suggestion, excitinib is probably a better suggestion because it's a more potent drug against these particular targets. Patient has a TSC1 alteration. And TSC1 activates the PI3 kinase AKT mTOR pathway. And drugs that are approved, there are several of these. But the two that are mentioned are Everolimus and Tempserolimus that downregulate the mTOR pathway. Now, remember, none of these drugs are actually approved for osteosarcoma. It's a rare disease. And what is approved is... chemotherapy, and then pazopanib is approved for sarcomas. CDKN2AB loss, this patient does have CDKN2AB loss. And there are several FDA-approved drugs. There's actually three. target this abnormality. One is palbocyclob, one is abemocyclob, and rubocyclob. So, there's three. He mentions abemocyclob here, but it could be any one of the three drugs. So, now we're beginning to think about how do we co-target all of these alterations at the same time. So, based on the tissue results, the preferred match therapy recommendation was for exitinib, which was preferred, or pisopinib. Pasopinib, the advantage is it's approved for the indication. The disadvantage is it's not as strong an inhibitor, as I mentioned. And in combination with a CDK4-6 inhibitor, such as Bebaciclib, And we'll show you in a little while a case report that's very similar of a patient that we treated in this way at UCSD. And we also, in order to maintain safety, we recommend starting both drugs at 50% of the dose, and then titrating up to patient tolerance. And this is what we did in the iPREDICT study at UCSD, which was the precursor to the TRACK study, and again, found to be a very safe way of dosing drugs. And then, if a third drug is to be added, we would add an mTOR inhibitor such as temsorolimus or everolimus, again, reducing the dose significantly, at least at the beginning. So, that would be the recommendations that came out of the MTB as far a customized combination. So, Dr. Nakanjam, did you want to talk a little bit about dosing?

Sure. For iPredict and for our TRACK study, as Dr. Kershrock mentioned, it's really important to start at lower doses. But there's a fine line between a super low dose and one that's efficacious. So we needed information to guide us on what safe starting doses would be. So Dr. Kershrock and I did several studies over the past few years, which are listed in the references here, which looked at clinical trials and dosing combinations from phase 1, 2, and 3 data. And these studies encompassed information from close to 100,000 patients. And the observations we saw from these clinical trials was that some sorts of drugs, mTOR, PARP, and HDAC inhibitors, tend to be more toxic when given in combination. Antibody drugs tend to be less toxic than small molecule inhibitors or the classical cytotoxic chemotherapy. And if you have overlapping targets, for example, 2-VEGF inhibitors, these small molecules can be a little more toxic when given together. So based on what we saw and these rules, in general for patients that are enrolled on track when we're giving novel combinations, we start most of the small molecules at a 50% dose. Many of the antibodies will consider starting at full dose. And certain other drugs, especially those in the mTOR, PARP, and HDAC class, will often start those even lower at a 25% dose. And as Dr. Kershrock said, it's really important to start low and then escalate the dose within the patient so we can get to a dose that's still safe but also efficacious. So these rules are important for the TRACK and the TRACK trial and also for iPREDICT. Going to the next slide. If we think about patients that are on clinical trials, standard of care drugs, most patients that are getting standard of care treatment don't represent the clinical trials population. They're older, they're sicker, they're on more medications. So some would argue it's important to consider dose reductions initially for patients even on standard of care combinations or single agent chemotherapy. chemotherapy, or other drugs. So Dr. Kershrock and I had put together a commentary addressing this. And you can see on the left, there are many factors which can affect dosing and need to be considered in the starting dose. And if patients have these, we want to start them at a lower dose. And it's important to take the tools that we have on the right to come up with personalized, optimized dosing for both clinical trials patients, patients on the track trial, and patients getting standard of care treatments.

So, thank you. So, and I want to really emphasize that last point by Dr. Nakanjam. Although we started doing lower doses and escalating, we escalate by seeing the patient weekly, doing blood work and seeing how they're doing, or we may de-escalate. We discovered that this was not only good for de novo combinations, it's actually good for everybody. because a lot of patients don't tolerate the approved doses. And this is, you know, it just makes sense. You have a 20-year-old in clinic that has, unfortunately, has cancer, and you have a 70- or 80-year-old in clinic that's just not going to tolerate the same dose. So, next, we also always talk about, in fact, we prioritize trying to get the patient on secondary clinical trials. And Dr. Vivek Subbiah is a world expert on clinical trials. And if you want to talk a little bit to us to what is available for this patient.

Thank you so much for the opportunity. As you can see here, this is one of the highest quality tumor boards that gives drug doses, combinations, combination regimens, and then clinical trial-based options now. So again, what are the clinical trial-based options based on the molecular profiling? As you saw that, there was a TAC alteration there. Based on that, Phase 2 basket study of napsirolimus in patients with malignant solid tumors with pathogenic alterations in the TSC 1, 2 altered genes, the precision 1 study. So that could be a potential option. In fact, this drug napsirolimus has an FDA indication for an extremely rare cancer. We call it PECOMA. And pecoma is probably 50 to 100 cases a year. And it's like a zebra con. So again, the drug has an indication. It's an albumin-bound form of serolimus. It has a deep activity in that. So now it's open for all tumors that harbor TAC12 alteration. So that could be an option for this patient. Another option is, again, based on the CKIT or PDGFRA, the Avopretinib option. Avopretinib basket study will also be an option for locally advanced metastatic solid tumors. And I see some folks smiling. I see folks from the precision one study and from the Avopretinib group here. It was not intentional. I just happened to see both of you guys here from the companies. And interestingly, CDKN2A loss. Patient has CDKN2A loss and B loss. So again, this can open up doors for MTAP testing, MTAP IHC testing. And if there is MTAP loss, this opens up to at least eight clinical trials with PRMT5 inhibitors or MAT2A inhibitor clinical trials. Again, you want to talk to us about MTAP loss and CDKN2A.

Well, so there's a couple of different ways to detect it. So we can detect the gene loss, but that's not the only way that you can lose them. So the coincident or downstream effect of losing the protein is also a possibility. So I think that's what you're referring to. But we don't do it in this trial, but I think that's one of the great things about the Molecular Tumor Board is that we also talk about additional diagnostic testing that might be sought by the patient at their local institution if it's warranted.

Oh, absolutely. I think we just want to don't talk about the next line of therapy, but we want to be ready for the next to next to next lines of therapy for these patients. Again, pazopanib, right? Again, why do we need some, you know, some are wondering why pazopanib Why do you need a molecular tumor board for pazopinib for osteosarcoma? In fact, the FDA label for pazopinib is soft tissue sarcoma. It's off-label use for osteosarcoma. Of course, pediatricians and pediatric oncologists and medical oncologists use that as a last line. In this case, we would not use this as a last line. Pazopinib is now indicated based on the molecular profile of this patient. In fact, it's interesting to see VEGF and mTOR pathway activated. There is a phase two study with sorafenib and everolimus. Did not meet the end point. It had a 45% patient adherence, clinical benefit rate at six months. So that did not meet the end point, but that's still an active regimen that has a phase two dose. So again, these are the clinical trial based options for our patient here. Thank you, Dr. Khesra.

So I think, thank you Vivek, so I think that the important thing here is that we try to, we have expertise in clinical trials and customized combinations, and we try to offer to the patient many possibilities, including clinical trials and including customized combinations. So this is a young patient. So if Catherine Skifos could speak to germline testing.

Absolutely. So as Dr. Elvin mentioned before, the TP53 mutation that was identified on the somatic testing was at a low variant allele fraction, which makes us less suspicious that it would be of germline origin. Nevertheless, this patient was a teenager when she was diagnosed with a sarcoma. And so because of that, she should consider genetic counseling and testing. In patients under the age of 30 with osteosarcoma, about 5% or so will be found to have a germline mutation in TP53. But as a patient gets younger, that number increases. And even though the TP53 mutation was not particularly suspicious on this test, I did include here that NCCN guidelines Give a bit of guidance for when to consider testing. So to echo what Allie was saying in her previous presentation as well, TP53 is the most commonly mutated gene somatically. But in patients where there is a TP53 variant identified on tumor only sequencing, germline testing should be considered. if there's relevant family history or if the patient is diagnosed under the age of 30 with any cancer. So that does provide helpful guidance in taking that next step as to whether or not to recommend germline testing. And then other genes may also be considered for this patient's germline testing based on family history. There's some preliminary evidence of genes like CDKN2A and POT1 being related to osteosarcoma risk as well.

Thank you, Catherine. So, again, I want to point out the multifaceted expertise, multidisciplinary expertise that we've tried to arrange for this molecular tumor board. And really, in the post-COVID era, it was made possible because we can bring together the best experts at the best places. We can bring them together weekly for a Zoom meeting, something that we really could have done before COVID, but we didn't. And now we do this regularly. So this is the update. This patient was, I think, presented around July, August of 2023. And she was on gemcitabine and Taxotere. and doing well, and she actually continues to do well with this therapy. And so one of the questions you might ask is, so why did she go on the protocol? Because she's doing well with her current therapy. And what I want to say is from a lot of experience with these types of protocols, she went on the protocol at the exact right time. So, once the patient has progressive disease, especially if it's aggressive, that's late. It's not too late, but sometimes it's too late because patients don't have a lot of time, especially if they've relapsed multiple times. Tumors tend to be aggressive. there may be a very short window in which the physician really needs to treat the patient before they're going to deteriorate or even die. So this is exactly when we want patients to go on. We want them to go on while they're still doing well on their prior therapy. Now, if she's cured, great. But the likelihood of her being cured is very small at this point, because she's had multiple relapses. So at some point, we think that she will have progressive disease. And now we have a treatment plan for her. And if it turns out that she's responding for another year or two, we can always do another liquid biopsy. We can always update the molecular tumor board. There may be new clinical trials that are available and so forth. And then I want to talk about an example of a patient that we published from the University of California while I was there with the iPREDICT study. Very similar story. This is a 31, this publication is on a 31-year-old woman with heavily pretreated metastatic osteosarcoma, just like this patient. Just like this patient, she had alterations in the cyclin pathway. They were a little bit different than the current patient's alterations, but they essentially did the same thing. She had a CDK4 and CCND2 amplification, which upregulates the CDK4-6 pathway. And so we got a CDK4-6 inhibitor for her called palbocyclob. And that was one of our suggestions for this patient, palbocyclob or abemacyclob. The patient in question also had abnormalities in the FGFR pathway, so a little bit different than the current patient. But again, very much in keeping with that every patient is unique, but they often have some commonalities. So, she was given together with palbocyclob linvatinib. Another FDA-approved drug. Both drugs were, even though she's only 31 years old, both drugs were given at a considerably reduced dose, probably about 40% of the normal dose level. And although we tried to increase the dose, despite the fact that the patient was only 31, She could not tolerate an increased dose. But in spite of that, more drug for these targeted drugs is not necessarily better. For chemotherapy, we always thought more drug is better. But for targeted drugs, once you hit the target, everything else may be toxicity. So, her PET scan showed 68% reduction in metabolic activity. So, she had a very strong partial response. And she continued to do well 51 months. from the start of therapy. So, very durable, ongoing response with a customized combination that she tolerated very well. So, I think a good example for our current patient with osteosarcoma as well who has similar but not identical So, I think we will stop there and then we're happy to address any questions that anybody has.

reference_conclusion: Molecular tumor board review supported a matched therapy strategy for relapsed metastatic osteosarcoma consisting of axitinib as the preferred agent, with pazopanib as an alternative, in combination with a CDK4/6 inhibitor such as abemaciclib. Both agents should be initiated at 50% of standard dosing with subsequent titration according to tolerance. If additional therapy is required, an mTOR inhibitor such as temsirolimus or everolimus may be added with significant initial dose reduction. Germline genetic counseling and testing should also be considered given osteosarcoma diagnosed before age 30 and the identified TP53 variant on tumor sequencing.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: In 2007, he presented with flushing and pain. Seven years after initial lung surgery, he was found to have elevated liver enzymes; subsequent ultrasound demonstrated liver lesions.

[ diagnosis ]: Typical lung carcinoid (low-grade well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor) of the right lower lobe, initially resected in 2007. Subsequent recurrent/metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor involving the liver, described as bilobar hepatic metastases.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Primary lung tumor pathology after right lower lobectomy and thoracic lymphadenectomy: typical lung carcinoid, 2.5 cm.  
- Mitotic rate: fewer than 2 mitoses per 10 high-power fields.  
- Ki-67: less than 5%.  
- Synaptophysin positive.  
- Chromogranin positive.  
- Liver biopsy from recurrent disease: well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial imaging in 2007 showed a lesion in the right lower lobe of the lung.  
- Seven years later, liver ultrasound showed liver lesions.  
- MRI of the liver at recurrence demonstrated a large hepatic lesion; disease was described as bilobar liver metastases with significant right lobe involvement.  
- Octreotide scan was performed at the time of hepatic recurrence.  
- Post-surgical imaging after hepatic debulking demonstrated two small residual subcentimeter hepatic lesions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were provided.

[ laboratory results ]:  
- Elevated liver enzymes were identified at the time hepatic recurrence was detected.  
- Elevated liver function tests/liver numbers were described in association with hepatic metastatic disease.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- 2007: Right lower lobectomy and thoracic lymphadenectomy for typical lung carcinoid.  
- No adjuvant treatment was given after initial surgery.  
- After hepatic recurrence, he underwent surgery consisting of removal of several confluent liver masses, microwave ablation, alcohol ablation, and lymph node dissection.  
- Residual gross disease remained after hepatic debulking, with postoperative imaging showing two small residual subcentimeter lesions.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor of pulmonary origin with bilobar hepatic metastases, status post hepatic cytoreductive surgery with microwave ablation, alcohol ablation, and lymph node dissection. Residual gross disease remained, with postoperative imaging showing two small residual subcentimeter hepatic lesions. The primary lung lesion had been completely resected and no thoracic recurrence was described; disease was described as confined to the liver at that stage.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Hepatic disease was described as bulky and not amenable to ablation at one stage because of lesion size.  
- Surgical candidacy for hepatic disease was limited by bilobar involvement, significant right lobe tumor burden, and abnormal liver tests.  
- After hepatic debulking, the patient was asymptomatic.
