reference_discussion.text: So the tumor board is a very important part of the care of our patients. And that's because a lot of the patients required more than one discipline. And as you know, in a hospital environment, I'm sure many of you have tried to get in touch with me. It's not so easy, right? And even us getting in touch with each other. And sometimes we need to get in touch with three or four people. And sometimes we all need to be looking at the same thing at the same time. in order to come to a decision. And as you'll see from today, there's not always one right decision. Sometimes these decisions in the care of a patient are quite nuanced. So it takes everybody coming together, reviewing the pathology, reviewing the radiology, the case, special considerations to develop a good treatment plan. Now, tumor boards tend to be recurring, and they should be not a looking back, so to speak, but looking forward. So they should be done on a – usually we do it weekly. Some places do it monthly. But as the patient care is being provided, it's an ongoing thing. So we're going to present a few cases today. And we have representatives from all the specialties. And this year we did something special is that we included the patient perspective. because I've noticed that a lot of times we'll have recommendations from our tumor board, and of course you know who has veto power, right? Right, right, okay. So case number one. So poor Josh, he's 53. In 2007. I wish, we'll get back to it one day. In 2007, he had flushing and some pain. He went to his primary doctor. He had some imaging that showed a lesion in the right lower lobe of his lung. Afterwards, he had a right lower lobectomy and thoracic lymphadenectomy. Here's a picture of the lesion. And this was the pathology results. It was a typical lung carcinoid, two and a half centimeters in size, Less than two mitoses per 10 high-powered fields. KI67 is less than 5%. Synaptophysin and comogranin was positive. Dr. Marchewski, any thoughts?

Well, this is basically a low-grade neuroendocrine tumor. We use a different terminology in different organs. In the lung, we like carcinoid. The tumor was 2.5 centimeters in size. which smaller than three centimeters is lower risk category. We use mitosis, how fast the tumor is growing. And there is a limit of two in 10 high power fields. That is good news. Higher than that makes it an atypical carcinoid. Tumors are known to have a little more aggressive behavior. So you have size is good, the number of mitosis is good, and then the Ki67 is less than five, which is another cutoff for good news versus not so less good news. The last two features are immunostains that we used to determine that a tumor is neuroendocrine. So both were positive, which classified the tumor as a low-grade neuroendocrine neoplasm.
Okay. Does anyone have any recommendations for this patient now that we're discussing in tumor board after surgery? Dr. Halperin, does this patient need any kind of treatment at this point?
No. Next question.
Okay.

Does anyone want to venture as to what the surveillance plan should be for a patient like this? Do they just need a chest x-ray once in a while and we're good? Anyone have any thoughts? What do we have to do to check to see if the tumor is going to come back or not? Dr. Lee, do you have a plan for this patient? Yeah, so surveillance imaging, I think there's not complete consensus in terms of guidelines. So this is a relatively low grade neuroendocrine tumor where the risk of recurrence is still low, but there is still that risk of recurrence. Imaging can either be CT of the chest imaging, usually about either three to six months intervals to see whether or not there's a recurrence moving forward. So this patient was told by the surgeon, you're good. This is done. Tumor's gone. You can maybe get a CT scan once in a while, you're in the clear. Giovanna, do you have any thoughts about this, this recommendation from the surgeon?

On the one hand, I think as a patient, I'm going to feel really good about that. Like, I want to believe that I'm cured. On the other hand, I may be a little suspicious. Like, is it really true? Am I doing the right thing? But if this is my first experience with being diagnosed with something really major, I'm probably going to believe the physician and just go with it, because I really want to believe that I'm done.

Yeah, it's a tough case. And then how long would you do surveillance for the medical oncologist? How long would you continue to check scans? Or surgeons? I know there's no thoracic surgeon here today, so I know it's a tough one. But you're tumor surgeons. How long would you do surveillance if you were going to do imaging? How long would it be done for?

Yeah, I think, you know, the movement more recently, particularly with GI, but I think even if we look at sort of the way we've adjusted the NCCN guidelines over the last year or two, has been to extend surveillance out, right? So I think we would typically say you may do the same number of scans, but over more years. So, you know, if you're doing them once a year, you may tend towards 10 years, I think The data aren't quite clear on, particularly with low-risk patients, exactly when and where those recurrences will be, but 10 or, for some folks, even longer may be appropriate.
Josh, how do you feel about all this? This is a tough problem.

I feel good so far, but I've read online that I'm never really cured and that I should be getting imaging or some other follow-up more often. So I'm a little nervous about waiting six months, but I'll try.

It's understandable. So this gentleman, seven years later, I think the idea that he had cancer even left his mind completely. He was found to have elevated liver enzymes, and an ultrasound showed liver lesions, and these are biopsy. So this is what an MRI at that time looks like. And here you see these, these are the tumors, and then this is the liver, normal liver here. So you see, it's a pretty large lesion. So not only is the patient, is Josh, shocked that it's come back, but he's also surprised again. That's concerning. And an actria scan, this is an olden days radiology. Gabe, what do you think about, you can't see it. It's not very impressive. Yeah, it doesn't look too good. But it's pretty similar to how we do with arterioscans. It's just kind of like blurbs of light, yeah. Anyways, so a biopsy was done. Dr. Marchevsky, what do you think about this biopsy result?

Well, again, the patient has a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor. In this situation, you have to consider could it be a recurrence of the tumor from many years ago. Or could the patient have a new tumor, as the neuroendocrine tumors are known to be multiple in some people. So before you make sure that this is a metastasis from the previous tumor, it's a good idea to compare the two lesions, which in this situation is not going to help all that much, because they all tend to look similar. But then clinically, you have to make sure the patient doesn't have a carcinoid tumor elsewhere, particularly in the small bowel. that may benefit from surgery before labeling this metastatic tumor from the lung into the liver.
And Giovanna, as a patient, how do you feel right now?

I think right now I'm pretty frightened. I was told I was good, and here I am some years later, and I feel like I have really greatly metastatic cancer. So I think one of the things that might cross my mind is, am I getting the best opinion that would come up?
Yeah.
How about you, Josh?

Josh, how are you feeling? I'm trying to find out what the next treatment would be, what my options are. I'm probably not running around yet to find what else to do. I'm waiting to see what comes back from the tumor board or from my oncologist.

OK. So does anyone from the surgical or interventional radiology have any perspectives on what they would recommend, or medical oncology at this point? So a patient with recurrent lung neuroendocrine tumor, well differentiated. by low-bar metastases to the liver seven years later. I think we would want to really discuss this kind of in this similar fashion in real life in terms of multidisciplinary team. One of the questions I would have for the surgeons as well as interventional radiologists is the tumors appeared relatively bulky. Whether or not that's going to potentially compromise venous outflow The patient already has elevated liver function tests, so the concern is that if it potentially leads to anus outflow obstruction, then that patient is in big trouble in terms of their underlying disease with the liver, and they can go into impending liver failure as a result of that. So that's, I think, question number one because that will really determine how aggressive we might want to be with our systemic therapies going forward. We know that the patient will need some form of systemic therapy because we're not going to be able to completely clear the disease. But question number one would be for, you know, the multidisciplinary team in that sense. Dr. Ganji, any thoughts? Our surgeon, if you haven't had a chance to meet her, she's our tumor surgeon specializing in endocrine tumors.

So, I apologize for my voice, but from the one cut, we see he has pretty significant disease in the right lobe of the liver, and you're saying he has bilobar metastases with some evidence of liver compromise based on his elevated liver numbers. So, I don't think he would be an optimal surgical candidate at this point. I think there would be some option to potentially see if our IR colleagues can offer some embolization therapies to kind of control or decrease the tumor size, followed potentially by some systemic therapy. and then reassess for potential resection depending on response.
That's my liver function.

Yeah, so I think there are several options for us in the interventional radiology realm. These are too big for ablation, so we're looking at the trans-arterial techniques. And we'd also, there are elevated liver enzymes here, so we'd look at the liver enzymes and make sure that it was safe to treat, actually, assuming that it is safe. I think bland chemo or radiation, it's kind of dealer's choice here, are all, they're all viable options.
So, Dr. Kasari knows what's happened.

So, I think one of the points that should be brought up is that, especially surgeons, I, first of all, I agree with all the comments of my colleagues. Surgeons are spatial, spatially oriented species. We like to see it, we like to have the information. So if you get calls from our offices saying, hey, we really got to have the actual images, that's the reason why. Because something that's in the report, most good surgeons will tell you they look at the images first, they make up their own mind about what's going on, and then they check to make sure that the radiologist read the film correctly. when it comes to liver disease for sure. So you got to see the images and see for yourself, what is the distribution of disease? What are the chances of resection now? What are the chances of resection later? How can we bring in this multimodality treatment to hopefully get the patient to the point where something more can be done, if it can't be done like this is right now.
Great. And Dr. Halperin, if someone's recommended to have a large cytoreductive surgery like this, How would you consult the patient as far as the risk-benefit ratio of doing something like that?

Yeah. This is really one of the things, sorry, like many things Giovanna says, like this was sort of true genius this morning when you said that really the calculation about quality of life and how much you're sort of buying with whatever sort of cost to yourself and your body you're willing to endure is so critical. Because the way I counsel my patients is when they see our surgeons, we tell them if you follow large surgical series long enough, almost everybody recurs eventually. And in fact, many series will show you an average time to recurrence on the order of a couple of years for many folks. And so it becomes very much how much risk is there to the surgery? What anatomic considerations will there be? How much of a hit to your quality of life? Like you guys, my surgeons are phenomenal. So, you know, the surgeons, we have very low morbidity and mortality, but what do you really get for that, even if it is just a week in the hospital or heaven forbid longer? And how do we weigh that against the other treatment options we might have in light of knowing what the benefits of all those things might be?

Great, so this patient did have a surgery. As you can see here, it was removal of several confluent masses, microwave ablation, and alcohol ablation, and a lymph node dissection. So even within the techniques, there's sometimes multidisciplinary, right? So now the patient has been debulked, or CIDR reduced. Anyone have any recommendations on what to do from here?
What should we do, tumor board? So I'm sorry, this was R2? Is that what we're saying? It was gross R2 debulking? Or did they... Let's assume it's R2.
Okay. Can you explain what R2 means?

Sorry, yeah, so the main question is do we still have visible cancer that was left behind sort of deliberately? Not deliberately, but because it was not... Forgive me, because it wasn't amenable to the many techniques that our colleagues had available at the time.

So let's say that, let's say for the sake of our tumor board, there's, there's about a couple of small sub centimeter lesions that you can see on post-surgical imaging. So there are two small lesions that you can see that they look like there's some residual left behind, which was expected.

Yeah. No, I mean, I think as a medical oncologist, you know, we're aware that our systemic therapies have significant benefit for folks, right? We know that progression through survival is significantly improved with the systemic agents we have. But we also know that in randomized trials, when patients cross over, everybody gets the benefit eventually. So a lot of times, if you're dealing with low-volume indolent disease, We'll take that opportunity to understand if and when the disease is going to grow before we start deploying the systemic therapies and really sort of try to maximize, because I think the lowest toxicity option you have is going to be observation, other than the anxiety, which is worth considering in that risk-benefit balance. And so we may try for that first.
Josh, how do you feel about all that? Do you feel like you're OK with waiting, or do you want to start treatment?

So I hate the word waiting. Waiting is a bad word for most of the patients. I didn't say it. I said it. And you said observation. You said waiting. I prefer learning. at our disease care, I do understand with enough explanation that you would give that maybe we need to see what type of stripe this is, whether it would start going in, whether we do some active surveillance and do some learning. There will be people who obviously won't be able to do that due to, you know, it's just too gut-wrenching to not be doing anything. But I would understand that. I do have one question as being the patient. Was I ever allowed to, be in my tumor board to listen to what happened and get the results of more than just what the final opinion is. That's been a big question in our group.
It's in the mezzanine. It's very hard to find.
There's no parking.
And coffee isn't that great.
Yeah, coffee is awful.
Coffee is awful, but we're used to that.

So that's a great question. Anyone on the board want to take that? I can take that if anyone else. Dan, you want to say, are patients allowed at your tumor board at City of Hope? I mean, patients are not traditionally, you know, allowed in the tumor board because we present a lot of different cases throughout the period. So you'll be kind of privileged to other patient identifiers and patient information. So what we do say is that, you know, we have a robust discussion and we do kind of keep notes in terms of what happened in the tumor board. We're very open in terms of how the case was discussed. So oftentimes for my patients, I do tell them that if there was discrepancies between different opinions, what are the different reasons why people had discrepancies so that we can really kind of weigh those risks and benefits and make a conscious decision together.

Can I comment on that too, please? So anyone shop on Amazon? Have you ever spent like three hours looking up, you know, a different type of wallet that you want to buy? The problem with information is that The more access to information you have, sometimes the harder it gets to try and interpret it correctly. It's not because we don't want you in the tumor board. It's that information has to be digested by someone that you trust and be given to you in the way that it makes sense. I bet you if you sat through tumor board for your own case, you're not going to understand maybe, you know, 30, 40% of sometimes the material that's being presented to you. And that's doing you a disservice. You shouldn't worry about the background stuff that goes out. You should find the right people that you trust, and then get that information. Check it with other folks if you'd like to. But that's part of the reason. I haven't seen anyone include patients in tumor boards across the country.
Keep this moving along. I'm going to assume I don't have any symptoms, and I'm OK. So I'll let it be active surveillance, and you tell me how often I should come back.

Yeah, that's so typically for well-differentiated, low-grade disease, our surveillance imaging plan is about every six months. But of course, depends on the situation, that might vary. So in April 2016, how long did you say, Dr. Halperin, the average amount of time was? Around a couple years. Yeah, well, two years later, there's some disease growth in the right lobe of the liver. So go back to the tumor board. Can you see it? Unfortunately, the screen is kind of dark. We can see it pretty good here.
My selfie doesn't look very good. Dr. Lipschitz, what do you think about that?
I would ask the surgeons if they want to resect again.
we'd have to see the rest of the images. Yeah, that's it.
Those are all the images. I mean, assuming that this- You would do a surgery again in two years?

Yeah, I don't rule things out. I mean, you have to have the full data set, as much data as you can, but repeat operations is doable. If this looks to be like in the right lower liver towards the back, and it's far enough away from the main vein that's draining the right side of the liver, So it is possible to go back in there and locally just excise that area.
Okay, any other ideas?

I think the question with excision I would have there is he's had a pretty extensive surgery so I'd like to know what remnant liver he has and what his liver function is and it looks, I assume it's about under two centimeters or so. So it's pretty central and I think an ablation would be another option for a short interval recurrence in this patient.
All right. So these are the options. How about Everolimus, Dr. Halperin-Ali, standard approved agent?
Agreed.
Agreed. That's true. That's true.

I think that I think the question in all of these situations is really, you know, what do we know about the biology of this? Sorry. It's sort of what's at the confluence of the anatomy of the situation as was described, the biology of the cancer and the condition of the patient. Right. And I think that the biology of the disease is telling us we just did the experiment that a local therapy is going to give us a relatively short interval recurrence. And my question would be, are we sure we want to bark up the same tree again, regardless of modality, IR surgery, or alternative technique, personally.
OK, great. So this patient did receive embolization, then received Everolimus and other therapies. But moving forward, we have a gallium 68 scan. Can you see that?
So another two years pass.
Yeah, we can say another two years, about the time the gallium is approved in the US. So we have a gallium 68 scan. Dr. Thompson, do you have any feelings about this scan?

Gallium 68 PET is a huge advantage over the octreotide because of the brightness of the lesions when they show up compared to background and the fusion of the lesions with the anatomy so you can see where the heart is up the top and the liver and then the blob down the bottom of the bladder. It's always surprising to our patients to find gallium 68 PET showing up things that they didn't know they had and that's the problem with sharpening the lens and taking a look at the fine detail is You're using a different tool. It's a more sensitive tool for detection of small things, and frequently it shows up things that you didn't know you had that were not evident on other imaging before. But sometimes that's really important to get a sense of the bigger picture of where the disease is rather than just focusing in on one organ.

And how does that change our treatment algorithm? Now that a patient has progressive disease, the gallium scan is positive, but they have a lung tumor. Does any of the medical oncologists have a feeling of what you would recommend for this patient? It's not an easy one. Yeah. So this is a, you know, I think you're going to get. You're probably four different opinions if you see four different medical oncologists. I'm being very honest. Yeah, yeah, maybe. Yeah, probably six different opinions on it. So at least off of your list here, I think a lot of major academic centers, we do encourage clinical trials. The reason why is we understand that for lung neuroendocrine tumors, there are limited FDA approved treatment options. Therefore, whenever we think about a clinical trial, We're really trying to give you another opportunity to see a medication that you might not have otherwise. So that we give you as many possibilities in terms of many chances to potentially respond to the various different types of treatments. Obviously that does require kind of a similar mindset from the patient perspective. and potential toxicities incurred in the clinical trial drug. But I think all of these are options. But usually, I would favor a clinical trial, in this case, over standard therapies.

And I'll do a quick follow-up. Would it matter the fact that my lung primary is completely removed and it doesn't seem to be re-showing up? That isn't the area recurrence, it's just my liver. Would that change some of the mathematics to what you were thinking?

Yeah, absolutely. So if it's just localized in one area, then potentially local regional approaches might be more appropriate, along with the same line of thought of being able to have as many therapies still on the table as possible going forward.

And can I just add, I think there's an important element here for the patient to understand how you are about information and decisions, and how do you make decisions, and how much information you feel you need. Like you said, I'm more the person who will be on Amazon for six hours looking for the wallet. So I feel my comfort level is there to make a decision once I feel like I have enough information. Some people are just the opposite. They're like, no, I don't wanna do the research, just tell me what to do. So it's important to know who you are in this process and what you need in terms of information or not having an overload of information. And that's individual.

reference_conclusion: Following resection of the typical low-grade pulmonary carcinoid, no adjuvant therapy was recommended. Surveillance imaging with chest CT was advised, initially at 3- to 6-month intervals and then extended over a prolonged period, potentially up to 10 years or longer. After hepatic recurrence with bilobar metastases and residual low-volume disease following cytoreductive surgery, the plan was for active surveillance with imaging approximately every 6 months rather than immediate systemic therapy. With subsequent progression, liver-directed embolization and everolimus were used, and for further progressive Ga-68-avid disease, clinical trial enrollment was favored over standard therapies, with consideration of additional locoregional treatment if disease remained confined to one area.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 53-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Pelvic pain and numbness in the left leg.

[ diagnosis ]: Poorly differentiated high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma, primary site not identified.

[ histopathology results ]: Biopsy demonstrated poorly differentiated high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Imaging showed abdominal/pelvic masses and lymphadenopathy. Enlarged lymph nodes were present in the abdomen surrounding a vascular structure. No large lung mass was identified.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: Tumor molecular profiling was performed and demonstrated PD-L1 amplification.

[ current disease status ]: Poorly differentiated high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma with abdominal and pelvic masses and lymphadenopathy; primary site not identified.

[ other clinical data ]: None provided.

reference_discussion.text: Okay, so the first case was a good example of We need everybody together to make decisions and come together. So this is a 53-year-old woman who presents with pelvic pain, numbness in the left leg, and imaging that shows masses and lymph nodes in the belly causing these problems. The biopsy shows a poorly differentiated high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma. And here's some lymph nodes. This picture is better. Here are the lymph nodes here surrounding this vascular structure. These are not normal lymph nodes. So for our medical oncology colleagues, how would you approach this problem?
chemotherapy. Next question.
Does it matter to you where it's coming from?

So it actually, to some extent it does. And that's only because I think that there's significant heterogeneity in sort of the biology of high-grade neuroendocrine neoplasms, such that the uptake of that sort of frontline atazolizumab immunotherapy incorporation that was discussed earlier is a little bit under It's a little bit, I won't say contentious, but debated in terms of whether it should be deployed outside or sort of with extra-pulmonary high-grade endocrine carcinomas. So if you told me this person had a large lung mass with regional adenopathy from that, which she didn't, they would see one of my lung doctor friends, and that person would get immunotherapy. If they see one of the sort of extra-pulmonary high-grade endocrine carcinoma people, beyond that I would say no, it's chemotherapy, chemotherapy, and chemotherapy. And if we don't know? If we don't, so it's an excellent question, right? Because epidemiologically, we actually can see that unknown primary high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma tracks exactly what small cell lung cancer of the lung. So as smoking went up and pulmonary high grades went up, extra pulmonary high grades went up, And then a smoking cessation took hold in our population. And then the incidence of the cancer went down. So did unknown primary. So yeah, it mirrors it beautifully. It's just an order of magnitude different.
Giovanna, your medical oncologist is telling you it's chemo and that's it. Is that OK? Next question. That's what he said.
I like options. I would say not it's chemo or that's it. I would say it's chemo or we need to have a conversation about what it would mean not to do chemo.
I think if I do my typical Amazon shopping information on Dr. Google that I'm going to probably see the same answers that chemo is going to be.
But would you send me out for any genomics testing? Just, I know that's later on this afternoon, and you kind of explained why you might not, but would you send me for a panel somewhere?

Male Speaker Dr. Lee? Dr. Lee, would you do that? Male Speaker I mean, given the fact that we have limited treatment options, I would genomically profile the tumor on the off chance that there are a targeted approach. This is an example where we don't talk to the surgeon.

I actually have a question, a learning thing for me. I'm wondering if you guys do any repeat biopsies of this, with the heterogeneity that's there with KI-67, and a lot of the decision you made on that.

That's a separate, totally separate question, actually. Fascinating one, but totally separate. So first, though, Dr. Lee's point, which is, I absolutely agree, like, genomic profiling, extremely reasonable, but do not wait. Right, it's go ahead and get it, but it has no relation to what you're about to do. Something actionable afterwards. Yeah, exactly as you said, Josh. It's great down the line to know, and this is when you have tissue you may be able to send, but absolutely don't wait for it. It's the same chemo no matter what.

This is the type of tumor where, you know, we always say normally For most neuroendocrine tumors, it's not a sprint, but a marathon, right? But this is a high grade, poorly differentiated neuroendocrine carcinoma. So this is a time where we do have to sprint. So you do need to start treatment right away. So my patient, well, here's the molecular findings. So we did molecular findings. We started the patient on chemotherapy like you recommended. When it was discussed with the patient that we need to do chemotherapy, She said, no, I don't want to do that. And I said, you really? I said, everything you guys said, you know. That's it. That's what you got to do. And she's like, nope, nope, nope, nope. We're going to do immune therapy. And I said, please, let's just do chemo. Let's do chemo. So she agreed. We started the chemo, and then we got molecular testing. And this is what the molecular testing showed. Anyone want to take a stab at this? Does this mean anything to the group? Some people would look at this and say, I don't know what this means. This doesn't mean anything to me. It's kind of complicated.
The graphs are much harder to read.
This is common. So we get molecular findings and a lot of times it's hard to interpret them, right?
So I think as a patient, I look at this and I just want to know, is there anything actionable?

Right. I mean, is there? Yeah, as a physician, I have exactly the same question. And what I honestly mean by that is, are there prospective data that tell us that acting on one of these things for this person will yield benefit or harm? And I think the answer really is no. in terms of outside of an experimental setting. That being said, as data are emerging, we may use this to influence among the various non-data driven or clinical trial options that we would have, but in the standard realm, this to me is not actionable.

Yeah, and this is a particularly tricky case because PD-L1 amplification is a pretty rare event and being discussed. So this patient, she was like, I do not want to do chemo. And she kept telling me over and over again. And she pushed me, and so we enrolled her into the DART clinical trial. which was the recent study that was actually showed positive results. So she was enrolled in Nevo IPI and she was on treatment for almost a year. She had some immune related side effects, but otherwise she stopped and her cancer hasn't grown for about two years now. And every day she comes, she brings me like a health juice and she's like, doc, let me take care of you. If you ever need any medical advice, I'm always available. And yeah, her disease is well controlled and almost gone without any treatment now.

Well, and if I could just take a moment. So this illustrates actually a number of really fantastic points, right? One is, you know, sorry. It's a chronic issue with me. So this illustrates really a couple of beautiful points, right? So one is, you know, how much you worked with your patient to decide together what the most appropriate thing for her was, and the fact that you were able to match her to a clinical study such that you were able to get her what she wanted, and also make this not just some pretty pictures on the screen, but data that other people can learn from and hopefully benefit from. Because we know, right? DART is a small study. We don't really totally know. [ chief complaint ]: Hematuria.

[ diagnosis ]: Incidentally detected pancreatic tail lesion, diagnosed on biopsy as a well-differentiated low-grade pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 45-year-old African-American woman; physician.

[ chief complaint ]: Left breast cancer.

[ diagnosis ]: Triple-negative invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast, clinical stage T1N1, grade 3. Germline BRCA1 mutation carrier.

[ histopathology results ]: Following neoadjuvant chemotherapy and bilateral nipple-sparing mastectomies, pathology showed complete pathologic response in the breast and lymph nodes. Twelve lymph nodes were removed; one of 12 nodes showed treatment effect.

[ imaging findings ]: Primary tumor size was reported as less than 2 cm on imaging, consistent with T1 disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRCA1 mutation positive.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Received neoadjuvant weekly paclitaxel plus carboplatin for 12 cycles, followed by doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide. Subsequently underwent bilateral nipple-sparing mastectomies with axillary nodal evaluation. Surgical pathology demonstrated complete pathologic response in breast and nodes.

[ current disease status ]: No residual invasive disease identified in the breast or sampled lymph nodes after neoadjuvant therapy and surgery.

[ other clinical data ]: Past medical history included hypertension requiring two medications. Family history was significant for heart disease. Ovaries remained intact.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 32-year-old woman. Member of the Air Force.

[ chief complaint ]: Palpable right thyroid nodule measuring approximately 3 cm.

[ diagnosis ]:  
- Right thyroid Hurthle cell neoplasm on fine-needle aspiration, with Afirma gene expression classifier result reported as suspicious.  
- Status post thyroid lobectomy.  
- Final surgical pathology demonstrated a benign 3.5 cm Hurthle cell neoplasm without capsular or vascular invasion.  
- Incidental 1.3 cm follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma in the same lobe.  
- Pathologic stage described as T1b, presumed N0, Mx.  
- One sampled lymph node was negative for malignancy.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- Fine-needle aspiration cytology: suspicious for Hurthle cell neoplasm.  
- Intraoperative frozen section: follicular lesion with Hurthle cell features.  
- Final pathology of dominant nodule: benign 3.5 cm well-encapsulated Hurthle cell neoplasm; no capsular invasion; no vascular invasion.  
- Separate nodule: 1.3 cm follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma.  
- Surgical margins were microscopically positive for the papillary carcinoma.  
- Multifocal disease within the involved lobe was described, including foci measuring 1.3 cm, 2 mm, and 3 mm.  
- One lymph node removed with the lobectomy specimen was negative for carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a well-defined, well-circumscribed complex thyroid nodule with cystic and solid components, without evident microcalcifications.  
- Neck ultrasound was negative for abnormal cervical lymphadenopathy.  
- An additional ipsilateral thyroid nodule measuring just over 1 cm was identified in the same lobe and was characterized as nonspecific/indeterminate.  
- The second nodule was later reported pathologically as 1.3 cm.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]:  
- Afirma gene expression classifier on the indeterminate thyroid nodule: suspicious.  
- Subsequent testing of the papillary thyroid carcinoma demonstrated BRAF V600E mutation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]:  
- Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy was performed and was suspicious for Hurthle cell neoplasm.  
- Thyroid lobectomy was performed.  
- Lobectomy pathology showed benign Hurthle cell neoplasm as the dominant lesion and incidental follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma in a separate nodule.  
- No metastatic carcinoma was identified in the single sampled lymph node.

[ current disease status ]:  
- Status post lobectomy with incidental multifocal follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma identified in the resected lobe.  
- Microscopic positive surgical margins were present.  
- No radiographic cervical nodal disease was identified preoperatively.  
- No nodal metastasis was identified in the single sampled lymph node.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Preoperative TSH was normal.  
- A low-TSH/hyperfunctioning nodule scenario did not apply in this case.

So from a surgical perspective, what comes next? Are you ready to take this thing out? And if so, what are you going to take out? So let's just take it from the far end to the close end, and we'll just address these questions. Dr. Farris.

So the positive predictive value of the AFIRMA suspicious was actually not that high. The main value of the AFIRMA test is its negative predictive value. So in a sense, the test here didn't help so much because you have a cytologic diagnosis, which is indeterminate, has a risk of 20 to 30% malignancy, and I'd say most practices would lead to a lobectomy. in the absence of other clinical or features such as hypothyroidism or contralateral nodules and so on, family history of thyroid cancer, radiation, and so on. So in this setting, without any of those adjunctive reasons for more than a lobectomy, this patient, if presented to me, we wouldn't get the AFIRMA test. I can tell you about the Pittsburgh test. With the Afirma test, I would say we're still back at the same lobectomy that the cytologic diagnosis would have indicated.
Okay. And any disagreement on the panel to a lobectomy as the next step in this patient's evaluation?

I don't disagree. I agree completely except that when I get a herthal cell dominant type of FNA, I think it's helpful to get a thyroid peroxidase antibody. And this snippet of ultrasound that you showed us did not look like a patient with Hashimoto's thyroiditis, but I think that sometimes there are patients with thyroiditis and that can lead to an interpretation on cytology of herthal cells when it really isn't a neoplasm.

Right, and I think that the presence of underlying autoimmune thyroid disease is a confounder in cytopathology, because Herthal cells are very common in that setting. And in that setting, the likelihood of malignancy may not be as high as the 30% we were mentioning earlier. It may actually be somewhat lower, simply because there are Herthal cells in the nodule. But nonetheless, cytopathology and molecular markers probably are not going to be enough to avoid a surgery. Just to clear the air and be sure, is there anybody here who would prefer to do a total thyroidectomy for this patient with a 3-centimeter and a 1.1-centimeter indeterminate right thyroid nodule. I'll take that as a no. We have consensus. Surgical consensus.
I would just like to know if anybody's ever seen a hurtful cell carcinoma in a 30-year-old woman.

That's a good question. Has anybody in the audience seen a hurtful cell cancer in a 30-year-old woman? I think she was 32, actually. Oh, sorry, 32. Yeah, it happens. It's uncommon, but it can rarely happen. a small smattering of such tumors myself. So she had a lobectomy, and frozen section said follicular lesion with hurtful cell features. So frozen section, useful in your practice or not useful in your practice for these hurtful cell lesions?
I almost never freeze thyroid nodules.
OK, Dr. Shah at Memorial.

I think for whatever action you take in surgery, you must have a good reason why you are doing it. If the frozen section is going to change the course of the operation, then you should do it. If the frozen section report is not going to alter your decision, then that's an unnecessary expense, an exhibition of your ignorance about the need for the test. I'm sorry, but I'm a bit harsh, but that's true. Because frozen sections are being sent knowing that this is a follicular lesion, knowing that the pathologist is not going to tell you whether this is low-grade follicular carcinoma or an adenoma. So what are you looking for on frozen section? Now, if you argue that I'm looking for medullary carcinoma, I would say do it. But then you don't need frozen section. You should have done the blood test before the operation.

So often these days, the pathologists are doing touch preps, which are useful in the diagnosis of follicular variant papillary in some cases. So that might be one reason to do an immediate assessment. Frozen section itself, outside of Mayo Clinic, seems to have a very poor reputation. And the primary reason for doing frozen section at Mayo, I think, is just because that's what we do with everything that comes out of the body at Mayo. Everybody gets a frozen section on everything. Our use of it at Moffitt is rather more selective, as I think you're suggesting. Final pathology confirmed a benign three and a half centimeter hurtful cell neoplasm, but no signs of capsular or vascular invasion, well encapsulated benign nodule. But you may remember there was a 1.1 centimeter second nodule, and it turned out to be a 1.3 centimeter follicular variant papillary thyroid cancer. So now we've got an incidental discovery of this T1B, presumed N0 because the preoperative ultrasound was negative, M unknown, follicular variant papillary cancer in a 32-year-old woman. So how would you move forward? Who on the panel, just a show of hands, who would do completion thyroidectomy?

I think that it's one of those discussions that is taking up more and more time in our clinics, this kind of case. I think if this patient isn't aware of the options, they very well may find another surgeon who tells them that you didn't offer that. And so I think it takes a lengthy discussion explaining the advantages and disadvantages of a completion thyroidectomy. And there are disadvantages. It's not a benign procedure and it's not clear that you can demonstrate any benefit from it.

So educate me, because I'm not a surgeon. You've done a lobectomy. You've entered the ipsilateral compartment of this tumor that was discovered to be a follicular variant papillary. Presumably, the contralateral compartment is a virgin compartment. You already know that the nerve is intact from the first side, presumably. Now, you already know the status of the parathyroids on the first side, so isn't a completion thyroidectomy actually safer than a de novo total thyroidectomy, where you wouldn't know the status of each nerve and you wouldn't know necessarily the status of the parathyroids until you've done it?

Simply, you didn't mention in the pathology, but simply because they don't appear on the pathology report does not mean that they're well vascularized. That would be the first point. The second is that there is scar tissue in the central pre-tracheal area prior to encountering the so-called virgin area you pointed out. Nonetheless, it's a procedure the patient may not need. I think that's the major risk of it, not in comparison to the upfront lobectomy. But can you demonstrate any benefit to the patient? And you can from the standpoint of the ability to use an annual thyroglobulin and so on. You know, you certainly will clarify for this patient the disease status of the contralateral lobe.

So this young woman is a member of the Air Force. We have a big naval and Air Force base in Tampa. And she's a member of the Air Force, and she is used to taking orders. And the first thing she says when she's asked the question about the completion is, I will do whatever you say, sir. What would you recommend to her?

I think as part of the discussion, one information that will be critical, because if you decide not to do the completion thyroidectomy, you're also leaning towards doing something instead of that, which would be the RAI ablation, presumably. Then the question to ask is, given that it's a young lady, we don't know what the family status is, what her wishes are for pregnancy down the line. While it is not absolute that patient treated with RAI would become amenorrheic, there is some considerable risk that that could happen. And I think that should come into the discussion as to what the optimal option would be for these patients.

We don't have a real endocrinologist on the panel, so I'm going to act as the panelist endocrinologist if that's okay. And I would say most of us would say that radioactive iodine is a poor substitute for surgery for completion thyroidectomy. requiring often multiple doses to ablate that remnant, and often with an incomplete ablation at the end of the day, requiring cumulatively large doses. So if I'm the endocrinologist seeing this patient, and I think she needs a completion, she's coming back to you. I'm not going to be doing that completion using RAI.

But you do bring up an important point. The first, as you said, being that I would not treat with RAI in the absence of an attempted total thyroidectomy. or completion in this case, but an important point to this case is to have a relationship with your endocrinologist that you know what they're going to be telling the patient with this diagnosis so that you present a united message and not confuse the patient.
Right. So anybody on the panel who's coming down hard towards a completion thyroidectomy given that the patient is neutral on this?

I would just like to back up to the prior discussion about frozen section as well as the, I would take issue with the staging of this lesion as a T1N0 if there were no nodes sampled at the time of the prior surgery. When I went in to operate on this woman for a hurtful cell lesion, I didn't want to have to go back into that compartment at a later date, so I would have sampled lymph nodes if I could find any, and that would have given me information on both the hurtful cell and the possible existence of metastatic papillary carcinoma at the time. So I would have liked to know what the actual pathologic nodal status of the original thyroid lobectomy side was.
So there was one node that came out with that lobe and it was node negative for cancer.

And that sort of points out the shortcomings of our staging system that with one single node you have a pathologic stage N0 which may not be reflective of the rest of the nodes in the area. But if, as the surgeon in that original case, you had at least inspected that ipsilateral side and confirmed that there were no other prominent lymph nodes, then I think that that's at least more supportive of this being a case of papillary carcinoma that's not metastatic to the highest risk area, which is the ipsilateral central net.

So we're going to talk a little bit more about central neck node management in the next case. So we'll skip on there. Anybody here on the panel willing to say this patient does not need the completion? She had a 1.3 centimeters. She's T1. She's a young patient. She's going to live forever. Why on earth are we going to go ahead and take out that other lobe? Dr. Shah, I know I can call on you to be a minimalist.

You know, there is a saying in medicine which is called primum non nocere, do no harm to the patient. This patient is cured, and you can't cure her more than 100%. Whether you do total thyroidectomy, you do total thyroidectomy and give radioactive iodine, you do elective central compartment dissection or elective lateral neck dissection, it's not going to improve the longevity of this patient. So doing more, you have to convince me that completion thyroidectomy, completion thyroidectomy in radioactive iodine, or elective node dissection has any statistical data supporting your recommendation. If you do not have statistics to support your contention, then I think we are talking about personal biases which should not apply into a forum like this.
But Dr. Shah, when did you ever see any statistics in thyroid cancer that were meaningful?

There's plenty of statistics. And there are very few meaningful statistics. And you will never find a prospective randomized trial because the biology of the disease is such that all of us will be long gone before you report a 20 or a 30 year survivorship and recurrence-free survivorship in a 32-year-old woman.
So would you treat her with thyroid hormone suppressive therapy with that?

That is a very provocative question. Does this woman need to be suppressed? Mind you, she's 32, and she's going to live at least another 60 years of her life. She will get older, and she will get osteoporotic. And do you want to precipitate her osteoporosis by keeping her TSH down to zero? And there are some enthusiasts to keep the TSH to zero. So I think I would get a baseline TSH perhaps two months out. I'm in no rush to put the patient on suppression the week after thyroidectomy. I'm not aware of any data which says that if you don't suppress within one week of thyroidectomy, the patient will die. No such thing exists. And if you do immediate post-op TSH, it's going to be elevated. You just took out a part of the thyroid gland. It takes that information some time to get to the brain to affect on TSH. So two months out, I'll do TSH. If the TSH is elevated or on the high range of normal, I may think about suppression. If it is one or around, I will not put her on thyroid suppression.
So are you going to treat her just to normalize her TSH or will you suppress her if you treat her with thyroid hormone?

Well, I think that is a question which is debatable. Again, there is no data to show that suppression of TSH to 1, 0.9, 0.05, or 0.04 has any statistical validity that higher suppression means better patient care or better survivorship.

All right, so we're going to take a vote from the panel first. Who on the panel then is going to be comfortable with a lobectomy alone? OK. And let's just take a brief poll from the audience. Is there anybody in the audience who feels strongly that this patient really should have the total thyroidectomy, the completion thyroidectomy? So we've got a few people who really do feel, maybe a dozen or 20 people who really feel that thyroidectomy is necessary. How about a show of hands who would say a lobectomy is sufficient? The majority of the audience would say lobectomy. I can tell you that amongst an endocrinology audience, this case would raise probably 95% of people's hands saying, let's get rid of that other half. Because otherwise, how do I monitor this patient into the future? So let's take this minimalist audience and ask the question, would it matter to you if those surgical margins were microscopically positive?
This is one of those that she would then be a T3. And that would put her in a category where she's a candidate for RAI.

If I can interrupt a second, it wouldn't necessarily make her T3. Only surgical margins are positive. You're assuming that the entire thyroid has been removed. So you could have a T1 that has positive surgical margins.

It would be hard to envision that, but usually those two go together. But that would raise my concern for whether this patient needs adjuvant RAI, at which point the completion thyroidectomy would be part of that package.
Okay, and the rest of the panel, any still want to stick with the lobectomy alone? Dr. Shah, justifying.

OK, so I think the most important part of this patient's care is educating the patient about the biology of her cancer. Needless to say, this patient will go and seek many consultations. She will get confused with a diversity of opinions. And then she'll come back to you that Dr. Ferris says thyroidectomy and radioiodine. Dr. Orloff says thyroidectomy and elective Guys, don't take it personally. Elective node dissection and what have you. So I think your first or second post-operative visit is going to be the longest one. Because you are now telling the patient that this cancer is symbiotic with you. Presence of microscopic cancer doesn't mean anything. I can prove microscopic cancer even in your lateral neck node. If I do elective neck dissection of the whole neck, there's a 50% probability that you will have myocardial metastasis. And all of this means very little. And it takes time for the patient to understand the biology of this disease. But once they do, they're in sync with you. This patient will be coming to see you once a year for the rest of her and your life, and your discussion at that time will be mostly social, how her family is doing.
So you're going to leave this residual cancer in the neck. Are the other panelists happy with that approach?

First of all, at the time of surgery, you should have put your cross clamp away from the nodule so that you don't get this scenario. But assuming that this was done elsewhere, then you need to go back to pathology. and help pull out the specimen, how microscopically positive it is. If there is gross transaction through tumor, and the cut margin shows the tumor throughout up and down, then I will take her back to the operating room. If I see a focal microscopic area of papillary carcinoma, that's fine. I'm not worried about it.
Focal microscopic. Rest of the panel happy to leave it behind, or do people want to be a bit more aggressive?

I think if you go by the HCA guideline, This patient will fall, going back to what Dr. Farris was alluding to, assuming that this is true extra thyroid extension, but not just positive surgical margin. You're now talking of someone in intermediate to high-risk category. But if you're only saying that this is microscopically positive, we don't know how he got there, and it may not be that you actually left tumor behind, then you have a lot of discussion to hold with the patient. And that would actually be a patient where you are thinking may be following the guideline of low normal TSH suppression. And Dr. Shah would not.
But isn't it the case that your endocrinologist with whom you work closely is going to freak out if you don't do something more?

That's exactly what I'm saying, that the endocrinologist in this instance would not be comfortable saying, we're not going to do anything. You're fine. And I think the multidisciplinary approach will actually help the patient to reach the most appropriate decision going forward.

Well, not only were her surgical margins microscopically positive, but she also has a BRAF V600E mutation, which we didn't know about ahead of time, but it was tested on the sample subsequently. Dr. Ferris, you're still leaving that cancer behind?

I'm just, my heart sunk. Because we could have packaged up this patient's entire surgical therapy with her upfront total thyroidectomy with the Nikki Forov panel We would have not had any frozen section. We would have saved the health care system.
But remember that we didn't biopsy the cancer. We biopsied the benign nodule. So we would have been no further ahead. Oh, you're right about that.

Fair enough. Well, I do think there's a question as to whether on the histopathology there's any value for doing molecular testing. I think there's a real stretch besides curiosity and research. But doing it after the fact, given Particularly, I think, is the point of this bullet point is to raise the question about the prognostic value of this common mutation, which is, I'd say, relatively controversial at present, particularly in the absence of other histopathologic features, which we already know have prognostic variables.
So how about in Kobe, Japan? Would we be following the same path, or would we have a different strategy in Japan?

So in this case, T1N0, M0, so I recommend Lobectomy. So this is surgical margin positive, mean external thyroid extension. But microscopically positive. So the prognosis is not changed. So I observe alone.

You would observe alone and not complete the thyroidectomy or treat with radioactive iodine. So you would fit very much into Dr. Shah's approach. All right. What happens if it's multifocal? Dr. Orloff.
Lisa, he's trying to corner you into completion.

It's getting tougher here. I would agree with the other panelists about the BRAF mutation itself. We did a study. I'm currently located at Stanford University, but while I was at UCSF, we did a review of our BRAF positive histology and agree with Bob's comment that It was present in the majority of our papillary carcinomas in the range of 80 plus percent of the cases and really did not have a direct correlation with more aggressive behavior. The additional foci does raise the question of if there are these microscopic foci that you saw, are there additional microscopic foci that you didn't see? And I have tended to rely on the three rule of three microscopic foci as a... Well, she has three because there's a 1.3 centimeter, a two, and a three millimeter.
Exactly.

So she would qualify as having three foci in this lobe, and therefore, and I'm sorry I can't recall the study that cited numbers of foci of microscopic disease, but the rule of thumb that I followed is three or more foci of disease is more predictive of diffuse disease in the other lobe.

So we looked at this at Mayo. I say we, it's really Ian Hay who looked at this at Mayo and demonstrated that multifocality predicts more than anything else the involvement of central compartment lymph nodes. And of course, central compartment lymph nodes then predict a higher risk for future recurrence of the disease, but didn't really impact on the long-term survival of these patients, which remains, of course, for normal life expectancy. But I think each of these adverse impacts, including the finding of lymphovascular invasion on pathology, arguably raises the risk of this patient, and I think pushes us more and more towards a completion. But I think this case, more than anything, illustrates why it's fascinating to be in a department of head and neck and endocrine oncology, as I am, because the challenge with thyroid cancer is not that the disease is so aggressive and nasty as it is with most of the head and neck squames. but rather that it is so benign and innocuous, and you have to make these terribly tough decisions about how aggressive to make the treatment. And so we're balancing the risk and the benefit of surgery against the risk of the disease. So I find thyroid fascinating, as I say. So let's talk about a second case, then. A 46-year-old woman. It's an incidentally discovered three centimeter nodule, so very similar to the last case, just a little older. No radiation history, no family history for thyroid cancer, no abnormalities of thyroid function. There's the nodule on the ultrasound.

reference_conclusion: Initial evaluation should include a dedicated thyroid ultrasound performed by an experienced thyroid ultrasonographer, comprehensive history and physical examination with palpation of the entire neck, serum TSH testing, and pre-decision laryngoscopy. Given the 3 cm thyroid nodule with normal TSH, ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration is indicated. After cytology suspicious for Hürthle cell neoplasm and a suspicious Afirma result, the agreed next surgical step is thyroid lobectomy rather than total thyroidectomy. Following incidental identification of a 1.3 cm follicular variant papillary thyroid carcinoma after lobectomy, the consensus favored observation with lobectomy alone, with completion thyroidectomy not routinely recommended.
reference_conclusion_quote: I would always want to have an ultrasound, and even one with one from the outside would repeat one by an experienced thyroid ultrasonographer [...] Ordering blood tests, part of the physical exam should always include a pre-decision making laryngoscopy, as well as palpation of the entire neck. [...] So I try biopsy and fine needle biopsy and US guide. [...] I'd say most practices would lead to a lobectomy. [...] we're still back at the same lobectomy that the cytologic diagnosis would have indicated. [...] We have consensus. Surgical consensus. [...] Who on the panel then is going to be comfortable with a lobectomy alone? OK. [...] The majority of the audience would say lobectomy. [...] So in this case, T1N0, M0, so I recommend Lobectomy. So this is surgical margin positive, mean external thyroid extension. But microscopically positive. So the prognosis is not changed. So I observe alone.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 46-year-old woman.

[ chief complaint ]: Thyroid nodule.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe.

[ histopathology results ]: Fine-needle aspiration/biopsy of the thyroid nodule was classified as Bethesda VI, diagnostic of thyroid cancer with papillary features. Cytologic features included nuclear clearing, prominent nucleoli, irregular nuclear contours, and nuclear grooves.

[ imaging findings ]: Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a right-sided solid nodule measuring 3.2 cm in longitudinal dimension and 2.0 x 1.5 cm in the other recorded dimensions. The nodule was heterogeneous, contained hypoechoic areas, and demonstrated internal blood flow. It was described as somewhat suspicious. Preoperative ultrasound of the neck showed no involved lateral cervical lymph nodes. The lesion abutted the thyroid capsule laterally and approached the trachea.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BRAF positive.

[ laboratory results ]: TSH 1.2.

[ current disease status ]: Biopsy-proven papillary thyroid carcinoma of the right thyroid lobe, at least 3.2 cm in size, abutting the thyroid capsule and approaching the trachea. No lateral neck nodal involvement had been identified on preoperative ultrasound. Distant metastatic status was not documented.
