reference_discussion.text: Can I ask what her TSH was?
TSH was 1.2. Thank you. So there is the nodule, Dr. Ferris.

This one looks a little more irregular, looks more worrisome, certainly less well-circumscribed. It's a little hard to tell from the projection whether those are cystic low-density areas or just poor projection, but certainly looks like a solid nodule.

And on ultrasound real time, it was definitely a solid nodule, but with those hypoechoic areas within it, somewhat heterogeneous. Blood flow pattern? So it contains blood flow. And so it was felt to be at least a somewhat suspicious nodule. That's the biopsy material. I don't think you can see it all that well, but there's nuclear clearing and prominent nucleoli and some irregularity in the shape of the nuclei. Nuclear grooves are present as well. And so this was classified as Bethesda 6 diagnostic for thyroid cancer with papillary features, so papillary thyroid cancer. So, ultrasound scan was done preoperatively, no lateral nodes were noted to be involved at the time. On then to management of the central neck in this case, clearly we're going to do a thyroidectomy. I suppose I should ask first, is anybody on the panel going to do a lobectomy?
Sure, why not?
Good, I'm glad.

No, no, what is it in this patient that makes her a candidate for total thyroidectomy. Unless you tell me she has gross extra thyroid extension, which matters. Unless you tell me this is poorly differentiated histology, that matters. Or unless you tell me that the tumor has invasion of central compartment viscera. Her age of 46 does not put her into the high-risk category. And I think, if you give me a moment, I want to address the myth of 45-year-age cutoff.
That's why I made her 46.

Because there is nothing that happens on your 45th birthday that makes you high risk. So we have carefully looked at this and validated that from data from our institution, from Toronto, from MD Anderson, from Brazil, and from Australia. So there is a validation by five different institutions. using recursive partitioning curves, ROC curves, to see where does the line for worsening of prognosis for recurrence and death due to cancer fall. That's not 45. That line actually drops at 56, and the recommendation to the AJCC-UICC staging committee in the coming year is going to shift the age cutoff line from 45 to 55. By doing that, we would be moving 17% of thyroid patients who get unnecessarily aggressive treatment because they just happen to be 46.

So let me challenge you just a little because here's a patient she's got. Although these two dimensions are 2 and 1.5 centimeters in longitudinal dimension, It's 3.2 centimeters. So this is going to be at least a T2 tumor. A large papillary of classic subtype is going to have lymph nodes involved in the central compartment in more than 60 to 70 percent of cases. So she's going to be a node positive T2, N1A at least, M unknown, papillary cancer when you have resected this. And that is going to give her a stage probably three designation at a minimum. So now we're talking about a stage three cancer in this woman, and you're only going to do a lobectomy. Let's take a poll of the audience and tell me.

Wait, wait, wait, before you take the poll. You exactly enumerated the problem of the staging system. Because thyroid cancer is not like a pregnancy test. There are many gradations of thyroid cancer. So this patient will go to the operating room at my institution with the following consent, right thyroid lobectomy, possible total thyroidectomy, possible central compartment dissection. Because those decisions are made intraoperatively. If she has no enlarged lymph nodes identified at the time of surgery, if she has no gross extra thyroid extension demonstrated at the time of surgery, there is no data that doing more than a lobectomy makes any difference.

So let us then say you're going to do a lobectomy at this end of the table, a total thyroidectomy at the other end of the table, but both of you would agree, I think, the central neck is very important. Dr. Shah, you would presumably do something in this ipsilateral central neck. Dr. Ferris, I'm assuming you would do something in the bilateral central neck. What something would you do? We'll explore the central nodule. Hold on. Dr. Farris answer.

I don't think there's an indication for a bilateral central compartment dissection in this case, unless you told me that the nodule was straight in the middle in the isthmus, for instance. But other than that, I think a ipsilateral central compartment staging procedure is reasonable.

So how are you going to stage it? Are you going to ignore it, inspect it, dissect it, reset it? What exactly are you going to do surgically? Again, remind me, remember I'm an endocrinologist here, I think in simplistic terms.
So if you're asking what is removed, are you saying whether to make the decision to do so or not?
Well, what I'm saying is you're going in to operate on this woman's thyroid. I presume you're going to do a removal of the thyroid and you will at least look into the central neck.
Sure.
And I think identify the nerve and those kind of things.

Dr. Shah makes the point that we always inspect the central neck nodes. And that would be one situation where a frozen section could be valuable if there was something concerning or if there are features with regard to the gland itself, that lobe that looked worrisome and it looked more aggressive than the ultrasound suggested. But I think in this case, I would say I would be leaning toward it. Leaning towards? Doing a central peritracheal dissection on that side.
So can you describe what you mean by a peritracheal dissection? What do you actually take out?
Skeletonizing the nerve, removing the peritracheal, pretracheal, and paralaryngeal lymph nodes.
And Dr. Orloff, is that what would happen in California?

I wouldn't be satisfied. I have to put in a plug for a dynamic ultrasound, because that ultrasound picture you showed us has other worrisome features. The tumor at least abuts the capsule laterally in the thyroid. It approaches the trachea immediately. I think you would see lymph nodes in the central compartment, in spite of what you read and hear about ultrasound being poor in the presence of the thyroid gland for the central neck. most often see macroscopic nodes in the central neck if you look for them. And so I think you would have a better sense preoperatively of whether there were bilateral or ipsilateral central nodes if you did a more, or you had a dynamic ultrasound to review. So depending on what that showed, I think I would most likely do at least an ipsilateral central neck along the lines of what Dr. Farris described, but possibly bilateral if there were nodes on ultrasound bilaterally.
So you would want to remove the node-bearing tissue, or you would pluck out the nodes?
No. Plucking is not in my vocabulary.
All right. And Dr. Shah, I presume you would say the same thing. If there were visible nodes, you would do something about them.
Visible or palpable, yes.
OK. What about this idea of a distinction between central compartment dissection and central compartment resection, which in ICD-10 are going to be two different codes? What's the difference?
Semantics.
Semantics, nothing other? So you do the same procedure? for those two codes? What do you code it as?

I think, you know, Brian, we need to clarify what does a central compartment lymph node dissection mean. And I would like to have the surgeons on the panel define when they do a central compartment dissection, what do they actually do?
So there's the challenge to the surgeons, please.

Well, in this setting where you're doing it at the time of the total thyroidectomy, the nerve is skeletonized. If we're not going to do it, there's a large portion of the nerve that's not usually exposed and dissected. In a case where you're doing a comprehensive ipsilateral dissection, then the nerve is going to be skeletonized so that the lymph node packet, lateral, medial, to the nerve as well as A pre-tracheal, the central portion of the pre-laryngeal and pre-tracheal nodes are also dissected. They're not always kept in continuity, just given their orientation. But it's a comprehensive dissection where the nerve is dissected in its entirety down to the level of the innominate artery from the cricoid insertion point.
And that sounds like a definition that I'm comfortable with.

So this lesion was on the right side, and I think it bears mentioning that the recurrent laryngeal nerve on the right divides the central compartment in a way different from the left, and that there's a substantial nodal packet posterior deep to the recurrent nerve on the right side. So it doesn't disagree with what Bob just described, but there is a larger volume of nodal disease posterior and lateral to the nerve. I think otherwise, you know, it's the management of the parathyroids is the real challenge in these central compartments. And so, to some extent, depends on where those parathyroids were and how their blood supply was oriented at the time of the thyroidectomy. I typically would do the thyroidectomy first and do the central compartment dissection after removing the thyroid. So, it's, there's some variation to it.

So one of the reasons that I bring this case up again is to emphasize the difference in mindset between surgeons and endocrinologists, because we tend to think as endocrinologists very simplistically, that you either operate and dissect those compartments in the central area, or you ignore them altogether. And I think the subtleties are often lost on us. And I think it's those subtleties that lead to some of these very heated debates about how we should actually manage the central neck. When you really sit down with at least the surgeons at Moffitt and you talk through exactly what they do, just as you described, it's actually exactly the same at Moffitt as at Mayo and I suspect as it is at Memorial. These terms that we use are used loosely and don't really describe what the surgeons truly do. So I would make a plea for clearer language and you know, clarity of communication back to the endocrinologists who get upset with you if you don't do something in the central neck. Would it change your management of central neck if it was BRAF positive? We've kind of answered that question before, but does everybody agree that it shouldn't change your management? Anybody in the audience disagree with that? Do you think BRAF is really important in managing the central neck? One hand, one hand.

Please, use. First question is for everybody's central neck in a second. Where is the fascial plane that divides the right and left central neck? I've never understood that. How do you know how far to go over on the other neck to know that you're staying on one side? That's one question. The other question is, do you guys have any pearls on how to preserve the parathyroids when you're taking all the soft tissue out with all the nodes that look like parathyroids?
Sounds like a question for the surgical team.

Well, I don't do elective dissections because I have not been convinced it has any benefit to the patient. And I was going to ask Lisa and Bob both, what do your patients benefit? And how many of them benefit out of the 100 you do? So maybe think about the response to that. Superior parathyroid is easier to preserve because it is tucked away from the lymph node bearing area. And a proper central compartment lymph node dissection means clearance of all lymph nodes from hyoid to innominate and from carotid to carotid. I bet my boots 80 out of 100 surgeons doing elective central compartment dissections don't do that and challenge me on that one.
But what about that definition of left versus right central compartment? Where is the dividing line?

Well, I think it's an arbitrary midline. You clear pre-tracheal lymph nodes up to the lateral aspect of the lower pole of the contralateral lobe. Is that about correct? So you clear pre-tracheal lymph nodes up to the lower pore of the contralateral lobe. But it's an arbitrary line. There is no finite division. Keep also in mind that there is crisscross lymphatic drainage also. Inject dye in one lobe of thyroid and you will harvest it from the contralateral paratracheal area. So it is not strictly unilateral. So Gary has his hand up. Gary, use the microphone. Thank you.

So there is going to be a VA cooperative trial that's going to be looking at elective dissection. This VA cooperative trial is not powered to look at recurrence. It's powered to look at morbidity of the surgery. They define the neck dissection as stopping at the contralateral thymus. I think that was as arbitrary as anything else. There is no fascial plane there. Actually, when you showed that one ultrasound, there's a posterior carotid lymph node there that's more than one centimeter in size. Would not be removed in a standard central compartment dissection, just as you know.

So not only were lymph nodes in the central compartment involved, this tumor was also BRAF positive, but also when the surgeon went in, it was clinically adherent or invasive into the trachea. So this is where head and neck surgeons excel, is doing stuff to the viscera of the neck. So what is the appropriate management of tracheal adherence versus invasion? Anyone who wants to volunteer, please.

Well, I can tell you what it sounds like would happen in my practice is if this were discovered intraoperatively, then attempts would be made to obtain a negative margin on the cartilage to the extent that even a ring could potentially be shaved. But this is where frozen section would be useful. I think in the absence of having a thorough discussion and a plan, I would not be more extensive than that at this stage.

So you would not propose to reset part of the trachea or do anything more aggressive with this disease? You would just shave it down to a negative surgical margin? How far will you shave it? Right into the lumen?
Well, that is occasionally what happens and requires buttressing that and supporting that with strap muscle or some other maneuvers, but hopefully avoidance.
And the rest of the panelists agree with that approach?

We haven't really talked about imaging, preoperative imaging, but I think the best management of tracheal invasion is to anticipate it and really be thinking about it before you get to the operating room. So if you have any suspicion of its presence, getting cross-sectional imaging is appropriate preoperatively. And performing bronchoscopy at the time of intubation to assess for intraluminal disease is also very valuable. difficult once you've already resected the thyroid and haven't really assessed the depth of invasion from the inside out or cross-sectional.

Which raises a crucially important question. When should we be doing cross-sectional imaging in the preoperative neck? And should we be doing it with CAT scan or MRI or some other imaging? And should we, if we're using CAT scan, do it with contrast material? So let's have a little discussion about that.

So if you're going to do a CAT scan, don't waste your time and money doing a non-contrast CAT scan. It's totally useless. And giving contrast dye and getting better imaging to give you better assessment of the central compartment viscera and the tumor is the crucial part. No inadequate operation is going to be patched off by RAI. So only administration of contrast to do a CAT scan implies that your radioiodine administration would be delayed by a few weeks, maybe two months even. I'm not aware of any patient ever even reported as a case report who has died because of delay in RAI administration by two months.

And as an endocrinologist, I would support your view on that 100%. You know, it doesn't take that long for the iodine load to be washed out. typically would check urinary iodine excretion rates to confirm that the iodine load is gone and then move ahead with RAI if that's indicated. But how about...

So Brian, you indicated adherence versus invasion. Yes. Adherence to me implies that you can peel the tumor off the trachea. Invasion to me implies you need to investigate more by imaging, by endoscopy, and be prepared for visceral resection.
So I agree with that, but then the question is, who should be submitted to cross-sectional imaging preoperatively? Is this something we do to every patient or not?
Go back to your ultrasound. Can you show the imaging back?
OK.

So if you see here, you do not see any intraluminal tumor. But you do have concern about the irregularity of the tracheal wall on the right-hand side. I would be inclined to do cross-sectional imaging on this. Keep in mind, you don't have to have intraluminal tumor to have full thickness tracheal wall invasion. The tracheal wall may look smooth. on ultrasound or on cross-sectional imaging, but simple hypervascularity of the mucosa of the trachea and fixation of the tumor to the tracheal wall is tracheal invasion. That tumor you will not be able to peel off. You will actually transact the tumor trying to peel it off. So endoscopic assessment of the trachea to see the area of hypervascularity or telangiectasia is a crucial point which will tell you that the tumor is just next to the trachea or it infiltrates the tracheal wall.
So you would recommend CT with contrast to evaluate this neck preoperatively? Absolutely. Is that the case in Kobe as well? Would you do cross-sectional imaging with contrast material?
Yes, relatively. I checked the CT scan, so contrast.
And in Emory, you would also cross-sectionally image?

Yeah, at times we try to do MRI pre-op, but eventually we end up doing the CT with contrast because you still end up with the same problem of we can't identify the planes, we don't know which one is lymph node and what is blood vessel and things like that.

So again, the question would be to the panel, is this something we should recommend in everybody going through thyroid surgery now, or should we be selective? And if we're going to be selective, what criteria should we use to select a patient for cross-sectional imaging pre-op? Dr. Arsha has suggested, because we're not really seeing the lateral wall of the trachea, medial to this tumor, maybe that's an indication. Should we base it on that? Should we base it on size? How are we going to make this determination? Because once again, I'll point out, ATA guidelines, ACE guidelines, and I think AAES guidelines, none of them call for routine cross-sectional imaging.

So I've been privileged to be part of a writing group from the ATA that is about to publish, and Bob is as well, guidelines on preoperative imaging in thyroid cancer. And most of the focus of this writing project was on nodal disease. and disease that appears to extend beyond the thyroid, not really focusing on characteristics of thyroid nodules within the thyroid. But I think a sort of simple summary is that if you are not confident that you can see everything that might be there to see with ultrasound alone, then cross-sectional imaging is complementary. So it may be the disease that appears to extend beyond your ultrasound limit, and it may be that the patient's body habitus or prior treatment of thyroid-related or unrelated in the neck distorts anatomy such that you just, you can't see completely around the disease, then it's appropriate to do cross-sectional imaging.

So again, I think the message to the endocrinologists would be, you know, be more liberal with your cross-sectional imaging rather than just relying on ultrasound. Sorry, question at the microphone if you will.

I'm Hisham Mahana from Birmingham. I guess what our discussion is saying is that, what Bob alluded to earlier, is that really it's the quality of your ultrasound that's pretty important and that, you know, we often get radiographers and community ultrasound operators doing these regular ultrasounds, and it really has to be somebody who's very experienced at doing ultrasound radiography, or else you get bitten by these, basically.

Absolutely, 100% agree with that. All right, so let's, since we're running remarkably short of time, let's move on to this case, case number three. She's a 28-year-old woman, You can see the problem there in her neck. It's been present for a few months and treated with antibiotics to no benefit. It's felt to be about four and a half centimeters in the right lateral neck, and that was confirmed on ultrasound. Ultrasound otherwise was reported to be negative. There was nothing in the thyroid gland visible. CT scan was otherwise negative, apart from a mass in the right region, too. and a core biopsy was performed elsewhere and was positive for papillary thyroid cancer. So this sounds like it's the old-fashioned lateral aberrant thyroid. Since we're 100 years into the Memorial Sloan Kettering Head and Neck Surgical Service, Dr. Shah, how often do you see lateral aberrant thyroid at Memorial?

reference_conclusion: The agreed operative plan is right thyroid lobectomy with possible conversion to total thyroidectomy and possible central compartment dissection, with final extent determined intraoperatively based on nodal status and gross extrathyroidal extension. In the absence of enlarged lymph nodes or gross extrathyroidal extension at surgery, lobectomy alone is considered appropriate; if central nodal disease is identified, at least an ipsilateral comprehensive central neck dissection/peritracheal dissection should be performed, removing the peritracheal, pretracheal, and paralaryngeal nodal tissue. Given concern for possible tracheal involvement, preoperative cross-sectional neck imaging with contrast-enhanced CT is recommended, with endoscopic assessment as indicated to evaluate for invasion and guide the need for visceral resection planning.
reference_conclusion_quote: So this patient will go to the operating room at my institution with the following consent, right thyroid lobectomy, possible total thyroidectomy, possible central compartment dissection. Because those decisions are made intraoperatively. If she has no enlarged lymph nodes identified at the time of surgery, if she has no gross extra thyroid extension demonstrated at the time of surgery, there is no data that doing more than a lobectomy makes any difference. [...] I don't think there's an indication for a bilateral central compartment dissection in this case, unless you told me that the nodule was straight in the middle in the isthmus, for instance. But other than that, I think a ipsilateral central compartment staging procedure is reasonable. [...] Dr. Shah makes the point that we always inspect the central neck nodes. And that would be one situation where a frozen section could be valuable if there was something concerning or if there are features with regard to the gland itself, that lobe that looked worrisome and it looked more aggressive than the ultrasound suggested. But I think in this case, I would say I would be leaning toward it. Leaning towards? Doing a central peritracheal dissection on that side. [...] Skeletonizing the nerve, removing the peritracheal, pretracheal, and paralaryngeal lymph nodes. [...] So you would recommend CT with contrast to evaluate this neck preoperatively? Absolutely.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female patient. Age was not stated.

[ chief complaint ]: Right lateral neck mass.

[ diagnosis ]: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with occult primary in the thyroid and metastatic right lateral cervical lymph node involvement. Pathologic stage was reported as T1a N1b. Distant metastatic status was not established.

[ histopathology results ]: Thyroid pathology demonstrated a microscopic 3 mm focus of papillary thyroid carcinoma. Nodal pathology demonstrated a single involved lateral neck lymph node. No extranodal extension was identified. No soft tissue invasion was identified.

[ imaging findings ]: Neck ultrasound performed at a cancer center showed an ultrasonographically normal thyroid gland and was otherwise negative apart from a large right lateral neck mass. CT neck with contrast was reviewed and considered adequate quality; it demonstrated a solitary mass in the right high neck. The mass was described as approximately 4.5 cm and consistent with a level II/right high neck node. No chest imaging had been performed.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: TSH was 0.9.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Surgical treatment had been performed, with postoperative pathology showing T1a papillary thyroid carcinoma and N1b nodal disease as above.

[ current disease status ]: Postoperative status following resection of papillary thyroid carcinoma with a microscopic intrathyroidal primary and a single metastatic right lateral cervical lymph node. No extranodal extension or soft tissue invasion was present on pathology. Distant metastatic disease had not been evaluated with chest imaging.

[ other clinical data ]: No family history was reported. No history of radiation exposure was reported.

reference_discussion.text: That's a misnomer, and I think that terminology should be removed from the vocabulary for thyroid surgeons. Literally every patient who was described to have lateral aberrant thyroid was indeed a metastatic papillary carcinoma completely replacing the lymph node where the tumor was so well differentiated and there was no lymphoid follicle seen that it looked like normal thyroid tissue. Incidentally, the picture you showed is not the location for lateral labyrinth thyroid. Lateral labyrinth thyroids occur at level four or in the supraclavicular fossa. That's where they were called lateral labyrinth thyroids. Higher up in the neck, they are clearly metastatic thyroid carcinomas. Nevertheless, the terminology lateral aberrant thyroid is equal to well-differentiated carcinoma metastatic lymph node. So in 2014, there is no lateral aberrant thyroid.

So I would agree with that. And I gather, at least my interpretation of that concept of the lateral aberrant thyroid was much more of an incidental observation than a clinically apparent, what's obviously a metastatic node anyway. It was removing lymph nodes and finding benign appearing thyroid tissue in an incidental sort of fashion, as opposed to somebody presenting clinically like this that isn't even the phenotype of a lateral aberrant thyroid.

All right. I think those are fair criticisms of a term that we shouldn't be using anymore anyway, but sometimes it's fun to go back to the old history books. So how should we manage the thyroid gland? How should we manage the lateral neck on that side? And what should we do about the central neck in this case, where the thyroid gland itself is ultrasonographically normal?
Is there any family history or radiation exposure?
No family history, no radiation exposure on her TSH was 0.9.

So this patient would get a ultrasound, both of the central and lateral neck. This is a patient that I will often get both CT, contrasted CT, as well as a good ultrasound, clearly repeating it at my center.

So just to reassure you, the ultrasound was done at a cancer center and was negative apart from this big lateral neck mass. And the CT scan also was reviewed from the outside, was felt to be of adequate quality, so it was not repeated. But the review also suggested a solitary mass in the right high neck.

So, as has been pointed out, she still has quite a good prognosis. She's probably very worried, but she has a big operation in front of her. She needs a total thyroidectomy. In my practice, I would do an ipsilateral central compartment dissection as well as a lateral comprehensive neck dissection, levels two through five.
I would include. So, you would do the transverse incision and turn the corner and go all the way up to the back of the ear?
I would carry a COCR incision laterally in a skin crease that's less obtrusive, if you will.

So tell me about the pros and cons, if you will, of the extended cochlear incision versus a true lateral neck incision running along the lateral border of the sternocleidomastoid or medial border of sternocleidomastoid.

Well, I tend to make for squamous cell carcinomas a hockey stick type incision vertically behind the sternocleidomastoid. It's relatively unobtrusive, but in a patient like this, you can usually get around all of those lymph nodes with a single low incision in a horizontal plane, extending that cochlear incision, even if you extend it posterior to the sternocleidomastoid muscle a bit for more superior exposure. Because that looked like a level two node, at least four and a half centimeter, some portion is going to be up in level two, 2A. I think you're obligated to dissect level 2B on this young woman as well. Of course, you have to be careful with the accessory nerve. That's the major concern. But level five is going to be, I think, of necessity as well. And so extending the COCR more posteriorly gives you access to level 5A and B.

And any other takers for an extended coca incision? Does everybody agree that that's an appropriate incision to reach this level 2 lymph node high in the neck and clear the remainder of compartments 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, at least ipsilateral?
It is not.
Good. Why not?

In 2004, The only incision for any type of neck dissection is a single transverse incision along an appropriate skin crease, regardless of the indication for the neck dissection. All you have to do is extend the length of the incision along the same skin crease, whether it's higher or lower. such that you should not be able to identify the neck incision in that patient standing six feet away, regardless of what neck dissection you have done. Cochlear incision is out of the vocabulary for modern day teaching in head and neck surgery. Double trifurcate incision is out of the vocabulary. And any incision that draws a vertical component in the neck is out of the vocabulary for head and neck surgery.
Out of the vocabulary for head and neck surgery, not only for thyroid surgery.
That is correct.
Those are fighting words, I feel sure. We'll have a squamous panel after this.
Squamous, carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, skin cancer, or thyroid cancer.

I think what you were describing is actually what Dr. Farris does, but maybe calls it a Cochra incision out of maybe tradition. I think another name that's sometimes used is the Addy decision or Addy incision after Joseph Addy. agree that you can access all of those levels of the neck through extension of your thyroidectomy incision. Maybe not calling it a cochlear incision, but designing the level of the incision to be able to adequately access the superior aspects of the central compartment and the thyroid as well as the inferior aspects of the central neck and just being able to extend that laterally.
So where for the hockey stick incision, where does that come in? Is there a role for a hockey stick incision in California?

You know, I think in this case dissecting level one, at least in my practice, is not a component that I spend a lot of time with. I think it's likely to be the area of most difficulty without a vertical portion. So I would say in that situation that it's when you're focused in the aerodigestive tract as opposed to level six and four where most of the lymph nodes metastatic from thyroid cancer are. That, to me, is where I distinguish the need for different incisions. And many more of these patients are young females where a less obtrusive scar is important. You know, it's a disease of morbidity as opposed to mortality, as opposed to squamous cell carcinoma where getting all of the disease out is obviously much more of a mortality issue.

So let me then turn to the audience because, again, I think there's some controversy potentially here. Who amongst the audience agree that the vertical component of an incision, call it what you will, but the thing that runs up behind the ear has gone out of the practice of head and neck surgery? Is there anybody here? So let me rephrase the question. I apologize. Let me make it clear. Is there anybody here who still feels that the vertical component of the incision is a requirement or a desirable attribute of a surgical approach? So we do still have some outstanding people.
What are we talking about? I think you need to rephrase that question for thyroid cancer.

I should make it clear. OK, let's try again. Vertical incision for metastatic thyroid cancer involving lymph nodes. Is there anybody who would still do that vertical incision? Wave your hands if you're raising them. There's a few smattered people, yes. And presumably, this is for ease of access to the upper part of the neck. How about morbidity of the vertical versus the skin crease incision? Is there a difference in morbidity in terms of neurologic function in the neck?
It's not the morbidity, Brian, but it's the aesthetic morbidity.
I count that as morbidity.

The functional morbidity of numbness of the skin is going to be the same. But the aesthetic morbidity of putting a hypertrophic scar in a woman's neck, or a man's neck for that matter, is not called for, because you can essentially do everything, including level 2B and 1A, through a single transverse incision. Bob, try it. Next time you will give me a call after the operation, Jay, you were right, I could do it.

All right, so pathology on this case revealed a T1A. There was a tiny microscopic focus, a three millimeter focus of papillary cancer. N1B, a single lymph node involved. No extra nodal extension, despite the size of that thing. There was not felt to be soft tissue invasion. How about adjuvant therapy? Is this somebody who should receive radioactive iodine? How about anemorrhy?

Yes, so this is a patient now with relatively small primary, but already you have evidence of node involvement. So this would be at least intermediate risk, so would benefit from adjuvant iodine therapy.
You said that very confidently, will benefit the data that supports you?

Well, that is the slippery slope there now to say I will benefit, so let me retrace my step. I will recommend the patient to receive adjuvant therapy for two reasons. One, given the nodal involvement, we know that the risk of recurrence in this patient is going to be higher than if you did not have lymph node involvement. Therefore, you want to closely monitor this patient in a reliable manner. So using iodine therapy at least as, not just as adjuvant, but to allow you to better monitor the patient in terms of thyroglobulin measurement will be of benefit.
So what if the post-operative thyroglobulin is not measurable? Would you still give RAI?
If you post-op thyroglobulin?
Yeah, six weeks after the operation, the thyroglobulin is not measurable, and there are no antibodies.
TG is less than 0.2 negative antibodies.

Well, at least the data out there will suggest that we know that pre-op thyroglobulin doesn't actually tell you what the survival outcome is going to be. The drop in thyroglobulin post-surgery also has not been shown to be a strong predictor of what the outcome is going to be. It may be that you have a tumor that is actually not thyroglobulin secreting. And then the question becomes, what would be the benefit of your iodine therapy in that instance? I guess that would be something that you have to discuss with the patient, that using iodine therapy in this instance is probably not going to help in terms of your monitoring. But I know where you're coming from, saying, show me the data, that adjuvant therapy will actually help with the outcome for this patient. I think there is some data to suggest that, not strong, a lot of it retrospective, showing that when you give I-131 as adjuvant therapy in this instance, it doesn't improve your overall survival, but it may at least reduce the risk of recurrence, which is what most of these patients will suffer from.

So I'll show my stripes at this point and emphasize that I'm a therapeutic minimalist when it comes to the use of radioactive iodine, having spent almost 20 years at Mayo Clinic under the tutelage of Ian Hay. So I come at this from a biased perspective. The data from Mayo, and we look very, very carefully at these patients, the data from Mayo is that node positive or node negative, size of tumor irrespective, so long as the patient was truly stage one and low risk by the prognostic scoring system of MASIS ages or aims, that we were unable to demonstrate any benefit to I131 ablative therapies in these patients. And the two groups had superimposable mortality rates and recurrence rates. And those data we've presented on a number of occasions. Having said that, there are others around the country who strongly disagree with us. It is the source of continuing exciting interactions at various national and international meetings. And of course, moving to Cancer Center as I have in Tampa, I've had to somewhat compromise my principles and acknowledge that most of my colleagues would be very uncomfortable not treating a patient like this with I131. So my bias then is to do it in a way that, if we're going to do it, minimizes the morbidity of the treatment and use low-dose remnant ablation using thyrogen stimulation to avoid hypothyroidism and use low doses of I-131, which are demonstrated to provide equally effective ablation of the thyroid remnant, which is all you're really achieving by doing this I-131. But could I get a comment from the Japanese perspective? Radioactive iodine, I understand, is less commonly used in Japan. Would you take an approach that involved RAI or not?
There is no merit to radioactive iodine, but recurrent and distant metastasis in the future is high, I think. So I recommend radioactive iodine.
You would administer radioactive iodine?
But I will check the thyroid globulin, the level of thyroid globulin. So if it's high, I strongly recommend.

So I think that one very strong argument in favor of some exposure to radioactive iodine in this patient is this search for distant metastatic spread. We've currently classified her as an MX. But we have no chest imaging. We haven't done a CT scan of the chest. It's quite helpful, I think, sometimes to do low-dose RAI and do a post-therapy scan to give yourself that extra level of reassurance that the chest is clear. I haven't found that to be a big issue with the N1B, just one or two lymph nodes. But if you have bulky lymphadenopathy extensively through the neck, I think that's a different beast.
Brian, you have been in the thyroid cancer business long enough. In this setting of this patient, how often have you found distant metastasis by RAI scan?
Never.
So I think we need to clarify that.
I'm trying to be nice.

Is Mike Tuttle in the audience? Michael? No. So our data of RAI mimics or reflects exactly what the Mayo Clinic showed. The administration of RAI post-operatively did not make any difference in local regional recurrence, recurrence pre-survival, or overall survival, whether they were treated or not. So our current philosophy is we do not give radioactive iodine unless the operative findings or the pathology report indicates an aggressive cancer. or the patient who is a low risk has persistently elevated thyroglobulin postoperatively done at about six weeks out, indicating that there may be a small node that we did not clear and that may need RAI treatment.

reference_conclusion: Management consisted of total thyroidectomy with ipsilateral central compartment dissection and a comprehensive lateral neck dissection encompassing levels II through V. Adjuvant radioactive iodine was discussed extensively; the panel noted that it is commonly recommended for nodal disease/intermediate-risk features, but also cited institutional practice to reserve postoperative radioactive iodine for aggressive pathologic findings or persistently elevated postoperative thyroglobulin approximately six weeks after surgery.
reference_conclusion_quote: She needs a total thyroidectomy. In my practice, I would do an ipsilateral central compartment dissection as well as a lateral comprehensive neck dissection, levels two through five. [...] Yes, so this is a patient now with relatively small primary, but already you have evidence of node involvement. So this would be at least intermediate risk, so would benefit from adjuvant iodine therapy. [...] So our current philosophy is we do not give radioactive iodine unless the operative findings or the pathology report indicates an aggressive cancer. or the patient who is a low risk has persistently elevated thyroglobulin postoperatively done at about six weeks out, indicating that there may be a small node that we did not clear and that may need RAI treatment.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 68-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Sudden-onset dysphonia and hoarseness after 3 months of progressive odynophagia, with more recent mild dysphagia.

[ diagnosis ]: Poorly differentiated follicular thyroid carcinoma with locally advanced invasive disease involving the trachea and esophagus. Right vocal cord paralysis was present.

[ histopathology results ]: Initial biopsy showed follicular neoplasm. Subsequent core biopsy of the primary lesion demonstrated poorly differentiated follicular thyroid cancer. Pathology reported no evidence of anaplastic thyroid carcinoma in the sampled core biopsy, although unsampled anaplastic component elsewhere could not be excluded on that specimen.

[ imaging findings ]: Clinical examination identified a large right neck mass with tracheal deviation to the contralateral side. Cross-sectional imaging demonstrated a large thyroid mass with posterior invasion extending toward the prevertebral fascia, tracheal involvement at multiple levels, and probable esophageal invasion. Imaging suggested at least 4 cm length of tracheal wall invasion. PET imaging showed the tumor to be highly FDG-avid. PET staging reportedly showed no distant metastatic disease prior to operative consideration.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic test results were reported.

[ laboratory results ]: No laboratory data were reported.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Laryngoscopy demonstrated right vocal cord paralysis. Bronchoscopy showed through-and-through tracheal invasion with tumor visible within the tracheal lumen; intraluminal tumor measured at least 3 cm. Esophagoscopy demonstrated frank invasion of the esophageal mucosal wall. The patient declined aggressive surgical resection because of anticipated loss of voice and possible loss of swallowing.

[ current disease status ]: Locally advanced invasive poorly differentiated thyroid carcinoma involving the trachea and esophagus, with right vocal cord paralysis. No distant metastatic disease had been identified on staging PET.

[ other clinical data ]: The patient reported several days of mild hemoptysis before bronchoscopy. He had a history of heavy smoking. Examination described a hyperinflated chest and a short, bulky neck. No stridor was present clinically.

reference_discussion.text: And certainly you're singing to the choir because that has always been my perspective as well. But I do find that the art of compromise is an important art to practice, which is why occasionally I will treat some of these folks nowadays with radioactive iodine that I would not have in the past, recognizing that we can do it with negligible risk. I think we need a trial. So we have enough time, I think, to deal with case four, if we're prompt about it. It's a 68-year-old man, sudden onset of dysphonia and hoarseness following three months of progressive discomfort on swallowing, and then more recently, a little dysphagia. He has a large right neck mass palpated in the neck with tracheal deviation to the contralateral side, and laryngoscopy reveals a right vocal cord paralysis. There's no stride or clinically. Imaging, in this case, I presume everyone would want some kind of cross-sectional imaging, CT with contrast. Anybody who wants a PET scan at this early stage? What are we getting out of our imaging? Dr. Orloff, what's the purpose of that CT versus the PET?
Well, your primary goal is to control the local disease, so the imaging is more focused on the surgical decision making and executing adequate surgery. So a PET scan is perhaps premature.
But you know this is a cancer, right? I mean, this is not going to be benign. Good luck getting it approved. You don't have a diagnosis.

Well, that's true. So CT with contrast, I would say that it really varies by institution, but MRI with contrast is also reasonable. I think there's probably a majority of people who favor CT. I personally had a lot of preference for MRI by my neuroradiologist and by just the goal of minimizing radiation exposure, but I think either type of study is appropriate. And it needs to be performed to include the mediastinum as well as the neck. So when you order a CT scan of the neck, you will often have the tumor cut off at the level of the clavicles. I think it's really important to emphasize CT from the skull base to and including the mediastinum. CT scans, I've been taught by my radiology colleagues, when a CT scan of the neck is done with the patient's arms down at their side, whereas a CT scan of the chest is done with their arms up over their head, so it does change the relationship of the anatomy. So, it just helps to know your regional protocol for imaging and to request that the scan go down below the clavicles. But as you're showing here, I mean, you are looking for where this tumor is invading. You already know that there's some invasive component because of the vocal fold paralysis. looking up and down from there to include the relationship with the trachea, the esophagus, the larynx, the retropharynx, and the mediastinum, as well as the great vessels.

So I've picked just one cross-sectional image of this tumor mass, which I think is evident there. You can see this big mass kind of invading posteriorly, heading at least towards the prevertebral fascia. It appears to be involving the trachea at multiple levels, and although we're not seeing a good view of the esophagus there, the read was that we probably had esophageal invasion of this tumor as well. So there was a PET scan done as part of staging for more distant metastases before this patient could be sent to the OR, and I'll explain the background to that in a moment. But you can see that this is very highly PET avid, as you might expect for presumably a poorly differentiated version of thyroid cancer. I would just make one comment about that, and that is that not all large and invasive cancers are necessarily poorly differentiated. And I think it's important to make a distinction between an aggressive cancer, which I believe this one actually is, poorly differentiated, deeply invasive, non-iodine avid, not a very effective thyroglobulin producer, probably. versus cancer that's just been sitting there for a long time and has had a long incubation period to become more locally advanced. I think there's a difference between those two things. But in this case, the time course, the invasion, the loss of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, the size of the tumor, and its invasive characteristics all suggest it's probably poorly differentiated thyroid cancer. A biopsy is performed, which reveals follicular neoplasm. Anybody still want to do Molecular markers on that you PMC. Would you do molecular markers on this follicular neoplasm?

It's a reflexive test for any indeterminate nodules So we would have this automatically and how helpful is that going to be at the cost of how many thousand dollars? You know, it's been analyzed as a cost-effective test since we use it with a high positive predictive value to avoid the lobectomy and second surgery But aren't you gonna have to take this guy to the OR? Yeah, well, this case is not, I mean, the cytology is inaccurate. It's not a follicular neoplasm. So if the cytology hit the appropriate malignant area of the tumor, you know, we would not do a molecular test. So this is one of the quirks where the reflexive test probably does it. On the other hand, it would likely be BRAF positive, and so we would have our diagnosis that we know. I think in this case, you want to make sure that you get excised tissue and not rely on cytologic tissue, honestly, because you want to know what the differentiation status is of this very likely, you know, malignancy.

Well, it's a topic for another day, but I think this business of reflexing tests is one that should be open to some additional discussion. I know it's very popular in the commercial field right now to simply take cytology that's indeterminate and reflex it. But I think, as this case demonstrates, we already know this is a cancer. I'm not convinced that a reflex test makes a lot of sense, whether it was the Afirma assay, the UPMC assay, a surgeon's version of this, you know, whatever it is, I think it's evident that the molecular markers, unless you think BRAF is useful, the molecular markers probably aren't all that helpful. But what would be the surgical approach? How are we going to manage this big, nasty, invasive cancer in this man who's lost a vocal cord already? Dr. Shah. Did everybody hear that? He said, carefully.

I think you need to sort out what is the level of understanding of the patient and the patient's willingness to have the type of surgery he may need. And that will allow you to decide whether you want to do a two-stage operation or one stage. And when I say two-stage, meaning endoscopic assessment to define what you will have to do and have the patient mentally prepared for that. Or if the patient is ready, doctor, do whatever is necessary. Cure me of my cancer. That makes your job easier, and you can do everything at one time. After imaging, this patient needs careful endoscopy of the trachea and the esophagus. You would probably find tracheal invasion through the mucosa on the right-hand side, where you saw the regular tracheal wall. At esophagoscopy, what you want to see more carefully, you may not see intraluminal tumor. but you want to see whether the mucosa easily glides over the involved muscular wall or not. And that would help you decide whether you need to do through and through esophagectomy or will a section of only muscular wall be adequate, leaving the mucosa and therefore the lumen intact. So endoscopic assessment is crucial before you put the incision.

So it turns out that prior to going through that procedure, the patient acknowledged a little haemoptysis over a couple of days. And at the time of bronchoscopy, there was indeed through and through tracheal invasion with disease visible in the lumen of the trachea.

So at that point, you need to be careful as to what is the length of invasion of the trachea that you may have to reset. you can easily dissect and do primary repair or primary anastomosis up to six or even seven rings of trachea, but it depends upon the physiognomy of the patient, long neck, short neck, et cetera. But those are technical issues. In most instances, the vertical involvement of the tracheal wall is within reach of the surgeon to be able to accomplish primary anastomosis.

So this was a man who had been a heavy smoker for much of his life. He had a hyperinflated chest, a rather short and bulky neck. He had imaging that suggested at least a four centimeter length of invasion into the tracheal wall. And intraluminally, there was at least three centimeters of tumor visible. In addition, when the esophagoscopy was performed, there was also frank invasion of the esophageal wall.
Mucosal wall of the esophagus.
Mucosal wall, correct.

So in this setting, now you are committing yourself to a much bigger operation, which may mean letting go tracheal resection and esophagectomy. And in that setting, I want to have the histology confirmed. I won't do that on follicular invasion or follicular lesion. So I would be inclined to do, after endoscopies, either an open biopsy frozen section, or if I have staged my endoscopies, then I want a core biopsy to give me a more clear histologic diagnosis.
So a core biopsy was performed of the primary lesion and it turned out to be a poorly differentiated follicular thyroid cancer.

So when you get that diagnosis, now you need to go to the pathology lab, because that to me is not enough. I want the pathologist to tell me, are you seeing this tumor leaning towards an aplastic carcinoma? or this is poorly differentiated carcinoma leaning towards differentiated carcinoma with focal areas of anaplasia. Because that will make the difference. If truly this is a poorly differentiated carcinoma with anaplastic features, the probability of surgical cure, mind you, my word, cure, becomes less and less. Surgical control of neck disease is possible. But surgical cure for anaplastic carcinoma is unlikely.

So the pathologist is adamant that they do not see any signs of anaplastic thyroid cancer. This is poorly differentiated cancer, and that's all they see in this core biopsy. But they could not exclude the possibility of having anaplastic cancer elsewhere that has not been sampled at this point. So other surgical views on this. Is this a surgically approachable disease?
I'd be looking for reasons not to do surgery on this patient.
Don't you have lots of them?

Very unlikely to cure this individual if there's true invasion of the laryngotracheal structure. So I would want to get a CT scan higher. I didn't quite see that cricoid in the larynx. But 68 years old, the patient, if fit, could certainly tolerate a major procedure. It's clearly the best curative chance, but you're going to have to reconstruct both the laryngotracheal complex with pull-up type procedures, microvascular procedures. It's a major problem that you'd want to make sure the distant disease, I gather the PET has been already cleared, but I think from the local regional standpoint, surgery would be not advised.

So just in the last few minutes, is there a role for a neoadjuvant approach to the management of these deeply invasive and rather nasty, poorly differentiated cancers? Could we give a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, for example, and shrink this cancer down, make it more easily operable?

I think the points that have already been raised is very critical because we need to know whether truly this is anaplastic thyroid cancer or poorly differentiated variant of well-differentiated thyroid cancer. And the reason for saying that is even when we are talking of neoadjuvant approach, that presupposes we are thinking of going back to surgery at one point or the other. If this is truly anaplastic, then the use of cytotoxic chemotherapy as a new adjuvant approach has been shown to be equivalent to doing adjuvant chemotherapy after debulking surgery. So if we think this is anaplastic, and the surgeons have already decided this is not something we want to jump into, at that point, it would be reasonable to use a platinum-based chemotherapy regimen as an either neoadjuvant approach along with radiation. I know some surgeons don't want the radiation in the mix. Or if it is a poorly differentiated follicular neoplasm, then one can then consider the use of tyrosine kinase inhibitors. But I think in that regard, the ability to actually shrink the tumor is relatively less. And therefore, you will not be looking at that as a neoadjuvant intervention with the plan of going to surgery.

So just to wrap this case up, the patient actually made the decision for us. He was not interested in accepting the aggressive surgical approach with loss of voice and the chance of loss of swallowing that that might ensue. And he elected for a chemo radiation program with cisplatin-based chemotherapy and external beam radiation, which I think completed about a week ago. So I can update this conference next year and let you know how he's doing. I'd like to thank the panelists for an interesting and fascinating discussion. I'd like to thank the audience for attention.

reference_conclusion: Following staging and endoscopic evaluation demonstrating transmural tracheal invasion and frank esophageal mucosal invasion, core biopsy confirmed poorly differentiated follicular thyroid carcinoma without definitive anaplastic features on sampled tissue. Extensive surgery was considered unlikely to provide cure and was declined by the patient because of the anticipated morbidity, including loss of voice and possible loss of swallowing. The agreed next step was nonoperative treatment with a cisplatin-based chemoradiation regimen consisting of external beam radiation and concurrent cisplatin-based chemotherapy.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 28-year-old female. ECOG performance status was 0 at initial presentation. Weight was reported as approximately 50–52 kg.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented in September 2020 with a large right breast mass measuring approximately 5 × 7 cm. During later follow-up after autologous stem cell transplantation, developed blurring of vision, dull aching right eye pain, and subsequently two convulsive episodes at home.

[ diagnosis ]: Primary breast diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), stage IIE at initial diagnosis, with subsequent right axillary nodal relapse and later secondary central nervous system lymphoma involving the brain parenchyma.

[ histopathology results ]: Excisional biopsy of the right breast mass showed an undifferentiated round cell tumor consistent with non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Morphology demonstrated diffuse pleomorphic infiltrate composed of mature and transformed lymphocytes with inflammatory cells, mainly plasma cells and histiocytes, separated by fibrous tissue bands. Final diagnosis was non-Hodgkin lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell type. Immunohistochemistry showed CD20 diffuse membranous positivity in neoplastic cells, Ki-67 positivity in more than 80%, and negative staining for cytokeratin and CD3.

Excisional biopsy of a recurrent right axillary lymph node later showed involvement by non-Hodgkin lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell type, with CD20 diffuse positivity.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial post-contrast CT in 2020 showed a right breast mass, enlarged right axillary lymph node measuring 20 × 24 mm, and a few bilateral small upper deep cervical lymph nodes measuring up to 13 × 7 mm. No other abnormalities were detected.

Bone marrow evaluation showed a small hypercellular marrow, approximately 30%, with no lymphomatous deposits.

Post-first-line PET-CT showed enlarged right axillary lymph nodes measuring 16 × 7 mm with SUV 1.8, considered likely residual, and a peripherally enhancing avid right iliac cystic lesion with SUV 5.1. Subsequent PET-CT demonstrated no nodal metabolic activity and anatomical resolution of the previously reported right axillary lymph node. The right iliac cystic lesion was characterized as a non-metabolically active ovarian functional cyst, largest 17 × 15 mm.

Ultrasound of the axillary region after approximately 6 months of follow-up showed an enlarged right axillary lymph node with loss of hilum, globular shape, and cystic degeneration, measuring 3.2 cm, with suspicious features, plus another subcentimetric ipsilateral lymph node; no left axillary lymphadenopathy was seen.

Restaging PET-CT after axillary relapse showed no other pathological lymph nodes.

PET-CT in May 2023 remained consistent with complete remission.

PET-CT in July 2025 showed a well-defined hypodense non-enhancing area in the right frontoparietal lobe with associated mass effect and mild compression of the ipsilateral ventricle.

MRI/MRS demonstrated a superficial cortical space-occupying lesion measuring 34 × 20 × 30 mm with moderate perifocal edema, effacement of adjacent cortical sulci, and mild leftward midline shift; imaging was suggestive of lymphoma.

CT brain after one cycle of CNS-directed therapy showed regression of the previously reported right parietal lesion to 13 × 9 mm with mild edema and minimal mass effect.

MRI in November 2025 showed regression of the frontal lobe subcortical space-occupying lesion but new faintly enhancing patches in different brain sites, including subthalamic and frontal subcortical regions.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: BCL2 and BCL6 testing were not performed. CD10, CD19, and CD30 were not performed. No double-hit lymphoma testing was reported.

[ laboratory results ]: LDH at initial presentation was approximately 600. Serum methotrexate level measured one week after high-dose methotrexate was 0.04 and was considered toxic. Serum creatinine was reported as normal, around 1. Liver function tests were reported as normal. Kidney function was reported as normal by serum creatinine assessment. During toxicity admission, neutropenia was present. No B symptoms were reported at initial presentation.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: Received 6 cycles of CHOP chemotherapy without rituximab as first-line treatment, completed in March 2021. Response assessment PET-CT showed likely residual right axillary nodal disease.

Subsequently received 6 cycles of rituximab. Re-evaluation PET-CT in January 2022 showed complete remission with no metabolically active nodal disease.

After isolated right axillary relapse approximately 6 months later, received second-line chemotherapy with R-GemOx-based treatment for 6 cycles; prophylactic intrathecal therapy was given during this treatment. PET-CT after 3 cycles in January 2023 showed complete remission, and PET-CT in May 2023 remained in complete remission.

Underwent autologous stem cell transplantation as consolidation, with day 0 stem cell infusion on 7 November 2023. Conditioning regimen was BEAM.

Following CNS relapse, received high-dose methotrexate plus cytarabine; methotrexate dose was 3 g/m². First cycle was administered on 8 July 2025.

One week after chemotherapy, developed febrile neutropenia, bullous skin eruption involving both arms and back, oral mucositis, diarrhea, scleral redness progressing to subconjunctival hemorrhage, and extensive ulcerative skin lesions. Dermatology assessment considered drug-induced skin toxicity and possible toxic epidermal necrolysis. Management included calcium leucovorin 50 mg every 6 hours for 2 days, then escalation to 100 mg every 6 hours, oral steroids, cyclosporine 100 mg every 12 hours, dexamethasone every 24 hours, and topical steroids. Marked improvement occurred on cyclosporine, which was continued for approximately 14 days and then tapered. Hospitalization lasted approximately 3 weeks.

After subsequent treatment, the patient received 3 cycles of the HAB protocol. Latest MRI in November 2025 showed regression of the original lesion but new enhancing brain lesions.

[ current disease status ]: After autologous stem cell transplantation, remained in complete remission until April 2025, approximately 18 months post-transplant. Subsequently developed secondary CNS relapse. After initial CNS-directed therapy, the dominant right frontoparietal/frontal lesion regressed radiologically, but MRI in November 2025 demonstrated new enhancing lesions in multiple brain regions, consistent with progressive intracranial disease.

[ other clinical data ]: Ophthalmology review during CNS relapse recommended retinal injection. CSF analysis had not been performed at the time the brain space-occupying lesion was identified. No lymphomatous bone marrow involvement was documented at initial staging.

reference_conclusion: The multidisciplinary panel concluded that no further conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy should be administered, given chemotherapy-refractory relapsed secondary CNS lymphoma and severe prior toxicity. Management should be palliative and include localized radiotherapy to the CNS lesion(s), with consideration of intrathecal therapy if leptomeningeal/CSF involvement is demonstrated. If available, treatment with a BTK inhibitor with CNS penetration in combination with rituximab, with or without lenalidomide or nivolumab, was recommended as the preferred systemic approach. Reduced-intensity allogeneic transplantation with a thiotepa-containing conditioning regimen could be considered only if good disease control/remission is achieved and a donor is available.

[...] I concur that radiation, localized radiation, is maybe your best first step in getting BTK inhibitors. I hope that Ibrazenib runab is available. I know Ibrunib is, along with Rituxan and Lunalidomide, is a reasonable move to try to get the patient in remission. [...] I mean, you are in the palliation realm at this point. [...] I don't recommend you give any more chemo, any more cytotoxic chemo. You can use targeted agent, you can do radiation, but I wouldn't give any different combination of chemo at this point.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 50-year-old man; previously healthy.

[ chief complaint ]: Right flank and rib pain associated with movement.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma of the right kidney with osseous metastases.

[ histopathology results ]: Right nephrectomy specimen showed clear cell renal cell carcinoma with abundant clear cytoplasm, enlarged round nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and delicate vasculature. Tumor was predominantly Furman grade 3 with focal Furman grade 4 atypia. Chest wall/rib resection specimen showed metastatic carcinoma morphologically consistent with the renal primary. Left medial clavicle wide excision specimen showed metastatic carcinoma morphologically consistent with renal cell carcinoma.

[ imaging findings ]: Initial contrast-enhanced abdominal MRI demonstrated a large mass in the lower pole of the right kidney with apparent invasion of the renal hilum; the renal vein was not involved. MRI also demonstrated metastases involving the right lower ribs, including a large soft tissue component associated with the right 11th rib lesion. Postoperative bone scan demonstrated abnormal uptake in the right calvarium, left clavicle, and left tibia, consistent with metastatic disease; dedicated calvarial views confirmed a right calvarial metastasis. Four months later, CT brain was performed. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis obtained five months after initial presentation demonstrated a right lower lobe pulmonary nodule and a soft tissue mass arising from the left acetabulum, consistent with metastatic disease.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Hemoglobin 12.5 g/dL; hematocrit 39%; white blood cell count 8.7 ×10^9/L; neutrophils 6.2 ×10^9/L; platelet count 212,000/µL; calcium 12 mg/dL; creatinine 1.2 mg/dL; LDH 108 U/L. Vital signs were normal. Karnofsky performance status was 100.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent right adrenal-sparing nephrectomy with right 10th, 11th, and 12th rib resection. He subsequently underwent left medial clavicle wide excision. He received radiation therapy to the skull to 30 Gy in 10 fractions. Following local therapies, subsequent imaging demonstrated additional metastatic disease, including right calvarium, left tibia, right lower lobe lung nodule, and left acetabular soft tissue mass.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic disease persisted after nephrectomy, rib metastasectomy, clavicle metastasectomy, and skull radiation, with osseous metastases involving the calvarium, clavicle, tibia, and left acetabulum, and a pulmonary nodule in the right lower lobe.

[ other clinical data ]: Physical examination showed a well-appearing man in no acute distress; examination was otherwise benign.
