reference_discussion.text: So we'll start with our first case today. This is a 50-year-old previously healthy man who initially presented with right flank and rib pain associated with movement. Physical exam revealed normal vital signs, a Karnofsky performance status of 100, and he was a well-appearing man in no acute distress. And otherwise, the physical exam was benign. His labs were significant for hemoglobin of 12.5, but a normal hematocrit of 39, white blood cell count of 8.7, with neutrophils of 6.2. His platelet count was 212,000. His calcium was high at 12 and his creatinine was normal at 1.2. LDH was normal at 108. This ultimately led to an imaging study. Dr. Ho will discuss our initial imaging for this patient.

The imaging that he first received was an enhanced MRI of the abdomen, and this image shows that there is a large mass in the lower pole of the right kidney, and it looks to invade the renal hilum, but the renal vein was not involved. In addition, he had metastases involving the right lower ribs, and the arrow is pointing to a large topotitia component to this right 11th rib metastasis.
So that brings us to the first discussion point of this case, and that is the necessity of biopsy. And for that, we will turn to Dr. Inman.

Well, when I look at these images, it's more likely to me to be a renal mass metastasized to the bone than a bone lesion metastasized to the kidney. So, in this case, the presumptive diagnosis is one of kidney cancer. The question of whether or not you need a biopsy depends on what you're going to do next. If the patient is going to be a candidate for a nephrectomy, then I wouldn't do a biopsy because the biopsy is not going to change what I do. On the other hand, if it's a patient who's not going to go to nephrectomy, then I would consider a biopsy because we'd need the tissue diagnosis to decide on how best to manage the patient next. So in this particular patient, because I think he would potentially be a candidate for nephrectomy, I probably would not be considering a biopsy.
Great. In terms of prognostic categories, Dr. Harrison will now discuss the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center criteria as well as the HENG criteria.

Sure. So this is summarized on this slide. There are several prognostic criteria that are used. The first one that's probably the most widely used is the Memorial Sloan-Kettering criteria. It consists of five criteria. This was published in 1999 by Dr. Mozart et al., and the reference is at the bottom of the slide there. But again, it takes into account five clinical factors. So having a low Karnofsky performance status is a risk factor, as is having a high LDH, a low hemoglobin, a high corrected calcium, and having had no prior nephrectomy. All of these are risk factors. Then based upon the number of risk factors, you can group the patients into prognostic categories. So if a patient has zero risk factors, that corresponds to a favorable risk category, one to two intermediate risk, and three or greater is a poor risk. And these correspond to different survivals. Now that's been updated. The initial Memorial Sloan-Kettering criteria were published in the cytokine era. Now that we're firmly in the TKI era where we're using drugs like sunitinib, these criteria have been updated. And the first four were retained. What was added was a short time to diagnosis to therapy of less than one year. Thrombophilia was added, neutrophilia was added, and I'm sorry, LDH was actually omitted, the second prognostic factor, because it is not routinely checked. So to summarize, what's called the HENG criteria has six risk factors. And again, you can group those patients into risk categories. A patient with favorable risk, as is shown on the slide, has a prognosis of about three to four years. Our patient has two risk factors, so that patient would be expected to have a median survival of about 27 months, whereas poor risk patients have a survival of about nine months. So in summary, I would say, you know, looking at this patient, he would appear to have a good enough prognosis to think about things like cytoreductive nephrectomy and other local therapies.
That leads us to our second discussion point, which is what is the role of cytoreductive nephrectomy in this case?

Okay, so cytoreductive nephrectomy is when we remove the kidney in the presence of metastatic disease and when we have not removed all of the cancer because presumably there's metastasis somewhere else that we haven't removed. And there's two main reasons we might consider cytoreductive nephrectomy. The first is symptoms. So, a symptomatic kidney tumor that's bleeding or painful, even if they're a poor risk patient from a cancer standpoint, might be a good candidate for nephrectomy to improve their quality of life for whatever time they have left. And the second reason we might consider would be to improve their survival. And there's two large randomized trials in the cytokine era that have been conducted. One was a SWOG trial, and the other one was done by the EORTC. And those trials were pooled in a large analysis, and it showed that there was a benefit to doing cytoreductive nephrectomy in combination at that time with interferon versus interferon alone, and it improved survival by about six months. We don't have any trials that have been published in the current TKI era, although there are two that have enrolled, the CARMINA trial and the SIRTIME trial, and those are expected to produce results in the next couple years. But we expect to see probably a similar benefit, although it's really not known. So for me and this patient, the best current data that we have suggests that patients who have their kidneys removed, even in the presence of metastatic disease, live longer and have less local symptoms. And the complication rate of cytoreductive nephrectomy is pretty low. About 25% of patients will have a complication, but of those, really only 5% are grade 3 or higher. Grade 3 or higher are complications you actually need to do something about. So the majority are minor complications. So because there's very few complications and because there's a potential survival benefit and because there's a symptomatic benefit, in general, if the patient's in good condition and can tolerate the surgery reasonably well, we would recommend cytoreductive nephrectomy.

Great, so this patient initially underwent a right adrenal sparing nephrectomy and right 10th, 11th, and 12th rib resection. We have the pathology of his initial resection and Dr. Fu will talk us through that.

So the image that's shown here is from his nephrectomy specimen, and basically everything that you're seeing is tumor. So the tumor morphology of his particular cancer is actually pretty classic. So the cells have abundant, very clear cytoplasm. The nuclei are fairly round, but they're pretty enlarged, and the nucleoli are very prominent. The vasculature is relatively delicate, and there is a fair amount of it. All of this is really good for a diagnosis of clear cell renal cell carcinoma, and this looks fairly high grade in appearance. The majority of the tumor was graded as a Furman grade 3. The next slide shows a higher magnification of some of the more focal areas of the tumor that had very large, very prominent pleomorphic nuclei that have some nucleoli that are actually the same size of the red blood cells that are on the slide as well. And that would be more consistent with the bizarre atypia that you see with the Furman grade 4 case. So, he had a very high grade clear cell renal cell carcinoma. Along with the nephrectomy came his chest wall resection, and along with the ribs, there was a large soft tissue tumor mass, and this is a representative section from that. If you take a look at the morphology of the tumor cells here, you can see that they look very similar to the initial image that I was showing of his kidney tumor. So morphologically, this is consistent with the metastasis from his clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
Thank you. Subsequently, the patient underwent a bone scan, and Dr. Ho will talk to us about that bone scan.

These are frontal and posterior images on the left from his bone scan. And you can see when the arrow is pointing to various sites, one in his right calvarium, his left clavicle, and his left tibia, are all sites of abnormal metabolic activity there, indicating that they're most likely to be metastases. The next image is a cone down view of his scalp, his calvarial region, again showing high activity in his right calvarium, consistent with metastatic disease.

So at this point, we considered local therapies for the patient, including metastasectomy, as well as external beam radiation. And I'll have Dr. Harrison talk a little bit about which to choose for this patient.

Okay. And, you know, I think the thing to recognize is that, you know, it doesn't have to be one or the other. It could be both. Dr. Edmund can maybe talk a little bit about this as well. Metastasectomy is appropriate when there are one or maybe a few lesions that we think we can remove, again, to debulk either all of the tumor or the vast majority of the tumor. Certainly, external beam radiation therapy is appropriate when a lesion can't be removed, for example, in the skull, not practical. So certainly, this is a multidisciplinary discussion amongst usually surgery, urology, that is, medical oncology, and potentially radiation oncology. I'll just add that several, you know, retrospective series looking at metastasectomy have shown that patients can have good outcomes. I don't know if you have anything to add there, Brian.

Well, I would comment that at the outset, this patient had a metastasectomy in his ribs. And the reason that was done was predominantly for symptoms, but also because at the time of initial treatment, it was the only known site of disease. And at this point, three months later, we now know that he has more extensive bony disease than we had previously. I think at this point, one of his metastases is in the clavicle, and it is quite symptomatic. So, one reason for doing a metastasectomy, other than for potential cure, would be for symptom control, because it can be very effective for that. And particularly in the clavicle, where it's prone to break, this is an area where we would consider bony resection. The data on metastasectomy for kidney cancer are actually pretty interesting. For patients who have lung-only metastases and that are completely resected, their five-year survival is almost 50%. For those patients who have disease in the bones, liver, or lymph nodes that are completely resected, it's not quite as good. It's maybe around 30 to 40%. but it's still a lot better than virtually any other treatment at five years for metastatic cancer. So, for me, if a patient is in good shape, has a good performance status, and that's key, has a limited number of metastases that we feel we can completely resect, then they're generally, and with minimal morbidity, I must say, because if you have to remove, for example, an entire leg, the morbidity of that would probably outweigh the benefit. So it has to be a procedure that has reasonable morbidity. Then there's a potential benefit to the patient, not only in terms of quality of life, but quantity of life. For those patients in whom we can't have a potential cure, then we really only consider it as a palliative maneuver and prefer radiation if it's possible. For example, for axial spine metastases, where there's multiple metastases, would prefer radiation in that setting.
Great, thank you.
So continuing on with our case, the patient underwent a left medial clavicle wide excision with pathology shown here.

So this is a representative image from his clavicle resection, and the bright pink material that you're seeing sort of in the upper right hand corner of the screen represents bone. So normal bone marrow is actually hypocellular. You should see hematopoietic elements and fat. And what you're seeing here in the majority of the screen is actually a very hypercellular infiltrate of epithelial cells. And if you sort of think back to the original morphology of his tumor, you can see that they look very similar. So this is consistent morphologically with a metastasis from his known renal cell carcinoma.

Thank you. So four months later the patient underwent a CT of his brain and he also underwent radiation to his skull to 30 gray in 10 fractions. After he underwent local therapy, he had a CT chest abdomen and pelvis five months after his initial presentation.

The image on the left shows lung bases. There is a nodule in the right lower lobe. And the image on your right is a soft tissue window image of his pelvis showing a soft tissue mass originating from his left acetabulum, also consistent with ptosis.
So at this point, we come to a role for systemic therapies for the patient. And Dr. Harrison, if you would discuss choosing his first line of systemic therapy at this point.

Sure. So now the patient has had a fairly aggressive surgical debulking, the patient has had a radiation therapy, and what systemic therapy do we choose? And certainly, based on the patient's risk factors, based on the patient's age, we did think about high-dose IL-2. High-dose IL-2, though, has a response rate in the neighborhood of about 15%, so maybe 7% complete responses, only half of which are durable, maybe 8% partial responses. So when we were thinking about how to treat this patient, we were thinking mainly of that lesion in his pelvis and thinking of the size of it and that if that continued to grow unchecked, he may start to have symptoms. So we needed something with a little bit higher response. And so for that reason, we actually chose sunitinib. Certainly, either sunitinib or pazotinib are first-line therapy choices in this setting, so a patient with clear cell metastatic renal cell carcinoma, good intermediate risk. The difference, again, between drugs like pazopanib and sunitinib and hydroxyl 2 are that the response rate is probably in the neighborhood of 30 to 40 percent. Now, they don't have the same chance of a long-term response, basically, if you just compare complete responses. So, complete responses are probably maybe 1 percent or non-existent with drugs like sunitinib. So, we did talk about this and counsel the patient very extensively about that. and elected to go at the agent with a higher chance of response. We also talked to the patient about anti-resorptive agents. So there are two drugs, zolandronic acid, which is a bisphosphonate or denosumab, a rank ligand inhibitor, which are reasonable to use in patients with skeletal metastases with renal cell carcinoma. If you look at the trial, which was in all solid tumors, it was a phase 3 trial. Actually, either one, they both included a significant proportion of patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma, and either one of these drugs did appear to delay or prevent skeletal-related events. So, I would say using a drug, either zoledronic acid or denosumab with the systemic therapy is important in this setting.
Do you think there's a role for any of these anti-absorption agents? Do they have an anti-neoplastic effect?

That's a good question. That's been investigated fairly extensively in different randomized phase three studies. It's not clear in renal cell carcinoma, at least clinically, that they do have an antineoplastic effect. But I would say they do add to the systemic therapy in terms of preventing important morbidity from the cancer. So they're very important in that regard.

Very good, thank you. That wraps up our first case and we'll move on to our second case. Our second case today features a 44-year-old man who presented with 18 months of fatigue, arthrages, night sweats, and weight loss. He had extensive infectious disease and rheumatologic workups, which were all negative, including two courses of treatment for tick-borne illnesses. An abdominal ultrasound was performed for fever of unknown origin, which demonstrated a right renal mass measuring 10 by 8 by 10 centimeters. He underwent a CT of the abdomen and pelvis which confirmed a 10 by 9 centimeter right upper pole renal mass with partial duplication of the collecting system, no lymphadenopathy, and a CT chest was negative for metastatic disease. He had an initial surgery with a right laparoscopic nephrectomy and regional lymph node dissection. Dr. Fu, can you describe his pathology?

reference_conclusion: The patient underwent cytoreductive management with right adrenal-sparing nephrectomy and resection of involved right 10th, 11th, and 12th ribs, followed by local treatment of metastatic sites including left medial clavicle wide excision and radiation therapy to the skull to 30 Gy in 10 fractions. With subsequent progression including a pelvic lesion, first-line systemic therapy with sunitinib was selected on the basis of the need for a higher response rate in metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma. Concurrent bone-targeted therapy with either zoledronic acid or denosumab was considered important to reduce skeletal-related events in the setting of osseous metastases.

[...] So continuing on with our case, the patient underwent a left medial clavicle wide excision [...] four months later the patient underwent a CT of his brain and he also underwent radiation to his skull to 30 gray in 10 fractions. [...] And so for that reason, we actually chose sunitinib. Certainly, either sunitinib or pazotinib are first-line therapy choices in this setting [...] So, I would say using a drug, either zoledronic acid or denosumab with the systemic therapy is important in this setting.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: 44-year-old man.

[ chief complaint ]: Eighteen months of fatigue, arthralgias, night sweats, and weight loss; fever of unknown origin prompted abdominal ultrasound.

[ diagnosis ]: High-grade clear cell renal cell carcinoma of the right kidney, stage II at initial surgery, with subsequent solitary pulmonary nodule in the right middle lobe.

[ histopathology results ]: Right nephrectomy specimen showed very high-grade clear cell renal cell carcinoma with 2% sarcomatoid features; reported as Furman grade 4.

[ imaging findings ]: Abdominal ultrasound demonstrated a right renal mass measuring 10 x 8 x 10 cm. CT abdomen and pelvis confirmed a 10 x 9 cm right upper pole renal mass with partial duplication of the collecting system and no lymphadenopathy. CT chest at initial staging was negative for metastatic disease. One year later, staging CT chest/abdomen/pelvis demonstrated a right middle lobe pulmonary nodule at the medial edge measuring 1.3 x 1.4 cm, increased from 0.8 x 0.9 cm three months earlier. No other definite evidence of metastases was identified on that study.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic data were available.

[ laboratory results ]: Infectious disease and rheumatologic evaluations were extensive and negative. Two courses of treatment for presumed tick-borne illnesses had been given prior to renal mass diagnosis.

[ prior treatments and outcomes ]: The patient underwent right laparoscopic nephrectomy with regional lymph node dissection for the primary renal tumor.

[ current disease status ]: One year after nephrectomy, a solitary enlarging right middle lobe pulmonary nodule was present, with no other identified sites of disease. Abdominal and pelvic CT remained negative.

reference_discussion.text: Very good, thank you. That wraps up our first case and we'll move on to our second case. Our second case today features a 44-year-old man who presented with 18 months of fatigue, arthrages, night sweats, and weight loss. He had extensive infectious disease and rheumatologic workups, which were all negative, including two courses of treatment for tick-borne illnesses. An abdominal ultrasound was performed for fever of unknown origin, which demonstrated a right renal mass measuring 10 by 8 by 10 centimeters. He underwent a CT of the abdomen and pelvis which confirmed a 10 by 9 centimeter right upper pole renal mass with partial duplication of the collecting system, no lymphadenopathy, and a CT chest was negative for metastatic disease. He had an initial surgery with a right laparoscopic nephrectomy and regional lymph node dissection. Dr. Fu, can you describe his pathology?

Sure, so he had a very high-grade clear cell renal cell carcinoma with 2% sarcomatoid features. So when we say that there are sarcomatoid features in a carcinoma, that typically means we're seeing morphology that is very atypical hybrid in appearance, often spindled in appearance, and that is generally associated with a poorer prognosis. And so even if it's very focal, we would still report a Furman grade four.

Great, thank you. One year later, he was undergoing staging CT when he had a chest, abdomen, and pelvis CT performed. This showed in the medial edge of the right middle lobe of the lung, he had a nodule that was previously measuring 0.8 by 0.9 centimeters. three months prior, and that had increased in size to 1.3 by 1.4 centimeters. There were no other definite evidence of metastases. So for this patient, we were hoping to discuss additional staging as well as role for biopsies or metastasectomies at this point.

I'd like to make a comment first about the history. The first question that pops up, I think, for many, many patients is, at the time of his first surgery, when he had stage 2 high-grade sarcomatoid renal cell carcinoma, was there a role at that point for adjuvant therapy? Should he have received systemic therapy after nephrectomy? And this is a common question that patients ask when I tell them they're at a little bit increased risk of recurrence because of the sarcomatoid features in their tumor. They ask if there's anything that we can give to prevent that. And I was wondering, Mike, if you could comment on that. What do you think?

Sure. No, this is a great question. And this, again, is a question that's commonly asked by patients. Given the activity of drugs like sutent, serafinib, et cetera, in the metastatic setting, it could be reasonably wondered, maybe we should try to treat high-risk patients to try to reduce the risk of recurrence, or at least delay recurrence. So as far as the evidence that is known right now, recently the ASURE study, which was looking at adjuvant sunitinib or serafinib, did not show a benefit to adjuvant treatment for high-risk patients with localized renal cell carcinoma. There are multiple other studies, S-TRAC, Everest, using other agents, including oxytinib, everolimus, et cetera, that have accrued and are waiting to read out. But at least the first results that we have do not support adjuvant therapy at this point, unfortunately, for patients.

Yeah, I think that's exactly what I would tell the patient, too. And the other thing is patients with sarcomatoid tumors in general are not generally very responsive to tyrosine kinase inhibition or mTOR inhibitors that we know of. So, you know, there's maybe those two reasons. As for this patient's lung lesion, it's small, it's unifocal. For me, at this size, 1.4 centimeters, it might be very difficult to biopsy. Generally, lesions at a centimeter in size can be tricky, but I would consider this potentially for a resection. This is a tumor on the imaging that is very peripheral in the lung. and would look to me to be amenable to thoracoscopic wedge resection. So my first thought would be, well, it's a unifocal site of disease. Maybe it can be resected, but before doing that, I'd want to make sure that there was no other disease elsewhere. And for me, that would include a bone scan to look for disease in the bone. And if he hadn't had a CT of the abdomen and pelvis, but I think he did, I would check that. But if the CT of the abdomen and pelvis was fine, the bone scan was clear, and with a solitary lung lesion, I personally wouldn't scan the brain. I would generally do that when the burden of disease above the diaphragm is high. So multiple or lung metastases is when I would, or multiple lung and bone metastases, that's when I would consider checking his head.

Yeah, no, I agree. And I think certainly in this patient, a metastasectomy would make sense. I think the thing to realize with systemic therapy is that it has real side effects. The progression-free survival, depending on what drug you use, sunitinib, pazopanib might be appropriate in this patient, would be about eight to nine months. But during that time, the patient is having side effects. fatigue, hypertension, et cetera, et cetera. Whereas if you could treat the patient with local therapy, potentially do a wedge resection or some other way, pluck out this nodule, even if all you did is delay the time to systemic therapy, that would be a benefit to the patient.

Yeah, and for thoracoscopic wedge resections, the recovery period is remarkably quick. Patients leave the hospital usually within a couple of days, and usually within six weeks are pretty much back to baseline, assuming that there's no complications.

So the patient did undergo a right thoracoscopic wedge resection when the pathology showed a 1.3 by 1.2 by 1 centimeter clear cell carcinoma with negative margins. Dr. Fu, do you want to comment on his immunohistochemistry staining?

Sure, so the immunohistochemical findings on the lung nodule showed positive staining for RCC and CD10, as well as some patchy staining for vimentin and anti-cytokeratins, and those are all very consistent with a diagnosis of metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma. A TTF1 immunostain was negative, and that was done to make sure that it wasn't a pulmonary adenocarcinoma, and those tend to be positive for TTF1, whereas a renal cell carcinoma would be negative, as this case was.

I think this case demonstrates really the role of metastasectomy in renal cell carcinoma. It also demonstrates the patients that tend to benefit. So metastasectomies tend to work best in people who have lung-only disease versus disease in other sites, although it can be beneficial in those other sites. It tends to benefit patients who have asynchronous recurrence of disease rather than synchronous disease. And it tends to benefit patients who have a low number of metastases, one or two versus three or more. So this patient basically had several risk factors that would suggest a good outcome with metastasectomy, solitary lung only disease.

Thanks very much for that commentary. And the patient has remained without evidence of disease now four years after metastasectomy. So he met all those criteria. That concludes this case. Thank you for joining us for this session of the Renal Cell Carcinoma Tumor Board.

reference_conclusion: Additional staging should be completed with bone scintigraphy to exclude osseous metastatic disease; if abdominal and pelvic CT remains negative and the bone scan is clear, brain imaging is not indicated in the setting of a solitary pulmonary lesion. Given the small, peripheral, unifocal right middle lobe nodule, thoracoscopic wedge resection/metastasectomy is the preferred next step rather than biopsy or immediate systemic therapy. Adjuvant systemic therapy after nephrectomy is not supported by the available evidence discussed.

And I think certainly in this patient, a metastasectomy would make sense. [...] But at least the first results that we have do not support adjuvant therapy at this point, unfortunately, for patients.

[ patient demographics ]: 46-year-old male.

[ chief complaint ]: Presented to the emergency department with epigastric pain.

[ diagnosis ]: Metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor involving the pancreatic tail with liver metastases.

[ histopathology results ]:  
- CT-guided biopsy of a liver lesion demonstrated a grade 2 well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with Ki-67 15%.

[ imaging findings ]:  
- Initial CT abdomen demonstrated a 15.8 cm pancreatic tail mass and multiple liver lesions, with the largest liver lesion measuring 3 cm.  
- MRI demonstrated a very large pancreatic tail mass and multiple enhancing liver lesions consistent with metastases.  
- Imaging review described the mass as away from the superior mesenteric artery and celiac axis, with draping over the splenic vein.  
- Ga-68 DOTATATE PET demonstrated high somatostatin receptor uptake in the large pancreatic mass and multiple liver lesions. The pancreatic mass contained areas of low uptake consistent with necrotic/nonviable regions. Local lymph nodes were also visualized.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: None reported.

[ laboratory results ]: None reported.

[ current disease status ]: Metastatic well-differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor with a 15.8 cm pancreatic tail mass and multiple liver metastases, the largest measuring 3 cm. Disease demonstrated high somatostatin receptor uptake on Ga-68 DOTATATE PET, with local lymph nodes also visualized. The pancreatic mass was described as away from the superior mesenteric artery and celiac axis, draping over the splenic vein.

[ other clinical data ]:  
- Necrotic areas were present within the pancreatic primary on imaging.

reference_discussion.text: Thank you. As we can see, we have an excellent panel today. And with that, we're going to discuss our first case. This is a 46-year-old male who presented to the emergency department complaint of epigastric pain. A CT scan of the abdomen reported a 15.8 centimeter pancreatic tilt mass with multiple liver lesions and with the greatest dimension being three centimeters in size. CT scan guided biopsy of the liver mass reported a grade two well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with a KI67 of 15%. So this is the scan. of the patient. And Dr. Mitra, as we're showing the scans, could you please describe what we're seeing in the scans and what would you recommend as the next step?

Sure. So for evaluation of these types of tumors, especially for staging, but also restaging, both CT and MRI have a very important role. So this is the MRI that was done. It's particularly good for the liver and for the pancreas, which is exactly where this patient has their disease. And so you can actually see the very large pancreatic tail mass, as well as multiple enhancing lesions within the liver, which are likely the metastases that are there.

I'm fond of MRIs, but I think sometimes when you're looking for vascular definition, I prefer a good CT for anatomical purposes and for planning surgery. I think a good CT for vascular definition and a delayed, you know, 20-minute delay on the ovious phase for the burden of liver disease.
And Dr. Singh, for our patients, could you please describe what is SMA and what is relevant in this case?

So the SMA is the superior mesenteric artery which supplies the entire intestines. And so it is critical to actually make an effort to save that, because if you compromise that, you're compromising the vascularity of the entire small intestines and two-thirds of the large intestines. The celiac axis, on the other hand, has three dominant branches. One goes up towards the liver, one goes up to the stomach, and the third goes up to the spleen and the body and tail of the pancreas. So once again, It's a good idea to save the celiac axis and not take it, although you can reconstruct these vessels. But I think it's always a better idea to have before you go into the operating room as to do you have the degree of freedom to be able to resect these without needing complex vascular reconstruction.
Okay. Dr. Mitra, anything that you would like to add?

No, I just wanted to reiterate Dr. Singh's point that both CT and MRI, as I mentioned, have an important role for the evaluation, but they do have different pros and cons. I think for patients, it's important to understand that in either case, it's important to get a multi-phase CT or a multi-phase MRI. Oftentimes patients only get one phase, and that's not quite sufficient to evaluate all the different things.
And Dr. Oz, anything else that you would like to add in this case?

Not much. I think it's a great discussion. I would probably echo a lot of what Dr. Singh said as a vascular interventional radiologist. You know, we are particularly keen on getting CTs for vascular planning, and I would agree that this mass looks like it's well away from the SMA and celiac axis. It does look like it's draping over the splenic vein, but I imagine the spleen is easier to sacrifice than other parts of the body.

So I think it's important to get good vascular definition on these scans, and particularly if the mass is encroaching on the superior mesenteric artery, which supplies almost two-thirds of the large intestine and the entire small intestine, it's important to make sure that the mass is away from that so it can be safely removed. And with regards to the celiac axis, that actually has three dominant branches, one that's going up towards the spleen, one to the stomach, and the other towards the liver. And once again, it's a good idea to actually save those blood vessels in surgery when you're doing that, except for the splenic artery and vein, which is going to come out in continuity with the mass itself. You can do complex vascular reconstructions, but you like to be well-prepared ahead of time before you go into these operations. You want to make sure you have good vascular definition on your scans before you go into the operating room.

And what I'm hearing in the discussions, especially in this case that we have a patient with a pancreas, large pancreas, mass, and liver lesions consistent with neuroendocrine tumors, and it seems that based on the discussions, surgery is an option. Would you recommend anything more, any other scans prior to surgery?

I'm actually fond of making sure that these are somatostatin receptor positive scans, tumors, because that determines a lot of the adjuvant treatment. So, a good gallium 68 PET scan is in order, I think.
And as we can see, this is the 68 gallium dot that they scanned. And Dr. Mitra, could you please describe what we see on the scans?

Yeah, so this scan is targeting the somatostatin receptors that are expressed on these tumors and based on the key 67. 15%, you would expect that most of these tumors should have high expression of somatostatin receptors. So it's a great thing that's an adjuvant to the CT scan or MRI scan to see what the expression there is. And as we're scrolling through, you're seeing all those same lesions in the liver as well as the large pancreatic mass that are showing that high uptake. The pancreatic mass also shows some areas of not high expression, which are probably necrotic or areas that have actually died within the tumor. And you can see that as sort of the holes within there as well. And you can probably make out some lymph nodes locally as well.

And can I ask you a follow-up question? Some of our patients ask whether there is any difference between 68 gallium dotted scans or 64 copper Could you please describe more in detail whether there's a difference or if any preference one versus the other?

Sure. So there's a lot of technical differences, but I think the bottom line that patients should understand is that there's these two different isotopes. Gallium 68 and copper 64, both of them are targeting the somatostatin receptor as we just talked about. And if the scanners are set up properly for the isotope, then essentially they're equivalent as far as imaging quality and effectiveness. So I don't think patients should really be worried too much about that. There are technical differences between them in terms of the half-life and the energies and things like that. But more or less, either one is good as long as the institution is set up for that.

Great. Thank you so much. Based on this information, Dr. Steens, now we have this patient that have a pancreas neuroendocrine tumors with liver metastasis. You already saw the dot of the scan, which is Abbott. So the tumor expressed the receptors. So what would you do next? Well, what would you recommend next on this patient?

the most important thing is to take the primary out. That is one single action that promotes longevity, okay? Whether you touch the liver, you don't touch the liver. And, you know, a lot of groups have published that, including our group. So that's one thing. So she would end up with a distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy for sure. Now, since there's no vascular reconstruction, and if the first portion of the operation is fairly straightforward. I'm a proponent of doing the liver at the same time. And as long as you think you can achieve in today's day and age what we say, 70% reduction of the total liver tumor volume, somewhere about eight or nine lesions is what I calculated, but there might be more, you know, which would definitely be more obvious on a 20 minute delay on the MRI. If there's no vascular reconstruction necessary, then I tend to do the liver at the same time. If there's going to be some major vascular reconstruction, I like to do it as a staged fashion. There is no data to suggest that the staged liver resection is anything wrong. So if you don't feel comfortable doing it at the first sitting, or you think the surgery's already taken, been fairly major, it's absolutely fine to stage it and do the liver in, you know, six weeks to three months.
Okay. And Dr. Oz, as an interventional oncologist, do you think that's something that you could address via liver directed therapies? And when would you recommend?

Yeah, that's a great question. I would echo what Dr. Singh said that, you know, in our practice, we would probably prefer if there is a surgical option with respect to obviously the primary, but also to the liver, to try to debulk as much as possible, especially if the tumor burden is feasible enough to do that. I think the role of interventional radiology or oncology here would be twofold. One would be If Dr. Singh, for example, felt that he could get 80% of the tumors, but maybe a few would be difficult to reach, then we could potentially offer local regional therapy like a percutaneous ablation. And or if he felt that the tumor burden was too high to address surgically, we could also offer what we call intra-arterial therapies, which are under that umbrella include things like bland embolization, as well as radio embolization.

I would like to add one more thing. You know, usually at the time of surgery, I tend to debulk them surgically. You don't need a margin on these tumors. All you need to do is enucleate these tumors. So it's like taking a hard-boiled egg out of a, you know, a shell basically, but you're not leaving any residual tumor behind. So you can do that safely. A couple of the deeper lesions, you can ablate in the operating room at the same time. But I think what Dr. Oz just said is there are certain, sometimes you're left with disease that you cannot get to, or you're going to be pushing the envelope a bit too much and, you know, not leave enough liver behind. At that juncture, you then, you know, put a pause on it and then do that either in a staged fashion or you get your interventional colleagues involved to address that disease while they're on systemic therapy.

Great. Thank you so much. Just as Dr. Singh recommended, this patient did underwent a distal pancreatectomy, a splenectomy, and cholecystectomy, meaning that the distal pan of the pancreas was resected, the spleen was resected, and the gallbladder was resected. Pathology was consistent with a grade three well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor. So the K67 is 30%. As we discussed earlier, the K67 was 15%. But now we can see that the final pathology said that it's 30% and there was lymph nodes that were also positive for neuroendocrine tumor. Patient then have a follow CT scans. The liver lynchings were unchanged and the patient was started on Lanreotide every four weeks with a follow scans every three months. After nine months of being on Lanreotide, follow scans revealed that the tumors in the liver grew. And at that moment, Landry type was stopped. And Dr. Mitra, what would you think? Would you do any other workup for this patient based on the Ki-67, based on what we've seen here?
Before I answer your question, I'm curious what your answer is. How often do you see that, that the Ki-67 changes? And what does that mean to you from an oncology perspective?

Right. So the initial KS67 of 15% was from a biopsy. And sometimes when the biopsy is done, it's possible that maybe they could biopsy a necrotic area. And sometimes when there is a necrotic area, sometimes the percentage of KS67 cannot be accurately calculated. So in the fact that this patient underwent surgery and there is a lot more tissue to kind of review this number. So I do believe that this KS67 is more accurate and it was 30% from the very beginning. And I feel like the initial KS67 that was done for a biopsy is possible that there is more necrotic tissue and unable to accurately calculate as I said, but now that this 30% seems to be more accurate in 30% is what I think has been from the very beginning of the diagnosis of neuroendocrine tumor. But yes, that's a good question. Sometimes I get the question that I get a K67 and a biopsy of this percentage and then a repeated one is higher. But usually we, our decision is to always take the highest K67 because as I said, you know, sometimes, you know, the lower K67, there may be an area that there was, like I said, necrotic tissue. And as I said, the pathology is the call of the pathologist to calculate this number. But I do believe that the higher guess 67 is a more accurate for the neuroendocrine tumor.

So let's say if the KI67 came back at 30% on the initial biopsy, based on the new data that's coming out with CAPETEM, would you start the patient on CAPETEM to see a response and then go to surgery? Or would you still want us to debulk it and then go to surgery?

Our recommendations for our patients with neuroendocrine tumors, as we all discussed, is multidisciplinary. And I think it's important always to have our surgeon, nuclear medicine, interventional radiologists, medical oncologists, because it's not one size fits all. And I think we all know that. So the treatment of neuroendocrine tumors is quite personalized from patient to patient. And in this situation, yes, I do agree that systemic therapy is an option. And the reason why is because of the volume of disease. It's important to know as well. What is the vol to know whether the tumors or outside the liver, wheth receptors because that a as well as what therapies in this situation because a large pancreatic mass, l metastasis. I do think th to my first follow up th line of therapy will be cap 10 just to see if that also shrink the tumors because we know that the tumors can shrink up to 40 percent. So and if we can do that, maybe it's possible that surgery it will be easier later on. But in this situation, yes, I think I will have opted to start Gibbs Iodine intramusolomide.

Yeah, so this brings up a couple of interesting points. So one is that, you know, we did see that area of necrosis on the initial scan. So what you said about the biopsy, you know, makes a lot of sense. And in addition to that, always the surgical biopsies is generally more accurate than the ones that are done with the core. Now we know that the patient has progressed based on the CT scan already. So just for that reason alone, it would be important to potentially restage again with somatostatin receptor PET, the DOTATATE PET, to see what is going on now. And then also because the Ki67 is increased, as the number goes higher, you begin to lose somatostatin receptor expression. At 30%, I would still expect to see good uptake, but it would be good to reevaluate that. And on the scan, as we're going through, You're seeing many, many more liver lesions than you saw previously. The majority of them appear to be still showing somatostatin receptor expression, but it would be very important to correlate that very closely with the CT or MRI to make sure that some of these small lesions are not beginning to lose the expression that was just mentioned. And then you also have their FDG scan. And that also starts becoming important as the Ki-67 starts going up, especially above 20%. Because you start losing somatostatin receptor expression, then those lesions will start having increased glucose uptake, which is what the FDG scan shows. So many people advocate that it would be ideal to do both types of scans to fully evaluate all the different tumors and what is expressing what.

Right. Thank you so much, Dr. Mitra. And as you suggested, this patient did had glucose scans, and the glucose scans is on the top end of the picture. And then the dot of the scan is on the bottom. And as we can see in this patient, it still highly expresses somatostatin receptor, which we know that is the tumor response to somatostatin receptors. It can open also the possibilities of other therapies as well. But as you suggested, I think you know, you say like, well, we need to sometimes do both the scans to really understand more about the biology of these tumors. Maybe there may be some tumors that may be more DOTATATE avid and maybe some tumors may be more FDG avid. But maybe if you could, for our patients, maybe to discuss more in detail, when would you do the two scans and how that help us to make clinical recommendations?

Yeah, in a very general sense, sort of rule of thumb, if the Ki-67 is less than 20%, you can probably get away with just the DOTATATE PET scan, again, as long as you correlate with the CT or MRI and you don't see any discrepancies there. Above Ki-67 of 55% on the opposite end of the spectrum, you almost always want to go with FDG. scan and it'll be less likely to show the DOTATATE expression. But that still leaves a very wide range between 20 to 55 percent where, again, you might need to do both types of scans. And the best advice I can give, again, is to correlate it with the CT and MRI. As far as therapeutic decisions, if you have somatostatin receptor expression, as you're alluding to, that opens up those types of therapies such as somatostatin analogs and PRRT, whereas the more you lose that and the higher the FDG uptake goes, then you're not going to be well served with those therapies and you'll want to do other types of systemic therapies such as CAPETEL. In this case, like you said, the FDG uptake is very, very low compared to the DOTATATE, so that's very good.

And one last question. Sometimes our patients have difficulties getting both scans approved. Is there any recommendation, anything that you will suggest, you know, for our patients or how to approach their physicians in order to get the scans done whenever it's needed?

Yeah, that's a really important point and frustrating for ourselves as well as for patients. And I think a lot of the difficulties, the fact that they're both two different types of PET scans and insurance companies often see them as sort of in the same bucket, even though they're completely ultimately types of scans. So oftentimes it's just an education with the insurance company and having them understand what is the benefit of these two different types of scans as we just discussed. So doing a peer-to-peer evaluation discussion with the insurance company can sometimes help alleviate that, but it is a problem and also there's a lot of regional variability. with that as well. But the first thing is to kind of understand the importance of it. And then secondly, is to kind of push for it with the insurance company.

Thank you. So just to follow with our case, this patient did get a combination oral chemotherapy with kefcidabine and temosolomide. And kefcidabine was discontinued due to coronary phase of spasms. And what is that mean is when your heart already suddenly constrict, causing spasms that trigger symptoms like a heart attack. It very rarely occur, it's less than 4%, but it has been documented. So this patient only got temosolomide alone for two more cycles. And as we can see on these scans, you know, there was evidence of the tumors grew and there were more tumors seen on the skins. And maybe that will be a question for Dr. Oz, you know, what would you recommend here?

This would be an ideal scenario for an interventional radiology intervention, particularly because the bulk, if not all of the disease seems to be confined to the liver, which is where most of our therapies are sort of confined to. Given the amount of tumors and the distribution of the tumors involving both lobes of the liver, we would typically favor doing something intra-arterial, meaning we go through the artery, deliver it, stage it into two procedures, right and left lobe. And we, in our practice, typically do what's known as bland embolization. So we would inject basically inert particles that would occlude the arteries and basically starve the tumors of their blood supply.

And could you please explain the difference between gland embolization, radio embolization, chemo embolization, because we know that there's different type of embolizations, and why would you recommend gland versus radio embolization? I know that some of our other colleagues may recommend radio embolization, and the question will be, if that's an option, when would you recommend that?

Yeah, that's a great question. You know, I think the procedures are all very similar in that the idea is that the tumors with neuroendocrine cancer are hypervascular. And hypervascular is a fancy word for they get a lot of blood flow or a lot of blood supply. So we take advantage of that by going into the artery of the liver and directly and injecting some material. And that material could be basically, like I said, just like grains of sand, just bland beads. That's called bland embolization. You can mix those beads with chemotherapy and or you could inject radioactive microspheres and that's called radio embolization. It's a form of radiation therapy. The sort of why one is picked over the other, a lot of that will just be variations in practice of the IR that you're seeing. And a lot of it is also just preference of the surgeon that you may be working with. The reason that we particularly like bland embolization is because A, it gets good results, but B, you can repeat the therapy with little to no sort of collateral damage to the liver. With neuroendocrine cancer, you know, radioembolization has become a little bit less favored because it causes sort of underlying liver damage. And we talked about other therapies like PRRT and things like that, where, you know, that will also directly target tumors and may cause some liver damage as well. So we want to try to minimize that as much as possible. Fortunately, because neuroendocrine cancer patients have generally a favorable prognosis, we want to minimize the chance of a patient developing cirrhosis down the road. So we favor bland embolization because it tends to sort of cause less cloud damage. It doesn't mean that you can't have Brady embolization, but more often than not, that will be sort of, at least in our practice, would be more of a bailout if the bland embolization didn't seem to work well.

Thank you so much for that answer. And Dr. Mitra, the fact that, you know, we have these tumors very avid on and this patient have not received 177 Lutetian DOTATAY, would you recommend in this situation?

Yeah, it's a great question, one that is very, very relevant right now in terms of the data that's coming out from several clinical trials, such as NEDR2, which is a big one that included patients with this type of high-grade tumors, but still expressed somatostatin receptors exactly as this patient does. At our institution, this patient would exactly go, as Dr. Oz is saying, between sort of these options, so the tumors are what, as he said, looks like either entirely or mostly limited to the liver. So liver-directed therapies would be a great option, but also because they're so somatostatin receptor avid, they would also potentially be a good candidate for PRRT. So that would, I think, be the big discussion point at our institution. And in often cases, it would go between one versus the other. It's just a matter of which one is done first.

Thank you so much. I think it's important to know and make our patients aware of the data with the NETR2 that it was given in the first line settings and for higher grade neuroendocrine tumors. And they saw that the tumors did shrink with that. And I think it's something that needs to be discussed as well with our patients.

Can I ask a quick question to the interventional radiologist? Do you tend to target the bigger lesions first and then leave the smaller lesions for the nuclear medicine people to take care with PRRT? Or do you randomly go after one side and then the other side? How do you plan treatment with bilobar disease like this?

Yeah, great question. So, the answer is somewhere in between. So, we do treat the whole liver when we do bland embolization, if you have tumors in both sides. If you only had it on the right or on the left, we would only treat that half. Typically, when we're doing interventions for neuroendocrine cancer, and if we're doing one of these arterial therapies like bland embolization, we're doing it because there's widespread tumors. If you only have a few tumors, then we're talking about surgery versus ablation or even something like histotripsy. So because we're doing it for patients who have tumors everywhere in their liver, more often than not, we will do what are called lobar infusions. So we go into the right hepatic artery. or the right side of the liver, and we inject the beads very proximally or very, you know, far away from the tumor and distribute the beads throughout the entire liver. Because the tumors are very hypervascular, meaning they're like vacuum cleaners, they kind of suck up those beads as you inject them. We indiscriminately inject those beads. So the intention is to treat all the tumors on that side that's being treated. And then we would repeat that procedure for the other side of the liver, you know, four to six weeks. The side of the liver we typically start with is the side that typically has the most tumor and the largest tumors. So more often than not, that tends to be the right side of the liver, but not uncommonly, we start with the left.
So with the bland embolization, do you feel that the smaller tumors completely go away and the bigger ones get a little bit smaller? What is your experience on that?

Yeah, I would say that's generally what I like to tell patients to expect is don't focus on the tumors disappearing. Focus hopefully more that these tumors are like light bulbs, as we've seen on these scans. We want to basically burn the light bulbs out. We want to basically get rid of the blood supply to them. So what we see more often than not is that those larger tumors, yeah, they may shrink a little bit, but we don't want to see them enhance or get contrast on the follow-up scans. Similarly, the tiny tumors, hopefully because they're so small, they may disappear, but we're looking for sort of a lack of enhancement more than anything.
Dr. Mitra, you wanted to make a comment?
Oh, I was just going to ask what your opinion is in this case between liver-directed therapy versus PRRT.

Right. And yes, we discussed our case, this case in our tumor board, and we discussed about liver-directed therapies. As Dr. Oz mentioned, that was an option. We also discussed about Lutathera. At that moment, the data of the NETHER2 was not out when this patient, you know, and what we know now is that 177 lutetium dodecane is approved for low grade neuroendocrine tumors. So the fact that we have this information that can also be used for higher grades is very important. But at that time, you know, we didn't have that information. So this patient actually was enrolled in our clinical trial with in combination with Olaparib. Dr. Kunz will discuss more about clinical trials, but this is a study that is available here at the NIH. And the idea is that we want to make 177-nutrition Dr. Tay more effective by adding Olaparib, but that will be. And just to mention, LACNATS has also a clinical trials information and a video about this study. Please refer to that video if you have an interest in this study. Now let's discuss our second case. This is a 45-year-old female. At age 40, she was complaining of intermittent flushing, postural hypotension, that means when the blood pressure drops when you go from lying down to sitting up, presyncope, so that's the feeling that you have when you faint or when you want to faint, and diarrhea. Five years later, she was admitted to the emergency room with no clear etiology of the symptoms, and she was having worse enough of diarrhea up to 20 times a day. Initially, her primary care physician thought that maybe there was an immune condition. She was sent to see a immunologist and it was him who recommended for evaluation. And as we can see here, the plasma serotonin was very elevated as well as the 5-HIAA was also elevated. She then underwent a CT scan of the abdomen and we can see here that there is multiple liver metastasis, which are the more darker area that we see in the liver. But maybe for further view, we can see the dot that they scanned. And the dot that they scanned also was positive as well with the tumors having the receptors. And as we can see, the scan is also positive. And a question for Dr. Mitra, what would you recommend here, Dr. Mitra?

reference_conclusion: Tumor board consensus favored resection of the pancreatic primary with distal pancreatectomy and splenectomy, with consideration of synchronous hepatic debulking if no major vascular reconstruction was required and at least 70% of total liver tumor volume could be reduced; otherwise, staged liver-directed treatment was considered appropriate. Following progression on lanreotide and intolerance/progression on capecitabine-temozolomide, repeat functional imaging with somatostatin receptor PET and FDG PET was used to reassess disease biology. Given liver-dominant, bilobar metastatic disease with persistent somatostatin receptor avidity, liver-directed intra-arterial therapy, particularly staged bland embolization, and PRRT were both considered appropriate options, with subsequent enrollment on a clinical trial combining 177-lutetium DOTATATE with olaparib.

case_summary:
[ patient demographics ]: Female patient.

[ chief complaint ]: Frequent diarrhea, reported at 18–20 bowel movements per day.

[ diagnosis ]: Widely metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor, suspected small bowel primary. Clinical features and imaging favored terminal ileum or right-sided colon origin. Hepatic metastatic disease was present.

[ imaging findings ]: Anatomic imaging demonstrated a mesenteric lesion/mass, suggesting a small bowel primary. No obvious primary mass was seen on the referenced scan. Disease was described as very widely metastatic with extensive liver involvement. DOTATATE PET was indicated for staging, and the tumor was described as having high somatostatin expression.

[ molecular/genomic findings ]: No molecular or genomic findings were provided.

[ laboratory results ]: Serotonin was markedly elevated. 5-HIAA was markedly elevated.

[ current disease status ]: Widely metastatic well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with extensive hepatic burden and a hormonally active syndrome.

[ other clinical data ]: The biochemical syndrome was consistent with hormonally active disease. Concern for carcinoid heart disease was raised in the setting of excess serotonin/5-HIAA.

reference_discussion.text: Imaging-wise, it's exactly what we need. We, again, want anatomic imaging and the DOTATATE PET for staging. Since this is the initial diagnosis, it would be important to find the primary tumor, which, again, can be done usually with a combination of those two things. There appears to be something there in the mesentery, which would suggest there may be a small bowel origin for the tumor. So that's something that would be important to find and can be helpful for the surgeons. But beyond that, it's clearly a very widely metastatic case.

And Dr. Sindh, what are your thoughts about this case? We think it's coming from this small bowel primary. So we know that serotonin and 5-HIA is very elevated, but there was not an obvious mass on this scan. So what are your thoughts about that?

I think the primary needs to come out. There's no question in my mind. I think there's a mesenteric mass. So this is most probably a terminal ileum or a right-sided colon primary. So if you don't see it, I would still recommend surgical intervention based on the mesenteric mass and go and do a right hemicolectomy if there is truly a mass in the right colon or in the terminal ileum. So that's number one. Number two, I think you have too much liver disease and this is not a liver that I could safely debulk to 70%. So I would again, actively engage my interventional colleagues and my med-on colleagues I would approach this in a stage-wise fashion. You could just do somatostatin analogs and watch this patient after the resection of the primary. And if there's no progression of the metastatic disease, you can delay the treatment of the liver metastases to a later time point. However, what's tricky in this particular case is the fact that she has 18 to 20 bowel movements a day. Now, you could make a case in that sort of a setting, deliver with interventional radiology. That's definitely an option, and that's what we did about 10 years ago. Today, you have Telerestat in your back pocket, so I've seen medical oncologists use Telerestat to control the bowel movements as well, and then keep an eye on the liver metastases. So I'd put that question back to you. and the interventional radiologist as to what your thought process is on this. Do you like to treat them up front or would you straight go to IR?

I'm an interventional radiologist. I like to do interventions. So, this patient is pretty symptomatic. And, you know, as you mentioned, you know, there's twofold goals of therapy, same as with our bland embolization procedures. is to not only to hopefully stop the growth of the tumor, stunt it, shrink it down, but also the second point would be for patients who are symptomatically affected by their tumors. And so in this case, doing a bland embolization I think would benefit this patient and has a high degree of sort of success when you're doing it for that purpose. So I would advocate for it, but as mentioned, I think it's also reasonable if there, if for any reason we wanted to hold off and see if medications could control it.

As a surgeon, I think it's imperative to remove the primary tumor because I think that largely determines the progression of metastatic disease and gives you an idea as to how the symptoms are controlled after the resection of the primary tumor. And so in that sort of a setting, I would definitely recommend proceeding with a right hemicolectomy in this patient and then reassessing. And if the diarrhea continues to be a big impending issue, then I think the options are to consider systemic therapy. with our medical oncology colleagues, and alternatively, interventional radiology to control the liver disease, which might be also participating in the secretion of the high 5-HIA.

Yeah, I just wanted to add, from my perspective as well, this is again why the NETR2 study was so powerful, because it was exactly in these types of patients who initially diagnosed, you know, it was within the diagnosis, that they were given Lutathera as long as they had high somatostatin expression, such as in this case. So I would throw that also into the mix as well, because in addition to controlling the tumor growth, it can definitely also help symptoms, and it can be given in conjunction with somatostatin analogs for additional symptomatic control. So just like all of these are options, and this is exactly why, you know, we have these types of multidisciplinary tumor boards to have all of these different perspectives and kind of choose the best path forward.

Absolutely. And as we all discussed, this patient underwent two radioembolizations. In this case, Dr. Oztet mentioned when it's needed or what, in terms of the difference between bioembolization or She also underwent surgery, as Dr. Singh mentioned, and underwent an elusive colectomy. Two separate tumors were identified, and three out of 12 lymph nodes that were resected was positive for neuroendocrine tumor. And pathology was consistent with a great one, well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with a KS67, more than 1%, but less than 3%. And she then underwent two blind embolizations. And the symptoms of diarrhea significantly improved. But then she was complaining of worsening shortness of breath. And here, the point I want to make is that every patient I have small bowel neuroendocrine tumors, where there is excess of serotonin and 5-HIAA, it's important to see a cardiologist and have a routine echocardiogram, surveillance echocardiogram, maybe once every year, once every two years, depending on how the clinical presentation of this patient is. But that can also, and the reason why I'm saying this is because when we see something like this, we need to consider about carcinoid heart disease, meaning that the hormone, can also go to the heart valve and it can cause scar of the heart valve. And that can also then put a risk for the patient to develop heart failure. So I think it's important also that we're patients with a small bowel near endocrine tumors that has this excess of hormones that be evaluated by a cardiologist and have routine echocardiograms as well. And my last question for Dr. Oz, a lot of our patients are asking about histotripsy. So I think we understood in this situation, resecting the primary was important, doing the liver directed therapy with embolizations is also important, or considering this patient for the symptoms. But we get a lot of questions about histotripsy. Maybe would you mind describing what is that and how this plays in terms of the management of neuroendocrine tumors?

Sure. Yeah, I'm glad a lot of people are asking me too. So I'm happy to chat about it a little bit. Histotripsy is a non-thermal. So non-thermal means doesn't rely on using heat or freezing to kill tumors. Mechanism of using ultrasound energy to ablate or kill tumors. It's also non-invasive. So it's very attractive because it's non-thermal and it's non-invasive. Most of the tumors that we've discussed today through our case presentations involve patients who had tumors throughout their liver. Histotripsy would be more applicable in situations where patients only had a few liver tumors, where we would consider doing what's known as ablation or percutaneous ablation, where we take a needle, put it into the tumor, and burn it away. Histotripsy would mitigate the risk of the needle puncture and also would allow us to potentially treat tumors that would be hard to treat with traditional ablation, meaning tumors that are next to blood vessels, bile ducts, which happen to, you know, occur a lot in the liver. So histotripsy is a technology, we just received it, and so it technically doesn't allow us to treat any new patient per se, but it's another tool that we have available to us to treat tumors the way that we think of when we do ablation. So it's a very exciting technology. One of the other final things I'll mention about it, it's very interesting, unfortunately doesn't apply yet to neuroendocrine. But it seems that when you do histotripsy, it promotes a very immunogenic response. Meaning when you kill the tumor, it basically disintegrates the tumor such that all the tumor antigens are released. And it really basically, you know, sort of to sum it up, it wakes up the immune system very much. So there's a lot of interest that you can get what's known as a non-target response. And that's particularly in cancers where we use immunotherapies. So there's also some excitement there with histotripsy as well. And because it's so new, we don't really know a lot of the answers yet, but now histotripsy is FDA approved. There are at least 10 centers that have the technology and are offering it and evaluating patients. But yes, it's a very exciting time because of, you know, having that technology available to us.
One quick question on that same thing. How big a tumor can you treat with histotripsy and what's your size cut off at this point?

Yeah, a great question. So, hisotripsy is very similar to percutaneous ablation in that the sort of maximum size that you can sort of do in one session is about four centimeters. So, we typically will target tumors. If we want to treat the whole tumor, we always want to have some margin. So, we'll typically treat a tumor that's up to three centimeters. It doesn't mean you can't treat tumors that are larger than three centimeters. You just have to do multiple treatments, you know, of that same area. So right now we're probably limiting it to, at least in my practice, limiting it to patients who would be eligible for ablation. And this would be an alternative to ablation.
Any major disadvantage or complications associated with histotrip?

Yeah, I would say the major disadvantage currently is we can't get to every tumor the way that we can get to with percutaneous ablation, largely because this is a technology using ultrasound waves, essentially, to create cavitation within the tumor. We have to have a good sonographic window, so we have to be able to see with an ultrasound very well, and there's some more physics to it, but we have to, in a geometric way, be able to align the robot so that the tumor is very well visualized. So that limits sort of the parts of the liver that we can treat. With that said, there's a lot of technological updates coming to the system over the next year or two that will hopefully be able to allow us to treat actually any tumor. We're a little bit away from that, but right now we're largely limited to tumors that you can mainly see with an ultrasound from a subcostal approach. So meaning, you know, if you take the ultrasound, you can only see the tumor from under the ribs.

reference_conclusion: Staging should include anatomic imaging and DOTATATE PET to identify the primary lesion, which is suspected to arise from the terminal ileum or right colon. The agreed management was resection of the primary tumor with right hemicolectomy, followed by reassessment of symptoms and metastatic disease burden. Given extensive symptomatic hepatic metastases, liver-directed therapy with bland embolization was supported for symptom control, with systemic therapy options including somatostatin analogs, telotristat, and consideration of Lutathera in the setting of high somatostatin receptor expression. Ongoing cardiology evaluation with surveillance echocardiography was recommended because of elevated serotonin/5-HIAA and risk for carcinoid heart disease.
